name: 1Backend
source_description: Self-hosted platform for building AI apps with microservices and microfrontends
upstream_docker_image: crufter/1backend (backend; upstream's own production docker-compose pins `default-1-latest`, or `cuda-12.2.0-latest` for GPU hosts — no numbered version tag exists on Docker Hub for this repo, only these two floating "-latest"-suffixed tags) + crufter/1backend-ui (frontend, tag `latest`, also unpinned)
version_health_notes: Six tagged GitHub releases from v0.4.0 (2025-05-05) through v0.9.0 (2025-10-12), roughly monthly — then no new tag in the ~10 months since (as of 2026-08-05). The project is not dormant, though: `main` was last pushed 2026-05-27 (~2.3 months ago, per repo `pushed_at`) and the Docker Hub `cuda-12.2.0-latest` image was rebuilt the same day, so commit and image activity continued well past the last version tag. Repo is not archived, has 2.3k stars and effectively one open issue. Read this as: still actively developed, but has stopped cutting versioned releases, and ships Docker images exclusively under floating tags (`default-1-latest`, `cuda-12.2.0-latest`, `latest`) rather than a pinned version — a recipe would have to pin an increasingly stale `v0.9.0`-era tag or accept a moving target, neither of which is the "pinned, current stable tag" af-create-recipe Phase 2 calls for.
differentiation: 1Backend is a developer runtime/framework for building custom microservice + microfrontend apps (built-in auth, request routing, an edge proxy that can replace nginx, and the ability to launch LLM containers on the host) — not a finished end-user application like the rest of the catalogue. It shares surface area with Runtipi (both launch and manage sibling containers via the Docker socket) and with Open WebUI/Ollama (both can run local LLMs in containers it starts), but unlike either of those its own admin console has no standalone function for a non-developer: there is nothing to "use" until someone writes and deploys a microservice or microfrontend on top of it.
usefulness_rationale: AF customers installing from the catalogue want a ready-made product (password manager, notes app, chat UI, Git host) they can start using immediately. 1Backend's admin console is a management/registry surface for a platform, not a product in itself — value only appears once a developer writes code against its SDK and deploys services on it, which is a different (and much narrower) audience than the rest of the catalogue targets, independent of any auth-mechanism question.
blocking_issues:
The app ships a fixed, documented default admin login (username `1backend`, password `changeme`, confirmed current in upstream's `using.md` docs) with no environment variable or first-boot configuration to set a custom password — it can only be changed manually after first login, which a one-click installer can't guarantee happens. Per the corrected SCHEMA.md guidance, this alone is NOT a blocker: gating the app behind a Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password is a legitimate real auth boundary, same as any app with no configurable login of its own.

However, 1Backend's official production docker-compose (two containers: `1backend-ui` on :3901 and `1backend` API on :11337) has the browser call the API origin *directly* — `BACKEND_ADDRESS` in the UI container must be a browser-reachable URL, not an internal one. That means there are two independently public HTTP origins, and the current basic_auth mechanism (IF-1312) is wired to gate a single declared public port per app (see `recipes/wud/metadata.yaml`'s IF-808 note: "the Traefik basic-auth feature (first-public-port opt-in) is not implemented" — confirming the feature's scope is one port, not the app as a whole). Gating only the UI port leaves the API port openly reachable with the same fixed `1backend`/`changeme` credential the correction is meant to neutralize — so for this specific two-origin app the credential problem is only half-solved by today's mechanism, not fully resolved the way it is for a single-public-port app like Adminer or n8n.

Backend container requires a `/var/run/docker.sock` bind mount to launch its own LLM/microservice containers. Precedented in the catalogue (runtipi, wud, portainer already mount the socket), so not a novel blocker by itself, but it compounds the exposure above: an unauthenticated or default-credentialed reach into an app that can start arbitrary sibling containers is a materially worse outcome than the same gap on a simple CRUD app.
summary: 1Backend is a developer platform for building microservice/microfrontend apps, not a ready-to-use end-user application — its value only appears once someone writes and deploys custom services on top of it, which does not fit a one-click catalogue aimed at finished tools; this holds regardless of the auth-mechanism question. On the credential point specifically, this re-run corrects the prior verdict's reasoning: 1Backend's fixed default admin login is not by itself disqualifying, since a Traefik basic_auth gate is a real auth boundary per the corrected SCHEMA.md guidance. But 1Backend's official deployment exposes two independently browser-reachable HTTP origins (UI :3901, API :11337), and today's basic_auth mechanism only gates one public port per app — so the default credential remains reachable unauthenticated on the ungated origin, a structural gap distinct from (and narrower than) the original "masks, doesn't fix" objection. Combined with low fit for a finished-product catalogue, overlap with Runtipi/Open WebUI/Ollama, a Docker Hub image line with no pinned version tag, and a stalled GitHub release cadence (last tag ~10 months ago, though `main` is still active), this remains not_recommended.

name: 2FAuth
source_description: Self-hosted two-factor authentication code manager for web and mobile
version_health_notes: Nine releases in 2026 alone (v6.0.0 on 2026-01-14 through v8.0.1 on 2026-07-05), roughly monthly cadence. Latest release v8.0.1 is about one month old as of 2026-08-05. Repo is not archived, issues/PRs are actively triaged — clearly active, well-maintained project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers TOTP/HOTP code management. Vaultwarden (password manager) is the closest neighbor conceptually — both are personal-security vaults — but 2FAuth specifically replaces a phone-based authenticator app (Google Authenticator/Authy-style) with a self-hosted, browser/PWA-accessible one, which is a distinct use case customers search for separately from password management.
usefulness_rationale: Clear, well-understood single-purpose app with broad appeal to anyone self-hosting security tools, and it is lightweight (single container, SQLite by default, no external DB dependency). Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because it stores a customer's live 2FA seeds — a single-user account signup with no built-in way for the platform to pre-provision or gate that first-run signup is a materially higher-risk exposure window than, say, a monitoring dashboard.
blocking_issues:
2FAuth has no admin-credential environment variables at all (confirmed against upstream .env.example and the official docker-compose install docs). The app boots with zero users and the first visitor to the public URL is presented with an open registration form; whoever submits it first becomes the sole account owner. There is no `type: password` parameter on the app's own login to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` — the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var, so the root-password-projection mechanism has nothing to attach to.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate could be placed in front of the whole app to close the open-registration race, but that only delays the same problem one layer out: the customer still needs a way to register the in-app account themselves before anyone else reaches the registration form, and today's basic_auth mechanism has no channel to hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential beyond the single root-password projection already used for the gate itself.
summary: 2FAuth is an active, well-maintained, single-container app (SQLite by default, no external DB required) that would fill a real gap in the catalogue — self-hosted 2FA code management, distinct from Vaultwarden's password-manager scope. It fails the installability test purely on the platform mechanism: the app provisions its one admin account via an open self-registration form with no env-var hook, so neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely hand the customer their own exclusive first-run credential. Revisit once the platform supports either injecting a preset admin login via env var (upstream would need to add that) or a customer-facing second credential channel beyond the single root-password projection.

name: 9Router
source_description: AI API routing proxy with token optimization for 40+ LLM providers
version_health_notes: Repo created 2026-01-05 (about 7 months old as of 2026-08-05) and pushed to the same day this analysis was written. GitHub releases show a multi-times-per-week cadence (v0.5.35 on 2026-07-16, v0.5.20 on 2026-07-07, v0.5.18 on 2026-07-03, v0.5.12 on 2026-06-26, v0.5.8 on 2026-06-21), and the Docker Hub tag list goes further, with 0.5.50 pushed only hours before this analysis. This is a very young, fast-moving project rather than a mature one — high feature velocity but no track record of API/config stability, and no LTS or versioning guarantees observed.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes does multi-provider LLM cost/routing optimization. Ollama and Open WebUI run/chat with locally-hosted models; Hermes Agent and OpenClaw are messaging-bot agent runtimes; Paperless-AI calls a single external provider for one document-tagging use case. 9Router is instead a generic OpenAI-compatible gateway that sits in front of 40+ commercial LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, GLM, MiniMax, Kimi, etc. plus OAuth-based coding-tool subscriptions), doing provider fallback and request-token compression. It targets developers/power users who already pay for multiple LLM providers/subscriptions and want one stable self-hosted endpoint plus cost savings, not end users wanting a chat UI.
usefulness_rationale: Real utility for a technical audience (developers routing Claude Code/Cursor/Copilot-style tools through cheaper or fallback providers), but it is a niche, single-purpose developer tool rather than broad consumer appeal, and its value is entirely dependent on the customer already holding accounts/API keys/subscriptions with third-party LLM providers.
summary: 9Router is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (20128) Node/Next.js app with its own dashboard login (INITIAL_PASSWORD, default "123456", used only until a password hash exists) plus a JWT_SECRET for session signing — both fit the mechanisms we already support: INITIAL_PASSWORD projects the customer's root-password hash the same way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does, and JWT_SECRET is a patternless server-generated value the customer never needs to see. Crucially, per upstream docs, the 40+ LLM provider connections (API keys and OAuth logins) cannot be pre-configured via env vars or compose at all — they are added entirely through the dashboard UI after boot, by the customer, the same self-service pattern as adding workflow credentials in n8n. That means the provider-credential problem that blocks Paperless-AI (enabled: false, requires an un-projectable OPENAI_API_KEY at compose time) does not apply here. The project is genuinely new and releasing multiple times a week, which is a stability caveat but not a version-pin blocker (MIT-licensed, active, tagged Docker images). Recommend building the recipe, front the dashboard route behind the domain param with INITIAL_PASSWORD projected from the root password, no basic_auth gate needed since the app has its own login.

name: Ackee
source_description: Ackee is a self-hosted Node.js analytics tool for privacy-focused website tracking
version_health_notes: Repo is not archived; last code push was 2026-07-25, so development is ongoing (as of 2026-08-05). But release history is lumpy: v3.4.2 shipped 2022-12-17, then nothing tagged for almost three years until v3.5.0 landed 2025-11-13, followed quickly by v3.5.1 (2025-11-19) and v3.6.0 (2026-04-08, ~4 months ago). Read as a project that went quiet for a long stretch and has recently picked back up, not a steady cadence — "slowing" fits better than "active" until a few more releases confirm the revival holds.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers website analytics/traffic tracking. Ackee is a lightweight, cookie-free alternative to Google Analytics/Plausible/Matomo that a customer running any of their own sites elsewhere (not necessarily hosted through us) could point a tracking snippet at. It's a genuinely new category, not a variant of an existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted privacy analytics has a real, recurring audience (indie site owners, privacy-conscious devs) and pairs naturally with IONOS-hosted sites, but it's a single-purpose tool with a narrower audience than e.g. n8n or Vaultwarden, and competes with more actively maintained alternatives (Plausible, Umami) a customer might expect instead.
blocking_issues:
ACKEE_PASSWORD has no expressible mechanism today. Ackee's login resolver (src/resolvers/tokens.js) compares the submitted password to the ACKEE_PASSWORD env var with plain string equality (`password !== config.password`) — it never hashes or verifies a hash, it does a literal match. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` produces a hash string (e.g. "argon2:$argon2id$...") to place into the parameter; that only works for apps that hash-verify the credential themselves (Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does this). Putting a hash into ACKEE_PASSWORD would require the customer to type that opaque hash string as their login password, which defeats the point — there is no channel today to hand Ackee a plaintext credential the customer actually knows, short of leaking their real root password verbatim into an env var, which we don't do.

Even if ACKEE_PASSWORD were solved, auto-generating it server-side (like a DB password) doesn't work either: unlike POSTGRES_PASSWORD or N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, this credential is customer-facing — it's the literal password typed into Ackee's own login screen every visit — so a random value the customer is never shown would lock them out.
summary: Ackee is a single-HTTP-port (3000), reverse-proxy-friendly Node.js + MongoDB app with no overlap in the current catalogue — analytics/tracking is a genuinely new category for us. It fails installability today purely on credential mechanics: its admin password field does a literal plaintext comparison against the ACKEE_PASSWORD env var, not a hash verification, so the `generated_from` root-password-hash projection (our only mechanism for an app's own login field) can't be wired to it, and auto-generating the password server-side would silently lock the customer out of a screen they need to use. Username is solvable (fixed constant), but password is not. Recommend revisiting only if a future mechanism can pass a customer-known plaintext credential through, or if Ackee itself adds hash-based password verification. Release cadence is also worth watching — a ~3-year gap before the current revival — before investing in a recipe either way.

name: Activepieces

Repo is not archived, pushed_at is today, 436 open issues actively triaged, 23.6k stars — clearly an active, fast-moving project.
differentiation: Direct conceptual overlap with n8n: both are visual, no-code/low-code workflow-automation platforms styled as open-source Zapier alternatives, both need Postgres, both expose a single web UI port behind Traefik. Activepieces' pitch leans harder into AI-agent/MCP-server pieces and a larger claimed integration count (200+ "pieces" vs n8n's node library), which could appeal to a customer specifically wanting AI-agent workflows rather than n8n's more general/technical node editor — but for a customer just wanting "workflow automation," n8n already covers the same job.
usefulness_rationale: Legitimate, popular, actively maintained tool with real demand (23.6k GitHub stars), but it duplicates the job n8n already does in the catalogue rather than filling a gap. Value to the customer is more "which brand of no-code automation do I prefer" than a new capability, which caps usefulness at medium rather than high.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the upstream docker-compose.yml and .env.example: there is no admin-username/admin-password environment variable at all. The app boots with zero users, and the first visitor to the public URL is presented with an open account-creation screen; whoever submits it first becomes the platform's sole admin. This is the same shape of problem as the 2FAuth gap analysis (see apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml) — no `type: password` parameter on the app's own login exists to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would close the "random internet stranger races to register first" version of this problem, but per the precedent set in the 2FAuth analysis, today's basic_auth mechanism has no channel to also hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential for the in-app signup form beyond the single root-password projection already used for the gate itself — so it does not fully resolve the underlying provisioning gap.
summary: Activepieces is an active, fast-moving, well-starred workflow-automation platform, but it lands in the catalogue as a near-duplicate of n8n rather than filling a new gap — both are Postgres-backed, single-web-port, no-code automation tools. It also fails the installability test for the same structural reason as 2FAuth: there is no environment variable to preset the sole admin account, so the app relies on an open, first-visitor self-registration screen that neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely provision for the customer. The internal Postgres/Redis/JWT/encryption secrets are all trivially server-generated and not blocking on their own. Revisit only if upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow, or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond root-password projection — and even then, weigh it against the existing n8n recipe before prioritizing.

name: Adminer
source_description: Full-featured database management interface supporting 11+ database systems
version_health_notes: Four releases in July 2024 (5.4.4 -> 5.5.1) closing security advisories, then no tagged release in the ~24-25 months since (as of 2026-08-05). Repo is not archived and issues/PRs are still being triaged, but there has been zero release activity for over two years, well past "slowing" into dormant. Docker Hub also ships a maintained 4.x track (4.17.1) alongside 5.x for anyone pinned to the older line.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes gives customers a generic database browser/admin UI. Recipes like n8n, paperless-ngx, gitea, immich, etc. run their own Postgres/MySQL internally but don't expose a UI to browse it. Adminer would let a customer manage any DB they run themselves (their own MySQL/Postgres, or the internal DB of another recipe) via a single lightweight PHP app.
usefulness_rationale: Useful for developers/power users who self-host a database and want a phpMyAdmin-style UI without provisioning one manually, but it's a niche/technical tool rather than a broad-appeal app, and it needs a reachable database to be useful at all (BYO or a separate recipe).
summary: Adminer is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8080) PHP app with no built-in admin login of its own — its "login" screen is a per-connection DB credential form the end user fills in interactively at each visit, not a secret af-api needs to provision. That makes it directly installable today: front it with the domain param plus a Traefik basic_auth:true gate (same pattern as n8n/WUD), with the basic-auth password itself projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from`, to keep the unauthenticated login page from being open to the internet. Release cadence has gone dormant (no tag since mid-2024, ~2 years now) but the project is still active/triaged, not EOL. Recommend building the recipe, with basic_auth as a required (not optional) gate given the app has zero auth of its own.

name: AFFiNE
source_description: All-in-one workspace combining docs, whiteboards, and databases with AI
upstream_license: MIT (editor/BlockSuite/client) + AFFiNE Enterprise Edition license (packages/backend/server — the component shipped in the official self-host image)
version_health_notes: Stable v0.27.3 tagged 2026-07-23, ~13 days before today (2026-08-05); v0.27.4-beta.1 already out 2026-08-04. Canary builds ship almost daily (e.g. v2026.8.5-canary.953 published today). Very high release cadence across stable, beta, and canary channels — clearly active development, nowhere near maintenance-only or EOL.
differentiation: Both AFFiNE and anytype-server target self-hosted personal/team knowledge management, but they differ sharply in shape: anytype-server is only a sync backend (three non-HTTP any-sync ports + MinIO) for Anytype's native desktop/mobile apps — no web UI at all, not reverse-proxy-friendly. AFFiNE ships a real single-port HTTP web app (docs, whiteboards, and a database/table view, with optional AI features) that works directly behind Traefik on affine.<base_domain>. It would be the first browsable "Notion/Miro-style" workspace in the catalogue, versus anytype-server's sync-only backend.
usefulness_rationale: Broad appeal — docs + whiteboard + lightweight database with AI is a popular self-hosted Notion/Miro alternative and a genuinely new UI-first productivity category for the catalogue, not a niche developer tool.
blocking_issues: Licensing: the self-host Docker image (ghcr.io/toeverything/affine, the one used in AFFiNE's own docker-compose.yml) bundles packages/backend/server, which upstream maintainers confirmed is not part of AFFiNE's MIT-licensed core — it ships under the AFFiNE Enterprise Edition license. Per that license, production self-hosting is unconditionally free only up to a 10-member/100GB tier; sustained use beyond that (or, arguably, systematic redistribution to many catalogue customers as a hosting reseller) falls under the EE Subscription Terms of Service. This needs legal/commercial review with AFFiNE before the recipe ships at catalogue scale — it is not resolved by any af-recipes mechanism.
summary: AFFiNE is a single-HTTP-port (3010), Traefik-friendly Docker Compose app (affine + postgres + redis, plus a one-shot migration job) with an active, fast-moving release cadence (stable v0.27.3, 2026-07-23; canaries almost daily). Mechanically it is installable today: the Postgres password can be generated server-side with no customer input, and the lack of any built-in admin-login parameter is handled the same way as Adminer/n8n — a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (projected from the customer's root password) protecting the first-run setup wizard from being claimed by a stranger. The real open question is licensing: the self-host server image ships under AFFiNE's Enterprise Edition terms, not MIT, with subscription requirements past a free tier — worth building as a recipe, but only after legal/commercial sign-off, hence build_with_caveats rather than build_now.

name: Agent Zero
source_description: Open-source AI agent framework with multi-agent cooperation and persistent memory
version_health_notes: v2.8 published 2026-08-01, four days before today (2026-08-05). Release history shows a near-weekly cadence through 2026: v2.0 (Jun 23), v2.1 (Jun 26), v2.2 (Jul 2), v2.3 (Jul 9), v2.4 (Jul 10), v2.5 (Jul 17), v2.6 (Jul 23), v2.7 (Jul 27), v2.8 (Aug 1). Docker Hub tags for agent0ai/agent-zero confirm the same cadence (latest pushed 4 days ago at time of research). Repo is not archived, has 18.7k stars and ongoing commits/PRs — clearly active development. Note the project migrated from the original frdel/agent-zero repo/image to the agent0ai organization; agent0ai/agent-zero is the current, actively-published image.
differentiation: Meaningful conceptual overlap with two existing recipes: openclaw and hermes-agent are both already "self-hosted AI agent" entries in the catalogue. Those two are messaging-app-first (Telegram gateway/bot with a secondary dashboard); Agent Zero is web-UI-first and pitches itself as a general-purpose autonomous coworker — a Dockerized Linux desktop, a browser with DOM annotation for computer-use tasks, hierarchical multi-agent delegation (an agent can spawn subordinate agents for subtasks), and a persistent long-term memory/vector store across sessions. It is closer in spirit to a self-hosted, model-agnostic "autonomous dev/ops agent" than either existing entry. Real differentiator for a customer who wants an agent to actually operate a computer (browse, run code, manage files) rather than just relay Telegram messages, but a third "AI agent framework" recipe risks crowding an already-covered niche.
usefulness_rationale: Popular (18.7k stars) and actively developed, with a genuinely distinct computer-use/multi-agent angle versus openclaw and hermes-agent. Capped at medium rather than high because the catalogue already has two AI agent recipes covering adjacent ground, and Agent Zero brings no integration a typical self-hosting customer couldn't already get by pairing an LLM API key with one of those.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against upstream source (helpers/dotenv.py, helpers/login.py, helpers/ui_server.py in agent0ai/agent-zero @ main): the app does ship its own optional login, gated by two env vars, AUTH_LOGIN and AUTH_PASSWORD, read from usr/.env at startup. Login is enabled only when AUTH_LOGIN is non-empty. However, the login handler (`ui_server.py::login_handler`) does a direct plaintext string comparison — `request.form["password"] == password` — not a hash comparison. This is the opposite shape of Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN (which detects and hash-compares an argon2-prefixed value). It means `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` cannot target AUTH_PASSWORD: the projected value would be a hash of the customer's root password, and the customer would type their actual root password at the login screen, which would never equal the stored hash. There is no plaintext-passthrough option in today's mechanism (only argon2/bcrypt hashing), so the app's native login has no usable input channel.

Workaround, same shape as n8n/OpenClaw/WUD/Open WebUI/Immich: leave AUTH_LOGIN/AUTH_PASSWORD unset (native login disabled, matching upstream's own default/documented state) and gate the single public port with Traefik `basic_auth: true`, projecting the root-password hash there instead. This is fully expressible today and is the recommended path — it does not require the app's own auth at all.

Model provider credentials (Anthropic/OpenAI/OpenRouter/Ollama, etc.) are configured post-provision via the Settings UI, not required as an env var at first boot — same deferred pattern already shipped in openclaw and hermes-agent, not a blocker.
summary: Agent Zero is an active, well-starred, weekly-shipping AI agent framework and is installable today by gating it entirely with Traefik `basic_auth` (the same pattern already used for n8n, OpenClaw, WUD, Open WebUI, and Immich) rather than trying to drive its own AUTH_LOGIN/AUTH_PASSWORD env vars, which do a plaintext comparison and are therefore incompatible with the hashed root-password projection mechanism. The bigger open question is fit, not installability: the catalogue already has openclaw and hermes-agent covering "self-hosted AI agent," and while Agent Zero's computer-use/multi-agent/persistent-memory angle is a real differentiator, a third entry in this niche should be weighed against those two before building, not treated as an automatic yes.

secrets_required_at_first_boot: admin_signup_credential; AGENTA_AUTH_KEY; AGENTA_CRYPT_KEY; AGENTA_RUNNER_TOKEN; AGENTA_STORE_ACCESS_KEY; AGENTA_STORE_SECRET_KEY; AGENTA_STORE_SIGNING_KEY; POSTGRES_PASSWORD; llm_provider_api_key_or_oauth_login
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the upstream env.oss.gh.example and compose file: there is no admin-username/admin-password environment variable at all. Sign-ups are open by default per the self-hosting docs — the first visitor to the public URL registers the sole admin account. Same structural gap already documented for Activepieces and 2FAuth: no `type: password` parameter on an app-owned login exists to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate would only add a second, unrelated credential in front of the app rather than provisioning the in-app signup itself.

The product is now fundamentally an agent-execution platform: to do anything beyond sign up, it needs either a model-provider API key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY / etc., all blank in the shipped env template) or an interactive OAuth login to a Claude/ChatGPT/Pi subscription mounted into the runner container. Both are customer-supplied external credentials with no projection channel under the current `/compose` mechanism — this is the same class of blocker as an external API key or OAuth registration described in apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md, and it is not optional: without it the app has no functional agent to run.

The `runner` service (which actually executes agent turns) requires `cap_add: SYS_ADMIN`, a mounted `/dev/fuse` device, and `security_opt: apparmor:unconfined` for its local FUSE-mounted sandbox. That is a materially more privileged container than any current recipe requests, independent of the secrets problem above.

The full oss compose stack is 13 services (web, api, worker-streams, worker-queues, cron, alembic migrator, services, runner, postgres, redis-volatile, redis-durable, seaweedfs object store, supertokens, plus an optional composio sidecar and traefik/nginx) — far heavier than any recipe in the catalogue today, raising the resource floor and operational surface for a use case two existing recipes already cover more simply.
summary: Hostinger's catalogue description of Agenta as an "LLMOps platform for prompts, evaluation, and observability" is out of date: the live upstream repo (checked today, 2026-08-05, with a same-day release) has pivoted to "the open-source workspace for building and running agents," putting it in direct conceptual competition with the catalogue's existing hermes-agent and openclaw recipes rather than filling a distinct niche. It fails installability on multiple independent grounds: no admin-account environment variable (open self-registration, same gap as Activepieces and 2FAuth), a mandatory external LLM-provider API key or OAuth subscription login with no customer-input channel today, a runner container that demands SYS_ADMIN/FUSE/apparmor-unconfined privileges, and a 13-service stack that is far heavier than the job requires. Not recommended — revisit only if a future dark-factory version targets a genuinely distinct LLMOps/prompt-eval product, since that would no longer describe what this repository ships.

version_health_notes: The GitHub repo was archived by its owner on 2023-04-22 (same day as the 3.2.0-alpha tag, "switched to yt-dlp instead of youtube-dl") and is now read-only — no issues, PRs, or further commits possible. That is just over 3 years and 3 months before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases: 3.1.1 (2023-03-11), 3.1.0 (2021-10-16), 3.0.3 (2021-03-08). The official Docker Hub image (rudloff/alltube, tags "latest" and "develop") is even further behind — both tags last pushed roughly 5 years ago, predating even the 3.1.x line, so the maintained image never shipped the yt-dlp switch. No official activity of any kind since the archive date; unofficial rebuilds exist (e.g. schklom/alltube, dnomd343/alltube-docker) but there is no vendor-maintained current image.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers video-download-from-URL as a function; the closest adjacent recipes (immich, paperless-ngx) are photo/document management, not video fetching. AllTube would be a novel category for the catalogue, but the specific gap it fills — a self-hosted youtube-dl/yt-dlp front end — is served better today by actively maintained forks/alternatives such as MeTube (ghcr.io/alexta69/metube, weekly-ish tagged builds through 2026) that solve the same problem with a live upstream.
usefulness_rationale: The underlying use case (self-hosted video downloader) has some appeal, but AllTube itself is a dead project: archived over 3 years ago, its own Docker image frozen even further back at ~5 years old (pre-dating the yt-dlp switch), and no security-patch path since youtube-dl/yt-dlp extractors break routinely as sites change their frontends. Shipping an archived, unpatched app whose core function (extracting third-party site URLs) is exactly the kind of thing that rots fastest is a poor trade versus building the same niche on a maintained alternative.
blocking_issues:
No official current Docker image: rudloff/alltube's "latest"/"develop" tags were last pushed roughly 5 years ago and do not include the 3.1.x/3.2.0-alpha era changes (yt-dlp switch, PHP 8 support, SSRF/open redirect fixes from 3.0.1-3.0.3). Building a recipe against the official image means shipping a multi-year-stale, pre-security-fix build; building against an unofficial fork (schklom/alltube, dnomd343/alltube-docker) means pinning to a third party with no relationship to upstream and no guaranteed maintenance either.

Repo is archived (read-only since 2023-04-22) — no path for the customer or IONOS to get a future security patch if a new vulnerability class is found in the URL-fetching/SSRF surface (this app already had two SSRF/open-redirect CVEs fixed in 3.0.1-3.0.3 before archival).
summary: AllTube is technically a simple, single-container, single-HTTP-port PHP app with no built-in login (structurally it would slot in cleanly behind Traefik basic_auth, same as Adminer/WUD), but the project itself is dead: archived by its owner in April 2023, and even its own Docker Hub image was last pushed about 5 years ago, predating the project's final yt-dlp-migration release. There is no maintained image to pin, no upstream to receive future fixes for an app whose core job (parsing third-party video-hosting pages) is exactly the kind of surface that needs frequent patching. Recommend not building this recipe; if the "self-hosted video downloader" niche is wanted, evaluate an actively maintained alternative such as MeTube instead.

It has no boot-time admin-provisioning env var: the app ships with open self- registration, and whoever completes the first sign-up through the web form becomes the admin. Release cadence is active (latest release 3 days ago) and the catalogue currently has no wiki recipe, so this is a real, currently-unfilled, high-usefulness candidate.

name: Anki Sync Server Enhanced
source_description: Self-hosted Anki sync server with multi-user support, backups, and web dashboard
version_health_notes: Third-party (not official-Anki-maintained) Docker wrapper that tracks upstream Anki releases with near-daily automated builds: 26.08 pushed within the last day (as of 2026-08-05), 26.05 five days prior, 25.09.4/25.09.3/25.09.2 roughly two-three months before that. Repo is small (single maintainer, chrislongros) but shows active CI/CD and release cadence as of today's date. Not archived, no EOL signal, but young/low community size relative to most of our current catalogue's upstreams — bus-factor risk with a single maintainer.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes serves flashcard/spaced-repetition sync. This would be a genuinely new category (personal education/productivity) rather than overlapping an existing recipe — closest analogues (Syncthing) are generic file sync, not Anki-protocol-aware.
usefulness_rationale: Real but narrow appeal — students/language-learners who want to avoid AnkiWeb's free-tier limits or keep flashcard data private. It's a single-purpose sync backend for one specific desktop/mobile app ecosystem, not a broad-audience tool, and the primary interface most customers would ever open is the optional dashboard, not the sync protocol itself.
blocking_issues:
The app's core credential is SYNC_USER1=<username>:<secret>, and the username half is not customer-chosen — the recipe can simply hardcode a fixed username (e.g. "customer") in the .env.template, so that part is not a blocker on its own.

With PASSWORDS_HASHED=true, SYNC_USER1's <secret> is a hash, and the Anki client authenticates by sending the plaintext password to the server at sync time (over TLS) — the server itself only ever needs the hash to verify against, the same shape as Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN. So this is NOT a case where the app needs the customer's plaintext; a customer syncing their Anki client would simply type their existing root password as the sync password, matching the generated_from model exactly. The genuine blocker is narrower: the app's hashing tool (user-manager.sh) produces PHC-format pbkdf2 hashes, and generated_from today only supports argon2/bcrypt. This is blocked_on_platform pending pbkdf2 (PHC pbkdf2-sha256) support in generated_from, not a structural not_recommended — per SCHEMA.md's corrected guidance, only a genuine plaintext requirement is a hard blocker, and this app has none.

The optional web dashboard (DASHBOARD_ENABLED=true) has its own independent secret, DASHBOARD_AUTH=user:pass, for the app's built-in basic-auth page. Since it's a plain HTTP basic-auth prompt with no backing user-management, the recipe can simply leave DASHBOARD_ENABLED off and instead gate the dashboard's route with Traefik basic_auth — same pattern as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI. That secret is fully expressible today.

Sync traffic (8080/8443) and the dashboard (8081) are two separate backend ports needing two separate Traefik routers/hostnames rather than the single-port-per-app shape most of our recipes use. Not a hard blocker (multi-service recipes like anytype-server/immich already front more than one port), but it is a step above our simplest single-container recipes and worth flagging as extra plumbing.
summary: Correcting the prior pass: this app's core sync credential does NOT require the customer's plaintext to reach the container — in PASSWORDS_HASHED mode the server only ever needs a hash to check the client-submitted password against, and the username half of SYNC_USER1 can be a fixed, non-customer-chosen value. The real, narrower blocker is that the app's hash tool produces pbkdf2 (PHC format), which generated_from doesn't support yet (only argon2/bcrypt) — this is blocked_on_platform, not a structural not_recommended. The optional dashboard's own auth can be bypassed entirely with a Traefik basic_auth gate instead. Once pbkdf2 support lands in generated_from, this becomes mechanically installable; independent of that, it remains a low-value, narrow-audience addition (single flashcard-sync ecosystem, single- maintainer upstream) so even post-unblock it's a low-priority build.

name: Annif
source_description: Multilingual automated subject indexing toolkit for libraries and research
version_health_notes: v1.4.1 shipped 2025-11-07 (confirmed via PyPI upload metadata); today is 2026-08-05, so ~9 months have passed with no new version tag — a noticeably wider gap than the project's prior cadence (1.0.0 Aug 2023, 1.1.0 Apr 2024, 1.2.0 Oct 2024, 1.2.1 Dec 2024, 1.3.0 Feb 2025, 1.3.1 Mar 2025, 1.4.0 Sep 2025, 1.4.1 Nov 2025 — roughly every 2 months for two years, then a stop). The repo is not archived, and the quay.io image for the `1.4.1` tag has been rebuilt repeatedly through 2026-05/2026-08 (base-image/dependency patches under the same app version), so the maintainer (NatLibFi, National Library of Finland) is still actively operating the project infrastructure even though no new functional release has landed in 9 months. Calling this "slowing" rather than "dormant" — the underlying Finto AI production service run by the same maintainer is still live, but the release pace has clearly cooled versus its 2023-2025 track record.
differentiation: Annif is a multi-algorithm automated subject-indexing/classification tool built for libraries, archives, and museums — given a document, it suggests controlled-vocabulary subject headings using statistical and ML backends (fastText, Omikuji, MLLM, etc.), exposed via a REST API and a lightweight web UI. This is a distinct capability from anything in the current 24-recipe catalogue: Ollama and Open WebUI are general LLM chat/inference tools, and Paperless-ngx/Paperless-AI do OCR/document archiving with LLM-assisted tagging, but none does controlled-vocabulary subject classification against a library taxonomy (e.g. YSO, LCSH). The catch is that this differentiation only matters to a narrow slice of customers — libraries, archives, and academic/research institutions doing metadata work — not the general self-hoster.
usefulness_rationale: Legitimate, actively-operated tool from a credible institutional maintainer (National Library of Finland), but it targets a very narrow professional audience (library/archive metadata specialists) and is non-functional out of the box: a fresh Annif instance ships with no vocabulary and no trained model, so the web UI and REST API have nothing to suggest until an operator manually trains a model or downloads a pre-trained one (e.g. from Hugging Face) and registers it in `projects.cfg`. That is a real setup burden with no self-service path in our one-click flow, well beyond what a domain name and a generated password can bootstrap. Combined with the niche audience, day-one value for a typical Application Factory customer is close to zero.
summary: Annif ships as a single container (quay.io/natlibfi/annif, Gunicorn on :8000, reference compose adds an nginx front-end we'd replace with Traefik) — structurally closest to the single-container web-app template (recipes/uptime-kuma/) rather than a multi-service stack. It has no built-in login of its own, so a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate projected from the customer's root password is the workable mechanism, making it technically installable today with no blocking secret-channel gap. The real problem is product fit: it needs a trained subject-classification model and vocabulary before it does anything useful, which our current per-customer parameter mechanism has no way to supply, and its target audience (library/archive metadata teams) is a sliver of our customer base. Recommend not_recommended — mechanically buildable but low value for a one-click catalogue entry, and upstream's release cadence has cooled sharply in the last 9 months on top of that.

name: Ant Media Server CE
source_description: Open-source WebRTC/RTMP/HLS streaming server with admin dashboard
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (COMMUNITY_EDITION_LICENSE; the separate Enterprise edition in the same repo is proprietary)
version_health_notes: Tagged release ams-v3.0.3 published 2026-05-04, ~3 months before today (2026-08-05). Prior tags (v2.17.0, v2.17.1, v3.0.0) land roughly every 4-8 weeks through early 2026 — steady cadence, no archive/EOL signal.
differentiation: No recipe today does live video ingest/streaming (RTMP/WebRTC/HLS) — closest neighbors (Immich, Syncthing) are file/photo sync, not real-time media. Would add a genuinely new category (self-hosted live streaming/broadcast) to the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real niche demand (self-hosted streaming for creators, security/webcam relay, WebRTC conferencing backends) but a narrower audience than general productivity/security apps already in the catalogue, and requires customers to understand RTMP/WebRTC concepts to get value from it.
blocking_issues:
No official Community Edition Docker image exists on Docker Hub. Ant Media only publishes 'antmedia/enterprise' officially; CE requires building your own image from the GitHub release zip (per the project's own Docker wiki) or relying on an unofficial third-party image (fluential/, rez0n/, boris1993/, etc.) with no upstream support guarantee — this alone fails the 'official Docker image + pinned tag' research bar.
First-boot admin account is created through a one-time web-panel setup form (username/email/password, or via REST POST) at http://<host>:5080, not read from an environment variable at container start. The generated_from: ROOT_PASSWORD mechanism only projects a password into an existing env-var-backed login field; it cannot pre-fill or drive a first-run HTML setup wizard, and the field set (email + password, not password alone) doesn't match the single-password projection model either.
Core value (RTMP ingest on 1935, WebRTC on a large UDP range 5000-65000, HLS/DASH playback) needs raw TCP/UDP ports exposed directly to the internet, not just the web dashboard — Traefik basic_auth can gate the :5080 dashboard but does nothing for the streaming ports, so the panel could be locked down while the actual media ingest stays open and effectively unauthenticated by our mechanism.
summary: Ant Media Server CE is an actively maintained, Apache-2.0 streaming engine, but it fails our installability bar on three independent grounds: there is no official CE Docker image to pin, the admin account is provisioned through a first-run web wizard rather than an env-var/root-password projection, and its primary value (RTMP/WebRTC ingest) lives on raw ports our basic_auth gate doesn't cover. It would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue (no live-streaming recipe exists today) but should wait for either an official CE image and a documented headless-provisioning API, or a platform mechanism beyond root-password projection.

However a 0.9.0 release-candidate cycle is actively in flight on top of that: rc1 (2026-05-08), rc2 (2026-05-16), rc3 (2026-05-21), rc4 (2026-07-23), roughly two weeks before today, and the Docker Hub `master-snapshot`/`master-snapshot-hadoop2` tags were rebuilt 2 days ago. Still an ASF Incubator podling (entered incubation 2024-03-11, not graduated, not retired) with quarterly board reports and an active committer/PPMC list — no archival or EOL signal. Net: GA tags ship slower than a typical top-level project (~4-11 months apart), but nightly builds and an active RC pipeline show the project is not dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches data-lakehouse/table-format management — this is a genuinely new category (Iceberg/Paimon table optimization, unified catalog service for Flink/Spark/Trino) rather than overlapping an existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: The dashboard/REST API (port 1630) is reverse-proxy-friendly on its own, but Amoro's actual value (self-optimizing compaction, catalog service) only materializes once external Flink/Spark/Trino compute engines and optimizer processes connect to its Thrift ports (1260 table service, 1261 optimizing service) — raw TCP, not HTTP, and not something Traefik fronts. Standing up AMS alone, with no compute engine attached, gives a customer little beyond an empty dashboard. summary: Amoro Management Service (AMS) ships with an embedded Derby metastore by default, so no external database is needed to boot. Its own dashboard login (`admin-username`/`admin-password` in config.yaml, default admin/admin) only accepts a plaintext value compared/decrypted at runtime — never a hash — so `generated_from` cannot project the customer's root password into it directly. That is not a hard blocker, though: following the same pattern used for Adminer, the fix is to leave Amoro's own admin/admin login untouched and gate the whole dashboard behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` credential (projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from`), which moves the actual customer-facing auth boundary in front of the app rather than through it. Mechanically installable today on that basis. The bigger open question is value: Amoro's headline feature (self-optimizing Iceberg/Paimon tables) needs external Flink/Spark/Trino engines talking to its raw Thrift ports, which sit outside what a single Traefik-fronted docker-compose recipe usefully exposes, and the audience (data engineers running a lakehouse stack) doesn't match the rest of the catalogue. Recommend build_with_caveats: ship it if there's a specific customer ask, but don't prioritize it as a differentiator.

differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is an API gateway / API management product — this would be a genuinely new category (dynamic request routing, rate limiting, auth plugins, canary/traffic-splitting, observability) if it worked end-to-end. But the product's core value proposition is customer-configured routing of arbitrary upstream domains/paths through its own data-plane ports, which is a different shape than every existing recipe: those are "one app, one subdomain, fronted by our Traefik," while APISIX itself *is* a reverse proxy meant to sit in that position for other services, not behind it.
usefulness_rationale: The category itself is defensible for a subset of technical customers doing multi-backend API management, but the actual product is unusable without a working control surface: there is no built-in web UI, only a REST Admin API, and the one official web UI (apisix-dashboard) has no current image compatible with a supportable APISIX version (see version_health.notes). A typical AF customer landing on a "gateway" tile with no browser-based way to configure a single route gets very little value; usefulness would be medium-to-high if the dashboard situation were resolved.
blocking_issues:
No officially maintained, pre-built Docker image for a web UI exists for the current APISIX line: apache/apisix-dashboard's last Docker Hub tag (3.0.1) is 3+ years stale and explicitly documented by upstream as untested outside APISIX 3.0. Building a compatible dashboard from a pinned git commit is outside what af-create-recipe supports (official image + pinned tag only).
Even ignoring the dashboard gap, the Admin API's own auth (X-API-KEY header checked by literal string equality against deployment.admin.admin_key.key) doesn't fit either supported secret-projection mechanism: generated_from only produces a usable login when the app hashes a customer-typed plaintext value itself to compare (as vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does) — APISIX does no such hashing, so a projected root-password hash can't double as a credential the customer can actually type in. And the admin_key isn't a fixed/unchangeable default we can gate behind Traefik basic_auth and ignore either — unlike Adminer, the Admin API *is* the entire product surface, so hiding it behind a gate without a way for the customer to also learn/use the real key leaves them locked out of the one thing the app does.
Structural mismatch with the recipe model: APISIX's raison d'etre is proxying arbitrary customer-configured upstream domains/paths through its own data-plane ports (9080/9443), which conflicts with the fixed one-app-one-subdomain-behind-Traefik shape every current recipe uses. Even a fully solved-credentials version of this recipe would need a different exposure model than the rest of the catalogue.
summary: Core Apache APISIX is a healthy, actively-released project (~2-month release cadence, no EOL signal), but it isn't installable as an AF recipe today and the blockers aren't the kind IF-1420/IF-1312 would fix. There is no current, officially published web UI image compatible with a supportable APISIX version (apisix-dashboard's Docker Hub tag is frozen at 3.0.1, 3+ years old), and the Admin API's plain string-equality API-key auth doesn't map onto either supported secret-projection mechanism the way a real password-based login does. On top of that, the product's whole point — routing arbitrary customer-chosen domains/paths through its own proxy ports — doesn't fit the one-app-one-subdomain-behind-Traefik shape every existing recipe assumes. This is an upstream tooling and architectural-fit problem, not a platform secrets-input gap, so `not_recommended` rather than `blocked_on_platform`.

name: Apache CouchDB
source_description: Multi-primary NoSQL document database with an HTTP/JSON API and offline sync
version_health_notes: 3.5.2 shipped 2026-05-14 (~2.9 months before today, 2026-08-05), with a 3.5.2.1 Docker-image-only respin shortly after. Prior patches: 3.4.3 on 2025-03-17, 3.4.0/3.5.0 branch split around 2024-09-20/2025-05-05 — a steady multi-month patch cadence on the current 3.5.x line, not slowing. Per endoflife.date, the project officially supports only the two most recent minor lines (3.4 and 3.5) for CVEs; 3.3 (EOL 2025-05-05) and 3.2 (EOL 2024-09-20) are already unsupported. ASF project, not archived, active commit and release history — clearly active, not dormant or EOL.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes give customers a standalone, general- purpose database engine with its own HTTP API. n8n, paperless-ngx, gitea, immich, etc. each run a Postgres/MySQL/SQLite instance internally as a private implementation detail, not something the customer provisions or talks to directly. CouchDB is the opposite: a document database customers deploy on purpose, then read/write over HTTP/JSON from their own apps (mobile/offline-first sync, IoT, custom backends) via CouchDB's built-in multi-primary replication. It also differs from Adminer (a generic admin UI *for* someone else's SQL database) — CouchDB is the database itself, with an admin UI (Fauxton) bundled on top.
usefulness_rationale: Valuable to developers who want a managed, ready-to-use NoSQL backend with offline sync (a well-known pattern for mobile/PouchDB-based apps), but it's infrastructure for other things a customer builds, not an end-user product — narrower appeal than the chat apps, password managers, and Git hosts that make up most of the current catalogue.
blocking_issues: CouchDB has its own admin login (no-admin-set "Admin Party" mode, where the HTTP API is fully unauthenticated, is explicitly not an option to ship) set via the official image's COUCHDB_USER / COUCHDB_PASSWORD env vars, which the entrypoint writes verbatim into local.ini's [admins] section. CouchDB accepts either a plaintext password there (which it then hashes itself on next read) or an already-hashed value prefixed `-pbkdf2-<hash>,<salt>,<iterations>` — but *only* that PBKDF2 format; it does not recognize bcrypt or argon2 hashes. `generated_from` today only supports `argon2` and `bcrypt` (per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md), so there is no way to project a CouchDB-compatible admin credential from the customer's root password yet. Per SCHEMA.md's guidance this is a genuine hash (not a plaintext) requirement, so it is a `blocked_on_platform` gap, not a structural `not_recommended` one: adding `pbkdf2` to `generated_from`'s supported-algorithm list would unblock it.
summary: Apache CouchDB is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (5984) app with a bundled web UI (Fauxton at /_utils) and no overlap with the current catalogue's internal-use relational databases — it would be the first recipe offering a customer-facing NoSQL database with its own HTTP API. Upstream is actively maintained (steady 3.5.x patch cadence, official two-minor-line CVE support policy) and reverse-proxy-compatible. The blocker is entirely mechanical: CouchDB's admin credential must be either plaintext or a PBKDF2 hash, and `generated_from` only supports argon2/bcrypt today, so there is no channel to project the customer's root password into it without an unauthenticated "Admin Party" API. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` pending PBKDF2 support in `generated_from`, not a hard pass.

name: Apache DevLake
source_description: Open-source DORA metrics and engineering team analytics platform
version_health_notes: v1.0.3-beta15 (2026-07-19) is the latest tagged release, about 2.5 weeks before today (2026-08-05); the prior tag (beta14) landed 9 days before that, and betas have shipped every 1-2 months back through mid-2025 with continuous `main_*` snapshot builds pushed to Docker Hub almost daily (latest 2 days before today). The project graduated from Apache Incubator to a full Apache Software Foundation top-level project in October 2025 — a strong independence/activity signal, not a dormancy one. The "beta" suffix has stuck around since v1.0.3-beta1 (2025-06) for well over a year; that looks like a versioning quirk (pre-1.0-stable naming inertia) rather than an indicator of instability, given the steady cadence and TLP graduation.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers engineering/DevOps analytics or DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, MTTR) computed from GitHub/GitLab/Jira/CircleCI/etc. activity. This is a genuinely new category — closest existing recipes (n8n, gitea) are automation/hosting tools, not analytics over them.
usefulness_rationale: Useful to engineering teams that already self-host their DevOps stack and want DORA/flow metrics without a SaaS subscription, but it is a narrower, more technical audience than most of the current catalogue (media, VPN, notes, automation). Its value is also back-loaded: on first boot it's an empty dashboard until the customer manually adds connections (GitHub token, Jira, etc.) through the UI after deployment — nothing blocking, but slower time-to-value than a single-purpose app.
summary: The official docker-compose stack is MySQL + the devlake backend + config-ui (port 4000) + Grafana (port 3002), plus an optional authproxy service for OIDC. Neither config-ui nor Grafana requires a customer-chosen credential at first boot: config-ui ships with no login by default (its ADMIN_USER/ADMIN_PASS basic-auth env vars are optional and off by default) and Grafana ships a fixed admin/admin default. Both are addressed the same way as Adminer/Amoro — gate the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password, rather than trying to feed a value into either app's own login. ENCRYPTION_SECRET (used to encrypt stored data-source tokens at rest) is a random value nothing customer-facing reads, so it generates server-side with no input channel needed. Mechanically installable today with no blockers; the open question is whether a DORA metrics platform is a strong enough differentiator for this catalogue's more consumer/prosumer-leaning customer base, and whether two public web UIs (config-ui + Grafana) on one Traefik host is worth the extra routing complexity versus the value delivered. Recommend build_with_caveats.

name: Apache DolphinScheduler
source_description: Visual workflow orchestration platform for big data and ETL pipelines
upstream_docker_image: apache/dolphinscheduler-api (full stack) / apache/dolphinscheduler-standalone-server (single-container, upstream explicitly marks this "not for production use")
version_health_notes: 3.4.2 (2026-05-30) is the latest GA tag, about 2 months before today (2026-08-05) — roughly quarterly cadence over the last three years (3.4.0 Jan 2026, 3.4.1 Mar 2026, 3.4.2 May 2026, 3.3.2 Oct 2025, 3.3.1 Aug 2025). Repo pushed 2026-07-30 (6 days ago), a `dev` tag rebuilt the same day, 14.4k GitHub stars, 127 open issues actively triaged. Apache top-level project (graduated from incubation in 2021), no archival or EOL signal.
differentiation: n8n (already in the catalogue) is general-purpose SaaS/API workflow automation with a drag-and-drop node canvas; DolphinScheduler is a DAG-based batch-job scheduler aimed at big-data/ETL pipelines (Shell, Python, SQL, Spark, Flink, Hive task types, cron-based dependency scheduling, backfill/retry semantics). Different audience and problem shape from anything in the current 24 recipes — closest conceptually is still n8n, but no functional overlap.
usefulness_rationale: DolphinScheduler can run plain Shell/Python tasks standalone, so it isn't worthless without external infra, but its headline value — Spark/ Flink/Hive/data-lake job orchestration — only materializes once a customer already runs that big-data stack elsewhere and points workers at it, which is a narrow, specialized audience compared to the general-purpose/consumer-facing tools already in the catalogue (VPN, photos, ad-block, notes, forms). Same pattern as apache-amoro: real software, small addressable customer base for a single-VM recipe.
summary: Upstream's own recommended docker-compose stack is multi-service: Bitnami PostgreSQL, Bitnami ZooKeeper, plus dolphinscheduler-api, -alert, -master and -worker containers all sharing one bridge network — a heavier footprint than most of the catalogue (comparable to immich/anytype-server in service count, but with a bigger combined RAM ask given master+worker+ Spark-class task execution). A `standalone-server` single-container image exists and bundles everything with an embedded DB/registry, but upstream explicitly documents it as "not for production use," so it isn't a sound basis for a customer-facing recipe. The web UI (single HTTP port 12345, path /dolphinscheduler/ui) is otherwise Traefik-compatible; the internal Netty RPC port (25333) is container-to-container only and would not be exposed publicly. Login is a fixed, non-configurable default (admin/dolphinscheduler123) — the password hash is a literal MD5 value baked into the schema-init SQL INSERT, not read from any env var or config at boot, so `generated_from` has no injection point at all (not even an unsupported-algorithm case — there is no runtime hook to write through). Per the fixed-default-credential precedent (Adminer, Amoro), this is not a hard blocker: gate the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password, and leave the app's own default login alone. Mechanically installable on that basis, but recommend build_with_caveats — build only if there's a specific customer ask, given the narrow big-data-engineer audience and heavier multi-service resource footprint relative to the rest of the catalogue.

name: Apache Doris
source_description: Real-time MPP analytics database for sub-second SQL and unified data warehousing
upstream_docker_image: apache/doris (separate fe-<version> and be-<version> tags, e.g. apache/doris:fe-4.1.3 / apache/doris:be-4.1.3)
version_health_notes: ~3.5 weeks between 4.1.3 (2026-07-13) and today (2026-08-05). Two parallel stable lines both getting regular patches: 4.1.x (4.1.0 Apr-21, 4.1.1 May-24, 4.1.2 Jun-17, 4.1.3 Jul-13 — roughly monthly) and 4.0.x (4.0.6 Jun-08, 4.0.7 Jul-12). Top-level Apache project, large active community, no slowdown or EOL signal.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is an analytics/OLAP database — this would be a genuinely new category (real-time MPP SQL analytics, unified data warehousing). But the product's core value is served over the raw MySQL wire protocol (port 9030) to BI tools and SQL clients, not through the FE's web console; the web console (port 8030) is a monitoring/admin surface, not the primary way customers get value from the app. That's a different shape from every existing web-app recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Real category, but Doris targets large-scale distributed analytics workloads: minimum viable deployment is already two containers (FE + BE) configured in "election mode" with FE_SERVERS/FE_ID coordination, and upstream's own production guidance is 3+ FE and 3+ BE nodes for HA. The BE image also requires AVX2 CPU support and JVM-backed FE tends to want double-digit GB of RAM. This is a heavier, more specialized footprint than a typical single-VM AF customer's use case, and the payoff (a MySQL-protocol endpoint for BI tools) doesn't map well onto the "one app, one browser tab" model most AF customers expect.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: root account password (FE web console at :8030 and MySQL-protocol access at :9030 share the same root account)
blocking_issues:
Doris's root account ships with an empty password by default and is changed only via a post-boot SQL command (SET PASSWORD) or the fe.conf `root_password` setting, which accepts only a doubled-SHA1 hash (MySQL PASSWORD()-style: SHA1(SHA1(plaintext))) — not argon2 or bcrypt. `generated_from` doesn't support that hash format today, so there's no channel to project the customer's root (server) password into it. Per the schema's guidance this is a 'not a hard no': it needs a supported-algorithm extension, not a plaintext requirement, so this is flagged blocked_on_platform rather than not_recommended.
Inspected the official FE init script (docker/runtime/fe/resource/init_fe.sh in the apache/doris repo) directly: it validates cluster-topology env vars (FE_SERVERS, FE_ID, FE_MASTER_IP, etc.) but has no env var for setting an initial password of any kind — confirming there is no init-time hook to inject a hash even if the algorithm gap were closed.
Even with the credential issue solved, the product's primary interface is the raw MySQL wire protocol on port 9030, not HTTP — usable as a `public: true, http: false` raw port (the platform already supports this for wg-easy/pihole), but it means the actual value of the app is delivered outside the Traefik-fronted browser flow every current recipe assumes.
summary: Apache Doris is an actively maintained, healthy ASF top-level project (monthly-ish releases, no EOL signal) and would fill a real gap — no analytics/OLAP database exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue. However it can't ship as a recipe today: its root account (shared by the FE web console and MySQL-protocol SQL access) only accepts a doubled-SHA1 password hash via fe.conf, an algorithm `generated_from` doesn't support yet, and the official Docker init script has no env-var hook for setting any initial password regardless. That's a genuine but closable platform gap (extend the supported-algorithm list), not a plaintext-only requirement, so this is `blocked_on_platform`. Separately, even once unblocked, Doris's minimum viable footprint (FE+BE multi-container cluster, AVX2 CPU requirement, upstream's own 3+3-node HA guidance) and its MySQL-wire-protocol-first interaction model make it a heavier, more niche fit for typical AF customers than most of what's in the catalogue today — worth deprioritizing relative to lighter-weight gaps even after the platform blocker is resolved.

name: Apache Druid
source_description: Real-time analytics database for sub-second OLAP queries on streaming event data

Prior majors: 36.0.0 on 2026-02-09, 35.0.1 on 2025-12-15, 35.0.0 on 2025-11-18, 34.0.0 on 2025-08-11 — a steady ~3-month major-release cadence going back years, plus patch releases (e.g. 35.0.1, 32.0.1/ 31.0.2 CVE fixes) between majors. ASF top-level project, actively developed (29+ contributors credited in the 37.0.0 release notes), not archived or slowing.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes offer a customer-facing analytics database. Existing recipes that embed Postgres/MySQL/SQLite (n8n, paperless-ngx, gitea, immich) use it as a private implementation detail; Druid is the opposite — customers stand it up on purpose to ingest streaming/batch event data and run sub-second OLAP queries over it via SQL or its native query API, then build dashboards or downstream apps on top. This is a genuinely new capability class for the catalogue (real-time analytics/data-warehouse infra), not an overlap with anything already offered.
usefulness_rationale: Valuable to a data-engineering audience wanting a turnkey managed OLAP engine, but it's infrastructure customers build on top of rather than an end-user product, and it is far heavier than every other recipe in the catalogue: the official docker-compose quickstart runs 8 containers (ZooKeeper, a Postgres metadata store, and six Druid services — coordinator, overlord, broker, router, historical, middleManager), each budgeted up to 7 GiB of memory in the reference "micro-quickstart" config. That's a materially larger resource floor and operational surface than anything currently in the catalogue, narrowing the realistic customer base to those who specifically want a full OLAP cluster, not casual self-hosters.
summary: Apache Druid is actively maintained (steady ~3-month major-release cadence, latest 37.0.0 on 2026-05-08) and would add a genuinely new capability — a customer-facing real-time OLAP database — with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue. Security is disabled by default (the console and query APIs use an AllowAll authenticator/authorizer out of the box, per upstream docs), so it has no login of its own to project a credential into; gating the router's single HTTP entrypoint (port 8888, which fronts the console and all service APIs) behind Traefik `basic_auth` is the correct mechanism and is expressible today, making it mechanically installable. The caveat is scale: the official stack is 8 containers (ZooKeeper + Postgres metadata store + six Druid services) with a multi-GB-per-service memory footprint, well beyond any recipe currently in the catalogue, and its audience (data engineers building analytics pipelines) is narrower than the general-purpose apps we currently ship. Recommend `build_with_caveats`: installable now, but worth confirming the resource floor and target customer fit before committing a recipe slot to it.

name: Apache Gravitino
source_description: Open-source metadata lake unifying Iceberg, Hive, and JDBC catalogs in one API
version_health_notes: ~1.2 months between 1.3.0 (2026-06-29) and today (2026-08-05). Prior releases landed at a healthy clip: 1.2.1 (2026-05-12), 1.1.1 (2026-04-01), 1.2.0 (2026-03-13), 1.1.0 (2025-12-16), 1.0.1 (2025-11-19), 1.0.0 (2025-09-30) — roughly monthly-to-quarterly, no gaps. Gravitino graduated from Apache Incubator to a full Apache Top-Level Project on 2025-06-03, which is a maturity signal, not a slowdown; the release rate has if anything increased since graduation. No archival, EOL, or maintenance-mode signal anywhere.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches data-lake/metadata management — this would open a new category. Gravitino is a metadata catalog service that unifies Iceberg, Hive, and JDBC-backed catalogs (plus newer additions like ClickHouse and Glue) behind one API and a web UI, aimed at customers building or federating a data lakehouse/warehouse. It doesn't compete with anything we ship today (n8n, Immich, Vaultwarden, etc. are all end-user or ops tools, not data infrastructure).
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely novel category with no internal competition, and the 1.2.0 web UI redesign makes it usable without hand-editing REST calls. But the audience is narrow and technical (data engineers already running or building a lakehouse) compared to the mass-market tools that make up most of the catalogue, and the product's core value — federating catalogs across Hive/Iceberg/JDBC/etc. — only pays off once a customer also has those backing systems (a Hive metastore, an S3-backed Iceberg warehouse, an external JDBC source) to point it at, which a fresh AF install doesn't provide out of the box.
summary: Apache Gravitino is a healthy, actively-released project (graduated to Apache TLP mid-2025, monthly-to-quarterly releases with no gaps) and is mechanically installable today: its default "simple" auth mode requires no login at all (falls back to an anonymous user), so the recipe can gate the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth exactly like Adminer — no external secret or plaintext-password channel is needed. Note that the alternative built-in "basic" auth mode requires setting GRAVITINO_INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD to a plaintext value before first startup (server hashes it internally but only accepts plaintext input), which would NOT be expressible via generated_from; the recipe should stick to simple-mode-plus-basic_auth-gate and avoid basic mode entirely. Two caveats keep this at build_with_caveats rather than build_now: the server ships with an embedded H2 store by default, which upstream explicitly says not to rely on for production durability (acceptable for a single-tenant AF instance but worth documenting); and the secondary Iceberg REST port (9001) is meant to be consumed directly by external query engines (Spark, Trino) rather than browsed, which doesn't fit neatly behind a single Traefik subdomain the way the Web UI/API port (8090) does — core catalog-management functionality works fine through 8090 alone, but customers wanting the Iceberg REST catalog protocol itself would need a raw port exposed outside the standard one-app-one- subdomain shape.

name: Apache HertzBeat
source_description: Agentless real-time observability platform with alerting and public status pages
version_health_notes: 1.8.0 (GitHub-tagged 2026-01-31, pushed to Docker Hub 2026-02-06) is the latest stable image tag — about 6 months before today (2026-08-05). A v1.9.0-rc1 GitHub release landed 2026-07-28 (~1 week before today), but no matching `1.9.0` tag exists on Docker Hub yet — the release is still in candidate/testing stage. A `nightly` image tag was rebuilt today (2026-08-05), so development is continuous even though the stable line has a ~6-month gap. Historical stable cadence (1.6.0 -> 1.6.1 -> 1.7.0 -> 1.7.1 -> 1.7.2 -> 1.7.3 -> 1.8.0) has run every 1-6 months since mid-2024 with no long stall, and the project is a full Apache Software Foundation project (~7.3k GitHub stars, ~2,900 commits, active issue triage) — this reads as active, not slowing.
differentiation: Uptime Kuma is the only existing "monitoring" recipe, and it is scoped to external up/down + latency checks on URLs and TCP ports. HertzBeat is agentless infrastructure/service observability: it polls hosts, DBs, middleware, cloud services, and custom protocols for real metrics (CPU/memory/disk, DB stats, JVM, etc.), stores them in a time-series backend, and layers alerting rules and public status pages on top — closer to a lightweight Zabbix/Prometheus+Grafana than a ping checker. Some conceptual overlap with Uptime Kuma at the "status page" surface, but the underlying data model and use case (deep host/service metrics vs. simple availability pings) are different enough to be additive rather than duplicative.
usefulness_rationale: Real value for a technical customer who already self-hosts several servers/services and wants one dashboard for metrics + alerting without standing up Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager by hand. Narrower appeal than consumer-facing recipes in the catalogue (media, notes, VPN), and it needs the customer to add monitors for their own infrastructure after deployment — the app is an empty dashboard on first boot until they do, similar to the DevLake/Adminer "bring your own thing to manage" pattern already flagged in this catalogue.
blocking_issues: HertzBeat's own admin login (default admin/hertzbeat) is not a database row — it is a static entry in a mounted `sureness.yml` file, and the only supported way to set a non-default password there is `credential: MD5(password + salt)`. `generated_from` today only supports `argon2`/`bcrypt`, so there is no channel to project the customer's root-password hash into HertzBeat's own login in the supported MD5(salt) form. Not a hard blocker per se (same "unsupported algorithm" case as any pbkdf2-only app) — it only blocks wiring the customer's password into HertzBeat's *own* login specifically.
summary: The official stack is a Postgres (or MySQL) database plus a time-series store (VictoriaMetrics/IoTDB/TDengine) plus the `apache/hertzbeat` app container, exposing port 1157 for the web UI/API and 1158 for manager-collector cluster traffic — a 3-container stack structurally similar to `immich`/`anytype-server`, with only 1157 needing to be public (1158 is only relevant for multi-collector clustering, not a single-node deploy). Rather than trying to feed the customer's root password into HertzBeat's own MD5(salt)-based `sureness.yml` login (no supported `generated_from` algorithm reaches that format today), the same pattern already used for Adminer/DevLake's config-ui applies: gate the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password, and leave HertzBeat's internal admin/hertzbeat login as an unexposed second factor behind that gate. That makes it mechanically installable today. The open question is value versus complexity: it is a genuinely new capability (real infrastructure metrics + alerting + status pages, not just uptime pings), but it targets a more technical customer segment and ships an empty dashboard until they configure monitors themselves. Recommend build_with_caveats.

name: Apache Hop
source_description: Visual data orchestration platform and modern successor to Pentaho Kettle
version_health_notes: ~1.6 months between 2.18.1 (2026-06-18) and today (2026-08-05). 2.18.1 is a patch release fixing regressions in 2.18.0 (released 2026-06-01, three months after 2.17.0 on 2026-02-06). That's a steady quarterly major/minor cadence with prompt patch follow-ups, and Docker Hub also carries active `Development`/`2.19.0-SNAPSHOT` builds updated within the last few hours at time of research. Apache Hop is a top-level ASF project under normal governance, not an incubator or dormant project — no EOL or maintenance-only signal.
differentiation: Apache Hop is a visual ETL/data-pipeline design and orchestration tool (successor to Pentaho Kettle) — drag-and-drop pipelines and workflows that move and transform data between databases, files, and APIs. n8n is the closest existing recipe (also visual, node-based, automation- flavored) but n8n is oriented around app/API integration triggers, not ETL-style batch data transformation with typed steps, JDBC drivers, and metadata-driven pipelines. No current recipe covers dedicated ETL tooling, so this would be a genuinely new category if it fit the platform's constraints.
