summary: Apache Hop is an actively-released ASF project (quarterly cadence, no EOL signal) with an official, regularly-updated Docker image (`apache/hop-web`, pinned tags like `2.18.1` on Docker Hub) that serves its browser-based pipeline designer on a single port (8080) with no path prefix or extra raw ports — reverse-proxy-compatible behind Traefik on `<slug>.<base_domain>`. Critically, Hop Web ships with no authentication of its own out of the box (the docs describe *manually* wiring Tomcat's `tomcat-users.xml`/`web.xml` for auth, which isn't something a recipe's boot flow can automate), so it is installable today only by treating the entire app as needing a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate — same pattern as Adminer. That makes it mechanically installable now (`build_with_caveats`) but the value delivered on first boot is limited to a design surface with no execution backend or data-source drivers configured; a customer gets a working pipeline editor, not a working data pipeline, without further manual setup. Note this recipe would target `apache/hop-web` specifically — the separate `apache/hop` image (Hop Server / CLI pipeline runner, default `cluster`/`cluster` plaintext credentials) is a different, non-web-UI artifact not covered by this analysis.

name: Apache IoTDB
source_description: Time-series database for industrial IoT and high-throughput sensor telemetry
version_health_notes: v2.0.10 shipped 2026-07-04 (~1 month before today, 2026-08-05). Release history shows a steady monthly-to-bimonthly cadence across both supported lines: v2.0.8 (2026-04-13), v1.3.7/v2.0.7 (2026-03-04), v2.0.6/v1.3.6 (2026-01-20/2026-01-07), v1.3.5 (2025-09-11). ASF top-level project, clearly active. One caveat: the separate `apache/iotdb-web-workbench` repo (the project's only web-console UI) was archived by its owner on 2024-01-08 and is read-only — that component is dead even though the core database is thriving.
differentiation: No existing recipe offers a standalone time-series database — the closest relatives (n8n, paperless-ngx, gitea, immich) embed Postgres/MySQL/SQLite purely as a private implementation detail, never expose it as the product. IoTDB would be a genuinely new capability class (industrial IoT / sensor-telemetry storage) if it weren't for the access-model mismatch below.
usefulness_rationale: The core value proposition — high-throughput sensor ingestion queried over its native Thrift RPC protocol (port 6667) or JDBC/CLI drivers — is not something a customer reaches through a browser or through Traefik at all; it's infrastructure other software (or a data engineer's own client) talks to directly. Its one HTTP surface, the REST API, is off by default and the project's only browser UI (iotdb-web-workbench) has been abandoned since 2024. That leaves a narrow, technical-only audience even before the installability problems below.
blocking_issues:
Primary interface is the Thrift RPC protocol on port 6667 (used by the CLI, JDBC/Session drivers, and virtually all real client traffic) — a raw non-HTTP protocol, so Traefik's basic_auth (HTTP-only) cannot gate it. reverse_proxy_compatible is false for the interface customers actually use.
Auth defaults to a hardcoded root/root account with no documented docker/env-var hook to set or hash a different password at first boot (confirmed against the official docker-compose-standalone.yml env vars and the Docker deployment guide — password can only be changed after boot via an authenticated 'ALTER USER' SQL statement issued through the CLI). Because the credential lives behind a non-HTTP port, the 'gate a fixed default password behind Traefik basic_auth' escape hatch (SCHEMA.md table) does not apply here — there is no HTTP entrypoint to put the gate on.
The only HTTP surface, the optional REST API (port 18080), is disabled by default, reuses the same un-projectable root/root credential, and is explicitly marked 'not recommended' by upstream for v1 — not a realistic substitute primary interface.
The project's own web console (iotdb-web-workbench) has been archived since 2024-01-08, so there is no maintained UI to front with Traefik even if there were an auth channel for it.
summary: Apache IoTDB itself is actively maintained (monthly-ish releases, latest 2.0.10 on 2026-07-04) and would fill a real gap — no recipe currently offers a standalone time-series database — but it fails our installation model on two independent counts. First, the interface customers actually use is a raw Thrift RPC port (6667), not HTTP, so it isn't reverse-proxy-compatible and Traefik basic_auth can't gate it. Second, the built-in root/root credential has no env-var/config hook to customize at container start; changing it requires an authenticated SQL session after boot, and there's no HTTP surface to put a basic_auth gate on regardless. The project's only web UI (iotdb-web-workbench) has also been archived since 2024, closing off that angle too. Recommend `not_recommended`: this isn't a "wait for IF-1420/1312" case since even the basic_auth escape hatch is structurally unavailable — it would need a native root-password env var or JWE-carried credential in the app image itself, plus a maintained web front-end, before it's a candidate.

name: Apache JSPWiki
source_description: Java-based Apache wiki engine with versioning, attachments, and access control
version_health_notes: 2.12.4 was tagged/published to Maven Central on 2026-04-08 — just under 4 months before today (2026-08-05). Recent stable-release gaps have been long and widening: 2.12.2 (2024-06-19) -> 2.12.3 (2025-07-29, +13 months) -> 2.12.4 (2026-04-08, +8 months). That is a genuinely sporadic cadence for a 2.x line, not a healthy monthly/quarterly rhythm. However the project is not stale: master had commits as recently as 2026-07-14 (3 weeks ago), and there is live work toward a 3.0.0 line (tag jspwiki-builder-3.0.0-RC1, dev version string "3.0.0-git-24" in July 2026 commits), so this reads as active-but-slow rather than maintenance-only. One naming oddity worth flagging for a reviewer: the git/Docker Hub tag for this release is literally named "2.14.2" (release-2.14.2 on Docker Hub, tag 2.14.2 on GitHub), but the pom.xml inside that tag is version 2.12.4 and Maven Central's maven-metadata.xml lists 2.12.4 as <latest>/<release> — "2.14.2" appears to be a mistaken tag label, not a real second version line. Treat 2.12.4 as the authoritative latest version.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a wiki/knowledge-base tool. Gitea hosts git repos and OpenGist hosts snippets, but neither gives a browsable, editable wiki with page history. JSPWiki's specific angle within "wiki" is fine-grained page/group ACLs and a mature versioning + attachment model (it predates Confluence and is still used by some legacy enterprise/documentation teams wanting that model) — a real but narrower niche than a generic Markdown wiki.
usefulness_rationale: Fills a genuine, currently-unfilled catalogue gap (self-hosted wiki) on its own merits, but is a heavier stack (JVM + Tomcat + JSP) with a sporadic, cooling release cadence compared to a same-category alternative already surfaced in this gap-analysis process (An Otter Wiki: single lightweight Python process, git-backed, dense/active release cadence — see apps-gaps/an-otter-wiki.yaml). If the catalogue only has room for one wiki recipe, An Otter Wiki is the stronger general-purpose pick; JSPWiki would only add value for customers specifically wanting its Java-centric ACL/versioning model or migrating from an existing JSPWiki instance.
summary: Apache JSPWiki ships an official single-container image (apache/jspwiki, pin e.g. release-2.12.3 or build-equivalent to 2.12.4) serving on one HTTP port (8080 in-container), storing pages/attachments/logs on a local volume with no external database — fully Traefik-compatible and mechanically simple to deploy. Like An Otter Wiki, it ships with an open default security policy: anonymous visitors can edit pages and self-register a profile out of the box, with whoever gets there first effectively claiming admin-equivalent standing before the customer does. That is not a hard blocker — the same Traefik basic_auth:true gate pattern used for Adminer/n8n/WUD/An Otter Wiki closes it — but it is a required secret, not an optional one. Mechanically installable_today with zero hard blocking issues, hence build_with_caveats. The bigger caveat is strategic rather than mechanical: release cadence has slowed to roughly one release every 8-13 months and the stack is heavier (JVM/Tomcat) than a comparable, more actively-released wiki candidate already flagged in this same gap-analysis pass (An Otter Wiki), which fills the same "self-hosted wiki" catalogue gap with less footprint and a much denser release cadence. Worth building only if the catalogue wants a second, ACL/versioning-focused wiki option alongside (or instead of) that one.

name: Apache Kvrocks
source_description: Redis-compatible disk-backed NoSQL database powered by the RocksDB engine
version_health_notes: 2.16.0 shipped 2026-06-22 (~1.4 months before today, 2026-08-05) with conditional SET ops, CLIENT PAUSE/UNPAUSE, expanded Redis 7.0+ command compatibility, a RocksDB bump to v11.1.1, and security hardening (Lua CVE patches, replication tightening, RDB validation). ASF top-level project (graduated from incubator), steady multi-week release cadence, active commit history and nightly Docker builds — clearly active, not dormant or EOL.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes give customers a standalone Redis- protocol-compatible key-value store. Kvrocks isn't a drop-in overlap with anything shipped today — the closest conceptual cousin is a Postgres/MySQL instance bundled *inside* another recipe (n8n, paperless-ngx), but those are private implementation details the customer never talks to directly, whereas Kvrocks would be a database the customer provisions and connects their own application to over the RESP protocol. It differentiates itself from an in-memory Redis by persisting to RocksDB on disk, aimed at larger datasets at lower memory cost.
usefulness_rationale: Pure developer infrastructure with no web UI and no HTTP surface at all — a customer would deploy it only to point their own external application at it over the Redis wire protocol. That's a narrower, more technical audience than the end-user apps (password managers, chat, Git hosting, photo management) making up most of the catalogue, and lower appeal than CouchDB's comparable "standalone database" gap since Kvrocks lacks even a bundled admin UI or HTTP API to browse data.
blocking_issues:
Kvrocks authenticates exactly like Redis: `requirepass` in kvrocks.conf is compared byte-for-byte against whatever the client sends via `AUTH <password>` — the server never hashes it, and there is no hashed-credential config option at all. `generated_from` can only ever project a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so this is not a "missing algorithm" gap like CouchDB's — extending `generated_from`'s supported-algorithm list would not help, because Kvrocks has no hash-verification code path to target in the first place. Only a genuine plaintext-password input channel would unblock it, and none exists today.

Traefik `basic_auth` is not an alternative gate here either: Kvrocks speaks the raw RESP (Redis) wire protocol on port 6666, not HTTP, so an HTTP-layer basic-auth gate in front of it is a no-op — Traefik would have nothing to intercept.
summary: Apache Kvrocks is an actively maintained (2.16.0, 2026-06-22), Apache- licensed disk-backed Redis-compatible database with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue. However it has no web UI, speaks a raw TCP protocol rather than HTTP, and its only auth mechanism (Redis-style plaintext `requirepass`) has no projection path from the customer's root password and can't be gated by Traefik basic auth since there's no HTTP layer to intercept. Combined with its narrow appeal as pure developer backend infrastructure rather than a customer-facing app, recommend not_recommended rather than blocked_on_platform — there is no near-term platform change (unlike CouchDB's missing pbkdf2 algorithm) that would unblock it, since Kvrocks has no hash-verification path to extend at all.

name: Apache Pinot
source_description: Real-time distributed OLAP datastore for sub-second user-facing analytics
version_health_notes: 1.5.1 shipped 2026-06-05 (~2 months before today, 2026-08-05) as a dependency/CVE-only security patch on top of 1.5.0 (2026-04). Prior minor releases: 1.4.0 (2025-09), 1.3.0 (2025-02), 1.2.0 (2024-08), 1.1.0 (2024-03) — a steady ~6-9 month cadence for minor/major releases with patch releases in between for security fixes. Top-level ASF project with commercial backing (StarTree) driving continued development; no slowdown or EOL signal.
differentiation: No existing recipe is an analytics/OLAP database — this would be a new category. Unlike Apache Doris (MySQL wire protocol) or Apache IoTDB (Thrift RPC), Pinot's customer-facing interfaces are both plain HTTP: the Controller's web Query Console (port 9000) and the Broker's REST query API (port 8099). That makes it more reverse-proxy-friendly than those two, in principle — Traefik can front either or both as normal HTTP routes, and even API clients can carry HTTP Basic Auth headers on every request, unlike a raw TCP wire protocol.
usefulness_rationale: The product's value is "sub-second queries for user-facing apps" — i.e. it's infrastructure a developer's own application calls programmatically via the Broker's query API, not something an AF customer browses in a tab. The Controller's Query Console is a real UI, but it's an admin/debugging surface for running ad-hoc SQL against tables, not a consumer-facing product. Minimum viable deployment is also a 4-container cluster (ZooKeeper + Controller + Broker + Server) with a JVM footprint per component; genuine real-time ingestion (the feature the source description leads with) additionally needs a Kafka-compatible stream the customer would have to bring or self-host separately, since a single-VM recipe realistically only exercises Pinot's batch-ingestion mode out of the box. That's a narrower, more technical audience and a heavier footprint than most of the current catalogue.
summary: Apache Pinot is an actively maintained, healthy ASF top-level project (latest 1.5.1, 2026-06-05) with no EOL signal. It has no built-in authentication by default on either the Controller (web Query Console, port 9000) or Broker (REST query API, port 8099), so — unlike Doris and IoTDB, which are blocked by non-HTTP wire protocols and unhashable passwords — Pinot is technically installable today by gating both HTTP surfaces behind Traefik basic_auth, the same pattern used for n8n/WUD. It's still `build_with_caveats` rather than `build_now`: the minimum viable deployment is a 4-container ZooKeeper+Controller+Broker+Server cluster with a per-component JVM footprint, and the app's real value — a query API for a customer's own application code — is developer infrastructure rather than a consumer-facing web app, a narrower fit for a typical AF customer than most of the current 24 recipes. Real-time ingestion (the feature in Hostinger's description) would also need a separately provisioned Kafka-compatible stream; a single-VM recipe would only exercise Pinot's batch-ingestion path out of the box.

name: Apache ShenYu
source_description: Java-native API gateway for service proxy, protocol conversion, and governance
version_health_notes: ~3 weeks between 2.7.1 (2026-07-13) and today (2026-08-05). Preceding releases landed on a steady ~3-month cadence (2.7.0.3 on 2025-11-24, 2.7.0.2 on 2025-08-25, 2.7.0.1 on 2025-05-03, 2.7.0 on 2025-01-15), each merging 50-250+ PRs per the project's own release announcements. Both official images (apache/shenyu-admin, apache/shenyu-bootstrap) publish versioned tags in step with releases. This is a healthy, actively maintained Apache top-level project, not incubating or dormant.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue is an API gateway, so the category itself would be new. Unlike apache-apisix (already analyzed: no web UI, not_recommended), ShenYu ships an official admin console image (apache/shenyu-admin) with a real browser-based dashboard for managing routes, selectors, and plugins — so the "no usable control surface" problem that sank APISIX doesn't apply here on its face. However, the product's actual value is that its second component (shenyu-bootstrap) is a data-plane proxy meant to sit in front of a customer's own backend APIs, accepting traffic on its own port(s) and routing it based on rules configured in the admin console — the same "gateway-shaped, not app-shaped" mismatch APISIX has.
usefulness_rationale: ShenYu targets enterprise microservices teams governing many internal services behind one gateway (originally built at Dangdang for that use case) — a mismatch for the typical AF customer running one self-hosted app per subdomain. Even a technical customer who wanted this would need to already have other services to proxy and the domain-specific knowledge to configure selectors/rules/plugins; there's no standalone value the way there is for e.g. Vaultwarden or n8n.
blocking_issues:
shenyu-admin ships a fixed, hardcoded default login (admin/123456) baked into its default H2 dataset. There is no documented environment variable or startup property to set/override the initial admin username or password (checked admin-property-config docs) — the password is only changeable after logging in with the default. Per SCHEMA.md this is not itself a hard blocker (gate the console behind Traefik basic_auth, as with Adminer/IF-1312), so this line is informational, not blocking.
Structural mismatch, independent of secrets: shenyu-bootstrap is a data-plane proxy meant to accept and route a customer's own arbitrary backend API traffic on its own port(s) (9195 default), based on rules the customer configures after the fact. That conflicts with the fixed one-app-one-subdomain-behind-Traefik shape every current recipe uses — the gateway's public port(s) can't be basic-auth-gated without breaking the API calls it's meant to proxy, and there's no fixed 'the app' behind a single subdomain the way there is for a normal web app. This is the same category of architectural-fit problem that made apache-apisix not_recommended, not a platform secrets-input gap.
Deployment requires wiring shenyu-bootstrap to shenyu-admin via a WebSocket sync URL (SHENYU_SYNC_WEBSOCKET_URLS) between two containers on a shared network, plus a database choice (H2 default, or MySQL/PostgreSQL/Oracle/OpenGauss for anything beyond a toy deployment) — more moving parts than a typical single-purpose recipe, though not on its own a blocker.
summary: Apache ShenYu is an actively maintained top-level Apache project (release 3 weeks ago, steady ~3-month cadence, no EOL signal) and, unlike apache-apisix, it does ship an official admin console image with a real web UI — so it clears the "unusable without a working control surface" bar APISIX failed. It still doesn't fit the catalogue: its actual product is a data-plane gateway meant to proxy a customer's own arbitrary backend APIs through its own open port(s) based on rules configured after deployment, which is fundamentally different in shape from every existing recipe's "one app, one subdomain, behind Traefik" model, and can't be basic-auth-gated without breaking the very traffic it's meant to proxy. Combined with a niche enterprise-microservices audience that doesn't match typical AF customers, this is not_recommended on fit and usefulness grounds rather than a platform secrets gap.

name: Apache SkyWalking
source_description: Open-source APM with distributed tracing, metrics, logs, and eBPF profiling
version_health_notes: 10.4.0 shipped 2026-04-20, roughly 3.5 months before today (2026-08-05). Recent cadence: 10.1.0 (2025-09-29) -> 10.2.0 (2025-11-?/2026-03, reporting inconsistent across mirrors) -> 10.3.0 (2025-11-10) -> 10.4.0 (2026-04-20), i.e. a new minor roughly every 3-5 months, and a 10.5.0 changelog already exists in the "next" docs tree, meaning development toward the following release is already underway. Sibling sub-projects (Horizon UI, NodeJS agent, BanyanDB) also released within the last 1-2 months of today's date. This is a healthy, genuinely active top-level Apache project, not a candidate for EOL/dormant flagging.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does distributed tracing / APM. Uptime Kuma is the closest existing "monitoring" recipe but it is external blackbox uptime/ping checking, not in-process trace/metric/log collection from instrumented applications — a fundamentally different use case (SkyWalking needs a customer to run language agents inside their own separately-hosted services and point them at this instance). That makes it a genuine, unfilled niche for teams running microservices elsewhere and wanting a central APM backend, but it is also a much narrower audience than our existing single-user consumer/prosumer recipes (password managers, wikis, file sync) — this appeals mainly to developers/SREs operating other software, not end users.
usefulness_rationale: Real, unfilled gap and a well-known, credible open-source APM brand, but the value only materializes for a customer who already has other instrumented services to point at it — it has no standalone utility. Combined with the operational weight below (multi-service stack, extra non-HTTP public ports for agent ingestion), this is a heavier, more niche addition than most of the current catalogue.
blocking_issues:
Not a single-HTTP-port app: the OAP server's whole purpose is receiving trace/metric/log data pushed by language agents running inside the customer's *other*, separately-hosted services (default gRPC receiver on 11800, HTTP alternative on 12801). Those raw TCP/gRPC ports must be reachable by external agents directly, not just browsers routed through Traefik on 80/443 — this is a structurally different exposure shape than every current recipe (all single browser-facing HTTP port fronted by Traefik). Mechanically possible to declare as extra public ports in metadata.yaml, but it is a real deviation from the reverse-proxy-only pattern and needs a product decision on whether AF wants to expose raw agent-ingestion ports per customer VM.

Multi-service stack: OAP server needs a real storage backend. H2/embedded storage was permanently removed as of the 10.2.0 line (2025) — the only supported backends now are BanyanDB, MySQL/ PostgreSQL, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch. A single-node BanyanDB instance is the lightest fit, but this is still a 3-container stack (OAP + BanyanDB + UI) more comparable to Immich/anytype-server than to the single-container recipes that make up most of the catalogue.

The current UI (Horizon UI, the actively-developed replacement for the now-archived skywalking-ui) ships with "no default account" — at least one local user (with an argon2id password hash) or an LDAP binding must be present in a mounted horizon.yaml before anyone can sign in at all. There is no env-var login mechanism and no customer-facing signup flow. This is expressible today only by shipping a fixed, non-customer-chosen local-user hash baked into the recipe and treating Traefik basic_auth as the real auth boundary (same pattern already used for Adminer/n8n/WUD/hermes-agent) — the Horizon UI's own login is not itself wired to ROOT_PASSWORD via generated_from today, and Horizon UI's hash format/CLI has not been verified compatible with af-core's generated_from argon2 output, so this path needs verification even after IF-1420 lands.
summary: Apache SkyWalking is an active, credible, Apache-governed APM project with no equivalent in the current catalogue — a real gap for teams running instrumented microservices elsewhere. It fails our "installable today" bar for structural reasons beyond the usual secrets-input gap: it is a 3-container stack (OAP + BanyanDB + Horizon UI) needing raw gRPC/ HTTP agent-ingestion ports exposed directly (not just a browser-facing HTTP port behind Traefik), and its UI login has no supported customer credential channel today (fixed local user + Traefik basic_auth as the real gate is the only expressible path, and even that needs the argon2-hash-format check against Horizon UI's own CLI). Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit only after a product decision on exposing non-HTTP public ports per recipe, and after generated_from/basic_auth (IF-1420/IF-1312) ship, given the audience is narrower (developers/SREs with other services to monitor) than most of the current catalogue.

name: Apache Solr
source_description: Enterprise open-source search platform built on Apache Lucene
version_health_notes: Solr 10.0.0 (announced 2026-03-04 on the Solr PMC mailing list) is ~5 months old as of today (2026-08-05) and is the most recent release, superseding the 9.x line (last 9.x release: 9.10.1, the closing release of that series). Solr is a top-level ASF project under normal PMC governance; the official `solr` Docker Hub image (maintained via `apache/solr-docker`, ownership transferred from the community maintainer to the Apache Solr project in 2019) has both `10.0.0` and `9.10.1` tags rebuilt within the last day at time of research (base-image security patching, not a new version). Historically Solr ships roughly one major/minor line per 1-2 years with patch releases in between — steady, not sporadic. No EOL or maintenance-only signal.
differentiation: Solr is a standalone full-text search/indexing engine (schema-based cores/collections, faceting, vector search as of 10.0) exposed over one HTTP port with a browser admin console. Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue provides this — the closest adjacent tools (paperless-ngx, immich) embed their own private search internally rather than exposing a general-purpose search backend a customer could point other apps or custom code at. This would be a genuinely new category (search infrastructure) rather than an overlap.
usefulness_rationale: Solr's admin UI is an operations console for managing cores/collections and running test queries, not an end-user application — there's nothing to "use" out of the box beyond an empty engine with no schema, no data, and no built-in ingestion pipeline for a customer's content. Value only materializes once a customer (or their own app) talks to the Solr HTTP API to define a schema and index documents, which is a developer-level task well outside the profile of a typical AF customer clicking through a recipe. Compares unfavorably to the (also-flagged-low-value) Adminer- style "raw infra tool with a mandatory basic-auth gate" pattern, but without even a familiar UI (a DB browser) — Solr's console is Solr-specific and has a steep learning curve.
summary: Apache Solr is an actively-maintained ASF project (latest release 10.0.0, 2026-03-04, ~5 months old, no EOL signal) with an official, regularly rebuilt Docker image (`solr:10.0.0`, single exposed port 8983, no path prefix) that runs fine in standalone mode (no ZooKeeper needed for a single instance) behind Traefik on `<slug>.<base_domain>` — reverse-proxy-compatible. Solr ships with no security.json / auth plugin configured by default, so the admin UI and the full read/write HTTP API (create/delete cores, index and query documents) sit open with no login of its own; that makes it mechanically installable today only by treating the entire app as needing a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate, same pattern as Adminer/Apache Hop. It's a genuinely new category for the catalogue (no existing recipe exposes a general-purpose search engine), but the admin console alone delivers little standalone value to a typical AF customer — it's empty infrastructure requiring developer-level follow-up (schema design, ingestion) to become useful, so `build_with_caveats` rather than a strong recommendation.

name: Apache StreamPark
source_description: Develop and operate Apache Flink and Spark streaming jobs from one console
version_health_notes: 2.1.7 shipped 2025-11-05, roughly 9 months before today (2026-08-05). Recent cadence: 2.1.4 (2024-05-14) -> 2.1.5 (2024-10-18) [~5 months] -> 2.1.6 (2025-07-09) [~9 months] -> 2.1.7 (2025-11-05, patches CVE-2025-54947) [~4 months], i.e. point releases have been slowing, with gaps stretching from ~5 to ~9 months apart rather than a tight cadence. No release in the last 9 months is consistent with that slowing trend but not yet dormant for a top-level Apache project, and the security fix in 2.1.7 shows the PMC is still responsive. The bigger concern is the official Docker Hub image (apache/streampark): the newest pushed tag is "2.1.6" (2025-07-09) with "latest" also pointing at 2.1.6 -- there is no "2.1.7" image tag at all as of today, so the containerized artifact lags the patched source release by one version and still carries the CVE fixed upstream in 2.1.7. Any recipe built today would have to pin to the vulnerable 2.1.6 image or build/publish an unofficial 2.1.7 image ourselves.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches stream-processing job orchestration -- StreamPark is a console for developing, deploying, and monitoring Apache Flink/Spark jobs, a distinct niche from workflow automation (n8n), infra dashboards (Portainer), or observability (Uptime Kuma). It would be a genuine first for that category.
usefulness_rationale: Real gap, but the audience is narrow and the value is mostly theoretical for a single customer VM: StreamPark itself is just a control-plane UI -- to do anything useful a customer must already have (or separately stand up) a Flink and/or Spark cluster for it to submit jobs to, and the local Flink install path even expects the Flink distribution to sit on the same server. That is a lot of surrounding infrastructure a typical AF customer would not have, making this a console with nothing to operate out of the box.
blocking_issues:
StreamPark ships a fixed, hardcoded first-boot login (admin / streampark) with no documented env var, config.yaml key, or CLI flag to set/override it at deploy time -- the customer would have to log in with the well-known default and change the password manually through the UI afterward. Not a hard blocker per SCHEMA.md (gate the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth as the real auth boundary, same pattern as n8n/WUD), but it does mean the app's own login stays a known-default credential until the customer manually rotates it.

Official Docker image is one version behind the patched source release (image pinned at 2.1.6, source patched CVE-2025-54947 in 2.1.7 with no corresponding image tag yet) -- shipping a recipe today means either pinning a vulnerable image or maintaining an unofficial rebuild, neither of which is a stable long-term posture.
summary: Apache StreamPark is an active, credible Apache project and a genuinely unfilled niche in the catalogue (no stream-processing console today), and mechanically it is a single-container, single-HTTP-port app that fits our Traefik-fronted pattern with the app's fixed default login gated behind basic_auth. It is held back from build_now by two real issues: the official Docker image lags the CVE-patched source release by one version, and -- more importantly -- StreamPark alone has no standalone value for a typical AF customer since it only orchestrates Flink/Spark jobs against a cluster the customer must provide separately. Recommend build_with_caveats: revisit once an image tag tracking 2.1.7+ exists, and weigh whether the narrow "already runs Flink/Spark elsewhere" audience justifies a slot in the catalogue.

Home Assistant (recipes/home-assistant, currently disabled) is the closest relative in spirit — both are "connect your own devices" platforms — but Home Assistant targets consumer smart-home devices via integrations, while StreamPipes targets industrial protocols (OPC UA, S7, Modbus) and streaming/analytics pipelines (Kafka, Pulsar, NATS) for a more technical, IIoT-focused audience. n8n is the closest workflow-automation analogue but has no built-in industrial-protocol connectivity or time-series storage. This would be a genuinely new capability class if built.
usefulness_rationale: The customer-facing web UI (pipeline builder, dashboards, adapter configuration) is real and would be reachable through Traefik like any other recipe, so it clears the bar the IoTDB/Pinot/Doris-style "developer infrastructure only" candidates don't. But the target audience — someone connecting OPC UA/S7/Modbus industrial sensors or Kafka/Pulsar streams — is narrow relative to our current catalogue, and the minimum viable deployment is a 6-container stack (backend, ui, extensions-all-iiot, CouchDB, InfluxDB, NATS), heavier than any single-purpose app we host today. A customer who actually has industrial sensor infrastructure to connect is a much smaller slice of the self-hosting market than, say, a photo library (Immich) or a password manager (Vaultwarden) user.
blocking_issues:
StreamPipes ships with a fixed, hardcoded first-boot login (admin@streampipes.apache.org / admin) with no documented docker/env-var hook to set or hash a different password at container start — the credential can only be changed from inside the UI after first login (confirmed against the official docs and installer/compose/docker-compose.yml). Per SCHEMA.md this is not a hard blocker on its own: gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth (as done for n8n/WUD) closes the exposure window before the customer logs in and changes the default password.
The bundled CouchDB (admin/admin) and InfluxDB (admin/sp-admin, plus a fixed admin API token sp-admin) sidecar credentials are also hardcoded in the shipped docker-compose.yml. Both are internal-only (no ports published to the host in the official compose file), so they are not customer-facing secrets and do not block installability, but they would need to be confirmed non-exposed in any recipe network config.
summary: Apache StreamPipes is an active, top-level ASF project with a real web UI and no existing catalogue overlap, but its release cadence has visibly slowed from quarterly (2022) to roughly annual (0.97.0 in Feb 2025, 0.98.0 in Dec 2025). It is mechanically installable today: the single public HTTP surface (the UI, port 8088/80) can be gated behind Traefik basic_auth to cover its fixed, unchangeable-at-boot default login (admin@streampipes.apache.org/admin), the same pattern already used for n8n and WUD. The bigger issue is fit rather than mechanics: the minimum deployment is a 6-container stack (backend, UI, extensions-all-iiot, CouchDB, InfluxDB, NATS) aimed at a narrow, technical audience — people with actual industrial sensors (OPC UA, S7, Modbus) or Kafka/Pulsar streams to connect — which is a much smaller slice of the self-hosting market than our current catalogue. Recommend `build_with_caveats`: worth building only if the catalogue wants to stake out an industrial-IoT niche despite the heavier footprint and narrower audience.

name: Apache Superset
source_description: Apache Superset is a modern data exploration and visualization platform for BI
version_health_notes: 6.1.0 shipped 2026-05-13 (~2.8 months before today, 2026-08-05), the first minor on the 6.x line after 6.0.0 (2025-12-18, a major visual and architectural overhaul). Before that: 5.0.0 (2025-06-23), with patch releases (e.g. 4.1.4, 2025-08-28) filling gaps between minors — a steady ~5-6 month major/minor cadence with patch releases in between, consistent with Pinot/other healthy top-level ASF projects. Top-level ASF project with heavy commercial backing (Preset.io); 6.1.0 alone gathered 1,500+ PRs from 136 contributors including 69 first-timers per Preset's release announcement. No slowdown or EOL signal.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers self-service BI/dashboarding — this would be a new category. Superset lets a customer connect to their own SQL data source(s) and build charts/dashboards via drag-and-drop, plus an ad-hoc SQL Lab query editor and scheduled alerts/reports. The web UI is a single HTTP port (8088 by default), so it's reverse-proxy friendly like most of the catalogue — no raw ports or extra protocols exposed to the customer.
usefulness_rationale: Superset ships with no data of its own — it is only useful to a customer who already has (or is willing to stand up) a separate database to point it at, which narrows the audience versus a self-contained app. The minimum viable stack is also heavier than most single-container recipes: Postgres for Superset's own metadata store, Redis for caching and as the Celery broker, plus web, worker, and worker-beat containers (worker-beat is needed for scheduled alerts/reports, one of the app's headline features). That said, it's a well-known, widely-adopted open-source BI tool, so there's real demand for a self-hosted deployment among customers who already run a database on the same VM or elsewhere.
blocking_issues:
Superset's own admin account is created at first boot by the upstream docker-init flow via `superset fab create-admin`, which takes ADMIN_PASSWORD as plaintext (Flask-AppBuilder hashes it internally with Werkzeug — pbkdf2 or scrypt depending on version, neither of which `generated_from` supports today anyway). There is no config path that accepts a pre-computed hash for this account, so root-password projection — which only ever produces a hash, never the plaintext — cannot supply it. This is a genuine structural blocker, not just an unsupported-algorithm gap: even if `generated_from` grew pbkdf2/scrypt support, the CLI still wants plaintext.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate (root-password projection, argon2 or bcrypt) can front the whole app to stop it sitting open on the internet, but that only gates transport — Superset still shows its own login screen behind the gate, and the customer has no way to know the ADMIN_PASSWORD needed to get past it. Superset's Flask-AppBuilder supports an AUTH_REMOTE_USER mode that trusts a proxy-set username header (which Traefik's basic_auth middleware does forward) to auto-login/auto-provision a user without its own password prompt. That could plausibly close this gap, but it's a nonstandard auth mode not used by any recipe in the current catalogue and would need real end-to-end validation before it can be called "installable today" — flagging it as an open engineering question, not a confirmed workaround.
summary: Apache Superset is an actively maintained, healthy ASF top-level project (latest 6.1.0, 2026-05-13, ~5-6 month major/minor cadence) with strong commercial backing and no EOL signal. It would fill a genuinely new niche in the catalogue — self-service BI/dashboarding — behind a reverse-proxy-friendly single HTTP port, but the minimum viable stack is heavier than most recipes (Postgres + Redis + web + worker + worker-beat) and the app only delivers value once the customer has a separate data source to connect it to. It is not installable today: the upstream admin-account bootstrap requires a plaintext ADMIN_PASSWORD with no hash-accepting alternative, so root-password projection (hash only) cannot supply it, and a Traefik basic_auth gate alone doesn't solve the app's own login screen behind it. A Flask-AppBuilder AUTH_REMOTE_USER trust-the-proxy-header mode might close the gap but is unvalidated and unlike any pattern currently shipped — `build_now` would need either a plaintext-password input channel or a validated AUTH_REMOTE_USER-based recipe design, not just an algorithm addition to `generated_from`.

usefulness_rationale: Apache Tika is a developer-facing REST microservice, not a product with an end-user workflow. AF customers are provisioning self-hosted apps to use directly; a bare text/metadata-extraction API with no UI has very narrow appeal outside customers already running custom integration code against it (and those customers are better served self-hosting it themselves alongside their own app, not via a standalone AF recipe).
summary: Mechanically installable: single container, single HTTP port (9998), no login of its own, so a Traefik basic_auth:true gate (password projected from the customer's root password) covers the only secret it would need — same pattern as adminer/n8n/WUD. Upstream is healthy and actively released. The blocker is fit, not mechanism: Tika has no web UI, its value is purely as a REST API consumed by other software, and it duplicates nothing while adding no direct end-user workflow to the catalogue. The project stopped tagging GitHub Releases after 0.9.64 (2025-07-04) and now versions purely via Docker Hub tags on appflowyinc/appflowy_cloud: 0.17.0 (2026-07-23), 0.17.1 (2026-07-30), 0.17.2 (2026-08-02) — 3 days before today (2026-08-05). No enabled recipe today covers a Notion-alternative workspace.

blocking_issues:
GOTRUE_ADMIN_PASSWORD is consumed by GoTrue as a plaintext value at container startup to create the bootstrap admin account for the AppFlowy admin frontend — GoTrue hashes it internally, it does not accept a pre-hashed value. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, so there is no channel to supply this credential today. name: Aptabase
source_description: Privacy-first SDK analytics for mobile, desktop, and web apps
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (server code; bundled SDKs are MIT)
version_health_notes: The repo has never published a single GitHub Release or version tag in its history — the only self-hosting artifact is `ghcr.io/aptabase/aptabase:main`, a rolling build re-published on every merge to main (last pushed ~6 days before 2026-08-05, i.e. ~2026-07-30). Commit activity is genuinely active (commits as recent as 2026-07-31, including a .NET 10 upgrade), so this is not an abandoned project — but there is no stable version to pin. "release_cadence: sporadic" describes the release process itself (none), not the underlying development pace, which looks healthy.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers app/product analytics. Aptabase targets mobile/desktop/web app event tracking (Firebase Analytics / Google Analytics alternative) rather than website traffic analytics — a distinct niche from a generic website-analytics tool like Ackee (already analyzed, apps-gaps/ackee.yaml, also blocked). It would be a genuinely new category if it shipped.
usefulness_rationale: App-event analytics has a real audience among indie/mobile developers who want to avoid sending usage data to Google/Firebase, and it's a novel category rather than a duplicate. But it's a narrower, more technical audience than n8n/Vaultwarden-style recipes, and the lack of any pinned release (see version_health) makes it a riskier pick to stand a recipe on today regardless of the installability blocker below.
blocking_issues:
Aptabase has no password-based admin login at all — first-run access is passwordless: a user registers with an email address and receives a magic-link JWT to activate the account (server/Controllers, AuthController.HandleMagicLink). There is no ADMIN_PASSWORD-shaped field for `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` to project into, because the app never asks for or verifies a password anywhere in the login flow — this differs from Ackee's case (plaintext-compare password field with no channel) in that here there is no password field to target in the first place.

Aptabase ships with no SMTP configured by default. Without SMTP, the activation magic-link is only ever written to container logs (confirmed via aptabase/self-hosting docs and issue #5/#7 in that repo) — a customer using our install flow has no way to read container logs to retrieve it, and af's install flow has no channel to surface log output as a credential either. Configuring SMTP so the customer receives the link by email would itself require an external SMTP relay/credentials — exactly the class of "external credential the customer must supply" that /compose has no channel for.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (our other supported mechanism) does not solve the underlying problem: it would only protect the login/registration screen from the open internet, it does not give the customer a way to complete Aptabase's own email-based account activation. The blocker is the account-creation flow itself, not lack of a perimeter gate.

Separately, upstream has never cut a tagged release — the only image available is the rolling `ghcr.io/aptabase/aptabase:main` tag, which RFC-002's pinned-tag requirement (no `:latest`-equivalent floating tags) would also reject even if the auth blocker were solved.
summary: Aptabase is a genuinely new category for us (app-event analytics, not website traffic analytics like Ackee) and is under active development, but it fails installability today for a different and more fundamental reason than Ackee: it has no password field at all, only a passwordless email-magic-link registration flow with no SMTP configured out of the box, so a customer has no channel to complete the first-admin-account setup through our install flow. Neither `generated_from` (no password field to target) nor Traefik `basic_auth` (doesn't touch account activation) close this gap. On top of that, upstream has never published a tagged release, only a rolling `main` image — a second, independent blocker against shipping a pinned recipe today. Revisit only if Aptabase adds a conventional password-based admin login or an env-var-settable activation bypass, and separately once it starts cutting real releases.

name: ArangoDB
source_description: Native multi-model database for graphs, documents, and key-value data
upstream_license: Business Source License 1.1 (core source, converts to Apache-2.0 after 4 years) for the OSS code; the shipped Community Edition binaries/Docker image are additionally governed by the separate "ArangoDB Community License" (effective with 3.12, released 2024-Q1), which is not Apache-2.0 despite older versions having used that license.
version_health_notes: 3.12.10 was pushed to Docker Hub about a day before today (2026-08-05); 3.12.9.x patches shipped roughly monthly before that (3.12.9 ~4 months ago, 3.12.8 ~5 months ago, 3.12.7 ~6 months ago, relative to today). Upstream states major releases are supported 18+ months and minor releases 12+ months from GA; 3.12 (GA 2024-03-21) and 3.11 (GA 2023-05-23) are both still in active support. 3.10 and 3.9 have already gone EOL on schedule. Clearly active development, not slowing or dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a standalone database — existing recipes (n8n, paperless-ngx, etc.) run Postgres/MySQL internally as a private backing service, never exposed to the customer. ArangoDB would be the first recipe where the database itself is the product: a single-port (8529) server with its own built-in web UI (query editor, graph visualizer, collection browser) that a customer — typically a developer building on graph/document data — interacts with directly, rather than a generic admin front-end for someone else's database (cf. the separate Adminer gap-analysis).
usefulness_rationale: Real but niche appeal: valuable to developers/teams building graph-native or document-native applications who want a managed instance without provisioning their own server, but it has no broad-consumer use case the way productivity or media recipes do.
blocking_issues:
The Docker image only accepts the root password as plaintext via ARANGO_ROOT_PASSWORD (or a random one via ARANGO_RANDOM_ROOT_PASSWORD) — there is no way to hand it a pre-hashed value, so it cannot receive a customer-chosen password through `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash). Workaround used here: generate ARANGO_ROOT_PASSWORD randomly server-side (a secret the customer never needs to know) and make the real customer-facing auth boundary a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate in front of port 8529, projected from the customer's root password — the same pattern used for Adminer/n8n/WUD.

Licensing: starting with 3.12, ArangoDB's Community Edition ships under a new "ArangoDB Community License" (not the old Apache-2.0) that explicitly disallows use "for your managed service (DBaaS, SaaS)" or "distributing it to your customers along with your software" without a commercial agreement. Offering ArangoDB as an Application Factory recipe — a hosting provider provisioning it per-customer at catalogue scale — reads as exactly the managed-service / distribution use case the license carves out. This needs legal/commercial review with ArangoDB before shipping; it is not resolved by any af-recipes mechanism (cf. the AFFiNE gap-analysis for a similar licensing caveat).
summary: ArangoDB is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8529) Docker Compose app with an active release cadence (3.12.10 shipped ~1 day before today) and no EOL risk. It would be the first standalone database recipe in the catalogue and fills a real gap for developers wanting managed graph/document storage, though it's a technical/niche audience rather than a broad-appeal app. Mechanically it's installable today via the same generate-server-side-secret-plus-mandatory-basic_auth-gate pattern used for Adminer, since the app's own root-password field only accepts plaintext. The bigger open issue is licensing: the Community Edition's post-3.12 terms explicitly restrict managed-service/DBaaS and customer-distribution use without a commercial agreement, which is close to a description of what shipping this as an AF recipe would be — recommend build_with_caveats pending legal sign-off, not build_now.

Actively developed: recent releases add a Graph Analytical View (OLAP acceleration), a built-in MCP server, TimeSeries data-model support, and native geospatial indexing. No signs of maintenance-only mode.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue is a standalone, customer-facing database service — Postgres/similar only appear as internal backing services inside other recipes (n8n, paperless-ngx). ArcadeDB would be the first recipe letting a customer stand up a queryable multi-model DB (graph/document/KV/time-series, SQL + Cypher + Gremlin + MongoDB/Redis wire protocols) with a browser Studio UI, useful for developers prototyping graph or document workloads without provisioning their own DB infra.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiator for a developer-tooling audience, but it's a raw database rather than an end-user app — narrower appeal than the catalogue's typical productivity/monitoring/media tools, and its value is capped by the installability blocker below (no working login channel for the customer's own credential).
secrets_required_at_first_boot: ArcadeDB server root user password (gates Studio UI and the HTTP/binary APIs — this is the app's only login)
blocking_issues:
ArcadeDB's root credential can only be set via arcadedb.server.rootPassword (system property, env var, or a root-password-path file) — all three accept the PLAINTEXT password only. ArcadeDB derives its own PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 hash internally from that plaintext; there is no server option to instead supply a pre-computed hash. generated_from only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password — it can never carry the plaintext value ArcadeDB actually requires. This is the genuine "plaintext required" case the schema calls a hard structural blocker, not a missing-algorithm gap that could be closed by extending generated_from's supported-algorithm list.

Gating the app behind Traefik basic_auth instead doesn't route around the problem: ArcadeDB has its own mandatory login (Studio and every HTTP/binary API call require an ArcadeDB user/password), so a customer who only holds a Traefik basic-auth credential still cannot log in to the app itself. A server-generated random root password (never disclosed to the customer) would work for internal secrets nothing customer-facing reads, but here the credential IS what the customer needs to use the product, so it doesn't fit that "generate and forget" pattern either.
summary: ArcadeDB is an actively maintained (monthly releases, latest 26.8.1 on 2026-08-03), Apache-2.0, multi-model database with a Docker image and an HTTP Studio UI on port 2480 that would add a genuinely new category — standalone databases — to the catalogue with no current overlap. It is blocked from installable_today, however: the app's only login (its root user) can only be provisioned with a plaintext password, and the platform's sole customer-secret channel (generated_from hashing the customer's root password) never carries plaintext. Recommend blocked_on_platform pending a plaintext-password input channel (distinct from the hash-only generated_from mechanism), not not_recommended, since the app itself is healthy and differentiated.

name: Argilla
source_description: Collaborative platform for AI engineers to build high-quality datasets
version_health_notes: v2.8.0 (2025-03-11) is both the latest GitHub release and the last commit on `main` — no commits or releases in ~17 months as of today (2026-08-05). The repo README carries an explicit maintainer notice: "The original authors have moved on to exciting new projects! ... the codebase is mature and stable ... we won't be adding new features going forward, but we're committed to solving bug fixes and publishing patches as needed," and the project is soliciting new maintainers. Not archived and not declared EOL, but self-described maintenance-only with a genuinely dormant release cadence — this is the aggressive-detection case the schema calls out, not a diplomatic "active" reading of a project that happens to be quiet.
differentiation: Argilla is a dataset-annotation / human-in-the-loop labeling tool for building and curating training data (text classification, NER, RAG relevance, preference/RLHF pairs). Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers this — ollama/open-webui are local-LLM chat/inference, paperless-ai/hermes-agent/openclaw are document/agent tooling, none do dataset labeling.
usefulness_rationale: Dataset annotation is a real, distinct niche with no catalogue coverage today, so differentiation is genuine. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because upstream has taken no new features and no commits in ~17 months with an explicit maintainer-succession notice — shipping a recipe on a stagnant project is a weaker bet than the differentiation alone would suggest.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: PASSWORD (owner/admin login for the built-in "argilla" account); API_KEY; POSTGRES_PASSWORD
blocking_issues:
The documented owner-bootstrap path for the v2.x Docker image is the `USERNAME`/`PASSWORD` env-var pair, consumed as plaintext at container startup — argilla-server hashes it internally (bcrypt) but gives the operator no way to supply an already-hashed value through that path. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, so there is no channel to reach this plaintext-only startup argument. Older (v1.x) docs describe a separate `hashed_password` field in a user-migration YAML file consumed by a CLI migration command, which in principle accepts a pre-hashed value and would fit `generated_from: "bcrypt:..."` — but it is undocumented for the current v2.8 owner-bootstrap flow, appears to be a distinct import/migration feature rather than first-boot user creation, and isn't confirmed to work as a first-boot substitute for `PASSWORD` today.

Traefik `basic_auth` does not substitute here: Argilla ships its own login (the "argilla" owner account), so a basic_auth gate would be a second, redundant login surface in front of an app that already has one — not a stand-in for a missing login, per the same reasoning that ruled out basic_auth for AppFlowy's admin frontend.
summary: Argilla fills a genuine catalogue gap (dataset annotation for AI/ML, no overlap with the existing 24 recipes) but is blocked on two fronts: the platform has no channel to supply the plaintext owner PASSWORD its standard Docker bootstrap requires (only a hash via `generated_from`, and basic_auth doesn't stand in for an app that already has its own login), and upstream has been in an explicit maintenance-only mode with no commits or releases for ~17 months. Even if a plaintext-credential channel were added to the platform, the dormant upstream makes this a weak long-term bet; not recommended for now.

name: AstrBot
source_description: AstrBot is an open-source multi-platform AI chatbot framework
version_health_notes: Latest release (v4.27.2) shipped today (2026-08-05); the two releases before it (v4.27.1, v4.27.0) shipped 2026-08-02, and v4.26.8 shipped 2026-07-28 — sub-weekly cadence, no gap over a few days in the last month. 5,000+ commits on the repo, actively maintained by AstrBotDevs. No archival notice, no EOL announcement.
differentiation: AstrBot's niche is IM-platform bot deployment — QQ, WeChat Work, Feishu, DingTalk, WeChat Official Accounts, in addition to Telegram/Discord/Slack — with a plugin ecosystem (1000+ community plugins) and built-in RAG/MCP/knowledge-base features layered on top of any LLM backend. This is a materially different audience than openclaw/hermes-agent (Telegram- first, coding/task-agent framing) and open-webui (single-user local-model chat UI, no IM integration at all).
usefulness_rationale: A real niche (self-hosted multi-platform IM chatbot, strong in the Chinese IM ecosystem) not fully covered by the two existing agent recipes, but it is the third AI-agent-with-messaging recipe in the catalogue and the value is concentrated in a specific audience segment rather than being broadly differentiating for most customers.
blocking_issues:
AstrBot has no environment variable for setting the dashboard admin password at first boot. On first start it auto-generates a random password for the fixed username `astrbot` and prints it only to container stdout logs — there is no channel in the current recipe mechanism to read those logs back to the customer, nor to inject a customer value into that flow.

The dashboard credential CAN be pre-seeded before first boot by writing `data/cmd_config.json` with a `pbkdf2_password` field, but that field is a `pbkdf2_sha256$<iterations>$<hash>` hash — `generated_from` today only supports `argon2`/`bcrypt`. Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md this is not a hard blocker (it's a hash, not a plaintext-password requirement), just a missing algorithm — flagging as `blocked_on_platform` rather than `not_recommended`. A legacy plaintext `password` field also exists in the same config file, but our mechanism only ever has a password *hash* available (`generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`), never the plaintext, so that field is not usable either way.

Full IM-platform functionality (the app's core purpose) needs more than the dashboard's single HTTP port: QQ integration via the NapCat adapter uses a reverse WebSocket port (default 6199) and upstream docs recommend opening the 6180-6200 range plus 11451 on a cloud server. The dashboard itself (port 6185) is a normal single HTTP service and works fine behind Traefik, but bot functionality beyond Telegram/Discord/Slack (which use outbound polling/webhooks, no inbound port needed) would require raw ports outside the Traefik-only model our other recipes use.
summary: AstrBot is an actively developed (sub-weekly releases), AGPL-3.0 licensed multi-platform AI chatbot framework with a real web dashboard and a differentiated niche (Chinese IM platforms, plugin ecosystem, RAG/MCP) versus the catalogue's existing openclaw/hermes-agent agent recipes. It is not installable today: the dashboard's first-boot admin password is randomly generated and only surfaced via container logs, and the one pre-seedable credential path (a `pbkdf2_sha256` hash in `cmd_config.json`) needs `generated_from` to support the `pbkdf2` algorithm, which it does not yet. Revisit once `generated_from` gains `pbkdf2` support; QQ/NapCat-style raw-port integrations would still be out of scope for a Traefik-only recipe but core Telegram/Discord/Slack usage would not need them.

name: Atomic Server
source_description: Realtime open-source headless CMS and graph database for structured content
version_health_notes: Not archived and not EOL — the `develop` branch shows commits as recent as today (2026-08-05), so upstream engineering is still alive. But the formal release cadence has stalled: the last tagged GitHub release is v0.41.0-beta.2 from 2025-08-02 (over a year ago as of today), and the last *stable* (non-beta) tag is v0.40.3 from 2025-07-06 (~13 months ago). More concerning for us specifically: the official Docker Hub image (joepmeneer/atomic-server) has not published a new version-numbered tag since v0.38.0 on 2024-06-12 (~26 months ago) — the maintainers now only keep a floating `latest` tag current (last pushed 2026-06-22) plus a `develop` tag, with no stable pinned tag corresponding to any 2025 release. Pinning to `v0.38.0` would mean shipping a build roughly two stable-release-cycles behind current `develop`; pinning to `latest` would violate RFC-002's no-`:latest` rule and track an unversioned moving target. Pre-1.0 project (upstream itself states breaking changes are expected until 1.0).
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes offer a generic structured-data / graph-database / headless-CMS layer with a browser-based data browser and table editor. The closest conceptual sibling, `anytype-server`, is a personal notes/knowledge sync backend with no web UI of its own and relies on raw TCP sync ports rather than a single HTTP surface — a different shape of product. Atomic Server would be a genuinely new category (developer/structured-content backend) rather than a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct capability (RDF-like linked-data store + CMS + table editor with JS/React/Svelte SDKs), but it targets developers building on top of it rather than an end-user self-hosting for its own sake — a narrower audience than e.g. Vaultwarden or Immich. Pre-1.0 stability caveats and the stale pinned-image situation (see version_health) also temper how confidently we could support it today.
blocking_issues:
Atomic Server has no username/password login of its own — identity is via public/private-key "Agents", not a hash-checkable credential — so there is no admin-login parameter to attach a `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` projection to. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate can still cover the front door (see secrets_expressible_today), but that only stops anonymous access — it does not complete setup.

The actual first-run admin bootstrap (`/setup`) requires a one-time invite token that the app itself generates and prints only to container stdout/logs at boot (confirmed against `atomic-server --initialize` / `ATOMIC_INITIALIZE`, which "recreates the /setup invite... prints it to console"). There is no env var to set this token to a customer- or platform-chosen value, and no current AF mechanism to surface container log output back to the customer. Even with a basic_auth gate in front, the customer has no way to retrieve the invite token needed to actually create the root Agent — this is the reverse of the usual "customer can't supply a secret" problem (here the app emits a secret the customer needs, and there's no channel to deliver it), so it is not something IF-1420 or IF-1312 as currently scoped would fix.

Official Docker image has no stable version-numbered tag newer than v0.38.0 (2024-06-12), roughly 26 months stale relative to `develop` and not matching any 2025 GitHub release — see version_health.notes.
summary: Atomic Server is a legitimately novel addition (structured-data/graph-CMS backend, no overlap with the current 24 recipes) and upstream engineering is still active, but it fails the first-boot secret-channel test for a reason distinct from the usual root-password-projection gap: its own setup flow needs an app-generated invite token surfaced to the customer, and no such log/output channel exists in the platform today. Combined with a stale pinned-Docker-tag situation (no version-numbered image in ~26 months) and pre-1.0 stability caveats, this should stay `blocked_on_platform` until either a log/first-boot-output surfacing mechanism exists or upstream adds a settable-invite env var — building a recipe now would mean shipping a stale image behind a gate that can't actually complete setup.

source_description: Open-source identity provider focused on flexibility and versatility
version_health_notes: Latest stable 2026.5.6 shipped 2026-07-22, about two weeks before today (2026-08-05). The project runs parallel supported branches (2026.5.x and 2026.2.x both received patches within the last two months) and already has 2026.8.0 release candidates in progress. Repo is not archived, commit and PR activity is continuous — this is a well-funded, fast-moving project, not a maintenance-mode one.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes provides identity/SSO functionality — Authentik is an IdP (SAML/OAuth2/OIDC/LDAP provider, forward-auth proxy-provider) that other self-hosted apps and even other AF recipes could federate against. Closest conceptual neighbor is Vaultwarden (also a "security" recipe) but that's a password vault for end users, not an SSO/identity broker for other services — genuinely distinct use case with real demand from customers running multiple self-hosted apps who want one login.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted SSO/IdP is one of the most commonly requested categories in the self-hosting community (competes with Authelia, Keycloak, Zitadel). A customer running several AF recipes side by side has an obvious use for a central identity provider, so this would meaningfully round out the catalogue rather than duplicate it.
blocking_issues:
Authentik provisions its initial `akadmin` superuser via two mutually-exclusive env vars: `AUTHENTIK_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD` (plaintext, explicitly discouraged by upstream) or `AUTHENTIK_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD_HASH` (a pre-hashed value, generated with `docker compose run --rm server hash_password '<pw>'`). The hash upstream produces is a Django-native hash — `pbkdf2_sha256` by default — not `argon2` or `bcrypt`, the only two algorithms `generated_from` currently supports. Per SCHEMA.md this is not a hard structural blocker (only a plaintext-only requirement would be) — it's a genuine gap in the supported-algorithm list. Flag as `blocked_on_platform` with `pbkdf2_sha256` named as the algo needed, rather than `not_recommended`.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the whole app is not a good substitute here: Authentik's own web UI is the product (it needs to stay reachable for end users completing SSO flows against other apps, not just the admin), so gating the entire origin behind a second, unrelated basic-auth layer would break the app's actual purpose rather than just protecting an admin panel the way it does for e.g. Adminer or WUD.
summary: Authentik is a mature, extremely actively maintained identity provider that would be a genuinely high-value, non-duplicate addition to the catalogue — nothing else we ship covers SSO/IdP, and demand for self-hosted identity brokering is real. It is mechanically a clean Postgres-backed multi-service stack (server + worker + postgresql, no Redis dependency in current releases) and is fully reverse-proxy compatible on a single public port. It fails installability today purely on the admin-bootstrap secret: the only supported hash format for `AUTHENTIK_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD_HASH` is Django's `pbkdf2_sha256`, which `generated_from` does not yet support (only `argon2`/`bcrypt`). Revisit as `build_now` as soon as `generated_from` gains `pbkdf2_sha256` support; until then this is `blocked_on_platform`, not a fundamental fit problem.

name: Authorizer
source_description: Open-source self-hosted authentication server with social login, MFA, and RBAC
version_health_notes: Last tagged *stable* (non-RC) release is 2.3.0, dated 2026-06-16 — about seven weeks before today (2026-08-05). Since then the project has been shipping near-daily release candidates toward 2.4.0 (rc.0 on 2026-07-11 through rc.14 on 2026-08-03, two days before today), so it is not stalled — it's mid-cycle on the next stable cut. Commit activity and the published ROADMAP_V2.md (phases through Q3 2027: rate limiting/bot detection now, M2M/SAML/SCIM/OIDC-provider later, then passkeys/DPoP) both indicate a well-funded, actively developed project, not maintenance-only. Note this is a significant v1→v2 rewrite (config moved from env vars to CLI flags only) — treat v1-era documentation found elsewhere online as stale.
differentiation: Authorizer is a developer-facing "auth backend" — an Auth0/Firebase-Auth alternative meant to be embedded into a customer's own application via OAuth2/OIDC client registration and SDKs, not a gateway that adds SSO in front of existing web apps. Authentik (also flagged in this catalogue, apps-gaps/authentik.yaml) is the closer fit for "single sign-on across my other self-hosted apps"; Authorizer only makes sense for a customer who is themselves building or running a custom application and needs an auth/RBAC provider for it. Real but narrower audience than Authentik within our current customer base.
usefulness_rationale: Useful for a developer-persona customer building their own app on top of the AF, but most of our current 24 recipes are turnkey end-user apps, not app-building platforms — so this serves a smaller slice of the customer base than a general SSO/identity-broker recipe would, and largely overlaps in intent (self-hosted identity) with the already-analyzed Authentik gap.
blocking_issues:
Authorizer v2 is configured entirely via CLI flags (no persisted admin-set password flow); `--admin-secret` is consumed by the process as a **plaintext** value used directly for admin-panel login — there is no hashed-secret input mode. Per SCHEMA.md, `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel to seed this admin credential from the customer's own password. This is the genuine plaintext-only case SCHEMA.md calls a structural blocker, not just a missing-algorithm gap like Authentik's.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the whole origin is not a substitute either: Authorizer's `/authorize`, `/oauth/token`, and hosted login-page endpoints must stay reachable for end users of whatever application the customer builds against it, so gating the entire app behind an unrelated second basic-auth layer would break its actual purpose (same reasoning as the Authentik analysis).
summary: Authorizer is an actively developed, Apache-2.0 self-hosted auth server, but it targets a different job than "add login to my existing self-hosted apps" — it's a backend for customers building their own applications, and it overlaps conceptually with the already-flagged Authentik gap for the identity/SSO niche. Mechanically it is a clean single-container app (quay.io/authorizer/authorizer, port 8080, reverse-proxy compatible), but it fails installability today for a harder reason than Authentik: its admin bootstrap secret (`--admin-secret`) is consumed as plaintext with no hashed-input mode, which SCHEMA.md treats as a genuine structural blocker rather than a missing-algorithm gap. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` and, given the medium (not high) usefulness versus Authentik's high, a lower re-evaluation priority even once platform constraints loosen.

name: Autobase
source_description: Open-source self-hosted Database-as-a-Service platform for PostgreSQL automation
upstream_license: MIT (core Ansible collection); console container images are tagged "_ee" (Enterprise Edition) even in the documented default deployment — see notes below
version_health_notes: Formerly vitabaks/autobase (né vitabaks/postgresql_cluster), now under the autobase-tech org. Releases have shipped roughly monthly for the last several months (2.6.0 2026-03-01, 2.7.0 2026-04-04, 2.8.0 2026-05-28, 2.9.0 2026-07-05, 2.10.0 2026-08-03 — 2 days before this analysis date of 2026-08-05). Clearly active, well-funded development, not remotely dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does Postgres cluster orchestration (automated failover via Patroni, backup/restore, blue-green major-version upgrades, connection pooling via PgBouncer/HAProxy). n8n and paperless-ngx consume Postgres as an internal dependency, not as a product. So on paper this fills a real gap — but see usefulness below for why that gap doesn't translate to our deployment model.
usefulness_rationale: Autobase's actual value is fleet orchestration: its Console SSHes/Ansible's into a set of target hosts (bare metal, VMs, or cloud instances) to deploy and manage Postgres clusters running on those separate machines. An AF recipe installs into exactly one customer container/VM with no other hosts attached to it. Deploying "Autobase" as a recipe would hand the customer a management console with zero targets to manage and no channel to supply the SSH keys or cloud-provider credentials needed to add any — the product's core loop doesn't map onto a single-instance recipe at all, independent of any auth/secrets question.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: AUTH_TOKEN (shared bearer secret gating the console-api/console-ui; the API healthcheck sends it verbatim as 'Authorization: Bearer <AUTH_TOKEN>', i.e. compared as plaintext, not hashed); SSH credentials / cloud-provider API keys for the target hosts the console would provision and manage (the app's core purpose)
blocking_issues:
Core function requires SSH credentials or cloud API keys for target hosts to manage — no input channel for either exists today.
Even solving the login gate does not help: a single-container recipe deployment gives the customer an orchestration console with no fleet to manage (see usefulness_rationale) — a structural mismatch with the recipe model, not just a secrets gap.
AUTH_TOKEN is checked as a literal bearer-token value against the API, not as a hash — generated_from only ever gives us a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so this field cannot be satisfied that way even if it were otherwise worth wiring up.
The documented default docker-compose (autobase.tech/platform.yml and platform.ssl.yml) pins autobase/console_api_ee and autobase/console_ui_ee — Enterprise Edition images — for what's presented as the free/Community path. Community-tier entitlements and limits are not documented publicly; licensing exposure for a customer expecting an open recipe is unclear.
Stack includes docker.io/bhavikagarwal2001/dbdesk-studio, an unofficial single-maintainer Docker Hub image (not published by autobase-tech) bundled as the SQL editor component — unreviewed supply-chain dependency.
console-api mounts /var/run/docker.sock — same privileged-access class as our existing Portainer recipe, which is currently shipped with enabled: false in this catalogue; that precedent suggests we already treat docker.sock-mounted infra-management tools cautiously.
summary: Autobase is a genuinely active, well-maintained open-source Postgres cluster-automation platform with no direct equivalent in our 24-recipe catalogue on differentiation grounds alone. But its value proposition — orchestrating Postgres clusters across a fleet of separate target hosts via SSH/Ansible and docker.sock — is fundamentally about managing infrastructure outside the single container the recipe would run in, so shipping it as an AF recipe would hand customers a console with nothing to manage and no channel to give it credentials for anything. Combine that with an unresolved Enterprise-Edition image question in the "default" compose file, an unofficial third-party image in the stack, and a docker.sock dependency we already treat cautiously (disabled Portainer recipe) — this is a not_recommended, not merely blocked_on_platform, since the mismatch persists even after IF-1420/IF-1312 land.

version_health_notes: As of today, 2026-08-05, it has been just under 12 months (~11 months, 28 days) since the last tagged release (v0.15.0, 2025-08-08), and the `automatischio/automatisch` Docker Hub image (`latest` and `0.15.0` tags) was last pushed the same day — no image update since. Classified `active` rather than `maintenance-only`/`archived` because feature commits are still landing, but the release/packaging pipeline has visibly slowed and this is worth re-checking before shipping a recipe.
differentiation: Same pitch and same job as n8n, already in the catalogue: both are self-hosted, open-source, no-code/low-code "Zapier alternative" workflow automation tools, both need Postgres (Automatisch also needs Redis for its job queue), both expose one HTTP port (3000) that sits fine behind Traefik. No concrete capability here that n8n doesn't already cover for a customer who just wants "workflow automation."
usefulness_rationale: Duplicates a job the catalogue already does well with n8n, and does so with a smaller integration set and a stalled release/image cadence. Would mostly serve a customer who specifically wants Automatisch by name (e.g. migrating an existing flow set) rather than filling a gap.
summary: Automatisch is mechanically installable today: it has no env-var-driven admin account, only a fixed, documented default login (`user@automatisch.io` / `sample`) seeded at first boot with no environment variable to change it, so per the SCHEMA.md precedent for a hardcoded/unchangeable default credential, a Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the whole app is the correct and sufficient fix — it becomes the real auth boundary, and the app's own fixed weak password behind it is no longer customer-facing risk. All internal secrets (Postgres password, encryption key, webhook secret, app secret) are patternless values the app never surfaces to the customer, so they're trivially server-generated. The blocker to prioritizing this isn't installability, it's fit: it duplicates n8n's job in the catalogue with a smaller integration set, and its release/image pipeline has been stalled for nearly a year even though `main` is still getting commits. Recommend `build_with_caveats` — buildable now if a customer specifically wants Automatisch, but not a gap-filling priority over the existing n8n recipe.
