What is independently corroborated: the GitHub org (casibase/casibase) is real, uses Apache-2.0, ships an official `casbin/casibase` Docker image, is not archived, and shows a live blog with posts as recent as 2026-01-02 plus multiple real release tags in the `v1.7xx` series — all consistent with an actively-developed project. A human reviewer should confirm the exact current tag directly from https://github.com/casibase/casibase/releases before any recipe work starts, since this analysis could not reliably pin it.
differentiation: Casibase positions itself as an enterprise "AI Cloud OS" — RAG-backed knowledge base, multi-model chat, MCP/A2A agent management, and admin UI with SSO/user management — on top of the same basic pitch as Open WebUI (self-hosted chat UI over multiple LLM providers). The knowledge-base/RAG and MCP-management angle is a real feature difference, but to a customer picking one self-hosted "chat with my LLM" app, it lands in the same slot Open WebUI already fills.
usefulness_rationale: Real, actively-developed, reasonably well-known project with a legitimate differentiated feature set (RAG knowledge base, MCP management) beyond a plain chat UI. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because it overlaps functionally with an existing recipe (open-webui) and, per installability below, cannot actually be onboarded under the current mechanism.
blocking_issues:
Casibase has no local admin username/password of its own — all login is delegated to Casdoor (casbin's separate SSO/IAM project) via OAuth. `conf/app.conf` requires a Casdoor endpoint URL plus a `clientId`/`clientSecret` pair for an OAuth application that must already exist on a Casdoor instance (either the publicly hosted `door.casdoor.com` or a self-hosted one) before Casibase can start serving logins at all. This is exactly the "OAuth app registration / third-party account linking" case `SCHEMA.md` calls out as having no input channel today — there is no root-password hash to project (`generated_from`) because Casibase has no password field, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate doesn't help because the missing piece is a functional dependency (Casibase won't run without valid Casdoor client credentials), not just an exposed-without-auth surface.

Self-hosting Casdoor alongside Casibase (to keep the OAuth dependency in-house) would add a second admin-configured application — registering the Casibase OAuth client inside Casdoor is itself a manual setup step with no automatable input channel via `/compose` today, and would need its own recipe/gap-analysis first.
summary: Casibase is a real, actively-maintained, Apache-2.0 AI knowledge-base and chat platform, but it overlaps functionally with the existing open-webui recipe and, more importantly, has a hard architectural blocker: it delegates all authentication to Casdoor via OAuth and has no local login of its own, so first boot requires a pre-existing Casdoor OAuth client ID/secret that the current `/compose` mechanism has no channel to supply. This is not fixable with `generated_from` or Traefik `basic_auth` — both assume the gated app can run and be configured without an external OAuth registration, which Casibase cannot. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`; revisit only if a Casdoor co-deployment/registration story (or a future af-api input channel for OAuth-style secrets) lands. Note also that automated research tooling in this session produced unreliable, self-contradictory version/date claims for this repo, so `version_health` above is deliberately conservative — a human should re-verify the current release tag directly from GitHub before further work.

Two-HTTP-port split (frontend 4018 / API 4019) behind one customer subdomain requires path-based Traefik routing not used by any existing recipe (see differentiation_caveat above) — not a hard blocker, but untested against the current recipe template and should be proven out before committing to build_now.
summary: Chartbrew is an actively maintained (release 5 days ago as of 2026-08-05, ~monthly cadence) self-hosted BI/dashboard builder with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue and broad appeal — genuinely useful to any customer who wants to visualize their own database/API data without hiring for it, sweetened by an AI chart-building assistant. Repo is not formally archived (archived: false on the GitHub API) and the issue tracker still gets occasional maintainer interaction (issue #125 "Add deployment badge for Hostinger" was updated 2025-11-20), but there has been zero code activity for over two years. Effectively a single-maintainer, feature-frozen project — treat as dormant rather than actively maintained, even though it isn't officially EOL'd.
differentiation: Chatpad is a static React/Nginx front end that talks directly to the customer's own OpenAI (or Azure OpenAI) account — no bundled inference, no server-side database; every conversation is stored client-side in the visitor's browser (IndexedDB). This is a much lighter deployment than open-webui (which bundles Ollama for fully local/private inference), but it depends entirely on the customer bringing an external OpenAI API key and trusting OpenAI with their prompts. It does not offer the "no cloud, no data leaves your server" story that open-webui already covers in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: A thin wrapper around a third-party paid API, with the core value proposition (privacy) already better served in-catalogue by open-webui's fully local model. Upstream has been feature-frozen for two-plus years, so shipping it now means shipping an unmaintained dependency for marginal differentiation.
blocking_issues:
The app itself has no login and requires no secret at container boot — it serves static Nginx content, and the customer's OpenAI API key is entered later, client-side, inside the running web UI (stored in browser IndexedDB, never passed through /compose or any env var). This isn't a structural blocker for /compose, but it does mean the app's actual usefulness depends entirely on a credential our mechanism has no visibility into or responsibility for.

Because the app has no built-in auth, leaving it ungated on the public internet lets any visitor open the chat UI and use their own (or, if left logged in, the deploying customer's) OpenAI key through it — mitigated by requiring the Traefik basic_auth gate, listed above.
summary: Chatpad AI is mechanically installable today — it needs only a domain and a Traefik basic_auth gate (it has no login of its own), both expressible via existing mechanisms, and the customer's OpenAI API key is supplied entirely inside the browser after deploy rather than through /compose. But it's a thin, single-maintainer client for a paid third-party API that has seen no code activity in over two years, and open-webui already covers the "private self-hosted chat UI" niche in the catalogue with a stronger privacy story (bundled local inference vs. Chatpad's dependency on OpenAI's cloud). Recommend build_with_caveats: technically buildable, but low differentiation and an unmaintained upstream make it a weak addition relative to the effort.

name: Checkmk
source_description: Infrastructure and application monitoring with auto-discovery and alerting
upstream_license: GPL-2.0 (Community/Raw edition; Enterprise/Cloud editions are commercial)
version_health_notes: 2.5.0 major released 2026-04-28, with patch releases landing roughly every 1-2 weeks since (currently 2.5.0p10, pushed ~8 days before today, 2026-08-05). The 2.3.0 and 2.4.0 lines are still in active/passive maintenance windows through 2026-2027, and the vendor publishes an explicit multi-year support calendar per major version. Repo is not archived, commit and werk (changelog) activity is continuous. Note the Docker Hub repo was renamed from `checkmk/check-mk-raw` to `checkmk/check-mk-community` when the "Raw" edition was rebranded "Community"; the old repo is legacy/frozen, the new one is current.
differentiation: Checkmk is a full infrastructure/host/application monitoring platform: it installs lightweight agents on target hosts (or polls via SNMP/APIs), auto-discovers services, and centralizes alerting across a fleet. This is materially different from Uptime Kuma, our only existing monitoring recipe, which is a self-contained external uptime/ping checker with no agent-based host metrics or auto-discovery. Checkmk would fill a distinct "monitor your own servers and their internals" niche versus Uptime Kuma's "is this URL/service reachable" niche.
usefulness_rationale: Server/infra monitoring with auto-discovery is a broadly useful, well-known category (Nagios/Zabbix/Checkmk-class tooling) for any customer running more than a couple of hosts, and Checkmk is a mature, actively developed, widely-adopted product in that space — a strong candidate on merit alone, independent of the installability problem below.
blocking_issues:
The container bootstraps its one site via `omd create --admin-password "$CMK_PASSWORD"` at first start, which requires the literal plaintext password for the `cmkadmin` account — there is no documented option to instead pass a pre-hashed credential (unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN, which is designed to store a hash). `generated_from` only ever produces a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so it cannot populate CMK_PASSWORD.

Unlike Alerta (which exposes AUTH_REQUIRED=False to disable its own login entirely, letting a Traefik basic_auth gate become the sole auth boundary), Checkmk has no documented way to disable or bypass its own cmkadmin login. Gating the reverse-proxy hop with basic_auth would not help: the customer would still hit Checkmk's built-in login screen behind it and have no way to know the cmkadmin password, since no channel exists today to hand them a customer-chosen or root-derived plaintext value.

Secondary, non-blocking note: full host monitoring also relies on the Agent Receiver on port 8000 (raw TCP, agent registration/push), separate from the web UI on port 5000. The web UI alone is single- HTTP-port and reverse-proxy-compatible, but exposing agent check-in for remote hosts would need a second, non-HTTP public port that our current Traefik-fronted recipes don't otherwise use.
summary: Checkmk is an actively maintained (2.5.0p10, patched roughly biweekly, July 2026), high-value infrastructure-monitoring platform with no overlap in our current 24-recipe catalogue — Uptime Kuma only covers external uptime pings, not agent-based host/service monitoring with auto-discovery. It is blocked from shipping as a recipe today purely on the installability mechanism: its admin account (cmkadmin) is created from a plaintext CMK_PASSWORD env var with no pre-hashed-credential path and no way to disable its own login the way Alerta does, so neither `generated_from` (hash-only) nor a Traefik `basic_auth` gate can supply a usable credential. This needs a genuine plaintext root-password-projection channel (or an equivalent) added to the platform before it's buildable — recommend `blocked_on_platform` rather than `not_recommended`, since the app itself is a strong catalogue candidate once that channel exists.

name: Checkrr
source_description: Media library scanner that auto-replaces corrupt files via Sonarr and Radarr
version_health_notes: v3.6.1 shipped 2026-02-18, about 5.5 months before today (2026-08-05) — no tagged release since. Release cadence between tags is uneven: 3.5.4 (2025-03-20) to 3.6.0 (2026-02-04) was a ~10.5-month gap, then 3.6.0 and 3.6.1 landed two weeks apart. Despite the tag gap, upstream commit activity is current — the default branch has commits as recently as 2026-07-11 (dependency bumps plus a real bugfix), and the repo is not archived. Single-maintainer project (aetaric) but actively triaged; treating the tag cadence alone as dormant would be misleading given the live commit history.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches media-library integrity checking. Checkrr scans a media directory (ffprobe/magic number/mimetype/hash checks against a local bbolt file) and, when it finds a corrupt file, can ask Sonarr/Radarr/Lidarr to delete and re-request it — but that "replace" behavior (the entire feature Hostinger's description highlights) is entirely dependent on Sonarr/Radarr, neither of which exists as an AF recipe today. Same structural gap already flagged for [[bazarr]]: it's a companion tool to the *arr stack, not a standalone app.
usefulness_rationale: Without Sonarr/Radarr present, checkrr degrades to a read-only "scan a folder and log which files are corrupt" utility — mechanically fine but a thin value proposition on its own, and there is no existing AF media volume/library for it to point at in the first place (no Plex/Jellyfin/ Sonarr/Radarr recipe populates one). Lower priority than Bazarr: Bazarr at least has a companion recipe precedent in this same gap-analysis pass, and Checkrr's headline feature is unusable without infrastructure AF doesn't offer.
blocking_issues:
Checkrr's web UI (port 8585) is a status/progress dashboard only — it has no login of its own, so it needs a Traefik basic_auth gate like Adminer/WUD. That part is installable today.

Unlike Bazarr, checkrr has no post-boot UI for entering Sonarr/Radarr API keys — they are static fields in checkrr.yaml, which must be fully written before container start. There is no channel for a customer to supply an external arr API key at first boot, so the "auto-replace via Sonarr/Radarr" feature named in Hostinger's own description cannot be wired up under the current mechanism even in principle (this is on top of Sonarr/Radarr not existing as AF recipes to point at).

Checkrr also expects the operator to pre-create empty checkrr.db and checkrr.yaml files as bind-mounted files (not directories) before first start, and to mount an existing media library into the container — no such shared media volume exists elsewhere in the catalogue for it to reuse.
summary: Checkrr (aetaric/checkrr, MIT, single official image, port 8585) is mechanically simple to containerize — one service, no database beyond a local bbolt file, reverse-proxy compatible — and the basic_auth gate for its UI is expressible today, so installable_today is true in the narrow mechanical sense. But its only differentiating feature, auto-replacing corrupt media via Sonarr/Radarr, has no path to working: those apps don't exist in the catalogue, and even if they did, checkrr has no channel to receive their API keys (config-file-only, no setup UI, unlike Bazarr). Shipping it today would hand customers a corrupt-file logger with no library to scan and no arr stack to talk to. Recommend not_recommended until/unless Sonarr and Radarr are added as recipes first, at which point this should be revisited alongside Bazarr as part of the same "media automation stack" decision.

The `1.9.2` image predates the 2.x rewrite the Hostinger description is actually referring to ("production AI agent framework... plugins, and function calling"), and upstream's own README calls 2.x "unstable alpha... not recommended for production use yet" — so even setting the image problem aside, the current source is self-described as pre-production.

name: Chibisafe
source_description: Self-hosted file vault for uploading and sharing files with shareable links
upstream_docker_image: chibisafe/chibisafe-server (backend) + chibisafe/chibisafe (frontend), both official on Docker Hub
version_health_notes: v6.5.5 shipped 2026-07-05, about 1 month before this analysis (2026-08-05). Prior releases (v6.5.4 2026-03-25, v6.5.3 2026-03-16, v6.5.0 2026-02-01, v6.4.2-6.4.5 clustered Jan-May) show a steady patch/minor cadence over the last year, multiple contributors, and an actively maintained GitHub Packages registry (dev tag rebuilt within the last 2 months). No archival notice, no EOL announcement.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes cover ad-hoc file upload + shareable-link distribution (ShareX/iOS-shortcut style). Immich is photo/video-specific with AI search; Syncthing is peer device sync, not link sharing; Opengist is text/code snippets only. Chibisafe fills a distinct "quick dropbox-style link sharing" niche.
usefulness_rationale: Clear, narrow use case (screenshot/file sharing tools, ShareX, invite-only file vaults) that a subset of self-hosters actively want, but it's a smaller audience than general-purpose apps already in the catalogue and has no differentiators (e.g. AI, sync) beyond "upload, get link."
blocking_issues:
Chibisafe creates a hardcoded first-run admin account (admin/admin) and only exposes an `ADMIN_PASSWORD` env var that sets that password as plaintext — not a hash. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash of ROOT_PASSWORD, so it cannot be projected into `ADMIN_PASSWORD` directly. Workaround: leave the default admin/admin credential as-is internally and put the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate (bcrypt hash of ROOT_PASSWORD), same pattern used for other apps with a fixed/unprojectable admin credential. This is not a hard blocker, just a required design choice.

Stack is 3 containers (chibisafe frontend, chibisafe-server backend, bundled Caddy reverse proxy) that upstream wires together with its own Caddyfile on one published port (24424->80). A recipe would drop the bundled Caddy and let our own Traefik front the frontend/backend pair directly — mechanically straightforward but needs the internal routing (frontend -> backend at :8000) reproduced without the upstream Caddyfile.
summary: Chibisafe is an actively maintained (latest v6.5.5, 2026-07-05), MIT-licensed file-vault/link-sharing app with no overlap in our current 24-recipe catalogue. It's mechanically installable today only via a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of its hardcoded admin/admin login, since its ADMIN_PASSWORD env var takes a plaintext value our `generated_from` hash mechanism can't supply. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth adding for the differentiated use case, but the 3-container upstream compose needs reworking to drop its bundled Caddy in favor of our own Traefik, and the admin login must ship behind a mandatory basic_auth gate rather than a customer-controlled credential.

differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches HR/employee onboarding — n8n covers generic workflow automation but has no onboarding-specific data model (to-do sequences, preboarding pages, knowledge base courses, hardware/access provisioning tracking). The Slack bot channel Hostinger's description highlights is a genuine differentiator versus a plain web app.

Medium rather than high because it's a narrow-audience B2B HR tool compared to broadly-applicable infra/productivity apps already in the catalogue, and its headline Slack integration needs an external Slack app registration this platform has no channel to configure (see below).

No first-boot channel to create the initial admin account. Self-service signup is explicitly disabled in the codebase (`UserAdapter.is_open_for_signup()` returns `False` in `back/users/adapter.py`), there is no `DJANGO_SUPERUSER_*`-style env var or admin-credential env var anywhere in `back/back/settings.py`, and no management command or data migration seeds a default user (the one user fixture in `back/fixtures/all.json` is dev/test-only — `FIXTURE_DIRS` is a Django test setting, not something loaded on `migrate`). The upstream Docker guide's own account-creation step is "from the logs, or specified yourself" with no elaboration, and the only concrete path anyone has documented is an interactive `manage.py createsuperuser` run inside the running container — not compatible with an unattended `/compose` bootstrap that must finish the container's first boot with no customer/operator shell session. This isn't a fixed/hardcoded credential we could gate with `basic_auth` and call solved (per SCHEMA.md's guidance on that case) — there is no account at all until someone runs an interactive command, so even a `basic_auth` front door would still leave the customer locked out of the app itself.

Slack bot integration (Hostinger's named headline feature) requires `SLACK_APP_TOKEN` and `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` from a customer-created Slack app — an external credential/OAuth-style registration with no input channel in the current mechanism. The web portal works standalone without Slack, so this doesn't block installing the app, but it does mean the differentiating feature named in the source description can't be delivered turnkey.
summary: ChiefOnboarding (chiefonboarding/chiefonboarding, AGPL-3.0, single official image, Postgres-backed Django app, port 8000) is mechanically simple to containerize and fills a genuine gap — no HR/onboarding tool exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue — but it fails the first-boot test on its own terms, not just on the Slack side-feature: there is no env var, management command, or data-seed path to create the initial admin account non-interactively, and self-service signup is hard-disabled in code. Until the platform has a way to run a one-off provisioning command (or the upstream project adds an env-var-driven superuser bootstrap), this can't ship as a recipe. Revisit if IF-1420/1312-style mechanisms grow an "run this command once at first boot" primitive, or if upstream adds `DJANGO_SUPERUSER_*`-style env vars.

name: Chroma
source_description: Open-source embedding database for AI applications and semantic search
version_health_notes: Very actively maintained as of 2026-08-05: tagged releases roughly weekly through the spring (1.5.5 on 2026-03-10, 1.5.6/1.5.7 in early April, 1.5.8 on 2026-04-16, 1.5.9 on 2026-05-05), plus a continuously published dev-build train on Docker Hub (1.5.10.dev24x tags landing within the last few days of research). No gap of concern; this is a fast-moving, well-funded project (Chroma Inc.), not a maintenance-only or dormant one.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a vector/embedding database. Chroma is a backend service, not an end-user app: it gives customers already running Ollama, Open WebUI, n8n, or Hermes Agent from this same catalogue a place to store embeddings for RAG/semantic-search workflows instead of standing up their own Postgres+pgvector or a hosted vector DB elsewhere. It's a genuinely new, complementary category rather than a variant of an existing recipe.

blocking_issues:
Chroma ships with no authentication enabled by default (the server boots fully open) and its own auth options (token auth via CHROMA_SERVER_AUTHN_PROVIDER/CHROMA_SERVER_AUTHN_CREDENTIALS, or basic auth via an htpasswd file) are configured through a static env var / mounted file, not a login screen — there is no "admin login parameter" to project `generated_from` into. A Traefik HTTP Basic Auth gate is usable from those clients (both SDKs support setting custom request headers/auth), but it is a rougher fit than for a human-driven web UI like Adminer's — every downstream integration (e.g. an n8n workflow node) needs to be configured to send the Basic Auth header on top of Chroma's own client config.
summary: Chroma is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8000) embedding/vector database with an official, actively maintained Docker image and no overlap in the current catalogue — it fills a real gap for customers building RAG pipelines on top of Ollama/Open WebUI/n8n. It has no built-in login of its own, so a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate (credential projected from the customer's root password) is the correct and available mechanism to avoid shipping it open to the internet, making it mechanically installable today. The caveat is fit, not mechanism: it's a headless, API-only service that's rarely used stand-alone, so it should be positioned/documented as an AI-stack building block rather than a general-purpose app, and any downstream integration needs to be told to send the basic-auth header.

name: CitrineOS

latest_version: v1.9.1 (latest tagged stable GitHub Release); v2.0.0-beta1 is a newer pre-release tag

The newest tag overall, v2.0.0-beta1 (2025-08-05), is a year-old pre-release that never graduated to stable. Despite this, the underlying repo is very actively developed — commits and merged PRs land on `main` almost daily (verified through 2026-08-03/08-05), and published Docker images (ghcr.io/citrineos/citrineos-server, -operator-ui, -ocpi) are only ever tagged `:latest`, tracking `main` directly rather than a versioned release train. So: active upstream, but no stable versioned artifact to pin a recipe to — a distinct problem from the project being dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches EV charging station management or OCPP. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue (charge-point operators / EV network operators), not a duplicate of any existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Real, growing niche demand (EU EV-charging operators needing OCPP 2.0.1 CSMS software) and no open-source competitor recipe exists in-catalogue, but the audience is narrow compared to general-purpose recipes, and the deployment is unusually heavy/operationally involved for that audience (see installability below).
blocking_issues:
No pinned, stable Docker image tag exists for any CitrineOS component (server, operator-ui, ocpi) — ghcr.io only publishes `:latest`, which tracks `main` directly. There is nothing to pin a recipe to that wouldn't silently drift underneath every install.
The stack's core function — charge points connecting over OCPP — depends on raw WebSocket/WSS listeners on multiple non-standard ports (8081-8083 plain, 8443-8444 TLS, plus 8080 HTTP API), not a single HTTP(S) port. Our Traefik-per-domain-on-443 model has no mechanism today to provision and expose a per-customer set of raw ports for charge-point traffic, so the product's primary purpose would not work out of the box behind our standard ingress.
The full stack is 6 containers (OCPP server, Operator UI, Postgres+PostGIS, RabbitMQ, MinIO/S3, Hasura GraphQL engine), plus an optional OCPI server profile — significantly heavier than any current recipe and a large surface to keep patched given the lack of pinned releases above.
The Operator UI has no login of its own: it bakes HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET directly into the client bundle (VITE_HASURA_ADMIN_SECRET) and auto-attaches it to every GraphQL call, i.e. anyone who loads the page gets full admin/DB access unless it sits behind an additional auth layer. Upstream's own docs recommend an external OAuth/IdP provider instead of the admin-secret approach in production — that OAuth registration has no input channel in our platform today. A Traefik basic_auth gate in front covers the immediate exposure risk (listed above) but is a workaround for a design upstream itself calls unsuitable for production, not upstream's intended auth model.
summary: CitrineOS would fill a genuinely new niche (EV charging / OCPP 2.0.1 CSMS) with no overlap in the current catalogue, and upstream is clearly an active project (Apache-2.0, LF Energy-hosted, daily commits). But it is not installable under today's mechanism: there is no pinned/stable image to build a recipe against, and its core value — charge points connecting over raw OCPP WebSocket ports — does not fit our single-domain-on-443 Traefik model the way our other recipes do. The admin-UI secret exposure is workaroundable via basic_auth, but the image-pinning and raw-port problems are structural. Revisit if upstream starts cutting real version tags and if the platform gains a way to provision extra raw ports per customer; until then this is blocked_on_platform, not a fit to build now.

name: CiviCRM

version_health_notes: Monthly-ish stable releases throughout 2026 (6.10 in Jan through 6.16.2 on 2026-07-27, about 9 days before this analysis) plus a separate security-release track (civicrm.org/security/releases). No sign of slowdown, archival, or announced EOL.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover CRM/constituent-management workflows (donor tracking, membership, event registration, case management for nonprofits/associations) — closest neighbors are dev-tool or infra recipes (Gitea, n8n) with no domain overlap. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists among nonprofits/associations as a free alternative to commercial CRMs, but it's a niche vertical compared to broadly-applicable infra tools already in the catalogue, and the standalone edition is comparatively young next to the CMS-integrated (Drupal/WordPress/Joomla) deployments most existing CiviCRM installs actually use.
blocking_issues:
The official civicrm/civicrm image does not self-install on container boot. Per the upstream civicrm-docker README, first-time setup requires running a separate `civicrm-docker-install` script via `docker compose exec` after the containers are already up, passing CIVICRM_ADMIN_USER and CIVICRM_ADMIN_PASS as env vars to that exec call. Our recipe mechanism only supports environment values injected at container start via docker-compose.yaml/.env — there is no post-boot exec step in /compose today, so the install can't complete without one.

Even setting aside the exec-based install, CIVICRM_ADMIN_PASS has no expressible mechanism: it's a plaintext admin password the app expects as a literal string at install time, not a hash, so generated_from:"argon2:ROOT_PASSWORD" (which only ever yields a hash) cannot supply it, and it isn't a login the customer authenticates with after the fact in a way that basic_auth could substitute for.
summary: CiviCRM is an active, well-maintained project (monthly releases, no EOL signs) that would fill a genuinely uncovered CRM/nonprofit-management niche in the catalogue, with a usable web UI and a single reverse-proxy-friendly HTTP port. It is not installable today, however: the official Docker image requires a post-boot `docker compose exec` install step that our /compose mechanism has no channel for, and that step needs a plaintext admin password our platform cannot project. Revisit once the recipe mechanism supports a post-boot init/exec hook; the root-password-hash and basic-auth mechanisms alone don't close the gap.

ClassicPress inherits WordPress's classic install flow: on first visit, wp-admin/install.php presents a browser form where a human picks the site title, admin username, admin password, and admin email — there is no env var on the official classicpress/classicpress image (built on the standard WORDPRESS_DB_HOST/USER/PASSWORD/NAME config pattern from the official WordPress image) that pre-provisions this account. This is not a structural blocker the way an external API key would be — the admin credential can be entirely server-generated and never customer-supplied, same pattern as Gitea's GITEA_ADMIN_PASSWORD in this catalogue — but the base image does not bundle wp-cli or any other non-interactive installer, so install.sh would need to either vendor wp-cli into the container or script a direct POST to install.php with the generated credentials. That's real recipe-engineering work beyond typical env-var wiring, not a missing input channel, so it doesn't block installable_today.
 | CONFIRMED (Task 4 sanity-check audit, 2026-08-24): the admin credential's install mechanism hashes plaintext internally (or, for alist/nextcloud, the post-boot CLI/occ command does) - generated_from can only emit an already-hashed value, so the customer's real root password will never match. Needs either a platform plaintext-passthrough mechanism or a per-recipe redesign (drop the auto-config, expose the app's own setup wizard behind basic_auth) before this is genuinely installable.
summary: ClassicPress is an actively maintained (2.7.0, 2026-03-25; official Docker image rebuilt as recently as 2026-06-19), GPL-2.0 WordPress fork that fills a real gap — the catalogue has no general-purpose CMS/website builder today. It's a single public HTTP port behind Traefik plus a MariaDB sidecar, structurally close to the Gitea recipe (web app + DB + a server-generated admin credential shown to the customer post-provision, never customer-supplied). The one caveat is that automating the admin account past WordPress's browser-based install wizard needs custom scripting (wp-cli or a scripted install.php POST) since the base image doesn't provide that out of the box — an engineering task, not a platform blocker. Recommend build_now.

The initial admin/org-owner account is created through the app's own web signup form (Better Auth) the first time a browser hits the domain, the same no-channel-needed pattern already used for Immich and Apache Answer; checking the actual Better Auth config in source (not just the self-host doc's general Email section, which reads as more mandatory than it is) confirms `requireEmailVerification` is not enabled, so that signup/login completes with a session with no SMTP configured — email is only needed afterward for verification, invites, and password-reset, none of which upstream gates login on. Reverse-proxy fit is single-domain-friendly in production deployments (per upstream's Coolify guide, the dashboard server-side-proxies all API calls, so only the dashboard's HTTP port needs to be public — the api and jobs containers, and MinIO, stay internal), which matches our one-HTTP-router-per-recipe constraint. name: ClickHouse
source_description: Columnar OLAP database for real-time analytics with millisecond query latency
version_health_notes: CalVer (Year.Month.Patch.Build) with a new minor cut roughly every month: 26.5 (2026-05-21), 26.6 (2026-06-25), 26.7 (2026-07-22) — 2 weeks before this 2026-08-05 analysis. Two LTS trains per year (typically March and August); current LTS is 25.8 (released 2025-08-29, supported through 2026-08-29) with 26.3 LTS (2026-03-26) already in parallel support. The last three minor releases are patched for bugs/security. No archival, no slowdown, no EOL signal — this is one of the more aggressively active upstreams reviewed in this batch.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a customer-facing database engine — existing recipes use Postgres/Redis/etc. only as internal sidecars for an app (n8n, paperless-ngx, CKAN-in-progress). ClickHouse would be the first recipe where the database itself is the product: a columnar OLAP store for real-time analytics/dashboards/event pipelines, aimed at developers rather than end users.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand from developers who want a fast, self-hosted analytics backend (event tracking, log/metrics analytics, BI query layer) without standing up a managed ClickHouse Cloud instance. Narrower audience than our general productivity/self-hosting recipes (needs SQL/analytics know-how, not a point-and-click app), but distinctive and non-duplicative if it ships.
blocking_issues:
ClickHouse's own auth is not usable through our mechanism: the official docker-entrypoint.sh only accepts the default user's password as a plaintext env var (CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD or CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD_FILE), which it writes verbatim into the user config for ClickHouse to hash internally at parse time. There is no pre-hashed-password input (no CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD_SHA256_HEX-style var supported by the entrypoint), so `generated_from` — which only ever carries a hash, never plaintext — cannot project the customer's root password into it. This is treated the same way as CKAN's fixed sysadmin default (IF-1312 precedent): rather than a hard blocker, the workaround is to leave ClickHouse's own auth unconfigured/default and put the real auth boundary at Traefik `basic_auth` in front of the whole app, the same pattern used for Adminer.

ClickHouse also exposes a native TCP client protocol on port 9000 (used by clickhouse-client and many BI/driver integrations), which is not HTTP and so cannot be gated by Traefik basic_auth. A recipe would need to simply not publish port 9000 (HTTP-only on 8123 behind Traefik), which is workable but limits the app to HTTP-interface clients (fine for curl/Grafana/DBeaver-over-HTTP, not for clickhouse-client's default native-protocol mode).
summary: ClickHouse is an aggressively active project (monthly CalVer releases, dual LTS trains, no EOL signal) and would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue — the first recipe where a database, not an app on top of one, is the product. It's mechanically installable today only with a workaround: ClickHouse's own user auth can't accept a projected root- password hash (the docker entrypoint only takes a plaintext password), so the recipe would leave the built-in `default` user unconfigured and rely entirely on a Traefik `basic_auth` gate over the HTTP interface (port 8123) for the real auth boundary — the same precedent already accepted for CKAN's fixed sysadmin default and for Adminer. The native TCP protocol port (9000) would simply not be published, limiting customers to HTTP-interface access. Given the narrower, developer-only audience and these two caveats, this is a build-with-caveats candidate rather than a clean build-now.

CloudBeaver is heavier (Java server, ~400MB image, persistent workspace) and more actively maintained than Adminer, with a richer UI (multi-connection management, SQL editor, ER diagrams) versus Adminer's single-page, per-visit connection form. The two are direct substitutes for the same customer need rather than complementary.
usefulness_rationale: Same audience as Adminer — developers/power users who self-host a database and want a management UI without installing DBeaver locally — so it doesn't expand the catalogue's addressable use case, just offers a heavier alternative. Worth having only if the product wants two DB-admin options at different weight/feature tiers, not as a first pick.
summary: CloudBeaver is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8978) Java web app with a persistent workspace volume, Apache-2.0 licensed and under active, fast-paced development (26.1.4 shipped 2 days before this analysis). It duplicates the same generic-DB-admin-UI niche already covered by the apps-gaps/adminer.yaml candidate, just with a heavier footprint and richer feature set. Unlike Adminer, CloudBeaver has its own persistent admin account, but it is not un-provisionable: CloudBeaver officially supports presetting the admin username/password via {WORKSPACE}/conf/initial-data.conf (adminName/adminPassword keys), applied at first server initialization in place of the interactive setup wizard (https://dbeaver.com/docs/cloudbeaver/Initial-data-configuration/). That file only accepts plaintext, not a hash, so generated_from can't project the customer's root password into it directly, but a server-generated random value written to initial-data.conf at container start works the same way CKAN's CKAN_SYSADMIN_NAME/PASSWORD do, with the whole app additionally gated behind Traefik basic_auth (root-password-derived) so the admin account is never customer-facing either way. Installable today with no blocking issues; given the overlap with Adminer and the added weight, this is a build-with-caveats on differentiation grounds, not on any provisioning gap.

name: Cloudflared
source_description: Cloudflare Tunnel daemon for secure remote access without opening ports
version_health_notes: Cloudflare cuts a new dated release roughly monthly (2026.2.0, 2026.3.0, 2026.5.0/2026.5.1, 2026.6.0/2026.6.1, 2026.7.3). Latest release is 13 days before today (2026-08-05). This is an actively maintained, first-party Cloudflare product with no signs of slowing.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes does this: cloudflared makes only outbound connections from the customer's server to Cloudflare's edge and exposes no inbound port at all — it's the inverse of our Traefik/domain model, not a variant of it. wg-easy is the closest thing we have to "secure remote access," but wg-easy is a self-contained VPN server we fully control, whereas cloudflared's routing, DNS, and access policy all live in the customer's own Cloudflare account and dashboard.
usefulness_rationale: The pitch (expose a local service without opening firewall ports) is genuinely useful, but it only works if the customer already has a domain on Cloudflare's nameservers and creates a tunnel + token themselves in their Cloudflare Zero Trust dashboard first. That's a heavier prerequisite than any app we currently ship, and the app itself has no UI, no login, and nothing for our own domain/Traefik machinery to front.
blocking_issues:
cloudflared needs a TUNNEL_TOKEN generated by Cloudflare when the customer creates a tunnel in their own Cloudflare Zero Trust dashboard. This is an external, per-customer, arbitrary credential with no projection mechanism — it is not a hash of the root password and there is no login screen to gate with Traefik basic_auth.
The app has no web UI and, in the standard remotely-managed-tunnel setup, publishes no inbound port at all — there is nothing for our Traefik/domain layer to front, so even the mechanically simplest secret channel (basic_auth gate on the app's own port) does not apply here.
Name is unambiguous: 'cloudflared' refers only to Cloudflare's own tunnel-connector binary/image (cloudflare/cloudflared); no other project shares the name.
summary: Cloudflared is an actively maintained, monthly-release first-party Cloudflare product, so there's no version-health concern. But it cannot ship as a recipe under the current mechanism: first boot requires a TUNNEL_TOKEN the customer generates in their own Cloudflare account, which is exactly the kind of external, arbitrary credential neither generated_from root-password projection nor Traefik basic_auth can carry. It also has no web UI and, in its normal configuration, no inbound port to put behind our domain/Traefik model at all, making it a poor structural fit even setting the secret problem aside. Blocked on a real external-token input channel, not just IF-1420/IF-1312.

It has no admin-credential env var of its own; first boot lands on an open `/install` wizard where the customer sets their own admin login, so that surface must be gated with a Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password, the same reasoning already applied to the Baikal and BookStack gap-analysis candidates (apps-gaps/baikal.yaml, apps-gaps/bookstack.yaml — neither is an existing recipe yet) — that clears `installable_today` with zero hard blockers. name: CockroachDB
source_description: Distributed SQL database built for resilience and horizontal scale
upstream_license: Business Source License 1.1 (converts to Apache-2.0 3 years after each version's release date) — CockroachDB Labs' "CockroachDB Core" build, per version-specific expiry dates.
version_health_notes: v26.2.5 pushed to Docker Hub ~6 days before this 2026-08-05 analysis; sibling patches v25.4.14, v26.1.8, v25.2.22 all shipped in the same 7-8 day window, and v24.3.35 ~8 days before — a broad, actively maintained patch train across every supported minor line, not a single stale release. Cockroach Labs runs quarterly major releases (vYY.R, alternating "Regular"/GA and "Innovation" cadence) with Regular releases getting 12 months maintenance + 6 months critical-only support, and some Regular releases promoted to Long-Term-Support (12+12 months) after a stability track record. Current latest is v26.2 (GA 2026-04-27); v25.4 (GA 2025-11-03) is still in maintenance support through ~2026-11. No slowdown, no archival, no EOL signal.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a standalone, customer-facing database — n8n, paperless-ngx, gitea, immich, etc. each run Postgres/MySQL/SQLite internally as a private backing service the customer never touches directly. CockroachDB is the same new category already flagged for ClickHouse/ArangoDB/Apache CouchDB: the database itself is the product. Its specific angle is Postgres-wire-protocol compatibility (any psql/JDBC/pg driver client can talk to it) plus built-in horizontal scale-out and multi-region resilience, which none of the other database gap-analyses offer — though on a single AF instance the multi-node/multi-region story is moot, so the practical pitch narrows to "a Postgres-compatible SQL engine with a bundled observability console."
usefulness_rationale: Real appeal to developers who want a managed, Postgres-wire-compatible SQL backend without provisioning Postgres themselves, but the value proposition (horizontal scale, multi-region survivability) is largely unrealized in a single-container AF deployment, and — per the installability section below — the primary interface (the SQL wire port) can't be safely exposed under the current recipe mechanism, which caps this well below ClickHouse/ArangoDB's already-medium rating.
blocking_issues:
CockroachDB's own auth is plaintext-only end to end: the Docker entrypoint's COCKROACH_USER/COCKROACH_PASSWORD variables (only honored on `start-single-node` with no pre-existing data directory) write a cleartext password, and even a manual `ALTER USER ... WITH PASSWORD` only accepts cleartext — CockroachDB hashes it itself at write time. Client-supplied pre-hashed passwords (SCRAM-SHA-256 or otherwise) are a long-standing open upstream request (cockroachdb/ cockroach#50757, cockroachdb/docs#12635), not shipped in any released version. `generated_from` only ever carries a hash, so there is no channel to project the customer's root password into CockroachDB's own login — the same fundamental mismatch already documented for ClickHouse, and the workaround is the same: leave CockroachDB's own SQL/DB-Console auth on a randomly-generated, server-side-only credential (or run `--insecure`, which has no auth at all) and put the real customer-facing auth boundary at Traefik `basic_auth` in front of the DB Console (HTTP, port 8080).

Unlike the DB Console, the SQL wire port (26257, Postgres protocol) is not HTTP and so cannot be gated by Traefik `basic_auth` — the same structural limitation already flagged for ClickHouse's native port 9000. A recipe would have to simply not publish 26257 (DB-Console-only exposure), but that guts the actual reason a customer wants CockroachDB: connecting a psql/JDBC/application client over the wire protocol. Exposing 26257 either unauthenticated (`--insecure`) or with a credential no customer input channel can set would leave root-level SQL access open on the internet, which is not an acceptable default. This is a materially worse version of ClickHouse's caveat, since ClickHouse still offers a usable HTTP query interface (8123) behind the same gate — CockroachDB's DB Console is observability/admin-only, not a query interface a normal client uses.
summary: CockroachDB (v26.2.5, actively patched across multiple supported minor lines, no EOL signal) would be the catalogue's first standalone SQL database sold as the product rather than an app's internal backing store — a real but niche developer audience. It clears the same plaintext-only-auth hurdle as ClickHouse via a Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the DB Console (port 8080), so it is mechanically installable today. The bigger problem is that the DB Console isn't the point of CockroachDB — the Postgres-wire SQL port (26257) is, and that port can't be gated by HTTP basic auth or given a customer-set credential under the current mechanism, so a compliant recipe can only safely expose an admin console, not the SQL interface customers actually want. Recommend `build_with_caveats`: technically shippable, but the caveat here removes most of the app's practical value rather than being a minor workaround.

name: Coder
source_description: Open-source platform for provisioning self-hosted cloud development environments
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (core), with a paid Enterprise license layer for SSO/audit-log/high-availability features
version_health_notes: Latest mainline release shipped one day before this analysis (2026-08-04, analysis date 2026-08-05). Release history shows a weekly cadence across both mainline (2.34.x/2.35.x/2.36.x) and stable-patch branches (v2.36.0, v2.35.3, v2.34.7, v2.35.2, v2.34.6, v2.35.1, v2.35.0 all within the two weeks before this analysis). Clearly active, well-funded, no signs of slowdown.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue provisions cloud development environments. Portainer and Guacamole are the nearest neighbors structurally, but neither does workspace/IDE provisioning: Portainer manages arbitrary Docker resources (and, like Coder, needs docker.sock mounted to do so), while Guacamole just proxies existing remote desktops over RDP/VNC/SSH with no privileged host access at all. Coder's actual product is spinning up per-developer dev containers/VMs on demand from Terraform-defined templates, with browser-based VS Code / SSH access — a genuinely distinct capability for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for self-hosted cloud dev environments, and unlike Autobase's fleet-orchestration model, Coder's default "Docker template" workspace provisioning targets the *same host* the Coder server runs on — so the product's core loop does map onto a single-instance recipe. The ceiling is lower than build_now-grade apps, though: it needs the Docker socket mounted into the app container (see below), which is a materially higher blast-radius ask than most of the catalogue.
summary: Coder is active, well-maintained, reverse-proxy-friendly on its single HTTP port, and fills a real gap (no dev-environment provisioning tool in the catalogue today). First-admin creation is a self-service web form (email/password chosen by whoever gets there first) with no environment-variable or hash-based seeding path — the official `coder server create-admin-user` CLI only accepts a plaintext password, which `generated_from` (hash-only) cannot supply. That makes it structurally identical to n8n/Open WebUI-style apps: gate the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` so only the customer reaches the setup page and claims the first-admin slot themselves, with no secret ever passed through our side. The remaining caveat is that Coder's workspace provisioning needs `/var/run/docker.sock` mounted into its own container to spin up dev-environment containers on the host — the same privileged-access class as our Portainer recipe, which this catalogue currently ships with `enabled: false`. Mechanically installable today, but the docker.sock exposure plus the "first visitor becomes admin" race (mitigated only by the basic_auth gate, not eliminated) argues for build_with_caveats rather than an unqualified build_now — a reviewer should weigh the docker.sock precedent explicitly before enabling.

blocking_issues: No current officially-published, pinned Docker image exists: quay.io/codimd/server has not been updated since 2020-11-12 (frozen at v1.6.0), while upstream GitHub has since moved to 2.6.1 (2024-10-01). summary: CodiMD is a Postgres-backed, single-HTTP-port markdown editor that would otherwise be Traefik-compatible, and its default open self-registration (no built-in root/admin concept) is a solved pattern — the same Traefik basic_auth gate used for An Otter Wiki and n8n would keep the signup form private to the customer until they create their own account, with the Postgres password generated server-side. The blocker is upstream health, not the auth mechanism: the official container image has been frozen since November 2020 while the project's own GitHub releases have moved on to 2.6.1, and there is no current image to pin. Combined with a sporadic release cadence and the fact that the actively-maintained continuation of this codebase is a separate fork (HedgeDoc, healthy releases through 2026), CodiMD as specifically requested is not a good candidate today. Recommend not_recommended for this slug; if live collaborative markdown editing is wanted in the catalogue, a future gap analysis of HedgeDoc under its own slug would be the better path.

Cadence is uneven — a ~5-month gap between v0.17.0 and v0.18.0 and an earlier ~4-month gap between v0.14.x and v0.15.0 — but the project keeps shipping (18.3k GitHub stars, active issue/PR triage, most recent commit activity recent), so it reads as active rather than slowing or dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers general-purpose file format conversion. Immich, Paperless-ngx, and Gitea handle domain-specific file storage/processing but don't offer an ad-hoc "convert any file to any format" utility. ConvertX wraps FFmpeg, ImageMagick, LibreOffice, Pandoc, and other converters (~1000+ format pairs across images, video, audio, documents, e-books, and 3D assets) behind one web UI, which is a genuinely new capability for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Broad, non-technical appeal — file conversion is a common everyday need (documents, images, media) and this is the only recipe candidate that covers it, unlike niche developer tools or apps that duplicate existing catalogue entries.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the upstream README and docker-compose example: ConvertX has no admin-username/admin-password environment variable at all. Accounts are created through an in-app registration form, gated only by the `ACCOUNT_REGISTRATION` env var (default `false`, which would also block the customer's own first signup unless set to `true`). With registration enabled, the first visitor to reach the public URL becomes the account holder — there is no `type: password` field on an admin login to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var. This is the same shape of problem documented in apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml and apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would close the "random internet stranger races to register first" version of this problem, but per the 2FAuth/Activepieces precedent, today's basic_auth mechanism has no channel to also hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential for the in-app signup form beyond the single root-password projection already used for the gate itself — so it does not fully resolve the underlying provisioning gap.
summary: ConvertX is an active, well-starred, single-container app (no external database required) that would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue — none of the current 24 recipes offer general file-format conversion. It fails the installability test for the same structural reason as 2FAuth and Activepieces: the app provisions its one account via an open self-registration form with no env-var hook for a preset admin login, so neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely hand the customer their own exclusive first-run credential. Revisit once upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow, or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond the single root-password projection.

name: Convex
source_description: Open-source reactive database platform for modern application development
latest_version: Precompiled 2026-08-05-38abb46 (rolling date+commit-hash tags, no semver releases)
version_health_notes: Releases are rolling precompiled builds tagged by date + short commit hash rather than semver — multiple tags cut on 2026-08-04 and 2026-08-05 alone (the day before/of this analysis), several hours apart. 7,500+ commits on main, 147 open issues, 50 open PRs, 12.3k GitHub stars; maintainers describe internal changes as synced to the public repo within days. No archival, deprecation, or EOL signal anywhere upstream — this is a venture-backed, actively-developed product at the core of Convex's commercial offering.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a backend-as-a-service / reactive database platform. Closest structural neighbors are n8n and paperless-ngx (Postgres-backed multi-container app), but those are finished end-user applications; Convex is an application *backend* with no end-user-facing product of its own — customers write and deploy their own TypeScript functions against it from a separate frontend (e.g. a Vercel-hosted app), using the Convex CLI. It's a genuinely distinct capability (live-query reactive database + serverless functions + file storage), but it targets developers building on top of the instance rather than someone using the instance directly, which is a different usage pattern than every other recipe in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for self-hosted Firebase/Supabase-style backends, and Convex is a well-funded, popular entrant in that space. The ceiling is capped by the fact that the value only materializes once a customer writes and deploys their own application code against this instance via the Convex CLI — it's a developer building-block, not a ready-to-use product, closer to a hosted database (which we don't otherwise offer standalone) than to any existing recipe.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: convex_admin_key (`convex-self-hosted|<hash>`) — required by the customer's own machine to run `npx convex deploy`/`convex dev` against this instance, and to authenticate in the dashboard UI; without it the instance is unusable by its owner; INSTANCE_SECRET; basic_auth_password
blocking_issues:
The customer-critical secret is the Convex admin key, not INSTANCE_SECRET. The admin key is not an env var at all — it is computed at runtime by running `./generate_admin_key.sh` inside the already-running backend container (a deterministic function of INSTANCE_SECRET + INSTANCE_NAME), and printed to stdout in the format `convex-self-hosted|<hash>`. It is not a login-form field on the app (so `generated_from` on an app parameter doesn't apply — there is no admin username/password screen to project a hash into), and it must reach the customer verbatim to be useful (so `traefik_basic_auth` and `server_generated_no_customer_input` don't apply either — this is a customer-facing plaintext value the customer needs on their own machine, not something gate-worthy or gate-satisfied).

No channel exists today to surface a value computed post-boot by install.sh (as opposed to a metadata-declared `auto_generate` parameter set at compose time) back to the customer. Even if install.sh ran `docker compose exec backend ./generate_admin_key.sh` automatically during provisioning and captured its output, there is no post-install "here is your credential" delivery surface in the current recipe/API mechanism to hand that string to the customer — this is a distinct gap from the three documented mechanisms, not a variant of any of them.

The dashboard itself (port 6791) has no server-side login wall — it loads for anyone who reaches it and simply prompts for the admin key client-side before it can do anything. That means it should sit behind a Traefik `basic_auth` gate purely as a network-exposure precaution (same as n8n/Open WebUI), but that gate is orthogonal to — and does not solve — the missing admin-key-delivery problem above.
summary: Convex is active, well-funded, and fills a real gap (no backend-as-a- service / reactive-database recipe exists today), but it doesn't fit the "self-contained end-user app" shape of the rest of the catalogue — the product only becomes useful once the customer deploys their own code against it via the Convex CLI, using an admin key that self-hosted Convex computes at container runtime rather than accepting or emitting through any env var. That admin key is customer-facing and mandatory from the very first use, and there is no existing mechanism (generated_from, traefik_basic_auth, or server-generated-no-customer- input) that can deliver it, nor any general post-install credential-reveal channel to fall back on. This is blocked on a platform gap distinct from IF-1420/IF-1312 — a way to compute a value after boot and hand it to the customer — not just on those two tickets landing.

differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover IRC or persistent-connection chat bouncing. openclaw, hermes-agent, and open-webui are AI-chat interfaces to LLMs, not IRC/human chat clients, so there's no functional overlap. blocking_issues:
Convos has no admin-login parameter of its own to project a root-password hash into: account creation happens through a self-service web signup form, and the app used to gate that signup behind a CONVOS_INVITE_CODE env var. The current Dockerfile no longer sets CONVOS_INVITE_CODE at all, meaning a fresh instance now defaults to open self-registration — whoever reaches the URL first can sign up and become the org owner. Left un-gated, this is a race an unrelated internet visitor could win before the customer does. No pinned stable Docker tag exists to build a recipe against today (see version_health) — only the rolling ':alpha' build. A recipe pinned to ':alpha' would silently pick up new (potentially breaking) builds on every redeploy, which conflicts with the pin-a-stable-tag expectation for new recipes.
summary: Convos is mechanically installable today — a single-container, single HTTP-port (3000) app with no raw IRC ports exposed inbound (it makes outbound IRC connections as a client/bouncer), and its lack of built-in admin auth can be closed with a standard Traefik basic_auth gate using root-password projection, the same pattern used for adminer/n8n/WUD. However it's a weak candidate to actually build: it fills a real gap (no IRC/chat recipe exists) but for a narrow, technical audience, and upstream has no pinned stable release to build against (last tag v8.07 from 2023-10-30, a stalled v9.0-rc1 pre-release since 2025-07-14, only a rolling ":alpha" image recommended today). Recommend build_with_caveats: revisit once upstream cuts a real v9 stable tag, and treat the basic_auth gate as mandatory given the app's own open-registration default.

name: COPS
source_description: Lightweight PHP OPDS and HTML server that exposes a Calibre ebook library to mobile readers and browsers
version_health_notes: The original upstream, seblucas/cops, is effectively dead — last tagged release 1.1.3 on 2019-06-24, over 7 years before today (2026-08-05), with no signs of maintenance. However, the project was forked and is now actively maintained as mikespub-org/seblucas-cops, which is the codebase LinuxServer.io's image actually tracks. That fork released 4.5.2 six weeks before today (2026-06-23), with prior releases at roughly 1-3 month intervals through 2026 (4.3.1 on 2026-03-03, 4.3.3 on 2026-05-15, 4.3.5 on 2026-06-07, 4.5.1 and 4.5.2 both on 2026-06-23). That is a healthy, active cadence. See the ambiguous-name note in blocking_issues below.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue serves a Calibre ebook library. COPS is deliberately minimal by design (a stateless PHP front-end that reads an existing Calibre metadata.db and library folder read-only, generating OPDS/HTML browsing and downloads) rather than a full library manager — it has no upload UI, no metadata editor, no format conversion, and expects the library to already exist and be managed elsewhere (e.g. desktop Calibre, or synced in). This is a near-duplicate of the `apps-gaps/calibre-web.yaml` candidate analyzed separately (also not yet a recipe): both read a Calibre library and serve an OPDS feed plus a browser UI, but Calibre-Web is the fuller "manage and read" experience (in-browser reader, upload, Kobo/Kindle sync, per-user accounts) while COPS is a much lighter "browse and download/OPDS-only" server with no editing or upload capability at all. If both were ever built, they would compete for the same customer need and shipping both would be redundant.
usefulness_rationale: Serving an existing Calibre library over OPDS for e-reader apps is a real, recognizable self-hosting use case, but COPS's minimalism cuts both ways: it's a smaller/simpler footprint than Calibre-Web, but it also can't do anything useful without a library the customer already has and must get onto the volume some other way (no upload flow), which raises first-use friction for anyone starting from empty. Usefulness is capped at medium and is really a choice between this and Calibre-Web rather than an addition alongside it.
blocking_issues:
Name ambiguity: "COPS" here refers to Calibre OPDS (and HTML) PHP Server (seblucas/cops, now maintained as mikespub-org/seblucas-cops and packaged by LinuxServer.io as linuxserver/cops), which matches Hostinger's source_description exactly. No other unrelated project shares the "COPS" name in this space, so this identification is not in doubt — noted here only because the upstream repo itself moved from seblucas/cops to mikespub-org/seblucas-cops mid-life, which could otherwise read as two different apps.

COPS has no runtime-configurable admin account of its own: any authentication is static htaccess/htpasswd-style config baked into config/local.php at build/deploy time, not something exposed via an environment variable af-api could populate at first boot. This is the same "app has no first-class login channel" shape as Adminer and Calibre-Web, not a harder blocker — it is solved by gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth rather than app-level auth.
summary: COPS is a single-container, single-HTTP-port PHP app (LinuxServer.io's lscr.io/linuxserver/cops image, pin to tag 4.5.2) with two bind mounts — /config for app config and /books for the Calibre library folder containing metadata.db — structurally closest to recipes/uptime-kuma or recipes/vaultwarden (single container, no external DB dependency). It needs no external API keys or OAuth to boot, and its lack of a built-in customer-settable admin login is handled the same way as Calibre-Web and Adminer: a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate derived from the customer's root password via `generated_from`. The real caveat isn't installability but redundancy: this is functionally the same "serve my Calibre library" job as the separately-analyzed Calibre-Web candidate, just with a lighter, read-only, no-upload feature set. Upstream health is fine once you track the actively-maintained mikespub-org fork rather than the long-dead original seblucas/cops repo. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically installable today, but only worth building if the fuller Calibre-Web is not built first (or vice versa) — building both would just split the same demand.

name: Copyparty
source_description: File server with WebDAV, SFTP, resumable uploads, and a built-in media library
version_health_notes: Latest tag v1.20.20 ("more wopi") landed 2026-08-03, two days before this analysis. Prior releases v1.20.19 (2026-07-27), v1.20.18 (2026-07-09) and v1.20.17 (2026-07-06) show a sub-monthly cadence, including two security-driven patches (GHSA-phv8-wgjp-g4p9 FTP path-traversal, GHSA-x5pq-m9p8-f4vx dirkey/filekey leak) fixed within days of disclosure. Single maintainer (9001) but very active commit history (4700+ commits). No archival notice, no EOL signal.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is a general-purpose browsable file server. Syncthing is device-to-device sync, not a shared upload/download hub with a browser UI; Immich and Paperless-ngx are domain-specific (photos, documents). Copyparty fills a distinct "personal cloud drive / drop server" niche: drag-drop uploads with resume, in-browser media playback/thumbnails, and WebDAV mounting from any OS, all from a single lightweight container.
usefulness_rationale: Clear, common self-hoster use case (ad-hoc file sharing, WebDAV drive, LAN media browser) with low resource needs and a single official image, but it's a narrower audience than general productivity/AI tools already in the catalogue, and FTP/SFTP/SMB — part of its headline pitch — aren't usable behind our Traefik-only exposure model.
blocking_issues:
Copyparty ships with no accounts configured by default (anonymous read-write to the served folder), so a login gate is required at first boot, not optional hardening.

Copyparty's own account system is not usable as the login gate today: its "ah-alg argon2" password hashing salts every hash with a server-local, auto-generated salt value ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME), so a standard argon2/bcrypt hash computed elsewhere (as generated_from would produce) will not verify against it — there is no plaintext channel to feed copyparty's own hasher. Gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth instead (rather than trying to project into copyparty's accounts.txt) sidesteps this and is fully expressible today.

WebDAV, SFTP, FTP/FTPs, TFTP and SMB — the multi-protocol pitch this app is chosen for — all need their own raw TCP ports exposed directly, which our recipes don't currently open (Traefik-only HTTP ingress). Only the HTTP/WebDAV-over-HTTP path and the web UI would work through the reverse proxy; SFTP and the other protocols would need additional port exposure this catalogue's recipes don't do today. Not a hard blocker (the web UI + WebDAV-over-HTTP alone is a usable recipe) but a real scope reduction from the Hostinger description.
summary: Copyparty is an active, single-maintainer project (releases roughly monthly, security patches within days) with an official Docker image and no overlap in our current catalogue. It can ship as a recipe today by gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth rather than trying to wire a customer credential into copyparty's own salted account system, which has no external input channel. The caveat: only the web UI and WebDAV-over-HTTP would work behind our Traefik-only exposure — the SFTP/FTP/SMB protocols central to Hostinger's description would need raw port exposure this catalogue doesn't support today, so a recipe would ship a reduced-scope version of the app.

name: Crafty Controller
source_description: Web-based control panel for managing multiple Minecraft Java and Bedrock servers
version_health_notes: Latest tag v4.10.8 landed 2026-07-29, about one week before this analysis (2026-08-05). Recent tag history (v4.10.4 2026-04-20, v4.10.5 and v4.10.6 both 2026-06-15, v4.10.7 2026-06-16, v4.10.8 2026-07-29) shows several releases per month through mid-2026. Repo has 6,300+ commits and 72+ releases, no archival notice, actively triaged issues. Primary development moved to GitLab (crafty-controller/crafty-4); the old craftycontrol GitHub org is a stale mirror — this is worth flagging since a search for "Crafty Controller" on GitHub surfaces several unrelated or abandoned forks (e.g. RMDC-Crafty/crafty, exzork/crafty-4) that are not the upstream project.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes touch game-server hosting/management. Crafty would be a genuinely new category: a panel for spinning up, scheduling, and monitoring Minecraft Java/Bedrock server instances from a browser, which is a common self-hoster use case with no equivalent in the catalogue today.
usefulness_rationale: Real, recognizable demand (Minecraft server hosting is one of the most common self-hosting use cases), but it's a narrower, hobbyist-leaning audience compared to general productivity/security/AI tools already offered, and the actual game servers it manages need their own raw TCP/UDP ports (25500-25600, 19132/udp for Bedrock, 8123 for Dynmap) that a Traefik-only, HTTP(S)-ingress recipe would not expose — so a recipe would ship a control panel that can create servers but players could not connect to them without additional port exposure this catalogue doesn't do today.
blocking_issues:
Crafty has no environment variable, config option, or setup wizard to set the admin credential at boot. On first start the app itself generates a random admin username/password pair internally and writes it in plaintext only to a container-local file (/crafty/app/config/default-creds.txt) — there is no supported channel to feed a customer-derived value (plaintext or hash) into that credential, so `generated_from` cannot be projected onto it.

Because the generated credential is random per-instance and only readable from inside the container filesystem, a customer with no shell access to the container has no way to ever discover it and log into Crafty's own UI. Fronting the app with Traefik `basic_auth` would only add an outer gate — the customer would still be locked out of the app itself behind that gate, unlike cases (e.g. Adminer) where basic_auth is hardening in front of an app with no login, or cases (e.g. n8n's setup wizard) where the customer sets their own credential once past the gate.

The panel backend is HTTPS-only on 8443 with a self-signed cert and requires WSS (WebSocket-over-TLS) for the UI to function, which is workable behind Traefik (backend TLS with cert verification disabled, standard websocket passthrough) but is an extra piece of Traefik config beyond the plain-HTTP backend pattern most current recipes use — not a blocker on its own, just a caveat if this is revisited later.
summary: Crafty Controller is an actively maintained (releases roughly monthly, latest one week old), GPL-3.0 Minecraft server panel with no overlap in the current catalogue — a genuinely new "game server hosting" category. It is blocked today, though, not just by weak defaults but by a hard structural gap: Crafty generates its own admin username/password randomly on first boot and only ever writes it to a file inside the container, with no env var, config, or wizard path for us to set it via `generated_from`, and no way for a customer without container shell access to ever retrieve it. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate doesn't fix this — it would just add a second wall in front of a UI the customer still can't log into. This needs either an upstream mechanism to pre-seed the admin credential (env var or mountable config) or a platform-side way to surface an app-generated secret to the customer post-install before it can ship as a recipe.

name: Crawl4AI
source_description: Open-source web crawler for AI applications with LLM-ready output
version_health_notes: v0.9.2 (2026-07-15, "maintenance bug fixes") is about 3 weeks old as of this analysis (2026-08-05). Prior releases v0.9.1 (2026-07-08), v0.9.0 (2026-06-18, a major "secure-by-default" Docker auth rework), v0.8.9 (2026-06-04) and v0.8.8 (2026-06-04) show a sub-monthly cadence with several security-driven patches (SSRF in proxy handling, path traversal, hardcoded JWT secrets) shipped within days of disclosure. Single primary maintainer (unclecode) but high commit volume and an active issue tracker. No archival notice, no EOL signal.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes does web crawling/scraping. Crawl4AI converts arbitrary web pages into LLM-ready Markdown/structured data via a REST API, with a browser-based Playground (manual request testing) and a Monitor dashboard (browser pool / job health). It would complement AI-automation recipes already in the catalogue (n8n, Agent-Zero-style agents, Open WebUI) as a scraping backend they could call, rather than duplicating any of them.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct use case (feeding scraped web content to LLM pipelines) with a single official multi-arch Docker image and a browser UI, but the product is fundamentally a developer-facing REST API — the web UI is a testing/monitoring surface, not an end-user application — so the addressable audience within a general self-hosting catalogue is narrower than for chat/productivity apps.
blocking_issues:
As of v0.9.0, the Docker server is secure-by-default: if CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN is unset, the process binds to loopback only inside the container, which would make it unreachable through our reverse proxy at all. So the token must be set to get a routable service, but that then makes CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN a mandatory secret the customer must know to call any endpoint (every route except GET /health requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>`) — this is the app's actual access-control boundary, not an optional extra, since there is no other login/account system in front of the API or the Playground UI.

Confirmed against the upstream source (deploy/docker/auth.py): CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN is checked via `hmac.compare_digest()` — a direct, constant-time comparison against the literal configured string. There is no hash-verification path (no bcrypt/argon2), so a hash projected via `generated_from` can never match what the customer would type in; the app only ever accepts the raw plaintext secret. Per SCHEMA.md, this is the genuine-plaintext-requirement case that is a structural blocker, not a "hash algorithm not supported yet" case.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (as done for login-less apps like Copyparty/n8n) does not solve this either: it would protect the reverse-proxy hop, but the customer still could not make a single successful API call afterward without separately knowing the exact CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN value, which our mechanism has no channel to generate-and-then-reveal to the customer (as opposed to projecting a hash of something the customer already knows, like their root password). This is a distinct platform gap from root-password projection — a "surface a server-generated secret back to the customer" channel — not one IF-1420/IF-1312 close.

Secondary, non-blocking note: the LLM-extraction features (the "LLM-ready" half of the pitch) accept `provider`/`api_token` as per-request parameters in the crawl API call body, not only as server-wide env vars, so a missing OPENAI_API_KEY/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY at boot is not itself a blocker — customers could supply their own key per call once they can reach the API at all.
summary: Crawl4AI is an active, well-maintained project (sub-monthly releases, fast security turnaround) with an official multi-arch Docker image and no overlap in our current 24 recipes. It is blocked from shipping as a recipe today: as of v0.9.0 the Docker server requires a CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN to be reachable at all, that token is checked via plain constant-time string equality with no hash-verification path, and it is the only thing gating every API/Playground call. Our mechanism can project a hash of the customer's root password (generated_from) or gate a reverse-proxy hop (Traefik basic_auth), but has no way to generate an opaque secret and then reveal it back to the customer so they can actually use the app — a platform gap distinct from the root-password-hash work already tracked in IF-1420/IF-1312.
