blocking_issues:
Name/upstream ambiguity: the Hostinger slug "cronicle" and description match jhuckaby/Cronicle, the original project, which ships NO official Docker image (its docs describe a manual POSIX/Node.js install only). The Docker-friendly option in wide use is a third-party fork, cronicle-edge/cronicle-edge (Docker Hub org "cronicle", image cronicle/edge, GHCR ghcr.io/cronicle-edge/cronicle-edge), which periodically re-syncs jhuckaby's upstream fixes and is itself actively released (v1.14.5, 2026-07-17). A recipe would have to be built against this fork, not the project a customer would find at the Hostinger-listed upstream URL — worth a human call on whether that substitution is acceptable before building. Other community images (soulteary/cronicle, intelliops/cronicle, etc.) were also considered and ruled out as unmaintained (soulteary's newest tag is roughly a year old and multiple major versions behind current upstream).

Cronicle's own login system ships a fixed default (admin/admin) with no documented environment variable or pre-seed mechanism to set the initial admin password (or a pre-computed bcrypt hash of it) at container first boot — the password can only be changed after logging in through the web UI. There is no channel to project the customer's root-password hash into it via generated_from. Per the schema's guidance this is not itself a hard blocker: gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth moves the real auth boundary in front of the app, making the unchangeable admin/admin default no longer customer-facing risk.
summary: Cronicle would fill a genuine gap (no cron/job-scheduler recipe exists today) and is mechanically installable now via a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of its fixed admin/admin login. The blocker is upstream identity: the project Hostinger's catalogue entry actually points to ships no official Docker image and has explicitly named a successor project (xyOps) while putting itself into bug-fix-only maintenance mode, so building this recipe today means depending on a third-party fork (cronicle-edge) instead of the upstream the customer would recognize. Recommend a human decision on the fork substitution before a build pass, rather than treating this as a plain build_now.

name: Cross-seed
source_description: Automatic cross-seeding tool for private and public torrent trackers
version_health_notes: Latest stable tag is v6.13.7 (2026-05-04), but the project is actively cutting v7.0.0 prereleases in parallel — most recently v7.0.0-22 on 2026-06-01, roughly 2 months before today (2026-08-05), with a dense cadence of prereleases through May-June 2026 (v7.0.0-9 through -22 in about 5 months). No archival or EOL signal; upstream is clearly actively developed, currently mid-way through a major-version transition (v6 -> v7).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches torrent/download automation, so on paper this would be a new category. In practice, though, cross-seed is not a standalone tool: its entire function is to watch an existing torrent client (qBittorrent/Deluge/Transmission/rTorrent) and query existing Torznab indexers (via Prowlarr or Jackett) to find cross-seedable matches. None of those companion apps exist in the catalogue today, so a customer deploying this recipe alone would get a daemon with nothing to connect to. Note: the documented/stable install path (ghcr.io/cross-seed/cross-seed:6, per cross-seed.org's own getting-started docker-compose example) is a genuinely headless daemon with only a webhook/job HTTP API on port 2468, no browser UI. A real Web UI (dashboard, torrent-client connection flow, API-key management screen) exists but only on the v7 prerelease track (introduced v7.0.0-15, iterated through v7.0.0-22 as of 2026-06-01, served from the same port 2468 via embedded Node SEA assets) — it has not shipped in a stable/tagged release yet.
usefulness_rationale: Useful only as part of a torrent-automation stack (torrent client + indexer manager + cross-seed) that we don't otherwise offer; shipped in isolation it has no functional value to a customer, and the target audience (private-tracker/cross-seeding hobbyists) is narrow relative to the rest of the catalogue.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: torrent client URL + credentials (qBittorrent/Deluge/Transmission/rTorrent); Torznab indexer URLs + API keys (from a customer's own Prowlarr or Jackett instance)
blocking_issues:
The stable/documented image (ghcr.io/cross-seed/cross-seed:6) is a headless daemon configured via a JS config file (config.js), plus a small HTTP API (port 2468) used for webhooks/triggers, not human administration — no login screen to project a root-password hash into. The v7 prerelease track does add a real browser Web UI on the same port, but it authenticates via an `apiKey` (config.js-set or auto-generated, shown/rotated in the UI itself) rather than a username/password login — that doesn't fit `generated_from`, which only ever projects a password hash, not an arbitrary API key value. So even once v7 stabilizes, the app itself gives us nothing to plug root-password projection into; the only available mechanism would be wrapping the whole Web UI in a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (treating it like a no-login app), which is expressible today in principle but moot while v7 remains unreleased.

The app is non-functional without a torrent client connection and at least one Torznab indexer URL/API key, both of which are customer-supplied, arbitrary, third-party credentials pointing at services outside this recipe (and outside our current catalogue entirely). There is no channel today (generated_from or otherwise) to get a customer-chosen value into config.js at /compose time.

Even if the credential-injection gap were solved, the recipe would depend on companion recipes (a torrent client, Prowlarr/Jackett) that don't exist in the catalogue yet, so it can't be usefully deployed standalone regardless of the secrets question.
summary: Cross-seed is an actively maintained (latest stable v6.13.7, prereleases as recent as June 2026) but narrow-purpose daemon. The documented stable install (v6) is genuinely headless; a real browser Web UI does exist on the v7 prerelease track (single port, would be reverse-proxy compatible), but it authenticates via an API key rather than a login, which `generated_from` can't project, and it hasn't reached a stable release. Regardless of that UI question, the app needs a customer-supplied torrent client connection and Torznab indexer API keys to do anything useful, with no channel today to get those values in at /compose time, and it depends on companion apps (a torrent client, Prowlarr or Jackett) that aren't in the catalogue — so it would ship as a non-functional standalone container even if the credential and UI-auth problems were solved. name: CryptPad
source_description: End-to-end encrypted collaborative office suite with zero-knowledge storage
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0-or-later (core), separate commercial license available from the project for proprietary use
version_health_notes: 2026.5.1 ("Spring fix release") shipped 2026-05-26, about 2.3 months before this analysis (2026-08-05); the preceding feature release, 2026.5.0, landed 2026-05-13. The project runs on a roughly quarterly seasonal release cadence (Winter 2026.2.0 on 2026-02-11, Spring 2026.5.0 on 2026-05-13, Autumn 2025.9.0 on 2025-10-22 the prior year) with fast point-fix releases in between (2026.2.1, 2026.2.2, 2026.5.1). No summer 2026 release has landed yet as of this analysis, which is consistent with the established seasonal rhythm (a "Summer" release would be expected roughly Aug/Sep) rather than a slowdown signal. Not archived, no EOL announcement; official Docker Hub image is actively republished (last pushed ~2 months before this analysis).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue provides real-time collaborative document/spreadsheet/presentation editing, and nothing provides zero-knowledge (server-blind) encrypted storage — the closest conceptual neighbor, Vaultwarden, encrypts a password vault, not general documents, and has no collaborative-editing surface at all. CryptPad would be a genuinely new capability, not a duplicate of anything already shipped.
usefulness_rationale: A self-hosted, E2E-encrypted alternative to Google Docs/Office 365 is a clear, differentiated customer draw — privacy-conscious teams and individuals specifically seek this out, and it needs no external database or third-party account to be useful out of the box. Usefulness is tempered only by the architectural fit issues below, which are about how it plugs into our reverse-proxy model, not about the app's value.
blocking_issues:
CryptPad's security model mandates two distinct customer-facing hostnames — a "main" domain (handles crypto key material) and a separate "sandbox" domain (renders the UI under a restrictive CSP) — configured via CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN / CPAD_SANDBOX_DOMAIN. Upstream's own admin guide states plainly that running production CryptPad without this second domain "may put users' information at risk." Every existing recipe in this catalogue provisions exactly one customer domain (a single `type: domain` parameter, one Traefik router, one TLS cert) for its single service; provisioning and certifying a second, distinct public hostname per customer instance for a single container is a capability the platform has never needed and doesn't have today. A recipe author could try to paper over this with a derived sub-hostname of the customer's one domain (e.g. "sandbox.<APP_DOMAIN>"), but that still requires the platform's DNS/TLS provisioning to issue and route a second hostname per instance, not something a recipe file alone can express — this is a platform gap, not a recipe-authoring choice.
CryptPad has no admin login of its own to project a root-password hash into. Admin status is granted by manually pasting a specific user's already-generated public signing key into config.js and restarting the container — a value that does not exist until after a human has already created an account through the running app's UI. There is no equivalent of Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN to seed at boot. This is not a hard blocker on its own (the admin console is optional; CryptPad is fully usable for anonymous/registered users without ever designating an admin), but it does mean no first-boot admin credential can be wired up via generated_from — only the general basic_auth access gate is expressible.
summary: CryptPad is an actively maintained (quarterly seasonal releases, latest 2026.5.1 in May 2026), single-container app with no external database and no third-party API keys — mechanically simple to run, and it would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue as the only E2E-encrypted collaborative office suite. It does not fit our current single-domain-per-recipe reverse-proxy model, however: CryptPad's own security guidance requires two separate customer-facing hostnames (main + CSP-sandboxed UI domain), and deploying it behind only one domain is explicitly called out upstream as putting user data at risk — shipping that configuration anyway would mean knowingly weakening the product's core selling point. Provisioning a second domain/TLS cert per instance is a platform capability gap, not something a recipe file can work around alone, so this is blocked_on_platform rather than a simple secrets-mechanism issue. Separately, its optional admin console has no first-boot credential channel (admin status is granted via a public key that only exists after a user account is created in the running app), though that alone would not block a basic-usable deployment. Revisit once multi-domain provisioning per recipe instance is supported.

Upstream's reference docker-compose.yml is a heavy stack: cvat_db (Postgres), cvat_redis_inmem, cvat_redis_ondisk (KVRocks), cvat_opa (Open Policy Agent for auth), cvat_server plus 8 separate worker containers (utils/import/export/annotation/webhooks/quality_reports /chunks/consensus — all the same cvat/server image running different queue-consumer commands), cvat_ui, an internal bundled Traefik instance as the actual HTTP entrypoint, and an analytics side-stack (cvat_clickhouse, cvat_vector, cvat_grafana) that the backend containers hard-depend on at boot (`depends_on: cvat_clickhouse` is baked into the shared backend-deps anchor, so it can't be trimmed without patching upstream's compose file). Not a structural blocker, but a real sizing/cost consideration for the recipe's minimum VM tier.
summary: CVAT is an active, corporately-backed, MIT-licensed computer-vision annotation tool with a tight weekly release cadence and no upstream end-of-life signal — a strong, differentiated addition that would open a brand-new "ML/CV data engineering" category in the catalogue with zero overlap against the current 24 recipes. Two real caveats keep this at build_with_caveats rather than a clean build_now: (1) the admin account has to be created via a scripted non-interactive `docker exec ... createsuperuser --no-input` rather than a plain container env var, a pattern no existing recipe uses yet and worth validating in Phase 3; and (2) upstream's reference stack is unusually heavy at ~17 containers (full worker fleet + OPA + an analytics sub-stack that's hard-wired as a dependency), which will push this recipe's minimum RAM/disk requirements well above anything else we ship today.

Installability hinges on a design choice the recipe author must get right: the upstream example docker-compose hardcodes AUTH_USERNAME=admin / AUTH_PASSWORD=admin as a plaintext DB-auth account created at container startup (create_account.php takes a raw password and hashes it internally with Cypht's own scheme, so `generated_from` cannot project a bcrypt/argon2 hash into it the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN accepts one — it would just re-hash our hash and lock the customer out). differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does auto-generated REST/GraphQL APIs over a customer-defined data model (a "backend-as-a-service" / headless-CMS style tool, in the vein of Directus or Supabase, neither of which we carry). n8n is workflow automation between existing apps/APIs, not a place to model and serve new data; nothing else touches this space at all. Docked from "high" mainly on name recognition/audience size, not on functionality or health.
blocking_issues:
Daptin has no env-var-driven admin bootstrap at all. Upstream's documented first-boot flow is three unauthenticated HTTP calls against the running instance: POST /action/user_account/signup (plaintext "password" + "passwordConfirm" fields, which Daptin bcrypts itself server-side), POST /action/user_account/signin to get a JWT, then POST /action/world/become_an_administrator to claim admin. Upstream's own docs state plainly: "On a fresh install, Daptin is WIDE OPEN — anyone can do anything" until that claim happens, after which public signup is disabled. Because Daptin's signup endpoint requires the plaintext password (it does the bcrypting itself), and `generated_from` only ever hands a recipe a pre-computed hash of the customer's root password — never the plaintext — there is no way to script an admin-claim that logs the customer in with their own root-password-derived credential the way CVAT's `createsuperuser --no-input` can. This is exactly the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case SCHEMA.md calls a structural blocker, not a workaround-able gap.

Worked around, not blocked: gate the entire domain behind Traefik `basic_auth` (credential from the root-password hash, same pattern as n8n/WUD/Immich) instead of trying to feed Daptin's own signup flow. This closes the "wide open" window at the ingress — nobody unauthenticated ever reaches the app — and the customer performs the three-call signup/signin/become-admin dance themselves, in their own browser, with their own chosen credentials, after authenticating through the gate. That's ordinary first-use onboarding (like a Vaultwarden user choosing their own vault master password post-install), not a `/compose`-time input problem, so it doesn't need a customer-supplied-value channel at all. Flagging as a caveat rather than folding into `secrets_expressible_today` cleanly: Daptin does have its own login system (unlike Adminer, the canonical no-login basic_auth example), so this is a slight stretch of the pattern's stated intent, even though it is mechanically sound and uses an already-shipped mechanism with no new install.sh pattern required.
summary: Daptin is a real, differentiated addition — nothing else in the 24-recipe catalogue does auto-generated REST/GraphQL over a customer-defined data model — and it's a healthy single container behind one HTTP port with active, if bursty, upstream releases and no EOL signal. It clears `installable_today` only via a workaround: its own admin-claim API needs a plaintext password that `generated_from` can never supply (a hash), so the fix is gating the whole domain with Traefik `basic_auth` and letting the customer do the three-call signup/become-admin dance themselves once inside, rather than trying to script their real admin identity into Daptin directly. That's a sound, already-used mechanism, but it is a deliberate reinterpretation of the basic_auth pattern for an app that (unlike its canonical no-login examples) does have its own login — worth a second pair of eyes in Phase 3 before treating it as settled.

name: Dasharr
source_description: Self-hosted history dashboard for private torrent tracker statistics
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/arcadia-solutions/dasharr (pin to a version tag, e.g. 0.3.0 — upstream's own compose.yml uses :latest, which we would not follow)
version_health_notes: As of today (2026-08-05), the latest tagged release (0.3.0, 2026-03-18) is about 4.5 months old. Release history before that was dense: 0.2.0 (2025-11-16), 0.1.9 (2025-10-31), 0.1.8 (2025-10-13), 0.1.7 (2025-10-11), 0.1.6 (2025-10-06), 0.1.5/0.1.4 (2025-10-04), down to the initial 0.1 release (2025-10-02) — a burst of near-daily point releases in the first month, tapering to roughly monthly, then nothing tagged since March. The repo is not archived and did receive two more commits after 0.3.0 (bug fixes, 2026-06-27, ~5.5 weeks ago), so it is not dormant, but the pace has clearly slowed: only 2 commits and 0 releases in the ~4.5 months since 0.3.0, versus dozens of commits/releases in the prior 5 months. Open issue #44 ("Blutopia broken", opened 2026-04-10) is still unaddressed as of this analysis. Small project (107 stars, 5 forks, single small team/maintainer per CONTRIBUTING.md) — active but low-velocity right now, worth re-checking before committing engineering time.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue tracks private-tracker statistics (upload/download/ratio/bonus-points history across trackers like RED, BTN, GGn, MAM, and ~20 others). Unlike cross-seed (previously analyzed, apps-gaps/cross-seed.yaml), Dasharr does not need a companion torrent client or indexer manager to be useful — it scrapes each configured tracker's own site/API directly using credentials the customer enters into Dasharr's web UI after boot, so it stands alone rather than depending on apps we don't otherwise ship.
usefulness_rationale: Real but narrow niche (private-tracker hobbyists checking their own ratio/bonus-point history over time) — smaller and more specialized audience than the cross-seed/torrent-automation space already scored low in prior analysis, and Dasharr itself is a young, low-star, single small-team project rather than an established brand.
blocking_issues:
Dasharr's own web UI login is gated by a single shared secret, API_KEY, set as a plaintext env var and checked in the backend (backend/src/middleware.rs) via a direct string-equality comparison against the `api-key` request header — there is no hashed/pre-hashed form accepted. The customer must know and type this exact value to log in and use the app at all, so it functions as Dasharr's real admin password. Our only customer-secret channel today (`generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`) only ever produces a *hash* of the root password — it cannot produce the plaintext value Dasharr's comparison requires, so this credential cannot be projected from the root password.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the app does not substitute here either: unlike Adminer/WUD-style apps with no login of their own (where the outer gate *is* the auth boundary), Dasharr still enforces its own mandatory API_KEY login behind any outer gate. Even with a fixed/hardcoded API_KEY value baked into the recipe and an outer basic_auth gate for perimeter security, the customer would still need to know that hardcoded API_KEY to pass Dasharr's own login screen — and there is no channel today to communicate a recipe-fixed secret to the customer, so this is a genuine plaintext-password requirement per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's blocking criteria, not a soft caveat.
summary: Dasharr is a small, single-container-plus-Postgres app (reverse-proxy friendly on one port) with real but narrow value: a history dashboard for private-tracker upload/ratio/bonus stats, with no overlap against the current 24-recipe catalogue. It is blocked from installable_today because its own web login is gated by a plaintext-compared API_KEY with no hashed-value support, which our root-password-hash-only `generated_from` mechanism cannot supply and which a perimeter Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not bypass, since the app's internal login still has to be satisfied separately. Combined with a slowing release cadence (no tagged release in ~4.5 months, only 2 commits since) and a fairly niche/low-usefulness audience, this is not a strong build candidate even setting the platform blocker aside — recommend `blocked_on_platform`, revisit only if a genuine external-API-key/plaintext-secret input channel is added to the platform.

name: dashdot
source_description: Minimalist server dashboard with real-time CPU, RAM, storage, and network stats
version_health_notes: ~5 months since v6.3.4 (2026-03-03) as of today (2026-08-05), but repo history shows a burst of 5 releases (v6.2.1–v6.3.4) between 2026-01-05 and 2026-03-03 after a longer gap from v6.2.0 (2025-08-10). Last commit (pushed_at) is 2026-07-30, five days before today, so the project is actively maintained even without a fresh tag. 55 open issues, not archived. Classified active, not sporadic/dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue shows live host-hardware telemetry (CPU/RAM/storage/network utilization graphs) as its primary purpose. Uptime Kuma monitors external service availability, not the host's own resource usage, so it is not a true overlap. dashdot would be a lightweight "is my VPS running hot" glance dashboard, distinct from log/uptime/update tooling already offered.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for at-a-glance server resource dashboards on small VPS/private-server audiences (dashdot's own stated niche), but it is a read-only nice-to-have rather than something customers depend on daily, and its core mechanism (privileged + full host-root mount, see below) is a heavier ask than most of our existing single-container recipes.
blocking_issues:
dashdot ships with zero authentication of its own — the upstream docker-compose example exposes the dashboard directly with no login screen, so it must sit behind Traefik basic_auth (expressible today, not a hard blocker) or it is wide open on the internet.

Upstream's only documented deployment path (docker/docker-compose installation docs) requires `privileged: true` plus a bind mount of the entire host root filesystem read-only (`-v /:/mnt/host:ro`) so it can read real hardware/OS stats from outside the container namespace. This is not a customer-supplied-secret problem, but it is a real platform-risk concern on shared customer VMs: it violates `bind-mount-under-opt` (WARN, host path is `/` not `/opt/dashdot/`) and triggers `no-privileged-without-justification` (WARN, would need an explicit `metadata.notes` justification). Neither is an RFC-002 ERROR, so it would not fail validation, but reviewers should weigh whether "read-only root mount + privileged" is an acceptable trade for a nice-to-have dashboard before this is built.
summary: dashdot is an actively maintained (last commit 5 days before this analysis), single-container, no-login server dashboard with no overlap in the current catalogue. Its one required secret — a Traefik basic_auth gate, since it has no built-in auth — is fully expressible today via the existing mechanism, so it is not blocked on missing platform features. The catalogue-fit concern is architectural rather than about secrets: upstream's only supported deployment needs `privileged: true` and a read-only bind mount of the whole host root filesystem, which are WARN- level RFC-002 flags worth a deliberate call before committing to a recipe, not a hard installability blocker.

name: Dashy

name: Databag
source_description: Self-hosted federated messenger with end-to-end encryption and topic-based threads
latest_version: 0.1.18 (Docker Hub tag); mobile-app release tags top out at v1.1.1021 (Jun 2024)
version_health_notes: Docker Hub's newest numbered tag, 0.1.18, was pushed 2025-10-15 — just under 10 months before today (2026-08-05) — consistent with the repo's last substantive commits on 2025-09-15/16 ("fixing dark colors on tablet", "updating go version format", merging an SDK-container branch). Since then, main has only received translation-string commits: 2025-11-08 (nginx-proxy doc example, non-code), 2026-01-01, 2026-04-17, and 2026-06-14 — the most recent activity is ~1.7 months old, but nothing functional or security-relevant has landed in the ~11 months since the Sep 2025 work. GitHub "release" tags (v1.1.x) are for the mobile client build number, not the server, and haven't moved since June 2024 (over 2 years ago). No archive banner, no announced EOL, issues/discussions still open — this reads as a project on autopilot (a maintainer merging community translations) rather than actively developed or abandoned outright.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers chat/messaging. Databag is a lightweight, self-hosted, E2E-encrypted, federated messenger (topic-based threads, audio/video calls, own public/private-key identity not tied to a blockchain or hosting domain) — distinct from anything in the current 24-recipe catalogue, which has no communication-category app at all.
usefulness_rationale: A self-hosted encrypted messenger is a recognizable customer want and would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue, not a rehash of an existing recipe. Rated medium rather than high because the project's own momentum has stalled (see version_health) and its federation model (direct app-to-server, own identity keys) is a niche fit compared to mainstream chat expectations — customers evaluating self-hosted chat are more likely to already know Matrix/Element or Rocket.Chat by name.
blocking_issues:
The `ADMIN` env var is the server's admin-panel credential, and it is compared as a raw plaintext string, not a hash: `entrypoint.sh` writes the env var's value verbatim into the `token` config row (`insert into configs (config_id, str_value) values ('token', '$ADMIN')`), and `net/server/internal/authUtil.go`'s `ParamAdminToken` checks `value != token` — a literal string comparison against that stored value. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of ROOT_PASSWORD into an app parameter; there is no way to make a hash satisfy a plaintext-equality check, so this is the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case SCHEMA.md calls a structural blocker, not an extensible-algorithm gap like IF-1420.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead does not substitute for this: Databag has its own real login layer (per-account bcrypt passwords plus the separate admin token), and the admin token specifically is required to do first-run setup — configuring the federated host domain and generating the invite link needed to create the very first user account. A customer who can pass a Traefik gate but never learns the (server-generated, non-customer-facing) ADMIN value would be locked out of ever configuring or using the app, so basic_auth only closes the "sitting open on the internet" gap, not the "customer needs working admin access" gap.

No other channel in `/compose` exists to carry a customer-chosen or customer-derived plaintext value.
summary: Databag is a single-container Go/SQLite app (balzack/databag:0.1.18, official image, pinned) that would be reverse-proxy-compatible on one HTTP port and fills a real gap — no messaging/chat recipe exists in the catalogue today. It is blocked, though: its admin credential is checked by exact plaintext string comparison with no hashing anywhere in the auth path, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash) cannot satisfy it, and Traefik `basic_auth` can gate the app's front door but can't give the customer usable admin access inside it. Combined with the upstream project having done no functional work in ~11 months (only translation-string commits since Sep 2025), this is not a good build-now candidate; revisit if af-api ever gains a genuine plaintext-projection channel, not just more `generated_from` hash algorithms.

name: Dawarich

name: DbGate
source_description: Open-source cross-platform SQL and NoSQL database administration tool
version_health_notes: v7.2.4 shipped 2026-08-04 — one day before today (2026-08-05) — adding built-in PostgreSQL backup/restore, alongside a run of beta/premium-beta tags in the same 2-day window (7.2.4-beta.10, 7.2.4-premium-beta.8/11). v7.2.3 preceded it by only ~16 days. This is a fast-moving, clearly active project with no dormancy signal at all; both the community (dbgate/dbgate) and premium (dbgate/dbgate-premium) Docker Hub images are kept current with each release.
differentiation: Nothing currently in the 24-recipe catalogue exposes a generic multi-engine database admin UI (n8n/paperless-ngx/gitea/immich each run their own internal Postgres/MySQL but don't surface a browser UI for it). DbGate is a direct analog to Adminer (already gap-analyzed, not yet built — see apps-gaps/adminer.yaml) but broader: single React/Electron- style web app covering MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MongoDB, SQLite, CockroachDB, Cassandra and more, plus a visual query designer, schema compare, and data import/export that Adminer's plain PHP forms don't offer. The two are not both "must build" — they'd serve the same customer need (BYO-database browsing/admin) with DbGate as the more feature-rich pick.
usefulness_rationale: Same audience and same first-boot friction as Adminer: useful to developers/power users who already run their own database (self-hosted or another recipe's internal DB) and want a real GUI instead of a CLI, but it needs a reachable database to be useful at all — an empty shell with nothing to browse until the customer supplies a connection. Rated medium (not high) for the same niche/technical-audience reasoning as Adminer, and not "low" like Datasette because DbGate connects to live, general-purpose databases rather than requiring a bespoke uploaded file.
summary: DbGate is a single-container app (dbgate/dbgate:7.2.4, official image, pinned) listening on one HTTP port (3000 internally) — reverse-proxy compatible on <slug>.<base_domain> with no other raw ports needed. Critically, it ships with NO authentication enabled by default: login is opt-in via either LOGIN_PASSWORD_<login> env vars or a single ADMIN_PASSWORD env var, and the admin path (packages/api/src/controllers/auth.js) checks that password with a plain `adminPassword == password` string comparison, not a hash — so `generated_from` (which only ever projects an argon2/bcrypt hash) cannot drive DbGate's own login the way it does for Vaultwarden. That's not a blocker, though: since DbGate ships unauthenticated by default anyway (same posture as Adminer), the fix is the same as Adminer's — leave DbGate's own login off and gate the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth: true`, with that gate's password projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from`. Worth flagging for the human reviewer: DbGate had a critical (CVSS 10.0) unauthenticated RCE via its JSON script-runner endpoint (GHSA-8v3q-9vmx-36vc, affecting <=7.1.8, fixed in 7.1.9) that was exploitable specifically because auth is disabled by default — another reason a mandatory (not optional) basic_auth gate is the right call here, and the pinned 7.2.4 tag is comfortably past the fixed version. Upstream is fast-moving and healthy (daily-ish releases as of this week). Recommend build_now, but note in triage that it covers the same customer need as the still-unbuilt Adminer gap — decide whether to build one, the other, or both rather than treating this as a clear net-new category.

name: DDNS Updater
source_description: Self-hosted dynamic DNS updater for 40+ providers, runs as headless agent
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release v2.10.0 shipped 2026-05-01 (also mirrored as qmcgaw/ddns-updater:v2.10.0 on Docker Hub), about 3 months before this analysis (2026-08-05). Tagged-release cadence is uneven: v2.9.0 landed 2024-12-24, then a ~17-month gap before v2.9.1/v2.10.0 both shipped 2026-05-01. However the `latest` image tag on Docker Hub was pushed ~23 hours before this analysis, meaning master is still built and published continuously between tagged releases — so the project reads as under active, if irregular, maintenance rather than dormant. No archived flag, no deprecation notice.
differentiation: Pi-hole and AdGuard Home (already in the catalogue) are DNS resolvers/ad-blockers for traffic leaving a customer's network — a different job from DDNS Updater, which periodically checks the server's public IP and pushes A/AAAA record updates to an external DNS provider (Cloudflare, GoDaddy, Route53, etc.) so a *changing* IP stays reachable at a fixed hostname. No existing recipe covers that.
usefulness_rationale: DDNS Updater's core use case is keeping a hostname pointed at a residential/home-lab server behind a dynamic IP. AF customers run on IONOS cloud infrastructure with a static IP and a domain the platform itself already provisions and resolves (<slug>.<base_domain>) — the problem this app solves largely doesn't exist in that context. It would mainly appeal to a customer additionally running services on a home network they want an AF-hosted watcher for, a narrow secondary use case.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: Per-DNS-provider API credentials (e.g. Cloudflare API token, GoDaddy key/secret, Route53 IAM keys) configured in config.json/CONFIG; Traefik basic-auth gate credential (app ships no login of its own)
secrets_expressible_today: Traefik basic-auth gate credential (app ships no login of its own):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues: Core function is entirely dependent on a customer-supplied, third-party DNS provider API credential (different per provider, e.g. Cloudflare token vs GoDaddy key+secret) passed via config.json or the CONFIG env var. This is an external API key with no current /compose input channel — not expressible via generated_from (which only projects a hash of the customer's root password) or via any other mechanism today. Without it the app cannot perform its one job at all, so this isn't a gate-the-UI problem like Adminer/Dashy — the whole recipe is non-functional without a channel for this secret.
summary: DDNS Updater is a small, actively-built, MIT-licensed single-container app with an official multi-arch image and a lightweight web UI on one HTTP port (8000, plus a 9999 health port), so it would be mechanically reverse-proxy-compatible. It fails installability for a more fundamental reason than most gated apps, though: its entire function depends on a customer-supplied DNS provider API credential that our current /compose mechanism has no channel to receive — gating the web UI behind Traefik basic_auth (as we do for Dashy/Adminer) would still leave the app unable to update anything. Combined with a use case (dynamic-IP home servers) that doesn't map well onto AF's static-IP cloud hosting model, this is a `not_recommended` rather than a `blocked_on_platform` — even a future arbitrary-secret input channel wouldn't make this a compelling recipe for our customer base.

name: Decidim
source_description: Open-source participatory democracy framework for citizen consultations
version_health_notes: Six days before this analysis (today 2026-08-05). Two release lines are maintained in parallel (0.32.x current, 0.31.x LTS-style backport line), with releases on both roughly monthly (0.32.0 on 2026-07-02, 0.32.1 on 2026-07-30, 0.31.6/0.31.7 in the same window). Governed by a foundation (Decidim Association) with corporate/municipal backing, not a single maintainer — low abandonment risk.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover participatory/civic-engagement tooling (voting, proposals, budgeting consultations, assemblies). Closest conceptual neighbors (n8n, gitea, opengist) are automation/dev-collab tools, not citizen-facing consultation platforms, so this would open a genuinely new category rather than compete with an existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Real niche (municipalities, NGOs, unions running participatory processes) with no substitute in the catalogue, but it's a heavyweight Ruby-on-Rails stack (app + Postgres + Redis, plus a background worker for notifications) aimed at a narrower customer segment than most of our current self-hosting audience.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: Decidim system-admin email; Decidim system-admin password
blocking_issues:
The only way to create the first Decidim account (`bin/rails decidim_system:create_admin`) is an interactive rake task that reads a plaintext email/password pair from stdin and hashes the password itself via Devise/bcrypt at that point. There is no env var or field that accepts a pre-computed hash, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext) cannot supply it — this is the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case SCHEMA.md calls a structural blocker, not the unsupported-hash-algorithm case.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate doesn't substitute here either: unlike Adminer-style tools, the customer must actually know a working Decidim system-admin (and later, organization-admin) login to use the product at all — putting a second, unrelated gate in front doesn't give them that credential.

Beyond the admin account, first-run organization setup emails an invitation to the organization-admin address, which needs a working SMTP relay configured — an additional external dependency with no customer-input channel today, though secondary to the admin-account blocker above.
summary: Decidim is an active, well-governed Rails app filling a real catalogue gap (participatory democracy / civic engagement) with a standard reverse-proxy- compatible web UI. It cannot ship today: the first system-admin account is created via an interactive CLI prompt for a plaintext password that the app hashes itself, which the current root-password-hash-only projection mechanism cannot feed, and no basic_auth gate can substitute for that missing login. Revisit once the platform has a channel for handing the customer an actual generated credential (not just a hash), or once Decidim ships a non-interactive/env-var admin bootstrap.

name: DeepWiki Open
source_description: AI-powered wiki generator for GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket repositories
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/asyncfuncai/deepwiki-open (sha-tagged only, e.g. sha-cbd1ebd — no semver-tagged image published)
latest_version: no tagged release; rolling main branch, most recent commit 2026-08-04 (PR #568)
version_health_notes: No GitHub Releases have ever been published for this repo (releases page is empty) and the container registry only ships commit-sha tags (sha-cbd1ebd, sha-b5e7666, ...), never :latest-as-a-version or a semver tag — there is no stable version to pin the way RFC-002 expects. Commit activity is genuinely active: 10 commits in the 10 days before 2026-08-05 (today), most recent 1 day prior. However, the top-level README has been gutted to a single paragraph pointing at a hosted commercial product, "Grok Wiki" (grok-wiki.com), branded "Deepwiki-Open 2.0" — the maintainer's setup docs, feature list, and self-host instructions have been removed from the OSS README in favor of the SaaS. Self-host instructions used here were recovered from `api/README.md`, `docker-compose.yml`, and `api/config.py` in the source tree, not the front-page README. Treat this as a signal the OSS edition may be de-prioritized even though commits continue.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes generate documentation/wikis from a code repository. Closest neighbors are open-webui and ollama (self-hosted AI compute) and paperless-ai (AI companion to an existing app), but none touch code-to-docs generation. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Useful niche for a dev-focused customer, but the app's real value (LLM-quality code understanding) depends on a frontier model (Gemini/ OpenAI/OpenRouter/Bedrock), and see installability below for why that can't be wired up as a customer-supplied credential today. Restricted to a bundled local Ollama model, output quality is materially weaker, which caps how compelling this recipe is versus the upstream's own positioning.
blocking_issues:
App has no built-in login by default; DEEPWIKI_AUTH_MODE/DEEPWIKI_AUTH_CODE exist but require a plaintext shared code compared server-side, not a hash — generated_from cannot supply this because it only ever emits argon2/bcrypt hashes, so a Traefik basic-auth gate is used instead.
Default config requires GOOGLE_API_KEY (default chat provider) and OPENAI_API_KEY (default embedder, text-embedding-3-small) — both external API keys with no customer-supplied-value channel today.
A no-external-key deployment is possible (DEEPWIKI_EMBEDDER_TYPE=ollama + PROVIDER=ollama, bundling an Ollama service the way recipes/open-webui does) but this is a recipe-authoring workaround, not something the app supports out of the box, and it meaningfully degrades the AI-generated wiki quality that is the app's whole value proposition.
Frontend (Next.js, port 3000) and backend (FastAPI, port 8001) are two separate containers; most HTTP calls are proxied by Next.js rewrites, but the chat WebSocket connects from the browser directly to the backend port (see src/utils/websocketClient.ts), so Traefik needs two routers on one host (path- or port-based) rather than a single pass-through port like most existing recipes.
summary: DeepWiki Open would fill a genuinely new "AI docs from a repo" niche in the catalogue, has an MIT license, a real web UI, and active upstream commits (most recent one day before this analysis). But it structurally needs an external LLM API key (Google/OpenAI by default) to do anything useful, and our only workaround — forcing it onto a bundled local Ollama model — is a downgrade the app's own README doesn't even document, produces materially worse wikis, and would need its own resource-floor and Traefik dual-router work on top. Recommend holding until a real customer-supplied-API-key channel exists (or Ollama-only is explicitly accepted as the shipped mode), rather than building now with caveats.

name: Defguard
source_description: Zero-trust access management with WireGuard MFA and built-in OpenID Connect
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (core); enterprise features under a separate proprietary Enterprise License — the enterprise directory is explicitly carved out of the AGPL grant
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/defguard/defguard (core), ghcr.io/defguard/defguard-proxy (Edge/proxy), ghcr.io/defguard/gateway (Gateway) — three separate official images, no single all-in-one image; pin each to a current 2.0.x tag, e.g. 2.0.3
version_health_notes: Latest release v2.0.3 shipped 2026-08-04, one day before this analysis (2026-08-05) — a patch fixing an SMTP settings regression from 2.0.2. Recent history is dense: v2.0.2 (2026-07-11), v1.6.7 (2026-07-10, a parallel maintenance release for the older 1.x line), v2.0.1 (2026-05-22), v2.0.0 stable (2026-04-30) after a beta/RC cycle (2026-04-10 through 2026-04-27). A v2.1.0-alpha1 pre-release is already out (2026-07-15). This reads as a healthy, actively developed project with both a current stable line (2.0.x) and continued backport support for the previous major (1.6.x) — no archived flag, no deprecation notice.
differentiation: Defguard and wg-easy both provide a web UI for managing a WireGuard VPN, but Defguard is a much larger zero-trust access platform built around that VPN core: per-connection MFA (TOTP/WebAuthn/email), an internal OpenID Connect provider plus external OIDC/LDAP/AD sync, firewall allow/deny policy, activity/audit logging, and webhooks — a genuinely different tier of product from wg-easy's single job of "add/remove WireGuard peers from a web page." For a customer who wants just VPN peer management, wg-easy already covers it; Defguard would appeal to a customer wanting VPN + identity/MFA/SSO consolidated in one place.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiated capability (zero-trust access + MFA + OIDC, not just VPN peer management) and an actively maintained upstream. Held to medium rather than high because the vendor's own recommended topology — three independently-deployed components (Core, Edge/proxy, Gateway), ideally on separate hosts, with Core needing gRPC/internal-only exposure while Edge needs a public domain and Gateway needs a public UDP port — is a materially heavier and more networking-specific footprint than anything else in the catalogue, narrowing the realistic audience to customers specifically wanting a self-hosted zero-trust/VPN gateway rather than a general productivity or self-hosting audience.
blocking_issues:
Defguard's own one-line installer and docs recommend three independently-addressable components: Core (identity/policy, internal-only), Edge/proxy (public HTTPS entrypoint), and Gateway (public WireGuard UDP endpoint). Docs explicitly warn the Core/Edge gRPC ports (50052, 50055) must never be exposed publicly, while Edge needs a public domain/DNS record distinct from Core's internal one, and Gateway needs its own public UDP port. This is a multi-surface, multi-domain topology beyond a single <slug>.<base_domain> HTTP app behind Traefik — closer to needing a small dedicated network topology than a docker-compose stack, even though the one-line installer can co-locate all three containers on one host.
The admin account is created through an interactive first-run browser setup wizard rather than a fixed environment variable, and the wizard's Certificate Authority step requires an administrator email address for cert generation. That address is a customer-chosen value, not a hash of the root password and not something the platform can auto-generate meaningfully (an email needs to be real/reachable) — it has no expressible mechanism today (not generated_from, not basic_auth, not a server-side-generatable secret).
summary: Defguard is an actively maintained (latest v2.0.3, 2026-08-04), genuinely differentiated app relative to our existing wg-easy recipe — it wraps WireGuard VPN in a full zero-trust access platform with MFA, an internal OIDC provider, LDAP/AD sync, and firewall policy, not just a peer-management UI. The blocker is architectural rather than mechanistic: upstream's supported deployment is three separately-addressable components (an internal-only Core, a public-HTTPS Edge/proxy, and a public-UDP Gateway), which doesn't map onto our single-domain-behind-Traefik recipe model the way wg-easy's single web-UI-plus-VPN-port container does. On top of that, first-run admin setup goes through an interactive wizard whose CA step needs a customer-supplied administrator email address — a value type /compose has no channel for today. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once the platform supports multi-domain/multi-surface recipes (or a documented single-host-with-one-domain topology is confirmed) and an arbitrary customer-supplied value (beyond password-hash projection) has an input channel.

name: Deluge
source_description: Lightweight BitTorrent client with web interface and plugin support
upstream_docker_image: linuxserver/deluge (pin to a version tag, e.g. 2.2.0-ls381 — do not follow upstream compose examples that use :latest)
version_health_notes: As of today (2026-08-05), the latest stable release (2.2.0) shipped roughly 15 months ago. Historical cadence is very uneven: 2.0.0-2.0.3 landed in a burst in June 2019, then 2.0.4/2.0.5 in December 2021 (~2.5 years later), 2.1.0/2.1.1 in June/July 2022, and 2.2.0 in April 2025 (~3 years after that). Development is not dead — the readthedocs "latest" doc build shows an active 2.2.1.dev tree as of March 2026, and 2.2.0 itself included fixes for three GHSL-tagged security advisories — but stable releases land maybe once every 1-3 years, so treat this as sporadic rather than active. It is a mature, single-well-known-project (essentially the reference GPL BitTorrent client with a web UI), not a fork or abandoned mirror. The deluge-torrent/deluge GitHub repo is explicitly a read-only PR mirror (canonical development happens on git.deluge-torrent.org), which explains why it shows zero GitHub "Releases" despite ongoing upstream work.
differentiation: No BitTorrent/download-client recipe exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue today. Deluge's web UI (port 8112) is a single HTTP endpoint and works behind Traefik the same way Syncthing's web UI does, even though — like Syncthing — the app also needs raw non-HTTP ports open for its actual protocol traffic (inbound torrent peer connections on 6881/tcp+udp, optional daemon port 58846 for thin clients). That precedent (Syncthing already ships with public non-HTTP ports alongside its web UI) means the raw-port requirement here is not a novel problem for the platform.
usefulness_rationale: BitTorrent clients are a perennial self-hosted-app request (frequently paired with Sonarr/Radarr/Jellyfin-style media stacks that we don't carry either), and Deluge is one of the two or three most recognized open-source options alongside qBittorrent and Transmission. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because: (a) the upstream release cadence is slow enough that security-fix turnaround could lag, and (b) without a companion media-server/*arr recipe in the catalogue, a standalone Deluge instance is a less complete story for the "media automation" audience than it would be alongside those.
summary: Deluge (via the linuxserver/deluge image) is a single-container app with a web UI on one HTTP port, so it is reverse-proxy compatible the same way Syncthing is, alongside raw torrent-protocol ports (6881/tcp+udp) that must stay open regardless of Traefik. Its WebUI ships a fixed, well-known default login (admin/deluge) with no environment variable or first-boot parameter to override it — the linuxserver image only exposes PUID/PGID/TZ/DELUGE_LOGLEVEL/UMASK, none of which touch auth — so the fix is the same pattern used elsewhere in this catalogue for apps with no overridable login of their own: a Traefik `basic_auth` gate projected from the root-password hash in front of the app (IF-1312). With that gate this is installable today. It's marked `build_with_caveats` rather than `build_now` because upstream's release cadence is sporadic (multi-year gaps between stable versions), so whoever owns this recipe should budget for manually tracking CVEs/point releases rather than expecting routine upstream cadence to carry that load, and because it delivers more value as part of a future media-automation grouping than as a totally standalone recipe.

name: DenoKV
source_description: The Denoland key-value database for Deno Deploy
version_health_notes: ~2 months since 0.14.0 (2026-06-06) as of today (2026-08-05) — still actively maintained. Cadence had been fairly regular every ~2-3 months from 0.8.1 (2024-06) through 0.12.0 (2025-07-29), but the gap between 0.13.0 (2025-11-21) and 0.14.0 (2026-06-06) stretched to ~6.5 months, the widest gap in the release history — worth flagging as a slowdown, not yet dormant.
differentiation: No existing recipe provides a standalone database/KV backend service. DenoKV is a self-hosted implementation of the Deno KV protocol (SQLite- backed, ACID transactions) so a customer's own Deno/Deno Deploy applications can point at an external, persistent KV store instead of the single-instance built-in one. It would be a genuinely new capability in the catalogue, not a duplicate of anything we ship today.
usefulness_rationale: Purely a headless API backend with no web UI and no admin surface at all — the customer interacts with it exclusively by pointing their own Deno code at it via `Deno.openKv(url)`. That's a narrow niche (customers already building Deno/Deno Deploy applications who specifically want an external KV backend) compared to the general-purpose, UI-driven apps that make up the rest of the catalogue, and it has no standalone value without that specific developer workflow.
blocking_issues: DENO_KV_ACCESS_TOKEN is not an internal secret nothing customer-facing reads — it's the one credential the customer's own external Deno application (`Deno.openKv(url)`) must be configured with to use the service at all. DenoKV has no web UI, admin API, or any log/output channel to surface a server-generated value after boot, so there is no way for the customer to ever learn a server-generated token. It also isn't a customer-chosen credential (so `generated_from` doesn't apply) and there's no login of DenoKV's own to gate with `traefik_basic_auth` instead. No expressible mechanism exists for this secret today.
summary: DenoKV needs a single bearer access token (DENO_KV_ACCESS_TOKEN) that its own external Deno client must be configured with, but there is no channel today for that value to ever reach the customer: it's not a customer- chosen credential (no `generated_from`), there's no UI or API to gate with `traefik_basic_auth`, and DenoKV has no web UI, admin surface, or log output through which a server-generated token could be retrieved post- boot. It exposes one plain-HTTP port with no other raw protocols, so it would be reverse-proxy compatible if this were solved, but as things stand it is not mechanically installable today. Combined with having no web UI and a narrow developer-only audience (customers already building Deno/Deno Deploy applications who want an external KV backend) plus a recently slowing release cadence, it is not recommended for the current catalogue; revisit only if a customer-supplied-secret input channel ships and Deno adoption among AF customers becomes a requested use case.

upstream_docker_image: dhis2/core (official, on Docker Hub — pin to a specific patch tag, e.g. 2.43.1, not :latest or a bare major-line tag like 2.43)

DHIS2 publishes one major version per year (v43 is current, following v42 and v41) but keeps at least the last two-to-three major lines under active patch support in parallel — the `dhis2/core` Docker Hub tags show 2.41.9 pushed about a month ago and 2.40.12 also about a month ago, alongside the 2.43.x line. This is a well-resourced, actively maintained project (University of Oslo/HISP Centre) with dense, overlapping release trains rather than a single thin cadence — clearly `active`, not slowing or dormant.
