name: Dialoqbase
source_description: Self-hosted chatbot builder with knowledge base and multi-provider LLM support
version_health_notes: Upstream repo (n4ze3m/dialoqbase) was archived by the owner on 2026-07-08 — about 4 weeks before today (2026-08-05) — and is now read-only. The maintainer's own README describes the project as "a side project" that "is not ready for production" and "may contain bugs and security issues." Release history before archival was fairly active (releases roughly monthly), so this is a hard stop, not a slow fade: v1.11.5 itself was a security fix (unauthenticated path traversal in `GET /api/v1/view/*`) with an explicit recommendation to rotate `DB_SECRET_KEY` post-upgrade, and there will be no further fixes. Ambiguity check: found two forks (elr9/dialoqbase-server, Cyberdeep/dialoqbase-1) that surface in search; both are plain forks of n4ze3m/dialoqbase with no evidence of independent active maintenance or a community takeover, not a separate active upstream to consider instead.
differentiation: Dialoqbase is a chatbot-builder (Chatbase-style): customers create named bots backed by ingested knowledge sources (PDF, URL, GitHub repo, sitemap, YouTube, Word docs) and can embed a widget, on top of a multi-provider LLM backend (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Fireworks, or local Ollama/ LocalAI). open-webui is a general chat frontend for local models. There would be real differentiation (build-a-bot vs. chat-with-a-model) if the project were alive.
usefulness_rationale: The feature gap is real, but shipping a recipe on top of an archived, admittedly-not-production-ready upstream with an unpatched-forever CVE history is exactly the risk this catalogue should avoid regardless of differentiation.
blocking_issues:
Upstream repository archived 2026-07-08 (read-only, no further security fixes) — v1.11.5 itself was a security patch, so this is not a project to build a recipe on regardless of the mechanism question.
Admin login has a fixed 'admin/admin' default with no env var to set it at deploy time (only changeable manually after first login) — not a hard blocker per se (Traefik basic_auth can gate it), but compounds the risk given no upstream fixes will ever land for that flow.
Multi-service stack (dialoqbase app + Postgres/pgvector + Redis + SearXNG) needing 4 containers just to reach first boot, for a feature set that's moot given the archival.
summary: Dialoqbase (n4ze3m/dialoqbase) is a Postgres/Redis/SearXNG-backed chatbot builder that would mechanically fit our recipe mechanism today — its only first-boot secrets are a server-generatable JWT key and a fixed default admin login that Traefik basic_auth can gate. It is not recommended anyway: the upstream repo was archived on 2026-07-08, about four weeks before this analysis, ending development for good and cutting off any future fix for a known unauthenticated path-traversal CVE class already found in v1.11.4/ v1.11.5. Building on a dead, admittedly-not-production-ready upstream would ship un-patchable risk into the catalogue for a feature gap (chatbot builder vs. open-webui's chat frontend) that's no longer worth taking on this codebase.

name: Dify
source_description: Open-source platform for building LLM applications with RAG, agents, and workflows
upstream_license: Dify Open Source License (Apache-2.0 based, with additional conditions restricting offering Dify itself as a multi-tenant SaaS to third parties without authorization) — source-available, not a plain OSI license
version_health_notes: Latest tag (1.16.1) was pushed ~9 days before today (2026-08-05); the 1.16.0 minor landed 2026-07-17 and 1.16.1 is a hotfix release on top of it. Project ships weekly patch releases and roughly monthly feature releases (1.16.0 introduced the new "Dify Agent" beta). No signs of slowdown — clearly active, well-maintained upstream.
differentiation: None of the 4 existing AI-category recipes (ollama, open-webui, hermes-agent, openclaw) offer this: Dify is a visual builder for multi-step LLM applications (agents, RAG knowledge bases, workflow orchestration, prompt/app publishing), closer to "n8n for LLM apps" than to a single chat UI or single-agent runtime. Ollama is a bare model runtime, Open WebUI is a chat front-end, hermes-agent/openclaw are fixed-persona messaging agents — none let a customer compose their own RAG pipeline or multi-step agent workflow. Genuine gap-filler.
usefulness_rationale: LLM app-builder platforms are a distinct and popular category (direct competitor set: n8n's AI nodes, Flowise, LangFlow) that IONOS AF currently has no equivalent for. Strong demand signal given the catalogue already leans into AI/automation (ollama, open-webui, hermes-agent, openclaw, n8n).
secrets_required_at_first_boot: POSTGRES_PASSWORD; REDIS_PASSWORD; SECRET_KEY; SANDBOX_API_KEY; PLUGIN_DAEMON_KEY; INNER_API_KEY_FOR_PLUGIN
summary: Dify boots cleanly with no customer-supplied secrets: every internal credential (DB/Redis passwords, SECRET_KEY, sandbox/plugin-daemon keys) is a random value the customer never needs to see, so it can be fully server-generated the same way n8n's POSTGRES_PASSWORD/N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY are today. Admin account creation follows the exact same "first visitor to the fresh domain completes the web setup wizard" pattern already accepted for n8n and Open WebUI — Dify's INIT_PASSWORD env var is optional and, left unset, skips the init-password prompt entirely, so there is no plaintext-password requirement blocking us. The catch is operational rather than mechanical: this is upstream's heaviest stack in the catalogue (nginx + web + api + worker + worker_beat + redis + postgres + sandbox + plugin_daemon, optionally a vector DB), needs a correspondingly high RAM floor, ships under a source-available (not pure OSI) license worth flagging to legal/product, and is functionally an empty shell until the customer adds their own LLM provider API key through Dify's own in-app settings post-login (no first-boot blocker, but worth calling out as a UX caveat). Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building, but scope the compose file carefully (drop optional vector-DB/agent-beta services not needed for a minimal working install) and flag the license terms before shipping.

name: Directus
source_description: Headless CMS that wraps databases with dynamic API and admin app
upstream_license: MSCL-1.0-GPL (Monospace Sustainable Core License v1.0, source-available, derived from the Fair Core License / former BSL). Converts to GPL-3.0 four years after each release. Free 'Core' tier for orgs under $5M annual revenue / 50 employees, no registration required; SSO, custom access-policy rules, and custom-LLM connections require a paid license key.
version_health_notes: Released 7 days before this analysis (2026-08-05) — active, roughly monthly cadence (12.0.0 on 2026-06-10, 12.1.0/12.1.1 on 2026-07-01, 12.2.0 on 2026-07-29). Not remotely dormant or EOL. The notable event is not release cadence but a license change: v12.0.0 (2026-06-10) switched from the prior Business Source License to MSCL-1.0-GPL and introduced active license-key enforcement for paid tiers.
differentiation: None of the 24 existing recipes cover a headless CMS / backend-as-a-service (dynamic REST+GraphQL API generated over a customer's own database, plus an admin app for schema and content management). Closest structural neighbors are n8n and paperless-ngx (both Postgres-backed single web app), but neither overlaps functionally — this would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue (build custom apps/APIs on top of a database) rather than a duplicate of automation, document management, or media tooling we already ship.
usefulness_rationale: Headless CMS is a real, distinct customer need (app/API backends, content modeling) with no current catalogue coverage, but the 2026-06 license change (see blocking_issues) makes "medium" rather than "high" the honest call until the legal question is resolved.
blocking_issues: Licensing/legal risk, not a technical mechanism gap: MSCL-1.0-GPL's "Competing Use" clause prohibits "making the Software available to any party ... that competes with the Licensor's commercial offerings," and the license text contains no carve-out for standard hosting providers or resellers offering it to their own customers. IONOS Application Factory packaging Directus as a one-click hosted recipe for third-party customers is plausibly exactly the "Competing Use" the clause targets (it would compete with Directus's own hosted/Cloud offering). This needs legal sign-off before a recipe ships, independent of whether the Core tier is technically free for the end customer.
summary: Directus is mechanically installable under the current recipe mechanism — its own admin login (ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_PASSWORD) fits the generated_from root-password projection exactly like Vaultwarden, and KEY/SECRET/DB_PASSWORD are ordinary server-generated secrets the customer never needs to see. The app itself is active and well-maintained (monthly releases). The blocker is not technical: as of v12.0.0 (2026-06-10) Directus ships under MSCL-1.0-GPL, a source-available license whose "Competing Use" restriction has no hosting-provider carve-out and plausibly prohibits exactly the use case of IONOS reselling it as a managed recipe to its own customers. Recommend not_recommended pending explicit legal review of that clause against AF's distribution model — flagging this as a real gap worth revisiting, not a dead end, if legal clears it or if we instead offer only the free "Core" tier under a documented revenue/headcount assumption.

name: Dittofeed
source_description: Open-source customer engagement platform for automated multi-channel messaging
upstream_docker_image: dittofeed/dittofeed-lite (all-in-one image; also requires postgres + clickhouse/clickhouse-server + temporalio/auto-setup as mandatory sidecars)
latest_version: v0.23.0 (stable); v0.24.0-alpha.17 (pre-release, most recent tag overall)
latest_release_date: 2025-11-30 (v0.23.0 stable); 2026-03-27 (v0.24.0-alpha.17, most recent tag of any kind)
version_health_notes: The project has never cut a stable release past v0.23.0 (2025-11-30); everything since has shipped only as v0.24.0-alpha.N pre-releases, itself a sign the 0.24 line has been stuck in alpha for 9+ months. Alpha releases and commits to `main` were frequent through Dec 2025-Mar 2026 (multiple alphas some weeks apart), but the most recent commit of any kind is v0.24.0-alpha.17 on 2026-03-27 — as of today (2026-08-05) that is just over 4 months with zero commits, following what had been a fairly active cadence. Not old enough to call archived/EOL, but the sudden 4+ month silence right after a busy stretch is a real slowdown worth flagging, not a project I'd call confidently `active` right now.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does customer-engagement messaging (multi-channel email/SMS/push/WhatsApp/Slack campaigns, segmentation, and journey/workflow builders driven by user events). n8n covers generic workflow automation but has no concept of customer segments, message templates, or engagement journeys; it would be a genuinely new category (marketing/CRM-adjacent) rather than a repeat of an existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiator for a segment (small marketing/growth teams, indie SaaS builders) not served by anything else we carry, and it has a proper dashboard web UI. Capped at medium because the self-hosted "lite" stack is heavy for what it does (Postgres + ClickHouse + Temporal + the app itself — 4 containers just to boot) and the product's own alpha-for-9-months status makes it a riskier long-term bet than a mature single-purpose tool.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: POSTGRES_PASSWORD; CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD; SECRET_KEY; basic_auth gate credential
summary: Dittofeed is mechanically installable today: run it in the default `anonymous` auth mode (no app-level login at all, same posture as Adminer/n8n-without-basic-auth) and put the mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the dashboard/API instead of using the app's own `single-tenant` mode — that mode's `PASSWORD` env var wants a plaintext shared password with no hash-projection support, which `generated_from` cannot supply, so anonymous-mode + Traefik gate is the only expressible path, not a blocker. All internal creds (Postgres, ClickHouse, the session `SECRET_KEY`) are server-generated with no customer input needed. The real caveats are shape and momentum: the self-hosted "lite" stack still needs 4 containers (app + Postgres + ClickHouse + Temporal) to reach first boot — closer to immich/anytype in complexity than our single-container recipes — and the upstream has gone quiet for 4+ months after a busy Dec 2025-Mar 2026 stretch, with no stable release past v0.23.0 and the 0.24 line still alpha-only. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth adding for the genuine customer-engagement gap it fills, but watch the release cadence before committing — if the silence continues past another quarter, revisit as a potential dormant/maintenance-only call.

name: Diun
source_description: Docker Image Update Notifier to receive notifications when images are updated
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release v4.33.0 (2026-05-30, ~2 months before this analysis on 2026-08-05). Commit history shows ongoing activity through 2026-07-11 (~1 month before this analysis), including dependency bumps and small feature work (containerd provider, healthcheck command), so the repo is maintained, not dormant. v4.31.0 (2025-12-24) to v4.32.0 (2026-05-28) was roughly a 5-month gap, a normal cadence for this project, with v4.33.0 following two days later. Treat the project as active.
differentiation: None found. Diun is a headless watcher: it polls Docker Hub/registries (or the local Docker/Swarm/Kubernetes/Nomad/containerd/file provider) for new tags or digest changes and fires an outbound notification (Slack, Discord, Telegram, Gotify, webhook, etc.) — it has no web UI, no API to browse results, and no update-apply mechanism. `recipes/wud/` already covers this exact use case (Docker image update monitoring) plus a web UI and a one-click "apply the update" trigger, which is strictly more capability for the same job. Diun would be a straight subset of an existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: A customer who wants "tell me when my containers have updates available" already has WUD in the catalogue with more functionality (UI + apply). Diun's only differentiator — being a lighter headless agent — isn't a customer-facing benefit in this catalogue, since WUD is currently shipped `enabled: false` as an auto-injected companion rather than something the customer picks and pays attention to for its footprint.
blocking_issues:
Diun has no web UI and no login of its own, so there is nothing to gate with generated_from root-password projection or a meaningful Traefik basic_auth front door (it exposes no HTTP endpoint to guard).
Diun is only useful once configured with an outbound notification provider (Slack webhook URL, Discord webhook, Telegram bot token, Gotify URL/token, generic webhook, etc.) — an arbitrary, customer-chosen external credential with no /compose input channel today. Shipping it without one means it runs and finds updates but can never tell the customer, which defeats the app's entire purpose.
Needs read access to the Docker socket (or Swarm/Kubernetes/Nomad API) to enumerate running containers, same class of privileged mount already accepted for wud, not a new blocker on its own.
summary: Diun is a well-maintained, MIT-licensed headless Docker image update notifier, but it duplicates functionality `recipes/wud/` already provides with a superset of features (web UI, one-click apply) — there's no customer-facing gap it fills. It also has no built-in auth surface to gate and no way to configure its one essential input (an outbound notification-provider credential) through the current /compose mechanism, so even setting overlap aside it can't ship as a working recipe today. Not recommended.

name: Dkron
source_description: Distributed, fault-tolerant cron-style job scheduler with web UI and REST API
upstream_license: LGPL-3.0 (core/free edition; "Dkron Pro" auth/ACL/executor add-ons are commercial)
version_health_notes: ~2 weeks since v4.1.2 (2026-07-22) as of today (2026-08-05). Release history is regular: v4.1.0 (2026-03-30) → v4.1.1 (2026-05-12) → v4.1.2 (2026-07-22), roughly every 6-8 weeks, with active dependency-bump and bugfix commits in between. No signs of archival, maintenance-only mode, or EOL — this is a healthy, actively developed project.
differentiation: Dkron is a standalone distributed job scheduler (cron replacement) with a web dashboard and REST API for defining, scheduling, and monitoring recurring jobs/commands across one or more nodes. n8n covers workflow automation triggered by events/integrations, but nothing in the current catalogue provides a dedicated cron/job-scheduling UI. It would be a genuinely new capability rather than a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Useful for customers who want a reliable, UI-driven replacement for server cron jobs (retries, execution history, alerting on failure), but it's a narrower, more technical audience than general-purpose apps in the catalogue — most customers who need scheduling already get it via n8n triggers or their own crontab. Single-node deployment (no real cluster) also gives up most of Dkron's headline fault-tolerance value, so the pitch is closer to "cron with a nice UI" than the full distributed-system use case.
blocking_issues: The free/open-source edition of Dkron (LGPL) ships with no authentication of its own — the web UI and REST API are open to anyone who can reach the port. Web UI auth, API auth, and ACLs are "Dkron Pro" commercial features (~$450/year), not available in the image we'd ship. This is mechanically solvable today via a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the app (same pattern as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI), so it is not a hard blocker, but the recipe MUST NOT expose Dkron's own port without that gate given it has zero built-in access control.
summary: Dkron is an actively maintained (v4.1.2, 2026-07-22), LGPL-licensed distributed job scheduler with an official Docker image and a proper web UI + REST API — no overlap with anything currently in the catalogue. The free edition has zero built-in authentication (auth/ACLs are a paid "Dkron Pro" add-on), so it must ship behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate to avoid an open-to-the-internet job scheduler; that mechanism is already supported today, so it is installable, just with the caveat that the whole app, not just an admin panel, sits behind the gate. Clustering (its main fault-tolerance selling point) needs multiple nodes and isn't practical in a single-instance recipe, so the value proposition narrows to "cron replacement with a UI and retry/history tracking" — reasonable to build, but medium rather than high priority.

name: docassemble
source_description: Open-source expert system for guided interviews and automated document assembly
version_health_notes: Latest tag 1.10.7 pushed 2026-08-01, 4 days before this analysis (2026-08-05). Release history shows near-weekly cadence through 2026 (1.10.0 on 2026-06-28, then 1.10.1 through 1.10.7 roughly every few days to a week through early August). Actively maintained by a single lead maintainer (jhpyle); no signs of dormancy, archival, or EOL. Note: the upstream GitHub repo has no tagged "Releases" (empty Releases page) — version history is tracked via the changelog on docassemble.org and Docker Hub / PyPI tags instead, not GitHub Releases.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers guided-interview / document-assembly ("expert system" that walks an end user through a Q&A interview and generates filled legal/business documents from templates). Paperless-ngx is the closest structural neighbor (Postgres- backed single web app) but solves a different problem — archiving and searching existing documents, not generating new ones from an interview flow. This would be a genuinely new category (document generation / legal-tech tooling) rather than a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct niche (law firms, HR, compliance teams automating form generation) with no current coverage, but it's a narrower, more specialized audience than most of the existing catalogue (e.g. n8n, Vaultwarden) and comes with meaningfully heavier resource needs (4GB RAM, 40GB disk minimum) for a single-purpose app.
blocking_issues:
DA_ADMIN_PASSWORD, the container's initial-admin-login mechanism, only accepts a plaintext password at first boot (used to create the admin account, then upstream docs recommend deleting it) — there is no option to supply a pre-hashed value in any algorithm. Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md, generated_from only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext itself, so this is a genuine structural blocker rather than an "unsupported algorithm" case: no channel exists today to get a customer-specific admin password into this app.

DA_ADMIN_API_KEY (optional but recommended for programmatic access) is an arbitrary API key with no customer input channel either, though it is not required to boot.
summary: docassemble is active and well-maintained (near-weekly releases, latest 2026-08-01), MIT-licensed, and fills a genuine gap in the catalogue (guided-interview document assembly, nothing comparable in the current 24 recipes). It is also reverse-proxy-compatible: BEHINDHTTPSLOADBALANCER=true plus USEHTTPS=false lets it sit cleanly behind Traefik with no internal TLS termination needed. The blocker is the admin-login mechanism: unlike Vaultwarden-style apps that accept a pre-hashed admin credential, docassemble's DA_ADMIN_PASSWORD only takes a plaintext password at container init, which the current /compose mechanism has no channel to supply (generated_from only ever carries a hash). Revisit once the platform supports projecting a plaintext value derived from the customer's root password, or if upstream adds a hashed-password init option.

name: Docker Registry
source_description: Private Docker registry for storing and distributing container images
version_health_notes: v3.1.1 (2026-05-01) is ~3 months old as of 2026-08-05. The v3 line reached stable in April 2026 (v3.0.0 on 2026-04-03) after a run of release candidates through late 2025/early 2026, with v3.1.0 following within days and v3.1.1 a few weeks later — a healthy, tightening cadence, not a stale project. Recent releases close CVEs, and the repo (formerly docker/distribution, now under the CNCF-adjacent distribution/ org) shows ongoing multi-contributor activity. Not ambiguous: this is the canonical OCI registry implementation behind the official `registry` Docker Hub image; not to be confused with third-party registry UIs (e.g. Joxit/docker-registry-ui) which are separate optional add-ons, not the registry itself.
differentiation: Gitea (already in the catalogue) ships a built-in OCI-compatible container/package registry as one of its many features, which covers the "push/pull private images" use case for anyone already running Gitea. Docker Registry is a dedicated, standalone alternative for customers who want just a registry without a full git forge attached — lighter weight, single purpose, and usable independently of any git hosting choice.
usefulness_rationale: Real but narrow demand (teams wanting a private image registry without Docker Hub/GHCR), further narrowed by Gitea already covering the same need for anyone using it as their git host. It's also a headless HTTP API with no web UI at all — a customer manages it purely via `docker login`/`push`/`pull`, so there's nothing to browse in the AF app catalogue beyond a working endpoint.
summary: Docker Registry (the `registry:3.1.1` official image) is a single container, single HTTP port (5000) service with no login or web UI of its own — upstream's own docs document running it behind a reverse proxy for TLS termination, which fits our Traefik-fronted model directly. It has no built-in admin auth mechanism reachable via our `generated_from` root-password projection (its own htpasswd-based auth requires customer-uploaded credential files, not a single hashed parameter), so the correct gate is the same Traefik `basic_auth: true` pattern used for Adminer/n8n, with the registry's own `REGISTRY_AUTH=htpasswd` left disabled since Traefik becomes the actual auth boundary. Mechanically installable today, but low differentiation given Gitea already provides an equivalent container registry, and the headless nature (no UI, CLI-only `docker push`/`pull` workflow) makes it a poor fit for a customer-facing app catalogue tile. Recommend building only with those caveats flagged, not as a priority addition.

name: Dockge
source_description: Dockge is a fancy, easy-to-use, and reactive self-hosted Docker Compose stack manager
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release is 1.5.0 (2025-03-30) — about 16 months before today (2026-08-05) with no tagged release since. The `1` and `latest` Docker Hub tags still point at that same 1.5.0 build, over a year stale. However, commits to `master` continued well past that tag (feature work like container control buttons and resource-usage stats, plus an XSS fix, as recently as 2026-04-19, ~3.5 months before today), and a `nightly` image tag is rebuilt continuously (within the last day). So the project is not dormant or abandoned — it's the same author/pattern as Uptime Kuma — but the versioned release train has stalled for well over a year while development moved to nightly-only builds, which is a real slowdown worth calling out rather than "active".
differentiation: Dockge is narrowly focused on editing and operating docker-compose.yaml stacks directly (compose editor with terminal, .env editing, multi-agent remote stacks, git-style file layout under /opt/stacks) rather than being a general Docker API management console. `recipes/portainer/` already covers the broader "web GUI for Docker" space (images, volumes, networks, RBAC/teams) and, being a heavier full Docker/Swarm management tool, is a superset of what Dockge offers for the specific "manage my compose stacks" job. Note portainer currently ships `enabled: false` in this catalogue, so there is no live customer-facing redundancy today, only a structural overlap against a disabled recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful for a customer who wants to run their own docker-compose stacks alongside AF recipes on the same Docker host and prefers a lightweight, purpose-built compose editor over Portainer's heavier full-Docker-management surface. Capped at medium because the value proposition is narrow (a nicer UI over `docker compose` commands) and it meaningfully overlaps an existing recipe's job, even though that recipe is currently disabled.
summary: Dockge is a single-container app (no database) exposing one HTTP port (5001) — directly Traefik-compatible on dockge.<base_domain>. Like Uptime Kuma and Actual Budget (same author's pattern), it ships with no default or env-var-based credential: on first browser visit it presents a setup screen where the customer creates their own admin username/password directly in the app UI, so af-api needs to pass no customer-specific secret at all — this clears the current /compose constraint with zero blocking issues, same as those two recipes. The app does need a read/write mount of the Docker socket (same privileged mount class already accepted for portainer and wud) to manage compose stacks. The two real caveats are: (1) meaningful functional overlap with the already-cataloged (but disabled) portainer recipe — both are "web UI over Docker" tools, and (2) the versioned release train has stalled for 16+ months (last tag 1.5.0, 2025-03-30) even though master/nightly development is ongoing, so the stable Docker Hub tag customers would pin to is over a year old. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically installable today and a lighter, compose-specific alternative to Portainer, but worth weighing against simply re-enabling portainer, and worth re-checking whether a new tagged release ships before committing engineering time.

name: Docmost
source_description: Collaborative wiki and documentation platform with real-time editing
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (Community Edition core); separate Enterprise Edition license for paid add-ons (SSO/SAML, LDAP, AI, advanced importers) — not required for or bundled into core functionality
version_health_notes: v0.95.0 shipped 2026-07-03 — 33 days before today (2026-08-05). Preceding history is dense: v0.90.1 (2026-05-28), v0.90.0 (2026-05-21), v0.80.2 (2026-05-02), v0.80.1 (2026-04-28), v0.80.0 (2026-04-14), v0.71.1 (2026-04-05), v0.71.0 (2026-03-31) — multiple releases most months, no gap over ~5 weeks anywhere in the last year. Repo is not archived, issues/discussions actively triaged. Clearly active, pre-1.0 but maturing steadily.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a wiki/knowledge-base or real-time collaborative-docs tool. Gitea hosts git repos and OpenGist hosts snippets, but neither gives a browsable, structured, multi-user wiki with live co-editing. Within this gap-analysis pass alone, several other wiki/docs-shaped candidates have already surfaced — BookStack (apps-gaps/bookstack.yaml, structured books/chapters/pages), An Otter Wiki (apps-gaps/an-otter-wiki.yaml, lightweight git-backed Markdown), CodiMD (apps-gaps/codimd.yaml, frozen upstream image), AFFiNE (apps-gaps/affine.yaml, docs + whiteboard + database, EE-licensing concern), and Colanode (apps-gaps/colanode.yaml, chat + pages + databases, stalled release cadence). Docmost's specific angle is a polished, actively-developed Notion/Confluence-style real-time collaborative wiki (live multi-cursor editing, nested pages, spaces with granular permissions, full-text search, diagram embeds) with a clean AGPL-3.0 core and no EE code required for baseline functionality — unlike AFFiNE's Enterprise-Edition-licensed self-host image. Among the wiki- shaped candidates surfaced so far, Docmost is the most directly "real-time collaborative Confluence/Notion alternative" positioned one, distinct from BookStack's static-hierarchy and An Otter Wiki's git-backed single-editor models.
usefulness_rationale: Team wikis/documentation with live co-editing are a very common self-hosting request, and Docmost is a modern, actively developed, cleanly-licensed (AGPL-3.0 core, no EE dependency for core features) option with growing name recognition as a Confluence/Notion alternative. It is a genuine, currently-unfilled gap in the catalogue.
summary: Docmost ships an official image (docmost/docmost, pinned e.g. v0.95.0) paired with a required Postgres 18 and Redis 8 sidecar (same Postgres-plus-cache shape as n8n/paperless-ngx), serving its UI on a single HTTP port (3000) — fully Traefik-compatible. Its boot-time needs are DATABASE_URL (carries the Postgres password) and APP_SECRET (a 32+ char signing key), both patternless secrets nothing customer-facing ever reads, so both can be server-generated with no customer input channel needed. The app itself has no admin- provisioning env var: like An Otter Wiki, the first visitor to reach a fresh instance is walked through a public setup screen that creates the first workspace and admin account — meaning an anonymous visitor could claim the admin account before the customer does if left open. Per the pattern already applied to An Otter Wiki/n8n/WUD in this catalogue, that is resolved with a mandatory Traefik basic_auth:true gate (projected from the customer's root password via generated_from) in front of the app until the customer completes their own setup. That clears the /compose constraint today with zero hard blocking issues — installable_today — and the Community Edition core is cleanly AGPL-3.0 with no Enterprise-Edition code required to boot (unlike AFFiNE's EE-licensed self-host image). Release cadence is unambiguously active. Still a workaround for the app's own missing boot-time admin credential rather than a clean built-in mechanism, hence build_with_caveats rather than a plain build_now.

name: Documenso
source_description: Open-source document signing platform for digital signatures
upstream_docker_image: documenso/documenso, pin to a semver tag e.g. v2.16.0 — do not use :latest
version_health_notes: v2.16.0 published 2026-07-21, ~15 days before this analysis (2026-08-05). No archived flag, no deprecation notice, active upstream org (documenso.com is a funded commercial entity running the same OSS core as a hosted SaaS).
differentiation: E-signature / document-signing workflow (a "DocuSign alternative") is a distinct category not covered by any of the current 24 recipes. paperless-ngx and paperless-ai are document *archiving and OCR* tools — they don't provide a signer workflow, audit trail, or certificate-based digital signatures. Documenso would be a genuinely new capability for the catalogue rather than a variant of something we already ship.
usefulness_rationale: Digital signing is a common SMB/professional need with no existing catalogue entry, and Documenso is an actively maintained, single-image, Traefik-compatible web app — a good structural fit if not for the email-relay blocker described below.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: POSTGRES_PASSWORD; NEXTAUTH_SECRET; NEXT_PRIVATE_ENCRYPTION_KEY; NEXT_PRIVATE_ENCRYPTION_SECONDARY_KEY; NEXT_PRIVATE_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE; SMTP_CREDENTIALS
blocking_issues:
Documenso requires a working SMTP relay (NEXT_PRIVATE_SMTP_HOST, NEXT_PRIVATE_SMTP_USERNAME, NEXT_PRIVATE_SMTP_PASSWORD, plus a from-address) to send the signup email-verification message and, more fundamentally, to send signature-request emails to signers — the core workflow the app exists for. This is the customer's own external mail provider's credentials, not something af-api derives or generates; it has no projection mechanism today (not generated_from, not basic_auth, not server-generatable).

Admin access is not exposed via any env var or setup wizard at all — upstream docs state every signup produces a regular user account and "admin access must be granted directly in the database." This is actually a non-issue for installability (core document-signing use doesn't require an admin role, and no first-boot admin secret is needed), noted here only so a reviewer isn't surprised there's no ADMIN_TOKEN-style parameter to add.

The .p12 signing certificate itself is not a blocker: upstream docs confirm a self-signed cert + random passphrase can be generated entirely server-side at install time (openssl req/pkcs12), with no customer-visible value — this is mechanically identical to the server_generated_no_customer_input secrets above and would be handled the same way in install.sh, not a genuine third-party dependency like SMTP.
summary: Documenso is an actively maintained, single-image, Traefik-fit web app that would fill a real gap in the catalogue (no existing e-signature recipe). The blocker is narrow and specific: it needs a customer-supplied external SMTP relay for signup verification and signature-request emails, which is the app's core function and has no input channel under the current /compose mechanism (not a root-password-hash projection, not a basic_auth gate). Everything else at first boot — DB password, NextAuth secret, encryption keys, and even the .p12 signing certificate passphrase — can be generated entirely server-side. Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit once /compose gains a channel for customer-supplied third-party credentials (e.g. an SMTP-relay input), which would likely unblock a useful, differentiated recipe.

name: Dograh
source_description: Open-source no-code platform for building AI voice agents in minutes
version_health_notes: 4 days since v1.44.0 (2026-08-01) as of today (2026-08-05). Release history is dense and regular: v1.43.0 (2026-07-25) → v1.42.0 (2026-07-15) → v1.41.0 (2026-07-06) → v1.40.0 (2026-07-03), roughly weekly ships going back over a year (1.34.0 → 1.44.0 tags all present on Docker Hub). No signs of slowdown, archival, or maintenance-only mode — this is a young, fast-moving, well-maintained project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does voice AI / telephony. n8n covers general workflow automation and Open WebUI/Ollama cover text-based local LLM chat, but Dograh's core value (inbound/outbound phone calls handled by an LLM-driven voice agent, visual call-flow builder, telephony provider integration) is a genuinely new capability class, not a duplicate of anything shipped today.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiator for customers who specifically want self-hosted voice AI, but it's a narrow, technical use case (needs a telephony provider account like Twilio/Telnyx/Vonage to originate real calls, plus BYOK for LLM/TTS/STT to move past the bundled defaults) and a heavier deployment than most of the catalogue — self-hosting docs recommend 8 GB RAM / 4 vCPU for a "remote" (public, real-call-capable) deployment, well above most existing recipes' footprint.
blocking_issues:
Dograh's own auth is self-service signup/login (local JWT, no customer-set admin password we could hash and project via `generated_from`). Same pattern as n8n's owner-setup flow: whoever reaches the URL first can create the first (owner) account, so the recipe needs a Traefik `basic_auth` gate as an interim shield until the customer completes signup — not a hard blocker given IF-1312, but worth flagging since ENABLE_SIGNUP defaults to open registration.

Upstream's own `docker-compose.yaml` is explicitly not self-contained: it depends on a setup script (`dograh-init` / `scripts/setup_remote.sh`) to render nginx and coturn configuration before `docker compose up` will come up correctly for a public ("remote") deployment — the repo's own comments warn a fresh checkout "will fail or come up misconfigured" without it. Portable to our install.sh, but meaningfully more setup logic than a typical single-compose recipe.

Real (non-demo) voice-agent functionality requires coturn (WebRTC TURN relay) exposed on TCP 3478/5349 plus a wide UDP ephemeral range (49152-49200) for actual call media — not a single HTTP port behind Traefik. Expressible as extra public ports (same pattern as `wg-easy`'s UDP 51820), so not structurally blocking, but it does mean this is not a clean reverse-proxy-only app the way most of the catalogue is.

Placing/receiving real phone calls also requires the customer's own telephony provider account (Twilio/Telnyx/Vonage/Plivo) and optionally their own LLM/TTS/STT keys to move past Dograh's bundled defaults — those are runtime, in-app BYOK settings entered after login (not a first-boot secret), so they don't block `installable_today`, but they do mean the app is much less useful out-of-the-box without post-provision customer setup.
summary: Dograh is an actively and rapidly maintained (weekly releases, v1.44.0 as of 2026-08-01), BSD-2-Clause self-hosted voice-AI platform with an official pinned Docker image and no overlap with anything currently in the catalogue — it would be the first voice/telephony recipe. It clears the installability bar (no first-boot secret needs an unsupported input channel; the open-signup landgrab risk is coverable with a Traefik basic_auth gate, same as n8n), but it's a heavier, messier fit than a typical recipe: upstream's compose file needs a companion setup script to render nginx/coturn config, real call functionality needs a wide raw UDP port range for WebRTC media relay, recommended sizing (8GB/4vCPU) is above the catalogue norm, and the product isn't very useful until the customer brings their own telephony/LLM/TTS/STT credentials post-install. Worth building, but as a caveated, higher-effort recipe rather than a quick win.

name: DOMjudge
source_description: Open-source automated programming contest judge for ICPC-style competitions
version_health_notes: 9.0.1 released 2026-06-11 (~2 months before this analysis on 2026-08-05); 9.0.0 released 2025-10-05; 8.3.0 released 2024-05-31. Roughly annual major releases with patch releases in between, consistent history since the project's 2004 founding, actively maintained by the ICPC/DOMjudge community (used to run real ICPC regional/world finals). No signs of slowdown or archival. Note: 9.0.1 is the latest source-level release (2026-06-11, per domjudge.org/download), but no domjudge/domserver Docker image has been built/pushed for 9.0.1 as of this analysis; the latest pullable Docker Hub tag is 9.0.0 (pushed 2026-07-31), which is what upstream.docker_image pins.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches programming-contest judging or automated code execution/grading. Closest neighbors (gitea, opengist) are source-control/snippet tools, not contest infrastructure. DOMjudge would be a genuinely new category (education/competitive- programming) if it were mechanically deployable.
usefulness_rationale: Real niche demand (university clubs, ICPC regional organizers) but a narrow, one-off use case (spin up for a contest, tear down after) rather than an always-on self-hosted app, and it needs the multi-container setup below just to boot, which raises the bar versus most of the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
No env var or config option lets the deployer set the initial `admin` account password. The domserver container generates a random password on first boot and writes it to /opt/domjudge/domserver/etc/initial_admin_password.secret inside the container (or prints it to container logs) — retrieval requires `docker exec`/log access our customers don't have. There is no `generated_from` channel: the app doesn't accept a supplied hash or plaintext for this field, it always generates its own, so we have no way to either set it to the customer's root-password hash or to surface the generated value to the customer afterward.

Requires a second container type (judgehost) running with `privileged: true` and host cgroup mounts (/sys/fs/cgroup) to sandbox and execute untrusted contestant-submitted code. This is a fundamentally different trust/isolation requirement than any current recipe and is a platform-level (not just secrets-mechanism) blocker on shared multi-tenant infrastructure, independent of the admin- password issue above.

Needs an external MySQL/MariaDB database (not bundled in the official image), adding a required extra service beyond the domserver + judgehost pair.
summary: DOMjudge is a mature, actively maintained (9.0.1, 2026-06-11) contest- judging system with no equivalent in our catalogue, but it fails the current recipe mechanism on two independent grounds: its admin login password is server-generated with no way for us to set it via generated_from or to hand the generated value back to the customer, and its judgehost component requires privileged containers with host cgroup access to sandbox untrusted code, which is a container-isolation requirement well beyond what our reverse-proxy/Traefik model or multi-tenant hosting was designed for. Even setting the secrets-channel gap aside, the privileged-container requirement alone makes this unsuitable for the current platform. Not recommended to build until both a customer-facing credential channel and a policy for privileged contest-judging workloads exist.

name: Dragonfly
source_description: High-performance Redis-compatible in-memory data store for modern hardware
upstream_license: BUSL-1.1 (converts to Apache-2.0 on 2029-03-01) — source-available, not OSI open source
version_health_notes: Latest tag v1.40.0 landed 2026-08-03, 2 days before today (2026-08-05). The `i1.39.x` incremental line (i1.39.3 through i1.39.11) shipped roughly every few days through June-July 2026, so cadence between minor/patch cuts is close to weekly. Repo is not archived, commits and releases are current as of this week — clearly active development.
differentiation: Dragonfly is not an end-user application — it is a Redis/Memcached protocol-compatible in-memory data store with no admin UI, meant to be a backend dependency for other software. The catalogue already consumes Redis internally as a bundled, non-customer-facing dependency inside recipes/paperless-ngx and recipes/immich, but no existing recipe offers a standalone key-value store as a customer-facing product, so there's no direct recipe-to-recipe duplication. The gap it would fill is a raw infra primitive (a cache/datastore for the customer's own external applications), not a turnkey self-hosted app like the rest of the 24-recipe catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Useful only to a developer audience that wants a managed Redis- compatible cache/store for their own external code — it has no web UI, no built-in account system, and nothing to click into after install. That's a fundamentally different shape of product than the rest of the catalogue (turnkey apps end users interact with directly), and it conflicts with the platform's HTTP-first, Traefik-fronted install model (see installability below).
blocking_issues:
Dragonfly speaks the raw Redis wire protocol over a single TCP port (6379) — it is not HTTP, so it cannot sit behind Traefik on <slug>.<base_domain> the way every other recipe does, and Traefik's basic_auth middleware (HTTP-layer only) cannot gate it.
Dragonfly has no admin login or web UI of its own, so there is no metadata parameter to project a `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` hash into — its auth (--requirepass / DFLY_requirepass) expects a literal plaintext credential compared directly against client connections, which af-api never forwards (only hashes).
A server-generated random password (mechanism: server_generated_no_customer_input) would satisfy 'don't ship it wide open,' but defeats the app's purpose: the whole point of a customer installing a data store is to hand that credential to their own external client code, and there is no channel today for the customer to ever retrieve a server-generated secret post-install.
Net effect: either the port ships open with no auth (unacceptable for a raw TCP service reachable from the internet), or it ships with a password the customer can never learn and therefore can never use — both are blockers under the current mechanism.
summary: Dragonfly (docker.dragonflydb.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly, latest v1.40.0, actively released as of 2026-08-03) is a fast, Redis/Memcached-wire- compatible in-memory store, not a customer-facing application — it has no web UI and speaks a raw TCP protocol rather than HTTP, so it cannot be fronted by Traefik the way the rest of the catalogue is, and there is no channel today (no admin login to project a root-password hash into, no HTTP layer for basic_auth) to give the customer a usable connection credential without either leaving the port open or generating a secret they can never retrieve. Redis-compatible caching is already consumed internally, out of customer sight, by recipes/paperless-ngx and recipes/immich, so the practical need this would serve is already met where it matters. Not recommended as a standalone catalogue recipe under the current mechanism, and even setting the mechanism aside, a headless data-store primitive is a poor fit for a catalogue of turnkey self- hosted apps aimed at end users rather than developers standing up their own backend infrastructure.

name: Drupal
source_description: Open-source CMS for building and managing dynamic websites
version_health_notes: 11.3.16 (a Drupal 10/11-cycle patch release) shipped 2026-07-23, ~2 weeks before this analysis on 2026-08-05. Drupal core follows a published semver-ish release-cycle policy: scheduled minor releases roughly twice a year, patch/security releases on a near-monthly cadence, all tracked publicly at drupal.org/about/core/policies/core-release-cycles/schedule. Drupal 12.0.0 is on the published schedule for the week of 2026-08-10 (days after this analysis). Older majors are being sunset on schedule, not abandoned: Drupal 9 reached EOL in November 2023, Drupal 10 is scheduled for EOL 2026-12-09 as Drupal 11/12 take over. The project (founded 2001, one of the largest OSS CMS communities, used for gov/enterprise sites worldwide) shows no slowdown; the official docker-library/drupal image is kept in step with core releases (Docker Hub official image, 100M+ pulls).
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is a general-purpose website CMS — closest neighbors (gitea, opengist) are developer/source-control tools, not content-management for a public-facing site. Drupal would fill a real gap for customers who want to build/manage a blog, brochure site, or larger structured-content site without hand-coding, which is exactly the kind of workload Hostinger's shared/VPS customers already look for.
usefulness_rationale: CMS is one of the most commonly requested self-hosted app categories and Drupal is a top-3 open-source CMS by install base, well beyond a niche audience. High customer pull if it can actually be installed through our current mechanism.
blocking_issues:
Drupal has no first-boot flow that accepts a pre-supplied credential for its own admin account in a form our platform can produce. The official image ships no env var for this; the only supported paths are (a) the interactive browser install wizard, where a human types a password into a form field, or (b) `drush site-install --account-pass=<plaintext>`, which requires the **plaintext** password — Drush hashes it internally and writes it to Drupal's own `users_field_data.pass` column using Drupal's password-hashing scheme (a `$S$`-prefixed PHPass/bcrypt-hybrid format), not a raw bcrypt/argon2 digest. `generated_from` only ever produces a bare bcrypt/argon2 hash of the root password — it cannot be written directly into that column (wrong format) and the plaintext root password is never available to project into `--account-pass`. There is no algorithm-support gap to add here (unlike a case where Drupal simply used raw bcrypt); the app-side format itself is incompatible with a bare-hash input.

Gating the whole site behind Traefik `basic_auth` (our fallback for apps with no login of their own) doesn't resolve this the way it does for e.g. Adminer or WUD: Drupal customers need an ongoing, distinct admin/editor login to manage their own content after install, not just a one-time gate to keep the install page private. A `basic_auth` wrapper only hides the problem; it doesn't give the customer a way to actually log into their new site's admin UI.
summary: Drupal is an actively maintained, high-usefulness CMS with no equivalent in our current 24-recipe catalogue, a single reverse-proxy-compatible HTTP port, and an official, regularly updated Docker image — mechanically it looks like an easy build. The blocker is entirely on the secrets side: Drupal's admin account can only be created with a plaintext password (via the interactive installer or `drush site-install --account-pass`), and its own password-hash format is incompatible with the bare bcrypt/argon2 hash `generated_from` produces, so there is no channel today to give the customer a working admin login. Recommend revisiting once either a plaintext-projection channel exists or Drupal's install path adds support for pre-hashed credentials.

summary: DSpace is an active, well-maintained project (dspace-10.0, 2026-05-28) filling a real gap — institutional repository / research digital preservation — with no equivalent in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It is mechanically installable today only via a workaround: DSpace has no admin-account input channel of its own (CLI-only, plaintext-password, no env var), so the recipe would need to seed a fixed, non-customer-facing admin password at first boot and rely on a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password projected) as the real customer-facing auth boundary, following the same precedent used for DolphinScheduler/Adminer-style fixed defaults. usefulness_rationale: DuckDNS's value proposition (tracking a customer's own dynamic IP) is largely moot on a hosted cloud VM with a static address and a platform-managed domain already provided at install time.
blocking_issues:
TOKEN is the customer's own DuckDNS account API token, generated on duckdns.org after they sign in (e.g. via GitHub/Google/Reddit OAuth) and tied to their personal subdomain(s) there. It is an arbitrary external third-party credential, not a hash of the server root password and not something af-api can generate or derive — there is no `generated_from`/basic_auth channel that can supply it.

SUBDOMAINS (the DuckDNS subdomain name(s) to update) is also a customer-chosen value tied to their duckdns.org account, with the same no-input-channel problem.

The container exposes no HTTP port and has no web UI or login of its own to gate with Traefik basic_auth — it's a headless background updater, so there is nothing to front with the reverse-proxy pattern even if the token problem were solved.
summary: DuckDNS is a headless dynamic-DNS updater requiring a customer-supplied, third-party DuckDNS account token and subdomain name — both external credentials with no projection mechanism under the current /compose constraint, and it exposes no web UI to gate instead. Even setting the installability problem aside, its core purpose (tracking a changing home IP) doesn't map onto AF's fixed-IP, platform-domain-assigned VMs, so it would add little value even if a token input channel existed. Recommend not_recommended.

blocking_issues:
Duplicati's web UI login is set via the plaintext DUPLICATI__WEBSERVICE_PASSWORD env var. Server-side, `SetWebserverPassword()` (Duplicati/Library/RestAPI/Database/ServerSettings.cs) takes the raw password and PBKDF2-hashes it internally — it does not accept a pre-hashed value as input, and the same method explicitly throws ("Disabling password protection is not supported") if the value is empty, so the login cannot be turned off either. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel to seed this credential with something the customer can actually log in with.

Fronting the app with Traefik `basic_auth` does not substitute for this the way it does for a login-less app (e.g. Adminer): Duplicati has a real, mandatory admin login gating the backup-configuration UI the customer needs to use, not a bare unauthenticated tool. Setting DUPLICATI__WEBSERVICE_PASSWORD to a server-generated random value nobody communicates to the customer would lock them out of the app's primary function (configuring and monitoring backups) even with basic_auth in front — unlike a backing-service secret (DB password, JWT key) the customer never needs to interact with directly.
summary: Duplicati would fill a genuine gap — the catalogue has no dedicated encrypted-backup-to-cloud recipe — and upstream is actively released (stable tag ~4 weeks old, canary/beta channels shipping roughly weekly). It's a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8200) web app that would sit cleanly behind Traefik. However, its own admin login only accepts a plaintext password (hashed internally with PBKDF2, no pre-hashed input path, and disabling it is explicitly unsupported in the source), so `generated_from`'s hash-only projection cannot seed a login the customer can actually use, and Traefik `basic_auth` can't stand in because the app's real admin UI — not just an open door — sits behind that credential. Revisit once the platform can supply a plaintext customer-derived credential, or if Duplicati adds support for a pre-hashed WEBSERVICE_PASSWORD.

Mosquitto is a standalone MQTT broker (pub/sub messaging for IoT devices, sensors, and home-automation integrations) — a natural companion to the existing Home Assistant recipe (which commonly integrates with MQTT for device communication) but a distinct piece of infrastructure, not a duplicate of it. blocking_issues:
Mosquitto ships with no authentication configured out of the box — an unmodified mosquitto.conf allows anonymous connections on 1883. Exposing that publicly (port: 1883/8883, protocol: tcp, no HTTP) would mean anyone on the internet can publish/subscribe to every topic, so a recipe needs to force password auth via a `password_file` entry at first boot; this isn't optional the way it might be for an app with a login-less admin tool.

There is no HTTP layer to gate with Traefik `basic_auth` — MQTT is a raw TCP protocol (optionally TLS on 8883), not a web UI request the Traefik middleware chain intercepts. The `basic_auth` mechanism this catalogue relies on for login-less apps (Adminer, etc.) does not apply here, so a broker credential is the only viable gate.

Mosquitto's password file format (`mosquitto_passwd`) stores credentials as PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 with a broker-specific iteration count and salt (`username:$7$<iterations>$<salt>$<hash>`) — not argon2 or bcrypt, the two algorithms `generated_from` currently supports. This is not a fundamental blocker (the customer's root password could in principle be hashed with PBKDF2 and written straight into that file format, without ever needing the plaintext to reach the app), but pbkdf2 isn't in the supported `generated_from` algorithm list yet.
summary: Eclipse Mosquitto is an actively-maintained, EPL/EDL-licensed MQTT broker with no catalogue overlap — it would be the first message-broker recipe and a natural companion to the existing Home Assistant recipe. It has no web UI at all, speaks a raw TCP protocol rather than HTTP, and needs a password-file entry to avoid running fully open to anonymous publish/subscribe once exposed. That credential can't be gated with Traefik `basic_auth` (no HTTP layer to intercept) and Mosquitto's own password format hashes with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512, an algorithm `generated_from` doesn't support yet (only argon2/bcrypt). Revisit once `generated_from` gains pbkdf2 support, or once there's a defined way to expose a raw non-HTTP TCP port with a broker-native credential.

summary: EdgeDB (now "Gel") is a Postgres-backed graph-relational database with an EdgeQL/SQL query layer — it would be our first standalone "database-as-a-product" recipe rather than an end-user web app, which is already a fit stretch for the catalogue. More decisively, the vendor (Gel Data Inc.) announced on 2025-12-02 that it is shutting down and its team has joined Vercel; Gel Cloud closed 2026-01-31, and both the GitHub repo and Docker Hub image have had zero activity since late December 2025 (~7 months as of 2026-08-05), with a community issue already asking that the project be labeled unmaintained. Recommendation: not_recommended.

name: Elasticsearch
source_description: Distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene
upstream_license: Elastic License 2.0 (default distribution) / SSPL / AGPL-3.0 (dual/tri-licensed, customer picks); Apache-2.0 pre-2021 code still applies to some modules
version_health_notes: 9.5.0 tagged 2026-08-04, i.e. yesterday relative to today (2026-08-05). Cadence over the preceding ~7 months: 9.3.0 (2026-01-28), 9.4.0 (~April 2026), 9.4.1 (2026-05-13), 9.4.2 (2026-05-28), 9.4.3, 9.4.4 (2026-07-21), 9.5.0 (2026-08-04) — a steady stream of monthly minor/ patch releases plus continuous 8.x backport releases (8.19.x still shipping in parallel, e.g. 8.19.17/8.19.18). This is Elastic's flagship product with a large, well-funded team; unambiguously active, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: No existing recipe provides a standalone search/analytics/indexing engine — the 24 current recipes are end-user applications (photo management, password manager, VPN, forms, document management, etc.) that at most embed Postgres/Redis internally. Elasticsearch would be the first "infrastructure-as-a-product" recipe exposing a raw search backend for customers to build on top of (via its REST API/SDKs), conceptually similar in shape to the EdgeDB gap-analysis case (apps-gaps/edgedb.yaml) rather than to any shipped recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Elasticsearch itself ships no web UI at all — it is a pure JSON REST API on port 9200 (the ELK Stack's UI, Kibana, is a separate product/ potential separate recipe, not asked about here). Its natural consumer is a developer wiring up their own application or a companion tool (Kibana, Logstash, an app's own search feature) against the API, not an end user clicking through a dashboard the way every other recipe in this catalogue works. It also has real production footprint concerns (JVM heap, recommended 2GB+ RAM minimum, ideally 8GB+) disproportionate to the self-hosted, single-tenant use case this catalogue otherwise targets. Useful as infrastructure, but a poor match for the catalogue's current end-user-facing audience on its own.
blocking_issues:
The credential channel is not a simple env-var pass-through like Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN. Elasticsearch's Change Password API (`POST /_security/user/elastic/_password`) accepts a `password_hash` field carrying a pre-computed hash instead of plaintext, and its default `xpack.security.authc.password_hashing.algorithm` is `bcrypt` — one of the two algorithms `generated_from` already supports, so a `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` value is structurally deliverable. But there's a bootstrap chicken-and-egg: the container needs *some* initial credential to authenticate the first API call before the real hash can be set (e.g. start with a throwaway `ELASTIC_PASSWORD` env var, then call the Change Password API to overwrite it with the customer's projected hash). This is a workable install.sh pattern, not a plain metadata.yaml parameter mapping — more bootstrap logic than most existing recipes need.

Elasticsearch auto-configures TLS on the HTTP layer (self-signed cert) by default from 8.x onward when security is enabled with no other config. To sit cleanly behind Traefik (which terminates public TLS itself), the recipe needs to explicitly set `xpack.security.http.ssl.enabled=false` and rely on Traefik for the public HTTPS leg — a standard, supported ES setting, not a blocker, but a config detail that must be gotten right or the container ships double/mismatched TLS.

Even if the mechanism above is wired up correctly, there is no web UI for a customer to log into and use — the "login" being protected is a REST API credential a customer would use from their own code/ client, which is a different usage pattern than every other recipe's browser-based admin login.
summary: Elasticsearch is an actively-maintained, monthly-cadence release from Elastic with no catalogue overlap — it would be the first standalone search/analytics engine recipe. Its admin credential (the `elastic` superuser) is mechanically expressible via `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` because Elasticsearch's own Change Password API accepts a pre-hashed bcrypt value, but wiring that up needs a two-step bootstrap (temporary password to authenticate, then overwrite via the hash) plus explicitly disabling ES's auto-configured internal TLS so it sits cleanly behind Traefik. The bigger issue is fit, not mechanism: Elasticsearch has no web UI of its own — it's a raw REST API meant for a developer's own application code, not the end-user-facing tools the rest of this catalogue serves, and its recommended RAM footprint (2GB+, ideally 8GB+) is heavy for the self-hosted single-tenant profile here. Mechanically buildable, but low-value as a standalone recipe absent a clearer target customer (e.g. paired with a UI layer like Kibana).

blocking_issues:
EmailEngine requires its own paid subscription License Key (EENGINE_PREPARED_LICENSE) once the 14-day trial expires — a third-party credential purchased from postalsys.com per installation, checked against Postal Systems' own licensing service. There is no channel for a customer (or af-api) to supply this today, and unlike a free API key this one costs money per instance — every install would silently stop functioning after 14 days without it. The admin login password (EENGINE_PREPARED_PASSWORD) must be supplied as a base64url-encoded pbkdf2-sha512 password hash, not plaintext and not argon2/bcrypt. `generated_from` today only supports `argon2` and `bcrypt`. The service exposes three ports for its actual purpose beyond the admin Web UI: SMTP message submission (2525) and an IMAP proxy (9993), neither of which are HTTP and so cannot sit behind Traefik the way every other recipe in the catalogue does — only the REST-API/UI port (3000) is reverse-proxy compatible.

Minimum recommended footprint is 8GB RAM / 4 CPU cores (16GB+/8+ cores recommended for production), heavier than nearly every existing recipe, plus a required external Redis instance used as a primary datastore (not a cache) that would need to ship as a second container.
summary: EmailEngine fills a real gap (no existing recipe offers a REST/webhook proxy over IMAP/SMTP/Gmail/Microsoft-365 mailboxes), is actively developed, and its admin-password hashing scheme is only a platform-extension blocker (pbkdf2 support), not a structural one. But it is not viable today: it requires a paid, per-installation Postal Systems License Key with no customer-facing input channel and no free tier beyond a 14-day trial, plus two non-HTTP ports (SMTP, IMAP proxy) that don't fit our Traefik-only exposure model.
