But the separate packaging repo that produces the official Docker image, github.com/emoncms/emoncms-docker, last cut a release (11.6.10) on 2024-12-18 — over 19 months ago — and that is also the newest numbered tag actually published to Docker Hub (`openenergymonitor/emoncms`); `:latest` on Docker Hub points at that same 11.6.10 build. So the only consumable Docker image is frozen roughly 9 minor-version lines behind the current app release (11.6.x vs 11.15.x), with no indication the packaging repo will catch up — its own release cadence (11.3.17 in Apr 2023, 11.3.24 in Jul 2023, 11.6.10 in Dec 2024) is sporadic even on its own terms. Treating "the project" as the thing we'd actually ship (the Docker image), this is maintenance-only/dormant packaging riding on top of an active core repo — flagging per SCHEMA.md's guidance to catch stale packaging rather than soften it for the sake of the upstream app looking active.
differentiation: EmonCMS is a narrow, purpose-built time-series logger/visualizer for energy, temperature, and other sensor feeds, built around the OpenEnergyMonitor hardware ecosystem (emonTx, emonPi, emonBase). It is not a general home-automation hub — no device control, no integrations marketplace — so it doesn't strictly duplicate recipes/home-assistant, but the two target an overlapping audience (self-hosters instrumenting their home/energy setup) and a customer already running Home Assistant can cover basic energy dashboards via its own energy dashboard/MQTT integrations without a second app.
usefulness_rationale: Real value is narrowly scoped to OpenEnergyMonitor hardware owners (a specific enthusiast niche) rather than general self-hosting customers; most prospective users already running smart-home gear are more likely to already have or want Home Assistant instead. Combined with the stale, far-behind Docker packaging (see version_health), this is a small addressable audience for the risk of shipping a frozen, 9-versions-behind image.
blocking_issues:
EmonCMS has no fixed/pre-provisioned admin credential to project a password hash into — the first visitor to the web UI self-registers an account via a signup form, and that first-registered account becomes the admin. This is not a structural blocker under the current mechanism (there is no customer-supplied value needed at all — same pattern already shipped in recipes/n8n and recipes/uptime-kuma, neither of which gates or pre-seeds the first account either), but it does mean the app sits open to "whoever visits first registers as admin" for the window between deploy and the customer's own first login, identical to those two existing recipes' accepted behavior today.

The upstream default docker-compose stack bundles an Eclipse Mosquitto MQTT broker exposed on raw TCP port 1883 (used for posting sensor data into EmonCMS outside the HTTP API) alongside the web UI on port 80. The web UI alone is single-HTTP-port and Traefik- compatible; MQTT ingestion is not (Traefik in this catalogue fronts HTTP(S) only). A recipe could omit the MQTT service for MVP and accept only the HTTP-based input API, but that drops a feature many EmonCMS/OpenEnergyMonitor users specifically rely on.
summary: EmonCMS is mechanically installable today — no admin credential needs a projection channel we lack (same self-registration pattern already shipped for n8n/uptime-kuma), and its web UI is a single reverse-proxy- friendly HTTP port once the optional MQTT broker is left out. The blocker is not the mechanism, it's the project itself: the only consumable Docker image (openenergymonitor/emoncms) has not been rebuilt in over 19 months and is frozen ~9 minor versions behind the actively-developed core app repo, and the addressable audience — owners of specific OpenEnergyMonitor hardware — is narrow and already substantially covered by recipes/home-assistant for customers who want a home/energy dashboard. Not recommended for now; revisit if the emoncms-docker packaging repo resumes cutting releases closer to the core app's cadence.

name: EMQX
source_description: High-performance open-source MQTT broker for IoT and real-time messaging
upstream_license: Business Source License (BSL) 1.1 as of v5.9.0 (May 2025), when EMQX merged its previously separate Apache-2.0 Community Edition and BSL Enterprise Edition into a single source-available product. Each BSL version converts to Apache-2.0 four years after its release. BSL 1.1 permits running a single-node instance in production for free, but prohibits offering EMQX itself as a commercial hosted/managed service and requires a paid license for multi-node clustering. Hostinger's "open-source" framing is only accurate for versions predating 5.9.0.
version_health_notes: 6.2.2 shipped 2026-07-02, about one month before today (2026-08-05). EMQ actively maintains three parallel minor branches at once — 6.2.x (6.2.0 2026-03-31, 6.2.1 2026-06-11, 6.2.2 2026-07-02), 6.1.x (6.1.0 2025-12-30 through 6.1.3 2026-07-01), and 6.0.x (6.0.1 2025-11-11 through 6.0.3 2026-06-17) — with patch releases landing roughly monthly on each. Docker Hub also lists a 6.1.4 build newer than 6.2.2. This is a clearly active, well-resourced project (EMQ Technologies, commercially backed), not remotely dormant or EOL.
differentiation: No existing recipe provides a message broker of any kind — this would be the first. EMQX is a clustering-capable, high-throughput MQTT broker with a built-in web Dashboard (unlike Eclipse Mosquitto, which is UI-less), aimed at IoT/IIoT fleets and real-time messaging rather than end-user apps. It pairs conceptually with the existing Home Assistant recipe (a common MQTT consumer) but is distinct infrastructure, not a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Having a web Dashboard is a real advantage over Mosquitto for this catalogue (fits our Traefik-fronted, browser-managed app pattern much better), but the audience is still narrow and technical (people wiring up their own MQTT clients/devices), and the BSL license introduces a business-model wrinkle Mosquitto's EPL/EDL license doesn't have.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: EMQX Dashboard admin login (default admin/public, changeable via EMQX_DASHBOARD__DEFAULT_PASSWORD, plaintext only); Traefik basic_auth gate for the Dashboard (defense-in-depth, since the Dashboard credential itself can't carry the customer's root password — see blocking_issues)
secrets_expressible_today: EMQX Dashboard admin login (default admin/public, changeable via EMQX_DASHBOARD__DEFAULT_PASSWORD, plaintext only):server_generated_no_customer_input; Traefik basic_auth gate for the Dashboard (defense-in-depth, since the Dashboard credential itself can't carry the customer's root password — see blocking_issues):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
The Dashboard's own admin credential (`dashboard.default_password`/`EMQX_DASHBOARD__DEFAULT_PASSWORD`) is documented only as "the password used to initialize the database record for the admin user" with no mention of accepting a pre-hashed value — the config key is named `default_password`, not `default_password_hash`, unlike Vaultwarden's `ADMIN_TOKEN` which explicitly documents argon2 support. This reads as a genuine plaintext-only requirement, which per SCHEMA.md is a structural blocker for `generated_from` (it only ever carries a hash, never the plaintext). Workaround: set this env var to a random server-generated secret the customer never sees, and put the actual customer-facing gate in Traefik `basic_auth` (projecting the root-password hash there instead) in front of the whole Dashboard endpoint — mechanically this works exactly like an app with no login of its own, it's just that EMQX happens to also have an inner login the customer will never use.

EMQX exposes non-HTTP raw ports that are the actual point of the app — MQTT (1883/tcp) and MQTTS (8883/tcp), plus MQTT-over-WebSocket (8083/8084) — alongside the Dashboard (18083/tcp, HTTP). Only the Dashboard port can sit behind Traefik; 1883/8883 need direct raw TCP exposure the way wg-easy exposes its VPN port, which is a workable but non-default pattern for this catalogue.

Licensing: BSL 1.1 (since v5.9.0) forbids offering EMQX itself as a commercial hosted/managed service. Whether IONOS Application Factory reselling EMQX instances to customers counts as exactly that is a real open question that should go to legal/licensing review before building, independent of the technical mechanism questions above.
summary: EMQX would be the catalogue's first message-broker recipe and, unlike the also-analyzed Eclipse Mosquitto, ships a real web Dashboard that fits our Traefik-fronted pattern well. It is actively and commercially developed with no sign of slowing. Two things block it today: the Dashboard's own admin-password field appears to require plaintext (no documented hash support), so `generated_from` can't project the customer's root password directly into it the way it does for Vaultwarden — the workaround is a server-generated Dashboard password plus a Traefik `basic_auth` gate carrying the real customer credential, same shape as our login-less-app pattern. Separately, EMQX's core purpose requires raw non-HTTP ports (1883/8883) that don't fit the Traefik-only exposure model most recipes use. On top of both mechanism questions, EMQX adopted a Business Source License in 5.9.0 that restricts offering it as a hosted service — worth a licensing check before this is built regardless of the technical answers. Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit once a raw-TCP-port exposure pattern exists (as needed for Mosquitto too) and the basic_auth-gate-in-front approach is confirmed as acceptable for apps with their own plaintext-only inner login.

name: Enclosed
source_description: Minimalistic web application for sending private and secure encrypted notes
version_health_notes: v1.16.0 (2025-07-22) is both the latest tagged release and the single most recent commit on `main` — no code has merged in ~12.5 months as of today, 2026-08-05. Earlier cadence was much denser (multiple releases a month through most of 2023-2024), so this is a sharp slowdown, not a project that was always slow. The repo is not archived and still receives community activity — 39 open issues, 31 open PRs, and issues as recent as 2026-07-22 (#479) — but none of that backlog has been reviewed or merged in over a year, which reads as an unofficially stalled single-maintainer project (CorentinTh) rather than a healthy "maintenance-only" one: a growing pile of unanswered community contributions with zero merges is a stronger warning sign than a quiet-but-responsive repo.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does ephemeral, client-side-encrypted, self-destructing note sharing (the PrivNote/"burn after reading" use case) — Vaultwarden is long-term credential storage for the account owner, OpenGist is unencrypted code-snippet sharing, Syncthing is P2P sync between the owner's own devices. However, `apps-gaps/cryptgeon.yaml` already analyzed a near-identical candidate for this exact same gap (also encrypted/self-destructing note+file sharing) and is currently healthier upstream (release 6 weeks ago vs. 12.5 months for Enclosed, still-merging single maintainer vs. a stalled PR queue). Enclosed's one real edge over Cryptgeon: it supports an *optional* login gate on note *creation* (`AUTHENTICATION_USERS`) while keeping note *viewing* open for recipients, so a customer could restrict who can send notes without breaking the recipient experience — Cryptgeon has no such option at all. Building both would be redundant; if only one ships, Cryptgeon is the stronger pick today on upstream health, with Enclosed's creation-gate design as the main argument in its favor.
usefulness_rationale: Real use case, but it's a second entrant into a niche another gap-analysis candidate (Cryptgeon) already covers more freshly, and Enclosed's own upstream has gone quiet for over a year with a stuck PR backlog — a real risk of shipping a recipe on a project that stops getting even security fixes.
summary: Enclosed is a single-container app (corentinth/enclosed, one HTTP port 8787, filesystem storage by default — no external DB) that is mechanically installable today: by default it needs zero secrets (both note creation and viewing are open, by design, so recipients don't need an account), and if the team wants to restrict who can create notes, `AUTHENTICATION_USERS` (email:bcryptHash pairs) can be projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from:"bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` without touching note viewing. The blocker is upstream health and redundancy, not the platform: `apps-gaps/cryptgeon.yaml` already covers this exact PrivNote-style niche with a currently more active upstream, and Enclosed itself has had zero merged commits in ~12.5 months despite an actively-growing backlog of 39 open issues and 31 open PRs — classic stalled-single-maintainer signal even though the repo isn't formally archived. Recommend not_recommended: don't build this on top of Cryptgeon covering the same gap more freshly, and revisit only if Cryptgeon is ruled out and Enclosed's maintainer resumes shipping.

name: Errbit
source_description: Self-hosted Airbrake-compatible error tracker for Ruby, Rails, and other apps
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release v0.11.3 shipped 2026-07-18 — only 18 days before today (2026-08-05). GitHub's release history (verified via the releases.atom feed, not relative-time UI text) shows a healthy, continuing monthly-ish cadence: 0.10.8 (2026-02-16), 0.10.9 (2026-04-07), 0.10.11 (2026-05-19), 0.11.0 (2026-06-10), 0.10.12 and 0.11.1 (both 2026-06-20), and 0.11.2/0.11.3 (both 2026-07-18). Commit history also shows daily activity through early August 2026 (dependency bumps, CI/Rails updates, and occasional maintainer commits from biow0lf), 4.3k stars, 989 forks, and dozens of open issues/PRs actively triaged. The Docker Hub image tracks this — `errbit/errbit` tags match each release, with 0.11.3 pushed around the same date as the 2026-07-18 tag. This is a currently-active, well-maintained project, not one that has gone quiet. Note also v0.11.0's release notes call it "last branch that support MongoDB" — a signal the project may be moving off MongoDB in a future major version, worth rechecking before building a recipe on the current Mongo-based stack.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers application error tracking/exception monitoring (a Sentry-like function) — this would be net-new ground aimed at developers self-hosting their own apps who want Airbrake-API-compatible error collection without sending exception data to a third-party SaaS.
usefulness_rationale: Useful specifically to a developer/technical customer segment running their own Ruby/Rails (or any Airbrake-client-compatible) applications; it has no standalone value for a customer not already shipping code that reports errors to it. Medium rather than high because the addressable audience within a general self-hosting catalogue is narrower than, e.g., password managers or workflow automation, but the "no login of its own to reuse" gap below caps it further regardless of audience size.
blocking_issues:
Errbit's first admin account is created by a `db:seed` task (`rails errbit:bootstrap`) that reads `ERRBIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD` (falling back to a random `SecureRandom` value if unset) and passes it straight to a Devise `User` model, which bcrypt-hashes whatever plaintext it receives on save. The platform's only per-customer secret channel, `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, projects an already-hashed value — feeding that into `ERRBIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD` would get double-hashed by Devise and produce a password the customer's actual root password can never match. This is a genuine plaintext-password requirement (not a hash-algorithm mismatch), so it is a structural blocker rather than something `generated_from` can be extended to cover.

Errbit's own login screen can't be bypassed with a Traefik `basic_auth` gate either, because (unlike n8n/WUD/Open WebUI) it has a mandatory built-in login of its own — gating the reverse-proxy edge doesn't get the customer past Errbit's internal sign-in, and there is no documented env var to disable that internal auth.
summary: Errbit is mechanically simple to deploy (one app container plus a MongoDB 7.0+ container, a single HTTP port on 3000, official pinned image tags on Docker Hub, e.g. errbit/errbit:0.11.3, works fine behind Traefik) and fills a real gap in the catalogue — nothing else here does error tracking — but it is blocked by the platform's secret-input constraint: its first-run admin password must be supplied as plaintext to a Devise model that hashes it itself, so the platform's hash-only `generated_from` mechanism cannot produce a working login, and Errbit's mandatory built-in auth can't be swapped out for a Traefik basic_auth gate the way it can for apps with no login of their own. Upstream health is good (active daily commits and a monthly-ish tagged-release cadence through 2026-07-18, just 18 days before this analysis); the blocker is purely the missing plaintext-secret input channel, so this should be revisited if/when the platform gains a way to pass a customer-facing plaintext credential rather than only a hash.

That makes it installable under the current recipe mechanism with no blockers. It fills a real gap versus the existing single `media` recipe (Immich, a photo backup tool) but targets a narrower audience, hence a medium rather than high usefulness rating.

name: ESPHome
source_description: System for controlling ESP8266/ESP32 microcontrollers with YAML
upstream_license: MIT OR GPL-3.0-only (dual-licensed: Python codebase MIT, C++/runtime firmware code GPLv3)
version_health_notes: Monthly stable release trains (2026.4.0, 2026.5.0, 2026.6.2, 2026.7.x) with frequent patch releases in between (e.g. four 2026.7.x patches within the first days of August 2026), plus active beta pre-releases for the next train (2026.7.0b1/b2). As of 2026-08-05 the latest tag (2026.7.4) is only days old. 16k+ commits, hundreds of open issues/PRs still being triaged — this is a healthy, fast-moving project, not remotely dormant.
differentiation: ESPHome is not a home-automation hub — it's a build/flash/OTA-update tool for ESP8266/ESP32/RP2040/BK72xx microcontroller firmware, defined declaratively in YAML and compiled server-side. recipes/home-assistant is the closest existing recipe (same "smart home" space, frequently paired with ESPHome in real deployments) but solves a different problem: Home Assistant consumes/orchestrates devices, ESPHome builds the firmware those devices run. No recipe in the current 24 touches firmware build/flash tooling.
usefulness_rationale: Strong appeal to the DIY/smart-home hobbyist segment that already wants Home Assistant, but it's a narrower, more technical audience than most of the catalogue (requires owning ESP-family hardware and editing YAML device configs) rather than a broad-appeal turnkey app.
blocking_issues:
The dashboard's own optional login (ESPHOME_USERNAME / ESPHOME_PASSWORD env vars) is compared as a plaintext credential the container reads directly, not a hash — it has no `generated_from`-compatible input. Not a hard blocker though: leave those env vars unset (dashboard has no auth of its own by default) and gate the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth: true` instead, same pattern used for n8n/WUD/Immich. The unused ESPHOME_USERNAME/PASSWORD pair could still be set server-side to a random value nobody needs to know, purely as defense in depth.

USB/serial device passthrough (`--privileged --device=/dev/ttyUSB0`) for flashing devices over a wired connection is not available to a cloud-hosted container and would need to be scoped out of the recipe description — initial flashing would rely on ESPHome's browser-based Web Serial installer (talks to the *customer's local* machine, not the server) or on devices that are already flashed and just need OTA config updates, which the hosted dashboard fully supports.
summary: ESPHome is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (6052) Python/Tornado app with no fixed default admin credential and no external API keys/OAuth requirement, so it fits the current recipe mechanism: front it with a domain param and a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate (the app's own optional login isn't hash-projectable and should just be left disabled). Upstream is very active (near-weekly patch releases as of August 2026), well outside EOL/dormant territory. It doesn't overlap any of the 24 existing recipes and pairs naturally with recipes/home-assistant, though it appeals to a narrower DIY-hardware audience than most of the catalogue. The one real caveat to flag for customers is that USB flashing needs a local browser installer rather than the hosted container — worth a documentation note, not a blocker. Recommend building the recipe.

name: EspoCRM
source_description: Free open-source CRM for managing contacts, deals, and customer relationships
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (project switched from GPLv3 to AGPLv3 in Dec 2023; a paid EspoCRM Commercial License is also offered for orgs that don't want AGPL obligations)
version_health_notes: 18 days since the latest release as of 2026-08-05 — well within an active cadence. Release history shows near-weekly patch releases (10.0.0 → 10.0.3 in 15 days during July 2026), plus a parallel 9.3.x maintenance line still receiving security-only fixes (9.3.10 on 2026-07-02, CVE patches roughly monthly through the 9.3 series). No archival notice, no EOL announcement; upstream is clearly under active, well-resourced development.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover CRM/sales-pipeline use cases — the closest adjacent categories are automation (n8n) and productivity/notes (Anytype), neither of which is a substitute for contact/deal management. EspoCRM would be the catalogue's first CRM offering, giving small businesses a self-hosted alternative to Salesforce/HubSpot for contacts, leads, opportunities, and basic sales-pipeline tracking.
usefulness_rationale: CRM is a common ask for small-business self-hosters and currently has no representation in the catalogue; EspoCRM is a mature, actively maintained, genuinely free (AGPL) option in that space, so the demand case is strong even though it's currently blocked mechanically (see installability).
blocking_issues:
ESPOCRM_ADMIN_PASSWORD is consumed by the container's first-boot setup script as the literal plaintext password used to create the "admin" login (documented default: username admin / password "password", meant to be overridden). It is not compared against a stored hash — EspoCRM's installer takes the raw string and sets it as the account's password. `generated_from` only ever projects a one-way hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel today to supply this value. This is the genuine-plaintext-requirement case the schema calls out as a hard blocker, distinct from an unsupported hash algorithm.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead doesn't resolve it: EspoCRM's own admin login is the thing the customer actually needs to reach to use the CRM (unlike Adminer/WUD-style tools with no native auth), so hiding it behind a second, unrelated basic-auth layer while leaving the internal ESPOCRM_ADMIN_PASSWORD as an unreachable server-generated random string would leave the customer unable to ever log in to the product they installed.

Full stack also requires a MariaDB/MySQL service (no official SQLite/embedded-DB path) plus a `espocrm-daemon` sidecar container that shares the app's volumes to run scheduled jobs — not a blocker by itself (n8n and paperless-ngx already carry a DB dependency in this catalogue), just adds container count. An optional `espocrm-websocket` service for real-time UI updates can be omitted from an MVP recipe without losing core CRM functionality.
summary: EspoCRM is an active, well-maintained, AGPL-3.0 CRM with an official Docker image and would fill a real gap — the catalogue currently has no CRM recipe. It fails the "customer-supplied secret" test today, though: the container's own installer needs the admin account password as plaintext, and neither `generated_from` (hash-only) nor a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (wrong login entirely) can deliver that. It's a strong `build_now` candidate the moment the platform gains a plaintext-password input channel (or EspoCRM adds a way to set the admin password via a pre-hashed value); until then it's `blocked_on_platform`, not `not_recommended`.

differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover e-commerce/storefront use cases. EverShop would be a genuinely new category — a self-hosted online store (product catalogue, cart, checkout, order management) rather than automation (n8n), documents (paperless-ngx), or media (immich).
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted e-commerce is a common ask and fills a real gap in the catalogue. The upstream project is small/young relative to Magento or WooCommerce but is modern (TypeScript/GraphQL/React), actively developed, and Docker-first.
blocking_issues:
EverShop has no browser-based first-run setup wizard for Docker deployments. The upstream-documented way to create the initial admin account is to exec into the running app container and run `npm run user:create -- --email ... --password ... --name ...`, which takes the admin password as a plaintext CLI argument that EverShop hashes itself internally. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext — there is no documented way to seed EverShop's admin_user table with a pre-computed hash instead of a plaintext password, so the admin login cannot be projected through the supported mechanism.
Traefik basic_auth is not a viable substitute gate here: EverShop serves a public storefront (product browsing/checkout) on the same domain as the admin panel, and gating the whole domain behind HTTP basic auth would block the customer's own shoppers from the store front-end, defeating the app's purpose.
summary: EverShop would be a valuable, differentiated addition (the catalogue's first e-commerce recipe) and the upstream project is actively maintained with a straightforward Postgres-backed docker-compose shape similar to n8n/paperless-ngx. It is blocked today purely on the installation mechanism: initial admin account creation requires a plaintext password passed to a CLI command inside the container, which the platform's root-password-hash-only secret channel cannot supply, and a basic_auth gate is the wrong fit for a public storefront. Revisit if EverShop adds a documented way to seed the admin account from a pre-hashed password (matching an algorithm generated_from supports) or a browser-based first-run setup flow.

name: Evolution API
source_description: Open-source WhatsApp API for chatbots, automation, and messaging integrations
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (with additional brand-protection/logo-notice clauses per NOTICE/TRADEMARKS)
latest_version: 2.4.0-rc2 (pre-release); v2.3.7 is the latest stable/non-license release
version_health_notes: Repo was renamed from EvolutionAPI/evolution-api to evolution-foundation/evolution-api in 2026 as part of a "Evolution Foundation" rebrand; not a fork or abandonment, same project. Release history is frequent through 2025 (v2.3.0 2025-06-17 through v2.3.7 2025-12-05, roughly monthly). Since then only two 2.4.0 release candidates have shipped (rc1 2026-05-06, rc2 2026-05-17) and neither has graduated to a full stable release as of today (2026-08-05) — about 2.9 months since rc2 with no stable cut. Cadence is still "active" (project is clearly maintained, GitHub issue #2534 shows maintainers actively responding to community pushback), but the v2.4.0 line has stalled at RC status longer than any prior release gap in 2025, likely because of the license-activation controversy described below.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes exposes a WhatsApp integration API. n8n (already in the catalogue) is the nearest neighbor — customers would likely pair the two (n8n workflows calling Evolution API to send/receive WhatsApp messages) rather than one replacing the other. This would be a genuinely new category (chatbot/messaging-automation backend), not a duplicate of anything shipping today.
usefulness_rationale: WhatsApp business/chatbot automation is a real, popular use case (heavily promoted alongside n8n in the self-hosting/no-code community), so there is clear customer pull. Capped at medium rather than high because of the version_health uncertainty above (the actively-developed line now requires third-party license activation) and because the app's core value depends on WhatsApp Web session pairing (Baileys), which is inherently fragile to WhatsApp's own anti-automation enforcement and outside our control.
blocking_issues:
AUTHENTICATION_API_KEY is a single global secret compared as a literal string (an `apikey` request header checked for exact equality against the env var) — it is not a hashed/bcrypt-style login field. It cannot be the target of `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because that mechanism only ever projects a *hash* of the root password, and Evolution API has no way to compare a hash — the customer would end up needing to know the raw hash string as their literal API key, which they cannot derive themselves. Workaround: generate AUTHENTICATION_API_KEY randomly server-side (customer never needs to see or type it), bake it into both the API container and the Evolution Manager container's env (Manager supports pre-configuring VITE_EVOLUTION_API_KEY so its own login screen is bypassed), and put the real customer-facing gate in front via Traefik `basic_auth: true` (root-password projection) on both the API and Manager ports. This follows the schema's guidance that a fixed/hardcoded credential the app itself gives no way to change is fine once Traefik basic_auth is the actual auth boundary — so this is a workaround, not a hard blocker, and is reflected in secrets_expressible_today above.

Starting at v2.4.0 (currently RC-only, see version_health), every instance must complete a one-time "license activation" handshake against the Evolution Foundation's own licensing server before the Manager dashboard becomes usable (unlicensed instances are redirected to an external registration/OAuth-style callback flow). This is exactly the "OAuth app registration / third-party account linking" case the schema calls a hard no — there is no channel for us to complete that handshake on the customer's behalf, and no channel for the customer to complete it themselves through our install flow. This only affects 2.4.0+; the last pre-license release, v2.3.7, has no such requirement and can be pinned instead.

Because of the item above, a recipe would have to pin to v2.3.7 (currently ~8 months old and not the line upstream is actively developing) to avoid the license wall, which conflicts with the version_health signal that v2.4.0 is where current development effort is going. Revisit once 2.4.0 either drops the mandatory-activation requirement (tracked in upstream issue #2534) or ships a self-hostable/offline activation path.
summary: Evolution API would fill a real, distinct gap (WhatsApp/chatbot messaging backend, pairs naturally with the existing n8n recipe) and is actively developed. It is not installable today for two compounding reasons: its global AUTHENTICATION_API_KEY only works as a literal-compare secret (workaroundable via server-generated key + Traefik basic_auth, as noted above), but the actively-developed v2.4.0 line additionally requires an external license-activation handshake with the vendor's own licensing server, which has no expressible input channel under the current mechanism. Pinning to the last unlicensed release (v2.3.7) avoids the license wall but means shipping a recipe already behind upstream's current development focus. Recommend revisiting once upstream issue #2534 (mandatory license activation breaking self-hosted deployments) resolves one way or the other.

name: Evolution Go
source_description: High-performance WhatsApp API gateway written in Go for messaging automation
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (with additional brand-protection terms: logo preservation + usage notification requirements)
version_health_notes: Latest tag v0.7.2 shipped 2026-07-03, about 5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Recent release history: 0.6.1 (2026-03-25), 0.7.0 (2026-04-17), 0.7.1 and 0.7.2 (both 2026-07-03) — roughly monthly to bimonthly cadence with no long gaps. Repo shows 594 stars, 323 forks, 49 open issues, 42 open PRs — an actively developed project backed by a commercial foundation (Evolution Foundation), not a solo/abandoned effort. This is a newer Go rewrite of the older, more established Node.js "Evolution API" project from the same foundation; the Go version is younger but shipping regularly.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue provides WhatsApp messaging/automation connectivity — this would be net-new ground for a customer segment doing WhatsApp-based customer support, chatbot, or notification automation (e.g. paired with n8n or a CRM). It has a "Manager" web UI (login + Swagger docs) so it is reverse-proxy friendly on a single HTTP port, similar in shape to n8n.
usefulness_rationale: Would be genuinely useful to customers building WhatsApp automation, a real and growing self-hosting use case with no existing catalogue coverage. Capped at medium (not high) because it is a narrower, single-purpose integration tool rather than broad general-audience software, and — independent of demand — the licensing mechanism below makes it non-trivial to install without human interaction regardless of usefulness.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: GLOBAL_API_KEY (server-side API auth key, no customer-facing login of its own); vendor license activation (either interactive browser registration at the Evolution Foundation licensing server, or headless auto-activation via EVOLUTION_OPERATOR_EMAIL tied to a pre-registered account at evofoundation.com.br)
secrets_expressible_today: GLOBAL_API_KEY (server-side API auth key, no customer-facing login of its own):server_generated_no_customer_input
blocking_issues:
The app enforces mandatory license activation before it will serve any request: it returns HTTP 503 on every endpoint until activated. Activation requires either (a) a human interactively visiting /manager/login and completing registration on the Evolution Foundation's external licensing server, or (b) setting EVOLUTION_OPERATOR_EMAIL to an email address the customer must have already manually registered with that same external service ahead of time. Both paths require a customer-supplied value (an email tied to an external vendor account, or direct interactive action) that /compose has no channel to carry — this is the same class of blocker as OAuth app registration, not a password we can hash and project.

Even setting aside the missing input channel, upstream's own community has flagged this activation gate as actively hostile to automated/headless deployments (see evolution-foundation/evolution-api issue #2534: "mandatory license activation... breaks automated and self-hosted deployments" for Docker Compose auto-restarts, k8s pod recreation, and CI/CD) — a concern that applies equally to evolution-go's identical activation flow, and one upstream itself has not resolved with a non-interactive env-var-only path.
summary: Evolution Go fills a real gap (WhatsApp automation/messaging), is actively maintained, and is technically reverse-proxy compatible with a single web UI port — but it cannot be installed today because it enforces mandatory license activation against an external vendor service (evofoundation.com.br) that needs either interactive browser signup or a pre-registered customer email, neither of which our /compose flow has any way to supply. This is blocked_on_platform rather than not_recommended: if a future input channel exists for a single customer-supplied value (e.g. an operator email) passed through at provisioning time, or if upstream adds a fully non-interactive activation path, this would be worth revisiting.

name: ExcaliDash
source_description: Self-hosted dashboard to organize, manage, and collaborate on your Excalidraw drawings
upstream_docker_image: zimengxiong/excalidash-backend, zimengxiong/excalidash-frontend (no single official image — two-service stack, no pinned-version tags published, only :latest)
latest_version: v0.5.1 (2026-06-21); v0.6.0-dev in active development as of 2026-07-20
version_health_notes: ~1.5 months since the last tagged release (2026-06-21 to today, 2026-08-05), with a steady release cadence through 2026 (v0.4.27 Feb, v0.4.28 Mar, v0.5.0 Apr, v0.5.1 Jun) and a dev branch already at v0.6.0-dev with new features (built-in AI canvas assistant, multi-provider LLM support, scheduled backups) as of 2026-07-20. Genuinely active, no EOL/dormancy concern. Note the project only publishes `:latest` Docker tags, not versioned image tags matching the VERSION file/GitHub releases — a pin-to-a-stable-tag recipe would need to pin by digest instead of a human-readable version tag.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers diagramming/whiteboarding. ExcaliDash adds persistent storage, organization (collections/search), version history, and multi-user real-time collaboration on top of Excalidraw's open .excalidraw format — a self-hosted alternative to excalidraw.com's cloud collaboration or commercial whiteboard SaaS (Miro, FigJam) for teams wanting to keep drawings on their own server.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct niche (no equivalent recipe today) but a narrower audience than our general-purpose recipes — mainly technical/product teams doing diagramming and light design collaboration, not a broad horizontal need.
blocking_issues:
The app's own admin-account creation is not projectable via `generated_from`: on first boot it enters an interactive "bootstrap setup" flow gated by a one-time code the operator must read from container logs (`docker compose logs backend | grep "BOOTSTRAP SETUP"`), then the admin chooses their own username/password directly in the web UI. There is no env var to preset the admin identity or a password hash — confirmed against the project's own AGENTS.md, which documents no such variable. A managed-hosting customer has no way to read container logs to retrieve the one-time code, so the documented bootstrap path is unusable as shipped.

The only documented escape is `DISABLE_ONBOARDING_GATE=true`, which upstream explicitly labels "not recommended" — it skips the code check entirely and leaves the instance open for whoever visits first to register as admin (a claim-race). This is mechanically the "app with no built-in login until first use" case our Traefik `basic_auth` gate pattern already covers (same shape as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI): gating the whole app behind a root-password-derived basic_auth credential closes the race window, so the app only becomes reachable — and thus claimable — by the customer. This works today, but it means shipping a recipe that runs against the vendor's own stated security guidance (disabling their onboarding gate) rather than through a channel they intended.

No single official Docker image, and no versioned tags — only `:latest` for both `excalidash-backend` and `excalidash-frontend` — so pinning to "a current stable tag" (our usual convention) isn't directly possible; would need to pin by image digest instead.
summary: ExcaliDash is an active, actively-developed self-hosted Excalidraw dashboard with no equivalent in our 24-recipe catalogue — genuine differentiation for diagramming/collaboration use cases. It clears the installability bar only via a workaround: its documented admin-bootstrap flow needs a one-time code from container logs that a managed-hosting customer can't retrieve, so `installable_today` relies on setting `DISABLE_ONBOARDING_GATE=true` (upstream's own "not recommended" escape hatch) and closing the resulting open-admin-claim race with a Traefik basic_auth gate — the same no-native-login pattern used elsewhere in the catalogue, but here achieved by deliberately bypassing the vendor's intended onboarding security rather than through a channel they designed for it. Combined with the two-service (backend+frontend) shape, no official single image, and no versioned Docker tags (only `:latest`), this is a build_with_caveats candidate: mechanically buildable today, but with more rough edges than a typical recipe.

name: Excalidraw
source_description: Virtual whiteboard for sketching hand-drawn diagrams and collaborative brainstorming

Despite the tagging gap, the repo itself is not dormant: ~4k commits, ~2.3k open issues and ~1k open PRs, and the excalidraw/excalidraw Docker Hub `latest` tag was rebuilt as recently as ~3 months ago (~May 2026), indicating upstream ships continuously off `master` without cutting discrete version tags rather than having stopped development. differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover a whiteboard/diagramming tool — closest conceptual neighbor is anytype-server (knowledge management), but that's a native-app sync backend with no web UI, not a browsable sketching canvas. Excalidraw would be the catalogue's first hand-drawn-diagram/whiteboard offering, a genuinely new category.
usefulness_rationale: Popular, well-known tool (widely embedded in docs/wikis, large existing user base) and a real gap in the catalogue's categories. Capped at medium rather than high because the official Docker image is a client-only static frontend: it has no accounts, no server-side persistence, and no built-in real-time collaboration relay — so what ships out of the box behind Traefik is closer to a solo local-storage sketchpad than the "collaborative brainstorming" tool Hostinger's description promises.

Upstream publishes no pinned semantic-version Docker tags for excalidraw/excalidraw — only a rolling `:latest` and a set of commit-sha tags last pushed roughly five years ago. RFC-002 forbids `:latest`; the only workaround is pinning to an image digest (`excalidraw/excalidraw@sha256:...`), which upstream doesn't version or document, so there is no stable, human-readable tag to track or bump on updates.

It would fill a genuine gap (no whiteboard/diagramming tool in the current 24 recipes) but comes with two real caveats: upstream ships no pinned version tags (only rolling `latest` and ancient sha tags), conflicting with the catalogue's no-`:latest` rule, and the official image alone is a solo local-storage sketchpad, not the collaborative whiteboard Hostinger's description advertises, since real-time collaboration needs a separate room/websocket server this image doesn't provide. build_with_caveats: worth building, but only with an explicit decision on image pinning (digest pin, most likely) and a call on whether a single-user recipe is an acceptable scope or whether the collab-server stack should be built out too.

name: Faktory
source_description: High-performance background job server with web UI for job management
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (open-source edition; a separate proprietary "Faktory Enterprise" tier also exists, dual-licensed under COMM-LICENSE — not evaluated here)
version_health_notes: No tagged release since v1.9.4 (2025-02-19) — about 17.5 months before today (2026-08-05). Release cadence was already slow before that (1.9.3 2024-07-22, 1.9.2 2024-05-19, 1.9.1 2023-09-11, 1.9.0 2023-05-20), averaging roughly one release every 6-9 months even at its most active. Repo is not archived and the maintainer (Mike Perham, also of Sidekiq) was still editing the project wiki as recently as 2026-02, so this reads as a stable, low-churn single-maintainer project in long-term maintenance mode rather than an abandoned one — but the release cadence itself has effectively stalled for a year and a half.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers a language-agnostic background job queue; n8n is workflow automation, not a generic job server for developers' own applications. Faktory's actual value only exists once a customer plugs their own app's producer/worker code into it over its native TCP protocol — it is not a standalone end-user tool the way most of the current catalogue is.
usefulness_rationale: Useful for developers self-hosting an app that needs a job queue, but it's infrastructure plumbing for a customer's own codebase rather than a self-contained product, which is a narrower audience than most of the current 24 recipes.
blocking_issues:
FAKTORY_PASSWORD is a single shared secret gating both the raw TCP worker/producer protocol (port 7419) and the web UI's HTTP Basic Auth (port 7420). The client auth handshake requires the plaintext password (client computes a nonce-based pwdhash from it, e.g. `tcp://:mypassword@host:7419`) — it is not a login form the server hashes on submit, so `generated_from` (which only ever projects a hash, never plaintext) cannot supply it. This matches the schema's "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case, a structural blocker rather than an unsupported-algorithm gap.

Gating the web UI alone behind Traefik `basic_auth` doesn't solve this: Faktory's actual purpose is other services connecting to the job queue over port 7419's binary protocol, and the customer has no way today to learn or set the plaintext FAKTORY_PASSWORD their own worker code needs to authenticate with. A server-generated random secret "nothing customer-facing reads" doesn't apply here since the customer's own application code is exactly what needs to read it.

Port 7419 is a raw TCP protocol, not HTTP — not reverse-proxy compatible with the Traefik-on-`<slug>.<base_domain>` pattern the rest of the catalogue relies on; exposing it would need a separate raw-TCP exposure mechanism (e.g. NodePort) independent of the secret question above.
summary: Faktory is a solid, stable, single-maintainer background job server, but it fills a gap the AF catalogue doesn't currently target (job-queue infrastructure for a customer's own app code, not an end-user product) and its auth model requires a plaintext shared secret for both the wire protocol and web UI — something our root-password-hash projection and Traefik basic_auth mechanisms cannot supply. It would need a new "customer-visible generated plaintext secret" input channel (distinct from a login-hash) before it's installable, plus a raw-TCP exposure story for port 7419. Release cadence has also stalled for ~1.5 years, though the project does not appear abandoned. Not recommended to build now; revisit if a plaintext-secret channel and non-HTTP port exposure both land on the platform.

blocking_issues:
FalkorDB Browser (the web UI on :3000) ships its own NextAuth-based login/user-management layer (auth.ts in the falkordb-browser repo), not a single fixed admin token/password field. Public docs don't document an env var to project a hashed initial-admin credential into it the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN works, so BROWSER_UI_AUTH has no confirmed expressible mechanism today — would need either upstream support for a generated_from-style hash injection, or fronting the whole UI with Traefik basic_auth instead of relying on its native login (unconfirmed whether that's compatible with its own auth flow).
The core database protocol (port 6379, Redis wire protocol) is raw TCP, not HTTP — Traefik can't front it the way it fronts a web app, so if this recipe's purpose is letting a customer's own external tooling query the graph, that port must be exposed directly rather than through the reverse-proxy pattern the rest of the catalogue uses.
License is SSPL-1.0, whose service-provision clause specifically targets exactly this scenario (making the software's functionality available to third parties as a service) and requires the entire management stack be released under SSPL in that case. This is a legal/business call for IONOS, not a technical one — flagging for review before any recipe work starts, independent of the technical blockers above.
summary: FalkorDB is an actively maintained, frequently released graph database (v4.20.1, released 2026-07-15) with a bundled web UI, but it doesn't fit the catalogue mechanically or strategically today. Its own login system (FalkorDB Browser) has no documented hash-injection hook compatible with our generated_from/basic_auth mechanisms, and its real value is a raw Redis-protocol port that doesn't reverse-proxy the way our other recipes do. On top of that, its SSPL-1.0 license has a service-provision clause that squarely covers offering it as an Application Factory recipe, which is a legal question independent of the technical gaps. Given a narrow developer-only audience versus the rest of the catalogue, this is a not_recommended candidate rather than blocked_on_platform.

name: Faraday
source_description: Open-source vulnerability management platform for security teams
version_health_notes: Latest release (v5.23.0) was 13 days before today (2026-08-05). Release history shows a roughly monthly cadence over the past year (v5.22.0 2026-06-19, v5.21.0 2026-05-14, v5.20.1 2026-05-08, v5.20.0 2026-04-10, v5.19.0 2026-01-26), with one ~2.5-month gap between v5.19.0 and v5.20.0. Repo has 14k+ commits and open PRs under active review by Infobyte. No signs of maintenance-only mode or archival.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover security/vulnerability-management tooling — Faraday would be the first. It aggregates and deduplicates findings from 80+ external scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS, Nmap, Burp, Nuclei, etc.) into one workspace, which is a genuinely distinct workload from the productivity/media/dev-tooling apps already in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: High value for a narrow audience (security teams, MSSPs, pentesters) who already run external scanners and want a self-hosted aggregation layer; low relevance to the bulk of AF's general SMB/hobbyist customer base, so overall catalogue usefulness lands medium rather than high.
blocking_issues:
Faraday has its own login (single "faraday" admin account) and does not accept a pre-computed password hash for it. The account is created by `faraday-manage initdb`, which either auto-generates a random password and prints it once to container stdout/logs, or accepts an explicit plaintext value via `--password`/ `--choose-password`. Our only customer-secret channel (`generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`) only ever carries a hash (argon2/bcrypt), never the plaintext Faraday's CLI needs — so the root-password projection mechanism cannot set Faraday's native login directly. This is the genuine-plaintext-requirement case, a structural blocker for that specific mechanism.

Practical workaround: gate the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (root-password-hash-derived, expressible today) and leave Faraday's own auto-generated admin password as an internal, behind-the-gate credential — the same pattern already used for apps with a fixed/unchangeable default credential. This makes the app installable, but the customer still needs some way to retrieve Faraday's own generated password (or run `faraday-manage change-password`) after first boot — e.g. via container logs. Hostinger's own existing Faraday catalogue listing handles this today by having the customer read the admin password out of the `faraday-1` container logs post-deploy; it is unclear whether AF customers have an equivalent log-access path today.
summary: Faraday is an active, actively-released (monthly cadence, last release 13 days ago), GPL-3.0 open-source vulnerability-management platform with a single-port web UI and no overlap with any of our 24 existing recipes — it would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue. It is installable today only via the Traefik `basic_auth` gate pattern, because Faraday's own admin login needs a plaintext password (from its CLI) rather than the hash our `generated_from` mechanism supplies, and its self-generated internal admin password is only ever surfaced via container logs today. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building behind a basic_auth gate, but flag the log-retrieval UX gap for Faraday's own login before shipping.

source_description: Self-hosted feature flag platform, an open-source LaunchDarkly alternative
upstream_license: MIT (core platform; a subset of "Professional"-tier features requires a paid license key — not evaluated here since the recipe would target the free Standalone/Standard deployment)

version_health_notes: Latest tag 5.4.4 published 2026-07-10, about 4 weeks before today (2026-08-05); it was a same-day follow-up patch to 5.4.3 (also 2026-07-10) fixing a version-display bug. Release history is dense and regular: 5.4.2 (2026-06-17), 5.4.1 (2026-06-12), 5.4.0 (2026-06-03), 5.3.6 (2026-05-22), 5.3.5 (2026-05-17), 5.3.4 (2026-05-14), 5.3.3 (2026-04-24), 5.3.2 (2026-04-20) — roughly weekly to bi-weekly cadence for months. Repo is not archived, has an active Discord community and regular commits on main. Clearly an active, well-maintained project.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers feature-flag/experimentation infrastructure; this is genuinely new ground for developer-facing self-hosted tooling that a customer would plug their own applications' SDKs into (similar audience shape to n8n or Gitea — infrastructure a developer builds on, not an end-user product).
usefulness_rationale: Feature flags / LaunchDarkly-alternative is a real, recognizable category with no catalogue overlap, so it would add distinct value. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because of the architectural mismatch described below — as currently deployed it is not a good fit for our single-domain-per-recipe Traefik model.
blocking_issues:
FeatBit is not a single-HTTP-surface app the way our recipes assume. Upstream's own compose file (ui, api-server, evaluation-server, da-server, postgresql — 5 containers even in the "Standalone" deployment tier) runs the UI as a browser SPA that calls API_URL and EVALUATION_URL as separate absolute origins configured at container-start time; there is no documented path-prefix/BASE_PATH option for api-server or evaluation-server to sit behind a single shared hostname via path-based Traefik routing. Per rfc/002-recipe- rules.md ("Declare at most one HTTP port per recipe: only the first gets a router"), only one of these services could ever get a Traefik router under a recipe — the other(s) would need their own publicly resolvable hostname or port, which the platform's one-subdomain-per-recipe (`<slug>.<base_domain>`) model doesn't support today. This is a structural reverse-proxy incompatibility, not merely a multi-container recipe (contrast with immich, a similarly multi-service stack that exposes exactly one public HTTP port).

Separately, the initial admin login is a hardcoded seed-data credential (test@featbit.com / 123456) baked into the Postgres init scripts, not exposed via any documented env var on api-server or the UI. Per the schema this alone would not block installability — it could be gated behind Traefik basic_auth like other apps with fixed default credentials (hence secrets_required_at_first_boot names basic_auth_password) — but secrets_expressible_today is left empty because that gate can't actually be wired up: Traefik basic_auth on a single router would only cover the UI's origin, leaving the separately-addressed api-server/evaluation-server origins unprotected, so the mechanism doesn't reach the multi-origin surface. The multi-origin problem above is the real blocker, not the secret-input mechanism.
summary: FeatBit is an active, well-maintained, MIT-licensed feature-flag platform that would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue (no existing recipe covers this category) and ships a web UI. However, its deployment architecture — a browser SPA calling separate API and evaluation-server origins directly, with no documented single-hostname/path-prefix mode — conflicts with the platform's one-public-HTTP-port-per-recipe Traefik model, not just with the "no arbitrary secret input" constraint. Its hardcoded default admin login would otherwise be handled cleanly via Traefik basic_auth, but that doesn't resolve the underlying multi-origin problem. Not recommended to build now; revisit if the platform gains a way to expose multiple HTTP services under one recipe (e.g. path-based routing with app-side base-path support, or multiple subdomains per recipe), or if a future FeatBit release adds a reverse-proxy-friendly single-origin mode.

Per SCHEMA.md this is not a blocker on its own — gate the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth as the real auth boundary — but it does mean the app's own login stays at the well-known default underneath that gate.
FC_LLM_API_KEY (and its paired FC_LLM_API_BASE/FC_LLM_API_MODEL/ FC_LLM_API_TYPE), which power the AI translation/summary features that are the whole point of Hostinger's 'AI-powered' description, are read from the container environment at boot. Unlike recipes/hermes-agent (which lets the customer paste an OPENROUTER_API_KEY into an authenticated in-app dashboard post-provision), no FeedCraft documentation surfaces an equivalent in-app settings page for these specific vars — the only UI-editable provider keys found relate to the separate 'search provider' (Search-to-RSS) feature, not the core LLM config. Absent a confirmed post-deploy input channel, there is no way for a customer to supply this key through the current /compose mechanism.
summary: FeedCraft is an actively developed (if sporadically tagged) RSS middleware with a genuine catalogue gap to fill — no existing recipe processes feeds — and it is mechanically installable behind Traefik basic_auth with no customer-supplied secrets required to boot: full-text extraction and plain RSS proxying work out of the box. But two caveats keep this from a clean build_now: neither of its container registries publish a version-pinned tag to build a recipe against (only latest/dev/nightly/main), and the AI translation/summary features Hostinger's own description leads with need an external LLM API key with no confirmed post-deploy input channel today, so a customer would get a working feed proxy but not the AI capability the listing implies.

name: Fenrus
source_description: Self-hosted personal dashboard and home page with smart app widgets

The newest published Docker image of any kind is the `develop` tag, last pushed 2024-04-04 (~2 years 4 months before today, 2026-08-05); the `latest` and `23.08` tags (identical digest) were last pushed 2023-08-18 (~3 years before today) and are what a recipe would actually pin to, since `develop` is not a stable channel. Source-repo commits continue sporadically into 2026 (most recent seen: 2026-04-29, adding a "Mediastarr" smart-app integration), so the project is not archived or abandoned at the code level, but no new Docker image has shipped in over 2 years — anyone deploying today gets ~3-year-old code regardless of ongoing upstream commits. That mismatch between "repo still gets occasional commits" and "no image has been cut since 2023" is why this is classified maintenance-only/dormant rather than active.
differentiation: None of the current 24 shipped recipes are a personal homepage/link-launcher dashboard. Uptime Kuma covers uptime *monitoring* with alerting, not a bookmark/widget landing page. Fenrus's pitch (multi-user dashboards, "smart apps" that poll Sonarr/Radarr/Jellyfin/etc. for live status, LiteDB file-based storage with no external DB) is functionally the same category as `dashy`, which already has an `apps-gaps/dashy.yaml` entry recommending `build_now` — Dashy is actively released (near-daily tags) versus Fenrus's ~3-year-stale image, so if the catalogue only wants one dashboard recipe, Dashy is the stronger pick in this category today.

summary: Fenrus is a single-container, MIT-licensed personal dashboard (port 3000, LiteDB file storage, no external DB) that would be reverse-proxy compatible and technically installable today by gating it behind Traefik basic_auth — it has no built-in login pre-provisioning (the first visitor to self-register on the login page becomes admin, with no env var or API to seed credentials), so basic_auth is needed as a gate before the customer ever reaches that registration form, the same pattern already proposed for Dashy. However, the project has not published a new Docker image since 2023-08-18 (nearly 3 years) despite sporadic ongoing source commits through 2026, and it directly overlaps in category with `dashy`, an already-analyzed, actively-released alternative. Recommend not_recommended: the mechanism gap is solvable, but there's no reason to ship a ~3-year-stale image in a category already better covered by a fresher candidate.

usefulness_rationale: Feedback/feature-request boards (the "UserVoice/Canny" self-hosted category) are a common ask for SaaS builders and open-source maintainers wanting to keep feedback data off a third-party service, and no recipe today covers this space.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: EMAIL/SMTP relay credentials (host, port, username, password) or an equivalent transactional-email provider (e.g. Mailgun) API key
blocking_issues: Fider has no built-in username/password login at all. Every sign-in (including creating the first admin/tenant on initial visit) goes through either (a) an email verification-code/magic-link flow, which upstream docs state is mandatory to configure or the app "will see panic errors" at startup, or (b) OAuth (Google/GitHub/ Facebook) app registration. Both require an external, customer- supplied credential (SMTP relay or transactional-email-provider API key, or an OAuth client id/secret) that has no projection channel today — there is no admin password field to hash via `generated_from`, and gating the site behind Traefik `basic_auth` does not help because the customer still cannot complete the in-app sign-up/sign-in flow without a working mail relay.
summary: Fider is a single Go binary web app (plus a required Postgres database) that would otherwise fit our recipe mechanism well — one HTTP port, reverse-proxy compatible, active upstream (releases every few weeks, latest 33 days old, currently clean AGPL-3.0 after a brief and since- reverted open-core detour). It fails installability today for a structural reason distinct from a missing password-projection channel: Fider has no password login of its own to begin with, and both of its auth paths (email verification code, requiring a working SMTP/email-API relay, or OAuth app registration) need an external credential the customer would have to supply with no input channel in `/compose` today. This is not fixed by Traefik `basic_auth` gating, since the customer still couldn't complete Fider's own sign-up flow behind that gate. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` — worth revisiting if/when an SMTP-relay-credential or OAuth-registration input channel is added to the bootstrap mechanism, or if Fider ever ships a password-based auth option.

name: File Browser
source_description: Web-based file manager for browsing, uploading, and managing files on your server
version_health_notes: v2.63.23 (2026-07-27), a "last planned release" per the maintainers, was tagged only 9 days before today (2026-08-05) — release cadence was active right up to the end. The README now carries an explicit end-of-life notice: "File Browser is winding down and this is the last planned release. The repository is archived on 2026-09-01. After that date there will be no further releases, bug fixes, or security fixes." (a follow-up maintainer post is titled "Goodbye File Browser, for Real This Time"). The project's own docs site, filebrowser.org, has already stopped resolving to its content and now redirects straight to the GitHub repo. The README additionally flags two unpatched vulnerability classes that will never be fixed: command-execution risk in the runner/hooks feature (disabled by default, "would require a complete rewrite") and JWT session handling (sessions cannot be revoked; leaked or logged-out tokens stay valid until they expire). The maintainers' own recommendation is to treat it as "unmaintained software" and not expose it directly to the internet. This is EOL by the project's own announcement, not an inference from silence — archival is dated three weeks after this analysis.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue exposes a general-purpose directory browser/upload UI (Syncthing is P2P sync, not a browsable single-tree file manager; OpenGist is code-snippet sharing). File Browser itself would have filled that gap — simple, single-binary, single-directory web file manager — but it directly overlaps two already-analyzed, unbuilt candidates in apps-gaps/: AList (apps-gaps/alist.yaml, actively maintained, aggregates 30+ storage backends) and Dufs (apps-gaps/dufs.yaml, actively maintained, simpler single-directory server). Both cover the same "browse/upload files over HTTP" niche and are not EOL.
usefulness_rationale: The underlying use case (browse/upload files in a directory via a web UI) is genuinely useful, but File Browser specifically is the wrong vehicle for it now: it is EOL with maintainer-acknowledged unpatched vulnerabilities, and AList/Dufs already cover the same need without that baggage.
summary: File Browser is a single-container, single-HTTP-port Go app (filebrowser/filebrowser) that on first boot creates a fixed "admin" user with a known default password; the documented way to set a real password is a post-start CLI call against the running container (same shape as apps-gaps/alist.yaml's pattern), so ADMIN_PASSWORD could in principle be projected via generated_from:"<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD" plus a docker-exec setup step — there is no mechanism-level blocker. The real problem is that the project announced its own end-of-life during this analysis window: the last planned release shipped 2026-07-27, the repo archives 2026-09-01, and the maintainers explicitly call out unpatched command-execution and JWT-session vulnerabilities while recommending against exposing it to the internet. Combined with two healthier, actively-maintained alternatives already covering the same niche (AList, Dufs — both unbuilt candidates in apps-gaps/), there is no reason to build this one. Recommend not_recommended despite technical installability.

name: FileFlows
source_description: Automated media file processor that reduces file sizes up to 90%
upstream_license: Proprietary (freemium) — core server/UI application is closed source; only auxiliary repos (community scripts/flows, Homebrew tap, Unraid packaging) are published on GitHub under the `fileflows`/`revenz` orgs. No license file found for the app itself.
version_health_notes: FileFlows uses a YY.MM.Release version scheme with a genuine monthly cadence: version tags on Docker Hub go 26.03, 26.04, 26.05, 26.06, 26.07 with the 26.07 image pushed ~8 days before today (2026-08-05), i.e. the catalogue is current within the last month. This is a clearly actively-developed, commercially-backed project (same publisher/org as Fenrus, `revenz`), not dormant or archived.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes do automated media transcoding/file-size reduction. Immich is a photo library/gallery, not a transcoding pipeline; nothing else in the catalogue touches video/audio processing. FileFlows fills a distinct niche: a customer with a media server (e.g. running Emby/Jellyfin/Plex elsewhere, none of which are in this catalogue either) could point FileFlows at a library to shrink storage costs via automated re-encoding pipelines.
usefulness_rationale: Clear, non-overlapping use case and genuinely active upstream, but the core value proposition (hardware-accelerated transcoding, Docker-based "node" workers, GPU passthrough for Intel QSV/NVIDIA NVENC/AMD AMF) is a poor match for a generic reverse-proxied cloud VM recipe — the realistic customer benefit depends on GPU access or heavy CPU headroom that a typical AF instance won't provide, and the free tier caps processing to 1 node / 5 concurrent "flow runners" / 30 flow elements, which limits how useful the shipped product is without a paid license.
summary: FileFlows is a single-container (`revenz/fileflows:26.07`, ~974MB, port 5000 internally) web app for automated media transcoding pipelines, under active monthly-release development. Security/login is a licensed (paid-tier) feature — the default free-tier UI has no authentication at all, so it needs the same Traefik `basic_auth` gate pattern already used for n8n/WUD/Open WebUI to avoid shipping an open admin panel, and that gate is fully expressible today. It's mechanically installable and fills a real gap (no transcoding/media-automation recipe exists in the catalogue), but the app also wants a mounted Docker socket to spawn processing containers and benefits most from GPU passthrough — neither of which fits a plain reverse-proxied compose recipe well, and the free tier's node/runner/flow-element caps limit real-world usefulness without a commercial license. Recommend build_with_caveats: technically shippable now via basic_auth, but scope expectations (CPU-only transcoding, free-tier limits, docker.sock exposure) should be called out explicitly if built.

name: FileGator
source_description: Self-hosted multi-user file manager with role-based permissions and no database
version_health_notes: Six tagged releases in the last ~9 months (v7.13.1 in Jan 2026 through v7.14.4 on 2026-07-13), the latest only ~3 weeks before this analysis (2026-08-05). Repo is not archived, last push 2026-07-23, still has 215 open issues being triaged. Clearly active, not dormant or EOL.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes offer a general-purpose, multi-user file manager/sharing UI over a plain local repository folder. syncthing does peer-to-peer sync, not a browsable web file manager with per-user roles and home directories; the rest are unrelated app categories. FileGator fills a "self-hosted Dropbox-lite / team file share" niche the catalogue doesn't currently cover.
usefulness_rationale: Broad appeal use case (share/upload/manage files for a team or family) and genuinely no-database, single-container simplicity make it an easy add. Rated medium rather than high because it's a fairly thin feature set compared to full cloud-storage suites (no OCR/preview ecosystem, no mobile app), so it competes more with "quick FTP replacement" than "Nextcloud alternative".
summary: FileGator is a single-container, single-port (8080) PHP app with no external database, license MIT, and an active release cadence (latest tag 3 weeks old). It ships with one hardcoded admin/admin123 account whose bcrypt password hash lives in a JSON user-store file (private/users.json, seeded from private/users.json.blank on first boot) rather than being read from an environment variable at container startup like every other generated_from recipe shipped so far (Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN). The hash algorithm FileGator itself uses is plain PHP password_hash(..., PASSWORD_BCRYPT), which matches a supported generated_from algorithm, so the root-password projection is expressible in principle — but wiring it in requires install.sh to render private/users.json with the generated bcrypt hash before first docker-compose up, instead of the simple ${VAR} substitution pattern used everywhere else. That's a real implementation gap worth flagging (hence build_with_caveats, not a clean build_now), but not a structural blocker the way a missing input channel would be. Recommend building it once the file-seeding approach is validated on one recipe.

name: Filestash
source_description: Self-hosted file manager for FTP, SFTP, S3, WebDAV, and 20+ storage backends
version_health_notes: Upstream has never adopted semver/tagged releases: GitHub Releases page is empty ("There aren't any releases here"), and the newest git tags are v0.0-v0.4 from the project's earliest days, long superseded. The project ships purely off a rolling `machines/filestash:latest` Docker Hub tag, rebuilt frequently — last pushed 2026-08-05 (today), with the underlying commit landing 2026-07-27 and a steady stream of commits through late July 2026 (multiple commits/week). Repo is not archived, 14.4k stars, 1k forks, 121 open issues under active triage. Genuinely active project, but the complete absence of a versioned release channel means a recipe cannot pin to "a current stable tag" the way our other recipes do — only a point-in-time image digest of `latest`, which upstream could change underneath without any changelog/tag to track against.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue is a universal storage client. Syncthing is P2P device sync, not a browsable multi-backend file manager. Filestash is architecturally the cleanest fit for our Traefik-only exposure model of the file-manager candidates seen so far: unlike Copyparty (whose headline pitch needs raw FTP/SFTP/SMB ports) or a server exposing its own storage, Filestash's 20+ "backends" (S3, FTP, SFTP, WebDAV, SMB, Git, Dropbox, Google Drive, IPFS, etc.) are all outbound connections the container makes to storage the customer configures through the UI — the container itself exposes a single HTTP port (8334) and nothing else, so the whole "FTP/SFTP/SMB" part of its pitch works without opening any raw ports on our side. Note this app competes for the same "unified file browser" niche as two other gap-analyzed candidates not yet built, apps-gaps/alist.yaml and apps-gaps/cloudreve.yaml — all three solve a similar problem with different tradeoffs, worth deciding as a group rather than shipping all three.
usefulness_rationale: Popular (14.4k stars), well-regarded "universal Dropbox-like front end" with a genuinely broad backend-plugin list and a document-editing integration (optional Collabora/WOPI companion container) that AList and Cloudreve don't offer out of the box. Single lightweight Go container for the base install. Real demand exists for this class of tool; the main open question is which one of the three candidates (Filestash / AList / Cloudreve) is the better single pick, not whether the category is worth adding.
blocking_issues:
No pinned, versioned Docker tag exists upstream — only a continuously-rebuilt `latest` tag and years-stale short-git-sha tags from 2023. A recipe would have to pin by image digest at creation time and manually re-pin later, since there is no tagged release stream to track for updates. Not a hard blocker (digest pinning is a valid workaround) but a real deviation from how every other recipe in this catalogue tracks upstream versions.

Filestash's admin-setup endpoint (POST /admin/api/config) is completely open/unauthenticated until the `auth.admin` config key is first set (verified in server/ctrl/admin.go and server/middleware/session.go on GitHub) — by design, this is meant to be filled in via the web UI on first visit. install.sh can instead call this endpoint itself immediately after container start, before the app is reachable by anyone else, to set `auth.admin` to a pre-computed bcrypt hash — verified in source that admin-login compares via `bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword`, i.e. `auth.admin` literally stores a bcrypt hash and is compatible with `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` (not `argon2` — the comparison function only accepts bcrypt-formatted hashes). This requires install.sh to win a first-boot race window rather than a documented env var, so it's the same class of caveat noted for apps-gaps/alist.yaml's post-boot CLI call, just via HTTP instead of docker exec.
summary: Filestash is a single-container Go app (machines/filestash, port 8334) whose admin password can be set at first boot via a scriptable, currently- unauthenticated config endpoint that stores a bcrypt hash directly — confirmed compatible with generated_from:"bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD" by reading the actual comparison code on GitHub. Its 20+ storage backends are all outbound client connections, not inbound ports, so it is fully Traefik/reverse-proxy compatible despite the FTP/SFTP/SMB-heavy Hostinger description. The real wrinkle is version pinning: upstream has no tagged releases at all, only a rolling `latest` tag, so a recipe would need to pin by digest and manage its own re-pinning cadence rather than tracking upstream version tags like every other recipe does. Active, healthy project (14.4k stars, frequent commits, image rebuilt as recently as today) and a real, currently-unfilled catalogue gap, but it directly overlaps in purpose with two other not-yet-built gap-analysis candidates (AList, Cloudreve) — worth a deliberate choice among the three rather than building all of them. Recommend build_with_caveats.

Within the broader candidate pool though, this overlaps two other finance gap analyses not yet built: apps-gaps/actual-budget.yaml (lighter envelope budgeting, SQLite, no separate DB, self-registration on first visit) and apps-gaps/akaunting.yaml (small-business double-entry accounting, BSL-licensed with usage caps). summary: Firefly III is a multi-container PHP app (fireflyiii/core behind a single HTTP port 8080, backed by a MariaDB/MySQL container, plus an optional Alpine cron sidecar for scheduled jobs) — structurally close to the paperless-ngx pattern already in the catalogue. Unlike paperless-ngx it injects no admin credential via env var at all: APP_KEY, the DB password, and STATIC_CRON_TOKEN are opaque random strings the app never surfaces to the customer, all generatable server-side by install.sh with no customer input.
