That clears the /compose constraint with zero blocking issues. Release cadence is active (near-continuous tags through the past year, latest stable 5 weeks old, a same-day develop pre-release confirming ongoing work) with no EOL signal. Recommend build_now: it's a well-known, fully free (no license caps) finance app that fills a real catalogue gap — though if apps-gaps/actual-budget.yaml is also greenlit, weigh whether the catalogue needs both personal-finance apps or just one.

name: Firefly
source_description: Simple WireGuard VPN server with web management interface
upstream_license: Proprietary/"personal free use only" — upstream README states "Firefly is only for personal free use. If you want to buy the source code, please contact us." Not an OSI/SPDX open-source license; the web frontend alone is derived from wg-easy under CC 4.0. A fork (bbroot/firefly-wireguard) exists but carries the same license note. Name is ambiguous: there is no relation to "Firefly III" (personal finance manager) or other unrelated "Firefly" projects — Safe3/firefly is the correct match for Hostinger's "WireGuard VPN server with web management interface" description.
upstream_docker_image: uusec/firefly:latest (no pinned-version tags published on Docker Hub beyond a stray v3.1 layer; upstream's own docker-compose.yml uses :latest)
version_health_notes: Latest GitHub release is v4.4 (2025-02-21), about 17.5 months before today (2026-08-05). Releases have historically clustered in bursts (v4.0-v4.3 all within June-Aug 2024, v4.4 in Feb 2025) with long gaps between bursts. Most recent commit to main is dated 2025-10-31 (~9 months ago, "update"), so the repo isn't abandoned, but there has been no tagged release in over a year and no evidence of active feature development — consistent with maintenance-only rather than active.
differentiation: None of substance. Firefly is functionally the same product category as the existing wg-easy recipe (WireGuard VPN server + web management UI for adding/removing peers) — in fact Firefly's own web frontend is a derivative of wg-easy's. It adds a TCP-relay/anti-QoS-throttling mode and multi-language UI polish, but no capability our catalogue doesn't already offer via wg-easy, which is open-source (Apache-2.0-family, actively maintained) versus Firefly's restrictive personal-use-only license.
usefulness_rationale: A second WireGuard-with-web-UI recipe would duplicate wg-easy for no customer-facing gain, while inheriting a license that explicitly forbids the commercial redistribution a hosted-catalogue offering constitutes, plus a deployment model (host networking, kernel module access) that's harder to sandbox per-customer than wg-easy's existing bridge-network setup.
blocking_issues:
License: upstream explicitly restricts Firefly to "personal free use" and requires purchasing the source for other use. Bundling it into a commercial hosting catalogue (Hostinger reselling it as a one-click app) is very likely outside that grant — this is a legal blocker independent of any technical mechanism question.

Web UI admin login: the app stores/compares the login as a plaintext value (docker-compose.yml sets `FIREFLY_PASSWORD=firefly` directly, and the on-disk config.json field is a plaintext `"password"` string with no documented option to accept a pre-hashed value). Per the schema, a genuine requirement for the plaintext password — not any supported hash — is a structural blocker for `generated_from`, since that mechanism only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) into the app. Gating instead with Traefik `basic_auth` would work as a workaround, but doesn't change the license blocker above.

Deployment shape: upstream's docker-compose.yml runs the container with `network_mode: host`, `cap_add: [NET_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE]`, and a bind-mounted `/lib/modules`, and exposes a WireGuard UDP port alongside the web UI TCP port. Host networking is a poor fit for a shared multi-tenant recipe platform (no port isolation from other containers on the same node) and only the web UI TCP port could ever sit behind Traefik — the UDP WireGuard port would still need direct raw-port exposure either way, same constraint the existing wg-easy recipe already documents and manages.

No pinned Docker image tag is published for general use — Docker Hub shows `uusec/firefly:latest` as the only documented tag in upstream's own compose file, violating the pin-a-stable-tag research bar before any recipe could be drafted.
summary: Firefly is a WireGuard VPN server with a web management UI whose own frontend is a derivative of the wg-easy project we already ship as a recipe — it adds no differentiated capability over wg-easy. Worse, its license explicitly limits it to personal, non-commercial use, which conflicts with reselling it via a hosted catalogue; separately, its admin login is a plaintext-only credential with no hashed-input path, its compose file only offers an unpinned `:latest` image, and its host-networking/kernel-module deployment model is harder to sandbox than wg-easy's. No tagged release in ~17.5 months also points to slowing maintenance. Not recommended — wg-easy already covers this need with a cleaner license and mechanism fit.

name: Firefox
source_description: Self-hosted Firefox browser accessible through web interface
upstream_license: GPL-3.0 (container packaging; Firefox itself is MPL-2.0)
version_health_notes: LinuxServer.io ships a new tagged build roughly every 3-6 days (ls110 on 07-23, ls111 on 07-25, ls112 on 07-31, ls113 on 08-01), tracking upstream Firefox/Xubuntu package updates. As of today (2026-08-05) the latest tag is 4 days old. This is a rolling-release image with no "version" in the traditional sense beyond the Firefox build baked in; it is actively maintained and not a fork someone could confuse with a different, EOL "Firefox" project.

Guacamole is the closest conceptual neighbor (browser-delivered remote access) but it's a gateway *to* other machines over RDP/VNC/SSH, not a browser session of its own — no functional overlap. This app would give customers an isolated, always-on Firefox session (streamed via Selkies/WebRTC, previously KasmVNC) reachable from any device, useful for browsing isolation, geo-fixed IP browsing from the server, or accessing internal-network sites only the server can reach.

summary: Single-container app streaming a full Firefox desktop over HTTP (port 3000, HTTPS on 3001) via Selkies (formerly KasmVNC) — no built-in admin login of its own (the optional CUSTOM_USER/PASSWORD basic-auth env vars are just an alternate way to do the same gate, not a customer-facing app login). That makes it installable today the same way as WUD/n8n: gate the single public port behind Traefik basic_auth:true, with the password projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from`. Needs shm_size: 1gb and security_opt: seccomp=unconfined at the compose level (both expressible in plain docker-compose, not blockers). Release cadence is actively maintained. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically installable, but the passwordless-sudo terminal inside the streamed desktop means the basic_auth gate must be treated as mandatory, not optional, and the recipe write-up should call out that this exposes a full Linux shell, not just a browser, to anyone who gets past the gate.

name: Fireshare
source_description: Self-hosted video and image sharing for game clips with unique shareable links
version_health_notes: 11 days between today (2026-08-05) and the latest tagged release (v1.7.4, 2026-07-26). Release history is dense: 15 tagged releases between 2026-04-28 (v1.6.7) and 2026-07-26 (v1.7.4), averaging roughly one release every 6-7 days over that span, with the longest gap being ~4 weeks (v1.7.3 to v1.7.4). Docker Hub shows a `develop` tag rebuilt as recently as 2026-08-05 (today), confirming ongoing active development, not just release-tagging. Repo not archived, 1.4k stars. Genuinely active, healthy single-maintainer project.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue targets link-based sharing of individual video/image clips. Immich is the closest existing recipe (media library with sharing) but is architecturally a full personal photo/video backup and library platform (mobile auto-backup, facial recognition, ML search, multi-service stack with Postgres/Redis/ machine-learning containers) aimed at replacing Google Photos, not a lightweight "drop a clip in a folder, get a shareable link" tool for gamers. Fireshare is a single container with no database service, purpose-built for the narrower "share this clip on Discord" use case named in Hostinger's own description.
usefulness_rationale: Real, narrow niche (game-clip sharing with Discord/Twitter embed support via Open Graph) with community traction (1.4k stars, active Synology/TrueNAS/Unraid community packaging) but a smaller total addressable audience than general-purpose media tools already in or considered for the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
Fireshare's own admin login (used to upload/manage/tag videos — the app's core function, not just an optional settings surface) only accepts a plaintext password via the `ADMIN_PASSWORD` env var. Verified directly against upstream source (app/server/fireshare/__init__.py on GitHub, main branch as of 2026-08-05): at boot the app reads `ADMIN_PASSWORD` as plaintext and hashes it itself with `generate_password_hash(..., method= 'pbkdf2:sha256')` (werkzeug's own scheme) before storing it — there is no code path that accepts a pre-computed hash instead. Our platform's only per-customer secret channel, `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, only ever carries a hash of the root password (argon2 or bcrypt), never the plaintext itself. Since this is a genuine plaintext-only requirement (not merely an unsupported hash algorithm like pbkdf2, which would be a softer, extensible gap), there is no way to project the customer's own password into this field today, and no other way for the customer to learn a server-generated value either.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (as done for Adminer-style apps with an unusable fixed credential) does not resolve this the same way it does for those apps: Fireshare's admin account is the actual mechanism customers use to upload and manage their videos, not a redundant/bypassable inner login. Leaving `ADMIN_PASSWORD` at its default ("admin") or a random server-generated value behind a basic_auth gate would still leave the customer unable to ever learn a working admin credential for the app itself, blocking core functionality rather than just an unauthenticated attack surface.
summary: Fireshare (shaneisrael/fireshare) is a healthy, actively-released single- container app (v1.7.4, 2026-07-26, ~weekly release cadence) that fills a real gap not covered by Immich or any other current recipe: lightweight, link-based sharing of individual game clips/videos, reverse-proxy compatible on a single HTTP port. It is blocked from `installable_today` by a structural mismatch rather than a missing algorithm: the app's own admin login — required for its core upload/manage functionality, not an optional extra — only accepts a plaintext password via `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, confirmed by reading the boot-time user-provisioning code on GitHub. Our root-password projection mechanism only ever produces a hash, so there is no channel today for a customer to end up with a working admin credential, and a Traefik basic_auth gate in front doesn't substitute for that the way it does for logins-that-don't-matter apps like Adminer. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit only if the platform grows a plaintext-carrying provisioning channel, which is a larger change than the argon2/bcrypt algorithm list `generated_from` already supports.

name: Flame
source_description: Self-hosted startpage and application dashboard for your homelab
version_health_notes: Not archived, and the master branch is not dead (a follow-up commit fixed a sqlite/amd64 crash on 2026-04-25, and the repo was last pushed to on 2026-06-25 — about 6 weeks before today, 2026-08-05). The maintainer has publicly floated a v3.0 rewrite on a "modern stack" with no committed timeline. Net: alive enough to patch critical bugs, but not under active feature development — treat as maintenance-only rather than actively developed.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes are a bookmark/startpage dashboard — portainer and uptime-kuma are admin tools for specific concerns (container management, uptime monitoring), not a general-purpose landing page/link hub for a customer's other self-hosted apps. Flame would be a plausible "front door" once a customer has installed 2-3 other recipes on the same VPS, letting them bookmark and search across those apps' URLs from one page.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful once a customer has multiple recipes running, but it's a convenience layer rather than something people seek out on its own, and the optional Docker-socket integration (auto-discovering running containers) — one of its more compelling features — is a security tradeoff we'd want to leave disabled by default in a hosted, multi-tenant context.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: Traefik gate credential (perimeter auth in front of the app); Flame's own PASSWORD env var (in-app login used to edit apps/bookmarks/settings)
secrets_expressible_today: Traefik gate credential (perimeter auth in front of the app):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
Flame's login (controllers/auth/login.js) does a plain string equality check — `process.env.PASSWORD == password` — with no hashing anywhere in the comparison. It is not a "hash algorithm we don't support yet" case; the app only ever accepts a value the customer can type literally, and `generated_from` only ever produces a one-way hash, not the plaintext root password. So the in-app PASSWORD cannot be projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from` — the customer would have to type in a hash string they've never seen and could not have derived themselves.

Workaround used elsewhere for unchangeable/default app credentials (IF-1312 precedent) applies here too: put Traefik basic_auth (generated_from the root password hash) in front as the real perimeter, and ship Flame's own PASSWORD as a fixed, non-customer-specific value baked into the recipe. That unblocks shipping the recipe, but it means every install of this recipe shares the same in-app edit password — acceptable per IF-1312 reasoning (the Traefik gate is the actual boundary) but worth flagging explicitly since it's not a per-customer secret.
summary: Flame is a small, real gap in the catalogue (no startpage/dashboard recipe exists today) and is mechanically shippable now via a Traefik basic_auth gate keyed off the customer's root password, the same pattern already used for n8n/WUD/Open WebUI. The catch is Flame's own in-app login: it does a plaintext string comparison with no hashing, so it cannot consume a `generated_from` hash the way Vaultwarden's admin token can — the recipe would have to ship a fixed, shared PASSWORD value behind the Traefik gate, same precedent as IF-1312's "unchangeable default credential" case. Combined with medium (not high) usefulness and a project that's alive but effectively maintenance-only after a 2.75-year release gap, this is a reasonable build_with_caveats candidate rather than a priority pick.

name: FlareSolverr
source_description: Proxy server to bypass Cloudflare protection for web scraping

differentiation: No current recipe does anything like this. FlareSolverr is not a standalone destination app — it's a headless REST API (a single POST endpoint at /v1) that other self-hosted apps (Jackett, Prowlarr, Sonarr/Radarr, various scrapers) call over an internal network to get past Cloudflare/DDoS-Guard JS challenges on third-party sites. None of those consumer apps are in the current catalogue, so FlareSolverr would ship with no consumer to call it and no UI for a customer to interact with directly.

FlareSolverr has no login or auth of its own — every request to /v1 is served to whoever can reach the port. A Traefik basic_auth gate is mechanically expressible (same pattern as WUD/Adminer), so this alone would not block installable_today.

Structural mismatch, not a secrets gap: upstream's own README states plainly "DO NOT expose FlareSolverr to the internet, as it can be abused" — it is a generic URL-fetching proxy, and putting it on a public subdomain (even behind basic_auth, which only the paying customer can pass) still hands that one customer an anonymizing fetch proxy reachable from the open internet, which is a different risk profile than every other app in the catalogue. Its documented deployment pattern is a sidecar container on an internal Docker network reached only by another app's process (e.g. Jackett), never a Traefik-fronted, publicly routable service — which is the only deployment shape our recipe mechanism currently produces.
summary: FlareSolverr (flaresolverr/flaresolverr, MIT, v3.5.0 as of 2026-05-26) is an actively-maintained-if-bursty single-container project, and mechanically it could ship: no login of its own, and a Traefik basic_auth gate is a supported way to close that off. The real problem is fit, not mechanism. It is a headless REST API with zero web UI, meant to be called by other self-hosted apps (Jackett/Prowlarr/Sonarr-style indexers) that aren't in our 24-app catalogue, so a standalone customer would get a bare JSON endpoint and nothing to do with it. Worse, upstream explicitly warns against exposing it to the internet at all, which is the exact opposite of how every AF recipe is deployed (public subdomain via Traefik). Recommend not_recommended: not a platform blocker, a poor-fit candidate — it's plumbing for apps we don't offer, not a destination app in its own right.

A customer wanting to run a public community/support forum on their own infrastructure (instead of a hosted forum SaaS or a free third-party platform) would reach for this. Flarum has no official Docker image. All community images researched (mondedie/flarum, kovah/flarum, shinsenter/flarum) create the admin account by taking FLARUM_ADMIN_USER/FLARUM_ADMIN_PASS/FLARUM_ADMIN_MAIL as plaintext at container start and calling Flarum's own account- creation path, which bcrypt-hashes the password itself. Flarum's other supported install paths (web installer, `php flarum install` CLI) work the same way — plaintext password in, app hashes it internally. There is no supported path to hand Flarum a pre-computed hash directly, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash) cannot express this credential — a genuine plaintext-password requirement, not just an unsupported hash algorithm.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` is technically available but does not make sense for a public forum: it would block the site's actual visitors and members, not just an admin panel — this isn't a case like n8n/Adminer where the whole app is a single-admin tool. Using it purely as a substitute for the admin-account password would defeat the product's purpose.

Even setting the credential issue aside, no researched community image publishes a version-pinned tag tracking current Flarum (1.8.17 / 2.0.0-rc.5). `mondedie/flarum`'s newest numbered tag is 1.3.0, last published roughly 4 years ago; only its unversioned `latest` tag is current. `kovah/flarum` is explicitly deprecated (6+ years stale). `shinsenter/flarum` publishes daily dev-track tags (e.g. `dev-php8.3-nginx`) rather than a stable numbered release tag. None of these satisfy the "pinned, current stable tag, never :latest" requirement without building a bespoke image ourselves.
summary: Flarum is an actively maintained, MIT-licensed forum platform that would fill a genuine (if niche) gap in the catalogue — no existing recipe covers community/discussion-board hosting. It is blocked today for two independent reasons: first, every install path Flarum supports (its community Docker images, its web installer, and its CLI installer) needs the admin password as plaintext so the app can hash it itself, which our `generated_from` root-password projection cannot supply (it only ever carries a pre-computed hash); gating the whole forum behind Traefik `basic_auth` as a workaround would block real visitors, defeating the app's purpose. Second, there is no official Docker image and no community image offers a current, version-pinned tag we could responsibly pin to today. Revisit if either a custom image/entrypoint that writes a pre-hashed admin credential directly to the database is built, or if the platform grows a channel for a genuinely customer-chosen (not root-password-derived) credential.

The image ships with no default `config.yml` (ENTRYPOINT is the bare `flexget` CLI, `VOLUME /config` is empty) — first boot requires a task-free but valid YAML config plus `web_server: {web_ui: yes}` to even start the daemon and serve the UI. install.sh can template a minimal empty-tasks config, but the app is functionally useless to a customer until they hand-author real `tasks:` YAML (RSS URLs, torrent client connection, series/movie matching rules) — there is no input channel for that today, and it isn't a "secret" so it doesn't block installable_today, but it does mean the shipped app boots to an empty shell.
summary: FlexGet is an actively maintained (weekly-release), MIT-licensed, single- container app with an official Docker image and a bundled web UI reachable on one HTTP port — mechanically it clears our reverse-proxy and Traefik basic_auth gating bar and would not duplicate anything in the current catalogue. The caveat is UX, not platform capability: FlexGet's own login can't be hash-projected (only plaintext CLI-set), so it would ship gated purely by Traefik basic_auth, and even then the app boots to an empty automation engine that requires the customer to hand-write YAML task config before it does anything useful — no on-ramp our setup flow can generate. Buildable today, but expect low activation without a companion onboarding doc or template task library.

Preceding v2.x tags (v2.10.0, v2.9.0) landed roughly one to two months apart, a steady cadence consistent with active development. differentiation: None of the current 24 shipped recipes cover feature-flag/experimentation management (closest neighbours — n8n, Gitea, Anytype, Opengist — are workflow automation, source control, notes, and pastebin). Flipt's own angle within that niche is "Git-native": flags can be stored as declarative files in a Git repo (or served purely from local storage, which is what a default single-VPS recipe install would use) rather than a database, and it ships as a single dependency-free binary/container. Note this is the same niche already covered by the `flagsmith` gap- analysis candidate (apps-gaps/flagsmith.yaml, recommended build_now, BSD-3-Clause, active) — the catalogue does not need both, and Flagsmith is the cleaner pick on licensing grounds (see below).
usefulness_rationale: Feature flagging is a genuine, recurring need for teams running their own backends, so the category itself is high-value (as reflected in the Flagsmith gap analysis). Flipt specifically is downgraded to medium here purely because of the license conflict below, which makes it a considerably riskier pick than Flagsmith for the same customer need.
blocking_issues:
LICENSE CONFLICT (not a mechanism/secrets gap): Flipt v2's Fair Core License explicitly prohibits creating a competing cloud/SaaS offering using Flipt or offering Flipt as a managed service to third parties (per docs.flipt.io/v2/licensing). The Application Factory's business model — packaging and provisioning Flipt for customers through our own recipe/bootstrap mechanism — sits uncomfortably close to exactly what that clause targets, even though the resulting instance runs on the customer's own VPS rather than IONOS-operated infrastructure. This is a legal-review question, not something a recipe author can resolve by choice of config; flagging explicitly so it isn't shipped on the assumption that "self-hosted" automatically clears FCL's non-compete bar.

Technically the app is otherwise straightforward to ship: single container, one HTTP port (8080) for the UI/API plus an optional gRPC port (9000) that a customer-facing recipe would not need to expose, and no external database is required for a default local/filesystem- backed install. The only first-boot secret is the Traefik perimeter gate, same pattern as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI. If the license question gets cleared (e.g. legal confirms the customer-operated-VPS model is fine, or a version ages into its MIT Future License window), this would be a fast build.
summary: Flipt is an actively developed (~monthly releases, not archived), single- binary, Git-native feature-flag platform that would be mechanically easy to ship — one HTTP port, no external DB, no built-in login so a Traefik basic_auth gate keyed off the root password covers the only first-boot secret. The blocker isn't the recipe mechanism, it's licensing: Flipt v2's Fair Core License bars using it to offer a competing managed/cloud service to third parties, which is uncomfortably close to what packaging it as an Application Factory recipe would do. Combined with the fact that the `flagsmith` gap-analysis candidate already covers this exact niche under a clean BSD-3-Clause license with no such restriction, recommend not building this one — pursue Flagsmith for feature-flag management instead, or revisit Flipt only after legal clears the FCL question.

name: FMD (Find My Device)
source_description: Self-hosted, privacy-friendly Find My Device server for Android phones
version_health_notes: 20 tagged releases since v0.3.1 (2021-11-14), most recently v0.16.0 (2026-06-17), v0.15.0 (2026-05-09), v0.14.2 (2026-03-23) — roughly monthly cadence sustained for the past year, as of today (2026-08-05) the latest release is ~7 weeks old. Actively developed by fmd-foss (maintainer Thore Göbel, continuing the project originally started by Nulide in 2021). No archival or EOL signal.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers personal device location-tracking/recovery. Closest adjacent recipes (Vaultwarden, 2FAuth-style security tools) are credential managers, not device tracking — this would be a genuinely new personal-security category: a self-hosted alternative to Google's Find My Device / Apple Find My, with location pings end-to-end-encrypted client-side before upload.
usefulness_rationale: Real privacy appeal (host your own device-tracking backend instead of trusting Google) but it's a single-user, single-purpose companion service to one specific Android app (FMD Android) — narrower audience than general-purpose tools like Vaultwarden or Syncthing, and it has no utility at all without installing that companion app on a phone.
blocking_issues:
FMD Server has no admin web login of its own to project a root- password hash into. Per-device accounts (an ID + password pair) are generated inside the FMD Android app itself at registration time and are not customer-chosen, so there is nothing analogous to Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN here.

The actual gate is `RegistrationToken` (config.yml / env var `FMD_REGISTRATIONTOKEN`): "if RegistrationToken is non-empty, FMD Server requires the FMD app to provide this token during registration." This is a single shared secret that the customer must type verbatim into their own Android app's settings, and (unlike Vaultwarden's bcrypt ADMIN_TOKEN) there is no documented hashed comparison for it — it reads as a plain server-side string match, so the server needs the literal plaintext value, not a hash. Our platform's only per-customer-secret channel (`generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`) only ever carries a hash of the root password, never the plaintext. Per SCHEMA.md, a genuine requirement for the plaintext (not any hash) is a structural blocker, not a missing-algorithm case like the pbkdf2 example.

Leaving `RegistrationToken` empty (open registration) is not a safe substitute: it would put an unauthenticated device-location-tracking server on the public internet, letting anyone register an account and use the service — an unacceptable default for a privacy/security app.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead (our other supported mechanism) is also not a clean substitute here: the FMD Android app talks directly to the server's HTTP API (not through a browser), and it is not confirmed whether that app supports supplying HTTP Basic credentials (e.g. via embedded URL userinfo) — if it doesn't, a basic_auth gate would break the app's core sync/locate function rather than just adding a login prompt, unlike WUD/n8n/Open WebUI where basic_auth only fronts a browser-facing UI.
summary: FMD Server is an actively maintained (monthly release cadence), genuinely differentiated addition — nothing in our current catalogue does personal device-location tracking. But its core access-control primitive, RegistrationToken, is a shared plaintext secret the customer's own phone app must be given verbatim, and our platform can only project a hash of the root password, never plaintext — this is a structural mismatch, not a missing-algorithm gap. Leaving registration open is unacceptable for a privacy-focused app, and fronting it with Traefik basic_auth risks breaking the Android client's direct API calls. Not recommended for a recipe today; revisit only if the platform ever adds a genuine plaintext passthrough channel or FMD Server changes RegistrationToken to a hashed comparison.

Corrected port research: 3000 (HTTP) and 3001 (HTTPS) are the same desktop-GUI web interface exposed twice, not two required services — Traefik should terminate TLS and front the single HTTP port 3000, the same one-HTTP-port shape as recipes/guacamole. The image's separate websocket data channel (SELKIES_PORT/CUSTOM_WS_PORT, default 8082) is multiplexed over that same HTTP(S) connection via a standard WebSocket upgrade — LinuxServer's own reverse-proxy guidance for this webtop base image (SWAG/Apache examples) proxies everything through one port with Upgrade-header handling, never exposing 8082 separately. Traefik supports WebSocket upgrades on a normal HTTP router out of the box, so no extra port or special routing is needed. The image ships with no built-in auth by default (its optional CUSTOM_USER/PASSWORD env vars are documented by LinuxServer as suitable only for a trusted local network, not internet exposure), so it needs a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate — expressible today via generated_from projection of the customer's root password, same pattern as Adminer/WUD/n8n. name: FreeScout
source_description: Lightweight open-source help desk and shared inbox system
version_health_notes: Latest tag 1.8.232 shipped 2026-07-31, 6 days before this analysis (2026-08-05). The preceding releases (1.8.231, 1.8.230, 1.8.229...) land roughly weekly going back through mid-2026, so this is a genuinely active, frequently-patched project, not a stale one.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a ticketing/shared-inbox help desk. n8n (automation) and the CRM-adjacent tools we don't yet carry are the nearest conceptual neighbors but serve a different job; FreeScout would be a genuinely new category — self-hosted customer support for small teams who don't want a SaaS help desk subscription.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted help desk is a common, well-understood SMB need with real demand for a free alternative to Help Scout/Zendesk, and FreeScout is the most established free option in that space (AGPL-3.0, no per-seat licensing, active weekly releases).
blocking_issues:
No official Docker image from the FreeScout team itself; the app's own docs (freescout.net/docker/) point to a third-party wrapper (nfrastack/container-freescout, MIT), which bundles PHP-FPM/Nginx plus a bootstrap script but is not maintained by the upstream project — a supply-chain/support caveat worth surfacing even though it doesn't block the /compose secret-projection mechanism.
The wrapper's ADMIN_PASS (documented default 'freescout') and FreeScout's own `php artisan freescout:create-user` console command both take the admin password as PLAINTEXT that the app hashes internally — there is no documented path to hand FreeScout a pre-computed hash. generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD" only ever produces a hash, so it cannot be projected onto ADMIN_PASS without turning the customer's real root password into an opaque string they'd never actually know or be able to log in with (same blocker already identified for apps-gaps/flarum.yaml). FreeScout's internal admin login therefore stays at whatever plaintext value the wrapper's env/default sets, unrelated to the customer's root password, and is not customer-meaningful — it's protected only by the outer Traefik basic_auth gate, not by generated_from.
summary: FreeScout is an actively maintained (weekly releases), AGPL-3.0 self-hosted help desk with no overlap in our current 24-recipe catalogue and clear differentiated demand (a free Help Scout/Zendesk alternative). It's a Laravel/PHP app needing its own MySQL/MariaDB database plus a scheduler/ queue worker, structurally similar to the paperless-ngx/akaunting app+db pattern, and sits behind a single HTTP port so it's fully reverse-proxy-compatible. Its own admin login only accepts a plaintext password that the app hashes internally (both the wrapper's ADMIN_PASS env var and FreeScout's `artisan freescout:create-user` CLI), so generated_from_root_password cannot express it — the same class of blocker already flagged for Flarum. Because FreeScout's UI is agent/admin-facing (customers interact by email, not by logging into the ticketing console), gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth with a generated_from_root_password credential is a legitimate substitute boundary here, unlike for a public-facing app like Flarum. Bootstrap then only needs that basic_auth gate credential plus a server-generated database password — no external API key or OAuth registration is required, so it clears the /compose constraint under this corrected mechanism. The one other real caveat: there is no image published by the FreeScout team itself, only a third-party Docker wrapper linked from their own docs, which should be flagged to whoever authors the recipe. Recommend build_with_caveats.

name: Friendica
source_description: Self-hosted fediverse social network with ActivityPub and Diaspora federation
version_health_notes: Today is 2026-08-05. 2026.05 (May 21, 2026, codename "Blutwurz") is the newest tagged release, about 2.5 months old. Release history is a steady few-times-a-year cadence: 2026.05 → 2026.01 (Jan 27, 2026) → 2024.12 (Jan 1, 2025) → 2024.08 (Aug 17, 2024) → 2024.03 (Mar 21, 2024), roughly every 4-5 months going back years. differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes touch federated/social networking — Friendica would be the first entry in that space. It lets a customer run their own ActivityPub + Diaspora-protocol node (interoperating with Mastodon, Lemmy, Diaspora, etc.), which is a genuinely different pitch ("own your social presence") than anything currently in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted fediverse nodes have a real and growing audience among privacy-conscious users leaving corporate social platforms, and Friendica specifically appeals to that crowd by bridging multiple federation protocols (not just ActivityPub) in one node. Capped at medium rather than high because it's a smaller, more technical niche than our typical productivity/AI-tool customer, and full usefulness depends on outbound email (SMTP) working for registration/notification mail, which is a separate manual setup step post-install.
blocking_issues:
Friendica's registration form has no password field at all — it only collects nickname, full name, and email (docs.friendi.ca / wiki.friendi.ca account-basics). The account's actual password is generated server-side and delivered only by outbound email ("An email will be sent to you providing your account login details... your initial password"), which the user must then change via Settings after logging in. This applies to every account, including the one matched to `FRIENDICA_ADMIN_MAIL` for admin rights — there is no separate admin-bootstrap path that skips this.

That means becoming admin (or even just getting a usable login at all) at first boot depends on outbound mail actually working. The Friendica docker image exposes `SMTP` / `SMTP_PORT` / `SMTP_AUTH_USER` / `SMTP_AUTH_PASS` / `SMTP_DOMAIN` for a real mail relay — real external mail-provider credentials the customer would have to supply. Per SCHEMA.md this is exactly the "external credential the customer must supply, no input channel today" case: nothing in `/compose` can carry an SMTP username/password into the container.

Traefik `basic_auth` does not sidestep this the way it does for n8n/WUD/Immich, because those apps have no login of their own — `basic_auth` becomes the only auth boundary. Friendica does have its own login, required for actually using the app (posting, following, managing federation, admin panel), so gating the reverse-proxy entrypoint with `basic_auth` still leaves the customer needing a working Friendica login underneath, which still requires the emailed password. `basic_auth` would only add a redundant outer lock, not replace the blocked credential.
summary: Friendica is mechanically simple to deploy (the official `friendica:2026.05-apache` image, a MariaDB/MySQL container, and a `cron`/worker instance for background federation delivery — a three-service stack similar in shape to n8n — behind a single HTTP port, Traefik-friendly), and the internal DB password is trivially server-generated. But its account-bootstrap mechanism is not a self- contained web install wizard: the registration form has no password field, and every account's password — including the one that becomes admin via `FRIENDICA_ADMIN_MAIL` (a fixed config value, not itself a secret, but one that must be set to match whatever address is used to register) — is generated server-side and only reachable by outbound email. That makes real SMTP relay credentials (`SMTP_AUTH_USER`/ `SMTP_AUTH_PASS`) a hard requirement for the customer to ever obtain a working login, and there is no channel today for the customer to supply those, nor does a Traefik `basic_auth` gate substitute for Friendica's own required login the way it does for apps with no built-in auth. This is a genuine bootstrap-mechanism blocker, not merely a low-value niche — recommend `blocked_on_platform` pending either an SMTP-credential input channel or an upstream option to set a password directly at first boot. Otherwise the catalogue-fit case (first fediverse/social-networking recipe, active steady release cadence, no EOL signal) still stands and this is worth revisiting if that platform gap closes.

Only 18 days since the last release as of 2026-08-05. Repo is not archived and shows continued feature development (taxonomy system, agent/AI adapter concepts, MCP server, OAuth2 authorization server) across the recent releases.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers API gateway / API management (build, document, and expose REST APIs with a backend admin UI, consumer developer portal, and OpenAPI/ReDoc docs). Closest existing recipes (n8n, activepieces-style automation) are workflow tools, not an API-first backend platform; Fusio would be a genuinely new category for developer-facing customers who want to stand up and monetize APIs.
usefulness_rationale: API management is a real, distinct niche with clear appeal to developer/technical customers, but it's a narrower audience than the productivity/monitoring/media tools already in the catalogue and requires the customer to already have an API-building use case in mind.
blocking_issues:
Fusio's own official docker-entrypoint.sh provisions the initial backend admin account by running `php bin/fusio adduser --password="$FUSIO_BACKEND_PW"`, which Fusio hashes and stores internally, then verifies via normal password_verify() at login. This requires FUSIO_BACKEND_PW to literally be the plaintext password the customer will type at every subsequent login — there is no pre-hashed-credential comparison mode (unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN) that would let a `generated_from` hash of the customer's root password stand in for the real login credential. Since `generated_from` only ever carries a hash, never the plaintext, this is a genuine plaintext-password requirement and a structural blocker, not just an unsupported-algorithm gap.

Gating the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth` credential (hash of the root password) does not solve this either: Fusio has its own separate backend login that the customer still needs valid credentials for once past the gate, and there is no channel today to surface a server-generated backend password back to the customer.
summary: Fusio is a single-container (plus MySQL) API management platform with a web backend UI, reverse-proxy compatible on one HTTP port, actively maintained with frequent releases and no overlap with the current catalogue. It is blocked from installability today because its official Docker image provisions the initial admin account via a plaintext FUSIO_BACKEND_PW environment variable used directly as the login password, which the platform's root-password-hash projection mechanism cannot express and which Traefik basic_auth cannot substitute for since it doesn't gate Fusio's own separate login. Recommend revisiting once a channel exists for customers to supply or retrieve a real login credential beyond hash projection.

name: FusionAuth
source_description: Self-hosted customer identity platform with OAuth, OIDC, SAML, and MFA

version_health_notes: Latest tag 1.68.0 was pushed to Docker Hub 2026-06-30, about five weeks before today (2026-08-05). Checking the prior ~12 months of tags shows a steady cadence of a new minor roughly every 3-5 weeks (1.67.1 on 2026-06-08, 1.67.0 on 2026-06-01, 1.66.0 on 2026-05-05, 1.65.0 on 2026-04-30, back through 1.62.0-1.64.x over late 2025/early 2026) with no gaps of more than ~7 weeks. No dormancy, archival, or EOL signal.
differentiation: FusionAuth is a CIAM platform (OAuth2/OIDC/SAML, MFA, breach detection, passwordless) aimed at the same "add centralized identity/SSO" job as the three identity apps already flagged in this gap analysis (Authentik, Casdoor, Authorizer). Its niche within that group is closer to Authorizer (a backend a customer wires into their own application via SDKs) than to Authentik (a general SSO gateway fronting other apps), though FusionAuth's SAML and enterprise-MFA feature set is broader than Authorizer's. It does not add a capability absent from the other three, and its Community edition is a free but closed-source binary rather than OSS, which is a negative differentiator against the already-flagged Authentik/Casdoor (both actively developed OSS).
usefulness_rationale: A fourth self-hosted identity/CIAM candidate in the same niche as three already-analyzed apps (Authentik, Casdoor, Authorizer) adds little incremental catalogue value, and its closed-source licensing model is less attractive than the OSS alternatives already flagged. Would only be worth prioritizing over those if a customer specifically needs FusionAuth's SAML/enterprise-MFA feature set, which is a narrow case.
blocking_issues:
FusionAuth has no env-var-driven admin bootstrap. The first admin account is created either (a) interactively through the browser Setup Wizard on first visit to port 9011, where the operator types an email and plaintext password (min 8 chars), or (b) via a Kickstart file (`FUSIONAUTH_APP_KICKSTART_FILE`) that POSTs a user-creation API call containing a `password` field — but that field is documented as plaintext too; FusionAuth hashes it server-side with its own configurable algorithm, it does not accept a pre-computed hash as input. Kickstart also only runs once, against a completely untouched instance (no existing API keys/users/tenants). Per SCHEMA.md, a genuine plaintext-only requirement (not just an unsupported hash algorithm) is a structural blocker, not a `blocked_on_platform` gap like Authentik's `pbkdf2_sha256` case — there is no channel here to project even a hash of the customer's root password.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the whole app is not a substitute: FusionAuth's single public port (9011) serves both the admin UI and the OAuth2/OIDC/SAML endpoints (`/oauth2/authorize`, `/oauth2/token`, hosted login pages, SAML ACS) that end users of whatever application the customer builds against it must reach — gating the whole origin would break the product's actual purpose, same reasoning as the Authentik and Authorizer analyses.
summary: FusionAuth is an actively maintained (release roughly every 3-5 weeks, latest 1.68.0 on 2026-06-30), mechanically simple recipe candidate — a single fusionauth/fusionauth-app container plus Postgres (Elasticsearch/ OpenSearch can be avoided by setting the search engine to `database`), one HTTP port, fully reverse-proxy compatible. It fails installability today for the same reason as Authorizer: its admin bootstrap accepts only a plaintext password (via the interactive Setup Wizard or a one-shot Kickstart file), with no way to supply a pre-computed hash, so `generated_from` cannot reach it and it is a genuine structural blocker rather than a missing-algorithm gap. It also overlaps heavily with three identity/CIAM apps already flagged in this catalogue (Authentik, Casdoor, Authorizer) and brings a closed-source license instead of their OSS ones, making it the lowest-priority of the four even once platform constraints loosen. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` with low re- evaluation priority.

name: FusionDirectory
source_description: Web-based LDAP, Samba, Kerberos, and mail account manager for sysadmins
version_health_notes: Today is 2026-08-05. Latest tagged release is fusiondirectory-1.5 (Feb 24, 2025) — about 17.5 months ago, with no 1.5.x point release since. Release history shows the cadence lengthening over time: 1.1 (2017) → 1.2/1.2.x (2017-2018) → 1.3 (Mar 2019) → 1.3.1 (Oct 2022, a ~3.5-year gap) → 1.4 (Jun 2023) → 1.5 (Feb 2025). The project is not archived or EOL — GitHub mirror activity (and the upstream GitLab at gitlab.fusiondirectory.org, the actual primary VCS) shows commits as recently as late July 2026 — but major/minor tagged releases have become infrequent and irregular rather than on a predictable schedule, hence `slowing` rather than `active`.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes touch LDAP/directory/identity administration. FusionDirectory would be the first entry aimed at sysadmins who want a self-hosted directory service (POSIX accounts, Samba, Kerberos, mail routing) with a web UI on top of OpenLDAP — a distinct pitch ("run your own company directory/IAM") from anything else in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real audience among small/medium orgs wanting a self-hosted alternative to hosted directory services, but it is a narrow, technical sysadmin niche (LDAP schema, Samba/Kerberos integration) compared to the productivity/AI/media tools that make up most of the current catalogue, capping it below high.
blocking_issues:
There is no official Docker image from the FusionDirectory project itself. Every available image (zsoerenm/fusiondirectory-docker, Fekide/docker-fusiondirectory-openldap, sebt3/fusiondirectory, nfrastack/container-fusiondirectory, hrektts/docker-fusiondirectory, among others) is a third-party community build, each with its own bootstrap conventions and none clearly canonical — there is no single "pin a stable tag from the official image" choice to make.

FusionDirectory itself ships an interactive, browser-based setup wizard (fusiondirectory-setup-wizard) for first-run configuration (organization name, LDAP base DN, schema selection, admin bind DN/password, TLS). Several community Docker builds route around that wizard with env vars instead (e.g. Fekide/docker-fusiondirectory-openldap's `LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and `FD_ADMIN_PASSWORD`), but those env vars are consumed as **plaintext** by the container's init script, which then hashes them internally (via `slappasswd`/similar) into LDAP's own userPassword format. That is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, not merely a hash-format mismatch — per SCHEMA.md this is the one case that is a structural blocker, since `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt), never the plaintext root password itself.

Even setting the plaintext-password issue aside, FusionDirectory's "login" is an LDAP bind against an admin DN that is created during directory bootstrap — not a single app-level credential field the way Vaultwarden's `ADMIN_TOKEN` is. Wiring a customer-facing secret through LDAP directory provisioning (organization, base DN, schema load) is a multi-step bootstrap process our mechanism has no channel for today, beyond the single root-password-hash projection.
summary: FusionDirectory would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue (self-hosted LDAP/Samba/Kerberos directory management), but it fails installability on multiple independent grounds: no official Docker image to pin a stable tag against (only a scattered set of community-maintained forks), and a first-boot bootstrap — either the app's own interactive setup wizard or the env-var shortcuts some community images offer — that fundamentally requires a plaintext admin/LDAP password rather than the hash our `generated_from` mechanism can supply. Release cadence has also visibly slowed (17.5 months and counting since the 1.5 release, following a history of widening gaps between majors), though the project is still commit-active upstream and not EOL. Recommend `not_recommended`: the blockers here are structural (no canonical image, plaintext-password requirement) rather than a single missing platform feature, so this is not simply a "revisit once IF-1420/1312 land" case.

No recipe in the current 24 covers industrial automation/SCADA, so this would open a genuinely new, more technical customer segment (small manufacturers, integrators, hobbyist industrial-IoT users) rather than duplicating anything shipping today.

The project's dense recent history of unauthenticated-RCE advisories (see version_health) is a genuine caveat for a SCADA/ICS-adjacent tool, but the same basic_auth gate this recipe needs anyway for the default admin credential mitigates that whole class of exposure, so it does not change the usefulness verdict.
summary: FUXA is a single-container, actively maintained (monthly releases, not archived, commits as recent as today) SCADA/HMI web app with an embedded SQLite/file-backed data store, no external database dependency, and a single HTTP+WebSocket port (1881) that is reverse-proxy compatible. Its official Docker image ships a fixed, hardcoded default login (admin/123456) with no environment variable to set or override it at boot — the password can only be changed manually after logging in with the default credential. Per the platform's schema guidance, a fixed default credential the customer would otherwise hit unprotected on first boot is not a hard blocker: gating the whole app behind a Traefik basic_auth credential (projected from a hash of the customer's root password) closes the real exposure window before the customer logs in and changes the in-app default. That same gate also happens to cover the five unauthenticated-RCE advisories the project shipped against this exact repo in the six months before the current release (see version_health) — all are patched in the pinned 1.3.3 image, but the frequency is a red flag worth tracking for a SCADA/ICS-adjacent app. This makes FUXA installable today and a reasonable build candidate, filling a genuinely new industrial-automation niche, albeit for a narrower, more technical audience than most of the current catalogue.

name: Gerrit
source_description: Enterprise-grade web-based code review system built on top of Git
version_health_notes: Docker Hub tag gerritcodereview/gerrit:3.14.2 was pushed ~3 weeks before 2026-08-05 (i.e. mid-July 2026). Gerrit maintains several concurrent stable branches (3.14.x, 3.13.x, 3.12.x all received patch releases on the same day), which is a sign of active, disciplined maintenance rather than a single moving HEAD. Canonical development happens on Google's own Gerrit instance (gerrit-review.googlesource.com); the GitHub mirror (GerritCodeReview/gerrit) shows zero "Releases" entries because upstream doesn't use GitHub Releases for this project — that is expected, not a sign of abandonment, and should not be read as EOL. The project backs Android's and Chromium's own code review, which is a strong activity signal on its own.
differentiation: Gerrit's patch-set/vote-based review model (per-change +2/-1 scoring, mandatory review before merge) is a genuinely different workflow from Gitea's GitHub-style PRs or Opengist's snippet sharing — it is the tool of choice for teams that want strict gatekeeping before code lands, and is the de facto standard behind large open-source projects (Android, Chromium, LibreOffice). It is not a drop-in substitute for Gitea (no issue tracker, wiki, or package registry) but targets a narrower, real need: rigorous pre-merge review.
usefulness_rationale: The workflow differentiation is real, but Gerrit is a heavyweight, enterprise/OSS-foundation tool with a steep learning curve (patch sets, Change-Ids, git-review tooling) aimed at teams already running LDAP/OAuth identity infrastructure and CI. It is a poor fit for the self-hosted small-business/solo-developer audience this catalogue otherwise targets, and (see installability below) its production auth model does not fit our current single-secret provisioning mechanism at all.
blocking_issues:
Gerrit ships with auth.type=DEVELOPMENT_BECOME_ANY_ACCOUNT by default — "no authentication at all," where anyone hitting the app can pick any existing account (including the initial admin account created by whoever logs in first) from a list and log in as them with zero credential. Gating the whole site behind a single Traefik basic_auth credential (our only "no login of its own" mechanism) does not fix this: anyone who gets past that one shared gate can then silently impersonate every user in the system, not just reach a single shared admin account. That is a materially worse security posture than the "fixed default password" case the schema explicitly allows behind basic_auth, so treating it the same way would be a mistake.

The only auth.type Gerrit supports for real production use without an external identity provider is HTTP — trusting a header set by the reverse proxy to say who the user is — which still requires something upstream (Apache mod_auth, an LDAP bind, OAuth) to actually authenticate the human and populate that header. Traefik basic_auth alone only gates the door; it doesn't supply per-user identity, so it cannot stand in for the HTTP/LDAP/OAuth auth backends Gerrit actually needs to be secure with multiple real users. Multi-user LDAP/OAuth identity provisioning has no customer-supplied input channel today.

A production deployment additionally needs an SSH port (29418) open for git push/review operations — a raw non-HTTP port outside Traefik's reverse-proxy model, though this is not a novel blocker on its own (Gitea and Opengist already ship recipes with an analogous public SSH port for git clone).
summary: Gerrit is an actively maintained, genuinely differentiated code-review tool (patch-set voting, not PR-style merging) but is aimed at teams with existing LDAP/OAuth identity infrastructure — an audience mismatch for this catalogue. More importantly, its only auth-free default (DEVELOPMENT_BECOME_ANY_ACCOUNT) lets anyone past the door impersonate any account with zero credential, and the only mechanism this platform supports today (a single shared Traefik basic_auth gate) does not fix that — it only adds one more locked door in front of an already-open house. Real production use needs LDAP/OAuth/HTTP-header identity, which has no customer-input channel today. Not recommended.

It's a single container (official `ghost` image, port 2368) plus a MySQL 8 sidecar, structurally close to a Gitea-style "app + DB" recipe, and Ghost's own docs recommend exactly the reverse-proxy setup (HTTPS + X-Forwarded-* headers) Traefik already provides for every other recipe. The one caveat, same pattern already accepted for Bludit/Baikal/An Otter Wiki in this apps-gaps set: the official image has no env var or config key to pre-provision the admin ("Owner") account — it's created through an unauthenticated browser wizard at /ghost on first visit, with no plaintext-password-accepting CLI path either. install.sh must therefore put a Traefik basic_auth gate (projected from the customer's root password) in front of the app at first boot so a stranger can't race the customer to claim ownership, with the customer expected to disable that gate once they've completed the wizard so their public blog is reachable without a password prompt — the same "temporary claim-race protection, not a permanent lock" tradeoff already accepted for those recipes. That clears the /compose constraint with zero hard blocking issues, but the extra wizard-then-unlock step and lack of a bundled MySQL/queue story (customer must keep the DB container healthy) keep this at build_with_caveats rather than build_now.

name: GitBucket
source_description: Open-source self-hosted Git platform with a GitHub-style interface on the JVM
version_health_notes: The GitBucket project itself is still active at the source level: 4.45.0 (Jan 2026), 4.46.0 (Mar 2026), and 4.46.1 (18 Apr 2026) show a steady ~6-8 week release cadence through early 2026. However, 4.46.1 is now ~3.5 months old as of this analysis (2026-08-05) with no newer tag, longer than the established gap between prior releases, so "slowing" rather than "active" pending confirmation of a mid-2026 release. Separately, and more importantly for this recipe's viability: the official Docker Hub image `gitbucket/gitbucket` has NOT been rebuilt in over 3 years — its newest tag is still 4.38.4, roughly 8 minor versions and 3+ years behind the current 4.46.1 WAR release. Upstream's own README documents only `java -jar gitbucket.war` or deployment to a servlet container (Jetty/Tomcat/JBoss) as supported installation methods; Docker is not mentioned as an official path at all. The Docker Hub image appears to be a community/CI artifact that was abandoned mid-2022 even though the underlying project kept shipping source releases — a distribution-level dormancy that would not be obvious from the app's GitHub activity alone.
differentiation: GitBucket's pitch is a GitHub-style UI plus GitHub API compatibility (useful for reusing GitHub-ecosystem tooling/plugins) on a Scala/JVM stack instead of Gitea's Go stack. Functionally the two overlap almost completely for a self-hoster: git hosting, PRs, issues, wiki, web UI, optional SSH access. GitBucket does not add a capability Gitea (already in the catalogue, actively maintained image, lighter footprint) lacks; if anything it trades a smaller, faster Go binary for a heavier JVM runtime for the sake of GitHub API parity most self-hosters won't use.
usefulness_rationale: Gitea already covers this need in the catalogue with a current, actively-rebuilt official image and lower resource footprint. GitBucket would be a near-duplicate offering with no meaningful workflow differentiation for our target audience, and (see installability) the only Docker artifact available to build a recipe on is itself 3+ years stale.
blocking_issues:
No actively maintained official Docker image exists. The only image on Docker Hub (`gitbucket/gitbucket`) was last pushed ~3 years ago at version 4.38.4, while the project has continued releasing through 4.46.1 (Apr 2026) via WAR file only. Pinning a recipe to 4.38.4 would ship a multi-year-old build missing since-added security fixes (e.g. the SHA-256 webhook signature support added in 4.46.0). There is no upstream-provided current image to pin to, and hand-rolling and maintaining our own Dockerfile around the WAR file is out of scope for a recipe (we pin to upstream-provided image tags, we don't invent/maintain our own container builds).

GitBucket's default admin account is a hardcoded root/root login with no documented env var or config-time override for the initial password — not a hard blocker on its own (a fixed default credential can sit behind a Traefik `basic_auth` gate per SCHEMA.md), but it compounds the stale-image problem: the shipped GitBucket build itself would be missing over three years of patches behind that one gate.
summary: GitBucket the open-source project is still alive (steady releases through 4.46.1 in Apr 2026), but the only Docker artifact available to build a recipe on has been dormant for 3+ years and is 8 minor versions behind current — upstream itself only documents WAR/servlet-container installation, not Docker. Combined with near-total functional overlap with the already-cataloged, actively-rebuilt Gitea, there is no case for building this recipe today: not installable on a trustworthy pinned image, and low differentiation even if it were. Not recommended.

name: GitLab
source_description: GitLab is a complete DevOps platform for Git repository management and CI/CD
upstream_license: MIT (Community Edition core); shipped as the free tier of the unified GitLab EE codebase — proprietary tiers are gated behind a license key, not a separate CE source tree, since the 2021 CE/EE code merge
version_health_notes: GitLab ships a minor release on the 22nd of every month plus mid-cycle patch releases for the last three minors (e.g. the 2026-02-10 patch release covered 18.8.4/18.7.4/18.6.6 simultaneously). 19.2 landed 2026-07-16, under 3 weeks before today (2026-08-05) — this is one of the most disciplined, predictable release cadences of any app considered in this catalogue. No indication of slowdown, archival, or EOL; GitLab is a publicly traded company (NASDAQ: GTLB) actively developing the product.
differentiation: GitLab is a genuine superset of what Gitea offers today in this catalogue: built-in CI/CD pipelines, a container registry, merge-request approval rules, security/dependency scanning, and project management (issues, epics, boards) in one product, versus Gitea's lighter Git-hosting-plus-basic-Actions scope. It is not a substitute for Gerrit's patch-set review workflow, but it does cover everything Opengist offers (snippets) as a minor feature. For a customer who wants "our own GitHub/GitLab-style DevOps platform," it is a stronger, more recognizable brand match than Gitea.
usefulness_rationale: GitLab is one of the most widely recognized self-hosted DevOps platforms and a plausible top request from customers who specifically want "GitLab," not just "a git server" — brand recognition alone drives demand distinct from Gitea. The catalogue currently has nothing that covers integrated CI/CD + container registry + Git hosting in one app. The cost is a materially heavier footprint (omnibus image bundles PostgreSQL, Redis, and Puma/Sidekiq internally; upstream recommends a minimum of 4 GB RAM, 8 GB for reliable operation, vs. 512 MB for Gitea) which should be reflected in `app_min_ram_mb` if this is ever built.
blocking_issues:
GitLab's own admin bootstrap variable, GITLAB_ROOT_PASSWORD (an omnibus `gitlab.rb`/env setting), only accepts a plaintext password that GitLab itself hashes internally on first boot — it has no "accept a pre-hashed value and compare against it at login" mode the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash of the customer's root/server password, never the plaintext, so there is no way to project a value into GITLAB_ROOT_PASSWORD that the customer could actually authenticate with afterward. This is the exact "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case SCHEMA.md calls out as a hard structural blocker, not a missing-algorithm gap.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (our other supported mechanism) does not substitute here either: GitLab has its own login (the root account) and public self-signup is disabled by default, so a customer still needs a working root credential to do anything inside the app once past a `basic_auth` door — unlike Adminer/n8n, where `basic_auth` alone is the entire auth boundary.

If GITLAB_ROOT_PASSWORD is left unset, GitLab auto-generates a random root password and writes it once to /etc/gitlab/initial_root_password inside the container, valid for only 24 hours. Retrieving it requires a shell into the container/VM, which is not a channel our current provisioning flow exposes to the customer — and it expires before most customers would think to look for it, effectively locking them out of their own first login.
summary: GitLab is an actively and predictably maintained project (monthly releases, no EOL signal) and would be a genuinely higher-value, higher-recognition addition than what Gitea covers today, bundling CI/CD, a container registry, and project management into one app. It is blocked purely on provisioning: GitLab's root-login bootstrap variable only accepts a plaintext password, which `generated_from` (hash-only) and Traefik `basic_auth` (gate-only, doesn't help once an app has its own login) cannot supply between them. This is a platform-mechanism gap, not a reason to rule the app out — recommend revisiting once a plaintext-secret projection channel exists, and separately budgeting for its notably heavier RAM/disk footprint versus the rest of the catalogue.

name: Glances
source_description: Glances is a cross-platform system monitoring tool with web interface
version_health_notes: v4.5.6 shipped 2026-08-01, just 4 days before today (2026-08-05), and the prior several 4.5.x patch releases (v4.5.5 on 2026-06-13, v4.5.4 on 2026-04-19, v4.5.3 on 2026-03-29, v4.5.2 on 2026-03-14, v4.5.1 on 2026-03-07, v4.5.0 on 2026-02-08) land every 2-6 weeks. Repo's last push was 2026-08-05 (today), not archived, 108 open issues still being triaged. Clearly active, not slowing or dormant.
differentiation: Glances is a live host-hardware telemetry dashboard (CPU, RAM, disk, network, sensors, per-process and per-container stats via the Docker socket) — a "top/htop in a browser" tool. Uptime Kuma, our only monitoring recipe, checks external service/URL reachability, not the host's own resource usage, so it is not a true overlap. Note: a nearly identical candidate, dashdot (`apps-gaps/dashdot.yaml`), was already analyzed for the same "at-a-glance server resource dashboard" niche and would overlap heavily with Glances if both were ever built — worth flagging to whoever triages these so only one of the two ships.
usefulness_rationale: A live host-resource dashboard is a genuinely useful, well-known utility for VPS/private-server owners, and Glances is a much more mature and widely adopted project than dashdot in this niche. Capped at medium rather than high because it is a read-only diagnostic convenience, not something a customer's workflow depends on, and it largely duplicates functionality available via SSH + a terminal tool.
blocking_issues:
Glances' own optional web-server auth (`--password` / `-P`) is not a viable channel even if we wanted to use it instead of a Traefik gate: it hashes with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (100,000 iterations, UUID salt), an algorithm `generated_from` does not currently support (only argon2/bcrypt), and setting it requires an interactive `getpass()` prompt on first run with no documented env-var or config-file path to supply the password non-interactively. This is not a hard blocker overall, though, since Glances runs with no auth by default and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (the same pattern as dashdot/dozzle/n8n) fully covers the "don't sit open on the internet" requirement.

Upstream's documented container deployment for full host stats needs `--pid host`, a Docker-socket bind mount (`/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro`) for per-container metrics, and recommends `--network host` (with `--privileged` when using host networking) to read real host network-interface counters from outside the container namespace. None of these are RFC-002 ERROR-level (no customer-secret channel involved), but they are the same class of WARN-level privileged/bind-mount flags already noted for dashdot, and worth weighing before committing to a recipe.
summary: Glances is an actively maintained (latest release 4 days before this analysis), single-container system-monitoring dashboard with a web UI that has no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue — Uptime Kuma only covers external URL/service reachability, not host resource telemetry. It ships with no built-in auth by default, so a Traefik `basic_auth` gate fully covers the one secret it needs at first boot and is expressible today; its own optional password feature would not have worked anyway (unsupported hash algorithm, interactive-only setup). The remaining caveats are architectural, not secret-related: full host/container stats want `--pid host`, a read-only Docker-socket mount, and optionally `--network host` + `--privileged`, the same WARN-level trade-offs already flagged for the very similar dashdot candidate. Recommend build_with_caveats, and recommend deduping against dashdot before building either, since the two would serve the same niche.

The companion GNS3/gns3-web-ui repo (separate project, see below) pushed as recently as 2026-08-05 (today). Clearly active on both the 2.2.x stable line and the 3.x development line, no dormant/EOL signal.
differentiation: A network-topology emulator/lab tool (virtual routers/switches/PCs via Dynamips, IOU, QEMU/KVM, and Docker-based node types, wired into arbitrary virtual topologies) — nothing else in the current 24-recipe catalogue does this; it's a distinct "CCNA/network-engineering lab" use case, closest in spirit to a hosted lab environment rather than any existing app (Guacamole is a remote-desktop *gateway* for real hosts, not a device emulator; Portainer manages the customer's own Docker containers, not emulated network gear).
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful to network engineers/students studying for certifications or building/testing topologies, and GNS3 is the de facto standard tool for this niche. Capped at medium rather than high because it's a specialist tool for a narrow audience, not general-purpose infrastructure most customers need, and (see below) its core workflow does not fit our reverse-proxy-only exposure model.
blocking_issues:
GNS3 server's own HTTP auth (`auth`/`user`/`password` in `gns3_server.conf`) stores the password as plaintext in the config file — there is no hashing at all, so `generated_from` (which only ever projects a *hash*) has no channel to reach it. This is not the blocker on its own, though: `auth` is `False` by default, so the app can ship with its own auth left disabled and rely on a Traefik `basic_auth` gate instead (same pattern as Glances/dashdot), which fully covers the "don't sit open on the internet" requirement for the management UI itself.

The actual structural blocker is architectural, not secret-related: GNS3's core function — opening a console (Telnet/VNC) to a running emulated device, and linking devices together — requires large dynamically-allocated raw port ranges (`console_start/end_port_range` 5000-10000 TCP, `vnc_console_start/end_port_range` 5900-10000, and `udp_start/end_port_range` 20000-30000 for inter-node links, 2 ports per link), assigned per-node at topology-build time, not known in advance. `metadata.yaml`'s `ports[]` is a static, enumerable list (RFC-002 `single-http-port`/`no-duplicate-public-port`) — it has no way to express "expose an on-demand slice of a 5000-port range," and even a token subset would still make consoles/links unreachable for any node outside that slice. A recipe could expose only the Traefik- fronted web management API/UI (topology editing, node start/stop) and nothing else, but without console/link ports that isn't a usable network emulator — the one thing customers install GNS3 for.

Secondary (non-blocking on its own, but compounding): meaningful node types (Cisco IOSv/NX-OS, Arista vEOS, any QEMU-based appliance) need `/dev/kvm` passthrough and typically `--privileged`; Docker-based node types need the Docker socket mounted so the GNS3 server can spin up nested containers. RFC-002's `no-privileged-without-justification` allows this with documented justification, so it's not an ERROR by itself — but combined with the port-range problem above it reinforces that GNS3 is built to run as a general-purpose Linux host/VM (this is exactly why upstream requires the dedicated "GNS3 VM" or a full Linux box for GNS3 3.0+), not as a single reverse-proxied container.
summary: GNS3 Server is an actively maintained, well-regarded network-topology emulator with no overlap in the current catalogue, but it does not fit the platform's reverse-proxy-only exposure model. Its own auth is a plaintext (unhashable) config value, but that's sidestep-able by leaving it disabled and gating the web UI with Traefik `basic_auth` — the real problem is that GNS3's actual purpose (opening device consoles, linking emulated nodes) depends on large dynamically-allocated raw TCP/VNC/UDP port ranges that `metadata.yaml`'s static port list cannot express, and that Traefik cannot route even if it could. Shipping only the web management shell without console/link access would not be a usable GNS3 install. Recommend not_recommended unless/until the platform supports exposing dynamic raw port ranges per app — a much larger platform change than the IF-1420/1312 secret-projection work this schema otherwise gates on.
