differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover CI/CD pipeline orchestration. Gitea (developer-tools) is a git host with a built-in Actions feature, and n8n (automation) is general-purpose SaaS/API workflow automation with a drag-and-drop canvas — neither is a build/test/deploy pipeline server with GoCD's value-stream-map view, fan-in/fan-out pipeline dependencies, and material-triggered stages. A customer already self-hosting Gitea on this platform is a plausible next step to also self-host CI next to it.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct capability with a genuine developer audience, but the server alone is inert: GoCD ships no bundled build capacity, so a customer needs at least one gocd-agent container registered before any pipeline can run a single job. That's mechanically solvable inside one docker-compose stack (server + agent, agent auto-registered via a server-generated key, no customer input needed), but it raises the resource floor and the "what did I actually get" bar versus a single self-contained web app — closer to n8n/immich territory than to uptime-kuma.
summary: GoCD ships with no authentication configured by default — "if the security element is not defined, anyone can use GoCD without logging in," and every unauthenticated user is implicitly an admin. There is no env-var or first-boot hook on the official image to pre-seed a password-file or admin account; enabling security is a post-boot UI/config action. That maps cleanly onto the documented "no login of its own" case: gate the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password, exactly like n8n/WUD/Immich already do, and leave GoCD's own (absent) auth alone. The web UI is a single HTTP port (8153, no TLS needed since Traefik terminates it) and works fine behind a reverse proxy. The real caveat is functional, not auth-related: a server-only deployment can't run pipelines, so the recipe would need a paired gocd-agent service in the same compose stack (agent auto-registration key can be server-generated, no customer input required) to be useful out of the box, which pushes this recipe's resource footprint and complexity above the single-container norm. Mechanically installable today via the basic_auth gate; recommend build_with_caveats given the added server+agent complexity and a narrower (developer/CI) audience than most of the current catalogue.

name: Gogs
source_description: Gogs is a self-hosted Git service for painless project management
version_health_notes: Not archived and commits are still landing on `main` (last commit 2026-07-19, git-module dependency updated 2026-08-01), so this is not a dead repo. But release cadence is slow and irregular: v0.13.0 shipped 2023-02-25, v0.14.0/v0.14.1/v0.14.2 all shipped within one month of each other in Feb 2025 (v0.14.0 was pulled shortly after release for a builtin-SSH-server bug, superseded by v0.14.1 the same day), then a 16-month gap before v0.14.3 on 2026-06-07 — about 2 months before today (2026-08-05). Recent release notes for v0.14.2/v0.14.3 are almost entirely security-fix batches (reverse-proxy auth bypass, SSRF in webhooks, stored XSS, LFS cross-repo object leaks, RCE-adjacent issues) rather than new features. Reads as a small-team, maintenance-only project rather than one under active feature development.
differentiation: None found. Gitea is a 2016 fork of Gogs that overtook and long since surpassed it in feature set, release velocity, and community size, and is already in the catalogue (recipes/gitea). Gogs offers the same core pitch (self-hosted, lightweight Git service with web UI, issues, and SSH access) with no capability Gitea lacks; picking Gogs today would mean shipping the slower-moving, less-maintained fork of a recipe we already have.
usefulness_rationale: A customer wanting a lightweight self-hosted Git host is already served by the existing gitea recipe, which is more actively developed and functionally equivalent-or-better. Gogs adds no differentiated capability to justify a second, overlapping recipe.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: Gogs admin account (username/email/password created during first-run setup)
blocking_issues:
Gogs has no environment-variable or app.ini-driven way to provision the initial admin account. First boot either serves an interactive web install wizard (a plaintext password form field, not scriptable via env/config) or requires running `gogs admin create-user --admin --password <plaintext> ...` via CLI after the container is up, which also only accepts a plaintext password argument — there is no field that accepts a pre-computed hash the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever produces a hash, so it cannot be projected into either path; this is the documented hard-blocker case (a genuine plaintext-only requirement, not a missing hash algorithm).
The remaining documented fallback, 'first user to sign up becomes admin,' is a race condition on a freshly booted public instance and not viable for unattended fleet provisioning.
Gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth (as done for no-login apps) doesn't cleanly fit here either: Gogs is a full multi-user Git host where HTTP Git operations (clone/push over HTTPS) already rely on Gogs' own HTTP Basic auth against per-user credentials, so a Traefik basic_auth layer in front would conflict with or break git client authentication, and it does nothing for the separate SSH git port (2222), which sits outside Traefik entirely.
summary: Gogs is mechanically blocked under the current recipe mechanism: its first-boot admin account can only be created via an interactive web wizard or a CLI command that both require a plaintext password, and there is no channel today to project the customer's root-password hash into either path, nor does a Traefik basic_auth gate fit cleanly for a multi-user Git host with its own HTTP/SSH auth. Even setting the mechanism issue aside, Gogs is the slower-moving original that Gitea forked and surpassed, and Gitea already covers this niche in the catalogue. Recommend not_recommended: duplicates an existing, better- maintained recipe and is blocked on top of that.

Distinct niche from anything currently offered.
usefulness_rationale: Real value for a self-hosted-stack customer running several other AF apps who wants a single place to search logs, but it's a developer/ops-facing tool rather than a consumer app, and on its own (without log shippers like Promtail/Alloy pointed at other containers) it has nothing to ingest — most of its value depends on setup work outside what a recipe installs.
blocking_issues:
Same underlying issue as apps-gaps/grafana.yaml, since "bundled Grafana query UI" (per Hostinger's description) means the customer-facing login is Grafana's own admin account, normally set via a plaintext-only, first-boot-only GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD that `generated_from` cannot populate (it only ever carries a hash of the customer's root password). Resolved the same way as grafana.yaml: Grafana supports fully disabling its own login (GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED=true, GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ORG_ROLE=Admin, GF_AUTH_DISABLE_LOGIN_FORM=true), which removes the in-app credential requirement and shifts the sole auth boundary to a Traefik basic_auth gate - an expressible mechanism today.

Unlike a bare Grafana recipe, this app is marketed specifically for its per-user login/RBAC (viewer/editor/admin roles a customer would reasonably expect to assign to a team), so disabling native auth in favor of one shared basic-auth credential is a lossier compromise here than in grafana.yaml. Not a hard blocker - mechanically identical to the accepted grafana.yaml resolution - but flagged as a caveat for reviewer judgment rather than a clean build_now.

Loki itself (the log-storage/query API on port 3100) has no authentication of its own and is not designed to be exposed directly to customers - only Grafana's UI should be public; Loki should stay on the internal docker network only. This is a recipe-design detail, not a structural blocker, but worth noting since it affects the ports/parameters section of any future recipe draft.
summary: Grafana Loki (image `grafana/loki`, pin `3.7.5`) is a log aggregation backend with no UI or auth of its own; the customer-facing product per Hostinger's description is Loki + a bundled Grafana container as the query UI, a clean two-container stack behind Traefik (only Grafana's port needs to be public - Loki's API port 3100 stays internal). Its login boundary is Grafana's own admin account, the identical issue already resolved in apps-gaps/grafana.yaml: Grafana's anonymous-auth settings (GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED=true, GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ORG_ROLE=Admin, GF_AUTH_DISABLE_LOGIN_FORM=true) disable the plaintext-only, first-boot-only GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD entirely and shift the sole auth boundary to a Traefik basic_auth gate - an expressible mechanism today via `generated_from` on BASIC_AUTH_GATE. Upstream is actively maintained (two parallel patch lines, releases every 3-5 weeks, a release as recent as today). Fills a genuine observability gap not covered by the current 24 recipes, but is a narrower ops-tooling play with most of its value dependent on external log-shipper setup, and the basic_auth gate is a lossier compromise here than in grafana.yaml since this app's differentiator is specifically its per-user RBAC - recommend `build_with_caveats`, flagging that RBAC-loss tradeoff for reviewer sign-off.

summary: Grafana Tempo (3.0.2, actively maintained, June 2026) is a competent distributed-tracing backend, but it is not a fit for the current recipe mechanism or catalogue. It has no web UI of its own — it's inert without a separately-run Grafana to query it — and its actual value-delivering surface, the multi-protocol trace-ingestion ports (OTLP/Jaeger/Zipkin), cannot be meaningfully gated by the one auth mechanism we can project today (Traefik basic_auth over HTTP). Confirmed via upstream docs that Tempo's monolithic/single-binary mode (the only sane fit for a single-instance recipe) does not require Kafka despite that being a hard requirement for 3.0's microservices mode, so that specific complexity concern doesn't apply here — the blocker is the missing auth story and the two-hop dependency on a separately-deployed Grafana, not deployment topology. name: GreptimeDB
source_description: Open-source unified database for metrics, logs, and traces with SQL and PromQL
version_health_notes: v1.1.4 shipped 2026-07-24 (12 days before today, 2026-08-05), a maintenance release fixing streaming Flow expiration correctness and MySQL timestamp presentation. Prior patches: v1.1.3 (2026-07-17), v1.1.2 (2026-07-02), v1.1.1 (2026-06-18, a critical JSON-compatibility fix for v1.0.x→v1.1.0 upgraders). v1.0.0 GA landed 2026-04-08. A v1.2.0-beta.1 (2026-08-04, adding Prometheus Remote Write v2 and a JSON2 column type) and nightly builds on the v1.2 line are also shipping in parallel. Patch cadence of roughly every 2-3 weeks on the stable line plus active beta work — clearly active, not archived or maintenance-only.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is an observability database. GreptimeDB positions itself as a unified replacement for Prometheus+Loki+Elasticsearch-style stacks: metrics, logs, and traces in one engine, queryable via SQL or PromQL, with object-storage-backed elastic scaling. Broader in scope than a single-purpose log store (compare apps-gaps/grafana-loki.yaml, logs only) — this is a genuine, distinct niche versus anything currently offered, aimed at a developer/ops customer who wants to centralize telemetry from their own other AF apps.
usefulness_rationale: Real value for a customer running several other self-hosted apps who wants one place to store and query metrics/logs/traces, especially given native OpenTelemetry/Prometheus-remote-write ingestion. But it's a developer/ops-facing backend, not a consumer app, and — like grafana-loki — most of its value depends on the customer pointing external agents (OTel collectors, Prometheus remote-write, log shippers) at it, which is setup work outside what a recipe installs.
blocking_issues:
GreptimeDB's bundled dashboard (served at /dashboard on the HTTP port, 4000) has no login of its own by default — the instance is wide open unless the operator enables GreptimeDB's built-in "static user provider". That provider's user file supports three password formats (per https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/deployments-administration/authentication/static/): `plain:<password>` (plaintext, the default), `mysql_native_password: <sha1-hash>` (MySQL wire-protocol handshake), and `pbkdf2_sha256:<iterations>:<salt>:<hash>` — a hash stored at rest, usable with the HTTP/gRPC and PostgreSQL protocols. So this is not the genuine-plaintext-requirement case; GreptimeDB's own auth CAN be populated with a hash. The real gap is that `generated_from`'s currently-supported algorithm list (`argon2`, `bcrypt`) doesn't include `pbkdf2_sha256` yet, so that hash can't be produced by the platform today. Per the schema, that makes GreptimeDB's own login a `blocked_on_platform` case (needed algo: `pbkdf2_sha256`), not a hard structural blocker — once `generated_from` supports `pbkdf2_sha256`, GreptimeDB's own per-app admin login would be the preferred customer-facing auth path over a shared gate credential. Until then, the practical mechanism expressible today is the same as grafana-loki.yaml: leave GreptimeDB's built-in auth disabled and put a Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the dashboard/HTTP port instead.

GreptimeDB exposes three additional raw (non-HTTP) protocol ports for actually writing/reading data — gRPC (4001), MySQL wire protocol (4002), PostgreSQL wire protocol (4003) — none of which a Traefik HTTP `basic_auth` middleware can gate, since that only applies to HTTP traffic. If these are made public (needed for a customer to ingest metrics/logs from agents running outside the AF customer's own docker network, the product's main use case) they would sit open on the internet with no authentication, because GreptimeDB's only auth mechanism (the static-user provider, discussed above) has no expressible path today — `generated_from` doesn't support the `pbkdf2_sha256` hash it needs, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate can't protect non-HTTP wire protocols. Mitigation: keep 4001-4003 un-published (internal docker-network only, reachable only by other containers on the same customer stack) and restrict the recipe to HTTP-based ingestion paths (OTLP/HTTP, Prometheus remote-write, InfluxDB line protocol — all available over the port-4000 HTTP API) behind the same Traefik basic_auth gate as the dashboard. This materially narrows what the recipe can offer (no MySQL/PostgreSQL/gRPC clients) versus GreptimeDB's full feature set, but keeps the instance closed to unauthenticated raw-protocol writes.
summary: GreptimeDB (image `greptime/greptimedb`, pin `v1.1.4`) is an actively maintained, Apache-2.0 unified metrics/logs/traces database with SQL and PromQL query support and a bundled web dashboard on its HTTP port (4000) — a genuine gap versus the current 24 recipes, none of which is an observability datastore. It has no login of its own by default; its built-in static-user auth mechanism does support a hashed credential (`pbkdf2_sha256`), but that algorithm isn't in `generated_from`'s currently-supported list (`argon2`, `bcrypt`) yet, so it's a `blocked_on_platform` gap rather than a structural blocker — until that lands, the dashboard needs a Traefik `basic_auth` gate the same way grafana-loki.yaml resolves it. The bigger caveat is its three raw non-HTTP protocol ports (gRPC 4001, MySQL 4002, PostgreSQL 4003) used for data ingestion/query — a Traefik basic_auth gate cannot protect those, so a recipe would need to keep them internal-only and restrict customers to HTTP-based ingestion (OTLP, Prometheus remote-write, InfluxDB line protocol), a real reduction from GreptimeDB's full protocol surface. Installable today with that design constraint; recommend `build_with_caveats`.

summary: Grimmory is a two-container app (its own image plus a MariaDB dependency) on one HTTP port (6060, default) with bind-mounted book/bookdrop/data volumes — structurally closest to recipes/paperless-ngx (app + relational DB, single web UI, no other raw ports) rather than the single-container recipes. It needs no external API keys or OAuth registration to boot, and its DB credentials can be fully server-generated with no customer input, matching our current mechanism. Its one wrinkle is that the admin account is created through a public first-visit setup wizard rather than via any settable env var, which SCHEMA.md's basic-auth-gate pattern (already used for n8n, WUD, Open WebUI, Immich) covers cleanly: front the whole app with Traefik basic_auth derived from the customer's root password so no one but the customer ever reaches that wizard. Upstream (grimmory-tools/ grimmory, an active community successor to BookLore) is releasing on a healthy multi-week cadence with no signs of stalling. Distinct, broadly applicable "build a lightweight internal tool or tracker" pitch with no catalogue overlap today.
usefulness_rationale: "Spreadsheet that's also a database, with a web UI, self-hosted" is a clear, well-known value proposition (Airtable-alternative positioning) with broad appeal beyond a single niche, and it ships as a single container with a bundled SQLite store by default — no extra database service required, fitting the catalogue's lightweight single-container pattern.
summary: Grist is a single-container Node.js app (official image gristlabs/grist, pinned e.g. 1.7.17) serving one HTTP port (8484 by default), with data persisted to a mounted volume via a bundled SQLite store — no separate database service needed, and fully Traefik-compatible on a single public port. By default a brand-new instance is gated by an interactive "Quick setup" wizard that requires a boot key (GRIST_BOOT_KEY) typed in as plaintext — that comparison is not hash-based, so a customer-supplied value could never be projected into it via `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash). That path is avoidable, though: Grist explicitly documents `GRIST_IN_SERVICE=true` to skip the boot-key check entirely for deployments that are only reachable on a private, already-authenticated path, and `GRIST_DEFAULT_EMAIL` to run in single-user mode with a fixed admin identity (no interactive login at all). Combining those two — boot check disabled, fixed single-user email set server-side, nothing customer-supplied at the app layer — turns Grist into an app with no login boundary of its own, exactly the pattern already used for Grav/Gramps Web/An Otter Wiki: gate the whole thing behind Traefik `basic_auth: true` with the credential projected from the customer's root password hash, so the app itself never needs a customer-facing secret. That clears the /compose constraint today with no blocking issues. Combined with an active, roughly-monthly release cadence (latest release 1 week ago) and a genuine, high-value gap in the catalogue (no spreadsheet/data-app tool today), Grist is a strong build_now candidate.

name: GrowthBook
source_description: Open-source feature flagging and A/B testing platform
version_health_notes: v5.0.0 published 2026-07-20 (confirmed via GitHub releases API), ~16 days before today (2026-08-05). Prior tags show a steady cadence: v4.4.0 (2026-05-27), v4.3.0 (2026-02-04), v4.2.0 (2025-11-11), v4.1.0 (2025-09-09), v4.0.0 (2025-07-09) — a new minor/major roughly every 2-3 months going back years, on top of daily `git-<sha>` image pushes to Docker Hub (dozens per week) between tagged releases. Repo is not archived and is clearly under active commercial development (GrowthBook Inc. also sells a hosted/enterprise edition on top of this open-source core).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does feature flagging or A/B testing/experimentation — n8n (automation) and the various dev-tooling recipes are the nearest neighbors by audience (engineering teams) but not by function. This would be a genuinely new category: ship-behind-a-flag / gradual-rollout / experiment-analysis tooling that competes with LaunchDarkly/Optimizely/Split as a self-hosted alternative, a well-understood pitch for a technical customer base. Note: `reverse_proxy_compatible: false` above is because GrowthBook splits its Node.js app across two HTTP ports on one container — 3000 (frontend, APP_ORIGIN) and 3100 (API, API_HOST) — and upstream docs are explicit that "the back-end and the front-end must run on unique ports... currently GrowthBook does not support running both the API and the front-end on the same port" (docs.growthbook.io/self-host/env). The two must additionally share a root domain for session cookies to work, so fronting this with Traefik would need two subdomains under the same base domain — the same split-port shape as apps-gaps/chartbrew.yaml, and likewise a deviation from the single-port pattern every existing recipe uses.
usefulness_rationale: Feature flags and A/B testing are a common need for any team shipping a web or mobile product, and "self-hosted LaunchDarkly alternative" is a clear, specific pitch with no catalogue overlap today. Architecture is a bit heavier than our typical single-container recipes (Node.js app + MongoDB, split frontend/API ports), adding routing complexity beyond our usual single-port pattern.
blocking_issues:
GrowthBook has no environment variable for presetting an admin account. On first boot with an empty MongoDB, the app shows an open, unauthenticated sign-up form where whoever submits it first creates the sole organization and becomes its owner (confirmed against upstream self-host docs and community reports: subsequent visitors are shown an "ask for an invite" screen instead, meaning the window to claim the first account only exists once). There is no `type: password` parameter on GrowthBook's own login to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` — the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var.

This is the same structural shape as the 2FAuth and Activepieces gap analyses (see apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml, apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml): a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would stop a random internet stranger from racing to claim the first account, but today's basic_auth mechanism only carries a single root-password projection for the gate itself — it has no channel to also hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential to complete GrowthBook's own sign-up form, so the underlying provisioning gap (no automated, customer-exclusive admin account at first boot) is not resolved, just moved one layer out.
summary: GrowthBook is an active, well-maintained, MongoDB-backed feature-flagging and A/B-testing platform that would fill a genuine, currently-empty gap in the catalogue with broad appeal to technical customers. It fails the installability test on the same platform-mechanism grounds as 2FAuth and Activepieces: the app provisions its sole admin account via an open, first-visitor self-registration form with no env-var hook, so neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely and fully hand the customer their own exclusive first-run credential. All other secrets (JWT_SECRET, ENCRYPTION_KEY, MongoDB credentials) are purely internal and trivially server-generated, so they are not blocking on their own. Revisit once the platform supports either an env-var-driven initial-admin flow (upstream would need to add that) or a second customer-facing credential channel beyond the single root-password projection — and separately plan for the two-subdomain routing GrowthBook's split frontend/API needs.

name: Hanko
source_description: Open-source passkey-first authentication backend with social login, MFA, and SSO
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (backend); MIT (hanko-elements web components + frontend SDK)
version_health_notes: backend/v3.0.4 ("Hanko v3: Multitenancy") shipped 2026-07-27, 9 days before today (2026-08-05). Prior tagged releases: v2.7.0 (2026-06-05), v2.6.0 (2026-06-05), v2.5.0 (2026-03-03), v2.4.0 (2026-01-20) — tagged releases land roughly every 1-3 months. Repo `pushed_at` is 2026-08-04, `archived: false`, 57 open issues still being triaged, and GHCR shows rolling `main-<commit>-<date>` image builds published within the last few days — main-branch commit activity is daily and clearly active, well beyond the tagged-release cadence alone.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is an authentication-as-a-service backend. Hanko provides a passkey/passwordless/MFA/SSO auth API meant to be embedded into a developer's own application via "Hanko Elements" (embeddable web components) and a frontend SDK — it does not ship a standalone product a customer opens in a browser and uses.
usefulness_rationale: Hanko is a developer-facing auth backend, not an end-user application — there's no bundled dashboard or admin console in the OSS self-hosted build (unlike Hanko Cloud's paid console). To get any value out of it, the customer must already be building their own web or mobile app and wire in hanko-elements/the SDK themselves; simply installing the recipe and opening the domain yields a bare JSON API with a demo "todo app" as the only example UI upstream ships. That's a poor fit for AF's install-and-use model, which the rest of the 24-recipe catalogue targets (a working web UI at the customer's domain immediately after install).
blocking_issues:
Hanko's default user flows (passcode email verification on signup, account-recovery, security notifications) require a real SMTP relay in production — upstream's own docker-compose quickstart only wires up `mailslurper`, a fake local mail catcher for demos, not a real mail path. A production deployment needs the customer's own SMTP host/port/username/password, which is an external third-party credential with no input channel today (same category as an external API key — not expressible via `generated_from` or Traefik `basic_auth`).

The Admin API (port 8001, used for user/session/webhook management) ships with no authentication of its own — upstream guidance is to keep it off the public internet entirely, reachable only from a trusted internal network. If a recipe needs to expose it (e.g. so the customer can actually administer their instance), it would need a Traefik `basic_auth` gate; if it's kept internal-only instead, the customer has no way at all to manage users short of calling the raw API by hand, which undercuts the point of a self-service recipe.

No published image carries a stable semver tag matching Hanko's own GitHub releases (e.g. `v3.0.4`) — GHCR only publishes rolling `main-<commit>-<date>` build tags off the main branch, with no `latest` or version-numbered tag at all. A specific commit tag can still be pinned (satisfies "pinned, not `:latest`"), but there is no clear "current stable" tag to pin to, and every future recipe bump means picking an arbitrary main-branch commit rather than a vetted release build.

Even setting aside the mechanism gaps above, there is no customer-facing web UI to reverse-proxy: the public API (port 8000) and admin API (port 8001) are both bare JSON/REST endpoints, and the "web UI" (hanko-elements) is a component library meant to be embedded into a separate application the customer builds and hosts themselves, not something this recipe can stand up on its own.
summary: Hanko (image `ghcr.io/teamhanko/hanko`, no stable semver tag published — only rolling `main-<commit>-<date>` GHCR builds, latest tagged release backend/v3.0.4 from 2026-07-27) is an actively developed, AGPL-3.0 passkey/passwordless/MFA/SSO authentication backend with daily main-branch commits and a healthy tagged-release cadence. It fills a genuine gap versus the current 24 recipes (nothing else is an auth-as-a-service backend), but it is fundamentally a developer integration product, not an end-user web app: the self-hosted OSS build ships no admin dashboard, requires the customer's own SMTP relay credentials for its core email-passcode flows (no input channel today), and its Admin API has no built-in auth of its own and isn't meant to face the public internet. Between the missing customer-facing UI, the external SMTP-credential requirement, and the lack of a stable release image to pin, this doesn't fit the current recipe mechanism or AF's install-and-use model — `not_recommended`.

name: Harness
source_description: End-to-end developer platform with SCM, CI/CD pipelines, and hosted dev environments
version_health_notes: "Harness" is ambiguous. The Hostinger description ("SCM, CI/CD pipelines, hosted dev environments") matches Harness Open Source (github.com/harness/harness, formerly Gitness) — a single-container, self-hostable platform. The project name is also used for the commercial Harness.io SaaS platform (closed-source, enterprise) and for a "Harness CD Community Edition" (harness/harness-cd-community, a Kubernetes-delegate-based CD tool with no bundled SCM). Neither of those matches the description as closely as Harness Open Source does, so this analysis targets the OSS repo. The repo itself is still active day-to-day (pushed_at 2026-08-05), but that activity is almost entirely a legacy "drone" branch that keeps cutting patch releases for the old Drone-CI runner component (v2.28.2 on 2026-04-20, v2.28.1 on 2026-03-30, v2.27.x through early 2026, roughly monthly). The actual Harness Open Source *platform* release line (release/3.x branch, what `harness/harness:latest` on Docker Hub tracks) has not cut a new version since v3.3.0 on 2025-08-19 — just under 12 months with no stable release against today's date (2026-08-05), even though an `unstable` nightly tag is still being pushed. Treating this as dormant/maintenance-only for the product a customer would actually install.
differentiation: Adds CI/CD pipelines (Drone-derived) and hosted dev-environment provisioning on top of Git hosting, which neither gitea nor opengist offer. But both existing recipes are already disabled (enabled: false) in the catalogue, and Harness needs a Docker-socket mount to actually run pipelines — a materially larger privilege/blast-radius ask than either.
usefulness_rationale: The differentiator (CI/CD + dev environments) only works if the container gets access to the host Docker socket to spin up build containers, which is a significant privilege-escalation surface in a shared/multi-tenant hosting environment. Combined with the platform line being effectively stale for a year, this is a weak candidate next to already-shelved, lower-risk alternatives (gitea, opengist) covering the SCM half of the pitch.
blocking_issues:
Harness's own admin login (GITNESS_PRINCIPAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD) only accepts a plaintext password that the app hashes itself at boot — there is no field that takes a pre-computed hash. generated_from can only ever carry a hash, so it cannot be projected into this env var directly (a genuine plaintext requirement, not an unsupported hash algo). Left unset, the app falls back to a fixed default (admin/changeit), so the workable path is to leave it at that default/a server-generated value and put the whole app behind a Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password hash, htpasswd-compatible) as the real auth boundary — mechanically installable, but the app's own login stays a credential the customer never actually sets.
Needs a bind mount of /var/run/docker.sock into the app container so pipelines can launch build containers on the host Docker daemon. That is a full container-escape-equivalent privilege grant, which is a materially different risk class than anything our current 24 recipes require, independent of the auth question above.
Exposes SSH (port 3022) for git-over-SSH in addition to the web UI on port 3000 — a second raw TCP port beyond a single HTTP surface, though our existing gitea/opengist recipes already show this pattern is not a hard blocker by itself.
summary: Harness Open Source (formerly Gitness) matches Hostinger's SCM+CI/CD+dev-environments pitch, but its own admin login can only be set via a plaintext env var (no hash-projection channel), so a customer-specific credential can only be delivered by falling back to a Traefik basic_auth gate over the app's unset default login — workable, but not what the app's own auth was designed for. More importantly, the platform needs a host Docker-socket mount to run pipelines (a large privilege grant for a multi-tenant host) and its stable release line has been dormant for roughly a year against today's date, while overlapping the SCM half of two recipes (gitea, opengist) that are already disabled in our catalogue. Not recommended.

name: Hasura GraphQL Engine
source_description: Open-source GraphQL engine with instant APIs over any database
version_health_notes: Docker Hub shows v2.48.15 pushed ~4 days before the 2026-08-05 analysis date, and it exists specifically to patch a CVE in the Ubuntu base image — i.e. active security maintenance, not just feature releases. GitHub releases show a steady stream of point releases on the v2.x line. Hasura v3 (DDN / new engine) exists in parallel as a separate product; this analysis targets v2, the OSS self-hostable engine matching the Hostinger description.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes offer instant GraphQL/REST API generation over an existing database. Hasura sits in front of a customer's own Postgres (or other) database and auto-generates a queryable/mutable GraphQL schema plus a web console for managing permissions and relationships — a distinct "backend-as-a-service" category versus our existing automation (n8n), monitoring (uptime-kuma), or file/photo apps (immich, paperless-ngx).
usefulness_rationale: Valuable for developers who want a fast BaaS-style layer on their own Postgres without hand-writing an API, but it is a developer tool rather than an end-user app, and its core value (the admin console + GraphQL API) is exactly what our current secret-provisioning mechanism can't safely hand to the customer — see installability below.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET; POSTGRES_PASSWORD (backing database, if bundled rather than customer-supplied)
blocking_issues:
HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET is verified by direct plaintext string equality — the client sends the literal secret value in the `x-hasura-admin-secret` header on every console/API request, and Hasura compares it byte-for-byte against the env var. This is structurally different from the password fields our `generated_from` mechanism targets (e.g. Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN), where the app itself hashes whatever the customer types and compares against a stored hash. Projecting `argon2:ROOT_PASSWORD` into HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET would mean the stored value IS a hash string, and the customer would have to type that exact hash (which they never see) as the header value to authenticate — their actual root password would not work. There is no verification-time hashing step on Hasura's side for this field, so `generated_from` cannot bridge it.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` does not solve this either: Hasura's actual product value (the admin console for managing schema/permissions, and the GraphQL/REST API itself) requires the customer to know and supply HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET directly to use the app at all. If we instead server-generate that secret randomly and never expose it to the customer (the "random secret nothing customer-facing reads" case), the customer can never actually administer Hasura or call its API as admin — which defeats the purpose of installing it. Unlike Adminer or n8n, there's no way to make this secret purely internal.
summary: Hasura GraphQL Engine is an actively maintained, well-differentiated candidate (instant GraphQL API over a database, a category none of the 24 current recipes cover) but is blocked by the current provisioning mechanism: its one required secret (HASURA_GRAPHQL_ADMIN_SECRET) is checked via plaintext equality rather than app-side hash verification, so neither `generated_from` root-password projection nor a Traefik basic_auth gate can hand the customer a working, self-known credential without either exposing a raw hash string or removing their ability to administer the app. Revisit once the platform supports projecting a plaintext (not hashed) customer-known credential into an app env var, or once Hasura exposes an alternative auth path our mechanism can drive.

name: Haven
source_description: Private self-hosted blog for personal journals shared with invited readers
version_health_notes: havenweb/haven has never cut a GitHub Release or a git tag (both `/releases` and `/tags` return empty) — it ships purely as a rolling `master` branch, rebuilt to `ghcr.io/havenweb/haven:latest` (plus a per-commit short-SHA tag) on every push via `.github/workflows/docker-image.yml`. There is no "pinned, current stable tag" in the sense our other recipes use; the closest available pin is a specific commit SHA tag, not a vetted release. Commit history is genuinely active: pushed_at 2026-07-31, updated_at 2026-08-04 (1-5 days before this analysis on 2026-08-05), with real feature/fix commits roughly weekly-to-monthly over the past year (e.g. "Fix Indieauth" 2026-07-14, "Refactor post editing validations" 2026-07-07, RSS relative-link fix 2026-06-30, Rails 7.1/7.2 upgrades 2026-07-07, routine dependency bumps in between). Not archived, not dormant. It is, however, effectively a one-person project: of ~470 commits attributed to contributors, 356 (76%) are from a single maintainer (mawise), with 72 more from dependabot; only a handful of one-off external contributions. 798 GitHub stars, 17 open issues. Small but real maintenance risk if that one maintainer stops.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes covers personal blogging/journaling. Haven is deliberately narrow and different from apps-gaps/ghost.yaml and apps-gaps/halo.yaml (also unbuilt candidates): it is not a publishing/CMS platform aimed at public audiences or monetization — it has no plugin marketplace, no themes marketplace, no newsletter/payments story. It's explicitly a *private* journal shared only with people the author invites (access-controlled posts, IndieAuth/Micropub support, a built-in private RSS-style reader for following other Havens/blogs). Closest existing recipe by shape is Gitea/Opengist (small Rails/Go app + Postgres, single admin-managed user base) but neither of those is a writing/publishing tool. Also distinct from recipes/anytype-server (structured notes/wiki for yourself) — Haven's whole premise is "write posts, choose specific people to share them with," a social-but-private use case anytype-server doesn't address.
usefulness_rationale: Fills a real, currently-empty niche (private family/friends journal, not a public blog), and MIT-licensed with an active-enough maintainer. But it's a small, single-maintainer hobby project with no formal release process and a much smaller audience/brand than Ghost or Halo, so expected customer demand is lower — this is a nice-to-have addition to round out the publishing category, not a must-have on its own.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: postgres_db_password (HAVEN_DB_PASSWORD); initial_admin_password (HAVEN_USER_PASS, consumed as plaintext at container boot to create the sole admin user); Traefik basic-auth gate credential
blocking_issues: HAVEN_USER_EMAIL/HAVEN_USER_PASS are read by deploymentscripts/lib/ruby/create_user.rb at boot and passed straight into `User.create!(password: PASS, ...)` — Devise/bcrypt hashes it internally, but the *input* the app requires is a plaintext password, not a pre-computed hash. This is the exact "genuine plaintext requirement" SCHEMA.md calls a hard blocker for `generated_from`, which only ever carries a hash of the customer's root password. Unlike Ghost/Halo (apps-gaps/ghost.yaml, apps-gaps/halo.yaml), this isn't a first-visitor claim race on an unauthenticated setup wizard — Haven's admin account is created deterministically at container start from these env vars, so a recipe would have to bake in a fixed, non-customer-specific default password (documented in metadata.yaml for the customer to change post-install). That is workable in principle: gate the app behind Traefik basic_auth (projected from the customer's root-password hash) so the fixed default credential is never internet-reachable, then have the customer log in with the documented default and change it themselves via Haven's own Devise `/users/edit` page before disabling the gate — the same "temporary claim-race-style protection, customer disables it once done" tradeoff already accepted for Ghost/Halo. Flagging as a blocking issue here (rather than marking installable_today: true outright) because, unlike those two, the fixed credential is knowable in advance from the published recipe source itself (not just racing an anonymous visitor), so this needs an explicit product/security call before treating it as equivalent.
summary: Haven is a small, MIT-licensed, actively-committed-to (weekly-to-monthly real commits, last push 2026-07-31) but single-maintainer private blogging app with no formal release process — only a rolling `latest` image and per-commit SHA tags, no version to pin against in the usual sense. It fills a real gap (personal/family journal sharing, distinct from the public-CMS Ghost/Halo candidates and from anytype-server's personal-notes use case) and is structurally simple: one Rails container (ghcr.io/havenweb/haven, port 3000) plus Postgres, reverse-proxy friendly. The installability wrinkle is that its only admin-provisioning path (HAVEN_USER_EMAIL/HAVEN_USER_PASS env vars) takes a plaintext password baked into the recipe rather than a customer-supplied hash, so clearing it the same way accepted for Ghost/Halo (Traefik basic_auth gate + customer changes the fixed default password post-install) works mechanically but ships a recipe-wide-known default credential rather than a per-customer-random one, which is a materially different risk profile worth a deliberate call rather than defaulting to yes. Marked build_with_caveats: worth building once that call is made, but not installable_today without it.

name: Headroom
source_description: Open-source LLM context compression proxy reducing token usage by up to 95%
version_health_notes: v0.34.0 published 2026-08-05, the same day as today. PyPI release history (headroom-ai) shows near-weekly shipping through 2026: v0.25.0 (Jun 12), v0.27.0 (Jun 22), v0.28.0 (Jun 29), v0.29.0/v0.30.0 (Jul 3), v0.31.0 (Jul 9), v0.32.0 (Jul 17), v0.32.1 (Jul 19), v0.33.0 (Jul 29), v0.34.0 (Aug 5). GitHub repo (65k+ stars, not archived) shows the same cadence via release-please automation. Clearly active development. The repo previously lived at github.com/chopratejas/headroom and was transferred/renamed to the headroomlabs-ai org (old URL redirects to the new one, confirmed via GitHub API) — use headroomlabs-ai/headroom as canonical going forward.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers this niche. Headroom is not an LLM runtime or chat UI (unlike ollama, open-webui) — it's a transparent HTTP proxy that sits in front of a customer's own OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API calls and compresses tool outputs, logs, files, and RAG chunks before they reach the model, cutting token spend without changing answers. It complements rather than duplicates the catalogue's existing AI entries: a customer already running claude-code, gemini-cli, openclaw, or hermes-agent could point that tool's base-URL at a self-hosted Headroom instance to cut their own LLM API bill. It has no web dashboard of its own upstream (a third-party "headroom-gui" project exists but is a separate, unofficial repo by a different author, not part of this recipe candidate).
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely novel niche (cost-reduction proxy) with no catalogue overlap and an exploding star count, but it's a pure infrastructure/API proxy with no browser UI of its own — value only materializes for a technically-savvy customer who reconfigures an external tool's base URL to point at it. That's a narrower audience than typical catalogue recipes, capping usefulness at medium despite high technical interest.
blocking_issues:
The upstream LLM provider API key (Anthropic/OpenAI/etc.) is supplied per-request by the client calling the proxy — Headroom forwards the caller's own Authorization header upstream rather than storing a key itself — so no external API key is required at first boot. This is good news for installability: it removes what would otherwise be a hard blocker (no channel exists today for an arbitrary customer API key).

The minimal proxy (`headroom proxy --port 8787`) has no database dependency and no built-in authentication of its own, so it would sit open on the internet unless gated — same pattern as n8n/OpenClaw/WUD: front the single public port with Traefik `basic_auth: true`, projecting the root-password hash there. The optional Qdrant/Neo4j "memory stack" in upstream's docker-compose.yml is for an advanced semantic-memory feature, not required for the core compression proxy, and should be left out of a recipe to keep the footprint to a single container.

Docker image tagging is a genuine build concern, not a secrets blocker: ghcr.io/headroomlabs-ai/headroom does not publish matching semver tags for its PyPI/GitHub releases (v0.34.0, etc.) — only rolling tags suffixed with a short git commit hash (e.g. `slim-2954e37`, aliased to `main-slim`), which are reassigned on every push (observed "published about 2 hours ago" at research time). There is no stable, citable pinned tag to reference the way RFC-002 requires; a recipe would need to either pin to a specific commit-hash tag (which will eventually roll off the registry) or build the image from the pinned PyPI package (`pip install "headroom-ai[proxy]"==0.34.0`) in a Dockerfile instead of consuming the upstream image directly.
summary: Headroom is an active, fast-growing, genuinely novel addition to the catalogue — a token-compression proxy with no overlap with existing AI recipes — and is installable today: it needs no customer-supplied API key at boot (that flows through per-request from the calling client) and can be gated with the standard Traefik basic_auth pattern since it has no login of its own. The open issue is packaging, not the secrets mechanism: upstream does not publish stable semver-tagged Docker images, only rolling commit-hash tags, so building this recipe means either accepting a tag that will eventually roll off the registry or building a Dockerfile ourselves pinned to a specific PyPI release. Given the narrow (developer-facing, no-UI) audience, recommend build_with_caveats rather than a high-priority build.

name: Headscale
source_description: Self-hosted Tailscale-compatible control server for WireGuard mesh networking
version_health_notes: v0.29.3 published 2026-07-29 (confirmed via GitHub releases API), only 7 days before today (2026-08-05). Prior tags show a steady, fast cadence: v0.29.2 (2026-07-01), v0.29.1 (2026-06-18), v0.29.0 (2026-06-17, preceded by four betas from 2026-05-22 through 2026-06-15), v0.28.0 (2026-02-04). Repo is not archived, last push 2026-07-30, and is under clearly active development by juanfont/ the Tailscale-alternative community.
differentiation: Headscale is a re-implementation of Tailscale's proprietary coordination-server API: customers install the standard Tailscale (or any tailscale-compatible) client on each device and point it at this server to form a mesh VPN, rather than configuring individual site-to-site WireGuard tunnels by hand. wg-easy, already in the catalogue, solves a related but architecturally different problem — a single hub-and-spoke WireGuard server with a web UI for issuing per-client configs/QR codes. Headscale's pitch ("run your own Tailscale") is a distinct, well-known one for technical customers who already use Tailscale clients, but it overlaps enough in "self-hosted VPN mesh" positioning that both would compete for the same buyer intent.
usefulness_rationale: "Self-hosted Tailscale" is a recognizable, frequently-requested product for technical/homelab and small-business customers, and there is real demand distinct from wg-easy's simpler hub model. However, the lack of any first-party web UI (see below) significantly limits how self-service this can be made for an AF customer without shell access.
blocking_issues:
Headscale ships **no first-party web UI** at all — confirmed against upstream docs (headscale.net/stable/ref/integration/web-ui/): "Headscale doesn't provide a built-in web interface but users may pick one from the available options," explicitly listing headscale-ui, HeadscaleUi, Headplane, and headscale-admin as "community contributions... not maintained by the headscale authors." The official image exposes only an HTTP control-plane API (port 8080) managed via the `headscale` CLI (typically `docker exec` into the container) — there is no web login, no admin account, and no way for a customer to create users or issue device-enrollment (pre-auth) keys without shell access to the container. Wrapping the whole domain in Traefik `basic_auth` (as we do for auth-less apps like Adminer) protects the control-plane API from anonymous internet access, but does not give the customer any actual UI to operate the app — the fundamental day-2 workflow (add a device to the mesh) is unreachable through the browser alone.

Bundling one of the third-party UIs (e.g. Headplane, headscale-admin) to fix the above would introduce its own unsolved credential problem: Headplane authenticates admin sessions via a Headscale-generated API key (treated as full-access, bypassing any role system) or via OIDC. Neither fits our mechanism — an API key is an opaque token, not a password hash field `generated_from` can populate, and OIDC requires third-party app registration, which the schema explicitly rules out as a blocker (no channel for arbitrary external credentials/app registration).

Practical mesh connectivity also typically requires the embedded DERP relay, which needs a raw UDP STUN port (3478) exposed publicly alongside the HTTPS control port — the same "extra raw port beyond one HTTP port" shape as wg-easy's 51820/udp, so this would not be purely reverse-proxy-compatible even setting the UI problem aside.
summary: Headscale is an active, fast-moving, well-regarded open-source Tailscale-control-server reimplementation with a real "self-hosted Tailscale" pitch distinct from wg-easy, but it is a poor fit for our current recipe mechanism: the official image ships no web UI whatsoever, and the app's actual day-2 operation (enrolling devices, managing users) requires CLI/shell access we cannot expose to an AF customer through a domain + login flow. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate can secure the bare control-plane API but cannot substitute for a missing UI, and the available third-party UIs introduce credential channels (API keys, OIDC) our mechanism has no way to project. Combined with the extra raw UDP port needed for the embedded DERP relay, this is not a good build_now or even build_with_caveats candidate today — it is a product-fit gap (no operable web interface), not primarily a platform-secrets gap, so `not_recommended` rather than `blocked_on_platform`.

name: Healthchecks
source_description: Open-source cron job and background task monitoring with instant alerts
version_health_notes: v4.3 tagged 2026-07-14, ~3 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Release history over the prior year is steady and roughly monthly-to-bimonthly: v3.10 (2025-05-09), v3.11/.1/.2 (Aug-Sep 2025), v3.12/v3.13 (Nov 2025), v4.0 (2026-01-22, Django 6.0 upgrade), v4.1/v4.1.1 (Mar 2026), v4.2 (2026-04-28), v4.3 (2026-07-14, includes an Argon2 password-hashing upgrade). Single maintainer (cuu508) but commits are signed/verified and the cadence has not slowed — clearly active, not dormant.
differentiation: Healthchecks is a "dead man's switch" / passive monitor: cron jobs and scheduled tasks ping it, and it alerts when an expected ping fails to arrive on schedule. This is a different failure mode than Uptime Kuma (the closest existing recipe), which actively polls URLs/services and alerts when a live check fails. Uptime Kuma cannot detect "a backup script silently stopped running" the way Healthchecks can, and vice versa Healthchecks cannot detect "the website is down" the way Uptime Kuma can. No existing recipe covers scheduled-job/cron monitoring.
usefulness_rationale: Broad appeal: any self-hoster running cron jobs, backup scripts, or scheduled automation (a very common case among this catalogue's technical audience) benefits from being alerted when a job silently stops running. Complements Uptime Kuma rather than competing with it, and unlike Alerta it is immediately useful out of the box — the customer's own cron jobs can be pointed at it directly, no external monitoring stack required first.
summary: Healthchecks is a two-service app (web app + Postgres), structurally close to the n8n/paperless-ngx template, exposing a single HTTP port (8000) — reverse-proxy friendly. It has no boot-time admin-credential env var: the official Docker setup requires an interactive `manage.py createsuperuser` exec after first boot, which af-api's bootstrap flow cannot drive (no channel for a one-off interactive command). However, the app also supports open self-service signup (REGISTRATION_OPEN=True by default) through its own web UI, so no Django-superuser step is actually required for a customer to create their own monitoring account. That default is unsafe unguarded (any internet visitor could self-register on the customer's instance before the customer does), so the recipe should front the whole app with a Traefik basic_auth:true gate — projected from the customer's root password via generated_from, same pattern as Adminer — so only the customer can even reach the signup page. Postgres password and Django SECRET_KEY are both server-generated with no customer input needed. Upstream is actively maintained (v4.3, July 2026) and the app fills a real gap (cron/scheduled-job monitoring) not covered by Uptime Kuma. Recommend build_now.

name: Hermes WebUI
source_description: Self-hosted Hermes AI agent and web chat UI bundled in one Docker deployment
version_health_notes: Release cadence is unusually high — multiple tagged releases per hour against today's date (2026-08-05/06), most as `exp-vX.Y.Z` prerelease tags with an occasional `vX.Y.Z` stable cut. This reads as an automated/CI-driven tagging scheme rather than a curated release process, which makes "pick a pinned, current stable tag" (the af-create-recipe Phase 2 requirement) harder than usual: the last plain `vX.Y.Z` tag (v0.52.106) is already several hundred experimental tags behind HEAD, so a future recipe would need to decide whether to track the stable line (likely stale within days) or an experimental tag (no stability guarantee). Repo not archived, actively maintained.
differentiation: None found beyond implementation choice. Hostinger's description ("Hermes AI agent and web chat UI bundled in one Docker deployment") is already exactly what `recipes/hermes-agent/` ships today: the official `nousresearch/hermes-agent` image running the agent gateway plus a supervised web dashboard in a single container, reverse-proxy compatible on one HTTP port. `hermes-webui` (repo owner `nesquena`, not Nous Research) is an unofficial third-party wrapper that runs the same underlying Hermes Agent CLI/config with a different, more feature-rich web frontend (three-panel chat/session/workspace layout, voice input, themes) bolted on around it — but it targets the same upstream agent, the same provider-agnostic LLM config, and the same core use case as our existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Would ship the identical Hostinger-visible pitch as `hermes-agent`, just backed by an unofficial community wrapper instead of the official NousResearch image, with a much less settled release process (see `version_health`). No new capability a customer would pick this over `hermes-agent` for; adding it mainly doubles the maintenance surface for the same product story.
blocking_issues: HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD is read by the app as a plaintext password (api/auth.py: `os.getenv('HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD', '').strip()`) and hashed internally with a fixed-salt PBKDF2 scheme the app owns — there is no field that accepts a pre-computed hash. generated_from only ever carries a hash (argon2/bcrypt), so it cannot be projected into this env var directly. Auth is optional by design ("off by default... required if you expose the port outside 127.0.0.1"), so the workable path is to leave it unset and put a Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password hash) in front instead — mechanically installable, mirroring the traefik_basic_auth precedent, but the app's own richer auth (passkeys, OIDC) goes unused.
summary: Hermes WebUI is a real, actively-developed, MIT-licensed community project (github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui) that bundles the same official Hermes Agent our catalogue already ships in `recipes/hermes-agent/` with an unofficial (non-Nous-Research) web frontend. It is mechanically installable today — single HTTP port, reverse-proxy compatible, and its only first-boot secret (a plaintext dashboard password) can be routed around with a Traefik basic_auth gate — but it duplicates `hermes-agent`'s Hostinger-facing pitch exactly with no differentiating capability, rides an unusually chaotic release-tagging scheme that makes picking a stable pin harder than normal, and comes from a third-party maintainer rather than the upstream Hermes Agent project. Not recommended: this would be a lower-provenance duplicate of a recipe we already have.

name: Hermes Workspace
source_description: Open-source web UI command center for the Hermes AI agent
version_health_notes: v2.3.0 shipped 2026-05-08, ~3 months before today (2026-08-05) — a clear slowdown from the release pace that preceded it (v1.0.0 on 2026-04-10, then five more tags through v2.3.0 inside the following four weeks). Not dormant, though: commit activity on `main` (dependency bumps, test fixes, feature PRs) continues at least through 2026-07-05, one month ago, and CHANGELOG.md has an "Unreleased" entry for a docker-pull default change. Repo is not archived. Reads as active development that has simply stopped cutting tagged releases, not maintenance-only or EOL.
differentiation: Hermes Workspace is a richer front-end for the exact same backend already in the catalogue as recipes/hermes-agent: it runs vanilla `nousresearch/hermes-agent` and adds a second container (chat with SSE streaming, a Monaco-based file browser, a cross-platform PTY terminal, a memory/skills browser, an MCP catalog, and a "Swarm"/"Conductor" multi-agent orchestration UI) on top of it. It does not introduce a new backend capability — a customer who wants the Hermes agent already has it via the existing recipe with its own dashboard. The differentiator is UI depth (terminal + file access + multi-agent ops) rather than a new job-to-be-done, and that added depth is also what drives the installability problem below.
usefulness_rationale: The extra surface (in-browser terminal, file browser, multi-agent Swarm/Conductor control plane) is genuinely more capable than the existing hermes-agent dashboard for a power user who wants to actively operate the agent rather than just message it — but it duplicates the same underlying product already in the catalogue, and the added terminal/exec access raises the stakes of getting the auth story right (see below), which caps this at medium rather than high.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against src/server/auth-middleware.ts (verifyPassword()): HERMES_PASSWORD is compared to the login form submission with a plain Buffer/timingSafeEqual comparison — there is no hashing on either side. The app never hashes the configured secret, so it cannot accept an argon2/bcrypt digest as its "password"; the value in the env var IS the literal string the customer must type at login. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever projects a hash, never the customer's plaintext root password, so it cannot target this parameter — this is the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case called out as a hard structural blocker in SCHEMA.md, not an unsupported-hash-algorithm gap.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate does not fully substitute either: the app has its own login by design (server-entry.js refuses to bind a non-loopback host at all unless HERMES_PASSWORD is set, specifically to protect "a high-privilege control plane: terminals, files, agents"). Satisfying that boot-time check without a real customer- known secret would require setting HERMES_ALLOW_INSECURE_REMOTE=1 to bypass the app's own fail-closed guard and relying solely on the Traefik gate — leaving the container's full terminal/file/exec surface unauthenticated at the application layer, one hop behind whatever fronts it. That is a materially bigger downside than the basic_auth pattern used for apps with no login of their own (Adminer, n8n), where the app has no privileged local-shell capability to begin with.
summary: Hermes Workspace is a real, actively-developed (if no-longer-frequently- tagged) two-container add-on UI for the Hermes Agent already in the catalogue via recipes/hermes-agent — chat, file browser, terminal, memory/ skills inspector, and multi-agent Swarm/Conductor orchestration in one workspace. It fails the installability test on its own login: HERMES_PASSWORD is compared as a literal plaintext string (Node's timingSafeEqual over raw buffers, no hashing), so `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` — which only ever carries a hash — cannot supply it, and there is no other channel for the customer to set it at order time. Bypassing the app's own auth guard to lean on a Traefik basic_auth gate instead would leave a terminal/file/exec control plane running with no application-level authentication, which is a bigger risk than the apps that pattern was designed for. Combined with the fact that it duplicates the backend already shipped as recipes/hermes-agent rather than filling a catalogue gap, and release cadence has cooled since May, this is not worth pursuing now — revisit only if upstream adds hash-based comparison for HERMES_PASSWORD.

name: HFS
source_description: Self-hosted HTTP file server with web UI for sharing files from your disk
version_health_notes: Stable 3.2.2 shipped 2026-07-24 (12 days before analysis date 2026-08-05), preceded by 3.2.1 (2026-07-13) and 3.2.0 (2026-07-05) — roughly weekly stable cuts. A beta/alpha channel (3.3.0-alpha1 on 2026-08-03, 3.3.0-beta2 on 2026-08-04) is being pushed in parallel, one day before this analysis. Repo is not archived; this is the actively-developed HFS v3 rewrite (Node/TypeScript), distinct from the legacy "HFS2" (rejetto/hfs2, Delphi/Windows-only, unmaintained) — that older project was considered and ruled out as the wrong upstream for a Linux container recipe.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes cover ad-hoc HTTP file sharing (a single-owner "point at a folder, get a link" server). Syncthing is peer-to-peer sync between the customer's own devices, not a public share-by-link tool, so the use case doesn't overlap. HFS would fill a real "quickly share files from this VM over HTTPS" gap.
usefulness_rationale: Useful, low-complexity single-container app with an active upstream, but a narrow niche (ad-hoc file sharing) next to heavier general-purpose storage/sync tools most customers already reach for.
blocking_issues:
The official rejetto/hfs image boots with a hardcoded default account (admin / please-change) and provides no way to seed a *different* admin password without the plaintext password: the only supported paths are the interactive `create-admin <PASSWORD>` console command, a `create-admin: PASSWORD` line in config.yaml, or the HTTP `add_account` API call — all of which take cleartext, not a hash. Internally HFS stores credentials as an SRP verifier (`srp` field), not a bcrypt/argon2 hash, so even if a hash-shaped input were accepted, `generated_from` has no SRP-verifier derivation today and SRP normally requires the plaintext password and a fresh salt on the client side to compute, which isn't a straightforward "just add the algorithm" extension.

Because of the above, HFS's own admin login can't be seeded from ROOT_PASSWORD today. Per SCHEMA.md's decision table this is not a hard blocker on its own — the whole app can instead sit behind a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (the WUD/Open WebUI pattern), which is the actual customer-facing auth boundary; HFS's own weak default admin login then becomes an internal implementation detail behind that gate, same as accepted for other recipes with fixed default creds.
summary: HFS is an active, single-container, single-port web app with no overlap in the current catalogue — a plausible small addition. It can't project the customer's root password into HFS's own admin login (SRP-based storage, cleartext-only seeding path), so it isn't installable via the `generated_from` mechanism; it is installable today by gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead, treating HFS's default admin account as an internal detail behind that gate. Recommend build_with_caveats: ship it with the basic-auth gate as the primary boundary and document that HFS's built-in admin login should not be treated as customer-facing auth.

name: Hollama
source_description: Minimal self-hosted browser chat UI for Ollama and OpenAI language models
version_health_notes: Releases were frequent through 2025 (0.32.0 -> 0.35.4 across May-Oct 2025, several within days of each other, including three Docker-only fixes on 2025-10-09/10/12), then nothing tagged since 0.35.4 (2025-10-12) — about 10 months with zero releases as of today (2026-08-05). Repo is not archived and no EOL statement has been made, but the sudden stop after a clearly active cadence is enough to call this "slowing" rather than "active"; worth re-checking closer to build time in case it's just a quiet patch, not a stall.
differentiation: Hollama is a static, client-only chat frontend for Ollama/OpenAI- compatible endpoints: no backend, no database, no server-side session -- everything (server URLs, API keys, chat history) lives in the visitor's own browser localStorage. That is a narrower, lighter-weight version of what Open WebUI already does in the catalogue (Open WebUI additionally provides multi-user accounts, a real backend/database, and is already bundled with Ollama in one recipe). Hollama adds no capability Open WebUI lacks; it trades Open WebUI's persistence and multi-user accounts for a smaller footprint and zero backend.
usefulness_rationale: A single-user, no-persistence chat client is a strict subset of the open-webui recipe already in the catalogue (which bundles Ollama and keeps chat history server-side across devices). The only customer who would pick Hollama over open-webui is one who specifically wants nothing stored server-side, which is a narrow niche and not enough to justify a second AI-chat-UI recipe.
summary: Hollama is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (4173) static app with no built-in login of its own (any server URL/API key is typed in by whoever opens the page, per-browser). Mechanically that makes it installable today the same way Adminer is: gate the domain behind Traefik basic_auth with the password projected from the customer's root password, no other secret needed. The blocker is fit, not mechanism -- it duplicates the already-shipped open-webui + ollama pairing while offering strictly less (no persistence, no multi-user accounts, no bundled inference engine), and its release cadence has gone quiet for the past 10 months after an otherwise active 2025. Not recommended for the catalogue as-is.

name: Homebridge
source_description: HomeKit bridge for non-Apple smart home devices using plugins
version_health_notes: Core homebridge npm package is at v2.2.1 (2026-07-19), preceded by v2.2.0 (2026-07-18), v2.1.1 (2026-07-12) and v2.1.0 (2026-06-04) — roughly monthly or faster, and only ~2.5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). The official homebridge/homebridge Docker image tracks this closely: its `latest`/`ubuntu`/date-tagged (e.g. `2026-08-05`) tags were rebuilt about 16 hours before this analysis. Homebridge v2 (2026) added Matter-standard support alongside HomeKit, showing continued active development, not maintenance-only. Repo is not archived; commits and releases are ongoing.
differentiation: Homebridge is not really a general home-automation hub like Home Assistant/Domoticz — it's a narrower HomeKit compatibility shim: it exposes non-HomeKit smart devices (via community plugins) as HomeKit accessories so they show up in Apple's Home app. Its entire value proposition depends on two local-network mechanisms that a cloud VM cannot provide: (1) mDNS/Bonjour advertisement so the customer's iPhone/iPad on their home Wi-Fi can discover and pair with the bridge, and (2) direct LAN reachability to the smart devices/hubs it bridges (Zigbee/Z-Wave USB dongles, local WiFi devices, etc. attached to the customer's home network). Both require Homebridge to run inside the customer's home LAN broadcast domain, not on an IONOS cloud VM reachable only via a public domain.
usefulness_rationale: Even ignoring the installability question, hosting this app on a cloud VM does not deliver its core function: without being on the same LAN as the customer's iPhone and smart devices, HomeKit pairing and device bridging simply do not work (short of the customer building their own site-to-site VPN back to their home network — a heavy, unsupported workaround, not something a hosting recipe can set up). This is a fundamentally local-network appliance, not a cloud-hostable web app, unlike Home Assistant/Domoticz whose web dashboards at least remain reachable and partially useful remotely even when local-device control is limited.
blocking_issues: The official docker-homebridge image documents network_mode: host as required for HomeKit accessory discovery (Bonjour/mDNS, ENABLE_AVAHI) — the container needs to share the host's network stack to participate in the customer's home LAN broadcast domain. That's already a poor fit for our bridge-network + Traefik model, but the deeper problem is architectural, not just a Docker networking flag: an IONOS cloud VM is not on the customer's home LAN at all, so even with host networking granted, the bridge cannot discover or reach the smart devices it exists to bridge, nor be discovered by the customer's phone for HomeKit pairing. There is no recipe mechanism (present or planned) that closes this gap — it is not something IF-1420/1312 or a future secrets channel would fix.
summary: Homebridge (image homebridge/homebridge, actively released, latest core v2.2.1 from 2026-07-19) is a HomeKit compatibility bridge, not a general home-automation hub — it exposes a customer's local smart devices to Apple's Home app via mDNS/Bonjour and community plugins. Its Homebridge Config UI X web login ships with a fixed admin/admin default with no env var to change it at boot, which would ordinarily be solvable with a Traefik basic_auth gate (installable per the secrets-projection mechanism). But that doesn't address the real blocker: Homebridge's core function requires it to physically sit on the customer's home LAN (for Bonjour discovery by their phone and reachability to their local Zigbee/WiFi devices), which a cloud VM at IONOS cannot provide. This is a structural, product-level mismatch with cloud hosting, not a platform feature gap — not recommended, and distinct from the home-assistant/domoticz overlap in the catalogue which at least retain a usable remote web dashboard.
