name: Hoop
source_description: Infrastructure access gateway with automatic data masking and audit trails
version_health_notes: Docker Hub shows tag 1.133.1 pushed within hours of today (2026-08-05), with a dense sequence of same-day/next-day patch and minor releases immediately before it (1.133.0, 1.132.0, 1.131.0, 1.130.0 all within the prior ~24-36 hours) plus a steady multi-week run of 1.12x.x releases before that. This is a fast-moving, actively developed project — release cadence is effectively daily, not just "active."
differentiation: Hoop and Guacamole are both "gateway in front of infrastructure" tools, but they solve different problems: Guacamole streams remote-desktop protocols (RDP/VNC/SSH) into a browser with no inspection of session content. Hoop is a wire-protocol-aware proxy for databases, Kubernetes, SSH, RDP, and MCP/LLM traffic that adds policy enforcement on top — ML-based PII/PHI masking of query results, blocking dangerous commands (DROP TABLE, rm -rf), Slack/Teams approval workflows for risky operations, and full session recording/replay for audit. It targets platform/security teams governing engineer (and now AI-agent) access to an existing fleet of internal systems, not an end-user application.
usefulness_rationale: The stated use case (governed, audited, masked access to a company's existing databases/clusters/servers, with Slack-based approval flows) assumes an enterprise platform/security team and pre-existing internal infrastructure to gate. Our self-hosting customer base is buying and running a single application, not deploying a compliance/audit control plane in front of a fleet they already operate elsewhere. A standalone Hoop instance with nothing registered behind it does nothing useful out of the box, unlike every other recipe in the catalogue which is immediately useful on its own.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: local-auth admin account credential; Traefik basic-auth gate credential (fallback if no admin-seeding channel exists); JWT_SECRET_KEY / JWK_KEY (local auth signing key); POSTGRES_DB_URI (internal Postgres password for Hoop's own metadata store)
secrets_expressible_today: JWT_SECRET_KEY / JWK_KEY (local auth signing key):server_generated_no_customer_input; POSTGRES_DB_URI (internal Postgres password for Hoop's own metadata store):server_generated_no_customer_input
blocking_issues:
No env-var channel to pre-provision a local-auth admin credential. AUTH_METHOD=local (the default, no-OIDC path) relies on a first-authentication auto-signup flow that assigns the user to a default org; the older ADMIN_USERNAME/AUDITOR_USERNAME/API_KEY vars are explicitly marked deprecated in current docs, and we could not confirm from public docs whether the first signed-up user is auto-elevated to the admin group or requires a separate 'hoop admin' CLI step post-boot. Without a confirmed bootstrap path there is nothing to project generated_from:"<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD" into.
Even with a Traefik basic_auth gate as a stopgap, that only blocks anonymous access to the signup page — it does not solve who becomes admin once someone (the gated customer) reaches it, so it doesn't fully substitute for a real admin-seeding mechanism.
The full feature set (data masking, the headline capability) requires the separate Presidio analyzer + anonymizer ML services in the upstream docker-compose.yml, which is a materially heavier stack than a typical recipe (extra containers, ML model downloads/runtime).
The product's core function requires raw TCP ports beyond the web UI — gRPC (8010), SSH tunnel (12222), RDP tunnel (13389), Postgres tunnel (15432) — for proxying actual infrastructure protocols, not just an HTTP admin console. This is architecturally different from a Traefik-fronted single-port web app and would need per-protocol port exposure the way wg-easy needs a raw UDP port.
summary: Hoop is a fast-moving, actively released (near-daily tags), MIT-licensed infrastructure access gateway aimed at platform/security teams governing engineer and AI-agent access to databases, Kubernetes, SSH/RDP, and MCP/LLM traffic, with ML-based data masking, command blocking, approval workflows, and session recording. It is conceptually adjacent to Guacamole but solves a different, more enterprise-shaped problem (governance/audit over infra you already run) that doesn't map to a standalone self-hosted app our customers install for its own sake. It is also not mechanically installable today: local-auth admin bootstrapping has no confirmed env-var or generated_from-compatible channel, the headline masking feature depends on a heavier Presidio ML sidecar stack, and its actual gateway function needs several raw TCP ports beyond a single Traefik-fronted HTTP port. Recommend not_recommended — both the fit and the installability case are weak.

name: Hoppscotch
source_description: Open-source API development and testing platform for developers and teams
version_health_notes: 2026.7.0 (2026-07-30) is the latest tagged release, 6 days before this analysis on 2026-08-05 — matches a consistent roughly-monthly cadence over the past several months (2026.4.0/2026.4.1 in April, 2026.5.0 in May, 2026.6.0/2026.6.1 in June, 2026.7.0 in July). The `hoppscotch/ hoppscotch` Docker Hub image was rebuilt for that same tag 6 days ago, confirming upstream is actively maintained, not just tagging source without shipping images.
differentiation: Hoppscotch is a Postman/Insomnia-style API client and testing tool (build/send REST, GraphQL, WebSocket, SSE requests; organize them into collections; run them individually or as automated test suites). No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers this developer-tooling niche — the closest neighbors (Gitea, Opengist) are source/snippet hosting, not API testing. It would be a genuinely new capability for a customer running other AF-hosted services who wants to develop or debug their own APIs without a local install or a SaaS account.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct value for developer customers, but the self-hosted Community Edition's persistence/collaboration features (saved workspaces, team sync, shared collections — the features that make it worth self-hosting instead of just using the free hoppscotch.io cloud app or a local desktop client) are gated behind a login system that requires either SMTP credentials (magic-link email) or an OAuth app registration (Google/GitHub/Microsoft), neither of which our recipe mechanism can provision today (see below). Without those, a deployed instance is usable anonymously as a stateless request-sender, which is a materially weaker product than what upstream is designed to offer.
blocking_issues: The app's own login (email magic-link or OAuth via Google/GitHub/ Microsoft) needs SMTP credentials or an OAuth client id/secret — neither is expressible via generated_from or basic_auth, so those features stay unusable unless the customer manually edits the admin dashboard config post-deploy. Not a hard blocker for shipping (the app functions without login), but it means the recipe would ship an intentionally crippled version of the app's headline feature set.
summary: Hoppscotch is mechanically installable today: the official AIO image (hoppscotch/hoppscotch, pin 2026.7.0) runs as a single container with ENABLE_SUBPATH_BASED_ACCESS=true routing frontend/admin/backend through one port behind Traefik, backed by an internal Postgres container (a server-generated DB password and DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY, both patternless secrets with no customer-facing value). Since it ships with no self-hosted username/password login of its own — only SMTP-based magic links or OAuth, both external credentials we have no channel for — the whole app should sit behind a Traefik basic_auth gate the same way Homepage and n8n-style no-login apps do. Upstream is actively released (monthly cadence, image rebuilt within the last week) and there's no overlap with any existing recipe, so the gap itself is real. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building, but flag to product that the self-hosted collaboration/workspace features customers likely expect from "self-hosted Postman alternative" won't work out of the box without a customer manually wiring up SMTP or OAuth after deploy.

But payroll and employee PII are high-stakes data classes to run on an unmaintained-image, dual-versioning project, and the maintainers' own "v1 deprioritized" notice plus the stale Docker Hub image undercut confidence this is a safe long-term pick today.
blocking_issues:
The container's entrypoint.sh hardcodes the admin account via `python3 manage.py createhorillauser --username admin --password admin --email admin@example.com` with no environment-variable override for username/password/email — the app itself gives no way to change this credential at boot, and no `generated_from` hash-based login field exists to project the customer's root-password hash into. Per SCHEMA.md this is not a hard blocker by itself: it is handled by putting the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth` gate, which is the mechanism recorded above — but it does mean the `admin/admin` Horilla login remains reachable (with default creds) to anyone who gets past that gate, so the gate is the only real auth boundary.

The official upstream `docker-compose.yaml` builds the app from a Dockerfile and bind-mounts the app source and media directories from the host (`./horilla:/app/horilla`, `./media:/app/media`) rather than running self-contained from the published image — the documented deployment path is closer to "clone repo and build" than "pull a pinned tag and run." A recipe would need to diverge from upstream's own compose file and pin `horilla/horilla:1.4` directly, which is already 2+ releases stale (see version_health).
summary: Horilla fills a real gap (no HR/CRM recipe in the current 24) and is mechanically installable today by gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth, since its admin/admin login is hardcoded with no override channel. However, the official Docker Hub image is stale (1.4, missing 1.5.0/1.6.0/1.6.1), the project runs two inconsistent version/tag schemes, and the maintainers themselves have deprioritized the v1 line the image is built from. Given payroll/HR data sensitivity, recommend build_with_caveats rather than build_now — worth revisiting once the image catches up to a current tag on the v2 line.

name: HortusFox
source_description: Self-hosted plant management system for tracking care routines and garden organization
version_health_notes: v5.9 shipped 2026-07-31, only 5 days before today (2026-08-05). Release history (v5.0 2025-05-30, v5.1 2025-07-10, v5.2 2025-07-30, v5.3 2025-10-25, v5.4 2025-10-30, v5.5 2025-12-03, v5.6 2025-12-15, v5.7 2025-12-23, v5.8 2026-05-02, v5.9 2026-07-31) shows a real, if uneven, cadence — bursts of weekly patch releases (Oct-Dec 2025) followed by two longer quiet stretches (~130 days v5.7-v5.8, ~90 days v5.8-v5.9), each still followed by active feature work (attachments for plants, list-sorting persistence, security hardening) rather than a slowdown to maintenance-only. Single maintainer (danielbrendel) but commit activity and issue triage both look current; no archival notice, no stated EOL.
differentiation: HortusFox is a plant-care and garden-organization tracker (per-plant care schedules, location assignment, care-due warnings, collaborative chat, task/calendar features). Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches this niche — Homebox is the closest analog structurally (single web app + own DB, home-organization category) but covers physical-asset/inventory tracking, not living-plant care routines. This would be a genuinely new category, not a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Real hobbyist demand (houseplant/garden enthusiasts, similar audience to Homebox and other homelab-organization tools) but a narrow, single-purpose niche rather than infrastructure most customers reach for. Comparable usefulness tier to Homebox for the same reasons: cheap to run, low support burden, but not a high-demand category.
blocking_issues:
The app's own admin account is created at container boot by docker-entrypoint.sh, which reads APP_ADMIN_EMAIL and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD as plaintext and hashes them itself (`php -r "echo password_hash(...)"`, bcrypt) before writing to MariaDB. It needs the plaintext password as an env var, not a pre-computed hash, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash) cannot supply it — per SCHEMA.md this is a genuine structural blocker, not a "generated_from doesn't support this algo yet" case. If APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD is left unset the entrypoint auto-generates a random one via `openssl rand -base64 12` that is never surfaced to the customer or to af-api, i.e. nobody could log in at all.

Workaround available: bake a fixed, non-customer-facing APP_ADMIN_EMAIL/APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD into the recipe (same pattern as "hardcoded admin credential the app gives no way to change" in SCHEMA.md) and put the whole app behind a Traefik basic_auth gate keyed to the customer's root-password hash as the real security boundary. This makes it installable today, but the app's in-product login stays a fixed shared secret across every install rather than something tied to the customer — a caveat worth flagging even though it clears the mechanical bar.
summary: HortusFox is a MariaDB-backed PHP web app (structurally similar to paperless-ngx/n8n's app+DB template) with a single HTTP port, no OAuth, and no external API dependency — mechanically installable today only via a workaround: hardcode its own admin login to a fixed non-customer value and rely on a Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password hash) as the actual access boundary, since the app's entrypoint needs the admin password in plaintext to hash itself rather than accepting a pre-hashed value. It fills a genuinely new niche (no overlap in the current 24 recipes) with an actively maintained upstream (latest release 5 days old), but the underlying demand is a narrow hobbyist niche similar in scale to Homebox, so build_with_caveats rather than a strong build_now.

Even setting the platform-mechanism gap aside, it overlaps with Open WebUI's existing "chat frontend for an LLM backend" niche without a stronger self-hosted story, since its flagship use case (Hugging Face's hosted router) depends on an external account and API key rather than a bundled, private inference engine. The blocker isn't the platform mechanism, it's fit and upkeep cost: it directly overlaps our existing n8n recipe in the "hackable Zapier/IFTTT" niche while being materially behind it on active integrations and UI, and upstream hasn't cut a tagged release since 2022 — despite otherwise-active commits — forcing us to pin and periodically re-pin a rolling commit-SHA image tag instead of a stable version. name: Hugo
source_description: Lightning-fast static site generator built with Go
version_health_notes: ~1 month since the last tagged release as of 2026-08-05. Hugo ships frequent releases (roughly monthly, sometimes more often) and the project is actively maintained by gohugoio with ongoing commits and issue triage. No sign of slowdown or archival.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes are static site generators or build tools — this would be a genuinely new category. However, Hugo is a CLI/build tool, not a hosted application with its own persistent admin surface: it compiles a customer-supplied source tree (markdown + theme) into static HTML. `hugo server` exists but is documented upstream as a local live-reload preview server for development, not a production-facing service.
usefulness_rationale: A "Hugo recipe" that ships with no site content is an empty shell — there is nothing for the customer to see or use until they supply their own markdown/theme source, and the value of self-hosting Hugo specifically (vs. any static file server) is the build step over that source, not a runtime service.
blocking_issues:
No channel for customer content: Hugo has no value without the customer's own site source (markdown content + theme). /compose carries no mechanism for arbitrary file/content upload at install time, so a deployed instance would have nothing to build or serve.
Not a persistent service by design: Hugo is a build tool. `hugo server` is documented upstream as a dev-only live-reload preview, not intended to be exposed publicly in production — there is no equivalent to an admin UI or long-running app process that the recipe model assumes.
summary: Hugo is an actively maintained, fast-moving open-source static site generator (latest v0.164.0, 2026-07-06) with no EOL or dormancy concerns. It doesn't overlap with anything in the current 24-recipe catalogue, but it is structurally a CLI build tool rather than a self-hosted application: it has no admin UI, no login, and — critically — no value at all without customer-supplied site source content, for which the recipe mechanism has no delivery channel today. Recommend not pursuing this as a recipe; it is a poor fit for the catalogue's "install and use" model regardless of the root-password/basic-auth secret mechanism, since the blocker is missing content, not missing auth.

name: HumHub
source_description: Open-source enterprise social network and intranet platform for teams

The official `humhub/docker` image is kept current with matching tags (`1.18.4`, `stable`, `stable-nightly`), unlike some other candidates in this catalogue whose Docker Hub image lags behind GitHub releases.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover a general-purpose enterprise social network / intranet (activity streams, groups/spaces, wikis, file sharing, member directory). Gitea and OpenGist are developer- focused code/collaboration tools, not a company-wide social intranet. This would open a genuinely new category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted intranet/social-network platforms are a real SMB use case (HumHub advertises 4,500+ organizations using it) with no current catalogue entry, so there's plausible demand. It is, however, a heavier, more configuration-heavy app than most of our single-purpose recipes (requires a MySQL/MariaDB backend, background cron/queue workers for mail and search indexing) and its value is most apparent for teams that will invest time in setting up spaces/modules — a smaller slice of self-hoster traffic than a password manager or monitoring tool.
blocking_issues:
HumHub's own admin account is not projectable via `generated_from`. Both the browser install wizard and its scriptable equivalent (Yii console command `yii installer/create-admin-account --admin_pass=<password>`, confirmed to exist for unattended/CI use) take the admin password as plaintext and hash it internally at account-creation time — there is no field that accepts a pre-computed hash, so a `generated_from` hash of the customer's root password could never be handed to it directly. This mirrors the SCHEMA.md "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case, not the extensible-algorithm case.

Workaround (same pattern accepted for `apps-gaps/horilla.yaml`): install.sh can run the console admin-creation command with a fixed, recipe-baked credential (not customer-supplied, not secret) and put the entire app behind a Traefik `basic_auth` gate keyed to the customer's root-password hash. This keeps the recipe installable today but means the customer never gets a HumHub admin login tied to their own root password — only the gate is.
summary: HumHub is active upstream (monthly release cadence, current release 2026-07-21, matching official Docker image) and would fill a genuine gap — no social-network/intranet recipe exists in the current 24. It is mechanically installable today only via the same workaround used for Horilla: a fixed, non-customer-facing admin login created via HumHub's console installer, with the whole app gated behind Traefik basic_auth as the actual security boundary, since HumHub's admin account has no hash-based credential channel. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building, but flag to the developer that the customer's HumHub-internal admin login is decoupled from their root password, unlike our `generated_from`-backed recipes.

name: HyperDX
source_description: Open-source observability platform unifying logs, traces, and metrics
version_health_notes: 2.33.0 (app/api/otel-collector) shipped 2026-07-31, just 5 days before today (2026-08-05); 2.32.0 shipped 2026-07-27, i.e. sub-weekly minor releases across the monorepo's component packages. The CLI package (v0.6.0) is slightly behind at 2026-07-17 but still within the same month. Nightly image builds (`2-nightly`) are also being pushed continuously. This is a fast-moving, clearly active project, not a dormant/EOL candidate.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does log/trace/metric observability. Uptime Kuma is the closest existing "monitoring" recipe, but it is external blackbox uptime/ping checking, not ingesting telemetry emitted by a customer's own instrumented applications — a different use case. HyperDX (built on ClickHouse + OpenTelemetry, aka "ClickStack") would fill a genuine, currently-unfilled observability niche, but like other APM/observability tools it only has value for a customer who has other services to instrument and point at it; it has no standalone utility on its own.
usefulness_rationale: Real gap and a credible, fast-moving open-source project with a convenient all-in-one image, but the audience is narrower (developers/SREs with other instrumented services) than most of our existing single-user consumer/prosumer recipes, and it carries real operational weight (ClickHouse storage, OTel ingestion) for that narrower audience.
blocking_issues:
Not a single-HTTP-port app: the all-in-one image's entire value is receiving logs/traces/metrics pushed by OpenTelemetry-instrumented apps, which by default requires the OTel collector's raw ports (4317 gRPC, 4318 HTTP) to be reachable directly by whatever is pushing telemetry — not just a browser routed through Traefik on 80/443. This is the same structural mismatch flagged for Apache SkyWalking: every current recipe is a single browser-facing HTTP port fronted by Traefik, and exposing raw ingestion ports per customer VM is a product decision that hasn't been made.

The upstream docker-compose.yml (the non-all-in-one deployment) is a 4-service stack — MongoDB (app metadata), ClickHouse (telemetry storage), an OTel collector, and the app/API — comparable in weight to Immich/anytype-server rather than the single-container recipes that make up most of the catalogue. The all-in-one image collapses this into one container but still needs a real ClickHouse data volume and is a heavier resource footprint than a typical recipe.

No first-boot secret is required by the platform itself: on first visit to the UI (port 8080) the app presents its own signup screen where the visitor picks their own username/password directly (no env-var-injected admin credential, no API key gate) — the same pattern already accepted for n8n and Immich in this catalogue, so this alone is not a blocker.
summary: HyperDX is an actively developed (near-weekly releases, latest 2.33.0 on 2026-07-31), MIT-licensed observability platform with no equivalent in the current 24-recipe catalogue. Its own first-run account creation is unproblematic (self-serve signup, same pattern as n8n/Immich), so it is not blocked by the usual root-password/basic_auth secrets mechanism. What blocks it is structural: like Apache SkyWalking, its purpose requires exposing raw OTel ingestion ports (4317/4318) directly to whatever external, separately-hosted apps are pushing telemetry, which is a fundamentally different exposure shape than our Traefik-only, single-HTTP-port recipes, plus a heavier multi-container/ClickHouse storage footprint. Recommend blocked_on_platform pending a product decision on exposing non-HTTP public ingestion ports per recipe; revisit alongside Apache SkyWalking if/when that decision is made.

name: Iceshrimp
source_description: Decentralized ActivityPub social network powered by a fast .NET backend
version_health_notes: v2026.1.2-beta shipped 2026-07-30, only 6 days before today (2026-08-05) — a security hotfix disabling unfuzzed libvips load/save paths. Prior releases show a steady, sub-monthly cadence: v2026.1.1-beta (2026-05-20), v2026.1-beta (2026-04-24), v2025.1-beta5.patch3.security4 (2025-12-19), .security3 (2025-11-03), .security2 (2025-07-29), plus several 2025 patch/security releases before that. Both feature releases (report system, feed support, .NET 9→10 migration in v2026.1-beta) and fast security hotfixes are present, indicating genuinely active development rather than maintenance-only drift. Still explicitly labeled beta software by the maintainers themselves.
differentiation: Iceshrimp.NET is a Mastodon-API-compatible ActivityPub microblogging server (Misskey/Firefish lineage) — federated social networking, not covered by anything in the current 24-recipe catalogue. Closest conceptual neighbor is Hermes-agent (also chat/agent-adjacent) but that's an AI agent, not a fediverse server; there's no real overlap. This would open a genuinely new "social/fediverse" category.
usefulness_rationale: Real and growing demand for self-hosted fediverse presence (post-Twitter exodus audience, tech-savvy self-hosters who already run Mastodon/Misskey forks), and Mastodon-client compatibility broadens the addressable app ecosystem. Still a beta-labeled, single small-team project competing with much better-established alternatives (Mastodon, Pleroma/Akkoma) for the same audience, so demand ceiling is lower than infra-category tools.
blocking_issues:
No admin/root credential is set via environment variable or config at container boot. Like Mastodon/Misskey-family servers generally, and matching the same shape documented in apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml, apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml, and apps-gaps/airtrail.yaml, Iceshrimp.NET's admin account is created through its own web-based registration flow after the instance comes up — the first account to register (or the first account an operator manually promotes) becomes admin. There is no `type: password` parameter on the app's own login to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var. With the server publicly reachable behind the customer's domain the moment the compose stack boots, an unrelated visitor (or a fediverse-scanning bot) could register first and claim the initial account before the customer does, on an instance that — per default fediverse-server posture — may allow open registration out of the box.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would close the "random internet stranger races to register first" version of this problem, but per the 2FAuth/Activepieces/AirTrail precedent, today's basic_auth mechanism has no channel to also hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential for the in-app signup form beyond the single root-password projection already used for the gate itself — so it does not fully resolve the underlying provisioning gap. Even if it did, the gate would need to come off after the customer claims the admin account for the instance to actually federate/serve the public web, and our current one-shot bootstrap-token mechanism has no lifecycle hook for that ("remove gate after customer completes setup" is not a step `/compose` or `/bootstrap` support today).

Full service topology needs confirming against a canonical docker-compose.yml before drafting a recipe: PostgreSQL 15+ is a hard requirement (confirmed via CHANGELOG), Redis appears required for caching/job queues, and Meilisearch is used for full-text search — unclear from available docs whether Meilisearch is optional or mandatory for a functional instance. Official upstream docs (iceshrimp.net/docs) were unreachable/404 during this research pass (domain now redirects to the dev/source browser, which doesn't serve rendered docs pages); a `af-create-recipe` pass would need to pull the actual `docs/install*.md` from the dev-branch source tree or a third-party deployment guide to nail down the compose file, image tag/registry, and ports before drafting.
summary: Iceshrimp.NET is an actively developed (latest release 6 days old), Mastodon-API-compatible ActivityPub server with no current catalogue overlap and a real niche audience. It fails the installability test for the same structural reason as 2FAuth, Activepieces, and AirTrail: there is no env var to preset the sole admin account, so the app relies on an open, first-visitor self-registration screen that neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely hand to the customer exclusively — and even a temporary gate would need to be lifted post-setup for the instance to federate, which our current one-shot `/compose`+`/bootstrap` mechanism has no lifecycle hook for. Also still beta-labeled software from a small team, competing with more established fediverse servers for the same audience. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow, or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond root-password projection (plus a gate-then-release lifecycle hook), and confirm the full service topology (Postgres/Redis/Meilisearch) against upstream's canonical compose file at that point.

name: Icinga 2
source_description: Open-source monitoring for hosts, services, and metrics with a modern web UI
version_health_notes: 2.16.4 released 2026-07-16, ~3 weeks before today (2026-08-05). The 2.16.x branch has shipped a steady stream of releases through 2026 (2.16.0 Apr 23, 2.16.1 May 21, 2.16.2 Jun 29 as a critical security fix, 2.16.3 Jul 1, 2.16.4 Jul 16) plus parallel backports to the 2.15.x and 2.14.x branches — the project is clearly under active, well-resourced maintenance, not dormant.
differentiation: Icinga 2 is a classic Nagios-style host/service monitoring engine: active checks (plugins, NRPE/Icinga Agent, SNMP), distributed master/satellite/agent topology, and a notification/escalation pipeline, fronted by the Icinga Web 2 PHP UI. Against the only monitoring recipe we actually ship today, Uptime Kuma (a single-container URL/service pinger with no agent concept), Icinga 2 adds real infrastructure/host monitoring capability that Uptime Kuma doesn't cover, but it targets sysadmins who want to actively monitor a fleet of hosts, not a single self-hosted app owner. (Alerta, which would sit closer to Icinga 2 as an alert-correlation console, is itself only another unbuilt gap-analysis candidate, not a shipped recipe, so it isn't part of this comparison.)
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely differentiated capability (agent-based host/service monitoring) that nothing else in the catalogue offers, but it has an "empty by default" problem: a freshly deployed Icinga 2 instance monitors nothing useful until the customer defines hosts/services and, for anything beyond localhost, installs and registers Icinga Agents on remote machines — a config-heavy exercise unlike, say, Uptime Kuma's zero-friction "add a URL" flow. It also ships as a materially heavier stack (core engine + Redis + MySQL + web UI, vs. our typical 1-3 container recipes), raising both resource footprint and first-boot complexity for a self-host customer base that skews toward simpler tools.
summary: Icinga 2 (core engine, icinga/icinga2 image) plus Icinga Web 2 (icinga/icingaweb2 image) is a heavier stack than our current recipes: the modern Icinga DB architecture needs the core engine, a Redis instance (Icinga DB), a MySQL database (both for Icinga DB and for Icinga Web 2's own config/session store), and the PHP web UI — 4+ containers versus our usual 1-3. Icinga Web 2's admin login (icingaweb.passwords.icingaweb2.icingaadmin=<plaintext>) is consumed directly as a plaintext env var by the setup process with no pre-hashed-credential support, so `generated_from` can't target it directly, but that's not a hard blocker: the admin password can be server-generated and never exposed, with the whole app instead gated behind Traefik `basic_auth: true` projected from the customer's root password (the same pattern used elsewhere in the catalogue for apps with no native pre-hashed-credential support). That makes it installable under today's mechanism, but between the multi-container footprint and the "nothing to see until you configure hosts/agents" cold-start problem, it's a higher-effort build for a narrower audience than broader-appeal gaps in the backlog. Recommend build_with_caveats.

Separately, ILLA Cloud (the commercial entity behind the project) announced on 2024-10-?? that it would shut down its hosted cloud service on 2024-11-11 due to unresolved financial issues, then reversed that decision days later (2024-11-09 CEO post) claiming the funding problem was fixed and the open-source project would keep being developed. This reads as a company in decline that nominally kept the OSS repo alive but has not shipped meaningful work on it in well over a year — maintenance-only at best, trending toward de facto abandonment.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover a low-code/no-code internal-tool builder (dashboards, CRUD apps, admin panels backed by an arbitrary external database). n8n is the closest recipe by category (developer/automation tooling) but is a workflow-automation engine, not a UI/app builder — the two are complementary, not redundant. A healthy ILLA Builder would be a genuine, non-duplicative addition.
usefulness_rationale: The use case (self-hosted Retool alternative) has real customer appeal for a business/developer audience, but ILLA Builder specifically is a risky pick to build on right now given the company's financial instability and stalled release cadence — a customer standing up internal business tools on an abandoned platform is a worse outcome than not offering it.
blocking_issues: ILLA Builder ships a single all-in-one container (illasoft/illa-builder, port 2022 internally / 80 by default) with a hardcoded default admin login (root / password) and no environment variable or first-boot config to set a different admin credential — the only supported deploy-time input for the container is its two data volumes. There is no channel to project a per-customer credential into the app's own login, so it must be treated as "no login of its own that customer can set" and gated with Traefik basic_auth rather than generated_from.
summary: ILLA Builder is mechanically installable today: it's a single container, single HTTP port, with a fixed default admin login that has no deploy-time override, so the standard fix is to gate the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth wall (basic_auth_password projected from the customer's root password) rather than trying to set its internal root/password credential. The blocker isn't the platform mechanism, though — it's the upstream project itself. Releases stopped exactly two years ago (4.8.5, 2024-08-05), commit activity has been essentially docs-only since early-to-mid 2025, the vendor's own docs site no longer resolves, and the company that maintains it publicly disclosed and then "resolved" a funding crisis in late 2024 without any visible follow-through in shipped work since. Recommend not building this recipe now; revisit only if upstream shows a real release resurgence.

name: Imaginary
source_description: Fast HTTP microservice for high-performance image processing powered by libvips
version_health_notes: No tagged release since v1.2.4 in August 2020 — 6 years as of 2026-08-05. The repo is not archived and still receives sporadic commits (most recent seen: a Dockerfile build fix merged 2025-11-08), but that work has not been cut into a new version or a refreshed `h2non/imaginary` Docker Hub image, which itself hasn't been pushed in about 6 years. Effectively unmaintained-but-not-dead: fine for a stable, narrowly-scoped image-resizing microservice, but a 6-year-old base image is a real supply-chain/CVE concern for anything shipped as a recipe today.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a generic image-processing/resizing API. Immich does its own internal thumbnail generation but doesn't expose it as a reusable service; Imaginary would be a standalone HTTP microservice a developer could point their own app at for on-the-fly resize/crop/convert operations.
usefulness_rationale: It's a backend-only JSON/binary HTTP API with no UI and no concept of end-user accounts — there's nothing for a non-technical customer to open or click on. Value is limited to developers wiring it into their own app as an image-processing backend, which is a narrow slice of the AF customer base, and the stale (6-year-old) upstream image dampens appeal further.
summary: Imaginary is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8088) Go microservice with no web UI and no built-in login — it optionally supports an `-key`/API-Key header scheme, but that key is an app-launch flag, not something a customer types into a login form. Left unauthenticated it would be an open image-processing endpoint on the internet, so it needs to be gated the same way as Adminer/WUD: a domain param plus Traefik `basic_auth: true`, with that password projected via the customer's root password (`generated_from`). Mechanically installable today, but not recommended to build now: it has no web UI (low appeal to most customers, developer-only use case), no functional overlap need in the current catalogue to justify urgency, and the upstream image is 6 years stale with only sporadic, unreleased commit activity — build only if a concrete developer-facing image-processing use case emerges.

name: imgproxy
source_description: Fast on-the-fly image processing server for resize, crop, and format conversion
version_health_notes: v4.0.12 shipped 2026-07-29 (~1 week before today, 2026-08-05) with security fixes (BMP loader heap overflow, SSRF boundary hardening). Preceding patch releases landed roughly weekly through June-July 2026 (v4.0.4 through v4.0.11), with the v4.x line branching off v3.31.x in early June. Clear active, fast-moving maintenance cadence with a responsible security-disclosure address; no EOL or dormancy signal.
differentiation: imgproxy is a standalone HTTP image-processing proxy: a customer's own application constructs signed URLs against it and imgproxy fetches, resizes/crops/converts, and returns the image on the fly, replacing image-processing code that would otherwise live inside the app. Nothing in the current 24 recipes offers this as a general-purpose, app- agnostic service — Immich does its own internal thumbnailing for its own photo library and does not expose a reusable resize/convert API for other applications to call. Like Apache Tika, imgproxy's entire value surface is a REST-ish API consumed by other software, not a page a customer visits and uses directly.
usefulness_rationale: Pure developer-infrastructure microservice with no end-user workflow and no web UI — visiting the root URL returns only a bare health check, not a functional interface. Useful only to a customer who already runs their own web/mobile app and wants to offload its image resizing to a separate service, which is a narrow, technical audience compared to the end-user apps making up most of the catalogue.
summary: Mechanically installable: single container, single HTTP port (8080, no TLS of its own — expects to sit behind a reverse proxy, which matches our Traefik setup exactly), no web login of its own, so a Traefik basic_auth:true gate (password projected from the customer's root password) covers the only secret it would need — same pattern as Tika/adminer/n8n. imgproxy also supports its own IMGPROXY_SECRET bearer-token header auth and URL-signing keys, but those are server-generated internal secrets an application caller uses, not a customer-facing login, so they don't change the installability picture. Upstream is healthy and actively released (v4.0.12, 2026-07-29). The blocker is fit, not mechanism: imgproxy has no web UI, its whole value is as a REST API consumed by other software, and it duplicates nothing in the catalogue while adding no direct end-user workflow. Recommend not_recommended on usefulness grounds despite being technically installable today, mirroring the apache-tika verdict.

name: ImmuDB
source_description: Immutable, tamper-proof database with cryptographic verification and web console
upstream_license: BSL-1.1 (Business Source License 1.1 — source-available, not OSI-approved open source; converts to Apache-2.0 four years after each version's release)
version_health_notes: 1.11.1 released 2026-06-25, ~6 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Tag history shows the release cadence has stretched out: 1.9.6 (2025-03-31) → 1.9.7 (2025-05-30, 2mo) → 1.10.0 (2025-10-21, 5mo) → 1.11.0 (2026-04-28, 6mo) → 1.11.1 (2026-06-25, 2mo, a fix release). That's roughly one release every 4-6 months over the last 18 months, down from a much faster cadence in immudb's early years. The GitHub repo (Codenotary) is not archived — ~9k stars, 4,894 commits, 33 open PRs, 70 open issues — and a `dev` Docker tag was pushed 2026-08-03 (2 days before analysis), so active development continues even though tagged stable releases have slowed. Not dormant, but clearly past its highest-velocity period.
differentiation: ImmuDB is a standalone cryptographically-verifiable, append-only key-value/SQL database aimed at developers who need tamper-evident audit trails inside their own applications (e.g. financial ledgers, compliance logs). Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a bare database server offered as a customer-facing app — our closest recipes (n8n, paperless-ngx) use Postgres internally as an implementation detail, never expose it as the product. ImmuDB would be the first "install a database and use it yourself" recipe rather than an "install a finished consumer app" recipe, which is a different value proposition for a self-hosting customer than the rest of the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiated capability (cryptographic tamper-evidence) but a narrow, developer-only audience: a customer needs to already be building or operating an application that talks to immudb over gRPC/pgsql-wire to get any value from a freshly deployed, empty instance — there's no "browse and use it" experience like the rest of the catalogue offers. That's a materially smaller addressable slice of self-hosting customers than apps with an immediate, standalone use (password manager, uptime monitor, file sync).
summary: ImmuDB ships with a fixed, hardcoded default login (immudb/immudb) that can only be changed after boot via the separate `immuadmin` CLI against the running server — there is no env var or config option to inject a pre-hashed or plaintext admin credential at container start, so `generated_from` cannot target it directly. That's not a hard blocker per the schema's "fixed default credential" case: the whole app (gRPC service on 3322, web console + REST on 8080, optional pgsql-wire on 5432) can sit behind Traefik `basic_auth: true` gating the real auth boundary, making it mechanically installable_today. The bigger problems are fit and value: it is not reverse-proxy-compatible in the way our other recipes are (its primary interface is a raw gRPC/pgsql-wire port, not a single HTTP surface Traefik can front — the web console is a secondary admin panel, not the product), its BSL-1.1 license is source-available rather than open source, release cadence has slowed to roughly one tag every 4-6 months, and its audience (developers embedding a tamper-evident database in their own software) doesn't match the rest of the catalogue's ready-to-use consumer apps. Recommend not_recommended.

name: Indico
source_description: Open-source conference and event management system created at CERN
version_health_notes: v3.3.12 shipped 2026-03-23, ~4.5 months before today (2026-08-05) — the longest gap between releases in the recent history (v3.3.9 2025-12-11, v3.3.10 2026-02-17, v3.3.11 2026-02-27, v3.3.12 2026-03-23 show a monthly-or-faster cadence up to that point). However, the `master` branch on GitHub shows commits as recent as 2026-08-05 (same day as this analysis), so upstream development is clearly ongoing; the gap looks like a slower release-cutting cycle rather than a stalled or abandoned project. Maintained by CERN with 100+ historical contributors.
differentiation: Indico is a conference/event-lifecycle management tool (call for abstracts, registration forms, timetabling, room booking, badge printing, video-conferencing integration) — nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers this space. Closest catalogue neighbor by audience (small orgs/teams self-hosting collaboration tooling) is Gitea or n8n, but neither overlaps functionally.
usefulness_rationale: Real niche demand from academic/research institutions, user groups, and conference organizers who want a mature, CERN-built, MIT-licensed alternative to commercial event platforms. Audience is narrower than general productivity tools — most self-hosters running a personal homelab have no use for conference/abstract-review workflows — but the project is credible and well-established (in production at CERN and many physics/academic institutions since 2002).
blocking_issues:
No official hardened/production Docker image exists. The only image upstream publishes, `getindico/indico` on Docker Hub (built from github.com/indico/indico-containers), carries an explicit warning in its own Docker Hub description: "DO NOT use this in production as it is. There are important things missing, such as HTTPS support." The indico-containers README repeats this: "we do not use this setup ourselves so it is not as battle-tested as one of our official installation guides... a good working knowledge of Docker is recommended." Indico's actual recommended/canonical deployment path is a bare-metal/venv install documented at docs.getindico.io/en/stable/installation/production/, not Docker.

The reference stack (indico-prod/docker-compose.yml in indico-containers) is a 5-service topology: indico-web (uwsgi), indico-celery, indico-celery-beat, indico-redis, indico-postgres, plus an nginx reverse-proxy container in front of the web container for static-file serving — comparable in complexity to recipes/immich/ or recipes/anytype-server/, not a single-container app. Our Traefik-fronted model would replace the bundled nginx, which is workable, but it means adopting a stack upstream itself doesn't stand behind for production use.

No env-var or config-file driven initial-admin bootstrap exists. The only way to create the first admin account is the `indico user create --admin` CLI command (indico/cli/user.py), which is fully interactive: it calls `click.prompt(...)` for email/first name/last name/affiliation/username and `prompt_pass()` for the password — there are no `--email`/`--password` flags to script it non- interactively. Beyond that, the identity's password setter (indico/modules/auth/models/identities.py, backed by indico/util/passwords.py's bcrypt-based `BCryptPassword`) takes and hashes a **plaintext** password itself; it has no path to accept a pre-computed hash. Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's own test — "an admin credential the app will only accept... a genuine requirement for the plaintext password (not any hash) is a structural blocker, since generated_from only ever carries a hash" — this is exactly that case: `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` can only ever produce a hash of the customer's root password, and Indico has no way to consume that hash directly for its own login.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate could be placed in front of the whole app to prevent an outside visitor from reaching the interactive setup at all before the customer runs it — but that only re-creates the 2FAuth/Activepieces/AirTrail/Iceshrimp shape: it still requires a second, distinct credential for the actual Indico admin account beyond the single root-password projection already spent on the gate, and our one-shot bootstrap has no mechanism to run an interactive CLI prompt sequence with customer-specific values, nor a lifecycle hook to remove the gate once the customer completes setup.
summary: Indico is a credible, actively developed (same-day commits on master), MIT-licensed CERN project with no functional overlap in the current catalogue and a real, if narrow, academic/events audience. It's blocked today on two independent grounds: upstream itself disclaims its only published Docker image as unfit for production (recommending a bare-metal install instead), and initial admin provisioning requires an interactive CLI prompt for a plaintext password with no non-interactive or hash-based entry point — a structural mismatch with the `generated_from: ROOT_PASSWORD` mechanism, which only ever carries a hash. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit only if upstream ships a hardened container image plus a non-interactive/env-var admin-bootstrap path, or the platform gains a channel for handing an app a plaintext customer secret at first boot.

name: Infisical
source_description: Open-source secrets manager for syncing env variables and API keys across teams and infrastructure
upstream_license: MIT (with a separate `ee/` directory of enterprise-only features gated by an Infisical license)
upstream_docker_image: infisical/infisical (standalone image, tags like `v0.162.16-postgres`; requires an external Postgres + Redis)
version_health_notes: Releases are landing multiple times per week (v0.162.6 on 2026-07-14 up to v0.162.16 on 2026-08-04, roughly 10 tagged releases in three weeks). As of today (2026-08-05) the latest release is one day old. No indication of maintenance-only mode or EOL; this is a VC-backed, actively developed product with frequent feature and security releases.

Infisical targets developers/teams syncing environment variables, API keys, and infrastructure secrets across services (CLI, SDKs, CI/CD integrations, dynamic secrets, PKI). No recipe in the current catalogue covers this "secrets-manager-as-infrastructure" niche.

summary: Infisical is an actively maintained, MIT-licensed, web-UI'd secrets manager with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue — the closest existing recipe (Vaultwarden) solves a different problem. Its self-hosted requirements (an app container plus Postgres and Redis, all secrets server-generatable, initial admin account created by the customer themselves via the app's own signup screen after deployment rather than through the /compose bootstrap channel) fit the current recipe mechanism cleanly, the same way n8n's owner-account setup does. Recommend proceeding to a full af-create-recipe pass using n8n as the closest structural template (Postgres-backed multi-service stack), adding Redis as a third service.

name: InfluxDB 2
source_description: Unified time series platform with Flux queries and integrated web UI
version_health_notes: 2.9.1 (2026-05-11) followed 2.9.0 (2026-05-01) closely, but nothing has shipped on the 2.x line in the ~3 months since, as of today (2026-08-05). InfluxData's actual current development focus has moved to InfluxDB 3 (v3.10.0 shipped 2026-06-17, with a roughly quarterly major/minor cadence and its own two-latest-minors support window), while 2.x now only receives occasional bug-fix patches. InfluxData has publicly stated that on 2026-09-15 (about 6 weeks from today) the `latest` Docker tag will stop pointing at 2.x and switch to InfluxDB 3 Core, and endoflife.date notes 2.x has no announced EOL date but is clearly in a reduced-cadence, maintenance-only posture relative to the actively developed 3.x line. Not archived and not EOL, but a customer picking "InfluxDB 2" today is explicitly choosing the superseded major version; a recipe would need to pin an explicit `2.9.1` (or `2.9`) tag rather than `latest`, since `latest` will silently become v3 in six weeks.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a time-series database. InfluxDB 2 is a purpose-built store for metrics/events (Flux/InfluxQL query engine, built-in web UI for dashboards and data exploration) that customers would pair with something like Telegraf or their own instrumentation to push data in, and optionally Grafana on top for richer visualization. It's a different niche from Uptime Kuma (self-contained external ping/uptime checker) — no existing recipe lets a customer stand up their own metrics backend.
usefulness_rationale: Useful to developers/power users who want a self-hosted metrics store (IoT telemetry, custom app instrumentation, Home Assistant long-term history, etc.), but it's a backend building block with a technical audience, not a broad-appeal end-user app, and a bare instance with nothing writing to it yet is an empty shell — same caveat noted for Grafana in this candidate set.
summary: InfluxDB 2's official image has no env var or CLI path that accepts a pre-hashed admin credential — the documented `DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_MODE= setup` path (INIT_USERNAME/INIT_PASSWORD/INIT_ORG/INIT_BUCKET) only accepts a plaintext password, which `generated_from` (hash-only) cannot supply. However, if that init mode is simply left unset, InfluxDB boots uninitialized and presents an unauthenticated first-visit setup wizard at :8086 where the visitor creates their own username, password, organization, and bucket directly in the browser — the same pattern already accepted for Ghost/Firefly III/Baikal in this candidate set, not a blocker. install.sh should put a Traefik basic_auth gate (projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from`) in front of the app at first boot so a stranger can't race the customer to claim the initial account, with the customer expected to remove the gate after completing the wizard. Version health is the real caveat here: the 2.x line has gone quiet (last patch 2026-05-11, ~3 months ago) as InfluxData's development attention has shifted to InfluxDB 3, and the Docker `latest` tag itself switches from 2.x to 3.x on 2026-09-15 — any recipe must pin an explicit `2.9.1`/`2.9` tag, and a reviewer should weigh whether building against the superseded major (rather than InfluxDB 3, not yet analyzed here) is the right long-term bet. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically installable now via the same setup-wizard-plus-temporary-gate pattern as Ghost, but on a major version InfluxData itself is de-emphasizing.

version_health_notes: Upstream Inkscape is actively developed: 1.4.4 released 2026-05-06 (a maintenance/bugfix release with ~20 crash fixes), following 1.4.2 (2025-05-12) and 1.4.1/1.4.3 point releases in between, with 1.5 in active development on GitLab. differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a full desktop creative application — the closest analogues are the gap-analysis candidates for GIMP and Blender (both linuxserver "webtop" desktop-in-browser images, both flagged low-usefulness/not_recommended for this catalogue) and, at a different layer, draw.io/Excalidraw, which are lightweight diagramming web apps rather than a full vector-illustration suite. The one structural precedent for "remote desktop in a browser", Guacamole, is itself currently disabled, and the catalogue has so far passed on this app category (GIMP, Blender) for the same reason.
summary: Inkscape is actively developed upstream (1.4.4, 2026-05-06) and the lscr.io/linuxserver/inkscape image is mechanically installable today: a single container serving a noVNC desktop over HTTP/HTTPS with no login of its own, gated cleanly behind Traefik basic_auth using the customer's root-password hash, same pattern as n8n/WUD/draw.io. The packaged app version does lag upstream by two point releases despite weekly image rebuilds (those rebuilds are base-image patches, not app bumps), worth watching but not itself disqualifying. The real issue is fit: this is a full desktop-in-browser tool, the same architecture already evaluated and passed on for GIMP and Blender, needing desktop-class resources for a single interactive user rather than matching the catalogue's lightweight-persistent-service shape. Recommend not building unless the catalogue decides to invest in the "creative desktop app via browser" category as a group, at which point GIMP, Blender, and Inkscape should be evaluated together rather than piecemeal.

name: Inngest
source_description: Orchestration platform for reliable background jobs and AI workflows
upstream_license: Server Side Public License (SSPL) 1.0, with a delayed relicense to Apache 2.0 (the "Apache 2.0 Future License" clause in LICENSE.md); SDKs are separately Apache 2.0. SSPL is not OSI-approved.
version_health_notes: v1.41.1 published 2026-08-05 (today, per GitHub API). Release history shows near-weekly cadence through July-August 2026 (v1.34.0 on 06-29 through v1.41.1 today), each shipping incremental REST/queue/tracing features. Repo is not archived, actively developed. Clear active signal, no dormancy or EOL concern.
differentiation: Inngest is a code-first durable-execution/event-orchestration engine: a customer writes functions in their own application using Inngest's TypeScript/Python/Go SDKs, and the self-hosted server (this Docker image) is the event bus + step-function runtime + dashboard that receives events, schedules retries/sleeps/waits, and shows run history for those externally-defined functions. n8n and activepieces (see apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml) are visual no-code/low-code builders where the workflow itself lives inside the app; Inngest has no visual workflow editor at all — its dashboard is purely an observability surface for code the customer deploys elsewhere. That is a real conceptual difference in audience (developers shipping their own app code vs. end users assembling no-code automations), but it also means the self-hosted Inngest instance alone does nothing useful until the customer separately builds and deploys an app with Inngest SDK calls — something this recipe mechanism does not provision.
usefulness_rationale: Legitimate, actively maintained developer infrastructure, but its entire value surface requires the customer to already be developing and hosting a separate application instrumented with Inngest SDKs. Installed on its own, the dashboard shows zero functions and zero events — there is nothing for a customer to do with it standalone, the same "pure backend API consumed by other software" profile that capped imgproxy (apps-gaps/imgproxy.yaml) and Apache Tika. Narrower than most of the catalogue's direct end-user apps.
summary: Mechanically installable: single container (`inngest/inngest`, `inngest start`), defaults to embedded SQLite and in-memory queueing so no mandatory Postgres/Redis dependency, single primary HTTP port (8288, dashboard + event/GraphQL/REST APIs — a secondary websocket port 8289 is only needed for the optional outbound "Connect" gateway mode and can be omitted). The dashboard has no login of its own, so a Traefik basic_auth:true gate (root-password projection) covers that, and the two mandatory boot env vars (INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY, INNGEST_EVENT_KEY) are patternless secrets the server can generate itself — same shape as n8n's N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Upstream is healthy and fast-moving (v1.41.1, released today). The blocker here is fit, not mechanism: Inngest is infrastructure for a customer's own separately-hosted, SDK-instrumented application, not a standalone tool a customer visits and uses — the self-hosted instance alone has nothing to show until code the AF platform doesn't host starts sending it events. Recommend not_recommended on usefulness grounds, mirroring imgproxy, despite being technically installable today.

name: InsForge
source_description: Open-source backend platform with auth, database, and storage for AI agents
upstream_docker_image: No pinned/published image for the main app service. `docker-compose.yml` and `docker-compose.prod.yml` both build the `insforge` service from a local `Dockerfile` (`target: runner`) rather than pulling a tagged release image — no `ghcr.io/insforge/insforge:<version>` (or similar) was found on GHCR/Docker Hub to pin instead. Only the *sidecar* services ship pinned images: `ghcr.io/insforge/postgres:v15.13.4`, `postgrest/postgrest:v12.2.12`, `denoland/deno:alpine-2.0.6`.
version_health_notes: Tagged GitHub releases roughly every 2-16 days through the last ~2 months (v2.2.0 on 2026-06-05 through v2.2.9 on 2026-07-28, one week before this analysis). Well within "active" — no gap, no dormancy signal, project is clearly under heavy development.
differentiation: InsForge is a backend-as-a-service platform (Postgres, auth, S3- compatible storage, an OpenAI-compatible model gateway, Deno edge functions) meant for AI coding agents to build and operate full-stack apps against via MCP or SDK — not a finished application an end user opens and uses. Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a BaaS/agent- backend platform, so there is no direct functional overlap, but it is conceptually adjacent to Open WebUI/Ollama (both touch local LLM workflows) without actually duplicating either.
usefulness_rationale: AF customers installing from the catalogue expect a ready-made product (password manager, notes app, Git host, chat UI) usable immediately after setup. InsForge's dashboard is a management console for a developer platform — there is nothing to "use" until a developer wires an agent or app against its API/MCP server. That is a narrower, technical audience than the rest of the catalogue targets, independent of the mechanism questions below (same shape of gap as `1backend`).
blocking_issues:
No pinned, published Docker image exists for the main app service — both compose files build it from source via a local `Dockerfile`. This fails the "pinned, current stable tag" requirement outright; there is no versioned image on GHCR/Docker Hub to substitute, and building from a git ref inside a customer's compose stack is not a supported recipe pattern.

`ROOT_ADMIN_PASSWORD` (paired with `ROOT_ADMIN_USERNAME`) gates the InsForge dashboard — the app's own admin login. Public docs give no indication it accepts a pre-hashed value the way Vaultwarden's `ADMIN_TOKEN` explicitly documents (plaintext or Argon2 hash both accepted); the variable name and absence of any hash-format guidance suggest InsForge expects a plaintext secret it hashes/stores itself. `generated_from` can only ever project a hash of the customer's root password, so this parameter's compatibility with that mechanism is unconfirmed at best, and likely unsatisfiable — needs upstream confirmation before treating it as expressible. Unlike Adminer/WUD, InsForge has its own persistent admin account rather than a stateless per-visit credential form, so a Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front does not substitute for it: the customer would still hit InsForge's own login wall behind the gate with no way to know the credential.

Full BaaS functionality (agents/SDKs connecting via MCP to auth, PostgREST, and Deno services) exposes several raw, non-HTTP ports beyond the dashboard — 5432 (Postgres), 5430 (PostgREST), 7131 (auth), 7133 (Deno) alongside 7130 (app/dashboard). That is not reverse-proxy-compatible the way current recipes are (one HTTP port per app behind Traefik on `<slug>.<base_domain>`); precedented as a disabled pattern in the catalogue already (`anytype-server`, also `enabled: false` for the same reason).
summary: InsForge is an actively-developed (weekly+ releases), Apache-2.0 backend platform for AI coding agents — but it is a developer tool, not a finished end-user application, which is the same fundamental mismatch that ruled out `1backend`. On top of that audience mismatch, it fails the recipe mechanism on multiple independent grounds: no pinned/published Docker image exists for the main service (compose builds it from source), its own admin login has no confirmed hash-compatible input path for `generated_from`, and full functionality needs several raw non-HTTP ports exposed beyond what Traefik fronts today. Any one of these would be worth flagging; together they make this a clear not_recommended rather than a narrower blocked_on_platform.

Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers inventory or manufacturing workflows; the closest adjacent recipe by "structured records + search" shape is paperless-ngx (document management), which solves a completely different problem. InvenTree's own admin account (the one a customer must actually use to log in and operate the app — add parts, categories, BOMs, etc.) is only created via the plaintext `INVENTREE_ADMIN_USER` / `INVENTREE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` (or `INVENTREE_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE`) env vars at container first-start, or manually afterwards via an interactive `docker compose run inventree-server invoke superuser` shell command. summary: InvenTree is an actively developed (release every 1-3 weeks), MIT-licensed parts inventory and BOM management app with a genuine, differentiated use case not covered by any of the current 24 recipes, and it runs cleanly behind a single reverse-proxied HTTP port (bundled Caddy proxy container). It is blocked today purely on the platform mechanism: its only first-boot admin account channel (`INVENTREE_ADMIN_USER` / `INVENTREE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`) demands a plaintext credential the customer must actually use to operate the app, and there is no self-service signup flow to fall back on — `generated_from` cannot help because it only ever carries a hash, and a Traefik `basic_auth` wall can't substitute for a customer-usable admin login. name: Isso
source_description: Lightweight, self-hosted Disqus alternative for blogs and static websites
version_health_notes: Confirmed via GitHub releases API. Release history is very lumpy: a steady trickle from 0.10 (2016) through 0.13.0 (2022-06-12), then a ~3.75 year gap with no tagged release until 0.14.0 landed 2026-03-26 (~4.5 months ago as of 2026-08-05). "sporadic" fits better than "active" or "slowing" — cadence is bursty rather than regular, but the project is clearly alive.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers blog/static-site commenting. Isso is a genuinely new category — a lightweight, privacy-friendly Disqus replacement a customer would embed into a Jekyll/Hugo/static site they run (possibly hosted elsewhere), similar in spirit to how Ackee/Plausible-style analytics tools would be a new category too.
usefulness_rationale: Clear, narrow, well-understood use case (static-site owners who want comments without Disqus's tracking) with real recurring demand in the static-site/blogging niche, but it's single-purpose and lower-traffic than broader-appeal recipes like n8n or Vaultwarden. It also needs the admin/moderation UI to be genuinely useful day-to-day, and that UI is exactly what blocks installability today (see below).
blocking_issues:
Isso's admin/moderation interface (`[admin] enabled = true` in isso.cfg) is gated by a single `[admin] password` config value. Confirmed in isso/views/comments.py (the /login handler): the submitted form password is checked with plain string equality against the configured value (`if data["password"] and data["password"] == password:`) — no hashing, no verification function. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only works for apps that verify a *hash* server-side (Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN pattern); it produces an opaque hash string the customer would have to type back verbatim as their password, which isn't workable, and there is no channel today to hand Isso a plaintext credential the customer actually knows and picked. This is the same structural blocker documented for Ackee's ACKEE_PASSWORD.

Traefik `basic_auth: true` can't substitute here the way it does for Adminer/n8n: Isso's core purpose is serving a public, unauthenticated commenting widget/API that blog visitors read and post to without logging in. Gating the whole app (or even just the public origin) behind basic_auth would break the actual comment-embedding use case, so basic_auth can only ever protect the /admin path specifically, and Isso's own broken admin login would still sit behind it needing the same plaintext password a customer can't be given today.

Running with `[admin] enabled = false` avoids the credential problem entirely (moderation then happens purely via emailed HMAC-signed activate/delete links, no login at all) but removes the only in-browser moderation UI, which is most of the point of self-hosting a comment system for a customer who wants to manage comments without digging through email.
summary: Isso is a single-container (SQLite-backed, no external DB), single-HTTP -port (8080) Python app that would fill a genuinely new category — blog/static-site comments — not covered by any of the current 24 recipes. It fails installability today on the same credential mechanics as Ackee: its admin/moderation login does a plaintext string comparison against a config value, so neither `generated_from` (produces a hash, not the plaintext the customer typed) nor a blanket Traefik basic_auth gate (would also block the public comment-posting API that must stay open) can wire a customer credential to it safely. Recommend revisiting only if a future mechanism can carry a customer-known plaintext secret through, or defaulting `[admin] enabled = false` and accepting email-only moderation as an explicit product tradeoff. Release cadence is bursty (long 2022-2026 gap before the current 0.14.0) but the project is not dormant or EOL — commits and issue triage are ongoing as of mid-2026.
