name: Jackett
source_description: Torrent tracker proxy translating queries for Sonarr, Radarr, and other automation tools
upstream_docker_image: linuxserver/jackett (pin to a version tag, e.g. v0.24.2330-ls484 — do not follow upstream examples that use :latest)
version_health_notes: Latest tag v0.24.2330 shipped 2026-08-05 (today). Preceding tags (v0.24.2327, v0.24.2323, v0.24.2315, v0.24.2307, v0.24.2304, v0.24.2297, v0.24.2292, v0.24.2288, v0.24.2277) land roughly daily through late July/early August 2026 — this is a CI-driven near-continuous-deployment cadence (indexer definitions break frequently as tracker sites change markup, so the project ships small fixes constantly). Repo is not archived; 18k+ commits and ongoing development activity. Clearly active, not dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches torrent-indexer automation. Jackett fills a narrow, well-defined niche: it normalizes dozens of public/private tracker sites into a single Torznab/API endpoint that other tools query. Like autobrr and Bazarr, it is a piece of a larger pipeline (indexer -> Jackett -> Sonarr/Radarr -> download client) rather than a self-contained destination a customer would use on its own — none of Sonarr, Radarr, or a download client (qBittorrent/Deluge/Transmission) exist as AF recipes today, so a standalone Jackett install has nothing downstream to feed.
usefulness_rationale: Recognized, widely-used tool in the self-hosted media-automation community, but of the three related niches researched so far (autobrr, Bazarr, Jackett), Jackett is the most upstream/dependent link in the chain: its only output is search results for other "*arr" apps to consume, so in isolation — with no Sonarr/Radarr and no download client in the catalogue — it produces literally nothing a customer can act on directly (no library, no downloads, no subtitles). Usefulness is lower than autobrr (which at least feeds a download client directly) and lower than Bazarr (which augments an existing library once pointed at Sonarr/Radarr). Recommend deferring until/unless AF decides to build a full media-automation stack.
summary: Jackett (via linuxserver/jackett) is a single-container app with a web UI on one HTTP port (9117), no database dependency — structurally as simple as uptime-kuma or WUD, reverse-proxy compatible behind Traefik. It ships with no admin password set by default; an operator can optionally set one through the web UI or API, but it is hashed with a salted SHA-512 scheme the platform's `generated_from` projection (argon2/bcrypt only) does not support, and there is no environment variable to preconfigure it at boot. The correct fix is the same pattern used for Adminer/WUD/Bazarr/Deluge: gate the whole app behind a required Traefik `basic_auth`, projected from the customer's root password, rather than relying on Jackett's own optional/unsupported password field. With that gate in place this is mechanically installable today (installable_today: true), but the recommendation is `build_with_caveats` rather than `build_now` because Jackett's real-world value depends entirely on Sonarr/Radarr and a download client existing downstream, and none of those exist in the current catalogue — shipping Jackett alone would hand a customer a search-result API with nothing to send those results to.

name: Jaeger
source_description: Jaeger is an open-source distributed tracing system for monitoring microservices
version_health_notes: v2.20.0 published 2026-07-20 (confirmed via GitHub Releases API), ~2 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Recent tag cadence is roughly monthly through 2026 (2.19.0 2026-06-03, 2.18.0 2026-05-13, 2.17.0 2026-03-30, 2.16.0 2026-03-07, 2.15.0 2026-02-06) — clearly active. Note a major architectural transition: Jaeger v1 (the classic collector/query/agent/ all-in-one component split, image `jaegertracing/all-in-one`) reached end-of-life 2025-12-31 and stopped receiving updates at 1.76.0; starting with 2.14.0 (2026-01-02) the legacy v1 binaries are no longer published separately and everything ships as v2.x, a unified binary built on the OpenTelemetry Collector framework (image `jaegertracing/jaeger`). Any recipe built today must target the v2 image/config format, not the deprecated v1 all-in-one image that older tutorials still reference.
differentiation: No shipped recipe touches distributed tracing today. Unlike Grafana Tempo (apps-gaps/grafana-tempo.yaml, already analyzed and not_recommended), Jaeger ships its own web UI for browsing and searching traces directly — it doesn't need a separately-deployed Grafana instance to be useful, which is a real self-containment advantage over Tempo. It still requires the customer's own services to be instrumented with an OpenTelemetry (or legacy Jaeger/Zipkin) SDK and configured to export spans to this instance, so it has no value in complete isolation, but it's a one-hop dependency (customer's own apps) rather than Tempo's two-hop one (customer's apps + a second self-hosted Grafana).
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful to a customer running multiple microservices who wants request-level tracing without standing up a heavier observability stack, and the built-in UI means it delivers value on its own once something is sending it traces. Held to medium rather than high because it's a developer/ops tool with a narrower audience than the catalogue's typical appliance (password manager, ticketing, file sync), and the all-in-one deployment's default in-memory storage means traces don't survive a restart unless a customer also wires up a real storage backend (Elasticsearch/Cassandra/ClickHouse) — out of scope for a single-instance recipe.
blocking_issues:
The Jaeger UI/query API (port 16686) has no built-in login of its own, so it fits the Traefik basic_auth gate pattern for a human browsing the UI. But that gate only covers one HTTP port — Jaeger's actual data-plane, the trace-ingestion endpoints (OTLP gRPC 4317, OTLP HTTP 4318, Zipkin-compatible 9411, legacy Jaeger Thrift/gRPC 14268/14250), also ship with zero built-in authentication, and a browser-style basic_auth prompt is not something OpenTelemetry SDKs/exporters can satisfy transparently in the general case — the app's core purpose (receiving traces from a customer's own instrumented services) needs those ports reachable, and there is no channel today to project any customer-chosen credential into an SDK the customer configures on their own infrastructure.
Same underlying limitation flagged for Grafana Tempo (apps-gaps/grafana-tempo.yaml): the ingestion surface that makes the app actually useful is not reasonably gate-able with the one supported mechanism (Traefik basic_auth), so leaving it open on the public internet is the only way the recipe would function as advertised.
Default all-in-one storage is in-memory only (traces lost on restart/redeploy) — not a blocker on the installability question but a real limitation worth surfacing to whoever scopes a recipe.
summary: Jaeger (2.20.0, actively maintained, monthly release cadence through 2026) is a healthier, more self-contained candidate than Grafana Tempo — it ships its own web UI and needs no second observability tool to be useful. It still fails the same installability test Tempo did: the UI's lack of built-in auth is coverable with Traefik basic_auth, but the trace-ingestion ports that are the actual point of running Jaeger have no built-in auth and no expressible mechanism to gate them today, so exposing them on the public internet (required for the app to receive traces from a customer's own services) is not something the current recipe mechanism can do safely. Also note the v1→v2 architecture cutover (v1 EOL 2025-12-31): any future recipe attempt must target the v2 image and config format, not the deprecated v1 all-in-one image most existing tutorials still show. Recommend not_recommended for now, on the same basis as Tempo — revisit only if a per-protocol credential/mTLS channel for the ingestion ports becomes expressible.

name: Jelly-Clipper
source_description: Open-source Jellyfin companion for creating and sharing clips from your library
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/arnolicious/jelly-clipper (pin to a version tag, e.g. v1.3.6 — do not follow upstream's :latest example)
version_health_notes: Latest release v1.3.6 shipped 2026-08-03, two days before today (2026-08-05). Preceding tags (v1.3.5, v1.3.4, v1.3.3, v1.3.2, ...) land within days of each other, driven by Renovate dependency-bump PRs plus the sole maintainer's own fixes — a healthy, near-daily-to-weekly cadence for what the author describes as "my first open source project." Repo not archived, 261 commits on main, 90 stars, 6 forks, 11 open issues. Clearly active, single-maintainer project (bus-factor risk worth noting but not an EOL signal).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does clip creation/sharing from a media library — Immich covers photo/video backup and organization, but not clipping from an existing Jellyfin library. The catch is that Jelly-Clipper is a pure companion app: it has no media library, no transcoding pipeline, and no user accounts of its own — it is useless without an already-running Jellyfin server for it to attach to. We do not offer Jellyfin (or any media-server recipe) in the current catalogue, so this app only pays off for a customer who already self-hosts Jellyfin elsewhere (their own box, another provider, or a manually-run container outside AF) and wants an add-on for it.
usefulness_rationale: Well-scoped, actively developed niche tool, but its entire value proposition depends on a Jellyfin instance that AF does not host and is not proposing to host. Standalone, it is a login screen pointing at nothing. Usefulness would jump to medium/high if/when a Jellyfin recipe is added to the catalogue; on its own today it is a thin, dependent add-on in the same vein as Jackett/Bazarr (upstream/downstream dependents with no anchor app present).
blocking_issues:
No blocker in the /compose sense: the app ships with no admin account of its own and no environment variable for a Jellyfin server URL/API key — deploy-time config is just JELLY_CLIPPER_ORIGIN (the public app URL) and optional cron/log-level settings, all non-secret. End users instead enter their own Jellyfin server address and Jellyfin username/password directly in the Jelly-Clipper login screen at runtime (delegated auth against Jellyfin's API), which is an in-app user action, not a customer-supplied /compose parameter, so it needs no generated_from/basic_auth projection.
Real-world blocker is architectural, not platform-mechanism: the app is non-functional without a Jellyfin server to log into, and we have no Jellyfin recipe. This is a 'nothing to point it at' problem the schema's secret-projection rules don't capture.
summary: Mechanically this is one of the simplest recipes imaginable — a single container, one HTTP port (3000), SQLite on a volume, no admin credential of its own to project, and no external API key baked into deploy-time config (Jellyfin login happens interactively in the app's own UI, not through /compose). installable_today is true on pure platform-mechanism grounds. But recommendation is not_recommended: the app is a companion to a Jellyfin server we don't offer anywhere in the 24-recipe catalogue, so shipping it alone gives customers a login screen with nothing to authenticate against. Revisit if/when a Jellyfin recipe is ever added — this would then be a natural, low-effort companion recipe.

name: Jellyfin
source_description: Free and open-source media server for organizing and streaming your media library
version_health_notes: 10.11.11 shipped 2026-06-06, about 2 months before today (2026-08-05). Stable point releases have landed roughly every 2-6 weeks through 2025-2026 (10.11.7 2026-03-31, 10.11.8 2026-04-05, 10.11.9 2026-05-21, 10.11.10 2026-05-24, 10.11.11 2026-06-06). In parallel, a 12.0 major rewrite is in active release-candidate cycling (rc1 2026-06-21 through rc4 2026-08-02, 4 RCs in 6 weeks). Repo is not archived; this is a clearly active, well-maintained project.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24 covers general-purpose personal video/TV library streaming (Plex/Emby-style). Immich is the closest neighbor by "self-hosted personal media" flavor but is strictly photo/video backup and AI-organized gallery, not a transcoding library server for movies and TV shows with wide smart-TV/mobile client support. This is a distinct, high-demand self-hosting category.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted media/TV streaming is one of the most commonly requested self-hosting use cases, has broad recognizable-brand appeal (Plex-alternative, fully open-source, no phone-home account requirement), and would meaningfully diversify the catalogue. Upstream is active with no abandonment signal.
blocking_issues:
Jellyfin has no environment variable, CLI flag, or config-seeding mechanism to set the initial admin username/password non-interactively. First boot always lands on an interactive web setup wizard where whoever visits the domain first chooses the admin credentials themselves — confirmed by upstream feature request github.com/jellyfin/jellyfin/issues/1940 ("Docker: add environment variables to skip setup wizard"), open since 2019, closed stale in 2020 with no fix shipped, and still being asked about as recently as 2026-02-19 with no resolution. A maintainer response on that issue states this "is definitely not doable now" short of hand-crafting a template system.xml, which is not an officially supported mechanism.

Even if the wizard could be pre-seeded, Jellyfin hashes its own passwords with PBKDF2-SHA512 (via its ICryptoProvider/ DefaultAuthenticationProvider), which is not in the currently supported generated_from algorithm list (argon2, bcrypt). Per SCHEMA.md this is not a hard structural blocker on its own — the algo list is extensible — but it means a genuine platform change (add pbkdf2 support to generated_from) would still be required even after an env-var/config-seed hook exists.

A Traefik basic_auth gate does not fully solve this: it would stop an anonymous internet visitor from reaching the wizard, but the customer would still hit the interactive Jellyfin setup wizard themselves on first login and have to choose their own admin password by hand in the app UI — there is no way to project a root-password-derived hash directly into Jellyfin's own admin account today. basic_auth could still be used defensively to close the open-wizard race, but it doesn't remove the manual step.
summary: Jellyfin is a single-container media server (official jellyfin/jellyfin image, HTTP port 8096, optional UDP 7359 for DLNA autodiscovery that would simply go unused behind a single-domain reverse proxy) structurally similar to Uptime Kuma/Vaultwarden-style single-container recipes, and it is an actively maintained, high-value catalogue gap with no current overlap. It is blocked today purely on the installability mechanism: Jellyfin's first-boot admin setup is an interactive web wizard with no env-var or config-seed hook (a 2019 upstream feature request for exactly this went nowhere), and even a future seeding mechanism would need generated_from extended to PBKDF2-SHA512 to match Jellyfin's own hashing. Traefik basic_auth can reduce the open-wizard race but doesn't eliminate the manual admin-password step. Recommend revisiting once either upstream ships non-interactive first-run provisioning or generated_from gains a pbkdf2 option and a config-seeding approach is validated.

name: Jellyseerr
source_description: Media request management tool for Jellyfin, Emby, and Plex with approval workflow
upstream_docker_image: seerr/seerr (pin to a version tag, e.g. v3.4.1 — do not follow upstream docs' :latest example)
version_health_notes: "Jellyseerr" as a standalone project name is superseded: as of v3.0.0 (2026-02-14), the Jellyseerr and Overseerr teams officially merged into one project and codebase called "Seerr". The old github.com/Fallenbagel/jellyseerr repo now redirects to github.com/seerr-team/seerr, and the old `fallenbagel/jellyseerr` Docker Hub image is stale (tags last pushed ~10-11 months ago, no recent activity) — the actively maintained image is `seerr/seerr` (mirrored at `ghcr.io/seerr-team/seerr`). This is not a case of two distinct unrelated projects sharing a name; it is the same lineage continuing under a new name, so a recipe built today should target Seerr/the `seerr/seerr` image, not the dormant `fallenbagel/jellyseerr` one, even though the Hostinger catalogue slug says "jellyseerr". Release history under the new name is active: v3.0.0/v3.0.1 (2026-02-14), v3.1.0 (2026-02-27), v3.1.1 (2026-04-13), v3.2.0 (2026-04-15), v3.3.0 (2026-06-02), v3.4.0 (2026-07-28), v3.4.1 (2026-07-30) — roughly monthly, with the latest release only 6 days old as of 2026-08-05. Repo is not archived; clearly active development.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches media-request management. Jellyseerr/Seerr sits on top of an existing Jellyfin, Plex, or Emby media server and lets non-admin household/family users browse a catalogue (via TMDB) and submit requests for movies/shows, which an admin approves and routes to Sonarr/Radarr. Closest catalogue neighbor conceptually is Immich (self-hosted media, own admin signup), but Immich is a photo library, not a request-approval front end for a video media server — no functional overlap. Critically, none of Jellyfin, Plex, Emby, Sonarr, or Radarr exist as AF recipes today, so this app is only useful to a customer who already runs one of those media servers somewhere else (self-hosted elsewhere, or a separate AF install) — like Jackett/autobrr/Bazarr, it is a dependent piece of a larger media-stack pipeline rather than a self-contained destination.
usefulness_rationale: Recognized, popular tool in the self-hosted media community and the natural next piece after a media server, but its entire value proposition requires an existing Jellyfin/Plex/Emby instance the customer already has elsewhere — the catalogue has no such recipe to pair it with, so on its own it is a request UI with nothing to serve requests, and its first-run setup is where its severest installability problem also shows up (see below).
blocking_issues:
Jellyseerr/Seerr has no standalone local-signup admin account. The first-run setup wizard requires selecting Jellyfin, Plex, or Emby and authenticating against that server (server URL plus that server's own admin username/password, or Plex OAuth) — the app's initial "admin" user is imported from the connected media server, not created inside Jellyseerr itself. There is no environment variable that pre-seeds an admin login, so `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` has no parameter to attach to.

This is third-party account linking, not a login the platform can hash or generate on the customer's behalf — the customer must already hold valid credentials for an external (or separately-hosted) Jellyfin/Plex/Emby server, and there is no channel today for the customer to hand that arbitrary third-party credential to `/compose`.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate could keep the public URL from sitting open before setup completes, but it does not solve the underlying problem: setup itself cannot complete without a real, working Jellyfin/Plex/Emby account, which the platform has no way to supply or substitute.
summary: Jellyseerr has effectively been superseded by "Seerr" (a 2026-02 merger of the Jellyseerr and Overseerr projects/teams under one codebase and one Docker image, `seerr/seerr`); the project itself is active and well-maintained under that name. It is a single-container, reverse-proxy- friendly web app with no exotic port requirements, but it cannot be installed via the current recipe mechanism: its entire first-run flow requires linking a real external Jellyfin, Plex, or Emby account, which is third-party account linking with no input channel today (not a root-password hash, not something Traefik basic_auth can substitute for). Even setting installability aside, the catalogue has no Jellyfin/Plex/Emby recipe for it to pair with, so its practical value here is capped until both a generic external-credential input channel and a paired media-server recipe exist. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`, revisit if/when the platform gains a customer-supplied external-credential channel.

name: Jellystat
source_description: Tautulli-style statistics and insights dashboard for Jellyfin media server
version_health_notes: Not archived — last commit to main was 2026-08-05 (today), and 1.1.11 shipped 2026-06-23, ~6 weeks before today's date. But the maintainer posted an explicit project-update in the README: accumulated tech debt means they are rebuilding Jellystat from scratch on a new backend/ frontend/possibly new DB, and "for now... the project is not going to be updated. I will probably push a few fixes for any major bugs that are easily reproduced." That statement, not the still-recent release date, is the reason to call this "maintenance-only" rather than "active" — feature development is explicitly paused pending a rewrite of unknown timeline. Release history itself (1.1.6 in 2025-05, then 1.1.7 through 1.1.11 roughly every 1-2 months through 2026-06) looks like a healthy small project, hence "slowing" rather than "sporadic" or "dormant".
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches media-server analytics. Jellystat is a Tautulli-alike for Jellyfin: session monitoring, watch history, per-user/per-library stats, backup/restore of that stats data. It is a companion/add-on app, not a standalone media server — it requires an existing, already-running Jellyfin (or Emby) instance to point at via an API key entered through its own setup UI after deploy. We do not currently have a Jellyfin recipe in the catalogue, so its addressable customer base is limited to those already self-hosting Jellyfin/Emby elsewhere (on IONOS or off it), not created fresh by this recipe's existence.
usefulness_rationale: Real niche demand (Jellyfin/Emby self-hosters commonly run Tautulli or Jellystat alongside their media server), and it's a lightweight single-container-plus-Postgres stack that's cheap to host. But value is capped by (a) no Jellyfin recipe of our own to pair it with, so it's a pure bring-your-own-server companion, and (b) the maintainer's own paused-development notice, which makes this a reasonable "works fine, not going anywhere fast" pick rather than a flagship addition.
summary: Jellystat is mechanically installable today: POSTGRES_PASSWORD and JWT_SECRET are opaque internal values the customer never needs to see or type, so both can be server-generated with no customer input channel required. Jellystat's own admin account is not set via an env var at all — it is claimed through a first-visit setup wizard in the web UI (the Getting Started docs). That means there is no login field to project a `generated_from` root-password hash into, and it leaves a race window where whoever loads the site first claims the admin account (the same shape as n8n's owner setup) — so a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the app is the appropriate fix, matching the mechanism already used for n8n/Immich-style first-run-setup apps. The Jellyfin/Emby API key the app needs to actually fetch stats is entered by the customer after deploy, through the authenticated UI itself, not at compose time, so it is out of scope for `/compose` and not a blocker. Net: build_with_caveats — installable now, but low-to-medium value given no Jellyfin recipe to pair it with and the upstream's own paused-development notice.

name: Jellyswarrm
source_description: Reverse proxy that merges multiple Jellyfin servers into one unified library
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/llukas22/jellyswarrm (pin to a release tag, e.g. v0.3.0 — upstream's own compose example uses :latest)
version_health_notes: v0.3.0 shipped 2026-07-27, about 9 days before today (2026-08-05). Releases have landed roughly every 1-4 months since the project's first tag (v0.1.1 2025-08-24, v0.1.4 2025-10-03, v0.1.5 2025-10-29, v0.2.0 2025-12-07, v0.2.1 2026-03-15, v0.3.0 2026-07-27), with the underlying repo pushed to as recently as 2026-08-04 (yesterday). Repo is not archived, has 825 stars and 28 open issues being actively triaged. Project explicitly self-describes as "still in early development" with some features (QuickConnect, WebSocket/SyncPlay, audio streaming, bitrate adaptation, media management) marked in-progress or unreliable in its own README — active but pre-1.0 and unstable in places.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches media-server aggregation. However Jellyswarrm is a companion/multiplier app, not a standalone media server: it has no value unless the customer already runs (or has access to) two or more separate Jellyfin instances elsewhere to merge — and we don't currently offer Jellyfin itself as a recipe either (see apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml, also blocked). Its addressable audience among AF customers is therefore narrower and more specialized than a general-purpose media server would be.
usefulness_rationale: Real but niche demand (self-hosters running Jellyfin at multiple sites or with friends/family "server federation") — visible in a dedicated awesome-jellyfin listing and community threads. Low priority for our catalogue specifically because it presupposes existing external Jellyfin infrastructure the customer manages themselves, and because the project is explicitly early/unstable on several features (SyncPlay, audio streaming, bitrate adaptation still listed as broken/incomplete by upstream itself).
blocking_issues:
Jellyswarrm's admin login (`JELLYSWARRM_USERNAME`/`JELLYSWARRM_PASSWORD` env vars) is deploy-time configurable, unlike Jellyfin's interactive- wizard-only setup — a structural improvement over that comparable gap. But the credential must be the app's real, usable plaintext login: its Rust backend (`crates/jellyswarrm-proxy/src/ui/auth/mod.rs`) authenticates the admin account with a direct `password == config.password` string comparison against the raw `Password` value loaded straight from the `JELLYSWARRM_PASSWORD` env var (`config.rs`) — there is no hash-verification step anywhere in that path (contrast with Vaultwarden's `ADMIN_TOKEN`, which is verified via bcrypt/argon2 against a stored hash and so accepts a `generated_from`-projected hash as the configured value while the customer still types their real root password). Projecting `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` into `JELLYSWARRM_PASSWORD` would store a hash string as the literal comparison value, meaning the customer would have to type that hash (not their root password) to log in — unusable, and not what `generated_from` is for.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (customer's root password hash) and setting `JELLYSWARRM_PASSWORD` to a fixed/internal default does not resolve this the way it does for Adminer-style no-login apps: the customer still needs to know and use the Jellyswarrm admin credential themselves afterward to add Jellyfin servers and manage user mappings through the `/ui` admin panel — it is the app's actual working login, not a redundant inner gate. A fixed default here would leave every deployment sharing the same admin credential with no customer-facing way to learn or change it via our pipeline.
summary: Jellyswarrm is a single-container (ghcr.io/llukas22/jellyswarrm), single-port (3000) reverse-proxy aggregator for Jellyfin libraries — structurally simple and Traefik-compatible, and an actively maintained, non-archived project with a release 9 days ago. It fills a real but narrow niche (merging multiple externally-run Jellyfin servers) that doesn't overlap anything in our 24 recipes, though its value is capped by requiring customers to already operate separate Jellyfin infrastructure, and by our catalogue not yet offering Jellyfin itself. It is blocked today because its admin login is a direct plaintext-equality check with no hash verification, so `generated_from` cannot project a usable credential into it, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate doesn't substitute since the customer still needs a real, individually-known admin credential to operate the app. Recommend revisiting only if upstream adds hash-based admin-password verification, or if the platform gains a plaintext-secret input channel (which per SCHEMA.md is a deliberate architectural exclusion, not just an unbuilt feature).

name: Jenkins
source_description: Jenkins is an open-source automation server for CI/CD pipelines
upstream_docker_image: jenkins/jenkins (official image maintained by the Jenkins project, built from https://github.com/jenkinsci/docker; the older unnamespaced `jenkins` image on Docker Hub is deprecated and has not been updated in 2+ years — do not use it)
version_health_notes: 2.568.2 LTS shipped today, 2026-08-05, with "important security fixes"; the prior two LTS releases were 2.568.1 (2026-07-08) and 2.555.3 (2026-06-10) — a steady ~monthly LTS cadence, on top of the separate weekly release train currently at 2.576. This is one of the most actively maintained projects considered in this catalogue: continuous CVE patching, an enormous plugin ecosystem still receiving updates, and no sign of slowdown, archival, or EOL.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes are a build/test/deploy pipeline server. Gitea (developer-tools) is a git host with a lightweight built-in Actions feature, and n8n (automation) is general-purpose SaaS/API workflow automation with a drag-and-drop canvas — neither is a general-purpose CI/CD engine with Jenkins's plugin-driven job model. Unlike GoCD (analyzed separately, not yet built), Jenkins can execute builds on its own controller node out of the box — no paired agent container is required for a useful first-run experience, though a customer would add agents for real workloads. Jenkins is also the most widely recognized CI/CD brand by a large margin, which drives name-recognition demand distinct from a feature comparison alone.
usefulness_rationale: Extremely well-known tool with a huge existing user base and plugin ecosystem; a natural next step for a customer already self-hosting Gitea who wants "real" CI/CD. Single-container, reverse-proxy-friendly web UI matches the rest of the catalogue's shape well.
summary: Jenkins is an actively and predictably maintained project (near-monthly LTS releases, no EOL signal) that would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue — no existing recipe covers general-purpose CI/CD. The default official-image boot flow (interactive setup wizard reading a random initialAdminPassword file inside the container) is not itself usable via our provisioning flow, but Jenkins core exposes `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm#createAccountWithHashedPassword(user, hash)`, which accepts a pre-computed bcrypt hash directly — the same shape as Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN. Combined with `-Djenkins.install.runSetupWizard=false` (JAVA_OPTS) to skip the wizard and a mounted `init.groovy.d` script that calls that API at boot, a `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` value can seed the initial admin account non-interactively, giving the customer a working login on first boot without ever seeing the wizard. This is mechanically installable today, but it is a materially more custom install.sh (a hand-written Groovy init hook + JVM flag) than the env-var-only pattern most current recipes use, so recommend build_with_caveats rather than a plain build_now.

name: jfa-go

Tagged-release history is sparse and irregular: v0.5.1 (2023-12-26), v0.5.0 (2023-09-08), v0.4.0 (2022-01-30) — gaps of 1-2 years between tagged releases, then a ~2-year gap before v0.6.0. We do not offer a Jellyfin (or Emby) recipe today (see apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml, itself blocked), so jfa-go only pays off for a customer who already self-hosts Jellyfin/Emby elsewhere — the same dependent-add-on shape as apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml, apps-gaps/jellystat.yaml, and apps-gaps/jelly-clipper.yaml.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful, well-known tool in the Jellyfin self-hosting community for anyone running a "family/friends" Jellyfin server, but its entire value proposition depends on an existing Jellyfin/Emby instance the catalogue does not host, and its installability is structurally blocked (see below) in a way that isn't a quick fix. Usefulness would rise if a Jellyfin recipe existed to pair it with, but even then the setup-time external-account requirement remains.
blocking_issues:
jfa-go's setup wizard has a mandatory server-connection step that calls the app's own /setup/test/jf endpoint (confirmed by reading setup.go on main), which authenticates the supplied username/password against the real Jellyfin (or Emby) server at the given URL and requires the resulting account to have IsAdministrator == true before setup can proceed. This is not an optional "add a feature later" step — jfa-go's core purpose (sending invites, applying library profiles to new users) is meaningless without a live, connected Jellyfin server, so setup cannot complete, and the app cannot do anything useful, without a real external admin credential the customer must already hold. This is the same shape as apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml's blocker, not apps-gaps/jellystat.yaml's (where the external API key is an optional feature added after a fully independent local admin login already works) — Traefik basic_auth can keep the wizard from sitting open to the internet, but it does not create an input channel for the mandatory external Jellyfin admin account itself.

Separately, jfa-go's own admin login (the wizard's "custom username/password OR connect your Jellyfin admin account" choice) has no environment variable or config-seed mechanism either — it is only ever set interactively in the wizard, so even that half of setup has no generated_from attachment point today.

Minor secondary issue, not the primary blocker: Docker Hub only publishes "latest" and "unstable" tags for hrfee/jfa-go, no semver-pinned tags, which is a normal pinning inconvenience rather than a platform blocker.
summary: jfa-go is a single-container, reverse-proxy-friendly Jellyfin/Emby companion app (HTTP on 8056, optional TLS on 8057) structurally similar to the other Jellyfin-ecosystem add-ons already analyzed (jellyseerr, jellystat, jelly-clipper), and shares their core problem: the current catalogue has no Jellyfin/Emby recipe of its own, so this only serves customers already self-hosting one elsewhere. Beyond that value-cap, jfa-go is structurally blocked on the installability mechanism today: its setup wizard requires successfully authenticating as a real Jellyfin/Emby administrator before setup can finish at all (confirmed in the app's own setup.go source), which is third-party account linking with no /compose input channel — the same blocked_on_platform shape as Jellyseerr, not the lighter build_with_caveats shape Jellystat got. Upstream itself is a single-maintainer, "active-ish" hobby project with sparse, irregular tagged releases (v0.6.0 landed 2025-11-27 after a ~2-year gap since v0.5.1) and no semver Docker tags, which further tempers enthusiasm even setting the installability blocker aside. Recommend revisiting only if a Jellyfin/Emby recipe and a customer-supplied external-credential channel both materialize.

name: Jitsi Meet
source_description: Self-hosted video conferencing platform with screen sharing and recording
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/jitsi/web (+ ghcr.io/jitsi/prosody, ghcr.io/jitsi/jicofo, ghcr.io/jitsi/jvb — multi-image stack, no single "jitsi-meet" image)
version_health_notes: Released the day before this analysis (2026-08-05); prior tags stable-11146 (2026-08-03), stable-11031 (2026-06-08), stable-10978 (2026-05-20), stable-10888 (2026-03-30) show a steady ~3-6 week release cadence with no gaps. Repo not archived, actively pushed to (last push same day as latest release). Clearly active, not EOL or dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers video/audio conferencing — closest is Guacamole (remote desktop) which is a completely different use case. Jitsi Meet would be the first real-time communication app in the catalogue, giving customers a self-hosted Zoom/Meet alternative with screen sharing.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted video conferencing is a broadly appealing, well-known category (privacy-conscious teams, schools, communities wanting to avoid Zoom/Meet). Jitsi Meet is the dominant open-source option in this space, well maintained, with no equivalent in our catalogue.
blocking_issues:
Not reverse-proxy compatible: the video bridge (JVB) requires a raw UDP port (10000/udp by default) exposed directly to the internet for WebRTC media (RTP), on top of the normal 80/443 HTTP(S) for the web UI/signaling. This is mechanically expressible (wg-easy already declares a raw public UDP port the same way), but it means Jitsi cannot sit purely behind Traefik like our typical single-HTTP-port recipes — it needs an additional publicly routable UDP port on the host, which the AF network layer would need to support per-customer.

Default configuration ships with no authentication at all — anyone with a room link can create or join a meeting (ENABLE_AUTH=0 by default). This is intentional product design (like a Zoom-style open link), not a missing admin login, so it does not block installability the way an unauthenticated admin panel would — but gating the whole domain behind Traefik basic_auth (our usual fallback for no-login apps) is not really usable here, since it would also block the external guests the app is meant to let in without a shared secret. Flagging this as a product trade-off a human should decide on, not a hard technical blocker.

Hostinger's description explicitly mentions "recording", which the base docker-jitsi-meet compose does not provide — that requires the separate Jibri component (its own service, its own XMPP recorder/transcriber passwords, and materially higher RAM, 8GB+ per upstream docs). A recipe built from the base compose would not match the advertised feature set unless Jibri is included, which raises the minimum spec well above our typical recipe footprint.

Minimum viable spec (web + prosody + jicofo + jvb, no Jibri) is ~2 CPU cores / 4GB RAM per upstream guidance, noticeably heavier than most of our current single-container recipes.
summary: Jitsi Meet is an active, well-maintained project (release the day before this analysis, ~monthly cadence) with zero overlap in our current catalogue and clear customer appeal as the first video-conferencing recipe. The credentials it needs at first boot (Jicofo/JVB internal auth passwords) are all server-generatable with no customer input required, so the usual secrets-projection blocker does not apply here. The real blocker is architectural: JVB needs a raw public UDP port for WebRTC media, which falls outside the single-HTTP-port-behind-Traefik model most recipes use, and the app's intentionally-open-by-default meeting access doesn't fit cleanly into our only no-login fallback (Traefik basic_auth) without breaking the guest-access use case. Recommend revisiting once the platform has a story for exposing a raw per-customer UDP port (comparable to what wg-easy already needs), and deciding deliberately whether an open-by-default meeting room is acceptable for a shipped recipe or whether auth should be mandatory.

name: Jitsu
source_description: Open-source customer data platform and event streaming pipeline for engineers
upstream_docker_image: jitsucom/console (plus jitsucom/rotor, jitsucom/bulker, jitsucom/ingest, jitsucom/syncctl — no single "jitsu" image for the current architecture)
version_health_notes: Releases are dated same-day as this analysis (2026-08-05) with daily/near-daily beta tags going back weeks — the project is clearly actively developed. However every visible release tag is a "-beta.N" pre-release; no stable non-beta channel was found, so "latest stable" doesn't exist as a concept here today. Name ambiguity: the GitHub repo's `master` branch (and the `jitsucom/jitsu` Docker Hub image, last pushed ~2 years ago) is the old Jitsu v1 "Segment alternative" architecture (configurator + server + Redis + ClickHouse). The active, default-branch project (`newjitsu`) is a ground-up rewrite ("Jitsu Next") with a different microservice architecture and different Docker images. This analysis covers the active `newjitsu` rewrite, since that's what upstream now ships and documents; the old v1 branch/image was considered and ruled out as effectively dormant.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers event streaming / customer-data-platform tooling (a self-hosted Segment alternative). It would add a genuinely new category to the catalogue rather than duplicating anything among the current 24 recipes.
usefulness_rationale: The audience is narrow (engineering/data teams wanting to self-host an event pipeline) and the operational footprint is heavy for a general VPS customer — upstream itself steers self-hosters toward Kubernetes for full functionality, which cuts against the profile of most AF customers who want a lightweight single-VPS app.
blocking_issues:
SEED_USER_PASSWORD is consumed by the console service as the literal credentials-login password (ENABLE_CREDENTIALS_LOGIN=true), not as a hash the app verifies against — a genuine plaintext-password requirement. generated_from only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, so it cannot satisfy this; it is a structural blocker, not just an unsupported algorithm.
Upstream's own self-hosting docs describe the Docker Compose deployment as legacy/deprecated for full functionality: it 'cannot run functions, profile builders or connector syncs' — core CDP features. The documented, supported path for a real deployment is a Kubernetes cluster + Helm chart, which is a different deployment model than our docker-compose recipe mechanism, not just a missing secret.
Heavy backing-infra footprint even for the degraded Compose setup: five first-party services (console, ingest, rotor, bulker, syncctl) plus Postgres, MongoDB, ClickHouse, and Kafka/Redpanda — well beyond the resource floor of a typical AF recipe and hard to justify for the single-VPS use case.
Several env vars are named for an 'EE' (Enterprise Edition) auth path (EE_API_AUTH_TOKENS, EE_CONNECTION), suggesting some functionality may be licensing-gated even in a self-hosted deployment; not fully verified but worth flagging.
summary: Jitsu's active codebase (the `newjitsu` rewrite) is a well-maintained but heavyweight, engineering-oriented CDP that needs its own plaintext admin password at first boot — a channel our recipe mechanism doesn't have today — and whose own docs say Docker Compose can't run its core features, pointing self-hosters at Kubernetes instead. Combined with a five-service-plus-four- datastore footprint and a narrow target audience, this is a poor fit for the AF catalogue independent of the secrets-mechanism gap; recommend not building a recipe for it.

name: JobOps
source_description: Self-hosted job hunting pipeline that searches boards and tailors CVs
version_health_notes: v0.11.0 shipped 2026-07-22, about 2 weeks before today (2026-08-05). 10 tagged releases visible between 2026-05-01 (v0.5.0) and 2026-07-22 (v0.11.0) — roughly weekly, with two patch releases (v0.6.1, v0.6.2) in the same week. 775+ commits on main, ~800 users reported by the project, and it was recently #3 on GitHub's TypeScript trending page. No archival or slowdown signal; this is a young, fast-moving project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches job-search/career tooling. JobOps aggregates listings across 10+ job boards (LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, Adzuna, Hiring Cafe, etc.), uses an LLM to score fit against a profile, generates tailored CV PDFs per role, and tracks application status via Gmail monitoring. It's a genuinely distinct niche, closer in spirit to Paperless-AI (LLM-assisted personal productivity tool) than to any media/infra/dev-tool recipe we ship today.
usefulness_rationale: Real, differentiated niche with no catalogue overlap, but the audience is narrower (active job seekers only, not an always-on service like most current recipes) and the app's core value proposition — AI scoring and CV tailoring — is fully dependent on a customer-supplied external LLM API key, which our platform has no way to accept today.
blocking_issues:
The app's headline features — AI fit-scoring and AI-tailored CV generation — require a customer-supplied API key for an external LLM provider (OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic/Claude, Google Gemini, or GLM/Zhipu), configured via env vars such as MODEL / LLM_PROVIDER and provider-specific key vars. There is no root-password-hash or Traefik-gate mechanism that can express an arbitrary third-party API key; this is exactly the "external API key the app can't function without" case SCHEMA.md calls a hard no. Without it the app still boots, but the feature Hostinger's own description leads with ("tailors CVs") does not work.

Several optional integrations have the same no-input-channel problem but are non-blocking on their own since the app degrades gracefully without them: RXRESUME_API_KEY (PDF export via Reactive Resume — CVs can otherwise be exported locally), GMAIL_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID/SECRET (Gmail-based application-status tracking), ADZUNA_APP_ID/KEY and APIFY_TOKEN (extra job-board coverage), and UKVISAJOBS_EMAIL/PASSWORD (UK visa-sponsorship board login). None of these unblock the core LLM dependency above.

Upstream ships with no mandatory login (BASIC_AUTH_USER/PASSWORD are optional env vars, unset by default), so a Traefik basic_auth gate is needed regardless to avoid the UI and its stored job/application data sitting open on the internet. That gate is expressible today via generated_from root-password projection into Traefik basic_auth, but it only solves the open-UI problem, not the LLM-key problem above.

Licensing: upstream is AGPL-3.0 layered with the Commons Clause, which explicitly withholds the right to "Sell" the software — defined broadly to cover providing it to third parties for compensation (including hosting fees) where the value substantially derives from the software itself. Shipping this inside a paid IONOS Application Factory recipe plausibly falls inside that restriction and would need legal sign-off independent of the technical blockers above.

Name ambiguity: "JobOps"/"jobops" is shared by several unrelated or derivative projects — isjiajia01/job-ops (a customized EU-focused fork) and becomdoup-spec/job-ops-1 / 0xSojalSec/AI-job-ops (mirrors of the same upstream), plus an unrelated project, HireBridge/jobops (an MCP server for job-search workflows driven from a chat client, not a standalone web app). DaKheera47/job-ops was selected as the canonical upstream because it matches Hostinger's description ("searches boards and tailors CVs") and is the original, most-starred, actively released repo.
summary: JobOps is a single-container app (ghcr.io/dakheera47/job-ops, versioned tags available, HTTP port 3001 mapped to 3005, has a /health endpoint, no extra raw ports) that would sit fine behind Traefik like our Uptime Kuma/Open WebUI-style recipes, is under genuinely active weekly release cadence, and fills a career-tooling niche nothing else in the catalogue covers. It's blocked today because its core AI scoring/CV tailoring functionality requires a customer-supplied external LLM API key with no expressible input channel under the current generated_from / Traefik-basic_auth mechanism — the same structural gap flagged for other AI-key-dependent apps. It also carries an AGPL + Commons Clause license that restricts commercial resale/hosting, which is a separate, non-technical concern worth legal review before this is revisited. Recommend re-evaluating once a real API-key input channel exists on the platform, and flagging the license question to legal in parallel.

name: Joplin Server
source_description: Self-hosted synchronization server for Joplin note-taking application
upstream_license: Joplin Server Personal Use License (non-commercial; the wider Joplin monorepo is AGPL-3.0-or-later, but packages/server/LICENSE.md carries its own proprietary personal-use terms)
version_health_notes: Recent server releases: server-v3.4.4 (2025-09-25), server-v3.5.1 (2025-12-03), server-v3.5.2 (2025-12-19), server-v3.6.1 (2026-04-20), server-v3.7.1 (2026-05-18). Roughly one release every 1-4 months, with one wider gap (Dec 2025 -> Apr 2026, ~4 months). As of today (2026-08-05) it has been just under 3 months since the last release — within the project's own historical cadence, not a sign of stalling. Repo is actively developed (desktop client had a v3.7 pre-release as recently as June 2026); not archived, not in maintenance-only mode.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover note-taking/knowledge-base sync — this would be the first. It's a backend-only sync target for the Joplin desktop/mobile apps plus a small admin web UI, not a general-purpose note editor itself.
usefulness_rationale: Joplin is a popular open-source note-taking app and self-hosting the sync server (instead of paying for Joplin Cloud) is a common self-hosting use case, so there is real demand. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because of the licensing problem below, which caps the realistic ceiling regardless of technical demand.
blocking_issues:
LICENSING BLOCKER (likely fatal on its own): packages/server carries a separate "Joplin Server Personal Use License", not AGPL-3.0 like the rest of the repo. It explicitly prohibits installing the software on infrastructure and "charg[ing] others for the use of the Software," installing it "behind a proxy and charg[ing] others," or granting third-party access "for a fee or for any commercial purposes" when the licensee is "engaged in commercial activities." IONOS offering this as a paid/commercial Application Factory recipe is exactly the scenario the license forbids; a commercial license would need to be separately negotiated with the vendor before this could ship at all, independent of any technical mechanism question.

No first-boot input channel for the admin credential even ignoring the license: Joplin Server ships with a hardcoded default admin account (admin@localhost / admin) and provides no environment variable to seed a different initial email/password/hash at container start — the only way to change it is to log in with the default credentials afterwards and use the admin UI's "change password" screen. This doesn't fit `generated_from` (no env var exists to receive a hash) or plain env-var injection (no plaintext channel either).

Traefik basic_auth is not a valid substitute gate here, unlike Adminer-style apps: Joplin Server's primary interface is a sync API consumed directly by the Joplin desktop/mobile client apps, which have no UI to supply a separate HTTP Basic Auth credential for the sync target. Wrapping the whole app in `basic_auth: true` would block real sync traffic, not just gate human browser access to an otherwise-open app — so it would break the app's core function rather than secure it.
summary: Joplin Server is a plausible-looking gap (no note-sync app in the catalogue today, active upstream, single reverse-proxy-friendly port), but it fails on two independent grounds: the server component's license explicitly forbids commercial/paid hosting of exactly the kind Application Factory would be doing, and even setting the license aside, the app has no channel — env var, hash, or otherwise — to set its admin credential away from the hardcoded admin@localhost/admin default at first boot, with basic_auth unable to substitute since it would break client sync traffic. Recommend not_recommended; revisit only if the vendor's licensing terms change.

Repo is not archived and receives ongoing commits, but every commit in the last 12+ months (through 2026-08-03) only touches the README (added blog posts, papers, and a "Hostinger one click install" reference) — no code, no docker-compose.yml, no Dockerfile changes. 169 open issues / 26 open PRs with no releases cutting against them suggests triage has effectively stopped even though the repo isn't formally declared EOL. Note the "Hostinger one click install" reference commit (2026-06-29) implies Hostinger may already surface this app via another channel outside the AF recipe catalogue — worth checking with the catalogue owner before duplicating effort.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue offers arbitrary multi-language code execution as a service. It would appeal to a narrow customer segment (developers building coding-assessment platforms, online IDEs, LMS integrations) rather than general self-hosting users — it is a REST API with no web UI of its own, unlike almost every other recipe we ship.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiator on paper, but the target audience (developers embedding a sandboxed code-execution backend into their own product) is narrow compared to the rest of the catalogue, and the app's only interface is an API — there's nothing for a typical AF customer to click into. Combined with the security profile below, the addressable value is low.
blocking_issues:
Judge0's own AUTHN_TOKEN is compared as a plaintext shared secret (an X-Auth-Token header value checked for exact string equality), not a hashed admin login — it cannot receive a generated_from ROOT_PASSWORD hash the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does, since the app never re-hashes the incoming value for comparison. Not a hard blocker: leave Judge0's own AUTHN_TOKEN unset and gate the whole public port with Traefik basic_auth (root-password-hash-derived) instead, the same pattern used for n8n/WUD/Open WebUI. This is expressible today and avoids leaving a remote-code-execution API open unauthenticated, but it means every API call from the customer's own client code must also carry HTTP Basic Auth, which is workable but adds integration friction for an app whose whole purpose is being called by other software.

Not a hard blocker either, but a real caveat: both the `server` and `worker` services require `privileged: true` (Judge0's `isolate` sandbox needs direct cgroup/kernel-namespace access to isolate submitted code). RFC-002's `no-privileged-without-justification` rule permits this with a documented justification. This is a code-execution service that must run privileged containers specifically to sandbox untrusted, customer-submitted code, and upstream has not shipped a security-relevant release in over 2 years despite 169 open issues.
summary: Judge0 CE is mechanically installable under the current mechanism (basic-auth gate on the one public port, internal DB/cache secrets server-generated) and fills a genuine gap — no other recipe offers code execution. But it's a poor fit for the catalogue: it has no web UI (pure API, unlike every other recipe we ship), targets a narrow developer niche, requires privileged containers to run its untrusted-code sandbox, and upstream has been effectively dormant on actual code/security fixes for over two years (one release since 2021, none since April 2024) while still accumulating open issues. The combination of a security-sensitive sandboxed-execution app and a stalled patch cadence is a bad pairing to recommend to customers; not worth building now.

name: KeeWeb
source_description: Web-based KeePass-compatible password manager running in the browser
version_health_notes: Repo is not archived and there is no announced EOL, but the release history is a long dormancy followed by a short revival burst, not a steady cadence. Releases ran v1.18.0 (2021-05-08) through v1.18.7 (2021-07-18), then nothing for ~4.75 years, then a burst of two releases in quick succession — v1.18.8 (2026-04-30) and v1.18.9 (2026-05-08) — with matching commit activity on master from 2026-04-30 through 2026-05-08 and no commits since. That is 3 months of silence as of today (2026-08-05), right after the first real activity in years. Too early to tell if this is a sustained revival or a one-off burst; treat as sporadic until another release lands. Separately, the published ghcr.io/keeweb/keeweb container image is only tagged up to `1.19.0`/`latest`, which resolves to the same commit as source tag v1.18.8 — the newest source release (v1.18.9) has not been published as a container image at analysis time, so a recipe pinning to a real image tag would actually be one release behind upstream's latest tag.
differentiation: Both are self-hosted password managers, so the category overlap is direct. KeeWeb's angle is KeePass (.kdbx) format compatibility for users migrating from desktop KeePass, and a fully client-side encryption model with no server-side account system at all — the server only ever sees an encrypted blob if one is even configured (see installability notes). Vaultwarden is a full Bitwarden-compatible server: multi-user, has native mobile/browser-extension clients, an admin panel, and org/sharing features. For a typical customer wanting "a password manager I can self-host," Vaultwarden is the more complete and more actively maintained answer; KeeWeb mainly adds value for someone specifically invested in the KeePass ecosystem.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiation is thin (KeePass-format niche) against an existing, more capable, more actively maintained recipe in the same category. It's also weakened by KeeWeb's own storage model: the official Docker image just serves the static web app over nginx — there is no bundled database/storage backend, so a database saved without configuring an external WebDAV/Dropbox/Google Drive/OneDrive target only persists in the browser's local storage, tied to one device/browser profile. That undercuts the primary reason someone self-hosts a password manager (cross-device sync), unless the customer separately stands up and wires in their own WebDAV server — which our recipe mechanism has no way to provision.
blocking_issues: App has no bundled persistent storage for the vault file (kdbx); usable cross-device sync requires a customer-configured WebDAV/Dropbox/Google Drive/OneDrive backend, none of which our /compose mechanism can provision or supply credentials for today. A recipe would either ship a KeeWeb instance whose saved vaults don't survive a container restart/browser change, or require the customer to wire up unrelated third-party storage entirely out-of-band.
summary: KeeWeb is mechanically installable today — single container, single HTTP port, no login of its own, so a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (with the password projected from the customer's root password) covers its only first-boot secret, same pattern as n8n/Adminer/WUD. But it directly overlaps an existing, more capable, more actively maintained recipe (Vaultwarden) in the same category, its own persistence story is weak without external storage wiring we can't provide, and its release history is a ~4.75-year dormancy that only just broke with a two-release burst in early May 2026 followed by 3 more months of silence. The combination of thin differentiation, a shaky storage story, and an unproven revival makes this a pass rather than a build, despite ticking the pure installability box.

name: Keila
source_description: Self-hosted newsletter platform with drag-and-drop editor and SMTP delivery
version_health_notes: Not archived; single primary maintainer (wmnnd) but commits continue past the 0.30.2 tag (e.g. bugfix commits on 2026-07-21 and 2026-08-01). Release cadence has been roughly monthly through 2026 (0.18.0 on 2026-01-04 through 0.30.2 on 2026-06-26, ~40 days before today, 2026-08-05). No EOL announcement found.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover email newsletter / mailing-list campaign management. Keila is a Mailchimp/Sendinblue-style tool (drag-and-drop or MJML/HTML campaign editor, sign-up forms, segmentation, unsubscribe handling) — a genuinely new category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct use case (customer-owned newsletter/mailing list) with no overlap in the current catalogue. Value is capped by the app's own requirement for a customer-supplied external SMTP relay to send any mail at all, which our recipe mechanism has no way to collect (see blocking_issues).
secrets_required_at_first_boot: KEILA_PASSWORD (root admin account password); MAILER_SMTP_HOST / MAILER_SMTP_USER / MAILER_SMTP_PASSWORD / MAILER_SMTP_FROM_EMAIL (customer's own SMTP relay credentials)
blocking_issues:
KEILA_PASSWORD (root admin login) is accepted by the app only as a plaintext value (documented minimum: 10 characters) — Keila stores and hashes it itself but gives no way to seed it from a pre-computed hash. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) into an app parameter, so there is no channel to supply this plaintext value. This is a genuine structural blocker, not an unsupported-algo gap.

Keila cannot send any mail — including its own transactional emails (double opt-in, password reset) — without a working SMTP relay. MAILER_SMTP_HOST/USER/PASSWORD/FROM_EMAIL are required at first boot and must be the customer's own external mail-provider credentials (or an AWS SES/Sendgrid/Mailgun/Postmark equivalent). This is an arbitrary external credential with no input channel today, same class of blocker as an external API key.
summary: Keila is an active, actively-released (monthly cadence through 2026), AGPL-3.0 self-hosted newsletter tool filling a category gap in the current 24-recipe catalogue, with a single-port Phoenix/LiveView web UI that is Traefik-compatible. It cannot ship today: the root admin password only accepts a plaintext value (no hash-seeding path via `generated_from`), and more fundamentally the app is non-functional without a customer-supplied external SMTP relay, which the current `/compose` mechanism has no channel to collect. Revisit once the platform supports either plaintext secret projection or a generic customer-supplied external-credential input.

name: Kestra
source_description: Open-source workflow orchestration platform for data pipelines and automation
version_health_notes: v1.3.31 published 2026-08-04 (2 days before this analysis), with v1.3.30 a week before that and v1.3.29 the week before — a tight, near-weekly cadence on the 1.3.x line. A parallel v1.0.5x backport/LTS line and a v2.0.0-rc6 pre-release (also dated 2026-08-04) are both shipping concurrently, and the develop branch's own default docker-compose.yml still points at :latest for day-to-day use. Repo is not archived, 27.6k stars, 381 open issues and 134 open PRs under active triage. Clearly an active, fast-moving project, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: Conceptually adjacent to n8n (both are "workflow orchestration" tools and both need Postgres + a single web UI port), but a different job: n8n is a no-code/low-code node editor for wiring together SaaS APIs, while Kestra is a declarative-YAML, event-driven scheduler aimed at data-pipeline and infrastructure orchestration (the open-source Airflow-alternative niche) — DAGs, triggers, backfills, millions of scheduled executions. No recipe in the current catalogue covers that data-engineering/DAG-scheduler use case, so for a customer specifically wanting pipeline orchestration rather than app-to-app automation, Kestra adds real incremental value over n8n.
usefulness_rationale: Popular (27.6k stars), actively developed, and fills a niche (DAG-style data-pipeline orchestration) that n8n doesn't really address. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because it's a fairly technical, engineer-facing tool (declarative YAML flows, plugin ecosystem) with a narrower target audience than most of the catalogue's simpler self-hosted apps, and the installability blocker below further limits near-term value.
blocking_issues:
Since OSS 0.24.0, Kestra requires basic authentication (username + password) to reach the app at all. There are exactly two ways to set it, and neither fits the current mechanism: (1) a first-boot "Setup Page" at /ui/main/setup where whoever visits first types in an admin email + password and self-registers as the sole admin — the same open first-visitor race condition flagged as a structural blocker in apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml — or (2) a `basic-auth: username / password` block baked into the KESTRA_CONFIGURATION env var (application.yaml), which per Kestra's own migration-guide examples takes the password as **plaintext**, not a bcrypt/argon2 hash. Confirmed against the migration guide's sample config (`password: Admin1234`) — no hashed-password field is documented. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever projects a hash, so it cannot populate this field; this is the genuine plaintext-only case the schema calls out as a structural blocker, not a solvable algo-support gap.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would stop it sitting open on the internet, but per the Activepieces precedent it can't also hand the customer a second, distinct credential for Kestra's own setup-page/basic-auth login beyond the single root-password projection already spent on the gate — so it doesn't resolve the underlying first-boot admin-provisioning gap either.
summary: Kestra is an active, well-regarded, near-weekly-shipping data-pipeline orchestration platform (Apache-2.0, Postgres-backed, single web UI port, Traefik-friendly) that would add a genuinely new DAG/data-engineering capability rather than duplicate n8n outright. It's blocked from shipping as a recipe today for the same structural reason as Activepieces: Kestra OSS now mandates basic-auth, and the only two ways to set it are an open first-visitor self-registration setup page, or a config-file field that Kestra's own docs only document as accepting a plaintext password — a case the platform's root-password projection (hash-only) cannot satisfy. Revisit if Kestra adds a hashed-password config option, or once the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond the single root-password projection.

name: Keycloak
source_description: Open-source identity and access management with SSO, OAuth2, and SAML
version_health_notes: Minor releases (26.x) ship roughly monthly (26.6.1 in 2026-04, 26.6.2 in 2026-05, 26.6.3 in 2026-06, 26.7.0 in 2026-07, 26.7.1 shortly after) — about 3 weeks since the last release as of 2026-08-05. CNCF-adjacent, Red Hat-backed (upstream of Red Hat build of Keycloak / RHBK), very active issue triage and security patching. No EOL or maintenance-only signal.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes provide identity/access management, SSO, OAuth2/OIDC, or SAML. Keycloak would let a customer stand up a central auth provider that other self-hosted apps (or their own external apps) delegate login to — a genuinely new capability, not a variant of anything already in the catalogue. Guacamole/Vaultwarden are the closest security-category neighbors but solve different problems (remote desktop gateway, password vault) with no IAM overlap.
usefulness_rationale: SSO/IAM is a common ask for small businesses and dev teams once they run more than one self-hosted app; Keycloak is the de facto open-source standard for it, well documented, and Red Hat-backed for longevity. Complexity of configuring realms/clients post-install is real, but that's normal for this class of app and doesn't reduce its value.
blocking_issues:
Keycloak's initial admin account is created from KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME / KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD (or the _FILE variants) at first boot. Keycloak takes the plaintext password and hashes it itself with its own internal credential-storage scheme (PBKDF2-based, configurable per realm) — it does not accept a pre-computed hash as input. This is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, not a hash in an unsupported algorithm, so generated_from cannot project a customer value into it.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth instead is not a substitute here: Keycloak's entire purpose is that the customer logs into its own admin console to configure realms/clients/SSO. A basic_auth wrapper would not give the customer a usable admin identity inside the app itself, only network-level access to a login screen whose credential we still can't set to something they chose.
summary: Keycloak is an active, Red Hat-backed IAM/SSO project with no equivalent in the current 24-recipe catalogue and clear customer demand for self-hosted SSO. It's a single reverse-proxy-friendly web app with a Postgres backend, structurally straightforward to package. The blocker is purely mechanical: its admin bootstrap requires a plaintext password that our root-password-hash projection can't supply, and a Traefik basic_auth gate doesn't substitute for a real admin login the customer can use. Revisit once the platform gains a channel for a customer-chosen plaintext admin credential (not just a hash) — this is exactly the kind of high-value app worth building the moment that lands.

name: Khoj
source_description: Open-source AI assistant for chatting with your documents and the web
version_health_notes: Master branch is genuinely active (commits as recent as 2026-08-02, e.g. "Make chat export robust and fix export truncation #1314"), and the repo is not archived (36k+ stars, 101 open issues, 30 open PRs). But the published container image has not been re-tagged in over 4 months: the last cut is 2.0.0-beta.28 on 2026-03-26, ~4 months and 11 days before today (2026-08-06), after a cadence of roughly monthly betas from late 2025 through March 2026 (beta.19 on 2025-11-18 through beta.28 on 2026-03-26). The project has also been in a "2.0.0-beta.*" versioning state for a long stretch with no GA cut in sight. Net: code is alive, but the artifact a recipe would actually pin to is stale relative to upstream dev — worth re-checking image cadence before building.
differentiation: Khoj combines document RAG chat, built-in web search (via a bundled SearxNG instance), custom agents, and scheduled automations in one app, versus Open WebUI (chat UI over local/cloud models, no built-in web search or document RAG by default) and Paperless-AI (narrowly scoped to auto-tagging Paperless-ngx documents, not general chat). Genuinely broader "second brain" positioning than either existing recipe, but the value proposition overlaps meaningfully with Open WebUI once a customer adds RAG/websearch plugins there.
usefulness_rationale: Real, popular (36k star) project with a distinct feature set, but the upstream reference stack is heavy (Postgres+pgvector, a code-execution sandbox, SearxNG, an experimental VNC-based "computer use" service, plus the main server — five containers) and recommends 8GB+ RAM and 16GB VRAM for good model performance. This service looks optional (it is not needed for core chat/RAG functionality) and can likely be dropped from a recipe's compose file, but that is a real recipe-authoring decision, not something this analysis resolves — flagging it as the reason reverse_proxy_compatible is marked false for the stack as shipped upstream.
summary: Khoj is mechanically installable under the current /compose constraint: KHOJ_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY and KHOJ_ADMIN_PASSWORD are opaque values the app itself consumes and never needs to surface to the customer, so both are plain server-generated secrets. The upstream reference deployment runs the main chat UI with `--anonymous-mode` (no login at all) by default, which is exactly the no-built-in-auth case the schema calls out — a Traefik basic_auth gate keyed off the customer's root password (generated_from) is the correct customer-facing security boundary here, same pattern as n8n/Open WebUI/Immich. The real caveats are catalogue fit and packaging effort rather than the secrets model: it overlaps meaningfully with the already-catalogued Open WebUI, the full upstream stack has a non-proxyable VNC service that would need to be trimmed out of any recipe, and the published container image hasn't been re-tagged in 4+ months despite active upstream commits. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building once someone confirms the "computer"/VNC service can be dropped cleanly and re-checks that image tagging has resumed, but it's not a priority pick over apps with cleaner single-purpose fit.

Elasticsearch itself was previously analyzed (apps-gaps/elasticsearch.yaml, low usefulness precisely *because* it has no UI); Kibana is effectively the missing UI half of that pair. None of the 24 shipped recipes provide log/search dashboarding. Shipping Kibana as a recipe requires also standing up an Elasticsearch instance underneath it (Kibana has no other supported backend), making this a two-service stack rather than a single container — closer in shape to recipes/immich/'s multi-service pattern than to a single-container web app.
usefulness_rationale: Kibana is the industry-standard log/search dashboard and, unlike a bare Elasticsearch recipe, gives a customer an actual browser UI to click through rather than a raw REST API — a meaningfully better fit for this catalogue's end-user-facing profile than Elasticsearch alone. Capped at medium rather than high because it is only useful once something is actually indexing data into the bundled Elasticsearch (Logstash/Beats/an app's own logs), which this recipe would not itself provide — an empty Kibana+Elasticsearch pair is dashboards over nothing, the same caveat noted for Grafana. It also inherits Elasticsearch's heavier resource footprint (JVM heap, 2GB+ RAM recommended for ES alone) atop Kibana's own footprint, disproportionate to the single-tenant self-hosted profile this catalogue otherwise targets.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: elastic superuser password; kibana_system service-account password/token
blocking_issues:
The customer-facing login is the same elastic superuser analyzed in apps-gaps/elasticsearch.yaml: Elasticsearch's Change Password API accepts a pre-computed bcrypt hash, so generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD" is structurally deliverable in principle, but only after the same bootstrap chicken-and-egg is solved (start Elasticsearch with a throwaway password, then overwrite via the hash-accepting API) — install.sh logic beyond a plain metadata.yaml parameter mapping, same as the ES-only case.

This recipe adds a second bootstrap problem on top of that: modern Elastic Stack (8.x+) wires Kibana to Elasticsearch via a Fleet/Kibana enrollment token and a CA fingerprint generated at Elasticsearch's first boot (or, for compose stacks, manually configured ELASTICSEARCH_HOSTS + ELASTICSEARCH_SERVICEACCOUNTTOKEN + xpack.security.http.ssl trust settings), all server-side and none of it customer-facing — expressible, but meaningfully more install.sh complexity than a single-container recipe, on top of the already-nontrivial ES password bootstrap.

Elasticsearch auto-configures TLS on its HTTP layer by default when security is enabled; as in the ES-only analysis, the recipe needs to explicitly disable that (xpack.security.http.ssl.enabled=false) so Traefik can terminate public TLS cleanly, plus configure Kibana to trust Elasticsearch's internal transport certs for the service-to-service leg.
summary: Kibana is Elasticsearch's actively-maintained (9.5.0, 2026-08-04), industry-standard dashboard/visualization UI, and would fill the gap the Elasticsearch-only gap-analysis flagged (no web UI, low usefulness standalone). Mechanically it is installable today: the customer-facing elastic-user login is expressible the same way as in the Elasticsearch analysis (generated_from bcrypt hash via ES's Change Password API, bootstrapped through a throwaway password), and the Kibana↔Elasticsearch service-account credential is a server-generated secret with no customer input needed. The catch is packaging cost, not a hard blocker: this ships as a two-container stack (Kibana + Elasticsearch, since Kibana has no other supported backend), needs the same TLS-disable and password-bootstrap workaround as the ES analysis, plus enrollment/service -token wiring between the two containers — more install.sh complexity than most existing single-container recipes. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building as the "UI half" that makes Elasticsearch's data usable, but usefulness to a customer still depends on them feeding data into it (via Logstash/Beats/an app's own logs), which this recipe alone would not provide.

source_description: Self-hosted time tracking for freelancers, agencies, and teams
version_health_notes: Actively maintained; kimai/kimai2 Docker Hub repo shows a steady monthly release cadence through 2026 (2.46.0 on 2026-01-07 through 2.63.0 on 2026-08-03, i.e. 2 days before today, 2026-08-05). differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover time tracking / timesheet / invoicing for freelancers or agencies. Kimai adds a genuinely new category: project/customer/activity-based time tracking with reporting and invoice export.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct use case with no catalogue overlap and a sizeable target audience (freelancers, agencies). Standard single-web-app + MySQL/MariaDB shape, structurally similar to recipes/n8n and recipes/paperless-ngx (app container + DB container behind Traefik). Value is capped by the same admin-credential blocker seen in Keila (see blocking_issues).
blocking_issues:
ADMINPASS (the initial ROLE_SUPER_ADMIN login) is accepted by the image only as a plaintext value — the entrypoint runs `kimai:user:create` with this password, and Kimai hashes it internally at creation time but gives no way to seed the account from a pre-computed hash. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of ROOT_PASSWORD into an app parameter, and the customer would then need to know and type that hash string to log in, which they don't. This is the same class of structural blocker documented for Keila's KEILA_PASSWORD — not an unsupported-algo gap, since no algorithm choice fixes a plaintext-only field.

Gating the app behind Traefik basic_auth instead does not resolve this: the customer still needs a working Kimai login (to track their own time, manage projects/customers, run reports) beyond the outer gate, and ADMINPASS would have to be some value the customer never learns, leaving them locked out of the actual application.
summary: Kimai is an active, well-maintained (monthly release cadence through 2026), AGPL-3.0 self-hosted time-tracking app that would fill a real gap in the current 24-recipe catalogue — no existing recipe covers freelancer/agency time tracking. It is structurally simple (single web app + MySQL/MariaDB, single HTTP port, Traefik-compatible), similar in shape to recipes/n8n and recipes/paperless-ngx. It cannot ship today because the only supported first-boot admin credential (ADMINPASS) is plaintext-only with no hash-seeding path, the same blocker already documented for Keila. Revisit once the platform adds a genuine customer-supplied plaintext-credential input channel (beyond hash projection via `generated_from`).
