name: Kodi
source_description: Headless Kodi server for sharing a centralised media library across clients
version_health_notes: Kodi 21.3 "Omega" shipped 2025-12-15, under 8 months before today (2026-08-05). The 21.x Omega line has had regular point releases since its 2023-04 debut, and a Kodi 22 "Piers" major rewrite is already in alpha/beta cycling (a1 2025-08, a2 2025-12, a3 2026-04-01, b1 2026-06-29) on the way to a future stable cut. Team Kodi/XBMC Foundation is clearly active. However, this health check is for the upstream Kodi application itself — it does NOT extend to the "headless server" packaging most relevant here (see blocking_issues): Team Kodi ships no official Docker image, and the community image that became the de-facto standard, linuxserver/kodi-headless, was archived by its maintainers on 2022-02-24 and last built Kodi 18.5 "Leia" (2020-01-07) — over 6 years and 3 stable major versions (19, 20, 21) out of date. The suggested replacement, a single independent developer's personal fork (matthuisman/kodi-headless), is more current (last bumped 2026-07/08 to track 22.0b1) but is a one-person side project, not a vendor-backed or widely-adopted image.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers this ground, but "headless Kodi as a shared library server" is a fundamentally different product than the personal-media-streaming category a customer would expect from a hosted Kodi recipe. Kodi's web UI (Chorus2) is a remote-control surface for a local Kodi instance's own playback, not a browser-based video player/transcoder the way Jellyfin or Plex are — headless Kodi has no video output at all. Its actual purpose, per Hostinger's description, is letting several separate physical Kodi installs (TVs, Android boxes, HTPCs on a home LAN) share one library database (MySQL/ MariaDB, configured by hand-editing advancedsettings.xml) and discover each other over UPnP/DLNA/EventServer (UDP 9777) — all LAN-local, multi-device protocols that don't map onto "one cloud VM behind one HTTPS domain for one customer."
usefulness_rationale: A cloud-hosted single-domain instance cannot deliver the feature that makes headless Kodi useful (multiple home-network Kodi clients discovering and syncing against a shared library over local UPnP/DLNA and a shared DB) — those clients live on the customer's LAN, not on the internet-facing VM. What would actually be reachable through Traefik is just the JSON-RPC/remote-control web UI, which is not itself a media-streaming or media-management experience a self-hosting customer is likely to want in isolation. Jellyfin (see apps-gaps/ jellyfin.yaml) already covers the "self-hosted video streaming server with a real web UI" niche far better structurally, if that's the gap being targeted.
blocking_issues:
No official Docker image. Team Kodi does not publish or endorse a container image; every option found is third-party. The one that became the de-facto community standard, linuxserver/kodi-headless, was archived 2022-02-24 and frozen on Kodi 18.5 (2020), so it cannot be used as a current, supportable base image. The maintained alternative (matthuisman/kodi-headless) is a single hobbyist's personal repo with no organizational backing, SLA, or multi-maintainer continuity — a materially weaker supply-chain position than every other image currently in the catalogue.

Kodi's web interface ships with authentication off by default (no env var to enable/seed a username+password at first boot in either community image); a Traefik basic_auth gate closes that specific perimeter gap and is expressible today, but it only secures the remote-control API surface, not the feature the app is being recommended for.

The actual value proposition Hostinger's description calls out — "sharing a centralised media library across clients" — requires pointing the instance at an external MySQL/MariaDB database by hand-editing advancedsettings.xml inside the container after boot; there is no env var for this in either community image, and even if there were, the "clients" that would consume that shared library are separate physical Kodi installs on the customer's home LAN, which cannot reach a UPnP/DLNA/EventServer-based discovery flow through a single Traefik HTTPS domain. This is a structural fit problem, not just a missing-secret-channel problem.
summary: Kodi the application is actively maintained upstream, but "headless Kodi server" as packaged for Docker is not: there is no official image, the community image that used to be the standard has been archived since 2022 and is 6+ years / 3 major versions stale, and the only current alternative is an unaffiliated single maintainer's personal fork. More fundamentally, the feature Hostinger's blurb is selling — a centralised library shared across multiple Kodi clients — depends on LAN-local protocols (UPnP/DLNA, a hand-configured shared MySQL DB) that don't translate to a single customer VM behind one Traefik domain; what would actually be reachable over HTTPS is just a remote-control web UI with no video playback of its own. A Traefik basic_auth gate makes it mechanically installable, but the resulting recipe wouldn't deliver the product a customer is expecting. Recommend not building; Jellyfin (see apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml, currently blocked_on_platform on the admin-setup wizard) is the structurally better candidate for the "self-hosted media streaming" gap this app is adjacent to.

Koel scans a music library and serves a Spotify-style web player (playlists, smart playlists, podcasts, radio, Last.fm/Spotify/MusicBrainz integrations), giving customers a self-hosted alternative to Spotify/Plex-for-music that this catalogue otherwise has no equivalent for.

Capped at medium rather than high because it's only useful once a customer has their own music library to upload/mount, similar to the "needs data fed into it" caveat noted for Kibana/Grafana, and it is a narrower audience (personal audio hoarders) than broadly-applicable tools like password managers or uptime monitors.
blocking_issues:
Koel's own login is not a customer-configurable credential at first boot: the official docker image runs `koel:init` on first start, which creates one fixed default admin account (admin@koel.dev / KoelIsCool per github.com/koel/docker's README) — there is no ADMIN_EMAIL / ADMIN_PASSWORD env var on the official image to set a different login during container startup. Changing it afterward requires an interactive `php artisan koel:admin:change-password` command (or the web UI once logged in), which needs the plaintext new password — something install.sh never has access to, since af-api only ever projects a hash via generated_from. That rules out generated_from for Koel's own login.

Given a fixed, publicly-documented default admin credential and no supported channel to rotate it at install time, this falls into the "fixed/default/hardcoded admin credential the app itself gives no way to [programmatically] change" case from SCHEMA.md — gate the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth:true using the root-password-derived hash, same pattern as n8n/WUD/Adminer. That makes the Koel-native admin@koel.dev/KoelIsCool login a behind-the-gate concern rather than an internet-facing one.

Storage layout needs a persistent `/music` volume for the library plus `storage/app/public/images` and `storage/search-indexes` — all server-side bind mounts, not customer secrets, but worth noting for the eventual recipe's volume plan.
summary: Koel is an actively-maintained (v9.11.0, 2026-07-13), single-container, single-HTTP-port music streaming server with no existing catalogue overlap and a genuine web UI — a good structural fit. It is installable today, but only via the Traefik basic_auth workaround rather than Koel's own login: the official docker image has no environment variable to set a custom admin email/password at first boot, only a fixed documented default (admin@koel.dev/KoelIsCool), and rotating it afterward needs a plaintext password our install flow cannot supply. Recommend build_with_caveats: gate the app behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth using the root-password hash (same pattern as n8n/Adminer/WUD), leaving Koel's own default admin account as a behind-the-gate detail rather than a customer-facing credential.

Recommend not_recommended pending legal review of that clause, and even absent the license issue this niche is already covered by two broader candidates (Grocy, KitchenOwl) under separate gap analysis. Note on identity: the only real candidate found was PanSalut/Koffan; chhinhsovath/KoffanLightWebApp is a fork/mirror of the same project, not a distinct upstream, and was ruled out as such.

source_description: Lightweight self-hosted server monitoring dashboard with real-time metrics
version_health_notes: 1.4.0 tagged 2026-08-05 — today. Preceding tags show a very tight cadence: 1.3.2 (2026-07-30), 1.3.1 (2026-07-28), 1.3.0 (2026-07-22), 1.2.5-fix2/fix1 (2026-07-20), i.e. multiple releases most weeks, plus frequent unversioned "Snapshot-*" pre-release builds between tags. Repo is not archived; last push 2026-08-05T13:17Z, ~5.6k GitHub stars. Unambiguously active — a young, fast-moving project rather than mature/stable (breaking storage-format changes between 1.3.x point releases per the release notes), so pin carefully and expect the pinned tag to age quickly. SECURITY: the upstream README links directly to a Huntress security-research post, "Komari: The 'Monitoring' Tool That Didn't Need Weaponising" (huntress.com/blog/komari-c2-agent-abuse, published 2026-04-30), documenting a real-world intrusion on 2026-04-16 in which a threat actor with stolen VPN credentials installed the stock, unmodified Komari agent as a persistent SYSTEM-level Windows service ("Windows Update Service" via NSSM) to get command-and-control with no custom infrastructure and no modification to Komari at all. The agent's server-to-agent control channel ships three capabilities enabled by default: exec (arbitrary PowerShell/sh command execution), terminal (interactive PTY reverse shell rendered in the operator's browser), and ping (network probing). Only `--disable-web-ssh` turns off the interactive-terminal piece, and it is opt-in at install time, not the default. Huntress' framing: "You do not weaponise [Komari]; you just point it at a server you 'own' and type an install command."
differentiation: The catalogue's one existing monitoring recipe, uptime-kuma, checks external endpoint availability (HTTP/TCP/ping probes against services you point it at). Komari is a different job: an agent-based system resource monitor — a lightweight agent runs on each server being watched and streams CPU/RAM/disk/network metrics back to a central Komari dashboard, multi-server fleet view included. No shipped recipe covers server-resource telemetry (a Netdata/Glances-style role), so this is genuine differentiation rather than a near-duplicate of uptime-kuma.
usefulness_rationale: There is a real gap (no resource-monitoring recipe today) and a clean single-port web UI, superficially similar to uptime-kuma which already shipped successfully. That would justify "medium" or higher on functional grounds alone. But Komari is not just a passive metrics dashboard with an incidental remote-control extra: its agent ships exec/terminal/ping control-channel capabilities enabled by default, and it has a documented, named real-world abuse case (see version_health.notes — the Huntress C2-agent-abuse writeup) of exactly that default-on capability being used to establish persistent SYSTEM-level backdoors with zero modification to the software. Hosting this on customer infrastructure means shipping a functioning C2 implant by default unless every deployment is deliberately hardened — a materially different (and higher) risk than any other app in the catalogue. That risk, not just "bigger blast radius", drives the rating down to low regardless of the monitoring-gap value.
blocking_issues:
No official docker-compose.yml is published upstream — only a `docker run` one-liner in the quick-start docs (ghcr.io/komari-monitor/komari, port 25774, /app/data volume). Not a blocker, just means a recipe's compose file would be authored from scratch rather than adapted from an upstream example.

Admin account creation is a first-run web wizard ("on first access, use the installation guide to create the administrator account and site settings") — the customer sets their own username/password interactively after deploy, the same pattern uptime-kuma already ships with. No af-api-projected secret is needed for this. However, upstream docs do not clarify whether the dashboard or its data is reachable before that wizard is completed, so this should be verified hands-on (deploy + curl before completing the wizard) before a recipe ships, rather than assumed safe by analogy alone.

Komari's agent control channel ships exec (arbitrary PowerShell/sh command execution), terminal (interactive PTY reverse shell in the operator's browser), and ping — all THREE ENABLED BY DEFAULT, not opt-in. Huntress documented a real-world incident (2026-04-16) where this default-on capability was used, with zero modification to Komari, to install a persistent SYSTEM-level Windows backdoor after a VPN credential compromise (see version_health.notes). The only documented mitigation flag, `--disable-web-ssh`, only disables the interactive-terminal piece — `exec` (arbitrary remote command execution) and `ping` remain enabled regardless, so there is no documented way to fully turn off the C2-capable surface even with hardening flags applied. This is not a customer-secret/input-channel gap the current `/compose` mechanism could close (it isn't about `generated_from` or `basic_auth` at all) — it is a property of the shipped software itself, so no platform change (IF-1420, IF-1312, or otherwise) would resolve it.
summary: Komari is an actively-maintained (1.4.0 released today, 2026-08-05, on a multiple-releases-per-week cadence), single-container, single-HTTP-port (25774) server-resource-monitoring dashboard with a genuine web UI and no overlap with the catalogue's existing uptime-kuma (endpoint-availability, not resource metrics) recipe, and it is mechanically installable today (the app's own first-run wizard lets the customer set their admin login directly, no customer secret needed at first boot). Despite that, it is not recommended: Komari's own README links to a Huntress security- research writeup documenting a real 2026-04-16 intrusion in which the stock, unmodified Komari agent was installed as a persistent SYSTEM-level Windows backdoor after a VPN credential compromise — enabled by the agent's exec/terminal/ping control channel, all three of which ship ENABLED BY DEFAULT, with only partial mitigation (`--disable-web-ssh` disables the terminal only; `exec` remains live regardless). This is a documented, named C2-abuse case in default configuration, not a theoretical concern, and no platform mechanism (current or pending) changes that risk — recommend not_recommended over pursuing a recipe.

name: Kong
source_description: Cloud-native API gateway built for hybrid and multi-cloud environments
version_health_notes: 3.9.3 released 2026-06-17, ~7 weeks before today (2026-08-05) — looks current at a glance, but the release history behind it shows the open- source line has effectively stalled: 3.9.0 (2024-12-13) -> 3.9.1 (2025-06-04, ~6 months later) -> 3.9.2 (2026-06-04, a full year after 3.9.1) -> 3.9.3 (2026-06-17, 13 days later, a security-only patch for CVE-2026-49975). No 3.10 or later has ever shipped as an OSS/free image. This is not incidental slowdown: Kong Inc. changed its licensing model around March 2025 (Kong Gateway 3.10) to drop the free/OSS mode entirely — running kong/kong-gateway:3.10+ without a paid Enterprise license behaves as an expired-license install with degraded functionality, and no further `kong:x.y.z` OSS images have been published since 3.9.x. The `Kong/kong` GitHub repo itself is not archived and still receives occasional security backports (hence 3.9.3), but new features, plugins, and the active development line have all moved to the paid Konnect/Enterprise product, which is already at 3.15.0.2 (2026-07-21) on a completely different, closed distribution. For a self-hostable, license-free recipe, the relevant upstream is functionally frozen in security-patch-only maintenance mode, not "active" the way the 7-week-old release date alone would suggest.
differentiation: Kong is an API gateway: it proxies, authenticates, and rate-limits traffic to *other* backend services that the operator configures via its Admin API or Kong Manager UI after boot. None of the current 24 recipes are gateways/infra-plumbing in this sense, so on paper there's no direct catalogue duplicate. In practice, though, every AF recipe already sits behind our own Traefik instance, which fills the "reverse proxy in front of a self-hosted app" role for the whole catalogue. A freshly-installed Kong recipe has no backend services of its own to route to — the customer would get a running gateway with nothing behind it, and configuring it to do anything useful requires Admin-API/decK work far beyond what a single-app recipe install flow supports. The product doesn't slot into "one useful app per subdomain" the way the rest of the catalogue does; it's platform plumbing that competes with, rather than complements, the platform's own Traefik layer.
usefulness_rationale: No functional gap filled (Traefik already covers reverse-proxying for every recipe), no natural standalone use for a customer who installs it with nothing to gateway, and the open-source track it would need to run on is in security-patch-only maintenance mode since Kong Inc. discontinued the free tier at 3.10 (March 2025).
blocking_issues:
Neither the Admin API (:8001) nor Kong Manager OSS (:8002) has any built-in authentication in the OSS build — RBAC/auth on the admin surfaces is an Enterprise-only feature. Left open, either port is a fully-privileged reconfiguration surface for the whole gateway. A Traefik basic_auth gate on both is expressible today (mechanism exists), but see the next two points on why that alone doesn't make this a useful recipe.
Even correctly gated, the recipe has nothing for the customer to use out of the box: Kong has no content or app of its own, only routing rules for backend services the customer must define post-install via the Admin API or Kong Manager, which is outside the scope of a one-click recipe install flow.
Full-featured/persistent mode needs a Postgres backend (DB-less mode is possible but requires hand-authoring a declarative YAML config off-platform, again with no supported input channel for that content).
Upstream OSS/free distribution is frozen at 3.9.x with new features and even routine (non-CVE) fixes redirected to the paid Konnect/Enterprise product since the March 2025 licensing change — building a recipe on a discontinued free tier is a durability risk independent of the fit issues above.
summary: Kong (kong/kong, pin 3.9.3) is mechanically installable under today's /compose constraints — it's a single official Docker image with plain HTTP ports, and the one credential it would need (a gate on the unauthenticated Admin API and Kong Manager UI) is expressible via Traefik basic_auth. The recommendation is not_recommended anyway, because the fit is wrong for this catalogue: Kong is a gateway meant to front other backend services the customer configures after boot, not a standalone app, and our own Traefik already plays the reverse-proxy role for every recipe. A fresh install would hand the customer a correctly-secured gateway pointed at nothing. Compounding that, the free/OSS distribution this recipe would have to run on has been frozen at 3.9.x since Kong Inc. discontinued the license-free tier in March 2025 (3.10+ requires a paid Enterprise license) — 3.9.3 (2026-06-17) is a security-only backport, not a live development line, so anything built on it inherits a maintenance-only upstream with no future feature path short of paying for Konnect.

name: Kotaemon
source_description: Open-source document Q&A chatbot with multi-LLM support and OCR
version_health_notes: ~9 weeks since v0.12.0 (2026-05-31) as of 2026-08-05. Repo is not archived and shows a push as recent as 2026-07-14 (~3 weeks ago), with 239 open issues still being triaged — this is actively maintained, not dormant. One caveat for a future recipe author: the versioned image tags on GHCR (`0.11.0-lite`, `0.11.0-full`, `0.11.0-ollama`) are ~1 year stale; all recent work only publishes to the floating `main-lite`, `main-full`, `main-ollama` tags (last pushed ~2 months ago). There is currently no versioned tag matching v0.12.0 to pin to — pinning today means either accepting a year-old versioned tag or the unpinned `main-*` tag, which RFC-002's pinned-tag rule would reject as-is.
differentiation: Open WebUI is a general chat frontend over local/any-provider LLMs with no document-specific pipeline; Paperless-ai bolts AI auto-tagging onto an existing Paperless-ngx archive. Kotaemon's core is retrieval-augmented document Q&A: multi-document upload, OCR/table/figure-aware parsing, hybrid full-text+vector retrieval with re-ranking, in-browser PDF citation highlighting, and agent-based reasoning (ReAct/ReWOO) over the user's own document set. That RAG-over-your-own-files use case isn't covered by anything currently in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely different niche (document RAG/Q&A) from the existing AI recipes, and it can run fully local via Ollama with no external API key required, matching the catalogue's self-hosted-first audience. Held to medium rather than high because the project is a research-lab-flavored tool (GraphRAG/LightRAG indexing options, agent reasoning modes) with a steeper first-run configuration surface than a typical AF one-click app, and the stale versioned-tag situation adds real packaging friction.
blocking_issues:
Kotaemon's own optional multi-user login (`KH_FEATURE_USER_MANAGEMENT`) is off by default; the app ships with no auth at all in that state, so it needs a Traefik basic_auth gate to avoid a document-QA app with arbitrary file upload sitting open on the internet. That gate is expressible today via generated_from(ROOT_PASSWORD).

If a recipe instead wanted to enable Kotaemon's built-in login (to get per-user document collections), the admin account is set via `KH_FEATURE_USER_MANAGEMENT_ADMIN`/`KH_FEATURE_USER_MANAGEMENT_PASSWORD` env vars, and per source (libs/ktem/ktem/pages/resources/user.py) that `..._PASSWORD` value is read as **plaintext** and hashed internally with `hashlib.sha256` at user-creation time — it is not a pre-computed-hash field. `generated_from` only ever emits a hash, so it cannot supply this parameter; per SCHEMA.md this is the genuine "app needs the plaintext, not any hash" case, which is a structural blocker for that path specifically. This does not block the app overall, since the no-login + basic_auth path above is available and is the same pattern already used for n8n/WUD/OpenClaw/Open WebUI/Immich.
summary: Kotaemon is mechanically installable today, but only via the "no built-in login, gate the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth" path — its optional native user-management feature is a dead end for our mechanism because its admin-password env var expects plaintext (which it then SHA-256-hashes itself), not a pre-computed hash that generated_from could supply. Single container, single HTTP port (7860, Gradio), reverse-proxy compatible, and can run fully local via Ollama with no external API key required at boot. It fills a real gap (document RAG/Q&A) not covered by open-webui or paperless-ai, but recommend build_with_caveats rather than build_now: the basic_auth path is the only viable one architecturally, and separately the upstream image situation is messy right now — the only current tags are the unpinned `main-lite`/`main-full`/`main-ollama` floating tags, since the last versioned image build (0.11.0) predates the latest v0.12.0 release by about a year, which a future recipe author will need to resolve before this clears RFC-002's pinned-tag rule.

differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers ML dataset preparation. Paperless-ai auto-tags an existing document archive; Open WebUI is a chat frontend over LLMs. Label Studio is a purpose-built human-in-the-loop annotation tool (bounding boxes, transcription, classification, NER, etc.) across text/image/audio/video/time-series, aimed at teams building or fine-tuning ML models — a distinct developer/ML-tooling audience the catalogue doesn't currently serve.

Label Studio has an in-app login, but with no admin pre-provisioned it defaults to open self-signup: any visitor can create an account and that account becomes an org member with no gate at all. Left as-is on a public <slug>.<base_domain> URL, a random visitor could race the customer to sign up first. Single app container behind a standard HTTP port, reverse-proxy compatible, and fills a genuine gap (ML data labeling/annotation) not covered elsewhere in the catalogue. Recommend build_with_caveats rather than build_now: the audience is narrower/more technical than most current recipes, the official production topology adds a Postgres dependency, and the ~5-month gap since the last stable tag (against an otherwise active, nightly-built repo) is worth revisiting at recipe-authoring time to confirm it hasn't stalled further.

This is a genuinely new category — appeals to customers building their own SaaS/API product who want self-hosted Stripe-Billing-style infrastructure rather than a general productivity or infra tool.
usefulness_rationale: High differentiation (fills a real gap) but a narrower audience than most of the catalogue — useful mainly to customers running their own metered SaaS/API business, not general self-hosters.
blocking_issues:
Lago structurally needs two independently public-facing HTTP services, not one: `api` (port 3000) and `front` (port 80). Verified against upstream docker-compose.yml (github.com/getlago/lago, main branch): `front`'s `API_URL` env var defaults to `${LAGO_API_URL:-http://localhost:3000}` and is consumed client-side — the *browser*, not the front container, calls the API directly at this public URL.

Confirmed there is no upstream reverse-proxy workaround: fetched getlago/lago-front's shipped nginx config (nginx/nginx.conf on main) and it only serves the static SPA build (location /assets/, location / -> index.html) — no location /api or proxy_pass to the api service. The front container cannot be configured to internally proxy API calls, so there is no single-domain path; the browser must reach the api service on its own public hostname.

rfc/002-recipe-rules.md (lines 270-272) is explicit that a recipe may declare at most one Traefik-routed port — the renderer emits exactly one Traefik router per app and strips the host binding of every other routed port, leaving a second routed port unreachable. No existing recipe establishes a working precedent for two separate public web UIs on two subdomains from one recipe (checked gitea: second port is raw SSH, not HTTP; runtipi: port 80/443 are the same UI via http/https, not two services; wud: only ever declares one public port) — this is a genuine platform-mechanism gap, not something a single-domain recipe can paper over.
summary: Lago is an active, well-maintained (v1.51.0, released 2026-07-27, ~biweekly cadence, 10.3k stars, AGPL-3.0) open-source usage-based billing platform with no equivalent in the current catalogue — a genuinely new billing/metering category customers building their own usage-based SaaS would want. It has no fixed admin credential to project (an open in-app signup wizard, like n8n's) and every other "secret" at boot (RSA key, DB/Redis credentials) is server-generatable, so auth alone is not the blocker. The blocker is structural: Lago's `front` (port 80) is a static SPA whose browser-side JS talks directly to the `api` service (port 3000) at its own public URL — verified against upstream docker-compose.yml and lago-front's nginx config, which has no `/api` proxy_pass to fall back on. That means Lago needs two independently public HTTP subdomains to boot a working UI, but our recipe mechanism supports only one Traefik-routed port per recipe (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md) with no existing multi-subdomain precedent to lean on. Not installable today; revisit once multi-domain Traefik routing per recipe exists, or if upstream ever ships a same-origin proxy option for `front`. Recommend blocked_on_platform.

summary: LakeFS (treeverse/lakefs, pin 1.86.0) is mechanically installable today. Run with `LAKEFS_DATABASE_TYPE=local` and `LAKEFS_BLOCKSTORE_TYPE=local` it needs no external Postgres or S3/MinIO service, so it fits a single- container docker-compose recipe with one HTTP port, cleanly reverse- proxyable through Traefik. LakeFS has no env var to preset an admin account at boot: the first visit to the base URL redirects to a one-time `/setup` wizard that itself generates and displays an access-key-ID / secret-access-key pair for whoever completes it, shown only once. That is the same "first-visitor race" shape as Appsmith's signup wizard — an anonymous visitor could reach `/setup` before the customer and claim the generated admin credential — so it needs the same fix: a Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front closes the race, after which the customer completes the wizard themselves and receives their own credential directly in the browser. No app-generated secret needs an out-of-band delivery channel (unlike Atomic Server's console-only invite token), so this doesn't hit the `blocked_on_platform` case. Upstream is clearly `active` — releases every 1-3 weeks including fast security patches, and the company behind it is funded and shipping both the OSS core and a paid Enterprise tier in parallel. The main caveat is audience: this is a data-engineering/dev tool, useful but narrower than most of the catalogue's general-purpose apps. Recommend build_now.

blocking_issues: Langflow's own login (LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER / LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD) only accepts a plaintext password via env var — there is no pre-hashed-credential input, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash) cannot project a value into it. Workaround: set LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=true (this is actually the upstream project default, though the official Docker image ships with it set to false) so Langflow's own login screen is bypassed entirely, and generate LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD server-side as a random value nobody needs to read. That moves the real auth boundary to a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the app, matching the pattern already used for n8n/WUD/OpenClaw. Flagging as a caveat rather than a hard blocker since a working mechanism exists today.
summary: Langflow is active upstream (stable release one day before this analysis, roughly biweekly stable cadence plus near-daily nightlies) and fills a genuinely open slot in the catalogue: a visual builder for LLM/agent workflows, distinct from n8n's general automation and from the chat/messaging-agent recipes we already have. Installability requires one workaround: Langflow's built-in login only accepts a plaintext superuser password (no hash input), so instead of projecting the customer's root-password hash into it, the recipe should disable Langflow's own login (LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=true, matching upstream's own default) and gate the app with Traefik basic_auth instead — the same pattern already used for n8n/WUD/OpenClaw. With that caveat applied this is installable today and worth building.

A recipe must rebind it to 127.0.0.1:9090:9000 like the other internal services to keep a single public port — this is a mechanical compose-level fix the recipe author needs to make, not something upstream provides out-of-the-box.

As shipped upstream it has TWO public ports, not one: langfuse-web:3000 (the HTTP UI/API) and minio:9090 (raw S3 API, gated only by MINIO_ROOT_USER/MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD env vars) — every other backing service (langfuse-worker, clickhouse, redis, postgres) is already 127.0.0.1-bound in the upstream compose. To reach the same single-public-port pattern used elsewhere in the catalogue (e.g. Immich: server + ML + redis + postgres, one public port), a recipe would need to rebind minio to 127.0.0.1:9090:9000 — a small, mechanical compose-level fix, not something upstream provides out-of-the-box. Every infra secret it needs at boot (NEXTAUTH_SECRET, SALT, ENCRYPTION_KEY, and the Postgres/ClickHouse/ Redis/MinIO credentials) is an opaque value the app never surfaces to the customer, so all seven can be server-generated with no input channel needed — no `generated_from`/root-password projection or Traefik basic_auth gate required for those. The admin account itself needs no env var either: email/password signup is enabled by default and the first person to sign up becomes the org owner, the same first-visitor-claims- admin pattern already accepted for Kutt, Uptime Kuma, and Gitea. `AUTH_DISABLE_SIGNUP` exists to lock signup down after that first claim, which a recipe should set post-bootstrap as good practice but isn't a platform blocker. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically installable today, but the 5-service ClickHouse-backed stack is heavier (RAM/disk) than most of the current catalogue and worth flagging to whoever prioritizes the backlog rather than treating it as a drop-in build_now.

name: LavinMQ
source_description: High-performance AMQP message broker with built-in web management UI
version_health_notes: v2.9.1 shipped 2026-07-01, about 5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). It followed v2.9.0 (2026-06-25, a major release adding disk-flushed publish confirms, durable clustered confirms, and OAuth2/OIDC SSO login), which itself followed v2.8.2 (2026-06-24), v2.8.1 (2026-05-18), and v2.8.0 (2026-05-06/07) — a steady roughly-monthly minor/patch cadence, with two release candidates (v2.9.0-rc.1/rc.2) preceding the 2.9.0 GA the way a maintained project typically stages releases. Built and maintained by CloudAMQP (a commercial RabbitMQ/ LavinMQ hosting company), actively developing new features (OAuth2/OIDC, Prometheus metrics, RabbitMQ-definitions compatibility) rather than just patching. Clearly active, not slowing, maintenance- only, or archived.
differentiation: No existing recipe provides a message broker of any kind — this would be the first, alongside the also-analyzed Eclipse Mosquitto (MQTT, no UI) and EMQX (MQTT, has a UI, BSL-licensed). LavinMQ is an AMQP 0-9-1 broker (RabbitMQ-protocol-compatible, drop-in client library reuse) with clustering/replication, stream queues, and a built-in web Management UI, released under a permissive Apache-2.0 license — no licensing wrinkle like EMQX's BSL. It targets developers wiring up their own applications' async messaging/task-queue needs (comparable audience to Centrifugo's pub/sub use case) rather than end-users, but is technically the cleanest-licensed, most actively developed broker candidate evaluated so far.
usefulness_rationale: Message queues are foundational infrastructure many self-hosted stacks (and custom customer apps) depend on, and having a Management UI plus a permissive license makes LavinMQ meaningfully better-fitted to this catalogue's Traefik-fronted, browser-managed pattern than Mosquitto and cleaner licensing-wise than EMQX. Capped at medium, not high, because — like Centrifugo — it's backend infrastructure a technical customer integrates into their own application rather than a stand-alone tool with immediate end-user value.
blocking_issues:
LavinMQ boots with a hardcoded guest/guest user, and the official Docker image starts with --default-user-only-loopback=false, i.e. that default account is reachable from any network interface, not just localhost, unless changed at deploy time. There is no environment variable or config-file setting to inject a first-boot password the way RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS works for RabbitMQ — the guest/guest credential is fixed at container start. Changing it requires an install.sh step that calls LavinMQ's HTTP Management API (PUT /api/users/guest) after boot, authenticating as guest/guest and immediately overwriting the password — the same bootstrap-then-overwrite shape already used for the Elasticsearch/ Kibana analyses, not a novel blocker on its own.

That overwrite call does support hash-based credential projection: PUT /api/users/:name accepts a password_hash field plus a hashing_algorithm parameter, and the server source (src/lavinmq/auth/user.cr) confirms bcrypt is one of the four supported algorithms (bcrypt, SHA256, SHA512, MD5) — so generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD" is structurally deliverable via that install.sh call, unlike EMQX's plaintext-only Dashboard field or Centrifugo's plaintext admin_password.

LavinMQ's actual purpose — accepting AMQP client connections — is a raw TCP protocol (5672 plaintext / 5671 TLS), not HTTP. Only the Management UI (15672, HTTP) can sit behind Traefik; the AMQP port(s) need direct raw TCP exposure the same way wg-easy exposes its VPN port, which is a workable but non-default pattern for this catalogue. A recipe would need to expose both: Traefik-fronted 15672 for the UI/API and a raw 5672 (+ optionally 5671) port for actual broker use — without the raw port, the broker is installable but functionally useless to any client.
summary: LavinMQ is an actively developed (v2.9.1, 2026-07-01, ~monthly cadence), Apache-2.0-licensed AMQP message broker with a built-in web Management UI and no catalogue overlap — it would be the first message-broker recipe, and the cleanest-licensed of the three brokers evaluated (versus Mosquitto's no-UI and EMQX's BSL license). Mechanically it is installable today: the fixed guest/guest credential can be overwritten post-boot via the Management HTTP API using a bcrypt password hash, matching generated_from's supported algorithm list, the same bootstrap-then-overwrite install.sh pattern used for Elasticsearch/ Kibana. The remaining caveat is architectural rather than a hard blocker: LavinMQ's core function is a raw AMQP TCP port (5672/5671), not HTTP, so the recipe needs both a Traefik-fronted management UI and a directly-exposed raw broker port for the broker to actually be useful to a connecting client. Recommend build_with_caveats.

upstream_license: GPL-2.0 (LAM community edition; "LAM Pro" adds paid features, not required for core function)

Verified via github.com/LDAPAccountManager/lam/releases.atom: 9.3 (2025-09-16) -> 9.4 (2025-12-13) -> 9.5 (2026-03-17) -> 9.6 (2026-06-12) -> 9.6.1 (2026-06-17), a steady ~3-month major cadence with bugfix point releases in between. differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes manages an LDAP/directory-services layer. LAM is a pure management UI for an existing OpenLDAP directory (create/edit users, groups, DHCP entries, etc.) — a genuinely different slice of infrastructure than anything we ship today. Closest cousin is Guacamole, which can *authenticate against* LDAP but has no directory management UI of its own.
usefulness_rationale: Niche/technical: only useful to a customer who already runs (or is about to run) their own OpenLDAP directory, which is a small slice of our self-hoster audience compared to broadly-appealing tools like Vaultwarden or n8n. Same "needs a pre-existing external system" caveat as Adminer, but for a narrower dependency (LDAP vs. any SQL database).
summary: LAM is a single-container PHP app (ghcr.io/ldapaccountmanager/lam, latest 9.6.1) exposing one HTTP port (80), reverse-proxy-compatible, no database dependency by default. Its architecture splits auth into two layers, and both fit our current mechanism without needing a customer to supply arbitrary values at /compose time: (1) the LDAP directory connection ("server profile") is edited through LAM's own config screen, gated by a master config password whose documented default is the fixed, well-known string "lam" — a hardcoded credential the app itself doesn't force you to change, which per our schema is fine to leave as-is behind a Traefik basic_auth:true gate rather than something we must project; (2) day-to-day login to browse/manage the LDAP tree is a per-session LDAP bind DN + password typed into LAM's login form at each visit — same runtime-entry pattern as Adminer's per-connection DB login, not a persisted secret we need to provision. So installable_today: true with a required basic_auth gate (password from `generated_from` on the customer's root password, same pattern as n8n/WUD/Adminer). The catch is usefulness, not installability: LAM only manages a directory that must already exist — we don't ship OpenLDAP itself in this recipe, and pairing one in isn't a drop-in fix since the LDAP admin bind password would then become the actual working login and OpenLDAP's default hash schemes (SSHA/CRYPT) aren't in the generated_from-supported algo list (argon2, bcrypt) today. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically installable and low engineering cost, but a narrow, technical audience that must bring its own LDAP server to get any value from it.

Repo is not archived, CHANGELOG.md is actively maintained, and the official Docker image (leantime/leantime) is tagged in lockstep with each release. Clearly active, well-maintained project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers project/task management. Leantime is a goals-and-tasks PM tool (kanban, Gantt, sprints, time tracking) aimed explicitly at non-project-managers/ADHD-friendly teams — a distinct customer search ("project management", "Monday.com/Trello alternative") from anything already shipped (n8n is workflow automation, Gitea is source control, not task tracking).
usefulness_rationale: Project management is one of the most commonly self-hosted SaaS replacements (Monday.com/Asana/Trello alternative), broad appeal beyond developers, and the app is architecturally simple: single PHP app container + MySQL, one HTTP port, standard Traefik-fronted deployment with no raw ports or protocols.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the official docker-leantime repo's sample.env and README: Leantime has no admin-username/admin-password environment variable at all. The app boots with zero users and directs the first visitor to a public /install setup wizard where they create the sole admin account interactively in the browser — whoever reaches that wizard first owns the instance. This is the same structural shape documented in apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml and apps-gaps/airtrail.yaml: there is no `type: password` parameter on Leantime's own login to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because the credential is created client-side through the setup wizard, not injected via env var at container start.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would close the open race to reach /install first, but per the 2FAuth/AirTrail precedent it only relocates the problem one layer out: the customer still needs their own distinct credential for the in-app wizard, and today's basic_auth mechanism has no channel to hand the customer a *second* credential beyond the single root-password projection already consumed by the gate itself.
summary: Leantime is an active, well-maintained, high-value catalogue candidate — self-hosted project management fills a real gap distinct from all 24 current recipes, and its architecture (single app container + MySQL, one HTTP port) is straightforwardly Traefik-compatible. It fails the installability test for the same structural reason as 2FAuth and AirTrail: the sole admin account is provisioned through an open, first-visitor web setup wizard with no env-var hook, which neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely resolve. The internal LEAN_SESSION_PASSWORD and MySQL credentials are trivially server-generated and not blocking on their own. Revisit once upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow, or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond root-password projection.

name: Letta
source_description: Open-source framework for building stateful AI agents with persistent memory
version_health_notes: letta-ai/letta shipped roughly monthly releases from v0.15.0 (2026-11-25) through v0.16.7 (2026-03-31), then only one more release, v0.16.8 (2026-05-14) — about 2.9 months with no follow-up as of today (2026-08-05). More importantly, the repo's own README now states this is "the legacy Letta server" and that "active development has moved to the Letta Agent repo" (letta-ai/letta-code), with self-hosting an API server "now done via the App Server". The repo is not archived (still 24k+ stars, open issues/PRs get triaged) but upstream itself frames the exact product matching Hostinger's description — a self-hosted, Dockerized stateful-agent API server — as superseded. Treat as maintenance-only rather than actively developed, even though the release cadence alone would look merely "slowing".
differentiation: Letta is a backend framework/API server for building custom agents with persistent, structured long-term memory (memory blocks, archival memory) plus an ADE (Agent Development Environment) web UI for inspecting/debugging that agent state — it targets developers writing against the Letta SDK/REST API, not end users chatting with a pre-built agent. That's distinct from open-webui (consumer chat frontend over local models) and hermes-agent (turnkey messaging-app agent), but it's a narrower, more technical audience than either.
usefulness_rationale: Mechanically installable, but low general usefulness for our hosting customer base: it's a developer framework consumed mainly through an SDK/API rather than a ready-to-use app, and the specific self-hosted server product it would package is the one upstream itself has deprecated in favor of a different architecture (see version_health).
secrets_required_at_first_boot: ADE/API access gate; Postgres password (internal, app-to-db only)
secrets_expressible_today: ADE/API access gate:traefik_basic_auth; Postgres password (internal, app-to-db only):server_generated_no_customer_input
blocking_issues:
Name/product ambiguity: 'Letta' today spans two divergent products under the same GitHub org — the legacy letta-ai/letta server (Dockerized, Postgres-backed, matches Hostinger's description, analyzed here) and the newer 'Letta Code'/App Server product (active development, CLI/coding-agent oriented, no documented docker-compose). This analysis targets the legacy server since it's the one that matches the catalogue description and ships an official Docker image; a reviewer should confirm that's the intended candidate.
ADE/API access gate: Letta has no customer-facing login form of its own unless SECURE=true is set; the API is open by default. This is gateable via Traefik basic_auth (see secrets_expressible_today) rather than a native login.
The app needs an LLM provider credential (e.g. OPENAI_API_KEY, or an OLLAMA_BASE_URL pointing at a reachable Ollama instance) to actually create/run agents. This is not required for the container to boot and is configured by the customer inside the ADE web UI after first login (same deferred-config pattern already shipped for hermes-agent's OPENROUTER_API_KEY), so it does not block installable_today, but it does mean the app is non-functional out of the box until the customer does that manual step themselves.
summary: Letta is mechanically installable under the current mechanism — no hard blocker exists (the LLM key gap is deferred to post-provision self-service like hermes-agent, and the missing native login is gateable via Traefik basic_auth) — but it's a poor catalogue fit: it's a developer-oriented agent framework/SDK rather than a ready-to-use end-user app, overlaps conceptually with three existing recipes (open-webui, hermes-agent, ollama), and the specific self-hosted server product matching Hostinger's description is one upstream itself describes as legacy, with development energy now going into a different, non-Dockerized product. Not recommended for the catalogue.

version_health_notes: Monthly (sometimes sub-monthly) release cadence throughout 2026 — 5.0.0 (2026-05-03), 5.0.1/5.0.2 (early-to-mid May), 5.0.3 (2026-06-03), 5.1.0 (2026-06-07), 5.2.0 (2026-07-03), 5.3.0 (2026-08-03, 2 days before this analysis). Repo has 5,000+ commits, dozens of open issues/PRs under active triage. Clearly active, not maintenance-only. Project is a continuation of the discontinued open-source "Booked Scheduler" (phpScheduleIt lineage), rebranded LibreBooking after Booked Scheduler went closed-source/SaaS-only in 2020 — LibreBooking itself has diverged substantially since and is the actively maintained upstream, not an abandoned fork.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover room/equipment/shared-asset booking or scheduling. Closest neighbors (Uptime Kuma, Portainer, Gitea) are unrelated domains. This would be a net-new category for the catalogue — useful to small orgs, coworking spaces, or teams wanting to schedule meeting rooms/equipment without a SaaS subscription.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct use case with no in-catalogue competitor, but resource booking is a narrower niche than the productivity/automation/AI tools that dominate the current catalogue — likely lower demand than a generic top-of-funnel app.
summary: LibreBooking is an active, GPL-3.0 room/equipment/resource-booking web app with an official single-container Docker image (needs a MariaDB companion), a single HTTP port, and monthly releases through August 2026 — no EOL or dormancy concerns. It fills a category gap none of the current 24 recipes cover. Setup is two steps, and both fit the current mechanism: the entrypoint only pre-populates config.php (DB connection string, install password) without creating the schema or an admin account, but install.sh can create the schema server-side by importing upstream's own database_schema/*.sql files in the documented order — the /install wizard is just a browser front-end over those, so no HTML form scripting is needed and every secret involved (LB_DATABASE_PASSWORD, LB_INSTALL_PASSWORD, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD) is patternless and server-generated. The admin account is then the n8n pattern: register.php is a public, unauthenticated page that is not behind the install-password guard, self-registration is on by default, and whoever registers with the configured admin.email gets admin — so the customer types their own plaintext credential into the app's own form and no hash projection is required. The one thing to be explicit about is that admin.email has no customer-input channel and must stay at a fixed default, which makes the mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate the real auth boundary protecting open self-registration until the customer completes signup. Recommend build_now; usefulness rated medium given the narrower niche relative to the catalogue's productivity/automation/AI focus.

name: LibreChat
source_description: LibreChat is an AI chat interface with RAG support for multi-provider LLM use
version_health_notes: v0.8.7 published 2026-06-24, ~6 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Preceding tags (v0.8.6 rc1/stable, v0.8.5, v0.8.4) shipped at a roughly monthly cadence through 2026, alongside a parallel `chart-x.y.z` Helm release track. Repo is not archived, has 41.7k stars, 4,870+ commits on main, and currently has 328 open PRs / 339 open issues — clearly active, ongoing development.
differentiation: Same "self-hosted chat frontend for any LLM provider" core as open-webui, and the same "chat + RAG + agents" pitch as anythingllm (which is only a gap-analysis candidate, not yet a recipe), but LibreChat goes further on both axes at once: built-in RAG via a dedicated pgvector-backed rag_api service (not just an Ollama pairing), a code interpreter and artifact/canvas rendering, MCP server integration, agents that can author their own skills, multi-user accounts with email/password plus optional OAuth/SAML/LDAP SSO, and a separate bundled admin panel for user/config management. It is the most feature-complete of the three, at the cost of being the heaviest stack (five containers: api, admin-panel, mongodb, meilisearch, vectordb (pgvector), plus rag_api) versus open-webui's two and anythingllm's one.

The five-service footprint (vs. open-webui's two) also raises the resource floor and operational surface for what is, from a customer's first-look perspective, the same category of app.
summary: LibreChat is active and well-maintained (monthly releases, 41.7k stars, no EOL signal) and is installable today with no customer-supplied secret at all: the required env vars (JWT_SECRET, JWT_REFRESH_SECRET, CREDS_KEY, CREDS_IV, ADMIN_PANEL_SESSION_SECRET) are all patternless strings the platform can generate server-side, and account creation happens through LibreChat's own first-visit registration/login screen (ALLOW_REGISTRATION defaults to true) — the same self-serve pattern already used by uptime-kuma and immich, needing neither root-password projection nor a Traefik basic_auth gate. Actually using it productively requires an LLM provider API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.), but that is configured post-provision through the app's own Endpoints settings UI, the same deferred pattern already shipped for openclaw and hermes-agent, so it is not a first-boot blocker. The open question is fit rather than mechanism: it overlaps meaningfully with open-webui (already a shipping recipe) and anythingllm (a separate build_with_caveats gap candidate), covering the same "chat with any LLM provider" ground with extra RAG/ agents/MCP/SSO capability, at the cost of a five-container stack instead of open-webui's two — worth building for the added capability, but only after weighing it against the two adjacent AI-chat entries already in or proposed for the catalogue.

name: LibreNMS
source_description: Auto-discovering SNMP network monitoring with rich alerting and graphs
version_health_notes: Monthly release cadence throughout 2026 (26.2.0 Feb 16, 26.3.0 Mar 16, 26.5.1 May 20, 26.6.0 Jun 15, 26.7.0 Jul 20 — with a 39-contributor changelog on the latest tag). Latest release is ~2.5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Clearly an actively maintained project, not maintenance-only or dormant.
differentiation: Uptime Kuma (our only existing monitoring recipe) does synthetic HTTP/TCP/ping checks against endpoints the customer configures by hand. LibreNMS is a different class of tool: SNMP-based auto-discovery and polling of network devices (switches, routers, APs, UPSes) with interface graphing, threshold alerting, and a device inventory — it monitors the network fabric itself, not application uptime. No existing recipe covers this ground.
usefulness_rationale: Real value for a customer running any amount of network hardware (a small ISP, an MSP, a homelab with managed switches), but it's a niche relative to our current app-hosting-focused catalogue and needs SNMP read access to the customer's own network devices to be useful at all — something no AF-hosted instance can assume by default. Value is real but narrower than a general-purpose app.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: MARIADB_PASSWORD (or MYSQL_PASSWORD); basic-auth gate credential for the LibreNMS web UI
secrets_expressible_today: MARIADB_PASSWORD (or MYSQL_PASSWORD):server_generated_no_customer_input; basic-auth gate credential for the LibreNMS web UI:traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
LibreNMS has no environment-variable or config-file channel to set the initial admin user/password at container boot. The official librenms/docker image either creates a default "librenms"/"librenms" account or prompts the visitor to set username/password via a first-visit web setup wizard, depending on version — in both cases the credential is not something af-api's /compose can project a hash into via `generated_from`. This is the exact "no login of its own worth wiring up, gate the whole thing behind Traefik basic_auth instead" case the schema describes, and that gate mechanism (IF-1312) is still unmerged.

Full functionality requires a multi-container stack (librenms app + MariaDB/MySQL + Redis + a poller "dispatcher" sidecar, plus cron for scheduled polling) — meaningfully heavier than our current single-container-plus-DB recipes, though mechanically no different in kind from immich/anytype-server.

Optional syslog-ng (UDP/514) and snmptrapd (UDP/162) receiver containers in the official compose are non-HTTP raw ports; they are NOT required for core SNMP-polling functionality and can be omitted from a recipe, keeping the shipped app single-HTTP-port and Traefik-compatible.
summary: LibreNMS is an active, well-maintained SNMP network-monitoring tool with a genuine gap versus our catalogue (nothing else does device/interface monitoring), and it's reverse-proxy-friendly on its core web UI port if the optional syslog/snmptrap receivers are left out. It cannot ship as a recipe today because it has no supported way to receive a customer credential at first boot — the only viable gate is Traefik basic_auth, which needs IF-1312 merged first. Revisit once that lands; the app itself is otherwise a reasonable build candidate.

The blocker is fit, not mechanism — it duplicates Immich, which already covers self-hosted AI-powered photo/video management in this catalogue, and Immich is the stronger pick on ecosystem and momentum. Not recommended unless the goal is explicitly to offer customers a choice of photo-library apps.

summary: Lidarr is a single-container app (linuxserver/lidarr, port 8686, no separate database service — config and its internal SQLite DB live in /config) that is mechanically as simple to deploy as uptime-kuma or vaultwarden, and reverse-proxy compatible behind Traefik on lidarr.<base_domain>. As of Lidarr v2+, authentication is required and set up through the app's own first-run wizard (choose "Forms" auth, set username/password interactively in-browser) rather than an environment variable — the same self-serve pattern already used by autobrr/immich/uptime-kuma, so no generated_from projection or Traefik basic_auth gate is needed to avoid an open-by-default install. installable_today is true with zero blocking issues. Recommendation is build_with_caveats rather than build_now: the app is a genuinely new category for the catalogue and mechanically ready to ship, but its core value proposition (hands-off music acquisition) is coupled to an indexer and download client that don't exist as AF recipes yet, so it would land as a capable library organizer with its headline automation feature dormant until a customer wires up external services on their own.

summary: Lightdash is installable today with no customer-supplied secret at all: every required env var (LIGHTDASH_SECRET, the internal Postgres password, the MinIO root credential used for result caching) is a patternless string the platform can generate server-side, and the admin/first-user account is created through Lightdash's own first-visit signup screen — the same self-serve pattern already accepted for n8n, uptime-kuma, immich, and (per apps-gaps/librechat.yaml) LibreChat. Upstream is exceptionally active (near-continuous automated releases, no EOL signal) and the app fills a genuine gap — no existing recipe covers self-hosted BI/dashboarding. The stack is four containers (app, Postgres, MinIO for query-result caching, a headless-browser service for scheduled/exported dashboard images), heavier than a typical single-service recipe but comparable to immich's multi-service footprint. The caveat is audience, not mechanism: Lightdash is only useful to a customer with (or willing to stand up) a dbt project and a data warehouse to connect it to — recommended to build, but expect a smaller addressable slice of the catalogue's customer base than general-purpose tools.

name: LightRAG
source_description: Simple and fast graph-based RAG framework with dual-level knowledge retrieval
version_health_notes: v1.5.5 shipped 2026-07-31, just 5 days before today (2026-08-05). PyPI/release history shows a tight, near-weekly cadence through 2026 (v1.5.0 on 2026-06-03, v1.5.1 06-09, v1.5.2 06-11, v1.5.3 06-14, v1.5.4 06-24, v1.5.5rc1 07-13, v1.5.5 07-31), on top of a steady monthly-ish cadence back through 2025 (1.0.x from Nov 2024, 1.1-1.2.x early 2025, 1.3.x through mid-2025, 1.4.x from Sep 2025). The `ghcr.io/hkuds/lightrag` image publishes matching versioned tags (not just `latest`), including the current `v1.5.5`. No archival or slowdown signal — this is one of the more actively maintained candidates seen in this batch.
differentiation: Neither open-webui nor bare ollama does document ingestion or knowledge- graph construction — open-webui is a chat frontend, ollama is just an inference runtime with no UI at all. LightRAG's actual value is the ingestion pipeline: upload documents, build a dual-level (entity + relationship) knowledge graph plus vector index over them, then query with graph-aware retrieval, and visually explore the resulting graph. That "turn a document pile into a queryable knowledge graph" capability doesn't exist anywhere in the current 24-recipe catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely new capability (document-grounded graph RAG) rather than a repackaging of open-webui/ollama, so there's a real reason a customer would pick it over what's already offered. Held to medium rather than high because it is a developer/technical-user tool (no first-run wizard, config is entirely env-var driven — see below) rather than a turnkey consumer app, and because a fully local, good-quality deployment requires bundling Ollama, which raises the resource floor and answer quality ceiling considerably versus a cloud-LLM-backed deployment.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: gate credential for the web UI/API (Traefik basic_auth)
secrets_expressible_today: gate credential for the web UI/API (Traefik basic_auth):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
LightRAG cannot answer a single query without a working LLM_BINDING (openai, azure_openai, bedrock, gemini, ollama, ...) plus matching EMBEDDING_BINDING — these, and any associated *_BINDING_API_KEY, are set via environment variables read at container start. Unlike AnythingLLM (apps-gaps/anythingllm.yaml), there is no in-UI first-run wizard to configure this after boot — upstream docs are explicit that the .env must be populated with LLM/embedding config before the server starts, and there's no account-creation flow in the WebUI either.
If the recipe pointed LLM_BINDING/EMBEDDING_BINDING at an external provider (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Gemini), the required LLM_BINDING_API_KEY / EMBEDDING_BINDING_API_KEY are external API keys with no customer-input channel today — this alone would make the recipe not installable as designed.
The escape hatch precedented by our own open-webui recipe is to hardcode LLM_BINDING=ollama / EMBEDDING_BINDING=ollama against a bundled Ollama sidecar with a pre-pulled default model, so no external key or customer secret is needed for the LLM at all (server-generated, no customer input, like open-webui + ollama today). That removes the hard blocker, but it is a real design decision, not a trivial default: it turns this into a 2-3 service stack (LightRAG + Ollama [+ a lightweight KV/vector store if not using the built-in file-based NanoVectorDB/JsonKVStorage/NetworkXStorage defaults]), pushes the RAM floor up to roughly open-webui's territory (~8GB+ for a usable local model), and yields materially weaker retrieval/answer quality than a cloud-LLM-backed deployment — acceptable for a "local-only, no data leaves the server" positioning, but a real quality/resource trade-off to surface to the customer, not a free lunch.
By default the server has no built-in login (LIGHTRAG_API_KEY / AUTH_ACCOUNTS+TOKEN_SECRET are opt-in), and upstream's own docs warn that on 0.0.0.0 "every endpoint is public" without them — so the WebUI/API must sit behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate the same way n8n/WUD/Open WebUI do, not be left open.
summary: LightRAG is under genuinely active development (latest tag 5 days old) and fills a real gap — document-to-knowledge-graph RAG — that nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers. It clears the auth bar cleanly: no built-in login, so a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password projected) is enough, the same pattern already used for n8n/Open WebUI. The catch is the LLM dependency: LightRAG cannot function at all without a configured LLM+embedding backend, that config is env-var-only with no in-UI setup wizard (unlike AnythingLLM), and pointing it at any external provider would need an API key we have no channel to collect today. The only installable-today path is bundling a local Ollama backend the way open-webui already does, which works but meaningfully raises the resource floor and lowers answer quality versus a cloud-backed deployment — hence build_with_caveats rather than a clean build_now.

name: Linkding
source_description: Linkding is a minimal, fast, self-hosted bookmark manager
version_health_notes: v1.45.0 tagged 2026-01-06, ~7 months before today (2026-08-05) — longer than the roughly 1-2 month gaps between the preceding releases (1.44.0 2025-10-05, 1.44.1 2025-10-11, 1.44.2 2025-12-13, 1.45.0 2026-01-06), so tagged-release cadence has slowed. However commit activity on `master` is current as of 2026-08-05 (commits the day before this analysis), so the project is actively developed, just without a recent tag cut — not dormant or abandoned.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover bookmark management. Linkding adds a lightweight, single-container, cross-device bookmark manager with tagging, full-text search, browser extensions, and automatic archiving (Wayback Machine snapshots) — a distinct productivity use case not served by anything in the catalogue today.
usefulness_rationale: Broad appeal for anyone wanting a private, self-hosted alternative to browser-synced or third-party bookmark services; small footprint and single container make it an easy, low-maintenance addition if it were installable.
blocking_issues:
Linkding has no self-registration and no anonymous/public-access mode — the only way to create a usable account is the container's LD_SUPERUSER_NAME / LD_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD env vars, checked directly in the upstream source (bookmarks/management/commands/create_initial_superuser.py): `user.set_password(superuser_password)`. Django's `set_password()` takes the raw plaintext and re-hashes it internally (PBKDF2 by default) — it does not accept a pre-computed verifier hash the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no way to provision this superuser account through the current mechanism.

A Traefik basic_auth gate does not substitute here: it would only protect network reachability, not solve the app's own login. Without a superuser account, the customer has no credentials to authenticate into Linkding itself and the instance is unusable on first boot.
summary: Linkding is a well-maintained, single-container, single-HTTP-port (9090) bookmark manager behind no existing recipe, and would be a clean addition to the catalogue on merit. It's blocked today because its only account- provisioning path (LD_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD) requires the plaintext admin password, not a hash, and af-api's root-password projection only ever produces a hash — there is no plaintext-credential input channel today, and Traefik basic_auth can't stand in for the app's own login. Revisit once a plaintext-projection mechanism exists, or if upstream adds a way to seed the superuser from a pre-hashed password.

name: LiteLLM
source_description: LiteLLM is an AI gateway to call 100+ LLMs using OpenAI format
upstream_license: MIT (core); enterprise/ subdirectory under a separate commercial license
version_health_notes: Weekly-cadence stable releases (v1.91.0 on 2026-07-04 through v1.95.0 on 2026-08-01, roughly one every 7-10 days), with day-0 support for new frontier models (Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.6) shipping the same week they launch. Latest release is 4 days before today (2026-08-05). No signs of slowdown, archival, or EOL.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes provide a unified LLM gateway. Ollama runs local models and Open WebUI is a chat frontend (optionally backed by Ollama) — neither lets a customer point many different apps at one OpenAI-compatible endpoint while load-balancing, cost-tracking, and swapping between OpenAI/Anthropic/Bedrock/Vertex/local Ollama models without changing client code. LiteLLM sits a layer below Open WebUI / n8n / any custom app and is a natural companion recipe for developer and AI-automation customers running multiple LLM-backed services.
usefulness_rationale: Fills a real gap for customers running several AI-integrated apps who want centralized API-key management, spend tracking, and provider failover instead of hardcoding provider keys into each app.
blocking_issues:
LITELLM_MASTER_KEY and UI_USERNAME/UI_PASSWORD are all plain strings that LiteLLM compares directly (bearer-token match / UI login) — none of them accept a pre-computed argon2/bcrypt hash the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash, so it cannot produce a value that equals the customer's own root password in LiteLLM's eyes. This is the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case the schema calls a structural blocker, not a missing-algorithm gap.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (root-password derived) solves the "don't sit open on the internet" problem, but LiteLLM's own UI login screen is still behind that gate and still needs a credential — the customer would hit a second login they have no way to know unless UI_USERNAME/UI_PASSWORD are fixed to recipe-documented static values. That works functionally (weak credential behind a real auth boundary, same shape as the Adminer pattern) but means every LiteLLM instance from this recipe would ship identical default in-app credentials, which is a product decision the recipe author should confirm, not an autonomous call for this analysis.

It needs Postgres (structurally similar to the n8n/paperless-ngx template pair) and has a real web UI, so it fits the catalogue's reverse-proxy pattern mechanically. The blocker is auth: its master key and UI login are plaintext-compared credentials with no hash-projection support, so `generated_from` cannot tie them to the customer's root password, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate alone doesn't clear LiteLLM's own login screen. Shipping it today would mean baking in a fixed, recipe-documented UI login behind the Traefik gate — workable but a deliberate product call, not something to default into silently. Recommend flagging as blocked_on_platform pending that decision (or a future secret-delivery mechanism beyond root-password hash projection).

name: Littlelink-Server
source_description: Stateless self-hosted Linktree alternative for personal link-in-bio pages
latest_version: latest (no versioned/semver tags published — Docker Hub and GHCR only ship a rolling `:latest` tag; the GitHub repo has zero tagged releases and zero git tags)
version_health_notes: No formal releases or version tags exist at all — checked both GitHub Releases (empty, "There aren't any releases here") and `git ls-remote --tags` (no tags returned) as of 2026-08-05. Docker Hub shows the `latest` image tag last pushed ~4 days before today (2026-08-05), and the repo has 817 commits and 1.1k stars, so development is active and current — just never cut into discrete versions. This means a recipe could not pin `app_version`/`image` to a stable tag the way RFC-002 expects; the only option would be pinning to a specific image digest (sha256@...) and manually bumping it, since there is no semver tag to track.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers a public "link in bio" landing page. The closest neighbors in apps-gaps (linkding, linkwarden, linkace) are private bookmark managers behind a login — a different use case from a single public page of outbound links meant to be shared on social media. If installable, it would be a genuinely new, low-footprint category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Broad appeal (content creators, small businesses, personal branding) and a tiny single-container footprint make this attractive in the abstract — but its entire value proposition is the customer's own name, bio, avatar, and links, which (see installability below) cannot actually be supplied through the platform today.
blocking_issues:
LittleLink-Server has no login, no admin UI, and no database — it is explicitly stateless. Every piece of page content (NAME, BIO, AVATAR_URL, META_TITLE, social/link URLs, custom buttons, theme, analytics IDs) is supplied only via container environment variables read at request time, and the only way to change any of it is to set new env vars and restart the container. There is no in-app onboarding or settings screen the customer could use after boot, the way most other recipes rely on the app's own first-run wizard.

Unlike the credential cases this schema is built around (root- password projection, Traefik basic_auth), what's missing here isn't a secret at all — it's the platform's total absence of a channel for *any* customer-supplied value beyond a domain and a root- password hash. `/compose` cannot pass through free-text content like a name, bio, or a list of social links. Deployed as-is, the recipe would boot successfully but publish either the upstream maintainer's own placeholder links (Techno Tim's bio/socials from the shipped `.env.example`/`docker-compose.yml` defaults) or a blank page — never the customer's actual profile, which is the entire point of the app.

This is a broader gap than IF-1420 (hash projection) or IF-1312 (basic_auth gate) can close; those solve one-credential-at-a-time login provisioning, not arbitrary multi-field content input. There's no existing IONOS platform ticket tracking generic customer content fields for `/compose`, as far as this analysis found.

Separately, no versioned tag exists upstream to pin (see version_health) — a secondary blocker for RFC-002's image-tag-pinned rule, though a digest pin could work around that one alone.
summary: LittleLink-Server is a well-maintained, single-container, single-port, MIT-licensed link-in-bio page generator with no direct equivalent in the current catalogue. It cannot ship as a recipe today, though, because its only configuration path is free-text environment variables (name, bio, avatar, links) with no login or in-app editor to fall back on, and `/compose` has no channel for arbitrary customer-supplied content — only a domain and a hash of the root password. summary: Livebook is a single official container (ghcr.io/livebook-dev/livebook, pin to a dated tag like "0.19.9") exposing one HTTP port (8080, the 8081 iframe port is only relevant when served over plain http:// — over https:// via Traefik, iframes default to loading from https://livebookusercontent.com, so no second port needs routing). The clean fit is to disable Livebook's built-in auth (`LIVEBOOK_TOKEN_ENABLED=false`, no `LIVEBOOK_PASSWORD` set) and gate the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth` credential instead, the same pattern already used for WUD/Adminer-shaped apps with no expressible native login. summary: LLDAP is an active (last commit 2026-07-19, weekly-ish cadence though official semver tags land unevenly every 9-14 months; latest tag v0.6.3, GPL-3.0), single-container Rust app with an official Docker image (lldap/lldap) and a single admin-facing HTTP web UI port (17170, Traefik-compatible) plus an LDAP protocol port (3890) that only needs to be reachable by other containers on the same stack, not the public internet — same "internal-only secondary port" pattern already used by adguard-home/pihole. Mechanically it is fully installable today: the one customer-facing secret is a single admin password (LLDAP_LDAP_USER_PASS) that doubles as both the LDAP bind credential and the web-UI login, which maps cleanly onto `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` (the exact Vaultwarden ADMIN_TOKEN pattern); the JWT signing secret and the private-key seed are both patternless values the customer never needs to see or supply. The caveat is entirely about usefulness, not mechanism: LLDAP alone is a directory with no consumer — it only becomes valuable once the customer separately configures another LDAP-aware app (several of which already exist in this catalogue) to authenticate against it, a manual post-install step in that other app's own settings. Recommend build_with_caveats: technically clean to ship, but document the "pair it with an LDAP client app" dependency prominently so customers don't install it expecting standalone functionality.

This is the same self-hosted-music-streaming niche already surfaced by prior gap analyses on Gonic ([[gonic]]), Airsonic Advanced ([[airsonic-advanced]]), and Ampache ([[ampache]]) — LMS is a fourth, distinct candidate in that space rather than a new category.

Ceiling is medium rather than high because it's only useful to a customer who already has a personal music library to mount, a narrower audience than general-purpose tools, and because it would be the fourth Subsonic-API candidate analyzed for this catalogue — the value of adding a specific one depends more on picking the best of the four than on this slot being uniquely compelling.
summary: LMS is a healthy, actively-maintained project (monthly tagged releases, most recently 2.5 weeks before this analysis) and is mechanically installable today. Unlike Gonic/Airsonic Advanced, it ships with no fixed default admin credential at all — on first HTTP request an interactive setup wizard lets whoever visits first create the admin username/password, stored internally (bcrypt) with no env var or config-file input to pre-seed it. That means `generated_from` root-password projection has no channel to hit (there is no parameter to project into before the wizard runs), and more importantly the app would sit open on the internet for anyone to race the customer to that wizard and claim the admin account. The recipe should gate the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth: true` (projected from the customer's root password) the same way n8n and WUD do, closing that race entirely; the customer then completes LMS's own admin setup wizard themselves once behind the gate. Single HTTP port (5082 by default), documented `behind-reverse-proxy`/`trusted-proxies` config options, so it sits cleanly behind Traefik on `<slug>.<base_domain>` with no extra raw ports. Needs at least two volumes (persistent working data, read-only music directory) — how the customer's library gets into the container is an open design question for a real recipe pass, out of scope here. Net: build_now, but worth comparing against the other three Subsonic-API candidates already analyzed (Gonic, Airsonic Advanced, Ampache) before committing engineering time to more than one.
