name: Logto
source_description: Logto is a comprehensive identity and authentication platform with OAuth and OIDC support
version_health_notes: Monthly release cadence going back at least a year (v1.35.0 2025-12-30 through v1.42.0 2026-07-30, roughly one tag every 4-5 weeks). Repo is not archived; last push to master was 2026-08-06 (yesterday relative to today, 2026-08-05, i.e. actively committed to within the last day). 181 open issues being triaged. No indication of maintenance-only mode or EOL.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes provide identity/access-management functionality (OIDC/OAuth2.1 provider, SSO, RBAC, social/enterprise connectors) that a customer could use to centralize login for their own apps. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue, not a duplicate of anything shipping today.
usefulness_rationale: High conceptual value (IAM-as-a-service is a common self-host want, especially paired with the AI/automation recipes already in the catalogue), but Logto's two-surface architecture (separate app and admin console ports, see below) makes it a heavier integration lift than most of our single-container, single-port recipes.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: POSTGRES password (internal, not customer-facing); admin console access gate (to prevent an unauthenticated third party from racing the customer to complete the one-time admin sign-up wizard)
blocking_issues:
Logto's official docker-compose exposes two distinct HTTP surfaces on two different ports: 3001 (the OIDC/OAuth provider + end-user sign-in experience, meant to be public) and 3002 (the Admin Console, where the customer configures applications, connectors, and RBAC). Both need to be reachable over HTTP with their own hostname for the product to be usable. RFC-001 §4.3 states a recipe may declare "at most one HTTP port ... only the first gets a router" — there is no mechanism today to give a second port its own Traefik-routed subdomain, so the Admin Console (3002) cannot be exposed correctly under the current single-router-per-recipe constraint.

Logto OSS has no env var or CLI flag to pre-seed the initial admin account. The first person to open the Admin Console's "Welcome" page after boot picks their own username/password through a one-time sign-up wizard, and only one admin account is supported. This isn't a `generated_from: ROOT_PASSWORD`-projectable login (no plaintext or hash input field exists at boot) — the only way to make this safe is to gate the Admin Console itself behind Traefik `basic_auth` so only the customer can reach the wizard first. That gate can't be wired up independently of the port-routing blocker above, since Admin Console exposure is already blocked.
summary: Logto is an active, well-maintained (monthly releases, MPL-2.0, no EOL signals) OIDC/OAuth identity platform that would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue - no current recipe offers IAM/SSO. It is not installable under the current recipe mechanism, though: the product architecturally needs two independently-routed HTTP surfaces (public app on 3001, Admin Console on 3002), but RFC-001 limits a recipe to one Traefik-routed HTTP port, and the Admin Console's one-time, env-var-less sign-up wizard has no first-boot credential channel other than gating that same Admin Console behind basic auth. Revisit once multi-router-per-recipe support exists; until then this is blocked on the platform, not on Logto itself.

name: Loomio
source_description: Open-source platform for group discussions, polls, and collaborative decisions
version_health_notes: Very active: 8 releases (v3.1.0 through v3.1.7) in the two weeks 2026-07-21 to 2026-08-04, several of them security patches (SSRF protection, Active Storage RCE fix, API auth hardening). Latest release is 2 days before today (2026-08-05/06). No sign of slowdown or maintenance-only mode; repo is not archived.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers group discussion/decision-making/polling. This is a genuinely new category for the catalogue (closest thing in spirit, n8n/anytype-server, are automation/note-taking tools, not deliberation tools) — a customer running a co-op, NGO, or open-source project would have a real reason to want this that nothing else in the 24 recipes addresses.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct niche (governance/consensus-decision tooling for co-ops, activist groups, open-source communities) but a narrower target audience than most of the current catalogue's general-purpose productivity/AI/ infra tools.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: SMTP_SERVER / SMTP_USERNAME / SMTP_PASSWORD (customer's own outbound mail account); DEVISE_SECRET; SECRET_COOKIE_TOKEN; POSTGRES_PASSWORD; dashboard basic-auth gate
blocking_issues:
Loomio has no username/password admin account at all — Loomio's own auth model is passwordless: the first person to sign up receives a 6-digit code / magic link by email and that establishes the group's admin. There is no `generated_from: ROOT_PASSWORD`-projectable login parameter to target because the app itself has no password field.

The app is non-functional without working outbound SMTP (SMTP_SERVER/ SMTP_USERNAME/SMTP_PASSWORD in loomio-deploy's env_template) — every sign-in and notification goes through customer-supplied third-party mail-provider credentials. This is exactly the "external credential the app can't function without, no input channel" case in the installability table; a Traefik basic_auth gate keeps the unconfigured instance from sitting open, but does not solve the deeper problem that the app cannot complete first-boot without an arbitrary customer-owned SMTP account.

Bundled haraka service listens on raw port 25 for inbound mail routing (MX-record based reply-by-email); this is optional but if enabled it's a non-HTTP port outside the reverse-proxy model our recipes rely on.
summary: Loomio is an actively maintained (weekly-release-cadence, AGPL-3.0), genuinely differentiated addition — group deliberation/decision-making is not covered by any of the 24 current recipes. It is blocked today, though, because it has no password-based admin login to project a hashed root password into (auth is 100% email-magic-link based) and it cannot boot into a usable state without a customer-supplied third-party SMTP account, which has no input channel in the current `/compose` mechanism. A Traefik basic_auth gate (IF-1312) covers the "don't sit open on the internet" half of the problem but not the "app needs a working outbound-mail credential to do anything" half. Revisit once there is a generic arbitrary-secret input channel, not just root-password projection.

Lowcoder would be a genuinely new category (Retool/Appsmith/Tooljet-style builder) rather than overlapping ground.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for self-hosted low-code app builders, and this fills a category gap. Medium rather than high because the app is heavier (bundles Mongo+Redis, higher RAM footprint than most current recipes) and the slowing release cadence adds some risk to shipping it as a flagship recipe right now.
summary: The all-in-one `lowcoderorg/lowcoder-ce` image is a single container on port 3000 that bundles MongoDB + Redis internally — no extra services, no raw ports, fully reverse-proxy-compatible. The signup path needs no secret projection at all — the customer sets their real password themselves, in-app — so the only genuine first-boot secret is gating the domain with Traefik basic_auth (root-password-derived) so an anonymous visitor can't race the customer to the first signup and claim the instance/workspace before they do. That makes it installable today with no platform blockers. The one soft caveat is a slowing release cadence (7 months since the 2.7.6 tag, though upstream dev activity on the `dev` branch is still ongoing) and a heavier resource footprint than most existing recipes — still a reasonable build_now given it fills a genuine category gap (no low-code app builder in the current 24-recipe catalogue).

name: LubeLogger
source_description: Comprehensive vehicle maintenance and fuel management system
version_health_notes: Releases roughly every 2-4 weeks throughout 2026 (1.6.1 on 2026-02-26 up through 1.7.0 on 2026-07-13, ~3 weeks before this analysis on 2026-08-05). Actively maintained single-maintainer project with a documented feature roadmap, official docs site, and hosted demo instance.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers personal/vehicle asset tracking; the closest analogues (Paperless-ngx for documents, Uptime Kuma for monitoring) are unrelated domains. LubeLogger fills a distinct "personal record-keeping" niche — service history, fuel economy, reminders — that has consumer appeal but isn't a duplicate of anything currently offered.
usefulness_rationale: Popular in the self-hosted community (active r/selfhosted mentions, dedicated docs/config site) and simple to run, but it's a single-user/household utility rather than a team or business tool, so the addressable customer segment for a hosting platform is narrower than for e.g. Vaultwarden or n8n.
blocking_issues:
Authentication is disabled by default (LubeLogger boots with no login at all unless "Enable Authentication" is toggled). The only non-interactive way to provision a root login is via the UserNameHash/UserPasswordHash environment variables, both documented as "SHA256 Hash of the root username/password" — no plaintext env var and no setup-wizard API. `generated_from` today only supports `argon2` and `bcrypt`; SHA256 is not on the supported list, so the root-password projection mechanism cannot currently populate UserPasswordHash. This is a genuine hash-algorithm gap, not a plaintext-password requirement, so it is a soft blocker rather than a structural one.

As a fallback, gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (leaving LubeLogger's own EnableAuth off) is mechanically expressible today and would avoid the SHA256 gap entirely, at the cost of the app's native per-user accounts/OIDC features being unreachable behind the shared basic-auth prompt.
summary: LubeLogger is a well-maintained, actively-released, single-container vehicle maintenance tracker with a clean web UI and no overlap with the current catalogue. It is not installable today because its only non-interactive root-credential mechanism (UserNameHash/UserPasswordHash env vars) requires a SHA256 hash, which `generated_from` doesn't support yet (only argon2/bcrypt) — add SHA256 support, or ship it behind a Traefik `basic_auth` gate with the app's own auth left disabled, to make this build_now.

name: M3DB
source_description: Distributed time-series database and Prometheus long-term storage backend
version_health_notes: No tagged release since v1.5.0 on 2022-04-07 — over 4 years and 4 months before this analysis (2026-08-05). The repo itself is not archived and still receives commits (last commit 2026-05-20, e.g. m3db-client circuit-breaker work), so this isn't a fully dead project, but it has stopped cutting versioned releases entirely. Worse for packaging: the quay.io/m3db/m3dbnode image's `master` tag (the only tag newer than v1.5.0) was itself last built 2023-11-01 — nearly 3 years stale — so even tracking `master` instead of a version tag would not pick up any of the 2024-2026 source commits. There is no current image to pin.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes touch metrics storage or observability infrastructure, so on paper M3DB would fill a real gap: long-term, horizontally-scalable storage for Prometheus remote_write. In practice though it's infrastructure that other infrastructure (a customer's own Prometheus/Grafana stack) talks to, not something a customer opens in a browser and uses directly.
usefulness_rationale: M3DB is built for horizontally-scaled, multi-node Prometheus deployments at a scale far beyond a single self-hosted VM customer's needs — most self-hosters running Prometheus rely on its built-in local TSDB and never need a dedicated long-term-storage backend. The audience that would actually want this (teams operating enough Prometheus volume to outgrow local storage) is a poor match for our single-VM, domain-per-recipe customer profile.
blocking_issues:
M3DB has no browser web UI at all — it exposes a REST admin/data API (placement + namespace management on :7201, metrics scrape on :7203) meant to be called by machine clients (a customer's own Prometheus for remote_write, Grafana for queries), not opened by a customer in a browser on <slug>.<base_domain>. Gating the whole thing behind Traefik basic_auth would satisfy our secret-projection mechanism, but it would also break the actual use case: Prometheus remote_write would then need that same basic-auth credential embedded in the customer's own Prometheus config, and we have no channel to hand that credential to an external system the customer configures themselves.

No current pinned image exists to build a recipe on: the last versioned tag is v1.5.0 (2022-04-07) and the `master` tag has not been rebuilt since 2023-11-01, despite source commits continuing into 2026. There is nothing recent to pin.

First boot is a multi-step imperative bootstrap, not boot-and-serve: POST /api/v1/database/create to define a placement + namespace, poll until all shards move from INITIALIZING to AVAILABLE (~1-2 minutes), then POST the namespace as ready. Scriptable in install.sh in principle, but adds real complexity on top of the two blockers above.
summary: M3DB does not fit our recipe mechanism or our customer profile. It has no web UI to gate or log into — it's a machine-facing REST API meant to receive Prometheus remote_write traffic and serve Grafana-style queries — so a Traefik basic_auth gate would technically satisfy the secret-input rule but would break the actual integration path with a customer's own Prometheus. On top of that, upstream has not cut a versioned release since 2022-04-07 and hasn't even refreshed its `master` Docker tag since 2023-11-01, despite the source repo staying nominally alive with sporadic commits through 2026 — there is no current image to pin. Combined with a usefulness case that's weak for single-VM self-hosters in the first place, this is a clear not_recommended.

Authentication__Password is read as plaintext at container start (it seeds the initial admin user via CreateUserAsync(username, email, plaintextPassword, isAdmin) in Program.cs, which hashes it internally) — it is not a `generated_from`-projectable field, since that mechanism only ever supplies a pre-computed hash, never a plaintext value. Per-mailbox IMAP/M365/Gmail credentials are added by the admin inside the UI after first login, not at container boot, so they don't block `/compose` — same as Paperless-ngx's document sources.
summary: Mail-Archiver (s1t5/mail-archiver) is an actively developed (weekly CalVer releases, latest 2 days before today), GPL-3.0, single-HTTP-port (5000) web app backed by Postgres — structurally close to Paperless-ngx and fully Traefik-compatible. name: Mailtrain
source_description: Self-hosted newsletter platform for mass email campaigns and list management
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release is v2.20210609.0 from 2021-06-09 — over 5 years before this analysis (2026-08-05). The official mailtrain/mailtrain Docker Hub image's `latest` and `v2.20210609.0` tags were both last pushed "about 5 years ago", matching the release date, so the image has not been rebuilt since. The repo itself is not marked archived on GitHub and still shows open issues/PRs (11 open issues, 103 open PRs at time of research), but none appear to be merging — that pattern (open contributions piling up, zero releases, frozen image) reads as an unmaintained/abandoned project in practice rather than a merely slow one, even though GitHub's own "archived" flag isn't set. Treating as eol_status: archived given the evidence, not the label.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers mass-email/newsletter campaign management (list segmentation, campaign sending, subscriber management, RSS campaigns) — this would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue, not a duplicate of anything we ship today.
usefulness_rationale: The use case (self-hosted newsletter/mailing-list tool) is real and distinct from anything currently in the catalogue, but the specific project is stale enough (no release or image rebuild in 5+ years, stalled PR queue) that shipping it now would mean putting an effectively unmaintained mail-sending app — a category where security patches and deliverability fixes matter — in front of customers.
blocking_issues:
Mailtrain ships with a hardcoded default admin login (admin/test) with no supported env var to set it at first boot, and an open upstream bug (Mailtrain-org/mailtrain#1115) reports the admin password reverting to the default on every container restart even after being changed in the UI — the app cannot be trusted to hold a customer-set credential on its own. Per SCHEMA.md this is expressible as a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the app (same pattern as Adminer), not a hard blocker by itself.
Also needs a three-container stack (Mailtrain app + MySQL/MariaDB + Redis) exposing three distinct ports (trusted UI 3000, sandbox/template-editor 3003, public subscriber-facing 3004) — only the trusted UI is reasonably put behind basic_auth; the public subscriber-facing endpoint (unsubscribe links, campaign tracking, web-view) must stay open to the internet without auth for the product to function, so a single blanket basic_auth gate does not cleanly cover the whole app the way it does for a single-port tool like Adminer.
Outbound mail delivery requires SMTP relay credentials (or a transactional-email API key) with no customer-supplied input channel today — same class of gap as any app needing an external API key.
summary: Mailtrain fills a real gap (no newsletter/mass-email recipe exists today) but the upstream project is effectively dormant — no release or Docker image rebuild since June 2021, a stalled queue of 103 open PRs, and a standing bug where the admin password resets to the hardcoded default on every restart. Even setting maintenance status aside, the three-port trusted/sandbox/public architecture means a single Traefik basic_auth gate can't cover the app the way it does for single-port tools, since the public subscriber-facing endpoint must stay open, and there's still no input channel for the SMTP relay credentials it needs to actually send mail. Recommend not_recommended: both the platform-mechanism gaps and the upstream abandonment would need to be resolved before this is worth building.

name: Maloja

The last commit to master of any kind was 2025-05-18 (a single PR merge); before that the most recent substantive commits were 2025-02-14/15/17. So it's been roughly 15 months since any code change and 18 months since the last tagged release, despite 114 open issues and 14 open PRs sitting untouched. The repo is not formally archived and no EOL has been announced, but the maintainer (krateng, a solo developer) shows no activity pattern consistent with ongoing upkeep. Treat as effectively dormant/maintenance-only rather than "active" — this is the kind of stall this analysis should flag rather than take at face value from the "actively maintained" framing on third-party mirror pages (e.g. LinuxLinks, awesome-docker-compose).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers personal music-listening tracking/scrobbling. Immich and Lychee cover photos, Paperless covers documents — Maloja would be the only recipe serving the "track and chart my own music listening history" niche (a self-hosted Last.fm-style stats page fed by scrobbler clients/plugins).
usefulness_rationale: Real but narrow niche — music-scrobble tracking appeals to a small slice of self-hosting hobbyists, well below the broad utility of monitoring, password-management, or automation tools already in the catalogue. Combined with the dormant upstream (no release in 18 months, no commits in 15), this isn't a project worth building a recipe on top of even before the installability question.
blocking_issues:
Maloja's admin login is set via the `MALOJA_FORCE_PASSWORD` environment variable, but the app takes this value as a **plaintext** password and hashes it itself internally (confirmed in `maloja/setup.py`: `auth.change_pw(password=forcepassword)`, feeding straight into `doreah.auth.AuthManager`). There is no env var or settings key that accepts a pre-hashed credential. Our only per-customer secret channel, `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, only ever produces an argon2/bcrypt hash digest — it cannot supply a plaintext value. This is the genuine-plaintext-required case (distinct from an unsupported-hash-algo case): no `generated_from` algorithm, present or future, can satisfy this parameter.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app does not substitute here, because Maloja's own login is not just an open/unprotected front door to gate — it's how the customer must authenticate to reach admin features they need for the app to be useful at all (registering scrobbler API keys, manual scrobbling, editing listening data). Gating at Traefik with the root-password hash and leaving `MALOJA_FORCE_PASSWORD` server-generated/unknown to the customer would lock the customer out of Maloja's own admin UI entirely, since they'd have no way to learn or set that password.
summary: Maloja is mechanically close but not installable today: its single customer-facing credential (the admin login used for scrobbler API key setup and data management) can only be provisioned via a plaintext env var that the app hashes itself, and our root-password projection mechanism only ever carries a hash, never plaintext — no current or planned `generated_from` algorithm closes that gap, and a Traefik basic_auth gate can't substitute since the customer genuinely needs to log into Maloja's own UI. Even setting the installability question aside, upstream has had no commits in ~15 months and no release in ~18 (v3.2.4, 2025-02-10), against a backlog of 114 open issues — a solo maintainer project that looks dormant. Given the niche appeal (no catalogue overlap, but a narrow audience) and the dormant upstream, this is not a priority even if a future generic plaintext-credential channel emerges.

name: Manticore Search
source_description: Open-source search engine with full-text and vector search via MySQL protocol
version_health_notes: Calendar-versioned, near-monthly release train through 2026: 25.0.0 (2026-03-30), 27.1.5 (2026-06-19), 28.4.4 (2026-07-10), 28.6.6 (2026-07-31, 5 days before this analysis on 2026-08-05). Repo is not archived, releases carry real feature work (v27.0.0 in June 2026 added built-in authentication/authorization; v25.0.0 added hybrid search and S3 backup/restore), and Docker Hub tags track releases within hours. Unambiguously active, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes provides a full-text/vector search engine. It would be positioned as infrastructure for developers/AI builders (e.g. RAG backends, site search) rather than an end-user app — closest in spirit to Ollama (headless engine, consumed via API by other software) rather than to any UI-driven recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Real capability gap it fills (search/vector search backend), but no web UI and a narrow, technical target audience (developers wiring it into their own app), and — per below — the flagship "talk to it over the MySQL wire protocol" angle from Hostinger's own description is the part that doesn't fit our exposure model cleanly.
blocking_issues:
Manticore's default listeners are three raw ports: 9306 (MySQL wire protocol), 9308 (HTTP/JSON API, including a /sql endpoint), 9312 (binary protocol for clustering). There is no bundled web UI. Traefik basic_auth is an HTTP-router middleware — it cannot gate the MySQL wire protocol on 9306 or the binary protocol on 9312, only the HTTP port 9308.

Built-in authentication (auth users/tokens) only shipped in v27.0.0 (June 2026) and is off by default — with it off, anyone who can reach 9306/9308/9312 has unrestricted read/write/DDL access. Turning it on doesn't give us an input channel either: bootstrapping the first admin (`--auth` / `--auth-non-interactive`) and `CREATE USER ... IDENTIFIED BY '<password>'` both take the admin password as plaintext, not a hash — `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, so it cannot supply what this flow needs. This is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, not a hash-algorithm gap, per SCHEMA.md's "not a hard no" carve-out.

Net effect: 9306 (the MySQL-protocol port Hostinger's own description calls out) and 9312 cannot be safely published publicly today — either leave them auth-off-and-open, or auth-on with no way to set the admin credential. Only 9308 (HTTP API) is realistically publishable, gated by Traefik basic_auth same as Adminer/n8n/WUD, at the cost of losing the MySQL-client-compatible use case entirely.
summary: Manticore Search is a genuinely active project (releases through 2026-07-31, five days before this analysis) filling a real gap (no search/vector-search recipe exists today), but its exposure model doesn't match ours cleanly: no web UI, and its two more interesting ports — the MySQL wire protocol (9306, the specific hook in Hostinger's own description) and the binary clustering protocol (9312) — are raw TCP, which Traefik basic_auth cannot gate, while the app's own built-in auth (new as of v27.0.0, June 2026) needs a plaintext admin password with no projection channel today. A recipe could still ship by publishing only the HTTP/JSON API (port 9308, including its /sql endpoint) behind a Traefik basic_auth gate and keeping 9306/9312 unpublished/internal-only — installable, but it drops the headline "connect over MySQL protocol" capability, leaving a narrower, more niche offering than the source description promises. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building for developers who're fine with the HTTP API, but flag the MySQL-port limitation explicitly before committing.

name: MantisBT
source_description: Open-source bug tracking system for issue management and project collaboration
version_health_notes: 2.28.4 shipped 2026-07-01 (a security release fixing CVE-2026-47156, a critical SOAP-API auth bypass, plus 7 other vulnerabilities) — 5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). It follows 2.28.3 (2026-05-14, also a security release), 2.28.2, 2.28.1, and 2.28.0 (2025-12), a roughly monthly cadence within the 2.28.x line over the last several months, with security patches shipped promptly. Upstream repo and blog are both clearly active. Clearly active, not slowing or dormant.
differentiation: Gitea (recipes/gitea) has built-in issue tracking, but it's tied to hosting the customer's git repos there — it doesn't help a team that wants a dedicated, standalone bug/issue tracker independent of where their code lives (or with no git hosting need at all). MantisBT is a long-established, purpose-built bug tracker (projects, issue workflows, custom fields, roadmaps, SOAP/REST API) with no equivalent in the current 24-recipe catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Standalone bug tracking is a real, recognizable self-hosting use case distinct from git-hosting-bundled issue trackers, and MantisBT is a long-standing, actively patched name in that space. It's a narrower audience than a wiki or password manager, though, and its PHP-era UI reads as dated next to newer competitors (e.g. a customer wanting project management is more likely to reach for something more modern-looking), which caps it at medium rather than high.
summary: MantisBT ships no official Docker image of its own; upstream only documents the interactive web installer (admin/install.php) against a manually-provisioned PHP/MySQL or PostgreSQL stack. The best available option is the community-maintained okainov/mantisbt-docker image, which wraps that installer with MYSQL_*/env-var-driven, non-interactive setup on first container start and is actively kept in step with upstream (rebuilt for 2.28.0 within the last ~2 months, a couple patch releases behind the current 2.28.4 at any given time but not stale). It's a single HTTP-port PHP app plus a MySQL/MariaDB sidecar — same shape as our n8n/paperless-ngx recipes — so it's fully Traefik-compatible. MantisBT's own "administrator" account is created by that installer with a plaintext password chosen at setup time, and no docker wrapper exposes an env var that MantisBT itself hash-verifies, so `generated_from` has nothing to project into for the app's real login. Per the same pattern already used for BookStack/Adminer/n8n in this catalogue, the fix is to leave the app's own admin account at a fixed value install.sh sets non-interactively and gate the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth: true` credential projected from the customer's root password — that becomes the real customer-facing auth boundary, and the internal DB_PASSWORD is a patternless secret nothing customer-facing reads, so it can be server-generated with no input channel needed. Clears the /compose constraint today with zero hard blocking issues, but the reliance on a third-party (not upstream-official) Docker image and the basic_auth workaround for the app's own security model keep this at build_with_caveats rather than a plain build_now.

name: Many Notes
source_description: Markdown note-taking app with vaults, full-text search, and OAuth
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release v0.16.2 landed 2026-06-13, about 7-8 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Release history over the trailing year shows real but uneven cadence: a burst of three releases (v0.16.0-v0.16.2) across 2026-05-25 to 2026-06-13, preceded by a roughly five-month gap back to v0.15.5 on 2025-12-08, and a run of three patch releases in 2025-10/2025-11 before that. Not archived, no EOL notice, ~1k GitHub stars, 9 open issues, actively developed — this reads as a small but healthy single-maintainer OSS project, not dormant.
differentiation: The closest existing peer is recipes/anytype-server, whose own description is "a privacy-focused note-taking and knowledge management app" in the same `productivity` category. It does not constitute overlap: anytype-server is a headless sync backend (any-sync-node, any-sync-filenode, any-sync-coordinator) consumed exclusively through the separate AnyType desktop/mobile client apps — its metadata.yaml ports are raw TCP sync protocols with `http: false`, no browser UI at all, and it is not reverse-proxy/Traefik-fronted the way our HTTP recipes are. Many Notes, by contrast, is a self-contained web app: you open a browser, log in, and write markdown — no separate client install, no sync protocol to expose. No other recipe in the catalogue covers personal markdown note-taking / knowledge-base use cases, so this would open a genuinely new, browser-first category alongside anytype-server's client-sync category.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted markdown notes with vaults is a popular, recurring self-hosting request and a natural complement to the existing productivity-adjacent recipes (Gitea, Opengist). Multi-vault, multi-user support and real-time collaboration make it more capable than a plain static-notes app.
blocking_issues:
Many Notes has its own local-auth login, but no admin-password env var or setup wizard — the first account is created through an open, unauthenticated self-registration form on the web UI, and there is no `generated_from` channel to project the customer's root-password hash into that registration (it is a web-form signup, not an app-managed credential field). Left unfronted, any visitor who reaches the domain before the customer registers could create the first (admin) account themselves. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate closes that exposure at the perimeter, but the customer still has to register their own in-app account manually after first login — the recipe can only secure the door, not pre-provision the account behind it.

OAuth (GitHub, Google, GitLab, Azure, Keycloak, and ~10 other providers) is optional, not required to boot, so it does not block `installable_today` — but it also cannot be offered as a customer feature under the current mechanism, since OAuth client ID/secret/redirect-URI registration has no input channel in `/compose` today.
summary: Many Notes is a small, actively maintained single-container markdown note app (PHP + SQLite by default, bundled Typesense for full-text search, one HTTP port) that would fill a real gap — no note-taking app exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It clears the installability bar only via a mandatory Traefik basic_auth perimeter gate, because its own account creation is an open self-registration form with no root-password projection channel; the customer must still complete in-app registration themselves after first login. OAuth support is a nice-to-have that stays unusable under today's mechanism (no channel for customer-supplied client secrets) but isn't a blocker since local auth works standalone. Recommend building with the basic_auth caveat called out explicitly in the recipe.

name: MariaDB
source_description: Open-source relational database server and MySQL drop-in replacement
version_health_notes: 12.3.2 (stable, noble-based LTS) released 2026-05-28, about 2.5 months before today (2026-08-05) — well inside a normal release cadence. MariaDB Foundation ships parallel maintained series (10.6 LTS until 2026-07, 10.11, 11.4, 11.8, 12.x) with regular point releases; the 10.6 branch is due to go EOL this month but the project itself is very much active, with a clear supported-series ladder for anyone who needs to move off an aging line. No ambiguity on upstream identity — this is the well-known MariaDB Foundation project, not to be confused with the commercial MariaDB Enterprise/SkySQL offerings which are separate products from the same foundation/company.
overlaps_with: gitea; guacamole; immich; n8n; paperless-ngx; runtipi
differentiation: None of the listed recipes expose MariaDB/MySQL as a standalone, customer-usable service — they each run their own MariaDB/Postgres instance internally, on the bridge network only, purely as private storage for that one app. A standalone MariaDB recipe would target a different use case entirely: a customer running their own external app (WordPress, a custom script, a BI tool) that needs a MySQL- compatible database to connect to from outside the VM. That's a real, distinct need, but it requires publishing the database port to the internet, which is exactly what the catalogue's own rules forbid (see `blocking_issues`).
usefulness_rationale: Would be useful to technical customers who want a managed MySQL- compatible backend for something they run themselves, but is a developer/power-user tool with no UI of its own, and its one useful exposure shape (a public 3306) is one our own recipe rules already reject on security grounds. Same class of app as Adminer (apps-gaps/adminer.yaml) but harder to ship: Adminer at least has an HTTP UI to gate; MariaDB is raw TCP with no application-layer presence at all.
blocking_issues:
The only useful shape for a standalone MariaDB recipe is a publicly reachable MySQL-protocol port so an external customer app can connect to it. Publishing host port 3306 is exactly what RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` rule forbids (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226) — 3306 is explicitly on the forbidden-host-port list. There is no alternate exposure path today: Traefik only routes HTTP, and MariaDB speaks a raw binary protocol, so it cannot be fronted the way our web-UI recipes are (no `basic_auth`, no subdomain routing).

Even setting the port rule aside, the root password can be projected via `MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD` (plaintext env var, which `generated_from` does not produce) or `MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASH` (a mysql_native_password-style hash, not `argon2`/`bcrypt`) — neither matches the currently supported `generated_from` algorithm list, so even the login-credential half of this would need a new supported hash algorithm or a plaintext-secret channel, neither of which exists today.
summary: MariaDB is an actively maintained, healthy upstream project, but a standalone MariaDB recipe has no viable shape in the current catalogue. Its only useful exposure — a public, customer-reachable 3306 — is explicitly forbidden by our own `no-public-db-port` rule, and it has no web UI to gate behind Traefik/basic_auth the way Adminer or other no-login apps do. This isn't a platform gap waiting on IF-1420/1312; it's a structural mismatch between what the app needs (a raw internet- facing DB port) and what our security rules and Traefik-only routing model support. Recommend not_recommended rather than blocked_on_platform, since no plausible mechanism change fixes this without relaxing a deliberate security rule.

name: Marimo
source_description: Open-source reactive Python notebook with SQL support and reproducible execution
version_health_notes: v0.23.16 shipped 2026-07-31, 5 days before today (2026-08-05). Release history is a steady roughly-weekly cadence across the 0.23.x line (0.23.14, 0.23.15, 0.23.16 all landing within the prior month), no gaps of concern. 22.2k GitHub stars, actively developed by marimo-team (a funded startup behind the project), heavy recent feature work (AI copilot integration, WASM/Pyodide bumps, SQL data-source discovery). No archival, deprecation, or EOL signal whatsoever — this is a healthy, fast-moving OSS project. One packaging note: the prebuilt ghcr.io/marimo-team/marimo image tags lag the PyPI/GitHub release by roughly a week or two (latest published container tag seen was 0.23.15-sql, ~13 days old, one release behind 0.23.16) — pin to whatever the newest published container tag is at recipe-build time, not necessarily the newest GitHub release tag.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue offers a notebook/coding environment. The closest analogues are two other not-yet-built gap candidates: apps-gaps/jupyter-notebook.yaml and apps-gaps/jupyterlab.yaml (both recommended build_now, still unbuilt), and the built code-server recipe (general-purpose browser IDE, not a notebook). Marimo is a real alternative to Jupyter rather than a duplicate of it: notebooks are stored as plain, git-diffable .py files (not Jupyter's JSON .ipynb), execution is reactive (changing one cell automatically re-runs every dependent cell, eliminating Jupyter's stale-hidden-state class of bugs), and it ships built-in SQL cells against DataFrames/databases plus a "run as script" / "deploy as app" mode absent from classic Jupyter. If the catalogue ends up shipping both Jupyter and Marimo they would coexist as differentiated options for the same broad "Python notebook" audience, similar to how the catalogue already carries multiple note-taking or media apps per CLAUDE.md's no-single-recipe-per-category stance — this is not a reason to reject either on its own.
usefulness_rationale: Reactive, git-friendly Python notebooks with built-in SQL are a distinctive, actively-requested niche (reproducibility and avoiding Jupyter's out-of-order-execution foot-guns are a recurring complaint in the data/ML community). Single official container, no external DB/cache dependency required to be useful, low resource footprint.
blocking_issues:
Marimo's own built-in login (the `--token-password` flag on `marimo edit`/`run`) only accepts a plaintext secret compared directly against what the visitor supplies — there is no hashed-password input mode analogous to Jupyter's/code-server's `--PasswordIdentityProvider.hashed_password` / `HASHED_PASSWORD`. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so it cannot feed this flag. Upstream docs are explicit that this built-in token is not meant for production/shared deployments anyway ("marimo does not provide a built-in authentication/authorization system... add your own through ASGI middleware") — the correct fix is `--no-token` to disable it and put the app behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate instead, same shape as many-notes and WUD. This is a build-time recipe decision, not a platform blocker: `traefik_basic_auth` fully covers it, so it does not block `installable_today`.

`marimo edit` (the interactive editor, as opposed to `marimo run` on a single fixed notebook) opens a file browser rooted at whatever directory the container is launched in and lets the customer create/ edit arbitrary `.py` notebook files, persisted to a bind-mounted volume — structurally identical in shape to code-server's workspace volume, not a blocker, just worth calling out for whoever plans the recipe (needs a `/opt/marimo/notebooks`-style volume, same pattern as code-server).
summary: Marimo is an actively maintained (weekly release cadence, 22.2k stars, no EOL signal), single-official-container Python notebook tool that would open a genuinely new category in the catalogue — no existing recipe offers a notebook/data-analysis environment, and Marimo's reactive-execution + git-friendly-.py-file + built-in-SQL model meaningfully differentiates it from classic Jupyter (itself still just a gap candidate, not a built recipe). Its own token-based login is plaintext-only and explicitly not production-hardened per upstream docs, so it cannot use `generated_from` the way Jupyter/code-server can; disabling it (`--no-token`) and fronting the app with Traefik `basic_auth` (customer root-password hash) closes that gap cleanly with a mechanism the platform already supports. No blocking issues remain. Recommend build_now.

name: Marreta
source_description: Self-hosted article proxy for clean, ad-free reading with intelligent caching
version_health_notes: v3.0.3 shipped 2026-07-27, about 9 days before today (2026-08-05) — very active. The v3.x line (Laravel rewrite) shipped four releases in three days (3.0.0-3.0.3, 2026-07-25 to 2026-07-27) stabilizing the rewrite, preceded by v2.3.10 (2026-07-18) and a long gap back to v2.3.9 (2026-04-01). Reads as a healthy, actively developed project mid major version transition, not dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes does this: paste a URL and get back a cleaned, de-paywalled, tracking-stripped, cached version of the article. It's a genuinely distinct use case from our existing media/productivity recipes (Paperless, Immich, n8n, etc). Note the app is explicitly branded upstream as a "paywall bypasser" (GitHub topics: bypasser, paywall, paywall-bypasser) — Hostinger's "clean, ad-free reading" framing undersells what it actually does, and the project itself maintains a DMCA-domain blocklist in response to takedown requests already received. That's a legal/reputational consideration for the catalogue, separate from the technical fit.
usefulness_rationale: Would appeal to a real, if narrow, slice of self-hosters (readers who want ad/tracker-free article rendering with their own cache), but the paywall-circumvention branding and DMCA history are a real risk profile for a hosting-company-curated catalogue — this needs a business call, not just a technical one, before building.
blocking_issues:
ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_PASSWORD gate the app's own `/admin` panel, which is where a customer would manage custom domain rules, extra blocked domains, and DMCA exclusions — the one piece of ongoing, customer- facing configuration this app has. Traced the seeder (database/seeders/AdminUserSeeder.php): it reads `config('marreta.admin.password')` (the plaintext `ADMIN_PASSWORD` env var) and calls `Hash::make($password)` itself at boot — there is no way to feed it a pre-computed bcrypt/argon2 hash instead. Per SCHEMA.md this is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, not a hash-algorithm gap, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash of ROOT_PASSWORD) cannot express it. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate on the whole app doesn't substitute either — it would let the customer reach the login page but not log into it, since Marreta's own admin credentials would still be an unknown, server-generated value.

Companion service `lightpanda/browser` (required for JS-heavy page rendering via `BROWSER_WS_ENDPOINT`) is only published under a `:nightly` tag in upstream's own compose.yml — no pinned stable release tag, which would separately fail `image-tag-pinned`.
summary: Marreta is an actively maintained, novel-to-our-catalogue app (article de-paywalling/cleanup proxy) with a real if narrow audience, but two issues block it under the current mechanism: its admin panel — the customer's only way to manage per-domain rules — needs a plaintext password that the app hashes itself server-side, which `generated_from` cannot supply, and its required browser sidecar has no pinned release tag. The core anonymous "paste a URL" flow needs no login and would work fine behind Traefik, but shipping it without working admin access loses the feature that makes the tool configurable. Recommend holding as `blocked_on_platform` pending a plaintext-secret input channel, and flagging the paywall-bypass/DMCA framing for a business decision independent of the technical gap.

name: Mastodon
source_description: Self-hosted federated microblogging server based on the ActivityPub standard
version_health_notes: v4.6.4 landed 2026-07-27, about 9 days before today (2026-08-05). Mastodon maintains four parallel release branches (4.6.x, 4.5.x, 4.4.x, 4.3.x) and ships security backports across all of them simultaneously — e.g. a critical FFmpeg CVE (CVE-2026-8461) was patched in 4.6.2, 4.5.13, and 4.4.20 within the same week in late June 2026. This is a large, well-funded project (Mastodon gGmbH) with a fast, structured release cadence and no signs of slowing.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers social/federated publishing — this would be a genuinely new category. The closest structural peers by "multi-service stack behind one domain" are recipes/immich (Postgres + Redis + app) and recipes/anytype-server (multi-service, non-HTTP sync backend), but neither is a real functional overlap.
usefulness_rationale: Mastodon is the flagship self-hosted ActivityPub server and a common, recurring self-hosting request (personal or small-community microblogging instance). It would be a strong catalogue addition on demand alone, independent of installability concerns below.
blocking_issues:
Multi-service HTTP surface on one hostname: the official docker-compose.yml runs three containers off two images — `web` (Puma, port 3000) and `streaming` (Node, port 4000) both need to be reachable under the *same* customer domain, with `/api/v1/streaming` routed to the streaming service and everything else to web. Every existing recipe in the catalogue maps one public HTTP port to one Traefik Host-based route per domain; none does path-based splitting of two HTTP services under a single hostname. This is plausible with Traefik PathPrefix routers but has no precedent in the current recipe/renderer mechanism and would need new plumbing, hence `reverse_proxy_compatible: false` for today's mechanism.

No channel to set the admin account's password. Mastodon has its own local login, but the only account-provisioning path is the `tootctl accounts create <user> --email <email> --confirmed` CLI command run once inside the web container — it has no `--password`/config-file field to accept a plaintext or pre-hashed credential; it always generates its own random password and prints it once to command output. This is not an "unsupported hash algorithm" case (the last row of the SCHEMA.md decision table) — there is no password input field of any kind, hash or plaintext, so `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` has no destination to project into. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate secures the perimeter but does not solve this: it does not give the customer a usable Mastodon admin login, since the real admin credential is a value the platform would generate but currently has no mechanism to surface back to the customer.

SMTP is not required to boot (the app starts and `--confirmed` bypasses the registration email), but standard operation — new member signups, admin password-reset flows — depends on a working outbound mail relay. Configuring that requires a customer-supplied external SMTP host/login/password, which has no input channel in `/compose` today. Not a hard blocker on its own since `--confirmed` avoids it at first boot, but it is a real functional gap once running.
summary: Mastodon is a high-value, actively maintained project with no equivalent in the current 24-recipe catalogue, but it fails installability on three independent fronts today: it needs two HTTP services split by path under one hostname (no precedent in our single-port-per-domain Traefik mechanism), its admin account has no password-setting channel at all (tootctl only ever generates and prints a random password, so `generated_from` has nowhere to project a hash), and full functionality depends on customer-supplied SMTP credentials with no input channel. These are platform-mechanism gaps rather than a low-value app — recommend revisiting once path-based Traefik routing and a way to surface platform-generated first-boot secrets to the customer both exist.

name: Mathesar
source_description: Spreadsheet-style web interface for exploring and editing PostgreSQL databases
version_health_notes: Roughly monthly minor releases through 2026 (0.9.0 Feb, 0.10.0/0.10.1 Apr, 0.11.0 May 28, 0.12.0 Jul 2), with a 0.12.0 PR log already open in late June 2026. As of today (2026-08-05) the gap since the last release is ~1 month, well within the established cadence — clearly active, not dormant. Project is stewarded by the Mathesar Foundation, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, not a single-maintainer side project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes gives customers a spreadsheet-style browser/editor for an existing Postgres database. It targets a different use case than the apps-gaps/adminer.yaml candidate (also un-built): Adminer is a generic, all-databases, form-based SQL admin tool for technical users; Mathesar is Postgres-only and explicitly designed as a non-technical, Airtable/spreadsheet-like data-entry surface with native Postgres access control. Recipes like n8n, paperless-ngx, and immich run their own internal Postgres but expose no UI to browse or edit it directly.
usefulness_rationale: Appeals to a broader (less technical) audience than a raw DB admin tool, which is a genuine differentiator, but it still requires the customer to already have (or want) a Postgres database to point it at — either their own external instance or Mathesar's bundled one, which starts empty. That's a real but narrower audience than general-purpose apps already in the catalogue.
summary: Mathesar's official docker-compose ships three services: the Django app (mathesar/mathesar, port 8000 internally), a bundled Postgres (pgautoupgrade/pgautoupgrade:17-bookworm), and a bundled Caddy reverse proxy (mathesar/mathesar-caddy) that claims host ports 80/443 for TLS. A recipe would need to drop the bundled Caddy service and point our own Traefik at the mathesar_service:8000 container directly (the same pattern used for other multi-service stacks like anytype-server/immich) — a build-time adaptation, not a platform blocker. Critically, Mathesar has no admin-credential environment variable at all: on first visit it walks the customer through an in-app setup wizard to create their own admin account interactively, the same pattern already accepted for immich. That means no customer-supplied secret needs to cross the /compose boundary — only a domain param and a server-generated (never customer-facing) internal DB password. Release cadence is active (monthly), the project is backed by a nonprofit foundation, and it is mechanically installable today with no changes to the current recipe mechanism. Recommend building.

name: Matomo
source_description: Leading open-source web analytics platform with complete data ownership and privacy
version_health_notes: 5.11.1 (2026-06-12) was a patch release fixing CNIL-related data-retention behavior on top of 5.11.0 (2026-06-08). That is about 8 weeks before today (2026-08-05) — well within Matomo's normal cadence of a minor release roughly every 4-6 weeks (5.10.0 on 2026-05-03, 5.8.0 on 2026-03-04). InnoCraft (the commercial entity behind Matomo) actively develops and funds the project; no signs of slowing.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers web/product analytics. Matomo is a genuinely new category for the catalogue — a privacy-respecting, self-hosted alternative to Google Analytics, single HTTP entrypoint, fits the one-port-per-domain Traefik model cleanly (structurally close to recipes/paperless-ngx and recipes/n8n: single web/app container + a relational database).
usefulness_rationale: Web analytics with full data ownership is a common, recurring self-hosting request, especially from customers avoiding Google Analytics for GDPR/privacy reasons. High recurring demand independent of the installability concerns below.
blocking_issues:
No first-boot channel to create (or gate) the Super User account. The official image auto-configures the database connection via MATOMO_DATABASE_* env vars, but that only skips the DB-connection step of the installer — Matomo still requires a human to complete the rest of the setup wizard in a browser (system checks, table creation trigger, then a "Super User" step where the admin chooses their own username/password interactively, followed by website/tracking-tag setup). There is no env var, CLI command, or config-file field that accepts a pre-hashed or plaintext admin credential at container start.

Even if such a field existed, Matomo's user-password hash is not a plain `bcrypt(password)`/`argon2(password)`: UsersManager first runs `hash_hmac('sha512', password, $salt)` using a per-install salt that is itself randomly generated during setup and stored in config.ini.php, and only *then* passes that intermediate value to `password_hash()` (bcrypt). `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only supports `algo(ROOT_PASSWORD)` directly — it has no way to reproduce Matomo's HMAC-with-install-specific-salt pre-processing step, so this is not merely an "unsupported algorithm" case (the extensible row in SCHEMA.md's decision table) but a structural mismatch in what the field expects.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not fully close this gap the way it does for apps with no login of their own (e.g. Adminer, WUD): the real problem here is a race, not a missing perimeter. Anyone who reaches the domain before the customer completes the wizard becomes the Super User. A `basic_auth` gate using a root-password hash would close that race (nobody untrusted reaches the installer first) and is the closest fit — but the wizard still requires the customer to manually click through several screens (including creating a website entry and copying a JS tracking tag) before Matomo is actually usable, which is a materially different post-install experience than every other recipe's zero-touch boot.
summary: Matomo is an active, well-maintained project and a genuinely new, high-demand category (privacy-first web analytics) with zero overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It is mechanically reverse-proxy friendly (single HTTP port), but first-boot account provisioning is a real blocker: the Super User account can only be created through an interactive browser wizard, Matomo's password hash requires an install-specific HMAC step that `generated_from` cannot reproduce even for supported algorithms, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate only mitigates the race for the installer rather than delivering the zero-touch, fully-provisioned boot our other recipes provide. Recommend revisiting once there's a way to surface a platform-generated first-boot secret through the wizard (or once Matomo ships a documented headless superuser-creation path), rather than building around a security race today.

name: Matrix Conduit
source_description: Lightweight Rust Matrix homeserver for federated, encrypted chat
version_health_notes: v0.10.12 (2026-02-12) is a security release mitigating a signing-key compromise; the prior two releases (v0.10.11, v0.10.10, both Dec 2025/Jan 2026) were also security-driven, following a tighter monthly-ish cadence through most of 2025 (v0.10.0 through v0.10.9, May-Sep 2025). Since v0.10.12 there has been no new version tag for ~6 months (today is 2026-08-05), though the GitLab project's `last_activity_at` is 2026-07-26 and untagged commits/container builds continued into mid-July 2026 — so development hasn't stopped, but the release cadence has clearly slowed relative to 2025. Upstream's own README still labels the project "Beta" with explicitly missing federation features (outgoing read receipts/typing/presence, E2EE emoji comparison). Note the project is ambiguous by name: this analysis covers the original `famedly/conduit`, not its more actively-developed forks `conduwuit` (itself now archived) or `continuwuity` (the current community continuation, releasing every 1-2 weeks) — Hostinger's slug `matrix-conduit` and description map to the original project's own Docker image name (`matrixconduit/matrix-conduit`), so that's the candidate evaluated here, but a reviewer picking this up should know the more active fork exists under a different name.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers real-time federated chat/messaging — this would be a genuinely new category, distinct from apps-gaps/mastodon.yaml (federated microblogging, different protocol and use case).
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosting a Matrix homeserver is a recurring, well-understood self-hosting request, but Conduit ships no client of any kind — it is a headless JSON API that only becomes usable once the customer installs a separate Matrix client (Element, Nheko, SchildiChat, etc.) and points it at the server. That's a materially higher setup bar than every other recipe in the catalogue, which are usable directly through a browser immediately after install.
blocking_issues:
No browser-reachable login or admin surface of any kind. Conduit exposes only the Matrix Client-Server and Server-Server JSON APIs; there is no web UI, so there is no page for a `generated_from` password hash to authenticate against, and no built-in "admin account" the platform could provision a credential for. The `emergency_password` config field logs in as a fixed `conduit` user via the same headless API, not a page a customer visits.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate — the fallback for apps with no login of their own — is not viable here, unlike Adminer or WUD. It would intercept every request to the Client-Server API, and real Matrix clients (Element, etc.) never send HTTP Basic Auth headers, so gating the whole domain would break the app's actual function rather than just adding a perimeter around unauthenticated access.

Federation — the feature Hostinger's own description leads with — is a second HTTP surface entirely: a Server-Server API conventionally reachable on port 8448 (or delegated via `.well-known/matrix/server` and `.well-known/matrix/client` JSON files served over plain HTTPS on 443). Our current per-slug single-domain Traefik model has no precedent for serving those two well-known static responses alongside the app's own routes on the same hostname (the closest parallel, Mastodon's path-split web + streaming services, was already flagged as unsupported in apps-gaps/mastodon.yaml). Running Conduit with federation disabled would sidestep this, but that guts the core value proposition Hostinger is describing.
summary: Matrix Conduit fills a category the catalogue doesn't have (federated real-time chat), but it is blocked on more than one front: it has no web login surface at all for `generated_from` to project into, a `basic_auth` gate would break the protocol itself rather than just securing it, and true federation needs well-known delegation/a second HTTP surface with no precedent in today's single-domain Traefik mechanism. Combined with a headless API that requires the customer to bring their own separate Matrix client to use it at all, and a release cadence that has visibly slowed since the Feb 2026 security release, this is a `blocked_on_platform` candidate worth deferring — and worth re-scoping toward the more actively maintained `continuwuity` fork if revisited later.

name: Matrix Synapse
source_description: Open-source Matrix homeserver for decentralized, encrypted communication
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (dual-licensed; Element also offers a commercial license)
version_health_notes: v1.158.0 shipped 2026-08-04, one day before this analysis (2026-08-05). Synapse ships roughly monthly stable releases (v1.155.0 on 2026-06-16, v1.156.0 on 2026-07-07, v1.157.0 on 2026-07-21, v1.157.1 and v1.157.2 as same-week security patches, v1.158.0rc1 on 2026-07-30 then v1.158.0 on 2026-08-04), each preceded by a signed release candidate. v1.157.2 alone patched ten security vulnerabilities. Synapse is Element's flagship homeserver, backed by a funded company with a commercial-license offering alongside the AGPL release — clearly active, not maintenance-only, archived, or EOL.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers chat/messaging or Matrix at all. Synapse would be the first Matrix homeserver in the catalogue, and would also materially raise the value of the existing apps-gaps/element.yaml candidate (Element Web), which today is capped at "low" usefulness specifically because there is no self-hostable homeserver for it to point at — Synapse fills that gap. Structurally closest to recipes/n8n and recipes/paperless-ngx (single app container + dedicated Postgres container behind one Traefik hostname); no functional overlap with anything shipping today.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosting a Matrix homeserver (own domain, own federation identity, own data retention) is a common, recurring self-hosting request and the natural anchor for a "communication" category the catalogue currently lacks entirely. Pairing it with Element Web would give customers a complete self-hosted chat stack.
blocking_issues:
Synapse has no web UI or first-run wizard of its own — it is a bare JSON API server. The only way a customer gets a usable account is (a) an admin-provisioned seed account via the `register_new_matrix_user` CLI script (gated by a `registration_shared_secret` in homeserver.yaml) or the `PUT /_synapse/admin/v2/users/<id>` admin API, both of which take the account password as **plaintext** and hash it internally — there is no config field or API parameter that accepts a pre-computed password hash — or (b) open self-registration through an external Matrix client (e.g. Element), which needs `enable_registration: true` and leaves the homeserver open to public sign-up by anyone who finds the domain until the customer manually disables it post-setup. Per SCHEMA.md's decision table, a genuine requirement for the plaintext password (not a hash) is a structural blocker — `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever produces a hash, so it has nowhere to project into either provisioning path.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not substitute here the way it does for Adminer-style apps: Synapse's single HTTP port carries both the Matrix client-server API (used by every Matrix client to log in and sync) and, when federation is enabled, server-server traffic. Layering HTTP basic auth in front of it would break normal client login and federation delegation, not just protect an otherwise-open admin panel — so it is not a viable stand-in credential gate for this app.

Directly writing a `generated_from`-produced bcrypt hash into Synapse's internal Postgres `users` table (bypassing its supported API entirely) is theoretically hash-format-compatible when the password pepper is left at its empty default, but this is not a documented or supported provisioning path — it depends on Synapse's internal schema staying stable across the version pin and is a materially different (and fragile) mechanism than the config/env-var style projection SCHEMA.md describes for other recipes. Flagging it here for completeness, not treating it as a shipped-quality workaround.
summary: Matrix Synapse is an actively developed (monthly release cadence, latest tag one day before this analysis), well-funded, AGPL-3.0-licensed Matrix homeserver with no equivalent anywhere in the current 24-recipe catalogue — it would open up a new communication category and make the existing Element Web gap candidate meaningfully more useful. Mechanically it is a straightforward single-container-plus-Postgres stack that works fine behind a single Traefik hostname via well-known federation delegation, so `reverse_proxy_compatible: true`. It fails installability today for a different reason than the usual API-key gap: Synapse has no web UI of its own, and every supported way to give a customer a working login (the `register_new_matrix_user` CLI script or the admin REST API) requires the plaintext account password rather than a hash, so `generated_from` has nothing to project into, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate can't substitute without breaking normal client and federation traffic on the same port. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` — revisit once the platform has either a way to seed a customer-usable account from a plaintext value it derives itself, or a supported plaintext credential channel distinct from the hash-only `generated_from` mechanism.

name: Mattermost
source_description: Open-source team collaboration platform with messaging, file sharing, and integrations
version_health_notes: 11.10.0 landed 2026-08-04, 2 days before today (2026-08-06), confirmed against Docker Hub tag push timestamps for mattermost/mattermost-team-edition. Mattermost ships a new minor server version roughly monthly (11.10.0 2026-08-04, 11.7.8 patch 2026-07-31, 11.9.0 ~2026-07-08) alongside an Extended Support Release track (11.7.x) that gets its own parallel patch cadence for customers who don't track monthly releases. This is a large, commercially-backed project (in the Slack/Teams alternative space) with a fast, structured release cadence and no signs of slowing.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers team chat/messaging — this would be a genuinely new category, distinct from the sync/file/dev tools already in the catalogue (n8n, gitea, opengist, syncthing, etc.). It's the self-hosted Slack/Teams alternative, a very commonly requested self-hosting workload.
usefulness_rationale: Team chat is a mainstream self-hosting use case with broad appeal (businesses wanting to avoid Slack/Teams SaaS pricing or data residency). Single Go binary + Postgres, one HTTP port, no unusual runtime needs beyond the admin-provisioning issue below — otherwise a clean architectural fit for the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the official mattermost/docker compose stack (docker-compose.yml + env.example) and Mattermost's own auth docs: there is no admin-username/admin-password environment variable or config field. `EnableOpenServer` (self-registration) actually defaults to false, not true — but that doesn't avoid the problem, it relocates it: the documented way to bootstrap a fresh install is to explicitly set `MM_TEAMSETTINGS_ENABLEOPENSERVER=true` (our install.sh would have to do this) so the first visitor can reach the signup form at all, at which point that first account is automatically promoted to System Admin with no email round-trip required (`RequireEmailVerification` defaults to false). This is the same shape of problem documented in apps-gaps/airtrail.yaml, apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml and apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml: the credential is created client-side via self-registration, so there is no `type: password` parameter on Mattermost's own login to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`.

Per the AirTrail precedent, a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate closes the "random internet stranger races to register first" version of this problem but does not resolve it: today's mechanism has no channel to hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential for the in-app signup form beyond the single root-password projection already consumed by the gate. Mattermost makes this worse than a single-user tool like AirTrail — it is explicitly multi-user team collaboration software, so a *permanent* basic_auth gate over the whole domain would also block every teammate the customer invites, since none of them know the customer's root password. Leaving the gate on defeats the product; removing it after bootstrap requires a manual out-of-band step our install flow doesn't support today.

Not required to boot, but standard operation (email invites to teammates, password-reset flows) depends on customer-supplied external SMTP credentials, which have no input channel in `/compose` today. Secondary to the admin-provisioning blocker above.
summary: Mattermost is a high-value, actively maintained, architecturally clean candidate (single Go app + Postgres, one HTTP port, Traefik-compatible) that would fill a genuine team-chat gap in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It is blocked today for the same structural reason as AirTrail/2FAuth/Activepieces: there is no env-var or config channel to preset the initial admin account, so the app relies on an open, first-visitor self-registration screen. Unlike those single-user tools, a Traefik basic_auth gate is an even worse fit here because Mattermost is explicitly multi-user — gating the whole domain would also lock out every invited teammate. Revisit once upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow or the platform gains a way to surface a platform-generated first-boot credential to the customer.

name: Mautic
source_description: Open-source marketing automation for email campaigns, lead scoring, and journeys
version_health_notes: 7.1.3 shipped 2026-07-07, about 4 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Mautic moved to a Long Term Support model starting with 7.0 (released 2026-01-20, "Columba Edition"): a 4-year support window per major (1 year active, 1 year security, 2 years Extended LTS), with monthly minor/patch releases (7.1 "Canis Major", 7.1.2, 7.1.3, and a 7.2 release already at RC) committed under that plan. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue.

Mature, widely deployed, GPL-3.0, no commercial-tier gating unlike some of the other business-app candidates reviewed.
blocking_issues:
DB credentials are fine: MAUTIC_DB_HOST/PORT/DATABASE/USER/PASSWORD on the official mautic/mautic image are genuine env vars, so MAUTIC_DB_PASSWORD and MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD are server-generated with no customer input needed — no blocker here.

The admin account is blocked. There is no MAUTIC_ADMIN_PASSWORD / MAUTIC_ADMIN_EMAIL env var on the official image at all — checked against github.com/mautic/docker-mautic's own README ("Environment Variables" section), which lists only DB connection settings, DOCKER_MAUTIC_ROLE/worker tuning, and PHP_INI_* settings. The only two supported ways to create the first admin account are (a) the `mautic:install` console command (`php ./bin/console mautic:install <url> --admin_email=... --admin_password=...`), which takes the password as a **plaintext** CLI argument and hashes it internally, or (b) the browser-based first-run web install wizard / REST API user-create endpoint, which takes a `plainPassword` field — also plaintext only. Neither path accepts a pre-computed hash. Per SCHEMA.md's decision table, a genuine requirement for the plaintext password (not a hash) is a structural blocker — `generated_from` only ever produces a hash, so it has nowhere to project into either provisioning path. This is the same failure mode as apps-gaps/matrix-synapse.yaml.
summary: Mautic is a PHP app (official mautic/mautic image, pin to 7.1.3-apache) that needs a MySQL/MariaDB backend plus a recurring cron/worker process for campaign triggers and email sending — a three-plus-container stack similar in shape to the paperless-ngx template, but with an extra always-on worker rather than paperless's auxiliary services. It exposes a single HTTP port and is Traefik-compatible with no other raw ports needed. DB/root MySQL passwords are server-generated with no customer input, so that part of the stack is fine. It fails installability today because the official image has no MAUTIC_ADMIN_PASSWORD/EMAIL env var at all: the only supported ways to provision the first admin account are the `mautic:install` CLI command or the web install wizard/REST API, and both take the account password as plaintext rather than a hash, so `generated_from` (hash-only) has nothing to project into. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` — a high-value, genuinely new category for the catalogue, but blocked on the same plaintext-password gap identified in apps-gaps/matrix-synapse.yaml until the platform gains a plaintext credential channel distinct from `generated_from`.

The one real gap: self-hosted Maxun has no built-in admin account — `POST /register` lets any visitor create the first account with an email/password of their choosing, so whoever reaches the URL first "owns" the instance. That's the same no-login-gate shape as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI, and the documented fix is a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app (root-password projected), same as those recipes, so it's still `installable_today`. Two structural caveats worth flagging before building: (1) the app ships as separate frontend (5173) and backend (8080) services split by path-prefix in upstream's own nginx.conf example, not a single port — a recipe would need an internal proxy container (nginx/Caddy sidecar) doing that same path split so only one HTTP port is exposed to Traefik, since no existing recipe demonstrates two HTTP services sharing one Traefik host by path; and (2) the browser-automation container needs multi-GB shared memory and `seccomp:unconfined`, plus a recommended 4-6GB RAM footprint for backend+browser alone — heavier than most current recipes. Mbin is a decentralized content aggregator, voting, discussion, and microblogging platform on ActivityPub (fork of the discontinued kbin project), interoperating with Lemmy, Mastodon, Pleroma, and PeerTube. Functionally this is the same niche already covered by the `lemmy` gap-analysis (Reddit-style federated link aggregation/discussion) — the two projects are close substitutes for a customer's "run my own federated community forum" use case, not independent additions. Per CLAUDE.md, overlap alone is not a rejection reason; this is noted for the later prioritization call, not as a disqualifier here.

blocking_issues:
Mbin has no web-based setup wizard and no self-registration path to an admin account. Per upstream docs (docs.joinmbin.org admin/running-mbin/first_setup and admin/running-mbin/cli), the only way to create the first (or any) admin user is the console command `php bin/console mbin:user:create <username> <email> <password> --admin`, and the only way to change a password afterwards is `php bin/console mbin:user:password <username> <password>`. Both commands take the password as a plaintext CLI argument — there is no config field, env var, or command flag that accepts a pre-hashed value. This is the genuine-plaintext-requirement case from SCHEMA.md's decision table (not merely an unsupported hash algorithm): `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever carries a hash of the customer's root password, and there is no destination in Mbin that accepts a hash for its own login.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not substitute, for the same reason documented in the `friendica` and `mastodon` gap analyses: Mbin has its own required login for actually using the app (posting, voting, moderating, admin panel), so an outer basic-auth perimeter still leaves the customer without a usable Mbin admin credential underneath.
summary: Mbin is an actively maintained (v1.10.1, released one day before this analysis) fork of the discontinued kbin project, filling a real gap in the catalogue — no existing recipe covers federated link aggregation/discussion. Mechanically it fits our model well: the official compose stack (php app with a built-in Caddy front end, a messenger worker, RabbitMQ+amqproxy, Postgres, and Valkey) already collapses to one public HTTP port with the built-in reverse-proxy auto-HTTPS disabled, the same pattern our Traefik setup already handles for other single-domain apps, and every internal service credential (Postgres, RabbitMQ, Mercure JWT, Symfony APP_SECRET) is an ordinary server-generated secret with no customer-facing exposure. The blocker is account bootstrap: Mbin has no web setup wizard, and its only admin-creation path (`mbin:user:create ... --admin` / `mbin:user:password`) takes a plaintext password as a CLI argument with no hash-accepting alternative, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash) has nowhere to project into, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate doesn't substitute since Mbin has its own required login for real use. It also functionally overlaps with the already-analyzed (and likewise unbuilt) `lemmy` candidate — same federated-aggregator niche, competing rather than complementary. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: worth revisiting if a customer-facing path to set an app-native plaintext admin password (not just a hash) is ever added to the platform.
