Meilisearch would be the first "search-infrastructure-as-a-product" recipe, similar in shape to the Elasticsearch gap-analysis case (apps-gaps/elasticsearch.yaml) but much lighter weight (single ~95MB binary/image, no JVM, low RAM floor) and aimed at developers wanting fast typo-tolerant search bolted onto their own site/app/docs rather than a big analytics platform.
usefulness_rationale: Meilisearch does ship a built-in web page (served at the root of its single HTTP port) offering a "Search preview" console — you paste an API key into the browser and can browse indexes and test queries interactively. That is a real web UI and it is reverse-proxy-compatible (plain HTTP on one port, no extra protocols), but it is a developer/API console, not an end-user-facing application the way every other recipe in this catalogue is. Its actual consumer is a developer's own application code calling the REST API/SDKs to power a search box elsewhere — the value only appears once the customer connects their own app to it. That's the same audience mismatch flagged in the Elasticsearch and EdgeDB gap analyses, just with a lighter footprint.
blocking_issues:
MEILI_MASTER_KEY is not an internal-only secret like a DB password — it IS the product's API credential. Every request except `GET /health` requires it as a Bearer token, so whoever holds the key controls (and can read/write) all of the customer's indexed data. The customer's own application therefore needs to receive this exact plaintext value to function at all — there is no dashboard channel today for surfacing a server-generated secret back to the customer for actual external use (the same gap noted for Gel/EdgeDB's root credential in apps-gaps/edgedb.yaml), so server_generated_no_customer_input does not really apply here: the customer must see it, and today they can't.

generated_from only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) onto a parameter; Meilisearch does not accept a pre-hashed master key at all — it takes the plaintext key directly and uses it verbatim as the Bearer token clients present. So even setting the "customer needs to read it" problem aside, a hash-shaped value would not work here regardless of algorithm support — a genuine plaintext requirement, which the schema treats as a structural blocker rather than an extensible gap.

Meilisearch also refuses to boot in `--env production` without a master key of at least 16 bytes — there is no "run it open" fallback that would be safe to ship publicly, so the credential can't just be left unset.
summary: Meilisearch is an actively and rapidly maintained (weekly-cadence, actively security-patched) lightweight search engine with no catalogue overlap — it would be the first standalone search/indexing recipe, lighter-weight than Elasticsearch but with the same fundamental audience mismatch: its web UI is a developer API console, not an end-user app, and its value only materializes once a customer's own code calls the API. That API call requires MEILI_MASTER_KEY, a plaintext credential the customer must actually receive and use — not an internal secret we can generate and hide, and not something generated_from's hash-projection mechanism can carry either. Mechanically simple to run (single container, single port, plain HTTP, low resource floor) but blocked today on the platform having no channel to hand a generated credential back to the customer for real use; worth reconsidering once such a channel exists.

Confirmed against upstream docs (Getting Started, Configuration -> Security) and the official docker-compose example: there is no environment variable to preset an admin username/password. The app boots with zero users; the first visitor to the public URL is shown an open sign-up form, and whoever submits it first becomes the "host admin" with full instance control. summary: Memos is an active, popular, genuinely lightweight note-taking app (single container, SQLite by default, one HTTP port) that would add real value to the catalogue's productivity lineup distinct from anytype-server's heavier sync-backend use case. It fails today's installability test for the same structural reason as 2FAuth and Activepieces: there is no env var to preset the sole admin account, so the app relies on an open, first-visitor self-registration screen that neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely provision for the customer. Revisit once upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow, or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond root-password projection.

name: MetaTrader 5
source_description: Browser-accessible MetaTrader 5 trading terminal for 24/7 forex and CFD trading
upstream_license: MetaTrader 5 itself is proprietary (MetaQuotes Software Corp., closed-source, free-to-use trading client). The community Docker wrapper (gmag11/MetaTrader5-Docker) is MIT, but its two runtime dependencies are copyleft: KasmVNC is GPLv2 and the LinuxServer.io base image is GPLv3 — bundling/redistributing the wrapper image carries those obligations even though MT5 itself is not open source.
upstream_docker_image: gmag11/metatrader5_vnc:2.3 (unofficial third-party wrapper; MetaQuotes ships no official Docker image or Linux binary at all)
version_health_notes: ~7.5 months since the wrapper's last tagged release (2.3, 2025-12-20) as of 2026-08-05. Full tag history: 1.0 (2023-10-15), 2.0 (2023-12-27), 2.1 (2024-05-29), 1.1 and 2.2 (both 2025-11-15), 2.3 (2025-12-20) — roughly 2-6 releases/year with uneven gaps, trending toward "slowing" rather than "dormant"; repo is not archived and has open issues/PRs being triaged. This assessment is for the third-party Docker wrapper, not MetaTrader 5 itself: MetaQuotes has no Linux/Docker distribution of MT5 at all, so "eol_status" here really tracks whether the community wrapper keeps up with upstream MT5/Wine changes, not whether MT5 the product is alive (it is; MetaQuotes actively ships MT5 updates for Windows/Mac/mobile, just never for Linux natively).
differentiation: MetaTrader 5 would be the catalogue's first finance/trading vertical app — none of the 24 current recipes touch trading, brokerage, or market-data workflows, so on category grounds alone it fills a gap. In mechanism, though, it is not really its own app in Docker form: MT5 has no Linux binary, so every "MetaTrader 5 Docker" project (gmag11's included) is Wine running the Windows .exe, screen-scraped into a browser via KasmVNC — i.e. a purpose-built instance of exactly what Guacamole already does generically (browser access to a remote desktop session). A customer wanting 24/7 MT5 gets a real, distinct outcome (their trading terminal always on, EAs/copy-trading running unattended) that Guacamole alone doesn't hand them out of the box, so there is user-facing value beyond the remote-desktop overlap — but architecturally this recipe is "Guacamole/noVNC + one specific pre-installed Windows app," not a native web or API-driven service like the rest of the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real, identifiable demand (Hostinger lists it as a named template, and community wrapper repos have hundreds of stars) from retail forex/CFD traders wanting an always-on terminal without leaving a desktop running. But it is a proprietary Windows app strapped to a VNC session via an unofficial third-party wrapper, not a maintained open web service — the fit is narrower and the operational risk (Wine compatibility breaking on MT5/Windows updates outside anyone's control) is higher than the median recipe.
blocking_issues:
The wrapper's web-access gate is controlled by two required env vars, `CUSTOM_USER` and `PASSWORD`, consumed directly (in plaintext, PAM/ KasmVNC-style auth) by the container — there is no `type: password` metadata parameter with a `generated_from` target, because the consumer here is not an app-level hashed-password field but a raw env var the VNC layer reads as cleartext. `generated_from` only ever projects a *hash* of the root password; it cannot supply a plaintext secret, so even the "gate credential" case this schema normally handles via `generated_from` doesn't apply here.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate could stand in for the login screen instead, but `CUSTOM_USER`/`PASSWORD` are two independent, freely-named values (arbitrary username, not just a password), and basic_auth's single root-password projection covers only one credential slot — it cannot also supply an arbitrary customer-chosen username to a second consumer inside the container.

Even with the VNC gate solved, the trading terminal itself is useless without the customer's actual MetaTrader broker account login (account number + broker-issued password, sometimes plus a TOTP code) entered inside the MT5 UI after boot — a third-party brokerage credential with zero input channel in the current `/compose` mechanism. This is the same "external account credential, no channel" shape as an OAuth registration, just typed into a UI instead of an env var.

Port 8001 (RPyC API) is a raw TCP protocol, not HTTP — it cannot sit behind Traefik/HTTPS the way the 3000 web-VNC port can, so even the reverse-proxy-compatible part of this app is only partial.
summary: MetaTrader 5 would be the catalogue's first finance/trading app, and there is genuine customer demand for an always-on browser trading terminal. But MetaQuotes ships no Linux/Docker build at all; every "MetaTrader 5 Docker" project, including the closest match to Hostinger's listing (gmag11/MetaTrader5-Docker), is really a Guacamole-shaped Wine-in-a-browser wrapper (Windows MT5 + KasmVNC), overlapping structurally with recipes/guacamole rather than standing as a novel service. It fails installability on three independent grounds: the VNC gate needs a plaintext username+password pair with no `generated_from` or `basic_auth` channel, the app itself needs the customer's real broker account credentials with no input channel at all, and one of its two ports is a raw TCP protocol that can't go behind Traefik. Not recommended under the current mechanism; revisit only if the platform grows a multi-credential, plaintext-capable provisioning channel — no version of `generated_from`/`basic_auth` alone would close this gap.

Treat the long 2023-2026 gap as a real dormancy risk that has only recently resolved, not as a settled "active" project with a long track record.
differentiation: opengist is a git-backed Gist clone (accounts, git push/pull, GitHub-style versioned snippets). MicroBin is a much lighter, anonymous-by-default paste/file/URL-shortener: a single ~5MB Rust binary with no git dependency, built-in optional client- and server-side end-to-end encryption, QR codes for shared links, configurable expiry, and URL shortening — a feature opengist doesn't offer at all. The use case is "drop a quick paste/file/link with no account" rather than "manage versioned code snippets like a mini-GitHub".
usefulness_rationale: Fills a genuinely different niche than opengist (ephemeral/anonymous sharing + URL shortening vs. git-based snippet management), but the general "self-hosted pastebin" ground is already covered by opengist, so this is a nice-to-have alternative rather than a clear catalogue gap.
summary: MicroBin is a small, actively-developed Rust pastebin/file-share/URL-shortener with a permissive BSD-3-Clause license and a pinned official Docker image (danielszabo99/microbin:2.1.4), exposing a single HTTP port (default 8080) that fits cleanly behind Traefik. It has no mandatory login of its own, so it installs today the same way n8n/WUD/Open WebUI do: gate the public port with Traefik basic_auth projected from the customer's root password. Its optional built-in admin console (MICROBIN_ADMIN_USERNAME/MICROBIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD) takes a plaintext password rather than a hash, so that specific feature isn't expressible via generated_from today — but it's not required, since the Traefik gate alone secures the app. Overlaps partially with opengist but differentiates via URL shortening, E2E encryption, and a much lighter footprint; recommend build_now, with a note that the project had a ~2.5-year release gap (2023-2026) worth keeping an eye on.

name: Microcks
source_description: CNCF API mocking and contract testing platform for multi-protocol services
version_health_notes: Latest release (1.15.0) published today, 2026-08-05, per the GitHub Releases API. Prior releases: 1.15.0-rc1 (2026-06-22), 1.14.0 (2026-04-29), 1.13.2 (2026-01-06), 1.13.1 (2025-12-08), 1.13.0 (2025-10-25), 1.12.1 (2025-07-21), 1.12.0 (2025-05-28) — a steady ~4-10 week cadence over the past year with no gaps. Repo is not archived, is a CNCF incubating project (not a sandbox/graduated-only signal but an active governance structure with a real TOC checkpoint cadence), and ships an official Kubernetes Operator and Helm chart alongside the core app. Clearly active, well-governed upstream.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers API mocking / contract testing — the closest adjacent recipes (n8n for automation, Gitea for source hosting) address a different stage of the dev lifecycle entirely. Microcks would be a genuinely new category (mock a REST/SOAP/GraphQL/gRPC/AsyncAPI service from its spec, so consumer teams can build/test against it before the real backend exists) with no overlap against anything currently shipped.
usefulness_rationale: Real, well-regarded tool in its niche (CNCF incubating, used by several enterprises for contract testing), but it targets API/platform engineering teams specifically rather than the broader self-hosting audience the rest of the catalogue serves — a narrower addressable customer than e.g. n8n or Immich.
blocking_issues:
Upstream's reference docker-compose ships two structurally different topologies, both incompatible with our current single-domain, single-HTTP-port-behind-Traefik model. The "standard" stack fronts the app with Keycloak for OIDC login: the app container publishes 8080 (HTTP API/UI) AND 9090 (gRPC mock port), Keycloak publishes a separate port (18080 in the reference compose), and the app's JVM options bake in a KEYCLOAK_PUBLIC_URL/OIDC issuer-uri tied to that exact second hostname:port at boot — this needs two publicly routable endpoints on two different hostnames/ports, not one <slug>.<base_domain> mapping.

The Keycloak-fronted login credential itself has no channel we support: the customer-facing account (admin / microcks123) is provisioned from a bcrypt hash baked into a static realm-import JSON file, not from an env var — it cannot be projected via generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD" without us maintaining a templated realm JSON per install, which the platform doesn't do today.

The "devmode" compose variant (KEYCLOAK_ENABLED=false) drops Keycloak and would in principle let us gate the whole thing behind Traefik basic_auth per the Adminer/WUD pattern — but doing so also gates the mock-serving ports (8080 HTTP mocks, 9090 gRPC mocks, plus Kafka 9092/19092 in the async profile) that Microcks' actual product value depends on: external test clients calling a mocked SOAP/GraphQL/gRPC/Kafka endpoint can't practically speak HTTP basic auth on those raw protocols, so gating breaks the feature the app exists for. There's no way to gate only the admin UI while leaving mock endpoints open without a per-path/per-port auth split the platform doesn't support today.
summary: Microcks is an active, well-governed CNCF project (1.15.0 released 2026-08-05, steady multi-month cadence, not archived) that would fill a genuinely new "API mocking / contract testing" category with zero overlap against the current 24 recipes. It is not installable under the current mechanism, though: its reference architecture is inherently multi-port and multi-protocol (HTTP UI, gRPC mocks, optional Kafka mocks), needs either a second public hostname for Keycloak or gating that would break the raw mock ports it exists to serve, and its customer-facing login credential is baked into a static Keycloak realm file with no generated_from-compatible input channel. Revisit if the platform gains multi-port-per-recipe support and a templated Keycloak-realm provisioning path; until then this is blocked on platform capability, not a "don't build" call on the app itself.

name: MicroRealEstate
source_description: Open-source rental property management for landlords, leases, rents and tenants
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/microrealestate/microrealestate/gateway (plus 8 sibling service images under the same org — no single "the" image; see notes)
version_health_notes: Latest tagged GitHub release is 1.0.0-alpha.3 from 2024-11-14 — 21 months before today (2026-08-05). Only three releases exist total, all alpha (1.0.0-alpha.1 2024-01-06, alpha.2 2024-10-19, alpha.3 2024-11-14), and the project has never cut a stable 1.0. However the repo itself is not dark: `pushed_at` is 2026-02-11 and commit history shows ongoing activity through at least 2025-12-09 (bug fixes, a feature request landed 2025-09-12, vulnerability fixes 2025-06-08). Not archived, 1,161 stars, 34 open issues. Docker images are published via CI on every push to a mutable `:latest` tag or a git-commit-SHA tag (`MRE_VERSION`) — there is no versioned/pinned stable image tag corresponding to a cut release, which is itself a signal of pre-1.0/alpha status rather than active abandonment.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches rental/property management, leases, or tenant billing — this would be a genuinely new category. The public surface is a single gateway container (port 8080) that reverse-proxies internally to /landlord and /tenant frontends, so it fronts fine behind Traefik on one hostname despite being a 9-service stack internally (mongo, redis, gateway, authenticator, api, tenantapi, pdfgenerator, emailer, landlord-frontend, tenant-frontend).
usefulness_rationale: The category is novel, but the app is stuck in alpha almost two years after its last tagged release with no stable image to pin, and — more importantly — its core authentication flow requires a working outbound email service before either the landlord or any tenant can even log in (see installability). That combination makes it a poor bet independent of the customer-parameter blocker below.
blocking_issues:
There is no admin-password env var at all. The landlord logs in via an interactive signup flow in the web UI (`SIGNUP: 'true'` on the landlord frontend/authenticator) rather than a credential set at deploy time, so `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` has nothing to project onto — the app never reads a pre-set admin password from an env var.

Both the landlord's own password-reset flow and — critically — every tenant login (tenant portal has no password of its own; it signs tenants in via emailed magic links) depend on the `emailer` service actually delivering mail. That requires the customer to supply one of: a Gmail address + app password, a Mailgun API key + domain, or SMTP host/port/username/password — all external third-party credentials with no input channel in the current `/compose` mechanism. Without one of these, the tenant-facing half of the app (arguably its main point, since landlords invite tenants to self-serve) is simply non-functional.

No official stable/pinned image tag exists to pin a recipe to (see version_health) — only a mutable `:latest` or a git-SHA, which RFC-002 pinning rules would reject even before the secrets issue.
summary: MicroRealEstate would fill a genuinely uncovered category (rental/lease management), and its public footprint — one gateway container on one port — is reverse-proxy-compatible in principle. But it fails installability on two independent grounds: the landlord account is created via interactive signup rather than an env-var password, so the root-password projection mechanism has nothing to attach to, and the tenant login flow (and landlord password reset) hard-requires the customer's own SMTP/Gmail/Mailgun credentials with no channel to supply them today. Combined with the project never having shipped past alpha in 21 months and having no pinnable stable image tag, this is a clear not_recommended rather than a build-with-caveats.

name: Milvus
source_description: Open-source vector database built for AI applications and similarity search
version_health_notes: Stable v2.6.x line ships roughly every 1-3 weeks (v2.6.16 2026-05-14 through v2.6.22 2026-08-04, i.e. yesterday relative to today 2026-08-05). A parallel v3.0.0 major line went GA on 2026-07-29, adding lakehouse/external-table integration on top of the same core. Both lines are actively maintained; no signs of slowdown or archival.
differentiation: No existing recipe is a vector database. Milvus would serve AI/RAG pipelines (embedding storage + similarity search) that customers build themselves, which is a different role than any of the 24 shipping recipes — closest in spirit is recipes/ollama (also an unauthenticated API-first backend with no bundled browser UI, and notably shipped with enabled: false in its own metadata).
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for a managed vector DB backing custom AI apps, but it's infrastructure a developer wires an SDK into, not something an AF customer opens in a browser and uses directly — narrower audience than our current UI-first catalogue.
blocking_issues:
Milvus's client protocol is gRPC (port 19530), not HTTP form-based login. Authentication is disabled by default, and when enabled the root user's password stays the hardcoded default ("Milvus") until an operator calls the runtime UpdateCredential RBAC API post-boot — there is no env var or startup config that accepts a pre-hashed password, so `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` has nothing to project into.

Traefik `basic_auth` assumes an HTTP browser login challenge; gRPC SDK clients (Python/Java/Go/Node) don't perform an interactive basic-auth handshake, so gating the gRPC port with basic auth would break normal client access rather than securing it. Exposing the port ungated leaves the database open to anyone who reaches the domain.

Standalone minimum viable deployment is a 3-container stack (Milvus + etcd + MinIO) with no bundled browser UI; the built-in port 9091 "webui" is a read-only health/metrics page, not an admin console. A real GUI would require bundling the separate Attu project, which itself needs the same root-password channel to connect to Milvus — doesn't resolve the underlying gap, just moves it.

recipes/ollama shows this catalogue already has a precedent for an unauthenticated-API-only backend, and it ships with `enabled: false` — suggesting this exact class of app (browser-less, SDK-driven, no auth channel) has already been judged not ready to expose to AF customers.
summary: Milvus is an actively maintained, well-regarded vector database, but it's architecturally a backend a developer's own code talks to over gRPC, not a browser-facing self-hosted app — it has no bundled web UI and no mechanism to receive a customer-supplied or root-password-derived admin credential at boot. Its default posture is no authentication at all, and neither of the two supported secret-projection mechanisms (generated_from hash, Traefik basic_auth) maps onto its gRPC client protocol. Recommend not building this recipe now; revisit only if a future platform version adds raw-TCP/gRPC-aware gating or Milvus itself grows a config-time password-hash input.

name: Miniflux
source_description: Minimalist and opinionated RSS feed reader with a clean web interface
version_health_notes: ~12 days since 2.3.3 as of 2026-08-05. Preceding releases land roughly monthly (2.3.2 on 2026-06-27, 2.3.1 on 2026-05-29, 2.3.0 on 2026-05-16, 2.2.19 on 2026-04-05) with real feature and security content in each — not a stalled or cosmetic-only cadence. 3,000+ commits on main, active issue triage. No archival notice, no EOL announcement.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers RSS/feed aggregation — this is a new category for the catalogue. A single lightweight Go binary with a Postgres backend, so it's a plausible "read all my newsletters/blogs/subreddits in one place" self-host for a customer, distinct from anything already offered (closest is n8n for general automation, which doesn't overlap functionally).
usefulness_rationale: Feed readers are a well-understood, evergreen self-hosting use case with steady demand (Google Reader's shutdown legacy keeps driving people to self-hosted alternatives), and Miniflux is one of the most polished, actively maintained options in that space — deliberately minimal dependencies (Go + Postgres, no Node/Python/Redis stack), single web port, no exotic hardware needs.
blocking_issues:
First-boot admin bootstrap (CREATE_ADMIN=1 / ADMIN_USERNAME / ADMIN_PASSWORD) only accepts a plaintext password — there is no option in Miniflux's config to seed the admin account from a pre-computed bcrypt/argon2 hash. generated_from can only ever project a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel to let the customer's own password become their Miniflux login. This is the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case the schema calls a structural blocker, not a supported-algorithm gap that IF-1420 could close by adding another hash type.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth (as done for n8n/WUD/ Open WebUI) does not fully solve this either, because Miniflux still presents its own separate login screen behind that gate — the customer would hit a second login they have no credentials for unless the admin password is also disclosed to them out-of-band, which isn't a supported flow today.

Miniflux does support trusting a reverse-proxy-supplied identity header (AUTH_PROXY_HEADER + TRUSTED_REVERSE_PROXY_NETWORKS + AUTH_PROXY_USER_CREATION=1), and Traefik's basicAuth middleware does emit an X-Forwarded-User header on successful auth — in principle this could bridge a Traefik basic_auth login (customer's root-password hash) straight into an auto-provisioned Miniflux account with no second login screen. That would resolve the blocker, but it is a novel wiring pattern no current recipe uses and isn't part of the documented generated_from/basic_auth mechanism pair — it would need to be vetted and adopted as a third supported mechanism before relying on it here.
summary: Miniflux is an active, well-maintained project that would fill a genuine gap (no RSS/feed reader in the current 24-recipe catalogue) with a light, reverse-proxy-friendly single-service-plus-Postgres footprint. It's blocked today only on the admin-bootstrap credential: Miniflux's first-run admin account can only be seeded with a plaintext password, which generated_from structurally cannot supply, and a plain Traefik basic_auth gate leaves a second, uncredentialed login screen behind it. A viable path exists (bridging Traefik basic_auth to Miniflux's AUTH_PROXY_HEADER trust so the gate IS the login), but it requires validating and adopting that as a new supported mechanism, not just building the recipe as-is.

ZEP_API_KEY is mandatory at first boot for the agent long-term-memory layer (Zep Cloud). Same problem: a third-party account credential with no input channel.

The app ships no login/admin account of its own (nothing in the README or compose file references an auth env var), so it would need a Traefik `basic_auth` gate just to avoid sitting open — that part is expressible today, but it doesn't fix the two API-key blockers above.

Architecturally split across two separately-exposed HTTP ports (3000 frontend, 5001 backend) with no reverse proxy or `/api` rewrite in front of them, unlike every current recipe's single public port — would need two routed hostnames/ports through Traefik, a pattern not yet used anywhere in the catalogue.

The shipped image runs the app via `npm run dev` (confirmed in the Dockerfile CMD), i.e. a development server, not a production build — a quality/stability concern independent of the secrets issue.
summary: MiroFish is a novel idea with no catalogue overlap, but it is not installable today: it hard-requires a third-party LLM API key and a third-party Zep Cloud API key at first boot, neither of which has a customer-input channel under the current `/compose` mechanism, and it also runs a dev-mode server across two separately exposed ports with no built-in auth. Even setting the platform blockers aside, the project's immaturity (single ~5-month-stale pinnable release despite active main development, `npm run dev` in production, and a star count that looks disproportionate to its age/commit history amid several same-named copycat repos from unrelated accounts) argues for treating this as low-priority even if a generic external-API-key channel is eventually built.

name: MiroTalk
source_description: Self-hosted P2P video conferencing with unlimited rooms and screen sharing
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (commercial/dual license also sold separately via CodeCanyon by the author)
latest_version: 1.8.75 (package.json; no git tags or versioned Docker Hub tags exist)
version_health_notes: No GitHub Releases and no git tags exist for this repo — it ships as a rolling `master` branch with `package.json` bumped ad hoc (currently 1.8.75) and a single `mirotalk/p2p:latest` Docker Hub tag (no versioned tags at all, last pushed 2026-07-31, 5 days before this analysis). Commit history is dense and recent (5 commits in the week before this analysis: dep bumps, a Node 24 base image bump, UI fixes), 4,665 GitHub stars, repo not archived, 0 open issues. Clearly active development, but the lack of any versioned tag (git or Docker) means a recipe could only pin by image digest, not a human-readable version — unusual among our current recipes and worth flagging even though it isn't disqualifying.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers real-time video/audio conferencing. Two other video-conferencing candidates (Jitsi Meet, Ant Media Server CE) were previously analyzed in apps-gaps/ but neither is an actual recipe yet, so overlaps_with is empty. MiroTalk's pure P2P architecture (no SFU/media bridge — video/audio flows directly between browsers) is the key differentiator from Jitsi Meet: it needs only the one HTTP signaling port, so unlike Jitsi it does not require a raw public UDP port for a video bridge and fits our single-HTTP-port Traefik model cleanly.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted video conferencing is a broadly appealing category (privacy-conscious teams/schools/communities wanting a Zoom/Meet alternative) with no equivalent in the catalogue today. MiroTalk is lightweight (single container, single port) compared to Jitsi's multi-service stack, making it a much easier first video-conferencing recipe to ship.
blocking_issues:
No versioned Docker tag exists (see version_health.notes) — only `:latest`. A recipe would have to pin by image digest instead of a human-readable tag, which is workable but a deviation from how every other recipe pins today; flagging for a human decision rather than treating it as disqualifying on its own.

MiroTalk's own host-protection feature (`HOST_PROTECTED` / `HOST_USER_AUTH`, default `false` in .env.template) stores credentials in `HOST_USERS`, a JSON array of one-or-more plaintext `{"username","password"}` pairs read directly from the env file — not a single hashed field. This does not fit `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash of the root password, never a plaintext value) and also does not fit the single-credential model even if it did (the sample default ships two accounts, admin and guest). The app's own login is therefore not expressible today; the recipe would instead have to leave `HOST_PROTECTED=false` (its default — no login, anyone with the room link can create/join) and rely on the Traefik `basic_auth` gate as the actual auth boundary.

Same product trade-off flagged for Jitsi Meet: MiroTalk's core value is letting external guests join a room via a shared link with no account of their own. Gating the whole domain behind Traefik `basic_auth` secures the deployment but also blocks those guests unless the host shares the basic-auth credential with them too — workable, but changes the app's intended sharing model. A human should decide if that trade-off is acceptable for a shipped recipe.

The upstream `.env.template` ships with `TURN_SERVER_ENABLED=true` pointing at a shared public TURN relay (`turn:a.relay.metered.ca:443`) with a hardcoded username/credential baked into the template alongside the public Google STUN server — not "no TURN server by default" as initially assumed. This is not an install blocker (it's a shared demo-tier credential, not a customer-specific secret our mechanism would need to provision), but a recipe should not ship that hardcoded third-party credential as-is: it's rate-limited/shared across every deployment of the template and could be revoked or abused. A human should decide whether to disable TURN by default, document it as customer-configurable via install-time env override, or find another resolution.
summary: MiroTalk is an actively developed (weekly commits, 2026-07-31 last push), lightweight, single-container P2P video conferencing app that would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue and is architecturally simpler to host than Jitsi Meet since it needs no raw UDP media-bridge port — just one HTTP port behind Traefik. It is mechanically installable today by leaving its own host-protection off and gating the domain with Traefik basic_auth (its built-in HOST_USERS login is plaintext-only and multi-account, so it cannot be projected via generated_from). The two open questions for a human before building are whether a basic_auth gate is acceptable given it also blocks the guest-link joining that is MiroTalk's core use case, and whether digest-only pinning (no versioned tag exists upstream) is acceptable for a recipe.

name: Misskey
source_description: Federated social media platform with emoji reactions and fediverse connectivity
version_health_notes: 2026.7.0 shipped 2026-07-31, 5 days before today (2026-08-05), following a full alpha → beta → rc → stable cycle (alpha.6 on 2026-07-17 through beta.4-6 and rc.0 on 2026-07-28) — roughly two weeks of pre-release hardening before stable. Prior stable, 2026.6.0, landed about a month earlier. This is a monthly-ish stable cadence with continuous alpha/beta activity in between (2026.7.0-alpha.2 for the *next* cycle was already on Docker Hub within hours of this analysis). Not archived, large active contributor base (syuilo + misskey-dev org), no EOL or maintenance-only signal.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers federated social/microblogging. Misskey is functionally closest to the already-analyzed (and unbuilt) `mastodon` and `friendica` candidates — same "run your own fediverse presence" pitch — so it's a competing option in that niche rather than an independent addition, but per CLAUDE.md that overlap is not itself a reason to reject it.
usefulness_rationale: Misskey is one of the most actively developed and distinctive ActivityPub servers (custom emoji/reactions, "Antenna"/timeline features, strong adoption in the Japanese fediverse), giving it real pull independent of Mastodon/Friendica. Architecturally it is also the simplest of the three fediverse candidates analyzed so far — a single web process on one HTTP port plus Postgres and Redis, no split web/streaming service and no mandatory outbound-SMTP dependency for account bootstrap.
summary: Misskey is the first fediverse/microblogging candidate analyzed that clears the installability bar. Its official image ships as a single web container (port 3000, no separate streaming service) plus Postgres and Redis, and its own account bootstrap is a plain web registration form with no email/SMTP requirement — the first account to register on a fresh instance automatically becomes admin (config.example.yml even documents an optional `setupPassword` gate explicitly aimed at "the provider of the service who sets up Misskey on behalf of the customer", but confirmed in source (packages/backend/src/server/api/endpoints/admin/accounts/create.ts) to be a plain-string-equality check against a config value, so it cannot carry a `generated_from` hash the way the customer's own password does). Left unset, that setupPassword gate is simply absent, which recreates the same race the platform already accepts for Immich/Open WebUI/n8n/WUD: a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (projected from the customer's root-password hash) in front of the whole domain is enough to guarantee the customer is the one who reaches the signup form first and becomes admin — no novel mechanism needed, just the existing basic_auth pattern. The only other secret at boot, the Postgres password, is an ordinary server-generated internal credential. One non-blocking caveat: as of 2026.7.0, automatic NSFW media detection moved to an optional external `sensitive-detector` service; omitting it degrades that one feature but does not affect boot or core functionality. Recommend `build_now`.

name: MistServer
source_description: Open-source media toolkit for building internet streaming applications at scale
upstream_license: Unlicense (public domain dedication, 0BSD as fallback for jurisdictions that don't recognize it); bundled mbedtls dependency is Apache-2.0/GPL-2.0
version_health_notes: ~12 days since 3.11.2 as of 2026-08-05. Recent cadence: 3.11.1 (2026-07-16), 3.11 (2026-07-15, new webcodecs player/protocol), 3.10 (2026-01-29), 3.9.2 (2025-11-27), 3.9.1 (2025-11-25), 3.9 (2025-11-24, Enhanced RTMP + JWT auth). Mix of feature releases every 1-7 months and fast-turnaround patch releases (3.11.2 shipped 9 days after 3.11.1 to fix a libSRT CVE) — real, security-conscious maintenance, not a stalled project. Maintained by DDVTech B.V., no archival or EOL notice.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches media/video streaming — closest neighbors (Immich for photo/video library, Home Assistant for camera feeds) are consumption/archival tools, not an OTT ingest-transcode-deliver toolkit. MistServer would open a genuinely new category: live RTMP/SRT/RTSP ingest with HLS/DASH/WebRTC output, aimed at developers or small broadcasters building their own streaming service rather than typical self-hoster productivity/monitoring use cases.
usefulness_rationale: Technically distinctive and well-engineered, but the audience is narrow (developers/integrators building a streaming product) compared to the rest of the catalogue's general-purpose self-hosting tools, and it needs real operational care (shared memory sizing, multiple raw protocol ports, stream-key management) beyond "set a domain and go."
blocking_issues:
MistServer ships with no accounts at all. On first HTTP connection to the controller (port 4242/8080) it returns a "NOACC" status and accepts an unauthenticated API call carrying new_username/new_password in plaintext to create the very first admin account — whoever gets there first wins. There is no config.json field or env var to pre-seed this account server-side before the port is public, so this is structurally the same "first HTTP visitor claims admin" race as n8n's owner-setup wizard, and needs the same fix: a Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password hash) in front of the whole app so only the customer can ever reach the account-creation screen. That gate is exactly the still-unmerged IF-1312 mechanism, so this is blocked on the same platform work as n8n/WUD, not something specific to MistServer.

Even once basic_auth lands, the app's core value — RTMP (1935), RTSP (5554), and raw UDP (8889, 18203) ingest/egress — sits on non-HTTP ports that Traefik cannot front at all; only the HTTP control panel benefits from the gate. This is inherent to the app's function (comparable to wg-easy's UDP WireGuard port) rather than a credential-input gap, so it doesn't block installability, but a recipe would need to expose those ports raw and rely on MistServer's own per-stream keys/JWT auth (3.9+) for ingest protection — worth flagging as a caveat for whoever builds this.

MistServer also recommends a non-default --shm-size (docs suggest 1-4GB vs Docker's 64MB default) and, per the official docs, a config file + video-storage bind mount rather than a self-contained volume — more infra-shaping than a typical single-container recipe, though not a hard blocker.
summary: MistServer is an active, well-maintained, genuinely differentiated candidate — no streaming/OTT toolkit exists in the catalogue today — but it is blocked on the same unmerged Traefik basic_auth mechanism (IF-1312) that gates n8n-style "first visitor creates the admin account" apps, since MistServer has no login at all until someone hits its account-creation API. Once that mechanism ships this becomes build_with_caveats: the HTTP control panel can be gated and reverse proxied, but the RTMP/RTSP/UDP ingest ports are raw by design and need to stay that way, and the niche technical audience makes this a lower catalogue priority than more broadly useful gaps.

name: Mitra
source_description: Lightweight Rust federated social network with full Mastodon API support
version_health_notes: 5 days since the latest release (v5.8.0, 2026-07-31) as of today (2026-08-05). Release history shows a new tag roughly every 2-4 weeks (v5.0.0 2026-03-23 through v5.8.0 2026-07-31, 8 releases in ~4.5 months). 4,300+ commits total, main branch under continuous active development. No signs of maintenance-only mode or abandonment.
differentiation: No existing recipe in the catalogue covers federated social networking / microblogging (ActivityPub, Mastodon-API-compatible). Mitra would be the first "run your own fediverse instance" offering, appealing to customers who want a personal or small-community Mastodon-compatible server without the heavier resource footprint of running actual Mastodon (Ruby/Rails + Sidekiq + Redis + Postgres).
usefulness_rationale: Fediverse self-hosting has a real, if niche, hobbyist/enthusiast audience, and "lightweight Rust alternative to Mastodon" is a genuine differentiator. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because Mitra is a much smaller, less-known project than Mastodon itself (fewer users familiar with the brand), and — see installability below — the admin bootstrap flow does not fit our current provisioning mechanism at all.
blocking_issues:
Mitra has no web-based signup for its first/admin account. The only supported way to create an account (admin or otherwise) is the CLI command `mitra create-account <username> <password> admin`, which must be run once against the running container before the instance is usable, and which takes the account's PLAINTEXT password as a literal argument — Mitra hashes it internally with its own scheme. `generated_from` only ever projects a pre-computed hash (argon2/bcrypt) of ROOT_PASSWORD, never the plaintext, so there is no way to feed this command a password that matches what the customer actually knows. Per SCHEMA.md's own criterion, a genuine requirement for the plaintext password (not any hash) is a structural blocker, and that is exactly the shape of this requirement.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not substitute here either: Mitra has its own real login system (Mastodon-API-compatible auth), so gating the whole domain behind basic auth would not give the customer a working admin login inside the app itself — it would just add an extra password on top of an admin account that still has no way to be provisioned with a customer-known credential.
summary: Mitra is a small but genuinely active Rust-based ActivityPub/Mastodon-API server with no overlap in our current 24-recipe catalogue and a real differentiation angle (lightweight fediverse hosting). It is reverse-proxy-friendly (single HTTP port, Postgres-backed, structurally similar to recipes/gitea and recipes/n8n). However, it cannot be provisioned under the current mechanism: the only account-creation path is a CLI command that demands the admin's plaintext password, and neither `generated_from` (hash-only) nor Traefik `basic_auth` (no substitute for a real in-app login) can satisfy that. Revisit if/when a plaintext root-password-projection channel exists, or if upstream adds a web-based first-run admin signup.

Prior cadence was otherwise roughly every 1-3 months (2.4.0 on 2025-11-13, 2.5.0 on 2026-02-24, 2.6.0 on 2026-03-16). It ships with a fixed, undocumented-as-configurable default admin login (admin@example.com / changeme per official docs) rather than an env-var-driven first-boot admin bootstrap — the supported artisan flow (`mixpost-auth:create`) is interactive and needs a plaintext password we never have, so generated_from cannot project the customer's root-password hash into it. Per the schema's guidance on fixed/default admin credentials, this is not a structural blocker on its own: gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth (root-password-derived) makes that gate the real auth boundary, with the unchanged default Mixpost login sitting safely behind it — the same pattern used for MindsDB. That makes it mechanically installable today with a caveat worth flagging to a human reviewer: release cadence has visibly slowed (~4.7 months since the last tag, the longest gap on record besides one prior 5-month stretch) and the free edition's social-network coverage (X/Facebook/Mastodon only) is narrower than what "social media scheduler" implies without the paid Pro tier. Recommend build_with_caveats.

name: Mobilizon
source_description: Federated event organizer for communities without ads or surveillance
version_health_notes: Mobilizon was originally a Framasoft project; Framasoft handed the project over to a new French non-profit, Kaihuri (funded by NLnet), in July 2024 after five years of in-house development — 4.1.0 was Framasoft's last release. Under Kaihuri the repo and Docker images moved from the `framasoft` namespace to `kaihuri` (framagit.org/kaihuri/mobilizon, Docker Hub `kaihuri/mobilizon`); the old `framasoft/mobilizon` image on Docker Hub is stale (last tag 3.0.3) and must not be used. Under the new maintainer, releases continue at a steady pace: 5.1.5 (2025-07-11), 5.2.0 (2025-10-17), 5.2.1-beta1 (2025-12-12), 5.2.2 (2026-01-11), 5.2.3 (2026-03-23), 5.2.4 (2026-06-29) — about 5 weeks before this analysis (2026-08-05). This is a genuine maintainer handover, not an abandonment: cadence and activity look healthy post-handover.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers federated community event organizing. Mobilizon is a Facebook-Events/Meetup alternative for communities and activist groups: it lets an instance's users create groups, publish events, and federate with other Mobilizon (and wider ActivityPub/Fediverse) instances, with no ads or tracking.
usefulness_rationale: Privacy-conscious communities and non-profits looking to leave Meetup/Facebook Events for event organizing are a distinct audience from anything else in the catalogue, and the federation angle (same space PeerTube/Mastodon-style tools occupy) has real pull for self-hosters already running other Fediverse software.
blocking_issues:
Mobilizon has no admin-account env var at all. The only way to create the first admin/moderator user is a post-boot CLI command (`mobilizon_ctl users.new <email> --admin --password <plaintext password>` via `docker compose exec`), which takes the password as a plaintext CLI argument rather than reading a pre-hashed value from an env var the way Vaultwarden's `ADMIN_TOKEN` does. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the root password, never the plaintext, so it cannot supply this argument. This is structurally the same blocker that keeps the existing `gitea` recipe disabled (`enabled: false`) — CLI-driven, plaintext-password admin creation with no env-var hash input.

Unlike apps such as n8n/WUD where the app itself has no meaningful login and Traefik `basic_auth` fully substitutes as the auth boundary, Mobilizon's own login is the actual product surface — organizers must authenticate as that user to create/manage groups and events. Gating the domain with `basic_auth` instead would secure the instance but not give the customer any way to actually use it as an event organizer, so it isn't a substitute mechanism here the way it is for login-less apps.

Secondary, non-blocking caveat: Mobilizon needs SMTP credentials to send registration-confirmation and notification emails for a fully functional multi-user instance. This isn't a hard blocker on its own (an admin-only/invite-based instance can run without it), but a built recipe would need to decide how to source or default this.
summary: Mobilizon is an actively maintained (steady ~quarterly releases post its 2024 Framasoft→Kaihuri handover, latest 5.2.4 on 2026-06-29), single-HTTP-port, Postgres/PostGIS-backed federated event platform that would be a genuinely novel addition to the catalogue (no overlap with any of the current 24 recipes) for communities wanting a Meetup/Facebook-Events alternative. It is blocked under the current recipe mechanism, though: the only way to create its first admin user is a post-boot CLI command taking a plaintext password, which neither `generated_from` (hash-only) nor a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (doesn't cover the app's own organizer login, which is customer-facing, not just an admin-panel lock) can supply — the same structural gap that already disabled the `gitea` recipe. Worth revisiting once the platform gains a channel for a customer-usable plaintext credential, or if Mobilizon adds an env-var-based admin bootstrap.

summary: Mongo Express is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8081) Node/Express app with no reachable-database dependency beyond a customer-supplied MongoDB connection string. Its own login is HTTP basic auth via plaintext env vars (ME_CONFIG_BASICAUTH_USERNAME/PASSWORD, comparing directly, not a hash), so it fits the same pattern as Adminer/DbGate: disable the app's own basic auth and gate the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth:true with the password projected from the customer's root password via generated_from — mechanically installable today with no blocking secret gap. It also duplicates ground already staked out by the healthier, unbuilt adminer/dbgate/cloudbeaver gap analyses, just narrowed to MongoDB only. Revisit only if upstream resumes shipping stable releases and Docker Hub un-deprecates (or a community fork takes over) the image.

name: MongoDB 4
source_description: Document-oriented NoSQL database with JSON-like document storage
upstream_license: SSPL-1.0 (MongoDB Server, since 4.0.4/4.2.x; earlier patch builds of the 4.x line are AGPL-3.0)
latest_version: 4.4.29 (final patch of the 4.x line; 4.0 and 4.2 series are older sub-lines of the same major version)

differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes exposes a standalone, customer-usable NoSQL database — recipes like immich, n8n, and paperless-ngx run their own internal Postgres/SQLite purely as private storage, not something a customer connects to directly. A standalone MongoDB recipe would target a customer running their own external app (a Node/Express backend, a custom script) that needs a MongoDB-compatible datastore to connect to from outside the VM. Same category of use case as apps-gaps/mariadb.yaml and apps-gaps/apache-couchdb.yaml, but on top of an EOL version of the engine rather than a live one.
usefulness_rationale: Even setting aside installability, shipping a recipe pinned to an EOL database version with no further security patches available is a poor fit for a hosting catalogue — customers would be running a database version whose known and future CVEs never get fixed. A live MongoDB version (7.x/8.x) would carry the same structural DB-port problem below but at least be a defensible offering; "MongoDB 4" specifically is not.
blocking_issues:
The only useful shape for a standalone MongoDB recipe is a publicly reachable mongod port (27017) so an external customer app can connect to it. Publishing that host port is exactly what RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` rule forbids (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226). MongoDB speaks a raw binary wire protocol, not HTTP, so there is no Traefik-based fronting option either (no subdomain routing, no basic_auth gate) — it has no application-layer presence to reverse- proxy the way our web-UI recipes do.

Even setting the port rule aside, the root user is provisioned via the official image's `MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME` / `MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD` env vars, which mongod's entrypoint consumes as a **plaintext** password to run its own SCRAM-SHA-1/256 credential derivation internally at first boot. There is no supported way to seed the root user from a pre-computed hash of any kind (bcrypt, argon2, or otherwise) — unlike CouchDB, which at least accepts a PBKDF2 hash. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash, never a plaintext value, so this is a genuine plaintext-password requirement per SCHEMA.md's guidance, making it a structural blocker rather than a missing-algorithm gap.
summary: "MongoDB 4" targets a database engine line (4.0/4.2/4.4) that is fully past MongoDB Inc.'s own end-of-life dates — the last patch (4.4.29) shipped 2024-02-28, over two years before today, with no further fixes coming for known or future CVEs. Independent of that, a standalone MongoDB recipe has no viable shape in the current catalogue: its only useful exposure is a public 27017 that RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` rule forbids, it has no web UI or HTTP presence to gate behind Traefik, and its root credential must be seeded as plaintext (not a `generated_from` hash), which the platform has no channel for. This combines the "raw DB port" structural mismatch already flagged for MariaDB with an EOL upstream version on top, making it a clear not_recommended rather than a platform gap worth tracking.

name: Moodle
source_description: Open-source learning management system trusted by over 489 million users worldwide
version_health_notes: Actively released: 5.0 shipped April 2025, 5.1 followed on the usual ~6-month minor cadence, 5.2 landed 2026-04-20 with a 5.2.1 point release 2026-06-08 (about two months before this analysis on 2026-08-05). Next release is 5.3, the LTS, scheduled for October 2026 (Moodle cuts an LTS roughly every two years with 36-month security support; non-LTS minors like 5.2 get 18 months). No sign of maintenance-only mode — active core development and a published forward roadmap.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes touch learning-management / course delivery. Moodle would be the catalogue's first education-sector app — genuinely new ground, not a variant of anything already offered (closest structural cousins are other PHP+DB web apps like Gitea or Paperless-ngx, not anything overlapping in purpose).
usefulness_rationale: LMS software serves a large, distinct customer segment (schools, training providers, corporate L&D) that none of our other recipes address, and Moodle is the dominant open-source player in that space (self-reported 489M users). High potential demand if it can be shipped responsibly.
blocking_issues:
No maintained, freely-available official Docker image exists to pin. bitnami/moodle (the de-facto standard self-hosting image for years) is "no longer available for free through Docker Hub" and now ships only as a paid Bitnami Secure Images OCI artifact; the free fallback bitnamilegacy/moodle is an explicitly frozen, unmaintained snapshot that "will receive no further updates or support." moodlehq's own moodlehq/moodle-php-apache is a PHP+Apache *base* image for Moodle's own CI/dev workflow — it does not bundle the Moodle application code at all; it expects a separately-cloned Moodle source tree mounted in as a volume (`MOODLE_DOCKER_WWWROOT`) and is explicitly documented for developer/Behat/PHPUnit use, not production. There is no single self-contained, actively-maintained, free image matching the "one official image, pinned tag" pattern every other recipe uses.

Even setting the image question aside, MOODLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD (the secret in secrets_required_at_first_boot) has no confirmed expressible mechanism today: Moodle's standard installer (admin/cli/install_database.php) only accepts the admin password as plaintext and hashes it internally — there is no built-in hook to accept a pre-computed hash. Projecting `generated_from` would need a nonstandard install script: run the installer with a throwaway password, then overwrite the resulting mdl_user.password row directly with a bcrypt hash (Moodle's default hash format happens to be PHP bcrypt, so the algorithm lines up) — plausible in principle but untested and well outside the standard install flow used by every other recipe in the catalogue, so not counted as expressible today.
summary: Moodle is a genuinely differentiated, high-demand catalogue addition (the first LMS/education app, actively released with a public roadmap through the 5.3 LTS in October 2026) but is not buildable today on our mechanism: there is no free, actively-maintained, self-contained official Docker image to pin — the historical answer (bitnami/moodle) is now paywalled, its free fallback (bitnamilegacy/moodle) is a frozen, unmaintained snapshot, and moodlehq's own image is a dev/CI base that requires mounting Moodle's source tree separately rather than shipping the app. That image-sourcing gap is upstream/packaging, not something IF-1420/1312 merging would fix, so this lands as not_recommended for now rather than blocked_on_platform — worth revisiting if Moodle or a trustworthy third party ships a maintained, free, self-contained image again.

name: Mopidy
source_description: Extensible music server unifying local files, Spotify, SoundCloud, and radio
version_health_notes: v4.0.0 (major, Pydantic-based data-model rewrite) shipped 2026-04-24, followed by the 4.0.1 patch release 2026-05-16 — under 3 months before today (2026-08-05). Commit activity on mopidy/mopidy as recent as 2026-07-29 and mopidy-spotify as recent as 2026-07-22, so upstream is actively maintained, not just tagging occasional releases.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers self-hosted music/media streaming; this would be the first in that category. Core value is unifying local audio files and internet radio behind one server, with the ability to bridge into Spotify/SoundCloud when the operator supplies their own service credentials.
usefulness_rationale: Mopidy itself ships no web UI or auth — a UI (e.g. the community Iris extension) has to be installed on top, and the two headline integrations named in Hostinger's own description, Spotify and SoundCloud, require an OAuth app registration / API key per customer that our platform has no channel to collect (see installability below). What's left after stripping those out — local-file playback and internet radio via MPD/HTTP — is a narrow, hobbyist niche compared to the rest of the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
No official Docker image. mopidy/mopidy ships no container at all; the community images found (wernight/mopidy, jee-r/docker-mopidy, firefrei/docker-mopidy) are third-party, and the most visible one (wernight/mopidy) hasn't been updated in ~5 years — building a recipe would mean either adopting an unmaintained image or maintaining our own Dockerfile, neither of which matches how the rest of the catalogue pins to a vetted official tag.
Mopidy's HTTP frontend (the interface any web UI, e.g. Iris, is served over) has no built-in authentication by design — upstream's own docs say to put it behind a reverse proxy that handles auth. This is expressible today via Traefik basic_auth, so it is not a hard blocker, but it must be treated as mandatory, not optional, or the JSON-RPC control API sits open.
Mopidy also exposes the MPD protocol (port 6600), a raw TCP protocol many desktop/mobile MPD clients use directly, not through the web UI. Traefik in this catalogue routes HTTP(S) by hostname; there's no mechanism today to expose a second raw-TCP port per customer, so MPD-native clients would be unusable and only the HTTP/web-UI path could ship.
Spotify and SoundCloud integration — the two most-marketed capabilities in Hostinger's own description — each require the customer's own third-party API key/OAuth app registration (mopidy-spotify needs a Spotify Client ID/Secret; mopidy-soundcloud needs a SoundCloud auth token). No customer-supplied-value channel exists for either, so a shipped recipe could only offer local-file playback and radio streams, not the headline features.
summary: Mopidy is actively maintained (4.0.1 shipped 2026-05-16, commits as recent as 2026-07-29) and would be the first music/media recipe in the catalogue, so there's no overlap concern. But it has no official Docker image, no built-in web UI or auth (requiring both a third-party extension and a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate), and its two headline features — Spotify and SoundCloud — need per-customer API credentials our platform has no channel to collect, leaving only local-file/radio playback installable. Given the missing official image and the value proposition being gutted down to a narrow hobbyist slice, this isn't worth building now even though a stripped-down version is mechanically installable.

name: Morphic
source_description: Open-source AI search engine with generative answers and source citations
version_health_notes: ~2 months between v1.5.0 (2026-06-10) and today (2026-08-05). Prior tags (v1.0.0 Feb 2026, v1.1.0 Mar 6, v1.2.0 Mar 30, v1.3.0 Apr 10, v1.4.0 May 24, v1.5.0 Jun 10) shipped roughly monthly through 2026, and the `ghcr.io/miurla/morphic` image is rebuilt on every merge to main between tagged releases. No archival or EOL signal; repo is under active, frequent development. One packaging caveat: the published container tags are commit SHAs (e.g. `bcda07c...`), not semver strings matching the GitHub release tags — pinning a recipe image tag means resolving the commit SHA that corresponds to a given release, not just quoting "v1.5.0". Name ambiguity: "Morphic" also names an unrelated 1990s Self-language GUI framework (ported to Squeak/Pharo/Lively Kernel) and a separate Raising the Floor accessibility desktop app; both were considered and ruled out — miurla/morphic is the only one matching Hostinger's "AI search engine with generative answers and source citations" description.
differentiation: Not another LLM chat frontend — Morphic is a Perplexity-style answer engine: it takes a search query, runs it through a bundled SearXNG meta-search instance, and has an LLM synthesize a cited, generative-UI answer (inline images, source cards) from the results. Open WebUI + Ollama cover "chat with a local model"; nothing in the current catalogue covers "search the web and get a sourced AI answer."
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely distinct capability (web-search-grounded answers with citations) rather than a repaint of open-webui/ollama, so there's a real differentiation case. Rated medium rather than high because good answer quality depends on a capable LLM backend — pairing it with a self-hosted Ollama model (the only way to avoid an external API-key requirement, see below) generally yields noticeably weaker synthesis than the hosted frontier models the upstream project is built around.
summary: Morphic is an actively maintained, Apache-2.0 answer-engine that fills a real gap in the catalogue (web-search-grounded, cited AI answers, distinct from the open-webui/ollama chat pairing already offered). Its Postgres, Redis, and SearXNG dependencies are all self-contained with server-generated secrets, and it is installable today provided the recipe follows the same escape hatch open-webui already uses: bundle a local Ollama container as the LLM provider (OLLAMA_BASE_URL) instead of asking for a customer-supplied OpenAI/Anthropic/Google API key, since those third-party keys have no input channel today. With ENABLE_AUTH left at its documented default (false) Morphic has no login screen of its own (unlike open-webui/anythingllm, there's no first-visit admin signup), so the recipe also needs a Traefik basic_auth gate rather than relying on built-in auth — Supabase-based auth (the only alternative) is itself an external third-party account with no customer-input channel. The main caveat is answer quality: this is a "hosted-frontier-model" product by design, and pinning it to local Ollama models will noticeably weaken the generative-answer synthesis that is its whole differentiator.

name: Multi-Scrobbler
source_description: Self-hosted scrobbler tracking plays from Plex, Jellyfin, Spotify, and more
version_health_notes: v0.15.0 released 2026-07-30, less than a week before today (2026-08-05). Release history through 2026 is dense: 0.13.2 (2026-05-05), 0.13.3 (2026-05-06), 0.14.0-beta.1 (2026-05-14), 0.14.0-beta.2/beta.3 (2026-05-28/30), 0.14.0 (2026-06-01), 0.14.1 (2026-06-03), 0.14.2 (2026-07-08), 0.15.0-RC1 (2026-07-28), 0.15.0 (2026-07-30) — multiple releases most months. differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers music-listen tracking or scrobbling. Immich (photos) and Paperless-ngx/Paperless-AI (documents) are the only other "personal media archive" recipes and don't overlap in domain. Multi-Scrobbler's actual value proposition is as a hub that watches Plex/Jellyfin/Spotify/etc. listening activity and forwards it to a scrobble target (Last.fm, ListenBrainz, or a self-hosted Maloja), so it's most useful to a customer who already has a media server or streaming account and wants unified listening history/stats.

blocking_issues:

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate closes that hole and is fully expressible today via root-password projection, so this part alone is not a blocker.

All of these are external accounts/keys the customer would create outside our platform, and several (Spotify, Last.fm) are completed via an OAuth redirect callback served from the dashboard itself (`BASE_URL`-driven). None of this is a hash of the customer's root password and none of it is server-generatable — there is no input channel today for any of it, matching the "external API key/OAuth" no-go rows in apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md.
summary: Multi-Scrobbler is an active, actively-developed, single-container app (MIT licensed, one web port, Traefik-compatible) that would be a genuine, non-overlapping addition to the catalogue for self-hosted media-server users who want unified scrobbling/listening stats. The dashboard itself has no built-in login, but a Traefik basic_auth gate fully covers that with today's root-password projection, so the container is mechanically safe to boot and expose. It is nonetheless not installable today: every source and client it supports requires a customer-obtained third-party API key or OAuth registration (Spotify, Last.fm, ListenBrainz, Jellyfin/Plex tokens, etc.), and none of that has an input channel under the current root-password-projection/basic_auth-only mechanism — matching the "external API key/OAuth" no-go case in apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` — revisit once the platform gains a customer-supplied arbitrary-value input channel beyond root-password projection.

Multica is a team-facing coordination platform: it assigns tasks/issues to multiple named coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, etc.), tracks their progress via WebSocket, and stores completed work as reusable "skills" across a workspace. No existing recipe covers this multi-agent, team-workflow orchestration use case, so there is no functional duplication — only a thematic adjacency (both are "AI agent" recipes).
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely novel category for the catalogue (dev-team agent orchestration hub) and the core web+API+Postgres stack is easy to containerize and front with Traefik. Rated medium rather than high because the actual coding agents run as a separate daemon process on the customer's own machine(s) with their own CLI credentials — the hosted instance is only the coordination/dashboard layer, so its standalone value depends on the customer already running that local daemon setup.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: RESEND_API_KEY (transactional email provider used to deliver login verification codes); site-access gate credential
blocking_issues:
Multica's only login mechanism is email-based: a user requests a verification code and Multica emails it via Resend (RESEND_API_KEY). There is no username/password admin account and no parameter that a root-password hash could be projected into — the app needs a real, working external email-delivery API key to let anyone log in at all. There is no customer-supplied-value channel for this today.

The only alternative to Resend is MULTICA_DEV_VERIFICATION_CODE, a fixed PLAINTEXT verification code documented upstream as "dev-only, dangerous in production." generated_from only ever yields a hash, so it cannot populate a field that must be compared against a plaintext code typed into a UI — this is the genuine-plaintext-requirement case the schema calls out as a structural blocker, not just a missing-algorithm gap.

A Traefik basic_auth gate can keep the deployment closed to the public internet, but it doesn't solve the above: once through the gate, the customer still cannot complete the app's own login flow without a working Resend key or the insecure dev code.

Optional Google OAuth login (GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID/SECRET) has no registration channel either, but since it's optional and email-code login is the primary path, this is secondary to the Resend blocker above.
summary: Multica is a legitimately new addition to the catalogue's AI-agent category — team-oriented coding-agent task orchestration, distinct from the personal/messaging-driven OpenClaw and Hermes Agent recipes already present — and upstream is under very active daily development. It is not installable today, however: its only account-creation path is an email-verification code sent via Resend (an external API key with no customer-input channel), and the sole production alternative is a plaintext dev-only code that generated_from's hash-only output cannot supply. A Traefik basic_auth gate can hide the deployment but cannot substitute for Multica's own login flow. Revisit once either a customer-suppliable external-API-key channel exists or upstream adds a password-based admin login that generated_from can target.
