name: MySQL
source_description: Fast, reliable open-source relational database for web and app workloads
upstream_license: GPL-2.0 (with commercial dual-licensing for enterprise features)
latest_version: 9.7.2 (current LTS line, oraclelinux9-based); 8.4.11 (previous LTS); 26.7.0 (Innovation track, not for production)
version_health_notes: 9.7.2 (LTS) released 2026-07-28, about 8 days before today (2026-08-05) — a very fresh release, well inside a normal cadence. Oracle now ships two parallel tracks: "Innovation" (currently versioned 26.x, calendar- style numbering, latest features, not recommended for production) and "LTS" (9.x, the stable/supported line customers should actually run), plus a still-maintained previous LTS (8.4.x). This is the official Oracle/MySQL Team-maintained Docker Hub image, actively updated within the last two weeks.
overlaps_with: gitea; guacamole; immich; n8n; paperless-ngx; runtipi
differentiation: None of the listed recipes actually bundle MySQL — on inspection they all run their own internal Postgres instance (or a Postgres-based fork, in Immich's case), not MySQL/MariaDB, purely as private storage on the bridge network. So there's no literal engine duplication. A standalone MySQL recipe would target a different use case than any of those: a customer running their own external app (e.g. WordPress, a legacy PHP app, a BI tool) that specifically needs a MySQL-protocol backend to connect to. That's a real, distinct need in principle, but see `blocking_issues` — it requires exactly the exposure shape our own rules forbid.
usefulness_rationale: Useful in principle to technical customers who want a managed MySQL-compatible backend for something they run themselves, but it's a developer/power-user tool with zero UI, and its only useful exposure shape (a public 3306) is one our own recipe rules already reject on security grounds. Same structural class as MariaDB (apps-gaps/mariadb.yaml) — effectively the same analysis applies, since both are raw-protocol RDBMS engines with no application-layer presence to gate behind Traefik.
blocking_issues:
The only useful shape for a standalone MySQL recipe is a publicly reachable MySQL-protocol port so an external customer app can connect to it. Publishing host port 3306 is exactly what RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` rule forbids (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226) — 3306 is explicitly on the forbidden-host-port list. There is no alternate exposure path today: Traefik only routes HTTP, and MySQL speaks a raw binary protocol, so it cannot be fronted the way our web-UI recipes are (no `basic_auth`, no subdomain routing).

Even setting the port rule aside, the root password can only be projected via `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD` (plaintext env var, which `generated_from` does not produce) or `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASH` (a `caching_sha2_password`-style hash, not `argon2`/`bcrypt`) — neither matches the currently supported `generated_from` algorithm list. This half of the problem is `blocked_on_platform`-shaped (a new supported hash algo could fix it), but it's moot given the public-port blocker above, which is a hard structural mismatch, not a platform gap.
summary: MySQL is an actively maintained, healthy upstream project (LTS 9.7.2 released just over a week before this analysis), but a standalone MySQL recipe has no viable shape in the current catalogue. Its only useful exposure — a public, customer-reachable 3306 — is explicitly forbidden by our own `no-public-db-port` rule, and it has no web UI to gate behind Traefik/basic_auth the way our other no-login apps do. None of the existing 24 recipes actually run MySQL internally (they use Postgres), so there's no literal duplication, but that also means there's no "internal-only, never publicly exposed" niche for it to fill either. This isn't primarily a platform gap waiting on IF-1420/1312; it's the same structural mismatch documented for MariaDB (apps-gaps/mariadb.yaml) between what the app needs (a raw internet-facing DB port) and what our security rules and Traefik-only routing model support. Recommend not_recommended.

name: Nango
source_description: Open-source OAuth and API integration platform for 300+ services
upstream_license: Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2) — source-available, not OSI-approved open source
version_health_notes: Latest release v0.71.3 shipped 2026-08-03, two days before today (2026-08-05). Release history shows a rapid, near-weekly cadence (v0.71.0 on 2026-07-14, v0.71.1 on 2026-07-20, v0.71.2 on 2026-07-21, v0.71.3 on 2026-08-03; v0.70.7-v0.70.9 through June 2026). Repo is not archived and shows active development with recent feature work (MFA sign-in gating added in the latest release).
differentiation: Nango is an OAuth/API-connector backend meant to be embedded into a product a developer is building (300+ prebuilt OAuth integrations, credential storage, API proxying, webhook handling) — it targets developers wiring auth into their own app, not end users automating tasks. n8n is a workflow-automation tool for end users connecting apps together interactively. The audiences and use cases differ enough that this isn't a straight duplicate, but it does compete for some of the same "connect my app to third-party APIs" mindshare as n8n's node library.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct developer-infrastructure niche (managed OAuth/token handling for building integrations) not covered by any of the 24 current recipes. But it's a narrower audience than most of the catalogue — useful mainly to customers who are themselves building a SaaS product with third-party integrations, not general SME/homelab users — and the free self-hosted tier is an intentionally feature-limited edition of a commercial product (see licensing note below), which caps how compelling it is as a catalogue addition.
blocking_issues:
Official docker-compose.yaml is a 4+ container stack (Postgres, Redis, the nango-server app, optional Elasticsearch for logs) and exposes two separate public HTTP ports from the same server container (SERVER_PORT 3003 for the API/dashboard, CONNECT_UI_PORT 3009 for the embeddable connect widget) plus the raw Postgres (5432) and Redis (6379) ports bound directly on the host in the shipped compose file — those two data-store ports need to be removed/firewalled, and the two HTTP ports both need Traefik routing (e.g. two host rules on the same domain), which is more surface than our single reverse-proxied port pattern is built for. Structurally closest existing template is recipes/immich/ (multi- container stack, Postgres + Redis dependencies) rather than a single-container recipe.

Elastic License 2.0: prohibits "provid[ing] the software to third parties as a hosted or managed service" that exposes a substantial set of its functionality. Each Application Factory deployment is a single customer's own dedicated instance rather than a shared multi-tenant service we operate, which is the more defensible reading of ELv2's exception, but this is a legal judgment call, not an engineering one — worth a compliance sign-off before treating this as clear to ship, independent of the mechanical installability question below.

The product's entire value proposition (300+ OAuth integrations) is unusable until the customer supplies an OAuth client ID/secret per third-party service they want to connect — that happens through Nango's own post-login settings UI (not a first-boot secret we'd need to inject), so it does not block installability, but it does mean the app is inert until the customer does non-trivial per-integration setup themselves after provisioning.
summary: Nango boots with only server-generated secrets (encryption key, DB password) plus a Traefik basic_auth gate in place of its own optional, non-forced dashboard login — the auth mechanism itself isn't the blocker. What blocks installable_today is shape: the official stack is multi-container (Postgres, Redis, optionally Elasticsearch) and exposes two distinct public HTTP ports from one container (dashboard/API on 3003, connect-widget UI on 3009) plus raw DB/cache ports bound in the shipped compose file, none of which fits our current single-port-behind- Traefik recipe pattern without real compose surgery. Separately, the Elastic License 2.0's hosted-service restriction and the fact that the free self-hosted tier is a deliberately limited edition of a commercial product both warrant a second look before prioritizing this — flagged as blocked_on_platform rather than not_recommended because the underlying app is active, well-maintained, and fills a real gap for developer-focused customers.

name: NATS
source_description: Cloud-native messaging system with pub/sub, request-reply, and JetStream
version_health_notes: v2.14.4 tagged 2026-07-30, less than a week before today (2026-08-05). The project maintains two parallel lines in lockstep: 2.14.x (current) and 2.12.x (LTS-style maintenance line) — 2.12.14 also shipped on 2026-07-30 alongside 2.14.4, and both lines had prior releases on 2026-06-29 (2.14.3 / 2.12.12), 2026-06-09 (2.12.11), and 2026-06-02 (2.14.2 / 2.12.10). That's releases in every recent month across both branches. NATS is a CNCF-hosted project (incubating), not archived, backed by Synadia. Clearly active.
differentiation: No existing recipe provides a message broker of any kind. NATS is general-purpose cloud-native messaging (pub/sub, request-reply, and JetStream for persistent/replayable streaming — a lighter-weight alternative to Kafka), aimed at connecting a customer's own applications/microservices rather than IoT devices specifically. This differs in target audience from the MQTT brokers (Mosquitto, EMQX) also analyzed as gap candidates: NATS speaks its own client protocol used from application code (Go/Node/Python/etc. client libraries), not the IoT-oriented MQTT protocol.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful piece of infrastructure for a customer running their own distributed apps/microservices and wanting a message bus without standing up Kafka, but — like Mosquitto/EMQX — it has no browser-usable surface at all; the entire point is other software connecting to it via a client library, so the audience is narrow and technical (people already writing their own services) rather than the general end-user apps most of the catalogue targets.
summary: NATS is an actively-maintained (CNCF, Synadia-backed), Apache-2.0 licensed messaging system with no catalogue overlap — it would be the first message-broker-style recipe. Unlike Mosquitto (blocked on generated_from lacking pbkdf2 support) and EMQX (blocked on a plaintext-only dashboard password plus a BSL license question), NATS's own config format natively accepts a bcrypt-hashed password in its authorization block (`nats server passwd` generates exactly this), which is a direct match for `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` — no workaround needed. Confirmed against upstream docs: NATS ships with no authentication enabled by default (anonymous access to publish/subscribe on 4222) so a recipe must force this password, and the HTTP monitoring endpoint on 8222 is unauthenticated by design and should sit behind a Traefik basic_auth gate (also root-password-projected) rather than being exposed directly. The main client port (4222, raw TCP) needs direct non-HTTP exposure, the same accepted pattern already used by wg-easy and Syncthing in this catalogue, not a structural blocker. Recommend build_now — mechanically ready today; the main open question is whether a technical, developer-facing message broker fits the catalogue's broader end-user-app profile, which is a product-fit call rather than a platform blocker.

name: Neko
source_description: Self-hosted virtual browser for collaborative web browsing and streaming
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/m1k1o/neko/chromium (one of several per-browser/app images under ghcr.io/m1k1o/neko/*; no single "the" image — chromium is the typical default)
version_health_notes: Latest release (v3.1.5) published 2026-08-05, one day before analysis date (2026-08-06). Multiple releases in the preceding months (v3.1.1-v3.1.4 in April 2026, v3.0.8-v3.0.10 across Sep 2025-Jan 2026). Actively maintained, no signs of slowdown.
differentiation: Guacamole (present but disabled in the catalogue) gateways to external RDP/VNC/SSH targets over TCP/websocket through the browser. Neko instead runs and streams a self-contained browser/desktop session via WebRTC, aimed at synchronous multi-user watch-parties and collaborative browsing rather than remote-desktop administration. Distinct use case, but both compete for the same "remote-access-in-a-browser" catalogue slot, and Neko's WebRTC transport is materially harder to expose than Guacamole's pure-TCP one (see reverse_proxy_compatible below).
usefulness_rationale: Real, differentiated use case (shared browsing sessions, watch parties, isolated browsing sandbox) not covered by any of the 24 shipped recipes. Value is capped by the infra mismatch below rather than by demand.
blocking_issues:
Neko's WebRTC media transport requires a dedicated UDP port range (NEKO_WEBRTC_EPR, commonly 56000-56100) to be publicly reachable and mapped 1:1 (host port == container port, per NEKO_WEBRTC_EPR) for each instance, plus NEKO_WEBRTC_NAT1TO1 set to the instance's own public IP. Traefik only fronts HTTP(S) on 80/443; it has no mechanism to route a customer-specific raw UDP port range. This is the same class of problem noted for Runner/af-api connectivity in CLAUDE.md — the fix is a routable per-customer UDP exposure (NodePort/LoadBalancer with a real public IP), not something the recipe layer can paper over with Traefik alone. Without direct UDP reachability the browser stream simply will not connect (WebRTC ICE fails).

Per-instance public IP / port-range allocation for NAT1TO1 is an infra-provisioning need beyond what any existing recipe requires (all 24 current recipes are single-HTTP-port, Traefik-fronted).
summary: Neko is an active, well-maintained project (Apache-2.0, latest release 2026-08-05) offering a genuinely differentiated use case — shared/streamed browser sessions — not covered elsewhere in the catalogue. Its two login passwords (user/admin) both map cleanly onto generated_from root-password projection, so the auth-secrets side is solvable today. The blocker is structural: Neko needs a customer-specific public UDP port range for WebRTC plus a 1:1 NAT mapping to a public IP, which our Traefik-only exposure model cannot provide. Recommend revisiting once a routable per-customer UDP/LoadBalancer exposure mechanism exists on the platform; not buildable as a standard recipe today.

name: Neo4j
source_description: The world's leading open-source graph database for connected data
upstream_license: GPL-3.0 (Community Edition); Neo4j Enterprise Edition is source-available/commercial, not OSS
version_health_notes: 2026.06.0 released 2026-07-02, about 5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Neo4j moved from semantic to calendar versioning (YYYY.MM) in January 2025 and has shipped a new minor roughly every month since (2026.02.3, 2026.03.1, 2026.04.0, 2026.05.0, 2026.06.0) — a genuinely active cadence. Only the latest minor is supported on the rolling line; a separate 5.26 LTS line is supported until 2028-06-06 for customers who want a slower-moving base. The official `neo4j` Docker Hub image is updated in step with each release (Debian trixie and UBI10 variants, community/enterprise tag suffixes).
differentiation: None of the 24 existing recipes are a graph database — n8n, immich, paperless-ngx, etc. all run Postgres purely as private internal storage, not as a customer-facing engine. A graph database serving connected-data use cases (recommendation engines, fraud/anomaly detection, knowledge graphs, dependency analysis) is a genuinely distinct niche the catalogue doesn't cover. See `installability`, though, for why that niche can't actually be served by our current mechanism.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct value in principle for technical customers building graph-backed apps, and it does ship a web UI (Neo4j Browser) rather than being purely headless like a raw RDBMS — but that UI cannot function through our reverse-proxy model (see below), which caps its practical usefulness at "yet another database a power user could reach only partially."
blocking_issues:
Neo4j Browser — the only web UI Neo4j ships — is a static page served on the HTTP port (7474) that then opens a live Bolt protocol connection to run any query. Since Neo4j 3.2, the browser hardcodes that Bolt connection to port 7687 regardless of the page's own URL path, so the HTTP port alone is not enough for the UI to do anything beyond loading its shell. Our Traefik renderer only routes a recipe's first `http: true` port (`single-http-port`, rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:267-272); a second Traefik-routed endpoint for 7687 has no rendering path today. Exposing 7687 as a second raw host port instead would put an unauthenticated-by-default binary graph protocol directly on the internet — the same risk class `no-public-db-port` guards against for MySQL/Postgres/Mongo/Redis etc. (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226), even though 7687 isn't literally on that forbidden list. Net effect: the app's one web UI cannot be made to work end-to-end through our reverse-proxy model without either renderer changes (multi-port/TCP routing) or accepting a raw public database-protocol port — the same structural mismatch already documented for MySQL (apps-gaps/mysql.yaml) and MariaDB.

Independent of the port problem, the initial admin credential (`NEO4J_AUTH=neo4j/<password>`, set once at first boot) only accepts a **plaintext** password — Neo4j hashes it itself internally with its own algorithm, and the Docker entrypoint gives no way to seed a pre-computed bcrypt/argon2 hash instead. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash, never plaintext, so it cannot populate this field. This is a genuine plaintext requirement per `apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md`'s own test table, not merely an unsupported hash algorithm — so it is a structural blocker, not something IF-1420 adding a new algo would fix.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead (à la Adminer) would not actually close the gap either: `basic_auth` only covers HTTP-routed traffic. It would protect the 7474 page but not a separately exposed raw 7687, so the one credential that matters for an unauthenticated graph database — the thing actually able to read and write all the data over Bolt — would stay unprotected. Neo4j's own (plaintext-only) auth is the only mechanism that actually covers Bolt, which is exactly the field we have no channel for.
summary: Neo4j is a healthy, actively released project (monthly calendar-versioned releases, latest 2026.06.0 from 2026-07-02) and would fill a real gap — no existing recipe covers graph databases. But it fails our mechanism on two independent fronts: its only web UI (Neo4j Browser) needs both the HTTP port and a hardcoded raw Bolt port (7687) to function, which our single-Traefik-router renderer can't route and which would otherwise mean a raw, unauthenticated-by-default database port facing the internet; and its initial admin credential only accepts a plaintext password with no hash-projection channel, so `generated_from` can't reach it and Traefik `basic_auth` can't cover Bolt anyway. Neither issue is a near-term platform gap (unlike a missing hash algorithm); both are structural mismatches with the current single-HTTP-port, hash-only-secret model. Recommend not_recommended, in the same structural class as `apps-gaps/mysql.yaml` and MariaDB.

It joins an existing NetBird network (the vendor's SaaS control plane or a separately self-hosted management server) and has no web UI, no exposed HTTP port, and no local admin/login of its own — a headless CLI daemon in the same category as claude-code/gemini-cli rather than a server a customer stands up and administers on its own domain. wg-easy, by contrast, is a full WireGuard server + web UI that IS the thing being administered — these solve different problems ("run a VPN client that joins a network I already have" vs. "stand up a new VPN server"), so no real overlap despite both being WireGuard-based.
usefulness_rationale: Provisioning an AF VM purely to run a mesh-VPN client has one legitimate use case: a customer who already runs a NetBird network wants a permanent cloud peer (e.g. a bastion/gateway reachable from anywhere over the mesh without exposing public ports). That's real but niche — most NetBird users install the client on devices they already have, not on a newly provisioned cloud instance whose only job is to be a mesh peer. Compared to the rest of the catalogue this is a narrow, single-purpose infra utility rather than a general-purpose self-hosted app.
summary: Re-evaluated as recipe_type: native (per the claude-code/gemini-cli precedent for headless CLI agents) rather than docker-compose: netbird's own install script (curl -fsSL https://pkgs.netbird.io/install.sh | sh) installs the client directly on the VM's own kernel/network namespace, so the earlier --network host/--privileged concern from a docker-compose framing doesn't apply, and SCHEMA.md explicitly carves out "no web UI" as a non-blocker for native recipes. NB_SETUP_KEY has no projection mechanism — it's an external credential from the customer's own NetBird control plane — but that mirrors ANTHROPIC_API_KEY on claude-code and GEMINI_API_KEY on gemini-cli: declare it as a required:false documentation-only parameter, install the agent unconfigured, and let the customer run `netbird up --setup-key=<their key>` over SSH post-provisioning. Mechanically this is installable today under the established native-CLI pattern. The remaining open question is usefulness rather than installability: a bare mesh-VPN peer is a genuinely useful but narrow product (cloud bastion/gateway for an existing NetBird network) rather than a general-purpose self-hosted app, so build_with_caveats rather than build_now.

name: NetBox
source_description: Open-source network infrastructure modeling for IPAM, DCIM, and documentation
latest_version: v4.6.7 (app); netbox-docker release-image tags track the same v4.6.x line
version_health_notes: v4.6.7 released 2026-07-30, about 6 days before today (2026-08-05). NetBox ships frequent patch releases within the 4.6 line (v4.6.3 on 06-16, v4.6.4 on 06-30, v4.6.5 on 07-14, v4.6.6 on 07-28, v4.6.7 on 07-30) — roughly every 1-2 weeks, a clearly active cadence. Now stewarded commercially by NetBox Labs but the core app and the official netbox-community/netbox-docker packaging remain Apache-2.0 and actively updated; no archival or EOL signal.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers IPAM/DCIM or network source-of-truth documentation. Portainer and Guacamole touch infrastructure/remote-access management but neither models IP address space, racks, or device inventory. NetBox would be a genuinely new category for technical/IT-admin customers managing their own network infrastructure.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct niche (no overlap) and a single HTTP web UI that fits our Traefik-fronted model well, but it's a specialist tool for network engineers/MSPs rather than a broad-appeal app — narrower audience than most of the current catalogue.
blocking_issues:
NetBox's own admin login is bootstrapped exclusively via the netbox-docker entrypoint's SUPERUSER_NAME/SUPERUSER_PASSWORD/ SUPERUSER_EMAIL environment variables (SKIP_SUPERUSER defaults to true, i.e. no superuser exists unless these are set), and SUPERUSER_PASSWORD is consumed as a **plaintext** value passed to Django's `createsuperuser --no-input` via DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD — there is no hashed-password input path for this variable. Per the SCHEMA.md decision table, a genuine plaintext-password requirement (not merely an unsupported hash algorithm) is a hard structural blocker: `generated_from` only ever produces a hash, never the plaintext root password itself.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead does not fix this: with SKIP_SUPERUSER left at its default, NetBox boots with no user account at all, so a customer landing on the (now basic-auth-gated) login page still has no NetBox credentials to sign in with. Unlike Adminer/WUD-style "no login of its own" apps, NetBox does have its own mandatory login — basic_auth would only add a second gate in front of a still-unusable app, not substitute for the missing admin account.
summary: NetBox is an actively maintained (v4.6.7, released 6 days before this analysis), Apache-2.0 licensed app with a real, non-overlapping niche (IPAM/DCIM/network documentation) and a single reverse-proxy-friendly web UI — a good structural fit for the catalogue otherwise. It's blocked today purely on the secrets mechanism: the only supported way to bootstrap its admin account, SUPERUSER_PASSWORD, requires the plaintext password rather than any hash, which `generated_from` cannot supply, and Traefik `basic_auth` can't substitute since NetBox still needs its own account to be usable at all. Recommend `blocked_on_platform` — revisit if a plaintext-capable projection channel (distinct from the current hash-only `generated_from`) is ever added, not `not_recommended`, since the app itself is healthy and the gap is purely platform-side.

name: Netdata
source_description: Real-time infrastructure monitoring agent with 800+ integrations
version_health_notes: Released 2026-07-15, three weeks before this analysis (2026-08-05). Frequent cadence: v2.10.0-2.10.4 landed April-July 2026 (four patch releases in one month), preceded by v2.9.0 (Feb 2026) and v2.8.x (Dec 2025-Jan 2026). No archival or EOL signals; this is a well-maintained, actively developed project.
differentiation: Netdata monitors the health of the host/infrastructure itself (CPU, memory, disk, network, per-process, container-level metrics via the Docker socket, 800+ integrations) with per-second granularity and zero-config auto-discovery. Uptime Kuma (our only other monitoring recipe) checks external endpoint availability from the outside; it does not look inside the host. No recipe in the current catalogue does host/infra-level observability, so this fills a distinct gap.
usefulness_rationale: Infrastructure monitoring is a broadly useful, well-understood need for anyone running a VM/server, and Netdata's real-time dashboard with no setup required (auto-detects services) makes it an easy sell as a one-click recipe.
blocking_issues: Netdata's own upstream deployment guidance runs the container with network_mode: host, pid: host, and privileged-ish capabilities (SYS_PTRACE, SYS_ADMIN, apparmor=unconfined) plus host bind-mounts (/proc, /sys, /etc/os-release, /var/run/docker.sock) to get full system-level metrics. That conflicts with running it as a normal bridge-network service behind Traefik on a per-customer subdomain. It can still run in bridge mode with a published port and the Docker-socket mount (giving Docker container-level stats), but full host hardware/process telemetry — the main selling point — would be degraded. This is a design/scope caveat, not a hard secrets-input blocker.
summary: Netdata is active, well-maintained (latest release three weeks ago) and fills a genuine gap versus our one existing monitoring recipe (Uptime Kuma checks external endpoints; Netdata watches the host from inside). Its local dashboard on port 19999 ships with no built-in login, so it is installable today the same way as Adminer/WUD: domain param plus a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate with the password projected from the customer's root password via generated_from. The open question is architectural rather than a secrets blocker — Netdata's recommended deployment wants host networking and host mounts for full-fidelity metrics, which sits awkwardly with our per-customer bridge-network/ Traefik model, so a recipe would need to scope down to container-level/Docker-socket monitoring rather than true host telemetry. Recommend building with that caveat made explicit to the developer picking this up.

name: NextChat
source_description: Self-hosted AI chat UI for OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and 20+ providers
version_health_notes: Recomputed directly from the GitHub releases API on 2026-08-06: v2.16.1 published 2025-07-29 — that is over a year old (~12.3 months) as of today (2026-08-05), not ~1 week as an earlier draft of this file incorrectly stated. Tagged-release history before it: v2.16.0 shipped 2025-02-16 (~5.3 months before v2.16.1), and v2.15.6 through v2.15.8 shipped roughly weekly in Oct-Nov 2024 (~3 months before v2.16.0). So the tagged-release cadence, already uneven, effectively stopped over a year ago — no new tag in the last 12+ months. However, the repo itself is not dormant: `pushed_at`/most recent commit on `main` is 2026-07-06 (~1 month old), 847 open issues, 88.5k+ GitHub stars, not archived. Classified `release_cadence: dormant` because the tagged-release track record shows nothing shipped in over a year; `eol_status: active` because ongoing commit and issue activity indicates the project is still maintained upstream, just not cutting tagged releases on a predictable schedule (or possibly moving to untagged/rolling `:latest`-style distribution — the Docker image itself was not checked for a same-period update cadence).
differentiation: Same "chat UI in front of an LLM" shape as Open WebUI, but a different model: NextChat has no bundled inference engine (no Ollama sidecar, negligible RAM/disk floor) and is built around bring-your-own-key access to 20+ hosted providers (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Azure, etc.) entered directly in the browser Settings panel, rather than local/self-hosted models. It would appeal to a customer who wants a lightweight, private front-end for API keys they already pay for, without also running a GPU/CPU-heavy local model stack.
usefulness_rationale: Legitimate, distinct niche (lightweight BYOK multi-provider chat front-end vs. open-webui's local-model-first design) and cheap to run, but it's still one more entry in the same broad "AI chat" category, and its core value depends entirely on the customer already holding paid third-party API keys they manage themselves post-install — the app itself contributes little beyond a UI shell around keys the platform has no visibility into.
summary: NextChat boots with zero required env vars: all provider API keys (OPENAI_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, etc.) are optional server-side fallbacks, and by default each visitor enters their own provider API key directly in the app's Settings UI, which the app then uses per-request — that key never needs to reach our recipe mechanism at all, since it's a runtime credential the customer manages themselves inside the app after install, not a first-boot secret we provision. The app's own `CODE` access-password env var is a plaintext shared-password comparison (not hashable via `generated_from`), so instead of using it we would leave it unset and put a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app on its public port — the same pattern already used for n8n and Open WebUI — to avoid shipping an open, unauthenticated public endpoint. That makes it mechanically installable today. The bigger prioritization concern: the pinned Docker image tag (v2.16.1) and its upstream GitHub tag are both dated 2025-07-29 — over a year stale as of today (2026-08-05), with no newer tagged release or image build since, even though the repo's `main` branch is still committed to monthly and issues are actively triaged (847 open). Combined with the conceptual overlap with open-webui in the same AI-chat category, this makes NextChat a lower build priority than a project with an active tagged-release track record, even though it remains mechanically installable and not abandoned.

Syncthing is the closest name association but solves a different problem — it's P2P device-to-device sync with no server-side web UI, no browsable file manager, no link sharing, no calendar/contacts/office integration. Immich is media-specific (photos/videos only) and Paperless-ngx is scanned-document-specific. Nextcloud is a general file drive (any file type) plus calendar, contacts, and optional office/collaboration apps — the "Google Drive/Workspace alternative" category the catalogue doesn't have yet.

High customer draw.
blocking_issues: CONFIRMED (Task 4 sanity-check audit, 2026-08-24): the admin credential's install mechanism hashes plaintext internally (or, for alist/nextcloud, the post-boot CLI/occ command does) - generated_from can only emit an already-hashed value, so the customer's real root password will never match. The one first-boot secret that is customer-facing is the admin login: the entrypoint's NEXTCLOUD_ADMIN_USER/NEXTCLOUD_ADMIN_PASSWORD are passed straight through to `occ maintenance:install --admin-pass "$NEXTCLOUD_ADMIN_PASSWORD"`, which stores its own internal hash of whatever string it receives — functionally identical to AList's `alist admin set <password>` post-boot call (apps-gaps/alist.yaml), so the value can be projected via generated_from:"<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD" with no plaintext-only requirement blocking it. DB and Redis passwords are pure internal secrets, generated server-side with zero customer input needed. No external API keys, no OAuth, no second customer-chosen credential. Active, healthy release cadence (34.0.2, 2026-07-23, ~13 days old) with three majors maintained in parallel. Recommend build_now.

Like several other candidates seen in this batch, Nexterm has no env-var admin bootstrap: the first visitor to reach the app hits an open "/register" first-time-setup endpoint and picks their own admin username/password with no channel to project the customer's root password into it, so that endpoint must sit behind a Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password-derived) until the customer completes real registration behind it — this makes it installable_today under the current mechanism. The bigger open question is fit and maturity rather than plumbing: it structurally overlaps with the catalogue's existing (disabled) Guacamole recipe, and the project itself is still pre-1.0/beta with every release tagged -BETA or -OPEN-PREVIEW, which is a meaningful risk for an app that will hold customer SSH credentials. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth a recipe if Guacamole is deprioritized in favor of covering the broader "server management" niche, but not a clear build_now given the overlap and beta status.

name: Nexus Repository Manager
source_description: Universal artifact repository manager for Maven, npm, Docker, and PyPI
upstream_license: Eclipse Public License 1.0 (Nexus Repository OSS); note the wrapping docker-nexus3 packaging repo is Apache-2.0
version_health_notes: 3.95.0 published the same day as this analysis (2026-08-05); the prior tag, 3.94.1, shipped 12 days earlier. Sonatype's own version-status page shows a steady monthly cadence through 2026 (3.92.0 on 05-07, 3.93.0 on 06-04, 3.94.0 on 07-09, 3.95.0 on 08-05) with 1 year GA support plus 6 months extended maintenance per release — a clearly active project, not maintenance-only. One caveat unrelated to release cadence: Sonatype's own FAQ warns that third-party community plugins often don't work with recent Nexus Repository versions or PostgreSQL mode — doesn't affect the core OSS product's health, but worth flagging.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is an artifact/package repository. Gitea covers git source hosting and Portainer covers container-host management, but neither stores or serves build artifacts (Maven/npm/PyPI packages, Docker images) the way Nexus does. This would be a genuinely new category serving dev teams / CI pipelines that need a private package registry.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct niche and a single reverse-proxy-friendly web UI (plus optional raw docker-registry ports customers wouldn't need for the baseline HTTP-only setup), but it's a specialist devops tool aimed at teams already running CI/CD — narrower appeal than broad consumer/prosumer apps in the catalogue, and the JVM footprint (2GB+ RAM recommended) is heavier than most existing recipes.
blocking_issues:
The official sonatype/nexus3 image has no documented environment variable for setting the admin password. On first boot it generates a random password itself and writes it to /nexus-data/admin.password inside its data volume; the customer is expected to read that file (via `docker exec ... cat /nexus-data/admin.password` or volume access) to log in the first time, then change the password through the setup wizard. Our recipe mechanism has no channel to read a container-generated file back out and hand it to the customer, nor to pre-seed the file with our own hash.

A community PR (sonatype/docker-nexus3#136, unmerged as of this analysis) proposes a NEXUS_ADMIN_INIT_PASSWORD variable, but even if merged it only accepts a **plaintext** password (it's hashed internally via Apache Shiro CLI before being written to the security database) — per SCHEMA.md, `generated_from` only ever projects a hash, never plaintext, so this would remain a structural blocker even with that PR merged.

Traefik `basic_auth` can't substitute here either: Nexus does have its own mandatory login (unlike Adminer/WUD-style loginless apps), so gating the reverse-proxy port would just add a second wall in front of an admin account the customer still has no way to discover or set.
summary: Nexus Repository Manager is an actively maintained (3.95.0 shipped the same day as this analysis, steady monthly cadence, EPL-1.0-licensed) app filling a real gap — no artifact/package repository exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue — behind a single reverse-proxy-compatible web UI. It's blocked today purely on the secrets mechanism: the official image bootstraps its admin account with a self-generated password written to a file inside the container, with no supported way to inject or read back a hash, and Traefik basic_auth can't cover for a genuinely missing admin credential the way it does for loginless apps. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`, not `not_recommended` — the app itself is healthy and worth building once a channel exists for either reading a container-generated secret back out or accepting a plaintext admin password input.

usefulness_rationale: No-code internal-tool builders (Airtable, Retool, Budibase) are a popular self-hosting category with no representation in the catalogue today; NocoBase is one of the most active open-source options in that space and would fill a real gap.
blocking_issues:
The app's own first-boot admin login is bootstrapped from INIT_ROOT_PASSWORD (documented default: admin@nocobase.com / admin123, username nocobase), which NocoBase's install routine reads and hashes itself internally — it needs the **plaintext** password, not a pre-computed hash. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password, so there is no channel to seed this field with a value the customer could actually use to log into the built app afterward. Unlike Adminer-style tools, NocoBase's core product *is* the logged-in app-builder session, so gating the whole thing behind Traefik `basic_auth` (leaving INIT_ROOT_PASSWORD at a fixed/random server-side value) would still leave the customer locked out of the NocoBase UI itself once past the gate — this isn't the "fixed default credential behind a proxy gate is fine" case, because there's no way for the customer to ever learn or set that inner credential.

Separately from the platform-mechanism issue above, NocoBase's Community Edition license (the custom "NocoBase License Agreement", not plain Apache-2.0 — see upstream.license) clause 5.4 explicitly prohibits using the Software to "provide to the public any form of no-code, zero-code, low-code, AI platform SaaS/PaaS products". An af-recipe hosting NocoBase for IONOS customers to build no-code apps on is arguably exactly this: a productized no-code/low-code SaaS/PaaS offering built on the original/modified Software. This is a legal/business blocker independent of the INIT_ROOT_PASSWORD issue — even if a plaintext-credential projection channel existed tomorrow, this licensing restriction would still need to be cleared (e.g. via a paid Commercial license, which itself still forbids the SaaS/PaaS use per its own clause) before this app could ship as a recipe.

Clause 5.2/5.3 of the same agreement also forbids removing or changing NocoBase's branding/name/version/license info from the UI or code without a paid Commercial license, constraining how any eventual recipe could present/white-label the app.
summary: NocoBase is strong on technical/catalogue merits — active development, official Docker image, single reverse-proxy-friendly HTTP port, and no functional overlap with anything currently in the catalogue. However it has two independent, unrelated blockers. (1) Platform mechanism: its first-boot admin account requires a plaintext INIT_ROOT_PASSWORD that only NocoBase's own install step can hash, and `generated_from` only ever supplies a hash — not fixable by wrapping the app in Traefik `basic_auth` the way Adminer-style tools are, since the customer still needs a working NocoBase login behind that gate. (2) Licensing: the Community Edition is governed by a custom "NocoBase License Agreement" (incorporating but overriding Apache-2.0) whose clause 5.4 bars using it to offer no-code/low-code SaaS/PaaS products to the public — which an af-recipe hosting it for IONOS customers plausibly is. Either blocker alone would prevent shipping this recipe today; both would need to be resolved (a plaintext-secret projection channel or post-boot password-set API for #1, and legal clearance or a Commercial license for #2) before revisiting.

name: NocoDB
source_description: Open-source Airtable alternative that turns databases into smart spreadsheets
upstream_license: Sustainable Use License (source-available, not OSI-approved; source-visible for internal/non-commercial use only — versions before 0.301.0 were AGPL-3.0)
version_health_notes: Latest release published the same day as this analysis (2026-08-05), confirmed via the GitHub releases API. Cadence is a steady ~monthly tag (2026.04.x through 2026.08.0, roughly one release every 2-4 weeks including point releases), with matching Docker Hub tags published same-day. No dormancy or EOL signal. Separately: the project relicensed away from AGPL-3.0 to the Sustainable Use License as of v0.301.0 (2024) — no longer OSI open source, restricting self-hosted use to internal/non-commercial purposes. That is a licensing-suitability question for a hosted-for-customers catalogue, not a version-health concern, but it should be flagged to whoever owns catalogue licensing policy before this ships.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers a no-code database/spreadsheet-hybrid tool. Closest neighbors in the catalogue (n8n for automation, paperless-ngx for document management) address adjacent but distinct needs. NocoDB would be the catalogue's first "structured data + spreadsheet UI" offering, filling a real gap for customers wanting an Airtable-style tool they host themselves.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely differentiated and popular upstream (turns any SQL database into a spreadsheet UI with API access), but the Sustainable Use License caveat and the plaintext-admin-password blocker below cap it below "high" until both are resolved.
blocking_issues:
NocoDB's own admin bootstrap (NC_ADMIN_EMAIL / NC_ADMIN_PASSWORD) only accepts a plaintext password (min 8 chars, one uppercase, one number, one special char) — there is no hashed-credential input on that path, so `generated_from` cannot project the customer's root password into it. This is a genuine plaintext-only requirement, not merely an unsupported hash algo, so it is a structural blocker for that specific channel.

Workaround exists and is recommended: omit NC_ADMIN_EMAIL/PASSWORD entirely. Without them, NocoDB has no preset admin — whoever visits the instance first and signs up through the web UI becomes the first (super admin) user. That first-come-first-served signup is itself a real risk on a public IP before the customer claims it, so it must be gated behind Traefik `basic_auth: true` (auto-generated credential, same pattern as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI) until the customer signs up, then the customer's own in-app signup becomes the durable login. This makes the app installable today via the basic_auth mechanism, just not via NocoDB's native admin-bootstrap env vars.

Needs a persistent database (Postgres recommended for production; falls back to embedded SQLite if NC_DB unset) plus NC_AUTH_JWT_SECRET — both are server-generated random secrets with no customer-facing value, so no blocker there.

Sustainable Use License is source-available, not OSI open source, and explicitly restricts running it as a service that competes with NocoDB's own paid offering — worth a licensing-policy sign-off before build, independent of the technical mechanism question above.
summary: NocoDB is an actively maintained (monthly releases, latest tag same-day as this analysis), single-container-plus-Postgres web app with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue, filling a real no-code/spreadsheet-on- database gap. It is mechanically installable today by skipping its plaintext-only admin-bootstrap env vars and gating first access behind a Traefik basic_auth wall until the customer signs up in-app — the same pattern already used for n8n and WUD. The remaining open question is non-technical: NocoDB's Sustainable Use License is source-available, not OSI-approved, and restricts hosting it as a competing service, which should get a licensing-policy review before this becomes a real recipe.

name: Node-RED
source_description: Low-code visual tool for wiring IoT devices, APIs, and online services
version_health_notes: 5.0.4 published 2026-07-30, 6 days before today (2026-08-05), part of a same-day patch burst (5.0.2, 4.1.12, 5.0.3, 5.0.4, 4.1.13 all landed 2026-07-30 per npm registry timestamps). Two release lines are maintained in parallel: 5.x (5.0.0 milestone released 2026-06-09, requires Node.js 22.9+, new editor) and 4.1.x (maintenance line for users not yet on Node 22). GitHub repo pushed to as recently as 2026-08-01, 23.5k stars, 317 open issues, not archived. Long-running OpenJS Foundation project with a steady multi-year release history — clearly active, no EOL or maintenance-only signal.
differentiation: Both are low-code, node-based flow editors for wiring APIs/services together, and both would sit in the same "automation" category — real overlap on the core value prop. Node-RED differentiates with a lineage and strength in IoT/hardware (MQTT, GPIO, Modbus, serial, BLE nodes) and a much larger free community node ecosystem (Node-RED Library), while n8n leans more toward SaaS/API business-workflow automation with a built-in queue-backed execution model and commercial support offering. A customer wiring together IoT devices or physical hardware would reach for Node-RED specifically; a customer automating SaaS/business workflows would reach for n8n. Distinct enough audiences to justify both, but the catalogue should expect some customer confusion between the two given the near-identical one-line pitch.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct demand (IoT/hardware integration) not fully served by the existing n8n recipe, backed by a mature, very actively maintained, widely-adopted (23k+ stars) OpenJS Foundation project. Not high because the catalogue already has an automation-category recipe covering adjacent ground, and Node-RED's typical use case (talking to local IoT/hardware devices) is a slightly awkward fit for a cloud VM deployment versus n8n's cloud-native SaaS focus.
summary: Node-RED is a single-container Node.js app (official image nodered/node-red, pin nodered/node-red:5.0.4) that needs only a persistent /data volume and exposes one HTTP port (1880) for its editor UI — no database, no extra raw ports, fully Traefik-compatible. The editor ships with authentication (adminAuth) disabled by default; it is not an env-var-driven login but a bcrypt-hash entry in settings.js, so the straightforward path under the current mechanism is the same one used for other no-built-in-login apps: gate the whole app behind a Traefik basic_auth challenge derived from the customer's root password, rather than trying to template a custom settings.js at install time. That makes it installable_today with no blocking issues. The open question is strategic fit rather than plumbing: it overlaps meaningfully with the existing n8n recipe on the "low-code automation" pitch, differentiated mainly by an IoT/hardware angle that may or may not resonate with typical AF customers running a cloud VM. Recommend build_with_caveats — a solid, actively maintained, low-effort recipe, but worth a product call on whether IoT-flavored automation is a differentiated enough niche to justify the overlap with n8n before prioritizing the build.

name: NodeBB
source_description: NodeBB is a modern, real-time discussion platform for building community forums
version_health_notes: NodeBB ships patch releases multiple times a week (v4.14.1 on 2026-07-22 through v4.14.7 on 2026-08-05, several within the same day — 0 days since the latest release as of today, 2026-08-05), on top of a steady 4.x minor cadence (4.9 → 4.14 across recent months). This is one of the more actively maintained projects reviewed in this series — no EOL signal, no archival, no slowdown. Note: the project's own Docker Hub image (`nodebb/docker`) is stale (newest tags ~3 years old, stuck around 1.19.x/3.0.0-rc), but the project has since moved to publishing current, version-pinned images on GHCR (`ghcr.io/nodebb/nodebb`, tag `4.14.7` published the same day as the release) — that is the image to pin to, not the Docker Hub one.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers community/discussion-forum hosting — the nearest neighbours (Gitea for code, Anytype for notes, Opengist for pastes) serve different purposes. A customer standing up a public support/community forum for a product or hobby project would reach for this instead of a hosted SaaS forum. (Flarum was evaluated separately for the same forum niche and hit the identical blocking issue below — the gap is real but the current mechanism can't reach either candidate.)
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted forums are a genuine but narrower need than the automation/dev-tooling/security apps dominating the current 24 recipes. NodeBB is well-maintained, Node.js-native (fits our container model more naturally than Flarum's PHP/community-image situation), and has a current official image — a reasonable pick if a forum recipe is wanted.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: admin__username; admin__password; admin__email; postgres__password (or mongo__password, depending on DB backend)
blocking_issues:
NodeBB's own setup path (`src/cli/setup.js`, `createAdmin()` in `src/install.js`) takes the double-underscore-nested env vars admin__username/admin__password/admin__email (or an equivalent `admin:*` setup-JSON block) as plaintext and calls `User.create({ password: ... })`, which bcrypt-hashes it internally. There is no supported path to hand NodeBB a pre-computed hash — this is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, the same structural blocker documented for Flarum, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash) cannot express it. If admin__password is omitted entirely, NodeBB will auto-generate a random 8-character password and print it once to container logs — not a usable customer-facing flow.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` is available mechanically but wrong for this app: a forum's entire point is public visitor/member access, so basic-auth-ing the whole domain would block real forum users, not just protect an admin panel (unlike n8n/Adminer, where the whole surface *is* the admin tool).
summary: NodeBB is an actively maintained (near-daily patch cadence), Node.js-native forum platform with a current official image (ghcr.io/nodebb/nodebb) — a solid pick for the forum/community gap in the catalogue if that gap is worth filling. It is blocked today for the same reason as Flarum: initial admin-account setup requires the password as plaintext so the app can hash it itself, which `generated_from` cannot supply, and gating the entire public-facing forum behind Traefik `basic_auth` would defeat the app's purpose rather than just protect an admin surface. Revisit once the platform gains a genuinely customer-chosen (not root-password-derived) credential channel, or if NodeBB adds a documented way to seed the admin account from a pre-hashed value.

name: nopCommerce
source_description: Open-source .NET e-commerce platform with full admin panel and 1,700+ plugins
upstream_license: nopCommerce Public License v4.0 (AGPL-3.0 + mandatory 'powered by nopCommerce' attribution on every UI screen, removable only via a paid per-URL copyright-removal key)
version_health_notes: 4.90.6 shipped 2026-07-08, about 1 month before this analysis (2026-08-05) — a minor/patch release fully compatible with 4.90.0-4.90.5. The 4.90.x line has been landing patch releases every few weeks (4.90.4 on 2026-03-16, 4.90.5 on 2026-06-29, 4.90.6 on 2026-07-08), and the official nopcommerceteam/nopcommerce Docker Hub image is kept in step with each tag. Project has run continuously since 2008 with a large plugin/theme marketplace and active GitHub repo (no archival notice). Clearly active, not dormant.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue covers e-commerce/online storefronts — closest neighbors (gitea, opengist, portainer, n8n) are dev-tooling/ops, not customer-facing storefronts. nopCommerce (.NET/ ASP.NET Core, MSSQL/MySQL/PostgreSQL-backed, self-hosted Shopify/ Magento-style platform with a large plugin ecosystem) would be a genuinely new category. Note this is not the only e-commerce candidate already surfaced in apps-gaps — see bagisto.yaml and evershop.yaml, both covering the same "self-hosted online store" gap and both currently blocked or unbuilt for their own reasons; a human reviewer should compare all three before committing build time to one.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted e-commerce is a real, commonly requested category with no coverage today, and nopCommerce specifically is one of the most established .NET-based options with a mature plugin/theme marketplace. Usefulness is high on fit grounds; see installability below for why it can't ship as a recipe today.
blocking_issues:
nopCommerce has no unattended/env-var-driven install path at all. First visit to the container redirects to an interactive browser install wizard (/install) where a human must manually type the database connection string (server, DB name, user, password) AND create the admin account (email + plaintext password) through HTML form fields. There is no CLI installer, no INSTALLATION_* / ADMIN_* environment variables, and no documented way to pre-seed DataSettings.json or the admin user record at container boot. Upstream's own feature request to make DB settings configurable via env vars (GitHub issue #4113) was closed/implemented for the dataSettings.json *location*, but the admin-account creation step itself still only happens through the wizard's form POST — there is no channel of any kind (env var, CLI flag, or hash injection) for `/compose` to supply either credential.

Even if the admin-credential gap were closed, nopCommerce's public storefront (/) and admin panel (/Admin) are served from the same container on the same HTTP port, the same structural problem documented for Bagisto (apps-gaps/bagisto.yaml): our Traefik `basic_auth` gate applies to the whole public port/domain, not a path prefix, so using it to protect the install wizard/admin area would also lock genuine shoppers out of the storefront itself — defeating the point of an e-commerce recipe. There is no path-scoped basic_auth mechanism in the current platform to gate only /install or /Admin while leaving / open.
summary: nopCommerce is an actively maintained, high-usefulness e-commerce platform with an official, regularly updated Docker image and a real catalogue gap to fill (no existing recipe covers self-hosted online stores). It fails installability today on two independent counts: there is no input channel whatsoever — not even a hash-projection path — for the database connection or the admin account it requires at first boot, since both are entered exclusively through an interactive browser install wizard with no env-var or CLI equivalent; and separately, its storefront and admin panel share one port/container, so a Traefik basic_auth gate (our usual fallback) would have to lock out paying customers along with the admin area. Recommend blocked_on_platform; revisit only if upstream ships an unattended/env-var-driven installer or the platform gains path-scoped basic_auth plus a plaintext-credential injection channel.

name: Norish
source_description: Self-hosted recipe manager with social media import and household sync
version_health_notes: Repo created 2025-12-03, last push 2026-08-05 (today). Releases every 1-4 weeks throughout its life (v0.16.0-beta through v0.19.1-beta from 2026-02-11 to 2026-07-17), latest release only 19 days before today (2026-08-05). Clearly under active development. Caveat: every tagged release to date carries a "-beta" suffix and the project is only ~8 months old — there is no 1.0/stable release yet, so upstream itself signals the app is not yet considered production-hardened.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers recipe/meal management. Paperless-ngx (document management) and n8n/Home Assistant (automation) are the closest productivity-category neighbors but serve unrelated use cases. Norish's household/family angle (shared groceries, meal planning, CalDAV sync) and social-media recipe import (YouTube Shorts/Reels/TikTok via AI) are novel to the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely new category for the catalogue with clear consumer appeal, but the single most-marketed feature per Hostinger's own description — social media import — depends on an optional AI provider that has no customer-input channel today (see blocking_issues), so a shipped recipe would only offer the app's baseline manual/URL recipe management, not the headline feature.
blocking_issues:
AI-powered social media import (the Hostinger-highlighted feature) is gated behind AI_ENABLED/AI_PROVIDER/AI_API_KEY env vars pointing at an external OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This is an external API key the customer would have to supply — no input channel exists today, so this feature cannot be part of an installable recipe as shipped. The app is still fully usable for manual/URL-based recipe entry without it.

Admin bootstrap is a self-service signup form, not a generated_from-projectable field: whoever first reaches the app's web UI after boot claims the "server owner and admin" role by choosing their own email+password there (PASSWORD_AUTH_ENABLED defaults to "Auto"), after which registration closes automatically. There is no ADMIN_PASSWORD-style parameter to project a root-password hash into. This matches the existing accepted pattern in recipes/uptime-kuma (also a bare first-visitor signup, no metadata admin parameter) rather than blocking installability, but it does mean the app sits open to a first-visitor race between boot and the customer's first login — worth a Traefik basic_auth gate as a belt- and-suspenders measure even though it's not strictly required by precedent.
summary: Norish is a real-time, household-first recipe manager (Postgres + Redis + headless-Chrome stack) with no equivalent in the current 24-recipe catalogue, and its core secrets (MASTER_KEY, DB password, Redis URL) are all server-generatable with no customer input needed, so it is mechanically installable today using the same first-visitor-signup pattern already shipped for uptime-kuma. However the feature Hostinger's own description leads with — social media import — requires an external AI provider API key that has no customer-supplied-secret channel today, so a recipe would ship without that headline capability. Combined with the project's still-beta (no 1.0) release status at ~8 months old, this is a build_with_caveats: real differentiation and an active upstream, but the marketed feature won't work out of the box and the app hasn't reached a stable release yet.

name: Notifiarr
source_description: Notifiarr.com client for Starr app notifications and media automation
version_health_notes: Releases roughly every 4-6 weeks (v0.9.0 2025-10-18, v0.9.1 2025-11-06, v0.9.2 2026-01-31, v0.9.4 2026-02-25, v0.9.5 2026-03-08). Latest release is ~5 months before today (2026-08-05), which is a bit longer than the prior gaps but still well inside "active" — no archival notice, no EOL announcement, repo/org actively maintained.
differentiation: None of the 24 shipped recipes touch the Starr ecosystem (Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, etc.) or Discord-based media-automation notifications — this would be a genuinely new category, not a competitor to an existing recipe (see project note: overlap is fine anyway, but there isn't any here).
usefulness_rationale: Useful to the self-hosted-media-server audience that already runs Sonarr/Radarr/Plex, but it is a companion/notification layer for other apps we don't ship (no Sonarr/Radarr/Plex recipe exists in this catalogue today), and it is entirely dependent on a third-party SaaS account (notifiarr.com) to do anything useful.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: DN_API_KEY (notifiarr.com account API key); DN_UI_PASSWORD (web UI login)
blocking_issues:
DN_API_KEY is a mandatory environment variable holding the customer's personal API key from their notifiarr.com account (Profile > API Keys). The client will not function at all without it — it's not an optional integration, it's the core purpose of the app. There is no form field or API param today through which /compose could receive an arbitrary customer-supplied external credential like this.

The web UI login is either the API key itself or a separately settable DN_UI_PASSWORD env var, both plaintext values the app reads directly (not a hash) — root-password projection via generated_from only ever carries a hash, so even the UI-login half of this (ignoring the DN_API_KEY problem) isn't expressible via generated_from. It could in principle be masked behind Traefik basic_auth instead, but that does not solve the DN_API_KEY blocker, which is unavoidable regardless of how the UI is gated.
summary: Notifiarr is an actively maintained, MIT-licensed, single-container Docker app with a web UI on :5454, and would add a category (Starr-app/media notifications) not currently in the catalogue. It is blocked from shipping today purely on the mechanism gap: it hard-requires a notifiarr.com account API key at first boot, which is exactly the "external API key the app can't function without" case the schema calls a structural no — there is no way to get a customer's own key into /compose. Revisit once an arbitrary-customer-secret input channel exists, or if a way is found to let the customer self-service that key inside the app's own web UI after boot (deferring only the login screen to Traefik basic_auth).

name: Notifuse
source_description: Self-hosted email marketing and transactional email platform
version_health_notes: Weekly-to-biweekly release cadence throughout 2026 (v32.0 on 2026-05-22 through v37.0 released ~1 day before this analysis on 2026-08-05, per Docker Hub tag history). Actively maintained, no signs of slowdown.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers email marketing/newsletter or transactional email sending (n8n does workflow automation, not email campaigns). This would be a genuinely new category: a self-hosted alternative to Mailchimp/Resend/Brevo with campaign broadcasts, A/B testing, an MJML visual editor, and a transactional email API/SMTP relay.
usefulness_rationale: Email marketing/transactional email is a common SMB need with no self-hosted option in the current 24-recipe catalogue; a working Notifuse instance would be an attractive, differentiated addition.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: ROOT_EMAIL; PASETO_PRIVATE_KEY; PASETO_PUBLIC_KEY; DB_PASSWORD; SMTP_HOST; SMTP_USERNAME; SMTP_PASSWORD
blocking_issues:
Notifuse has no password-based login: the admin/root account authenticates via a passwordless "magic link" emailed to ROOT_EMAIL, which requires a working outbound SMTP (or Amazon SES / Mailgun / Postmark / SparkPost) connection to even complete first login — there is no `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` login field to project the customer's root password into.

SMTP_HOST/SMTP_USERNAME/SMTP_PASSWORD (or an equivalent ESP API key) are mandatory at first boot for the app to send any email at all — its entire purpose. This is a third-party credential the customer must supply themselves; there is no `/compose`-time channel for arbitrary customer-supplied secrets today, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not help since the app's own SMTP configuration, not just its web UI, needs this secret to function.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` would protect the web UI but would not satisfy the app's internal requirement for real SMTP credentials to send the magic-link email or any campaign/transactional email — the blocker is functional, not just an auth-boundary gap.
summary: Notifuse is an actively maintained (releases roughly every 1-2 weeks, latest v37.0 as of 2026-08-05), AGPL-3.0 self-hosted email marketing and transactional email platform with a single-container web UI and no overlap with the current catalogue — a genuinely new, high-value category. However it cannot be installed under today's recipe mechanism: its admin login is a passwordless magic-link sent by email (no root-password login field to project into), and its core function requires a real SMTP/ESP credential the customer must supply, for which there is no customer-input channel today. This needs a generic external-secret input mechanism (or a first-run web setup wizard the customer completes themselves) beyond IF-1420/IF-1312's root-password/basic-auth mechanisms before it can ship.

Less broadly useful than a general productivity or infra tool since it targets developers building on top of it via API, not end users directly — actual email/SMS/push delivery also requires the customer to bring their own provider (SendGrid, Twilio, etc.) credentials via the app's own UI after first login.
summary: Novu is a fast-moving, MIT-licensed (community edition), actively maintained notification-infrastructure platform with no direct overlap in the current catalogue. The stack is heavier than most existing recipes — 6 containers (mongodb, redis, api, worker, ws, dashboard) — and the dashboard's frontend talks to the API and WS services on their own origins/ports rather than everything flowing through a single port, but Novu documents GLOBAL_CONTEXT_PATH / API_CONTEXT_PATH / WS_CONTEXT_PATH specifically for single-domain, path-based reverse-proxy setups, so it is Traefik-compatible with some extra routing rules. All first-boot secrets are server-generated random values (JWT_SECRET, STORE_ENCRYPTION_KEY, NOVU_SECRET_KEY, Mongo root password) with no customer input required; the admin account itself is created via Novu's own self-signup flow on first dashboard visit (the same pattern already used by the n8n and Immich recipes), not through /compose. No structural blocker — worth a real af-create-recipe pass, with the multi-service Traefik routing as the main implementation risk to scope up front.

name: NSQ
source_description: Realtime distributed messaging platform for high-throughput event streams
version_health_notes: v1.3.0 tagged 2023-12-27 (verified against the GitHub releases API published_at field) — about 32 months before today (2026-08-05), not the ~20 months an earlier draft of this analysis miscalculated from a wrong year. Prior tags: v1.2.1 (2021-08-16), v1.2.0 (2019-08-28), v1.1.0 (2018-08-19). The gap between releases has been widening, not holding steady: v1.1.0→v1.2.0 ≈ 1 year, v1.2.0→v1.2.1 ≈ 2 years, v1.2.1→v1.3.0 ≈ 2.3 years, and now ≈ 2.7 years and counting since v1.3.0 — a slowing cadence, not "roughly one release per year." The master branch is not fully dead: commits landed 2026-07-20 (a dependency bump) and 2025-06-20/06-29 (a genuine new feature, `max-defer-delay`), and a January 2025 PR merged topology-aware message delivery — real, if infrequent, ongoing development. No archive notice, no announced EOL. Given the corrected 32-month gap and the widening trend across the last three release intervals, "dormant" is the honest read on cadence even though scattered commits keep this short of a full EOL/archived status — hence maintenance-only rather than active or abandoned.
differentiation: No existing recipe provides a message broker of any kind. NSQ is a realtime distributed pub/sub messaging platform aimed at connecting a customer's own applications/microservices (comparable audience to the also-analyzed NATS and LavinMQ), built around three cooperating daemons: nsqd (the broker itself, stores/delivers messages), nsqlookupd (a discovery service nsqd instances register with), and nsqadmin (a read-mostly web UI for cluster stats/topic-channel management). Unlike NATS or LavinMQ, a useful NSQ deployment is a small cluster (at least one nsqd + one nsqlookupd) rather than a single container, which is a heavier footprint than the other broker candidates for the same "give a customer a message bus" job.
usefulness_rationale: Same narrow, technical audience problem as NATS/LavinMQ — the entire point is other software connecting to it via a client library, not a browser-usable end-user tool — compounded by NSQ needing multiple cooperating daemons to be useful at all (nsqadmin alone shows nothing without at least one nsqd registered with an nsqlookupd) and a 32-month-stale release with only dormant upstream activity since. Capped at low, below NATS/LavinMQ's medium, because it combines the narrow-audience ceiling both share with a materially weaker version trajectory and a heavier multi-daemon deployment shape for the same underlying customer need.
blocking_issues: nsqd's client protocol port (4150, raw TCP — what publishing/ consuming applications actually connect to) and nsqlookupd's TCP port (4160, what nsqd instances use to register) are not HTTP and cannot sit behind Traefik; they would need direct raw TCP exposure, the same accepted pattern already used by wg-easy and Syncthing in this catalogue, not a structural blocker on its own — but it does mean nsqadmin alone (the only piece that could be Traefik-fronted) is not a functioning deployment; a real recipe needs nsqd + nsqlookupd + nsqadmin as three services with two raw ports opened, for a broker whose primary interface has no authentication mechanism at all (not even a hash-based one) to layer beyond the external Traefik gate on the admin UI.
summary: NSQ is a real, MIT-licensed message broker with no catalogue overlap — it would join NATS and LavinMQ as a message-broker-style candidate — but it is the weakest of the three on every axis evaluated. Its last tagged release (v1.3.0) is 32 months old against a release cadence that has been widening (1yr, then 2yr, then 2.3yr between successive releases), landing it in dormant-cadence, maintenance-only territory (real but infrequent master-branch activity, no archive notice). It is mechanically installable today only in a narrow sense: nsqadmin's lack of built-in auth maps cleanly to a Traefik basic_auth gate, but nsqadmin alone isn't a useful deployment — a working recipe needs nsqd and nsqlookupd too, both raw-TCP services with zero built-in authentication of any kind (nothing for generated_from to project into), sitting on the public internet behind nothing but network exposure choices. Combined with the narrow technical-integrator audience already noted for NATS/LavinMQ and a heavier multi-daemon footprint for the same underlying need, recommend not_recommended — this is a worse pick than NATS or LavinMQ for the same "give a customer a message bus" slot in the catalogue.

name: ntfy

differentiation: None of the 24 shipped recipes is a general-purpose push-notification hub. ntfy is a single self-contained pub/sub HTTP server: any script, cron job, monitoring tool, or CI pipeline can POST/PUT a message to a topic URL and it fans out to the ntfy Android/iOS/desktop apps or web push — genuinely new category, not a competitor to anything we ship (per project note, overlap wouldn't disqualify it anyway, but there isn't any here).

Single tiny Go binary/container, minimal resource footprint, real web UI for managing topics/subscriptions.

Out of the box it has no login of its own — the server is open for everyone to read and write any topic — so it needs a Traefik basic_auth gate, which is fully expressible today via generated_from root-password projection into the gate's Basic Auth credential, exactly like n8n/WUD/Open WebUI. Because ntfy clients (curl, scripts, the ntfy apps) already send credentials as HTTP Basic Auth when the server requires auth, gating the whole public port this way is a natural fit, not a workaround. Adds a genuinely new, broadly-useful category to the catalogue with no mechanism blockers — recommend building now.

name: Nuclio
source_description: High-performance open-source serverless platform for real-time data processing
version_health_notes: Very active release cadence — multiple point releases per month across two parallel branch lines (1.16.x and 1.17.x), most recently 1.16.8 on 2026-07-30 and 1.17.3 on 2026-07-22, both within the last two weeks of today's date (2026-08-05). No signs of maintenance-only mode or archival.
differentiation: Nuclio is a FaaS/serverless function platform (deploy and invoke event-driven functions in various languages), which nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers — Portainer and WUD manage existing Docker workloads but don't let a customer write and deploy new serverless functions. However, Nuclio's core mechanism is fundamentally at odds with our single-container-behind-Traefik model: the dashboard (port 8070) mounts the host's /var/run/docker.sock and uses it to spin up a new container per deployed function, each bound to its own dynamically-allocated host port. Those function containers are not known at recipe-build time, so Traefik can only front the dashboard UI itself — invoked functions would need ad hoc port exposure our platform doesn't provision. Docker-socket-only ("local") mode is also positioned upstream as the getting-started/dev path; real Nuclio deployments run on Kubernetes for scaling and multi-node function placement, which a single AF VM doesn't provide either.
usefulness_rationale: Interesting category (serverless/FaaS) with no catalogue overlap, but the standalone-Docker mode is a stripped-down dev/demo path, not what upstream considers production Nuclio, and giving a customer's function deployments direct docker.sock access on their own VM is a meaningfully larger blast radius than any current recipe (arbitrary container creation, not just management of existing ones).
blocking_issues:
Nuclio's dashboard auth is controlled by NUCLIO_AUTH_KIND, with only two supported values: "nop" (no auth at all) and "iguazio" (delegates to an external Iguazio identity/session service — a third-party enterprise product, not something we can wire up as a customer credential). There is no built-in username/password login we can project a root-password hash into via generated_from; a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the whole UI is the only way to avoid shipping this open to the internet.

Even with the dashboard gated, deployed functions run as separate, unproxied containers with their own dynamically-assigned host ports — outside Traefik's static routing and outside what our recipe mechanism can express or expose safely today.
summary: Nuclio is an actively maintained (weekly-ish releases, Apache-2.0), genuinely novel category for the catalogue — nothing else here does serverless function deployment. But it's not installable as a normal single-container web app: it has no native login (only "nop"/open or an Iguazio-only auth backend), it needs raw docker.sock access to spawn function containers, and those function containers get their own ports Traefik can't front. A basic_auth gate covers the dashboard itself but not the underlying architecture mismatch with our fixed single-VM, single-port-per-recipe model. Not recommended for the current mechanism; would need a materially different exposure model (e.g., a proxy that discovers and fronts per-function ports) to reconsider.

name: NZBGet
source_description: Efficient C++ Usenet binary downloader with PAR2 repair and web UI
version_health_notes: Name is ambiguous: the original project at github.com/nzbget/nzbget (maintainer "hugbug") was archived by its owner on 2022-11-18 with a last stable release of v21.1 (2021-06-03) — that upstream is dead. However, a community fork at github.com/nzbgetcom/nzbget has continued development under active maintenance, with releases roughly every 6-8 weeks (v25.3 2025-09-01, v25.4 2025-10-09, v26.0 2026-02-02, v26.1 2026-04-07, v26.2 2026-06-18, ~7 weeks before today 2026-08-05, plus a 2026-08-03 testing pre-release). The widely-used linuxserver.io Docker image (lscr.io/linuxserver/nzbget) now tracks this fork's v26.x line, not the archived original. This analysis treats nzbgetcom/nzbget as the real upstream — the "NZBGet" a customer would get today is this fork, not the dead original repo.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches Usenet/binary downloading — there is no *arr-style media-acquisition app in the catalogue at all (no Sonarr/Radarr/SABnzbd equivalent either). NZBGet would be a first entry in that space: a single lightweight container that fetches and PAR2-repairs binaries from Usenet via a web UI, appealing to self-hosters building a media-automation stack.
usefulness_rationale: Solid utility for a specific audience (Usenet users), but it's most valuable paired with indexers/*arr apps we don't offer either, and requires the customer to already have a Usenet provider account — narrower appeal than broad-audience recipes like Vaultwarden or Uptime Kuma.
summary: NZBGet is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (6789) web app installable today, but its own login is HTTP Basic Auth against a fixed username ("nzbget", not configurable) and a ControlPassword that the app only accepts as plaintext (env var NZBGET_PASS on the linuxserver image) — it has no way to accept a pre-hashed value, so `generated_from` cannot target it directly. The workable pattern is the same as Adminer/WUD: set NZBGET_PASS to a random server-generated secret the customer never needs (mechanism: server_generated_no_customer_input, closing off the known default credential), then put the actual customer-facing auth boundary at Traefik with `basic_auth: true`, whose password is projected from the root-password hash via `generated_from`. Structurally this ships fine. The name is ambiguous, though: the original nzbget/nzbget project is archived and dead since 2022, and the linuxserver Docker image now tracks a different, actively-maintained community fork (nzbgetcom/nzbget, releases every 6-8 weeks). Recommend build_with_caveats — flag the fork provenance to reviewers, and weigh usefulness against the fact we have no companion *arr/indexer recipes to pair it with yet.
