Its own login (Config > Auth > Login form) is off by default and configured interactively after first boot, with no environment variable to pre-seed a username/password or hash at container start, so — exactly like Jackett — the correct fix is gating the whole app behind a required Traefik basic_auth projected from the customer's root password rather than relying on the app's optional built-in auth. With that gate this is mechanically installable today (installable_today: true), but the recommendation is build_with_caveats: the app's real value is entirely as an upstream feed for a Usenet download client and/or Sonarr/Radarr/Lidarr, none of which exist in the current catalogue, so shipping it alone hands a customer an aggregated search API with nothing downstream to send results to.

differentiation: No existing recipe in the 24-app catalogue touches crypto trading or portfolio automation. OctoBot (pinned to the classic :2.1.1 tag) would be a genuinely new category: self-hosted automated trading (grid/DCA/ TradingView-signal strategies) across 15+ exchanges (Binance, OKX, Kucoin, Hyperliquid, etc.), with a single-container web UI on port 5001 behind Traefik like our other single-service apps.

Pinning to :2.1.1 to get a usable self-contained UI also means shipping a version already superseded by upstream's default architecture (node mode/cloud pairing as of 3.0), with no clear path to track upstream's actively developed line without introducing a third-party cloud-account dependency.
blocking_issues:
OctoBot's own web-UI password is off by default on :2.1.1 and, per upstream docs, can only be set through the UI itself (Accounts > Interfaces) or by hand-editing user/config.json after first boot — there is no environment variable or startup argument to seed it. This rules out generated_from projection onto the app's own login; a Traefik basic_auth gate is the only available boundary.
The current :stable/:latest tags (3.0.0-beta1 onward) default to node mode, which pairs the self-hosted instance with a cloud-hosted OctoBot interface/account — a third-party account-linking dependency with no input channel today per SCHEMA.md. A recipe must pin the explicit :2.1.1 tag to avoid this; tracking upstream's :stable going forward would reintroduce the blocker the moment a recipe's compose file is refreshed.
Core function (placing real trades) requires the customer's own exchange API keys, entered through OctoBot's own UI after the app is running. This is not a first-boot blocker (the app boots and serves its UI, including paper-trading/demo mode, with zero exchange keys configured) — it's ordinary post-install customer configuration, same pattern as n8n credentials. Noted here for completeness, not as a blocker on installable_today.
summary: OctoBot is mechanically installable today only if pinned to the explicit :2.1.1 tag: single container, one HTTP port (5001), no login of its own configured at boot, so a Traefik basic_auth gate is a sufficient and available first-boot secret channel. The current :stable/:latest tags are NOT equivalent to :2.1.1 — verified against Docker Hub digests, they already point at the 3.0.0-beta1 node-mode release, which pairs with a cloud-hosted account and has no confirmed local-only path, making it a structural blocker rather than a caveat. OctoBot would fill a genuinely new category (self-hosted crypto trading automation) with zero overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue, but the caveats are real: a narrower, higher-liability niche than the rest of the catalogue, and a recipe pinned to :2.1.1 ships a version already superseded by upstream's actively developed, cloud-tied architecture, with no clear upgrade path that preserves local-only operation.

summary: Odoo is a single-container Python app (official `odoo` image, HTTP UI on :8069) backed by its own PostgreSQL instance — structurally the same app+DB pattern as n8n/paperless-ngx, and reverse-proxy-compatible behind Traefik with no extra ports or protocols. The image takes PostgreSQL connection settings (HOST/PORT/USER/PASSWORD) as plain env vars, which install.sh can server-generate with zero customer input. The wrinkle, same pattern already accepted for Ghost/Bludit/Baikal in this apps-gaps set: Odoo has no env var to pre-provision its actual Administrator login. The official image ships no ADMIN_EMAIL/ ADMIN_PASSWORD hook — the first database (and its admin user/password) is created through an unauthenticated browser wizard at /web/database/manager, protected only by a separate `admin_passwd` master password that itself is config-file-only (no native env-var support; install.sh would template it into odoo.conf, which is fine since it never needs to reach the customer). Per SCHEMA.md's guidance on wizard-only admin provisioning, gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth (projected from the customer's root-password hash) closes the claim-race exposure and clears installable_today with zero hard blocking issues — the customer completes Odoo's own database-creation wizard (picking their own admin email/password) after authenticating through the gate, then can drop the gate once the wizard is done. That extra wizard-then-unlock step, plus templating admin_passwd into a config file rather than a first-class env var, keeps this at build_with_caveats rather than a clean build_now. Odoo is actively developed on a yearly major-release cadence with a continuously-rebuilt official Docker image and no EOL signal, and Community Edition is plain LGPL-3.0 with no usage-tier caps. Recommend build_with_caveats: high customer-recognition value, technically installable today, but the wizard-gating flow needs to be spelled out clearly in install.sh/docs, and it should be weighed against the other open ERP/CRM apps-gaps candidates before more than one ships.

No archive notice, no EOL signal — this is a healthy, actively maintained project.
differentiation: OliveTin exposes a curated set of admin-defined shell commands as buttons/forms in a single-page web UI (Go backend, single HTTP frontend on port 1337, REST + Connect RPC API, explicitly documented as compatible with Traefik/Nginx/Caddy/HAProxy reverse proxies). It is not a workflow engine like n8n (no branching/scheduling/node graph) — it's a much narrower "turn a shell script into a safe web button" tool aimed at letting a less-technical user (or a teammate without SSH access) trigger a fixed set of ops actions (restart a service, run a backup, tail a log) without giving them a shell. No existing recipe in the catalogue covers this niche; Portainer manages Docker objects, n8n orchestrates workflows/API calls, neither runs arbitrary admin-defined host/container commands from a button.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct niche and a clean single-container web app, but the audience is narrower than a general infra tool: it only pays off once someone has authored a config.yaml `actions:` list of real commands to expose, which is a technical, per-deployment authoring step, not a turnkey experience. See installability below — under our current mechanism that authoring step can't happen post-install anyway, which caps day-1 value further.
blocking_issues: Not a blocker on basic installability, but a real usefulness cap: OliveTin's core value is running admin-authored shell commands defined in config.yaml's `actions:` list. That list has to be written into the image/volume at recipe-build time — there is no customer-facing channel in `/compose` today to let a customer supply their own arbitrary command definitions post-install (that would be exactly the "arbitrary customer-chosen value" the schema says has no input channel). A shippable recipe would boot with only whatever fixed example actions the recipe author bakes in; using OliveTin for its actual purpose (running *this customer's* scripts) would still require them to SSH/file-manager in and hand-edit config.yaml on the mounted volume — the same raw server access OliveTin exists to let them avoid granting to other people.
summary: OliveTin is an actively maintained (weekly-cadence releases, AGPL-3.0), single-container Go web app with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue, a single reverse-proxy-friendly HTTP port, and a login mechanism (Argon2id-hashed local users in config.yaml) that maps cleanly onto our `generated_from: "argon2:ROOT_PASSWORD"` mechanism — mechanically installable today. The catch is product-level, not platform-level: its entire reason to exist is running commands the deployer defines, and our current provisioning flow has no channel for a customer to supply their own command list, so a shipped recipe could only offer a fixed, recipe-author-chosen set of example actions until the customer gets raw file access to the app's config volume. Worth building as a build_with_caveats candidate — genuinely differentiated and cleanly authenticatable — but the caveat should be surfaced to whoever scopes the recipe, since "customize your own actions" (the app's main selling point) isn't reachable through the AF UI on day one.

name: OMERO
source_description: Open-source image data management platform for scientific microscopy
upstream_license: GPL-2.0 (OMERO.server); GPL-2.0 (OMERO.web) — Open Microscopy Environment, commercial licenses also available from Glencoe Software
version_health_notes: OMERO.server 5.6.18 shipped 2026-05-19 (~2.5 months before today, 2026-08-05); OMERO.web 5.33.0 shipped 2026-08-03 (2 days before today). Prior server/web pairing (5.6.17 / 5.31.0-5.31.1) went out in February 2026. Both `openmicroscopy/omero-server` and `openmicroscopy/omero-web` images on Docker Hub are updated in step with each release (omero-web "latest" pushed 3 days ago as of this analysis). Steady, ongoing cadence — actively maintained by the OME consortium, no EOL signal.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue serves scientific/research image data management. Immich is the closest structural neighbor (self-hosted media library with a web UI, Postgres-backed, single admin account) but is built for personal photo/video libraries, not the multi-user group/permission model, OME-XML metadata, and microscopy-file-format (proprietary vendor formats via Bio-Formats) handling that OMERO exists for. This would open a genuinely new "scientific data management" category rather than compete with an existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: OMERO is the standard self-hosted platform for microscopy image management in academic/core-facility bioimaging — a real, specific audience (universities, imaging cores, biotech labs) that has no other catalogue option today. But it is a narrow vertical compared to general-purpose recipes: unlike Immich (broadly useful to any customer with photos), OMERO is only useful to someone who already has microscopy data and workflows built around OME's ecosystem (Bio-Formats, OMERO.insight/Fiji plugins), a much smaller slice of the general self-hosting customer base this catalogue targets.
blocking_issues:
OMERO.server's admin ("root") account password is set at first boot via the `ROOTPASS` environment variable, which the server consumes as plaintext and hashes internally using its own scheme — there is no way to hand it an already-hashed value the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN accepts a bcrypt hash. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's server root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel today to get the customer's actual chosen admin password into OMERO. Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` does not solve this either, since the customer still needs a working OMERO login (root/admin account) to use the product at all — an inert or unknown admin credential leaves the app unusable, not just extra-gated.

Full OMERO functionality (desktop OMERO.insight client, Fiji/ImageJ plugin, most third-party integrations) depends on raw TCP ports 4063/4064 (the Ice protocol) in addition to the OMERO.web HTTP UI on 4080. Those raw ports have no path through our Traefik-only HTTP ingress, so even if the admin-password blocker were resolved, a recipe could only expose the web UI, not the full client ecosystem OMERO is normally used with.
summary: OMERO is an actively maintained, real gap in the catalogue — no existing recipe touches scientific image/microscopy data management, and OMERO is the de facto standard tool for that niche. It is mechanically close to installable (official images for server/web, Postgres backend, HTTP web UI compatible with Traefik) but is blocked today by the admin credential: OMERO.server's `ROOTPASS` variable requires the customer's actual plaintext admin password, which our `generated_from`/root-password-hash mechanism cannot supply, and no basic-auth gate substitutes for a working admin login the customer needs to actually use the product. Revisit once a plaintext-carrying secret channel exists, and note the audience is a narrow but real vertical (bioimaging labs) rather than a broad win.

name: OmniRoute
source_description: Self-hosted AI gateway routing 231+ LLM providers through one unified endpoint
version_health_notes: Confirmed directly against the Docker Hub tags API for `diegosouzapw/omniroute`: numbered tags run from 3.6.4 (2026-04-12) through 3.8.49 (2026-07-30), often multiple pushes per day (e.g. 3.8.16 through 3.8.19 all pushed within 24h on 2026-06-08/09) — an unusually fast, near-continuous-deploy cadence. Latest push was six days before today (2026-08-05). By raw release-cadence numbers this reads as actively developed, not dormant. However, corroborating web research for this repo returned wildly inconsistent and mutually contradictory "reputation" signals across sources queried in the same session: GitHub star counts of 9.8k, 17k, 33.9k, and 41.1k were each reported by different sources for what claims to be the same project, and multiple distinct GitHub accounts (diegosouzapw/OmniRoute, marcpadz/omniroute, BunsDev/omniroute, ChrisCompton/omniroute) publish near-identical READMEs describing the same tool. This pattern — many mirror/fork repos with copy-pasted descriptions plus self-contradictory inflated star counts — matches known GitHub fake-star / reputation-farming campaigns, which the security research community associates disproportionately with malware distribution rather than organic popularity. Independently, web research also surfaced a report that Socket.dev blocked the `omniroute` npm package at v3.8.5 (May 2026) for suspected malware, obfuscated code, and install scripts, with the maintainer reportedly patching two real vulnerabilities in the following v3.8.6 release. None of this could be fully independently re-verified from this sandbox (GitHub's REST API was unreachable during this research session), so treat the star-count and Socket.dev claims as corroborated-by-multiple-sources but not directly re-verified — a human reviewer should re-check Socket.dev's advisory database and the repo's actual star history directly before any further action.
differentiation: OmniRoute is a multi-provider LLM *gateway/router* (OpenAI-compatible `/v1` endpoint, provider failover, token-compression, free-tier aggregation across 90+ providers) rather than a chat UI or a local model runner — functionally closer to LiteLLM than to Open WebUI. Neither open-webui nor ollama covers "unify many third-party LLM provider accounts behind one endpoint for other tools to call," so on pure feature grounds it would fill a real, currently-empty slot (API-gateway/proxy for LLM traffic) rather than duplicate an existing recipe outright.
usefulness_rationale: The gateway/router niche is real, but this specific project's value proposition is aimed at individual developers wiring up coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot) to free/cheap LLM tiers on their own laptop — not a typical "install this on my server for my business" self-hosted app. Combined with the credibility red flags in `version_health.notes` (inconsistent/inflated popularity signals, reported malware flag on the npm package), usefulness is capped low regardless of the mechanical fit questions below: this is not a project IONOS should be comfortable running unreviewed on customer infrastructure.
blocking_issues:
Provenance/trust concern (see `version_health.notes`): this research surfaced credible-looking but unverified reports of a Socket.dev malware/obfuscated-code/install-script flag on the `omniroute` npm package, plus a fake-star-campaign-shaped pattern of multiple near-identical mirror repos with mutually contradictory star counts. Neither claim could be independently re-verified from this sandbox. This is a supply-chain trust question that sits above the mechanical `/compose` constraint — even if every secret below were expressible today, shipping a recipe for a project with credible malware-distribution signals would need a clean bill of health from a human security review first, not just a working docker-compose file.

The dashboard's `ADMIN_PASSWORD` env var appears (per upstream docs) to gate login to the web UI, and could plausibly be projected via `generated_from` the same way Vaultwarden's admin token is — but whether the app accepts a pre-hashed value (argon2/bcrypt) or requires the plaintext password itself was not confirmed from available documentation in this session. If it turns out to require plaintext, this becomes a genuine structural blocker per `SCHEMA.md`, not just an unconfirmed detail.

Full value (routing across paid/premium providers) requires the customer to supply their own per-provider API keys after first boot — this is a legitimate post-install, in-app configuration step (not a `/compose`-time secret) since OmniRoute ships with 90+ keyless free-tier providers pre-configured and is usable without any provider key at all, so it is not counted as a blocking issue here.
summary: OmniRoute is a real, very actively-released (near-daily Docker Hub pushes) multi-provider LLM gateway that would technically fill a gap our catalogue doesn't cover today (a routing proxy in front of many LLM providers, distinct from the chat-UI/model-runner niche open-webui and ollama already fill). Mechanically it looks close to installable — a single Docker image, a web dashboard with its own `ADMIN_PASSWORD` login that may be projectable via `generated_from`, and no hard requirement for a customer-supplied provider API key to boot. The recommendation is `not_recommended` anyway because this research surfaced serious, unresolved provenance red flags: multiple near-identical mirror GitHub repos reporting mutually contradictory, implausibly large star counts, and a separately-reported claim that the npm package was flagged by Socket.dev for suspected malware and obfuscated code. Neither claim was independently re-verifiable from this sandbox, but together they describe exactly the shape of a fake-popularity/malware-distribution campaign, and that risk should be cleared by a human security review before this project is considered further — regardless of how the mechanical secret-projection question above resolves.

This is the same niche already surveyed in apps-gaps/hemmelig.yaml (build_now) and apps-gaps/cryptgeon.yaml (build_with_caveats) — OneTimeSecret is in fact the original/reference implementation of the one-time-secret-link pattern that both of those apps were inspired by, and is the most widely recognized name in this space (SaaS product at onetimesecret.com plus long-running OSS project). If more than one of these three ships, they will visibly duplicate each other in the catalogue — a reviewer decision point, not a technical blocker, since none is a recipe yet.
usefulness_rationale: Best brand recognition of the three one-time-secret candidates surveyed so far (widely used SaaS + long OSS history, AGPL-3.0, actively developed), and the simple/anonymous deployment mode needs no login at all for its core feature — cheap to run (one app container + Valkey, no Postgres/RabbitMQ/worker processes required in this mode). Scored high on its own merits; actual priority depends on whether the catalogue wants one, two, or all three of Hemmelig/Cryptgeon/ OneTimeSecret.
summary: OneTimeSecret's official "simple" deployment (onetimesecret/onetimesecret web container + Valkey 8.1, per docker/compose/docker-compose.simple.yml in the upstream repo) is a two-service, single-HTTP-port (3000) stack behind Traefik with no raw ports or extra protocols. With AUTH_ENABLED= false (the anonymous/guest mode) its core feature — creating and viewing a self-destructing secret link — needs no account or login, so the only secrets it needs at first boot are SECRET (site encryption key) and VALKEY_PASSWORD, both patternless values nothing customer-facing ever reads and can be generated server-side, same as a DB password. The optional "Colonel" admin console and full-auth signup/SMTP flow are not needed to boot and are managed via CLI, not a web credential we'd need to project. Mechanically installable today with zero blockers; the reason this is build_with_caveats rather than a clean build_now is that apps-gaps/hemmelig.yaml and apps-gaps/cryptgeon.yaml already stake out the identical burn-after-reading secret-sharing niche — a human should pick one (or accept deliberate overlap) rather than all three shipping as near-duplicate recipes.

differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue provides MS Office-compatible document editing (docx/xlsx/pptx). Paperless-ngx and paperless-ai are document *archival/OCR* tools, not editors — no functional overlap. However, ONLYOFFICE Docs (the "Document Server") is architecturally not a standalone office suite with its own file storage or accounts: it is an editing/rendering *API service* meant to be embedded behind a host platform (Nextcloud, ownCloud, a DMS, a custom integration) that owns file storage, user accounts, and calls the Document Server's API/iframe to render and save documents. Standalone, the container only serves the JWT-protected editing API plus an optional bundled "example" test page (documentserver-example) that lets anyone create/edit throwaway files with no login at all — it is explicitly a developer test harness, not a file manager for end users. It only becomes genuinely useful once paired with a file-storage host that isn't in this catalogue, making it a satellite/integration component rather than a complete product for an AF customer today.
blocking_issues:
Document Server has no admin login of its own (community edition has no account system at all), and the only user-facing surface when run standalone is the bundled unauthenticated example/test page — shipping it open to the internet is not acceptable, and gating it behind Traefik basic_auth (mechanically doable) does not solve the deeper product-fit problem below.
Product-fit gap, not a mechanism gap: without a companion file-storage/DMS host (Nextcloud, ownCloud, etc., none of which are in our catalogue) there is no real deliverable for the customer beyond the test page or a raw API — recommend against building until/unless such a host recipe exists to pair it with.
summary: ONLYOFFICE Docs (Document Server) is actively maintained (v9.4.0, May 2026, steady ~2-month release cadence) and mechanically clears the current root-password-projection constraint — JWT_SECRET is a server-generated value the customer never needs, and the one open surface it exposes (the bundled example test page) can be closed with the existing Traefik basic_auth gate. The real problem is product fit, not installability: run by itself it is an embeddable editing API with no file storage, no accounts, and no standalone workflow — its intended host (Nextcloud, ownCloud, or a DMS) isn't in our catalogue, so a customer who installs it alone gets a JWT-gated API and a disabled/gated test page rather than an office suite they can actually use. Recommend not_recommended until a companion document-storage host is also on the roadmap.

name: Onyx
source_description: Open-source AI chat and enterprise search platform that works with every LLM
upstream_license: MIT (Community Edition); separate Enterprise Edition (SSO, advanced collaboration, analytics) is a paid, proprietary tier layered on top. A pure-MIT mirror without any EE code paths exists at https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx-foss.
version_health_notes: Formerly named Danswer, renamed to Onyx. Extremely active: tagged releases roughly daily (v4.5.0, v4.5.1, v4.5.2, v4.5.3 all landed within the 2026-08-03 to 2026-08-05 window) plus continuous nightly builds and a separate onyx-cli release train. 9,500+ commits, 31k+ GitHub stars. No EOL or maintenance-mode signal anywhere in the project.
differentiation: Both are "chat with any LLM" web apps, but Onyx is positioned as an enterprise-search / RAG platform: 40+ first-party connectors (Slack, Confluence, Google Drive, GitHub, Salesforce, SharePoint, etc.) that sync documents and permissions into a searchable knowledge base the chat layer queries, plus custom agents with tool actions. open-webui is a thinner, single-purpose chat frontend with no built-in document-connector ingestion. A customer who wants "ask questions over our company's docs" rather than just "chat with a model" is not served by open-webui today.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiation from the existing AI-category recipes, but the standard deployment is a heavy multi-service stack (Postgres, a vector/keyword search engine, Redis, MinIO, multiple model/worker containers, nginx) at ~10GB RAM / 32GB disk minimum — a "lite" profile drops this to ~4GB/16GB by disabling indexing/connectors, but that also drops the feature that differentiates it from open-webui in the first place. Sizeable to run, and the primary value (connector-based enterprise search) needs an LLM API key configured post-install to be useful at all, same as open-webui/anythingllm already do.
summary: Onyx is a legitimate, actively-developed AI chat + enterprise-search platform distinct from what open-webui already covers in the catalogue — the connector-based document ingestion is the differentiator. It boots with just a domain: authentication defaults to email/password with the first person to sign in through the web UI becoming admin (same pattern as Immich/Gitea already in the catalogue), so there is no customer-supplied secret needed at first boot and no `generated_from`/`basic_auth` gate is structurally required. The caveat is resource cost and stack complexity (5+ containers, ~10GB RAM standard) plus the fact that its headline feature needs an LLM API key added after install to do anything useful — build_with_caveats rather than an unqualified build_now.

name: Open Agent
source_description: Self-hosted AI assistant with LLM, RAG, agent loops, and MCP tool support
version_health_notes: Extremely active: 7+ tagged releases between 2026-07-07 (v2.81.1) and 2026-08-03 (v2.87.1), i.e. multiple releases per week right up to two days before today (2026-08-05). Docker Hub `casbin/openagent` shows the same v2.87.1 tag pushed 3 days ago. Repo is not archived, has 5.5k+ stars, 2,400+ commits, 43 open issues with ongoing PR activity. No indication of maintenance-only mode or slowdown.
differentiation: Open Agent is a broader "agent platform" than any single existing recipe: it combines a RAG knowledge-base/vector-store layer, a visual agent-workflow builder, native MCP-server tool integration, and computer-use/browser-use automation, on top of 28+ swappable LLM providers. OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are narrower single-agent runtimes driven through messaging apps (Telegram etc.); Open WebUI is a chat front-end paired with Ollama for local inference. Open Agent's RAG + MCP-tool + workflow-builder combination isn't fully covered by any one of the three, but it sits squarely in the same "self-hosted AI agent/ assistant" niche as all three put together.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely more feature-rich than the existing agent recipes (RAG stores, MCP tools, computer-use), so it's not a pure duplicate — but the catalogue already has three entries competing for the same "AI agent that needs a model-provider key" customer, and Open Agent's differentiators (workflow builder, computer-use) are power-user features that raise support-surface risk without an obviously distinct buyer from OpenClaw/Hermes Agent.
blocking_issues: Upstream docs and Dockerfile give no evidence of any built-in login screen or admin account — `docker run -d -p 14000:14000 casbin/openagent` opens straight to the app UI with no auth step. A Traefik basic_auth gate is therefore mandatory (not optional hardening) to avoid the agent/RAG/tool-execution UI sitting open on the internet; this is expressible today via traefik_basic_auth, so it does not block installability, but it must be wired as a hard requirement, not a toggle.
summary: Open Agent (the-open-agent/openagent, "casbin/openagent" on Docker Hub) is a single lightweight Go binary/container defaulting to embedded SQLite — no external database required — exposing one HTTP port (14000), which makes it mechanically simple to ship behind Traefik with a mandatory basic_auth gate, matching the pattern already used for OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. Upstream is unusually active (releases multiple times a week, most recently two days before this analysis) with no EOL signals. The blocker isn't platform mechanics but catalogue fit: it overlaps meaningfully with three existing AI-agent recipes (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Open WebUI), and while its RAG + MCP-tool + workflow-builder feature set is a real differentiator, it's an incremental "more agent features" pitch rather than a new category. Worth building if the catalogue wants a fuller-featured agent platform, but not a priority pick over its closer competitors already in the catalogue.

name: Open Archiver

version_health_notes: Roughly monthly-to-biweekly tagged releases since the project's first tag v0.3.1 on 2025-09-04 (v0.3.1 -> v0.3.2 -> v0.3.3 -> v0.3.4 -> v0.4.0 -> v0.4.1 -> v0.4.2 -> v0.5.0 -> v0.5.1 -> v0.5.2), i.e. 10 releases in ~11 months. No archive notice, no EOL announcement; this is a young (~1 year old), actively developed project, not dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does mailbox-level compliance archiving. Paperless-ngx (already in the catalogue) is document/scan management, not email; Immich is photo management. Open Archiver ingests from Gmail/Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, generic IMAP, and PST/Mbox/EML file imports, stores messages as immutable hash-verified .eml with an audit trail, and indexes them with Meilisearch full-text search — a genuinely distinct SMB/compliance use case (regulatory mail retention, eDiscovery, decommissioning a mailbox without losing the record).

secrets_required_at_first_boot: ADMIN_SETUP_GATE; POSTGRES_PASSWORD; REDIS_PASSWORD; MEILI_MASTER_KEY; JWT_SECRET; ENCRYPTION_KEY
summary: Open Archiver has no admin-account environment variable at all: on first visit any client is redirected to an unauthenticated `/setup` page where whoever gets there first creates the sole admin account, a real first-visitor-wins race condition, not the "app ships one fixed default password" case. That's structurally identical to the "no login yet, needs gating" row in SCHEMA.md, so a permanent Traefik `basic_auth` gate keyed to the customer's root password (same pattern as n8n/Open WebUI/Immich) closes the race: only the customer can reach `/setup`, and the real admin credentials they then choose there never need to pass through our bootstrap mechanism at all. Every other required value (Postgres/Redis/Meilisearch/JWT/encryption secrets) is a patternless server-generated secret nothing customer-facing reads. Its 5-service stack (app + Postgres + Valkey + Meilisearch + Apache Tika) mirrors Paperless-ngx's shape and exposes a single web port (3000), so it's Traefik-compatible with no raw-port needs. Gmail/M365 OAuth app registration is needed only to configure an *ingestion source* after login, inside the app's own UI — that's the customer's problem to solve post-boot, not a bootstrap-time secret our mechanism has to carry, so it doesn't block `installable_today`. Net: a real, non-overlapping compliance-archiving niche, mechanically installable now with the basic_auth gate, but a narrower audience than most of the catalogue — hence build_with_caveats rather than a clean build_now.

The bigger question is fit: it is a well-built but narrow vertical tool for drone pilots specifically, with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue but also a much smaller addressable audience than our existing general-purpose apps, and its tagged-release cadence has gone quiet for three months after a very active spring. name: Open Journal Systems

Backed by an academic non-profit (Simon Fraser University) with a 20+ year track record, not a venture-dependent single-maintainer project.

Closest adjacent tools are paperless-ngx/paperless-ai (document archival/OCR, not editorial workflow) and gitea/opengist (developer collaboration, not academic publishing) — no functional overlap with any of them.

Medium rather than high because it is a narrow vertical audience compared to broadly-applicable tools already in the catalogue (n8n, Vaultwarden, Immich).

blocking_issues:
OJS has no unattended/env-var install path: both the web installer and the CLI installer (tools/install.php -> PKP\cliTool\InstallTool::readParams(), see pkp-lib classes/cliTool/InstallTool.php) prompt for and store an admin username + PLAINTEXT password that OJS hashes itself during setup. There is no field that accepts a pre-computed hash, so root-password projection via `generated_from` cannot reach it — this is the genuine-plaintext-requirement case SCHEMA.md calls a structural blocker, not just an unsupported hash algorithm.
Gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth does not resolve the above: a customer still needs to complete the OJS install wizard and set an admin password themselves to actually use the journal (submit articles, manage editorial workflow) — basic_auth only protects the door, it doesn't substitute for the app's own required account-creation step.
summary: Open Journal Systems is an actively maintained, well-established scholarly-publishing platform (PKP, Simon Fraser University; LTS 3.5.0-5 shipped 2026-06-30, ~5 weeks before this analysis) with an official Docker image and no overlap in our current 24-recipe catalogue — it would fill a genuine, if narrow, gap for university/journal customers. It is blocked today purely on the installation mechanism: OJS's installer (web or CLI) requires the customer to set a plaintext admin password during setup, and neither `generated_from` (hash-only) nor a Traefik `basic_auth` gate can substitute for that required first-run account creation. Revisit once a customer-chosen-plaintext-password input channel exists on the platform, or if PKP ever adds a pre-hashed/env-based unattended install path.

name: Open Monograph Press
source_description: Open-source editorial workflow and catalog software for scholarly books
version_health_notes: Public Knowledge Project (PKP) ships OMP on the same release train as OJS (Open Journal Systems). Tag history shows a steady cadence: 3_5_0-0 (2025-06-16), 3_5_0-1 (2025-07-09), 3_5_0-2 (2025-11-29), 3_5_0-3 (2025-12-19), 3_5_0-4 (2026-04-10), 3_5_0-5 (2026-06-30) — roughly every 1-3 months, with parallel backport point releases on the 3.3 LTS and 3.4 lines. As of today (2026-08-05) the latest tag is ~5 weeks old. The official pkpofficial/omp Docker image is explicitly labeled BETA on Docker Hub, distinct from the maturity of the underlying application.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers scholarly/academic publishing workflow (peer review, ONIX metadata, book catalog and sales pages). paperless-ngx and paperless-ai are personal document archiving, not editorial/publication workflow; gitea/opengist are dev tools; none overlap OMP's actual use case.
usefulness_rationale: The differentiation is real but the addressable customer base (academic presses, scholarly societies, university library publishing units) is a narrow niche compared to the rest of the catalogue's general self-hosting audience. Worth building only if there's a specific customer ask for it.
blocking_issues:
OMP's normal first-boot path is an interactive web installer where the operator freely chooses a site admin username, email, and plaintext password (like OJS). There is no confirmed mechanism for projecting a generated_from-style hash into that field — the installer expects the plaintext, which it then hashes with its own internal scheme, not argon2/bcrypt supplied pre-hashed.

The Docker image's alternative unattended path (PKP_CLI_INSTALL env var, documented in pkp/containers' easyOJS.md) is explicitly called out by the maintainers as "under construction" and untested with the current images ("This feature was not tested yet with the new images. Report if you got any issue."). There is no reliable automated install path today regardless of the credential-mechanism question.

Even if PKP_CLI_INSTALL matures, it still requires supplying an arbitrary customer-chosen admin username *and* password pair — two independent values our JWE bootstrap token has no channel for beyond the single root-password projection.
summary: Open Monograph Press is an actively maintained, GPL-3.0 scholarly publishing platform with a genuinely novel niche versus our current catalogue, but it fails installability on two independent grounds: its only documented unattended-install path is explicitly experimental/beta and untested by its own maintainers, and even a working version of that path would still require an arbitrary customer-chosen admin username/password pair with no projection mechanism today. Combined with a narrow target audience, this is not worth pursuing now; revisit if PKP_CLI_INSTALL matures and if generated_from ever needs to support this case (still gated on the plaintext-vs-hash question).

source_description: Open-source secrets manager for storing and accessing sensitive credentials
version_health_notes: Latest stable release (2.6.1) shipped 2026-07-22, ~2 weeks before this analysis (2026-08-05). Prior releases: 2.6.0 on 2026-07-14, 2.5.5 on 2026-06-17, 2.5.4 on 2026-05-20, 2.5.3 on 2026-04-20 — a steady multi-week release cadence with both patch and feature releases. OpenBao is a Linux Foundation project (fork of HashiCorp Vault, created after Vault's 2023 BSL relicensing) with backing from IBM and other members; governance and cadence look sustainable, not a one-vendor side project.
differentiation: Vaultwarden (already in the catalogue) is a personal/team Bitwarden- compatible password manager for end users. OpenBao is a machine/infra secrets manager: dynamic secret generation (cloud/DB credentials), PKI issuance, encryption-as-a-service, and audited API-driven access for applications and pipelines — a different audience (DevOps/platform engineers) and use case with no functional overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Legitimate demand from customers running their own infra/CI who want a Vault-compatible secrets store without HashiCorp's BSL license. Value is capped for a single-VM AF deployment: OpenBao's dynamic-secrets and PKI features assume it's wired into other infrastructure (clouds, databases, CAs) that a lone AF instance doesn't provide out of the box, so much of its value only shows up once the customer does further integration work themselves.
blocking_issues:
OpenBao boots sealed and has no admin username/password concept at all — production storage backends require an operator-driven `bao operator init` (which mints a fresh root token and a set of Shamir unseal-key shares) followed by `bao operator unseal`. Both the root token and the unseal keys are generated by the app itself at init time and are the ONLY way to ever log in or unseal after a restart; they cannot be pre-supplied via env var/config for a production storage backend the way `generated_from` or `auto_generate` parameters work today.

Even if install.sh runs init/unseal automatically during provisioning, there is no existing mechanism to capture that app-generated root token/unseal keys and surface them back to the customer post-deploy. Today's `auto_generate` pattern only covers secrets generated by af-api BEFORE the app boots and injected in via the env template (e.g. Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN) — not values the app itself produces once running. Without a delivery channel, the customer would receive a running-but-unusable, permanently sealed or inaccessible vault.

A `-dev` mode exists that allows a fixed root token and auto-unseal, but it is explicitly unsuitable for anything beyond local testing (in-memory storage, no persistence, all data lost on restart) and is not a real option for a hosted recipe.
summary: OpenBao is an actively maintained, Linux Foundation-governed Vault fork with a real and distinct use case from anything else in the catalogue (infra/API secrets management vs. Vaultwarden's personal password vault). It is not installable under the current mechanism, though: it has no admin login to project a root-password hash into, and its actual login credential (a root token) plus its unseal keys are generated by the app itself at init time with no existing channel to hand them back to the customer. This needs a new "capture app-generated secret and return it to the customer" mechanism — a bigger platform gap than the root-password-projection or basic-auth-gate work already in flight — so it should be revisited once that lands rather than attempted now.

name: OpenBudgeteer
source_description: Open-source bucket budgeting app for personal finance management
version_health_notes: Latest tag v1.11 published 2025-12-17, ~7.5 months before today (2026-08-05). Not archived, still a single-maintainer project with ongoing commits/releases. Cadence has clearly slowed over time: patch releases were days-to-weeks apart in 2022/2024 (v1.8 -> v1.8.3 in about two months), but the last three feature releases are 7-8 months apart each (v1.8.3 2024-05-20 -> v1.9 2025-01-04 -> v1.10 2025-04-30 -> v1.11 2025-12-17, with a quick v1.9.1 patch in between). Today's elapsed gap (7.5 months) is right at the upper end of that recent pattern rather than clearly overdue, so this reads as "slowing" (small team, low cadence) rather than dormant/EOL.
differentiation: Both target self-hosted personal budgeting and would sit in the same "finance" category as an existing apps-gaps candidate (actual-budget, not yet built). Per catalogue policy, overlap alone isn't a rejection reason — OpenBudgeteer's "bucket budgeting" model (inspired by YNAB / Buckets, envelope-style buckets/bucket groups with reporting) is a distinct product angle from Actual's envelope budgeting, and some customers will prefer one UI/methodology over the other. It would be the second finance-category recipe rather than the first, competing directly with actual-budget for the same shelf slot.
usefulness_rationale: Personal budgeting has broad consumer appeal, but OpenBudgeteer is a much heavier install than the category's likely first pick (actual-budget is a single container with bundled SQLite; OpenBudgeteer mandatorily needs a separate MariaDB/Postgres and a separate Redis service). Smaller community (single maintainer, ~1k GitHub stars) and slower release cadence than Actual Budget. Worth having as a second option in the category, but not the priority pick.
summary: OpenBudgeteer is a .NET/Blazor Server web app that mandatorily requires a SQL database (MariaDB or Postgres) plus Redis alongside the app container — a three-service stack, heavier than Actual Budget's single container but structurally similar to n8n's app+Postgres pattern. It exposes a single HTTP port (8080) and is Traefik-friendly. All database/Redis credentials can be generated server-side with zero customer input. OpenBudgeteer does ship its own optional login (APPSETTINGS_AUTH_ENABLED, added in v1.11), but it's disabled by default and takes username/password as plaintext env vars with no hash-based option, so `generated_from` can't drive it — the recipe should leave it disabled and instead gate the app with a mandatory Traefik basic_auth (same pattern as Adminer/n8n), which is expressible today. That keeps the customer-facing credential need to just the basic_auth password, clearing the current /compose constraint with no blocking issues. Release cadence has slowed to roughly two releases a year but the project remains actively maintained, not EOL. Recommend building now, understanding it would be the catalogue's second finance-category recipe alongside the not-yet-built actual-budget candidate and a heavier install for a somewhat smaller upstream community.

OpenCloud fills a distinct "self-hosted Google-Drive-alternative" niche the catalogue currently lacks.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted file sync/sharing with office collaboration is a high-demand, well-understood category (Nextcloud-class) that the catalogue has no entry for today. OpenCloud is the actively developed successor project from the ownCloud team and ships an official, reverse-proxy-friendly single-container deployment path.

It's actively developed (releases every 2-4 weeks, latest 2 days old) and fills a real gap: the catalogue has no Nextcloud/ownCloud-class file-sync-and-collaboration app today. Recommend building a recipe now, using the official opencloud-compose "external-proxy" overlay as the template and pinning to a specific rolling tag (not :latest or the rolling floating tag).

name: OpenFGA
source_description: Google Zanzibar-inspired fine-grained authorization engine for apps
version_health_notes: Latest release (v1.18.3) shipped today (2026-08-05); the prior four releases (v1.18.2, v1.18.1, v1.18.0, v1.17.1) landed 2026-08-03, 2026-06-29, 2026-06-17, 2026-06-05 respectively — a steady multi-week cadence with no gaps. CNCF-hosted (Auth0/Okta-originated), actively maintained, no archival or EOL signals.
differentiation: OpenFGA is a Zanzibar-style relationship-based authorization API server — nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue provides fine-grained permission/authz-as-a-service for other applications to call. It is not an end-user app; it's infrastructure other apps' developers embed into their own software via SDK calls over its HTTP/gRPC API.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely differentiated (developer-tools/security infra we don't have), but its audience is developers building their own apps against the API, not the typical AF customer standing up a ready-to-use app. Value is real but narrower than most of the current catalogue.
blocking_issues:
OpenFGA ships two HTTP surfaces: the API (port 8080, meant to be called by the customer's own applications) and a "Playground" (port 3000), which upstream docs explicitly describe as a local-development-only tool with no authentication of its own — not something to expose on a public domain. There is no browser-facing admin UI suitable for a customer-facing AF app the way every other recipe in the catalogue has.

Default authentication mode is OPENFGA_AUTHN_METHOD=none — the API accepts any request unauthenticated out of the box. Securing it means OPENFGA_AUTHN_METHOD=preshared plus one or more OPENFGA_AUTHN_PRESHARED_KEYS values, which are plaintext bearer-token API keys the customer's own external applications must be configured with to call OpenFGA — not a login/password pair on an app the customer clicks into.

This breaks the current mechanism in a way distinct from every existing blocked case: the problem isn't lack of an *input* channel for a customer-chosen secret (a random preshared key can be generated server-side just fine), it's lack of an *output* channel — nothing in the current recipe/`/compose` flow surfaces a generated secret back to the customer so their external application can actually use it. All three existing mechanisms assume the secret is either supplied by the customer (root-password hash) or never needs to leave the server (backend DB password); OpenFGA's preshared key is generated server-side but MUST reach the customer to be useful, which none of the three cover.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (as done for WUD/ Adminer-style apps with no login) does not substitute here: that protects a human clicking through a browser, not an SDK making Bearer-token API calls, so it would not give the customer's own application a usable path to authenticate against OpenFGA.
summary: OpenFGA is an actively maintained, differentiated addition (no existing recipe covers authorization-as-a-service) but doesn't fit the current recipe mechanism: it has no customer-facing web UI, defaults to open/ unauthenticated API access, and its real secret — a preshared API key the customer's own external apps must be configured with — needs an output channel (surfacing a generated secret back to the customer) that `/compose` doesn't have today, not just an input channel. Revisit once the platform can hand a generated secret back to the customer post-install, or once OpenFGA is paired with OIDC-based auth wiring specific to AF.

name: OpenHands
source_description: Open-source autonomous AI agent for software engineering tasks
version_health_notes: Extremely active, releasing today (2026-08-05): v1.10.0 (2026-08-05), v1.9.0 (2026-08-03), v1.8.0/v1.7.2/v1.7.1 (2026-07-30), v1.7.0 (2026-07-29), v1.6.1 (2026-07-24) — multiple tagged releases per week. 83k+ stars, 10.7k forks, ~8k commits on main. No archival, EOL notice, or maintenance-mode signal. The project started as OpenDevin (early 2024), rebranded to OpenHands under the All-Hands-AI org, and in 2026 the GitHub org itself moved from All-Hands-AI to OpenHands with the web UI consolidated around a new "Agent Canvas" interface — an active rebrand/restructure, not a sign of decline.
differentiation: Closest existing recipe is claude-code (native, terminal-only, single agent backend, Anthropic models only). OpenHands/Agent Canvas is a browser-based control center that can drive multiple coding-agent backends (its own OpenHands agent, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or any ACP-compatible agent) against real project repos, plus scheduling, webhook-triggered automation, and GitHub/Linear/Slack integrations — a materially different, broader product from a single CLI tool. Hermes Agent and OpenClaw are messaging-driven personal-assistant agents (Telegram-first); OpenHands is squarely a software-engineering tool (reads/writes/runs code in a project directory, opens PRs) with no messaging-app angle, so the overlap with those two is thin.
usefulness_rationale: Distinct "autonomous coding agent with a web UI" niche not covered by any of the 24 current recipes; claude-code covers only the terminal case. Genuine differentiator (multi-backend, PR automation, project scheduling) for customers who want a persistent hosted agent rather than a local CLI session.
blocking_issues:
Upstream Docker setup (`ghcr.io/openhands/agent-canvas`) ships with no built-in login of its own — `docker run -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/openhands/agent-canvas` opens straight into the UI. Third- party self-hosted deployment guides (e.g. the Azure Marketplace listing) all layer HTTP basic auth via a reverse proxy in front of it, confirming there is no first-party auth to project a root- password hash into. A mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate is therefore required, same pattern as OpenClaw/Open Agent — expressible today, not a hard blocker.

Its "Docker" sandbox backend (the mode used to actually execute agent-written code safely) works by mounting the host's /var/run/docker.sock into the container so it can spawn sibling sandbox containers on demand — i.e. it requires giving the container root-equivalent control of the host Docker daemon. Upstream's own docs warn this grants the container access to all other Docker resources on the host. That is a materially different and larger blast radius than any current recipe's docker-compose footprint and needs an explicit platform/security decision before this ships, independent of the customer-input constraint that is the focus of this schema.

Functionally requires an LLM provider API key ("bring your own model" — Anthropic/OpenAI/etc.) to do anything useful. Like hermes-agent/openclaw, this has no first-boot input channel today; it would ship undocumented as an empty value and be set by the customer post-provision via the authenticated (basic-auth-gated) UI settings screen, not at order time. Not a hard blocker (app boots and the settings UI is reachable without it) but it does mean the app is non-functional until the customer performs an extra manual step.
summary: OpenHands (GitHub org OpenHands/OpenHands, image ghcr.io/openhands/agent-canvas, MIT) is an unusually active, high-star autonomous coding-agent platform with a real web UI, distinct from every current recipe including claude-code (native/terminal-only). It has no built-in login, so it needs the same mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate already used for OpenClaw/Open Agent, and the LLM provider key is set post-provision like Hermes Agent/OpenClaw — both are handled by existing patterns, not new blockers. The real open question is its Docker-in- Docker sandbox requirement (mounting /var/run/docker.sock to spawn sibling containers), which is a bigger host-access footprint than any current recipe and warrants an explicit platform decision before building. Note: the name "OpenHands" is also used by an unrelated, no-longer-maintained sign-language-recognition project (AI4Bharat/OpenHands) — not a candidate, ruled out.

name: OpenHuman
source_description: Self-hosted personal AI core with memory, agents, and 118+ app integrations
version_health_notes: Latest tag v0.63.9 shipped 2026-07-28, 8 days before this analysis (2026-08-05). Release history shows multiple tags per month (v0.57.44, v0.57.52, v0.57.53, v0.58.0, v0.58.7, v0.61.2, v0.61.8, v0.63.0, v0.63.1, v0.63.9 across June-July 2026) — a genuinely active, fast-moving project (36k+ GitHub stars, 3.6k forks), not dormant or maintenance-only. Still pre-1.0 / "Early Beta" per upstream's own framing, so breaking changes between releases are plausible.
differentiation: OpenHuman's pitch is a persistent local-first "memory tree" (Markdown + SQLite, Obsidian-compatible) plus a broad OAuth integration wallet (118+ third-party services: Gmail, Notion, Slack, GitHub, etc.) and agent-to-agent orchestration over Signal-protocol messaging. That's a materially different value proposition from hermes-agent/openclaw (messaging-triggered task agents with a web dashboard), but in self-hosted/server mode OpenHuman ships none of the UI that makes that differentiation usable — see installability below.
usefulness_rationale: The differentiating features (memory tree browsing, OAuth integration setup, agent orchestration UI) all live in the desktop app, not the self-hostable core. A customer provisioning this recipe would get a backend they cannot productively use without separately installing desktop software on their own machine and manually pairing it with a bearer token — a fundamentally different delivery model from every other recipe in the catalogue, where provisioning yields a directly usable browser web app.
blocking_issues:
No production browser-based web UI. Upstream's own Cloud Deploy docs state explicitly that "the deployed core does not serve the full React/Tauri UI as a production web app yet" — self-hosting only stands up the headless openhuman-core JSON-RPC backend (GET /health, POST /rpc, GET /events, GET /ws/dictation). The actual UI is the desktop app (Tauri/React), which the customer would have to install separately on their own computer and point at OPENHUMAN_CORE_RPC_URL/OPENHUMAN_CORE_TOKEN to get any usable product. There is nothing meaningful for Traefik to front for a browser-only customer — this breaks the "provision → open URL in browser → working app" model every current recipe assumes, independent of the secrets question below.

OPENHUMAN_CORE_TOKEN is technically auto-generatable server-side (e.g. `openssl rand -hex 32`), so unlike an external API key it doesn't strictly need a customer-input channel — but because there is no web UI to log into, there is no natural surface to hand that token back to the customer the way an admin-login page does for other recipes. It would depend on the AF customer portal's generic generated-parameter-reveal mechanism (as used for hermes-agent/openclaw auto_generate params) rather than anything in-app.

Most of the advertised value (118+ OAuth integrations: Gmail, Notion, Slack, GitHub, etc.) depends by default on the vendor's own backend (api.tinyhumans.ai) for OAuth brokering, or on the customer registering and supplying their own OAuth app credentials per integration in "Run Custom" mode. Neither has an input channel in the current `/compose` mechanism (no arbitrary customer-supplied values, no per-service OAuth registration flow) — so even if the web-UI gap above were solved, the integrations that differentiate this app from hermes-agent/openclaw would still be inert on first boot.
summary: OpenHuman is a genuinely active, fast-releasing project (weekly tags, latest 8 days old), but its self-hosted "core" is a headless JSON-RPC backend with no production web UI — upstream is explicit that the actual interface is a separate desktop app the user must install and pair locally, which is incompatible with the AF model of a browser-usable app behind Traefik. On top of that, the feature set that would differentiate it from already-catalogued agent recipes (hermes-agent, openclaw) — 118+ OAuth integrations — has no expressible input channel under the current `/compose` mechanism. Not recommended: even resolving the secrets gap (IF-1420/IF-1312) wouldn't fix the missing-UI structural blocker.

name: OpenLIT
source_description: OpenTelemetry-native observability and cost monitoring for LLM apps
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/openlit/openlit (paired with clickhouse/clickhouse-server — two-image stack, no single "the" image)
version_health_notes: openlit-1.24.2 published 2026-07-28, 8 days before today (2026-08-05). Preceding platform tags (1.24.1, 1.24.0, 1.23.0) shipped 2026-07-15, 2026-07-13, 2026-07-09 — roughly weekly to biweekly cadence for the last month, on top of separate near-weekly Python/TypeScript SDK releases in the same repo. GitHub repo confirmed not archived, pushed_at 2026-08-03, 2.7k stars, 58 open issues. Unambiguously active.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does LLM-call observability, tracing, or cost monitoring — ollama and open-webui are inference/chat endpoints, not instrumentation targets. OpenLIT would fill a real gap for a customer who has their own LLM-integrated app and wants to trace calls, GPU usage, and cost against it. That said, this is the same niche as the still-unbuilt Langfuse candidate (see apps-gaps/langfuse.yaml) — both are self-hosted, ClickHouse-backed, OpenTelemetry-based LLM observability platforms with SDK auto-instrumentation for 50+ LLM providers. Langfuse is materially further ahead on installability (see below) and would fill this niche with fewer platform blockers, so OpenLIT is redundant against that candidate even though it doesn't duplicate anything already shipped as a recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct demand from the developer/AI-builder audience, and a credible fast-moving project. Not high because it's a narrow developer-tooling niche (valuable only to customers instrumenting their own LLM apps, not the broader self-hoster base), and it is currently blocked on the same structural issue as HyperDX/Apache SkyWalking (see installability) rather than being a clean drop-in.
blocking_issues:
Not a single-HTTP-port app: the upstream docker-compose.yml (confirmed live today) publishes the web UI/API on 3000 AND the OpenTelemetry collector's raw ingestion ports 4317 (gRPC) and 4318 (HTTP) directly on the host. OpenLIT's entire value proposition is receiving traces pushed by a customer's own OpenTelemetry-instrumented application — which is typically a separate service the customer runs elsewhere, so those OTLP ports must be reachable directly by that pusher, not just routable to a browser through Traefik on 80/443. This is the exact same structural mismatch already documented for HyperDX (apps-gaps/hyperdx.yaml) and Apache SkyWalking: every current recipe is a single browser-facing HTTP port fronted by Traefik, and exposing raw ingestion ports per customer VM is a product decision that hasn't been made yet.

Login uses a hardcoded default credential with no environment-variable override: the upstream README instructs first login with email user@openlit.io / password openlituser, and neither the shipped docker-compose.yml nor the documented configuration env vars expose a way to set this at deploy time (auth-related env vars are limited to NEXTAUTH_SECRET and optional Google/GitHub OAuth client IDs/secrets — no admin email/password var exists). Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md this is not a blocker on its own — a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the app would be the correct mitigation — but it stacks with the raw-port issue above, since basic_auth only gates the browser-facing port 3000 and does nothing for the OTLP ports that also need to stay open.
summary: OpenLIT is an active, fast-shipping (roughly biweekly releases) open-source LLM observability platform that would fill a real gap in the catalogue — nothing currently does LLM-call tracing/cost monitoring — but it fails installability today for the same structural reason as HyperDX: its core function requires the OpenTelemetry collector's raw ports (4317 gRPC, 4318 HTTP) to be reachable by a customer's own instrumented application, not just a browser through Traefik, and no per-customer raw-port exposure mechanism exists yet. All four infra secrets it needs (ClickHouse password, NextAuth secret, vault encryption key, cron secret) are patternless and server-generatable with no blocker, and its hardcoded default admin credential is a soft issue Traefik basic_auth could cover — but that doesn't resolve the OTLP-port gap. It's also the same niche as the still-unbuilt Langfuse candidate, which reaches installable_today without this blocker, making OpenLIT a lower-priority pick even once raw-port exposure ships. Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit once per-customer raw-port/NodePort exposure exists, at which point Langfuse should likely be built first given its cleaner installability.

name: OpenObserve
source_description: Cloud-native observability platform for logs, metrics, traces, and dashboards
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (open-source edition; separate commercial Enterprise Edition also exists)
upstream_docker_image: public.ecr.aws/zinclabs/openobserve (mirrored on Docker Hub as openobserve/openobserve)
version_health_notes: Patch releases roughly every 3-7 days (v0.91.1 2026-07-02, v0.91.2 07-17, v0.91.3 07-21, v0.91.4 07-27, v0.91.5 07-30), plus a v0.92.0-rc3 release candidate cut 2026-08-05 (today). Latest stable is 6 days old as of today's date. Project passed 20,000 GitHub stars in July 2026 per upstream announcements. No signs of slowing, maintenance-only, or EOL.
differentiation: Uptime Kuma (our only existing monitoring recipe) is a lightweight up/down status checker. OpenObserve is a full logs/metrics/traces observability stack (Datadog/Splunk/Elasticsearch-style), a materially different and heavier use case — customers running multi-service self-hosted stacks (e.g. our own n8n, Immich, Gitea recipes) would use it to centralize log/metric ingestion and dashboards. No true duplicate in the current 24-recipe catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Observability is a common, high-intent self-host category with no representative in the catalogue beyond basic uptime checks. Single binary/single container deployment, low resource floor, and an active, well-adopted upstream make it an attractive candidate on merit alone.
blocking_issues:
OpenObserve has its own built-in login (root user) that gates all functionality — there is no way to use the app meaningfully without logging in as ZO_ROOT_USER_EMAIL / ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD. This is not an app with "no login of its own" that a Traefik basic_auth gate could stand in for; the customer must actually authenticate to the app itself to get any value from it.

ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD is read by the container as a plaintext password at startup (set directly via env var, e.g. ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD="Complexpass#123") — the app does not accept a pre-computed hash in any supported or unsupported algorithm. Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md this is the genuine-plaintext case, which is a hard structural blocker: generated_from only ever projects a hash of the customer's root (server) password, never the plaintext, so there is no way to pass a customer-meaningful password into this variable today.
summary: OpenObserve is an active, well-maintained, high-value observability app with no equivalent already in the catalogue (Uptime Kuma covers uptime pings only, not logs/metrics/traces). It is mechanically simple to deploy (single container, local-disk storage is fine for self-host scale, one HTTP port, reverse-proxy friendly) but its own admin login only accepts a plaintext ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD, which the current /compose mechanism has no channel to supply (generated_from projects a hash, not plaintext, and a Traefik gate can't substitute for the app's mandatory internal login). OR_ADMIN_PASSWORD is forwarded as KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD to bootstrap Keycloak's initial realm admin user, and Keycloak's admin-bootstrap env var only accepts a plaintext value (it hashes internally once the container starts) — there is no supported way to hand it a pre-computed hash in any algorithm. name: OpenSearch
source_description: Open-source search and analytics engine, community fork of Elasticsearch
version_health_notes: 3.8.0 tagged 2026-08-05 (today), per the GitHub Releases API (published_at 2026-08-05T17:20:33Z) and confirmed present on Docker Hub (opensearchproject/opensearch:3.8.0, last_updated 2026-08-04). Recent history on the 3.x active line: 3.4.0 (2025-12-16), 3.5.0 (2026-02-10), 3.6.0 (2026-04-07), 3.7.0 (2026-06-09), 3.8.0 (2026-08-05) — a steady ~8-week minor-release cadence, matching the project's own stated goal ("release a new minor version approximately every eight weeks"). Repo is not archived, was pushed to today (2026-08-05T17:20:16Z), has 13.4k stars and 3k+ open issues under active triage. This is an AWS-backed, CNCF-adjacent fork with a large contributor base; unambiguously active, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: OpenSearch is architecturally identical in role to Elasticsearch (apps-gaps/elasticsearch.yaml, analyzed separately, also not a shipped recipe) — a headless REST search/analytics backend with no web UI of its own, with OpenSearch Dashboards as its Kibana-equivalent UI counterpart (same relationship as apps-gaps/kibana.yaml describes for the Elastic Stack). Its one real differentiator is licensing and provenance: OpenSearch is the Apache-2.0-licensed fork AWS created in 2021 specifically in response to Elastic relicensing Elasticsearch under the (non-OSI) Elastic License/SSPL, so it's the option for a customer who wants an Elasticsearch-API-compatible engine without Elastic's licensing terms. None of the 24 shipped recipes provide a search/analytics backend; if either engine were built, the licensing difference — not any technical capability gap — would be the deciding factor between them, not a reason to build both.
usefulness_rationale: Same structural ceiling as the Elasticsearch analysis: OpenSearch ships no web UI at all on its own (port 9200 is a raw JSON REST API); its natural consumer is a developer wiring up their own application or a companion tool (OpenSearch Dashboards, or an app's own search/ RAG feature) against the API, not an end user clicking through a dashboard the way every other recipe in this catalogue works. It also carries the same disproportionate-for-single-tenant footprint (JVM heap, ulimits for memlock/nofile, 2GB+ RAM realistic minimum even for a single-node demo config) as Elasticsearch. Slightly more relevant than a plain "low" given growing self-hosted interest in OpenSearch as a vector-search/RAG backend and its permissive license, but that doesn't change the fundamental no-UI, developer-only audience problem for this catalogue.
blocking_issues:
OPENSEARCH_INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD itself only accepts plaintext — the container's demo-config bootstrap script bcrypt-hashes whatever string it's given at first startup, so a `generated_from` hash cannot be passed through that env var directly. But OpenSearch's Security plugin exposes an Internal Users API (`PUT _plugins/_security/api/internalusers/admin`) that accepts a `hash` field carrying a pre-computed hash instead of plaintext, and its default `plugins.security.password.hashing` algorithm is bcrypt — one of the two algorithms `generated_from` already supports. This is the same two-step bootstrap pattern already flagged for Elasticsearch (apps-gaps/elasticsearch.yaml): start the container with a throwaway OPENSEARCH_INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD to get a live credential, then call the Internal Users API to overwrite the admin account with the customer's projected `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` hash. Workable, but more install.sh bootstrap logic than a plain metadata.yaml parameter mapping.

The Security plugin's demo configuration auto-enables TLS on the REST layer (port 9200) with a self-signed cert by default. To sit cleanly behind Traefik (which terminates public TLS itself), the recipe needs to explicitly set `plugins.security.ssl.http.enabled: false` in opensearch.yml — a supported, documented setting, not a blocker, but a config detail that must be set correctly or the container ships double/mismatched TLS. (Transport-layer TLS, port 9300, is mandatory and unrelated to public exposure since that port is never published.)

Even with the credential mechanism and TLS wired up correctly, there is still no web UI for a customer to log into — the "login" being protected is a REST API credential meant for a customer's own code/client, a different usage pattern than every other recipe's browser-based admin login. (OpenSearch Dashboards would be the UI layer, but that's a separate product/separate recipe question, same caveat apps-gaps/kibana.yaml raises for the Elastic Stack.)
summary: OpenSearch is an actively-maintained (3.8.0 tagged today, 2026-08-05, on an ~8-week cadence), AWS-backed Apache-2.0 fork of Elasticsearch, created specifically to offer an Elasticsearch-API-compatible engine without Elastic's non-OSI license — that licensing difference, not any technical gap, is its only real differentiator from the already-analyzed apps-gaps/elasticsearch.yaml, since the two are architecturally identical (headless REST search backend, no web UI, OpenSearch Dashboards/Kibana as the respective companion UI). Its admin credential is mechanically expressible via `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` using the same two-step bootstrap Elasticsearch needs (throwaway initial password, then overwrite via the Internal Users API's hash field), plus disabling the Security plugin's auto-configured REST-layer TLS so it sits cleanly behind Traefik. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically buildable on the same terms as Elasticsearch, but low standalone value for this catalogue's end-user-facing audience absent a UI layer — if only one of the two forks is worth building, the choice comes down to which license a target customer segment prefers, not which is easier to package.

name: Openship
source_description: Self-hostable deployment platform with built-in CI/CD for any stack
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/oblien/openship-api, ghcr.io/oblien/openship-dashboard, ghcr.io/oblien/openship-edge (no Docker Hub image; GHCR only)
version_health_notes: 5 days before today (2026-08-05) at time of writing. Repo created 2026-03-05, last push 2026-08-05 (today). Release history shows near-daily tags through July 2026 (v0.1.6 on 2026-07-13 up through v0.5.0 on 2026-07-31 — 7 releases in 18 days). 10.3k GitHub stars, 118 open issues, not archived. This is a young but rapidly-shipping, clearly active project, not dormant.
differentiation: Unlike runtipi (one-click installs of pre-packaged apps) or Portainer (manual container/stack management), Openship is a git-push CI/CD platform: point it at a repo and it detects the stack, builds an image, runs the container, and reverse-proxies + TLS-terminates it on a customer-chosen subdomain, with webhook-driven redeploys on every push. That "push-to-deploy PaaS" niche (closer to a self-hosted Vercel/Heroku) isn't covered by anything in the current 24 recipes.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiated niche and an actively-growing project, but it is architecturally a mini-PaaS that wants to own the whole box (see installability below), which cuts against how narrowly-scoped our other recipes are.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: POSTGRES_PASSWORD; BETTER_AUTH_SECRET; INTERNAL_TOKEN; first admin account (username/password)
blocking_issues:
Openship ships its own reverse-proxy/TLS edge: the `edge` service is OpenResty running with `network_mode: host`, binding the host's :80/:443 directly (Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 handled by the app itself, not Traefik). This has a precedent in the catalogue (`recipes/runtipi/` does the same), so it is not disqualifying on its own, but it does mean our Traefik never sits in front of this app — so Traefik `basic_auth` is NOT available as a gating mechanism for anything Openship exposes.

Confirmed by reading source (apps/api/src/modules/auth/auth.routes.ts, apps/api/src/middleware/loopback-peer.ts): the open self-registration race does NOT exist. A guard runs before Better Auth's catch-all and unconditionally blocks POST /sign-up with 403 SIGNUP_DISABLED unless (a) zero users exist yet AND (b) the request's kernel-reported TCP peer address is loopback (127.0.0.0/8 or ::1) — not a spoofable header. The real blocker this creates is structural, not racy: there is no remotely-reachable channel to create the first admin at all. The only path in is on-host (the `openship up` CLI, or a raw loopback curl to the API's sign-up endpoint, which the compose file's `127.0.0.1`-only port binding would permit if run from the host during install.sh). But that loopback signup needs the customer's actual plaintext password to produce a login that will later match what the customer types — and our `/compose` mechanism only ever hands install.sh a hash of ROOT_PASSWORD via `generated_from`, never the plaintext (per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md). So even the loopback path cannot provision an admin account the customer can subsequently log into. This is confirmed from the public repo, not an open question for upstream.

`api` mounts the host Docker socket (Docker-out-of-Docker, so it can build/run whatever the customer deploys) and optionally reaches the host over SSH (`OPENSHIP_HOST_SSH_*`) for host-level ops. Socket mounts alone have precedent (`recipes/portainer/`, `recipes/runtipi/`, `recipes/wud/`), so not a blocker by itself, but combined with the other two points it reinforces that this app is a full mini-PaaS control plane, not a single scoped application — a materially larger trust boundary than anything else in the catalogue.
summary: Openship (oblien/openship — not to be confused with the unrelated openshiporg/openship e-commerce order-router, ruled out since it doesn't match Hostinger's "deployment platform with built-in CI/CD" description) is a genuinely active, fast-moving self-hosted PaaS with a real differentiated niche (git-push CI/CD) versus our existing app-store/container-manager recipes. It is blocked today because there is no remotely-reachable way to provision the first admin account at all: self-host sign-up is unconditionally gated to loopback-only-while-zero-users (confirmed in source, not a race), and even that loopback path needs the customer's plaintext password to produce a working login, which our `/compose` mechanism never has access to (only a hash, via `generated_from`). Combined with its own host-network reverse-proxy edge (precedented, not fatal, but meaning Traefik `basic_auth` can't front it either), this app has no channel through which our current recipe mechanism could hand it a customer-usable first login.

Development is clearly active: 15.0 shipped 2026-01-01, and the next major line is already in beta (16.0-beta1 2026-06-25, 16.0-beta2 2026-07-12).
