differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches game-server hosting; this would open a new "gaming" category. Customer value is real (self-hosting a multiplayer Transport Tycoon server for friends/community is a common ask), but it's a different shape of product than our productivity/dev-tool recipes: no HTTP surface, no admin web UI, connects via a native game client.
usefulness_rationale: Legitimate niche demand, but the app speaks a raw custom TCP/UDP protocol (game port 3979 TCP+UDP, admin/rcon over the same channel) with no HTTP component at all — it can't sit behind Traefik like the rest of the catalogue, and per CLAUDE.md a raw port needs NodePort/LoadBalancer-level exposure rather than a domain-based reverse-proxy route.
blocking_issues:
No HTTP/web UI at all — the game client and rcon admin console both speak OpenTTD's native TCP/UDP protocol on port 3979, so there is no surface for Traefik to front and no basic_auth gate is possible.
rcon (admin console) access is gated by rcon_pw, a config value the server compares against the plaintext password the client sends over the game protocol — it is not a hashed login. generated_from only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password, so it cannot supply what this parameter actually needs. This is a genuine plaintext requirement, not just an unsupported hash algorithm, so it is a structural blocker rather than something IF-1420 could later extend to cover.
Even the optional in-game server_password (gates joining the game itself) has the same plaintext-comparison requirement, so it has no expressible mechanism either.
summary: OpenTTD is an active, well-maintained open-source project (latest stable 15.3, next major line already in beta) with genuine customer demand for self-hosted multiplayer game servers, but it doesn't fit the AF recipe mechanism as it exists today: it has no HTTP surface for Traefik, and both its admin (rcon) and optional join password are plaintext comparisons that generated_from's hash-only projection cannot supply. Not recommended for now — would need a first-class plaintext-secret input channel (not just a new hash algorithm) plus raw TCP/UDP exposure support before revisiting.

name: OpenViking
source_description: OpenViking is an open-source context database built for AI agents
version_health_notes: v0.4.12 released 2026-08-03, 2 days before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases: v0.4.11 (2026-07-23), v0.4.10 (2026-07-16), v0.4.9 (2026-07-13) — a new tagged release roughly every 5-10 days, plus dev pre-releases (v0.4.12.dev01-03) landing within hours/days of the stable tag. Backed by ByteDance/Volcengine, 1,900+ commits on main, thousands of stars. Clearly active, fast-moving development. Pre-1.0 (still 0.x) — expect breaking config/API changes between minor versions, which matters for a recipe that hand-writes ov.conf.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 built recipes is a context/memory backend for AI agents. OpenViking is a virtual-filesystem-style store (viking://) that unifies an agent's memory, resources, and skills, with a bundled "Studio" web UI for browsing/debugging that context and an HTTP API other tools consume. Upstream explicitly names openclaw — already in our catalogue (recipes/openclaw/) — as an example consumer, so this would plug into an existing recipe rather than compete with one: a customer running openclaw could point it at a self-hosted OpenViking instance for durable, inspectable memory instead of an opaque vector store. It is conceptually adjacent to open-webui/ollama (both can run fully on local models) but serves a different job — agent context persistence, not a chat frontend.
usefulness_rationale: Real and growing category (agent memory/context layers), and the openclaw synergy gives it a concrete use case in our existing catalogue rather than being a standalone curiosity. Held to medium rather than high because it is primarily infrastructure consumed via API/CLI by other agents or developer tooling, not a self-contained end-user product — closer to Letta's audience (developers wiring up agent memory) than to a turnkey app a non-technical customer would install for its own sake. It is also pre-1.0 software from a fast-moving repo, so day-one config stability is a real risk.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: OpenViking root_api_key; Embedding + VLM model provider (external LLM API key OR a local Ollama sidecar with pulled embedding/VLM models)
blocking_issues:
root_api_key is consumed by the app as an opaque string it compares for auth, not as a plaintext credential with a specific required hash scheme, so projecting a bcrypt/argon2 hash of ROOT_PASSWORD into it via generated_from is plausible — but public docs never describe the Studio login UX (whether the browser prompts for this key, expects it in a URL, or trusts anything behind the reverse proxy). Without confirming that flow against a running instance, there's a real risk the customer has no discoverable way to actually enter the projected value into Studio, in which case a Traefik basic_auth gate (with the app's own root_api_key generated randomly and never surfaced) would be the safer mechanism instead. This needs to be resolved with a live smoke test before build, not assumed either way.
Core function (embedding + VLM calls for retrieval and self-evolving memory) requires either an external provider API key (no input channel today) or a bundled Ollama sidecar with specific pulled models (e.g. an embedding model plus a VLM like llama3.1) configured into ov.conf at first boot — heavier and less turnkey than open-webui's model-picker-after-install pattern, since OpenViking's config wizard normally runs interactively before the server can even start. Scripting this in install.sh is likely feasible but unverified beyond docs.
ov.conf must be authored and mounted before the container starts (no full env-var equivalent for the embedding/VLM block); combined with a pre-1.0, fast-moving config schema, this is more fragile to automate than a typical single-env-file recipe.
summary: OpenViking is an active, well-backed context/memory database for AI agents with a genuine differentiator (nothing else in the catalogue covers this, and it has a direct synergy with the already-shipped openclaw recipe) and a pinned official Docker image. It is not a clean ship today, though: the mandatory root_api_key could plausibly be projected via generated_from(ROOT_PASSWORD) since it appears to be a simple opaque string comparison, but the Studio login flow that would actually need to accept that value is undocumented publicly and must be verified live before relying on it; and first-boot embedding/VLM configuration either needs an external provider key (no channel today) or a scripted local-Ollama setup baked into ov.conf, which is more fragile than any current recipe's boot sequence. Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit once the generated_from mechanism ships and the Studio auth UX and a local-only embedding/VLM boot path have been hands-on verified against a running instance.

name: OpenVPN Access Server
source_description: Full-featured VPN server with web-based administration and client management
upstream_license: Proprietary (free for up to 2 concurrent connections; paid subscription/fixed license beyond that)
version_health_notes: Docker Hub shows a 3.2.2 tag pushed ~5 days before today (2026-08-05), with a prior 3.1.0 tag from ~5 months earlier — consistent with the documented 3.0/3.1/3.2 release-notes cadence (multiple point releases in 2025-2026, including CVE-2025-2704, CVE-2025-50055, and CVE-2025-13086 fixes). Vendor (OpenVPN Inc.) is actively shipping security and feature updates; no EOL or archival signal anywhere.
differentiation: Both are self-hosted VPN servers with a web UI for managing peers/clients, the same niche wg-easy already fills. OpenVPN AS adds the OpenVPN protocol (broader legacy client/firewall compatibility than WireGuard) and enterprise-ish admin features (LDAP/AD, 2FA, per-user access policies), but its free tier is hard-capped at 2 concurrent VPN connections — beyond that a customer must buy an OpenVPN subscription license key, which itself has no input channel through our mechanism (see blocking_issues).
usefulness_rationale: Overlaps directly with the VPN niche already covered by wg-easy, and its practical free-tier ceiling of 2 simultaneous connections makes it a weak general-purpose VPN offering compared to WireGuard Easy, which has no such cap. Only differentiator (broader legacy client support) is a niche need, not enough on its own to justify a second VPN recipe today.
blocking_issues:
No env var or compose-time config exists to set the initial admin password. The image creates a built-in 'openvpn' admin user with a password that is randomly auto-generated at first boot and printed only to `docker logs` — a channel af-api's /compose flow has no access to and cannot surface to the customer.
Even if that channel existed, the only documented way to set/change the admin password non-interactively (`sacli --user openvpn --new_pass <PLAINTEXT> SetLocalPassword`) takes a plaintext password, not a hash. generated_from only ever produces a hash (argon2/bcrypt), so this is a genuine plaintext-password requirement — a structural blocker per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md, not a missing-algorithm gap.
A Traefik basic_auth gate does not substitute here: the app already has its own admin login with a real (if unknown-to-the-customer) password, so gating the port doesn't solve provisioning a credential the customer can actually use to log in.
The VPN listener (1194/udp) and admin GUI (943/tcp) are raw ports, not a single HTTP surface — not reverse-proxy-friendly, though this alone is not blocking (wg-easy ships the same shape).
summary: OpenVPN Access Server is an actively maintained, well-documented product, but it fails our installability bar on the same structural point every time: the built-in admin account's password is auto-generated at first boot and only recoverable from container logs, with no env-var override and no hash-accepting API to set it via generated_from. That is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, which apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md treats as a hard blocker rather than a missing-algorithm gap to file against IF-1420. On top of that it overlaps with wg-easy's already-covered self-hosted-VPN niche and its free tier caps out at 2 concurrent connections. Recommend not_recommended rather than build_with_caveats or blocked_on_platform.

name: OpnForm
source_description: Open-source form builder with conditional logic, embeds, and response management
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (core), proprietary add-ons for Enterprise features (open-core model)
version_health_notes: Latest release v2.2.4 was 8 days before today (2026-08-05). Releases are frequent (v2.0.0 on 2026-06-08, v2.0.1 on 2026-06-12, v2.0.2 on 2026-06-25, v2.1.0 on 2026-06-30, v2.2.0/2.2.1/2.2.2 on 2026-07-14, v2.2.3/2.2.4 on 2026-07-28) — roughly weekly cadence over the last two months, clearly active development, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers form-building/data-collection. n8n covers workflow automation but has no purpose-built form UI, conditional logic, or response management. OpnForm would be a genuinely new category (Typeform/Google Forms alternative) for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Clear, distinct use case (forms, surveys, lead capture) with no overlap, but it ships as a 7-container stack (api, api-worker, api-scheduler, ui, redis, postgres, nginx ingress) — heavier operational footprint than most single-container recipes, and the free self-hosted tier caps at 2 total users (Enterprise license needed for more), which limits appeal for teams.

Admin account creation happens through an interactive first-visit setup wizard (customer sets their own email/password directly in OpnForm's own UI), the same pattern already used by n8n's recipe, so it needs no `generated_from` projection or Traefik `basic_auth` gate — installable today with just a domain. Caveats: it's a 7-container stack (Postgres + Redis + 3 Laravel/Nuxt processes + nginx ingress), needs `TRUSTED_PROXIES` configured correctly behind Traefik, and the free self-hosted tier is capped at 2 users, which may disappoint customers expecting team use. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building, but scope customer expectations around the user cap and budget for the heavier multi-service compose file.

name: OrangeHRM
source_description: Open-source HR platform for employee, leave, and recruitment management
upstream_license: GPL-3.0 (GPL-2.0-or-later prior to v5.6, converted to GPLv3 in v5.6)
version_health_notes: Verified via `api.github.com/repos/orangehrm/orangehrm/releases` (general web search results for this project were unreliable/ inconsistent about dates, so the raw API timestamps were used instead). v5.9 published 2026-06-28T23:46:59Z, ~5.5 weeks before this analysis (2026-08-05). Recent cadence: v5.6 (2024-01-28) -> v5.6.1 (2024-03-27, ~2mo) -> v5.7 (2024-07-19, ~4mo) -> v5.8 (2025-11-21, a ~16-month gap) -> v5.8.1 (2026-04-06, ~4.5mo) -> v5.9 (2026-06-28, ~3mo). The one long gap (mid-2024 to late-2025) is real, but the last three releases have landed on a normal 3-5 month rhythm and the repo shows continuous commit activity (7,900+ commits, dozens of open issues/PRs actively triaged), so this reads as active, not slowing or dormant. Docker Hub's orangehrm/orangehrm image tracks releases closely: 5.9/latest pushed the same day as the GitHub tag.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers HR/people-management (employee records, leave/time tracking, recruitment pipeline). The closest adjacent gap is apps-gaps/akaunting.yaml (business accounting), a different function entirely. OrangeHRM would open a genuinely new business-software category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: HR record-keeping (PII: salaries, leave, performance, applicant data) is a strong self-hosting/compliance draw for small-to-mid businesses, and the open-source "Starter" edition includes Employee Info, Leave, Time, and Recruitment modules out of the box, matching Hostinger's description exactly. The free edition is capped mainly by missing premium modules (Performance, Compensation, Surveys, an AI assistant) and by no REST API/payroll-connector access — those are paid-tier upsells, not artificial usage caps like Akaunting's BSL limits — so it remains a fully usable, unrestricted free product for its target audience (guidance suggests under ~50 employees).
blocking_issues:
A Traefik basic_auth gate (generated_from a hash of the customer's root password) can stop a random internet visitor from reaching the wizard before the customer does, but it does not solve the underlying problem: the wizard's DB-connection screen (host/port/ name/user/password) and admin-account screen both require values typed in by whoever completes it, and there is no channel today for install.sh to hand a server-generated DB password to "whoever that is" — the customer would have to invent their own DB credentials by hand, which the app's own MariaDB container was never told to expect. WIZARD_DB_CONNECTION and WIZARD_ADMIN_ACCOUNT are listed as required but have no expressible mechanism.

The official orangehrm/orangehrm image has no DB-config env vars at all — the Dockerfile (verified against github.com/orangehrm/orangehrm main branch) sets no ORANGEHRM_*/DB_* ENV and has no custom ENTRYPOINT/CMD; it's a bare php:8.3-apache image with the app code baked in. There is no install.sh-wireable channel for DB connection details, so `generated_from`/server-generated-secret projection onto a DB credential (as done for paperless-ngx-style apps) is not available for this image.

Docker Hub's own README says to "install OrangeHRM using the web installer" — this is the only documented setup path for the image. The browser wizard (Fresh Install) asks for BOTH the DB connection (host/port/name/user/password) AND the admin account in the same flow, unlike Uptime Kuma's wizard which only asks for the admin account. Whoever visits first fills in both; there's no server-side pre-fill of DB details and no way to gate only the admin-creation step, so a first-boot race lets a random visitor set the DB credentials and admin login together.

Two alternate non-wizard install paths exist and neither fits the current mechanism either: the deprecated installer/cli_install.php reads a static installer/cli_install_config.yaml that ships with a hardcoded default admin password (Ohrm@1423) and hardcoded default DB root/root credentials — usable only if the entire app sits behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (per SCHEMA.md's guidance on fixed/unchangeable default credentials), which is not how this analysis is currently scoped. The newer `php installer/console install:on-new-database` command explicitly refuses non-interactive execution (`if (!$input->isInteractive()) { ... return self::INVALID; }` in installer/Command/InstallOnNewDatabaseCommand.php), so it cannot be scripted by install.sh at all.

A viable path would be install.sh pre-generating installer/config/Conf.php directly from the Conf.tpl.php template (host/port/name/user/pass filled with a server-generated DB password) and running the DB migrations install.sh would otherwise leave to the wizard — but this bypasses the installer entirely, is not exercised by any upstream CI or documented flow, and would need to be re-validated against Conf.tpl.php's exact placeholder names and the migration invocation on every OrangeHRM release. That's a materially more fragile, unsupported-by-upstream mechanism, not a like-for-like match to the documented env-var pattern used for paperless-ngx.
summary: OrangeHRM ships as a single web container (orangehrm/orangehrm, PHP/ Apache) with no DB-config env vars and no scriptable installer: the Dockerfile bakes in the app code with no ENTRYPOINT, the browser-based web installer (the only path Docker Hub's README documents) asks for both DB connection details and the admin account in one first-visit wizard with no server-side pre-fill, the deprecated static-YAML CLI installer ships hardcoded default credentials (admin password Ohrm@1423, DB root/root) that would need a whole-app Traefik basic_auth gate to be acceptable, and the new interactive installer console command explicitly refuses non-interactive execution. None of these match the current `generated_from`/env-var projection mechanism used for paperless-ngx-style multi-container apps, and there's no channel today to hand the wizard a server-generated DB password before a customer (or an internet-facing race) reaches it. Pinned Docker tags exist and track releases closely, and the project remains actively released (last tag ~5.5 weeks old) despite one unusually long historical gap in 2024-2025, so this is not an EOL/version concern. It fills a real HR/people- management gap in the catalogue and would be worth building once install.sh can either drive the DB connection step of the wizard programmatically or pre-generate Conf.php directly — but as things stand today it is blocked on the installer having no scriptable, non-interactive DB-setup path.

name: Organizr
source_description: Homelab services organizer with tabbed access, user groups, and multi-auth
version_health_notes: Confusing two-eras situation. "V1" (the original PHP app, tagged releases like 1.90) was explicitly sunset by the maintainer on 2019-02-26 — the 1.90 release notes literally say "Update before FEB 28 to keep v1 working" and told users to pin to a v1-master branch if they didn't want to move to the V2 rewrite. That branch/version line has had no release in over 7 years and is dead. "V2" (current, on the `v2-master` branch) is where all activity now happens — last commit 2026-05-19, about 2.5 months before today (2026-08-05), with ongoing feature/security work (e.g. an SSRF-hardening commit). So the project is alive, but it has never cut a single tagged/versioned release for V2 in its ~7 years of existence — there is no "latest stable version" number to point to, only "whatever HEAD of v2-master is right now." Compounding this: the official `ghcr.io/organizr/organizr` Docker image is a thin Alpine/s6 wrapper that does not bundle the app at all — per its own README, "the preferred way to update organizr is to restart the container, as we grab the latest commit on startup" from whichever `branch` env var you set (default v2-master). That means even pinning the Docker image tag does not pin the app version: two customers deploying the same recipe on different days (or the same customer restarting their container) can silently get different app code with no version number attached to either. This is incompatible with this repo's "pin a specific, current stable tag, never :latest" convention, because there is no stable tag to pin — the mechanism has no concept of one.
differentiation: Same "front door" startpage/dashboard niche as five other already-analyzed candidates: homarr.yaml, heimdall.yaml, dashy.yaml, flame.yaml, and glance.yaml (mafl.yaml is the same niche too, already rated not_recommended). None of the current 24 shipped recipes are a bookmark/launcher dashboard, so the underlying gap is real, but Organizr would be the sixth candidate competing for the exact same catalogue slot with no other recipe yet built for it. Organizr's one distinguishing pitch versus the other five is tabbed iframe embedding of an app's own UI inside the dashboard (not just a link-out tile) plus built-in SSO against Plex/Emby/LDAP — a genuinely different feature set from Homarr/Dashy/Glance's tile-and-widget model, but that only matters if a customer already runs Plex/Emby/LDAP, which none of our 24 recipes provide.
usefulness_rationale: The startpage/dashboard slot is already thoroughly covered by higher- quality, better-versioned candidates (Homarr and Dashy are both build_now with active weekly/near-daily tagged releases). Organizr adds no capability those don't already offer for our customer base, its signature SSO integrations (Plex/Emby/LDAP) target a use case outside our current catalogue, and — separate from the redundancy — it cannot be version-pinned the way every other recipe in this repo is, which is a real cost independent of how many dashboard apps we already have candidates for.
blocking_issues: No stable, pinnable app version exists. Organizr's admin account is created through an in-browser setup wizard (choose SQLite/MySQL, create username/master password) rather than any env-var-settable login, so — like Homarr/Dashy/Glance — a Traefik basic_auth gate keyed off the customer's root-password hash is mechanically fine for the secrets side. But the app itself is fetched live from git at every container start regardless of which Docker tag is deployed (per upstream's own README), so this repo's "pin a specific current stable tag" convention has no valid target here — there is no tag that corresponds to a fixed, reproducible app version.
summary: Organizr is mechanically installable under the current secrets mechanism (Traefik basic_auth gate, same pattern as Homarr/Dashy/Glance), and the underlying v2-master branch is under active development (last commit ~2.5 months before this analysis). But it is a weak candidate on two independent grounds: it is the sixth already-analyzed app targeting the identical startpage/dashboard catalogue slot (after Homarr, Heimdall, Dashy, Flame, Glance, Mafl) with no clear advantage for our customer base over the strongest of those (Homarr, Dashy), and unlike all of them it has never cut a tagged release in ~7 years — the official Docker image pulls whatever the live git branch HEAD is at each container restart, so there is no version to pin, undermining the reproducibility every other recipe in this repo relies on. Recommend not_recommended: redundant niche plus a real, structural versioning gap, not just a preference call.

name: OSRM
source_description: OpenStreetMap routing engine with a built-in directions UI for self-hosting
version_health_notes: v26.8.0 published 2026-08-01, 4 days before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases confirm a steady cadence: v26.7.3 (2026-07-10), v26.7.1/v26.7.0 (2026-07-01), v26.6.x cluster (2026-06-03/04). Upstream automates a scheduled release on the 1st of every month (version format (YYYY-2000).M.patch) with additional patch releases landing between them. 9,000+ commits, active issue/PR triage, no archive notice. Clearly active, not slowing.
differentiation: No existing built recipe covers geospatial routing/directions. OSRM is a C++ routing engine over OpenStreetMap data (route, nearest, table/ matrix, match, trip, tile services) plus an official companion "osrm-frontend" (Leaflet-based directions map UI, ghcr.io/project-osrm/ osrm-frontend) that can front the backend's HTTP API. The bundled UI is the main differentiator from openrouteservice, an unbuilt gap-analysis candidate covering the same routing-API niche (apps-gaps/ openrouteservice.yaml) but with no web UI of its own — OSRM would be the version of that same idea with a turnkey directions frontend a customer can actually click around in, rather than an API-only service.
usefulness_rationale: Genuine self-host motivation (avoid per-request quotas/costs on Google/Mapbox/HERE directions APIs) and, unlike openrouteservice, ships a ready-to-use web UI. Held to medium rather than high because, same as openrouteservice, its real-world usefulness is gated by the OSM-extract problem below — a generic recipe can only serve whatever one region is baked in at build time, which will not match most customers' actual routing needs.
blocking_issues:
Neither osrm-routed (backend, API-only, default port 5000) nor osrm-frontend (UI, default port 9966) has any login of its own, so per SCHEMA.md the publicly-exposed frontend needs a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate. That gate credential is expressible today via generated_from/basic_auth, so this alone does not block installable_today.

osrm-backend ships with zero bundled map data — worse than openrouteservice, which at least ships a small default Heidelberg test extract. The operator must always supply an .osm.pbf for a specific region and run it through a multi-step CLI preprocessing pipeline (osrm-extract, then osrm-partition+osrm-customize for MLD or osrm-contract for CH) as separate one-shot container invocations before osrm-routed can serve anything. There is no channel today for a customer to choose their region/extract at install time (the same class of "no input field for a customer-chosen value" problem as openrouteservice, just with an extra manual build step on top). A recipe could still ship by baking one fixed default region (e.g. a single country) into install.sh and running the extract/partition/ contract pipeline during install, but that is a one-size-fits-nobody compromise, not a real per-customer configuration, and adds install time proportional to the baked-in region's size.

Two services to run (backend + frontend), with the frontend as the only one that needs public Traefik routing and the backend kept internal-only — mechanically fine, but combined with the extract/partition/contract preprocessing step this is a more involved compose setup than a typical single-container recipe.

Resource floor scales with the baked-in region size: osrm-contract/ osrm-partition RAM and disk usage for graph construction are meaningfully higher than a small extract (worth flagging for app_min_ram_mb/app_min_disk_mb sizing — e.g. a single mid-size country extract is modest, but there is no way to cap this per customer since the region is fixed at build time, not chosen by them).
summary: OSRM is an active, actively-released (monthly cadence) routing engine with no equivalent among the 24 built recipes, and it differentiates from the unbuilt openrouteservice gap-analysis candidate by shipping an official directions-map web UI (osrm-frontend) rather than being API-only. It has no login of its own, so both services need a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate — mechanically expressible today, so not structurally blocked. The real caveat, shared with and slightly worse than openrouteservice, is that osrm-backend ships with no bundled map data at all and requires a multi-step CLI preprocessing pipeline (extract/partition/contract) against a customer-chosen OSM region before it can serve a single route — something the current /compose mechanism cannot let a customer choose at install time. A recipe would have to bake in one fixed region, limiting who it is actually useful for out of the box. Recommend build_with_caveats: technically installable now via a fixed baked-in region, but flag the data-provisioning limitation and the added install-time preprocessing step before prioritizing it.

name: OTOBO
source_description: Open-source help desk and ITSM ticketing system with SLA and automation
version_health_notes: Two lines are under active security support in parallel: 11.0 (latest 11.0.17, released 2026-07-27, ~9 days before today 2026-08-05) and 10.1 (latest 10.1.18, also 2026-07-27). Monthly-ish patch cadence with frequent security fixes (e.g. 11.0.16 closed a CVE in April 2026). The prior 10.0 line reached EOL on 2026-01-01, so upstream does retire old minors on a published schedule — pin to 11.0.x, not 10.x. OTOBO is a 2019 community fork of ((OTRS)) Community Edition, maintained by Rother OSS GmbH; not to be confused with the original OTRS project (now proprietary under a different vendor) or other OTRS forks (Znuny) — RotherOSS/otobo is the correct upstream for the Hostinger "OTOBO" slug.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue covers help desk / ITSM ticketing — closest neighbors (gitea, opengist) are dev-tooling, not support workflows. OTOBO would open a genuinely new category: customer service ticketing, SLA tracking, and ITSM (CMDB, change management) for small teams that want an on-prem alternative to Zendesk/Freshdesk/OTRS SaaS.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for self-hosted help desk software, and OTOBO is a credible, actively-maintained option in that space. Usefulness is "medium" rather than "high" because the stack is heavy for a single-VM recipe (see installability) and the admin-onboarding blocker below means it can't ship as smoothly as our single-container or basic-auth-gated recipes today.
blocking_issues:
OTOBO's own documented production install path has no env-var or CLI hook to set the initial admin (root@localhost) agent password. The supported flow is the interactive web installer wizard (http://<host>/otobo/installer.pl), a multi-step, CSRF-tokened HTTP form flow that a human must complete in a browser — there is no env-var equivalent to project a `generated_from` root-password hash into it, unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN.

The one scriptable shortcut, `bin/docker/quick_setup.pl`, is documented by upstream as a dev/test-suite convenience, not a supported production path, and it auto-generates a random root@localhost password that it only prints to container stdout — there is no channel today for install.sh to read that value back out and no channel to hand the customer's own credential in instead.

Full stack (web, daemon, db/MariaDB, Elasticsearch, redis, optional nginx) is heavier than most current recipes — not a hard blocker but raises the min-spec bar and install-script complexity.
summary: OTOBO is an actively maintained, single-HTTP-port, Traefik-compatible ticketing/ITSM app that would fill a genuinely empty category in the catalogue. It is not installable today because the only two supported first-boot secret mechanisms (root-password-hash projection, Traefik basic_auth) have no way to reach OTOBO's admin account: the app's own installer requires a live interactive browser wizard, and its scripted shortcut only yields a self-generated password with no output channel. Revisit once there's either a way to run install.sh through the installer wizard headlessly (scripted HTTP form submission) or an OTOBO CLI command confirmed to accept a pre-hashed admin password directly.

There is no "local admin account" fallback the way Vaultwarden/n8n/Paperless-ngx have. Provisioning any of these requires the customer to first register an OAuth application with a third party (or stand up and configure their own OIDC IdP, e.g. Authentik/Authelia, which then has the exact same problem one level down) and hand back a client_id and client_secret — an external credential our `/compose` mechanism has no channel to accept today (per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's table: "Domain + OAuth app registration / third-party account linking" → no).

Traefik `basic_auth` cannot substitute here the way it does for login-less apps (Adminer, WUD): Outline does have its own login/account system, it's just entirely OAuth-backed, so gating the whole app behind basic_auth would sit in front of a UI that still can't complete first-run sign-in without a working OAuth/OIDC provider already configured.
summary: Outline (outline/outline) is an actively maintained, actively released (v1.9.2, 15 days old) self-hosted Notion/Confluence-style team wiki with real-time collaboration — a genuinely useful, currently-unfilled niche distinct from the lighter-weight an-otter-wiki candidate. It is blocked today because Outline has no built-in password login of any kind: every account, including the first admin, is provisioned through an external OAuth/OIDC identity provider (Slack, Google, Azure AD, Discord, or generic OIDC), which the customer must pre-register and whose client_id/client_secret our `/compose` mechanism has no channel to accept — this isn't a root-password hash and Traefik basic_auth doesn't help since Outline's own login flow still requires a working OAuth provider to complete. Recommend blocked_on_platform: worth revisiting if Outline ever ships a local-credentials auth mode, or once the platform gains a channel for customer-supplied third-party API/OAuth credentials.

But Overseerr's entire value proposition is a companion to a customer's own external Plex server plus Sonarr/Radarr instances — none of which are things AF provisions or manages — so even a healthy Overseerr would only be useful to a narrow slice of customers who already self-host a full media-server stack elsewhere.
usefulness_rationale: Independent of the EOL finding, the app only has value bolted onto an existing Plex/Sonarr/Radarr setup that AF does not provide, so its addressable share of our customer base is small; the archival makes the question moot regardless.
blocking_issues:
Upstream repo archived 2026-02-15 with an explicit "superseded by Seerr" notice and no future releases — not a candidate for a new recipe regardless of the auth question below.

First-run setup requires signing in with a Plex.tv account (OAuth- style token exchange against plex.tv), not an app-local admin password — there is no env var or setup field that accepts a plaintext or hashed customer-chosen credential, and root-password projection has no way to satisfy a third-party Plex account login. This is the same "OAuth / third-party account linking" blocker pattern documented in apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md, independent of the EOL issue.
summary: Overseerr is EOL: upstream archived the repository on 2026-02-15 (about 6 months before this analysis), shipped its final release the same day, and explicitly told users to migrate to a successor project ("Seerr"). Even setting that aside, Overseerr's first-run flow requires a Plex.tv account OAuth login rather than any customer-suppliable password, which has no expressible mechanism under the current root-password-projection or basic_auth model — a second, independent blocker. Recommend not_recommended: don't build on an archived, superseded upstream, and if the successor "Seerr" project is later worth evaluating, that needs its own gap analysis rather than being folded into this one.

name: Owncast
source_description: Self-hosted live streaming and chat server with RTMP and Fediverse support
version_health_notes: 0.2.5 shipped 2026-04-11, ~4 months before today (2026-08-05). History is bursty rather than steady: 0.2.0 (2025-01-11) and 0.2.1 (2025-01-17) landed 6 days apart, then a ~3.5 month gap to 0.2.2 (2025-05-03), a 7-day gap to 0.2.3 (2025-05-10), then an ~8 month gap to 0.2.4 (2026-01-10), then a 3 month gap to 0.2.5. Tagged releases are infrequent and irregular, but the project shows no archive/EOL notice, the repo has 150+ open issues and ~28 open PRs, and development continues on the `develop` branch between tags — read as a small-team OSS project maintained at a slow but real pace, not abandoned.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does live video ingest/broadcast. Two other live-streaming candidates have already been analyzed in this gap-analysis pass (ant-media-server-ce.yaml, mistserver.yaml) but neither overlaps functionally with Owncast: Ant Media targets WebRTC/low-latency conferencing-style delivery and MistServer is a developer-facing OTT ingest/transcode toolkit, whereas Owncast is a simple, single-purpose "run your own Twitch" app — RTMP ingest from OBS-style software, HLS playback, a built-in web chat, and optional Fediverse (ActivityPub) federation so followers on Mastodon etc. get notified when a stream starts. It would be a genuinely new catalogue category, and the simplest/most consumer-facing of the three streaming candidates analyzed so far.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand from creators/communities who want to self-host streaming instead of using Twitch/YouTube, and Owncast is dramatically simpler to operate than Ant Media or MistServer (single container, no transcode-farm concerns). Capped at medium rather than high because the audience (people who actively stream) is narrower than general self-hosting/productivity tools already in the catalogue, and getting real value requires the customer to already own streaming software (OBS or similar) and understand RTMP basics.
blocking_issues:
Owncast's admin password has no env-var or config-file input at container start. It can only be set two ways: a `-adminpassword` CLI flag (confirmed in the current `main.go` source) or an interactive login into the `/admin` web panel — both take the **plaintext** password directly, with Owncast hashing it internally. There is no field that accepts a pre-computed hash. Per SCHEMA.md this is the genuine "app requires the plaintext password, not any hash" case: `generated_from` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, so it structurally cannot reach this field — same category of blocker as Castopod's superadmin wizard.

The stream key (the credential the customer must type into OBS or similar software to publish video) is likewise only viewable/settable through the authenticated `/admin` panel after login — it is a value the customer genuinely needs to read and use, not a secret that stays server-side, so `server_generated_no_customer_input` does not apply either. Both default to the well-known value `abc123` out of the box.

Traefik `basic_auth` cannot substitute here the way it does for Adminer/n8n-style apps. Owncast's root path (`/`) is the public live-stream viewer page and chat — the entire point of the app is for anonymous visitors to watch without any login. Our `basic_auth` toggle gates the whole public port, not a specific path, so applying it to protect `/admin` would also lock out every viewer and defeat the app's purpose (the same reasoning that ruled out basic_auth for BroadcastChannel, an intentionally-public app).

Separately from the credential-input gap: core functionality needs a raw RTMP ingest port (1935, TCP) in addition to the HTTP port. This is not a blocker on its own — wg-easy and gitea already ship raw non-HTTP ports in this catalogue — but it does mean the app is not purely reverse-proxy-compatible.
summary: Owncast (official image `owncast/owncast:0.2.5`, MIT, sporadically but not abandoned-ly released) would add a genuinely new, simpler-than-the- alternatives live-streaming category to the catalogue with no overlap against the two other streaming candidates already analyzed. It fails installability today for a structural reason, not a soft one: both the admin password and the stream key are set via plaintext-only channels (a CLI flag or the authenticated admin UI), which `generated_from` cannot reach since it only ever carries a hash, and Traefik `basic_auth` can't substitute because it would gate the intentionally-public viewer page along with the admin panel. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit if the platform ever gains a plaintext-credential channel or a path-scoped auth gate, neither of which exists today.

Both the original brand and its fork are therefore live, separately maintained projects today — see the "ambiguous name" note below.

Syncthing (recipes/syncthing/) is P2P device-to-device sync with no server-side web UI or link sharing; Immich is media-specific; Paperless-ngx is scanned-document-specific. ownCloud (via Infinite Scale) would fill the same "self-hosted Google-Drive-alternative" niche already identified as a gap for Nextcloud (apps-gaps/nextcloud.yaml) and OpenCloud (apps-gaps/opencloud.yaml) — none of the three are actual recipes yet, so there is no catalogue overlap to reject on, but a human reviewer should be aware all three gap-analyses target the same customer need and likely only one (at most a couple) would get built, per this repo's build-bandwidth-is-a-later-decision stance.
usefulness_rationale: ownCloud is one of the most recognized names in self-hosted file sync/sharing, with a large existing install base and brand recognition comparable to Nextcloud. Infinite Scale in particular is a modern, single-binary/single-container deployment ("all batteries included: no external database, no external IDP needed") that is easy to stand up behind a reverse proxy.
summary: ownCloud Infinite Scale (owncloud/ocis, pin to a stable tag like 8.1.0, not :latest or the rolling floating tag) is a single container exposing its whole web UI + WebDAV/CS3 API on one HTTP port (9200), needs no external database or IDP for a basic deployment, and takes its only first-boot secret — ADMIN_PASSWORD for the built-in admin account — as a plain env var, a direct fit for generated_from root-password projection. Mechanically this is installable_today with no blockers. The caveat is strategic, not technical: ownCloud, Nextcloud, and OpenCloud (the last a literal 2025 fork of ownCloud's own Infinite Scale team) are three actively-developed products competing for the exact same "self-hosted file sync and sharing" customer need, and only ownCloud's own brand carries the added baggage of a recent ownership acquisition (Kiteworks, closed March 2025) and a team split that a customer researching the space will likely surface. Recommend build_with_caveats — worth building, but decide alongside (not instead of) the Nextcloud/OpenCloud gap-analyses rather than in isolation, since the catalogue only needs one or two of the three, not all.

So the project itself is active, it just batches source changes for a long time before cutting a tag/image — a real caveat for freshness of whatever image we'd pin, but not archived, maintenance-only, or EOL.

OwnTracks Recorder is the backend companion to the OwnTracks mobile app (iOS/Android): it ingests location pings from a customer's own phone and serves a live map + history via a small built-in web UI and REST API. summary: OwnTracks Recorder is a single-container app with no built-in authentication of its own — confirmed from upstream docs and community deployment guides, which uniformly rely on a fronting reverse proxy for HTTP Basic auth to protect both the map/API web UI and the `/pub` endpoint the phone app posts to. Run with `OTR_PORT=0` it needs no external MQTT broker either, so it fits our single-HTTP-port, Traefik-fronted pattern cleanly (same shape as Adminer/WUD): gate the one public port with `basic_auth: true`, with the password projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from`. The customer then configures the OwnTracks mobile app with that same domain and basic-auth credentials to start reporting location — a real setup step, but not a platform blocker. Version health is the main caveat: tagged releases and the published Docker image have gone quiet for about a year even though upstream source commits continue, so `installable_today` is true but the pinned image would already be a year stale on day one. Mechanically installable_today with no blockers. The caveat is about OxiCloud's own project maturity, not competing gap-analyses: it is roughly one year old (first tagged release 0.1.0-rc1 just over a year before this analysis), appears to be a single-maintainer-flavored project, and its Docker image still publishes under the maintainer's personal `diocrafts/oxicloud` namespace rather than an org-owned one — real bus-factor and long-term-support-responsiveness risk for a security-sensitive file-storage app, even though the release cadence is currently active and healthy. Paisa's differentiator is architectural, not functional: it is a thin web UI wrapped around the plaintext-accounting toolchain (ledger-cli by default, with hledger/beancount image variants), so the underlying data is a hand-editable ledger file rather than a database — appealing to a narrow "plaintext accounting" power-user niche (3.2k GitHub stars) rather than the mainstream consumer audience Firefly III/Actual Budget/Ghostfolio target.
usefulness_rationale: The personal-finance category already has three stronger, more actively developed candidates queued (Firefly III, Actual Budget, Ghostfolio) that together cover both of Paisa's selling points (double-entry bookkeeping and investment tracking) for a broader audience. Paisa adds a plaintext-accounting angle that is real but niche, and its upstream has slowed to maintenance-only with no new features in over a year, making it a weak addition relative to what's already on the list.
summary: Paisa is a single-container Go app (image ananthakumaran/paisa) exposing one HTTP port (7500) with data kept under a mounted volume, so it's mechanically reverse-proxy-compatible the same way Uptime Kuma is. It ships with no authentication configured out of the box — a user account is only created later, by hand, through the app's own Configuration page after the UI is already reachable — so there is no first-boot credential to inject via `generated_from`; the correct fit is a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate, the same pattern used for Ghostfolio and Adminer. That clears the /compose constraint with zero blocking issues, so it is mechanically installable today. The recommendation is nonetheless not_recommended: upstream release cadence has slowed to maintenance-only (latest tag is exactly 12 months old, with only build-fix commits since), and its feature set — double-entry accounting plus investment tracking — fully overlaps two already- queued, more actively developed candidates (Firefly III and Ghostfolio) that better serve the same customer need for a broader audience.

name: Pangolin Newt
source_description: Userspace WireGuard tunnel client for secure remote access via Pangolin
upstream_license: Dual-licensed: AGPL-3.0 or Fossorial Commercial License
version_health_notes: Latest release (1.15.0) shipped 2026-07-19, about 2.5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases: 1.14.0 (2026-07-02), 1.13.0 (2026-06-10), 1.12.5 (2026-05-08) — a roughly monthly cadence with substantive feature work each time (native WireGuard mode, SSH/RDP/VNC browser gateway, auto-update, SIGHUP config reload). Fossorial, the company behind Newt/Pangolin, is a 2025 Y Combinator company; this is a young, fast-moving, actively-funded project, not dormant.
differentiation: Newt is not a standalone VPN server the way recipes/wg-easy/ is — it is a headless client that dials out from the customer's network to an already-running Pangolin control-plane server (either the fosrl-hosted app.pangolin.net or a self-hosted Pangolin instance the customer already operates elsewhere) and only becomes useful once paired with that server. Pangolin itself (the server side: identity-aware tunneled reverse proxy, admin UI, site/resource management) is not in our catalogue at all and is a materially different, heavier app than Newt. Shipping Newt alone gives a customer a client with nothing to connect to unless they already run Pangolin elsewhere, which is a much narrower and more confusing value proposition than wg-easy's self-contained "stand up a VPN server with a web UI" story.
usefulness_rationale: Newt only has value to a customer who already runs (or is simultaneously being sold) a separate Pangolin server. As an isolated recipe it is a background daemon with no UI and nothing to configure beyond credentials issued by that external server — not something a customer would install on its own from an app catalogue browse.
blocking_issues:
NEWT_ID and NEWT_SECRET are not customer-chosen credentials — they are opaque tokens minted by a specific Pangolin server instance (self-hosted or app.pangolin.net) when the customer creates a 'site' there, then copy-pasted into Newt's config. There is no mechanism today for /compose to accept an arbitrary customer-supplied external value (this is the same class of gap as an external API key or OAuth token, per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md) — root-password projection and Traefik basic_auth don't apply because neither NEWT_ID nor NEWT_SECRET is a password Newt itself authenticates a user with; they're issued by a third-party system we don't control.
PANGOLIN_ENDPOINT (the URL of the customer's Pangolin server) is also a required, customer-specific, non-derivable value with no input channel today.
Newt has no web UI and exposes no HTTP port of its own — it is an outbound-only client, so it isn't reverse-proxy-fronted the way our other recipes are; Traefik has nothing to sit in front of.
summary: Newt (fosrl/newt) is an actively-maintained (monthly releases, most recently 2026-07-19), young but well-funded userspace WireGuard client built to pair exclusively with Pangolin, a separate identity-aware tunneled-reverse-proxy server that is not itself in our catalogue. Structurally it fails our installability bar in two independent ways: every value it needs at first boot (NEWT_ID, NEWT_SECRET, PANGOLIN_ENDPOINT) is minted by an external Pangolin server the customer must already operate, with no channel for /compose to carry such arbitrary external values today; and it has no web UI or HTTP port at all, so there is nothing for Traefik to front. Even if the input-channel gap were solved, Newt alone has little standalone customer value — it is a companion client, not an app. Recommend not_recommended; if Fossorial's Pangolin server itself were proposed as a candidate, that would need a separate gap analysis and would still hit the same external-credential problem for its own first admin account or license activation, so it is not an automatic yes either.

name: Paperclip
source_description: Paperclip is an AI/ML orchestration platform for autonomous teams
version_health_notes: ~2 weeks since the latest release as of 2026-08-05 (v2026.722.0, 2026-07-22), consistent with the project's observed cadence of a tagged release every 1-2 weeks since its public launch (v2026.525.0, 2026-05-25). Project is very young (~5 months old) but growing fast (75.7k GitHub stars, 14.1k forks, 3,480 commits, 453K image pulls) with active commit and release activity — no sign of slowing. The official container registry (ghcr.io/paperclipai/paperclip) only publishes `latest`, `buildcache`, and `sha-<commit>` tags rather than tags matching the named releases above, so a real recipe would need to pin to a specific `sha-<commit>` rather than a clean semver-looking tag.
differentiation: Unlike hermes-agent and openclaw, which each run a single AI agent against messaging apps, Paperclip is a meta-orchestrator that sits above multiple agent runtimes at once (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or arbitrary HTTP bots) and coordinates them via an org chart with roles, reporting lines, per-agent budgets, and an audit trail — closer to a fleet-management console than a single agent. It's not a workflow engine like n8n either (no node-based flow builder); its unit of work is an autonomous agent with a role, not a wired-together pipeline.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiator for a customer already running several AI agents and wanting governance/budget/audit across them, but that's a narrower and more advanced audience than hermes-agent/openclaw's "run one agent against Telegram" use case. Popularity (75k+ stars) is a strong signal of interest but the project is only ~5 months old, so durability of that interest is unproven.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: POSTGRES_PASSWORD; BETTER_AUTH_SECRET; dashboard basic-auth gate credential
blocking_issues:
Paperclip's own admin account is created through a first-run web signup (name/email/password entered in the UI), not through an env var the recipe can populate at container start — so there is no metadata parameter to project a `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` hash into, unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN. Left ungated, the first visitor to reach the instance after boot could claim the admin account. Recommend the Traefik `basic_auth: true` pattern already used for hermes-agent's dashboard as the practical gate, even though Paperclip technically has its own (just not-boot-time-settable) login — same precedent, applied to a slightly different shape of problem.

Functioning agents need at least one LLM provider API key (Anthropic/OpenAI/OpenRouter/etc.), which has no customer-supplied input channel today. This does not block *installability* — like hermes-agent and openclaw, Paperclip boots and is reachable/loggable into with zero agents configured, and the customer adds provider keys post-provision via the authenticated dashboard's Connections UI — but it does mean the app is inert out of the box until the customer brings their own key.

Name/ecosystem note: search results surfaced numerous GitHub repos across unrelated accounts (Made-By-Adem/paperclipai-docker, penclipai/paperclip-cn, osodevops/docker-paperclip, operator888/paperclip, codingmatty/paperclip-ai, agencyenterprise/paperclip-ai) all carrying the identical tagline "Open-source orchestration for zero-human companies" as unofficial Docker packaging/mirrors of the same project. The canonical upstream is confirmed as github.com/paperclipai/paperclip (75.7k stars, MIT, Paperclip Labs, Inc.) — a recipe should pull from ghcr.io/paperclipai/paperclip only, never from any of these third-party mirrors.
summary: Paperclip is a legitimate, MIT-licensed, actively-developed (weekly-ish releases) multi-agent orchestration platform with a single reverse-proxy- friendly web UI (Node.js server + Postgres), genuinely differentiated from our existing hermes-agent/openclaw/n8n recipes by its org-chart/governance layer over multiple agent runtimes at once. It's installable today — server-generated secrets cover the DB/auth secrets, and a Traefik basic_auth gate can stand in for the fact that Paperclip's own admin login isn't settable via env at boot — and it works with zero LLM provider keys configured, with the customer adding their own via the dashboard after first login. Caveats: the project is only ~5 months old with an unproven long-term trajectory despite fast early growth, the official image only ships `latest`/`sha-*` tags rather than clean version tags to pin against, and the audience (teams already running several AI agents) is narrower than most of our current catalogue.

name: Papermerge
source_description: Open-source document management system for scanning, OCR, and organizing PDFs
version_health_notes: No tagged stable release since 3.5.3 (2025-08-18) — about 12 months as of today (2026-08-05). Development has continued in the open in the meantime as an unreleased 3.6.0 alpha line (tags up to 3.6.0a16, last pushed to Docker Hub ~7 months ago, i.e. ~Jan 2026), including new `-oidc` image variants. Repo itself is not archived and shows commits as recently as March 2026, so the project is active, just slow to cut a new stable tag. Not EOL, but the stable line is aging and a recipe pinned to 3.5.3 would be a year behind the project's own alpha work.
differentiation: Papermerge offers group ownership/sharing, hierarchical folders (vs. paperless-ngx's flat tag model), and custom metadata fields with a REST API. Functionally it covers the same job as paperless-ngx (scan, OCR, index, search PDFs) with no capability paperless-ngx lacks for a typical customer, and paperless-ngx already has a purpose-built AI companion (paperless-ai) in the catalogue that Papermerge has no equivalent to.
usefulness_rationale: Near-total feature overlap with paperless-ngx, which is roughly two orders of magnitude larger by community size (~44k GitHub stars vs. Papermerge's ~400-500) and already in our catalogue alongside its AI companion. Papermerge adds no capability a customer choosing a document scanning/OCR app would miss from the existing option.
summary: Papermerge is a competent, single-container-plus-Postgres-and-Redis document management/OCR app that would be mechanically installable today — its admin login password can be derived from the customer's root password (generated_from_root_password), while the app secret key and DB password can be server-generated with no customer input, the same pattern already used by the paperless-ngx recipe, with no external API keys or OAuth needed. The blocker is fit, not mechanism: it duplicates paperless-ngx almost feature-for-feature while being far smaller, slower to release (no stable tag in ~12 months, still on an unreleased 3.6.0 alpha), and less battle-tested. Not recommended while paperless-ngx already covers this niche.

name: Papra
source_description: Minimalistic open-source document management and archiving platform
version_health_notes: Papra uses a calendar-flavored version scheme (26.5.0, 26.6.0, 26.6.1). 26.5.0 shipped 2026-06-07, 26.6.0 on 2026-07-02, and 26.6.1 on 2026-07-04 — three releases in about 8 weeks, roughly monthly minor releases with same-week patch follow-ups. Latest release is ~1 month before today (2026-08-05). Repo has 5.1k stars, 1,085+ commits, 132 open issues and 32 open PRs, no archive notice — a young but clearly active project shipping regularly, not a maintenance-only or dormant codebase.
differentiation: Directly competes with paperless-ngx (currently `enabled: false`, pending its own UAT) on the core pitch — self-hosted document archiving with full-text search and tagging. The differentiation is architectural rather than feature-based: paperless-ngx is a multi-service stack (Django app + Postgres + Redis + Gotenberg + Tika, ~2GB RAM minimum) whereas Papra is a single container with an embedded SQLite-backed data dir and no required external services — a meaningfully lighter operational footprint for the same customer need. It also adds AI-assisted auto-tagging and OCR/text-extraction out of the box, which paperless-ngx only gets via the separate paperless-ai companion recipe (also disabled, and itself dependent on a running paperless-ngx instance). A customer choosing between the two would pick Papra for simplicity/lower resource use and paperless-ngx for its larger ecosystem/maturity (2.x release line, much larger community) — genuine overlap, not a clear "why not both" case.
usefulness_rationale: Document archiving is a proven self-hosting use case (evidenced by paperless-ngx + paperless-ai already existing in-catalogue), so demand is real. Capped at medium rather than high because it's a second entry covering ground paperless-ngx already covers — value here is offering a lighter-weight alternative, not opening a new category, and paperless-ngx's larger, more established ecosystem may already satisfy most of this demand once it clears UAT.
summary: Papra (official image `ghcr.io/papra-hq/papra:26.6.1-rootless`, AGPL-3.0) is an actively developed, single-container document-archiving app with no external service dependencies (embedded SQLite + local/S3 file storage) and a standard first-user-becomes-admin registration flow — the same self-serve-signup pattern already shipping in the n8n and Immich recipes, needing no customer credential to be projected through our compose mechanism. The only boot-time secret, `AUTH_SECRET`, is a patternless random value the platform can generate server-side and the customer never needs to read. It is mechanically installable today with no blockers. The open question is prioritization, not mechanism: it overlaps meaningfully with the already-in-catalogue (if currently disabled) paperless-ngx/paperless-ai pairing, differentiated mainly by a much lighter resource footprint. Recommend `build_now` on its own technical merits, while flagging the overlap for a human to weigh against paperless-ngx's UAT timeline and existing ecosystem maturity.

name: Para
source_description: Open-source backend framework with REST API for object persistence and search
version_health_notes: 1.54.7 was tagged 2026-06-04, roughly 2 months before today (2026-08-05) — well within normal cadence for this project. Releases over the preceding months (1.54.6 on 2026-06-03, 1.54.5 on 2026-05-05, 1.54.4/1.54.3 on 2026-04-28, 1.54.1 on 2026-04-24, 1.54.0 on 2026-04-20, 1.53.0 on 2026-03-24, 1.52.5 on 2026-02-13) show a steady multi-release-per-month pace including recent feature work (1.54.0 added an MCP server implementation based on Spring AI). Repo has 2,100+ commits, single primary maintainer (albogdano / Erudika) still actively pushing Docker Hub builds (`latest` tag updated within the last few days as of research). Not archived, not EOL, not slowing.
differentiation: Para is a headless backend-as-a-service framework — it stores arbitrary JSON objects, auto-indexes and makes them searchable, and exposes that through a signed REST API (AWS Signature V4-style request signing, plus JWT and access/secret key auth). It ships no end-user-facing screens at all; you talk to it exclusively via API calls or one of its client SDKs (JS, Java, PHP, C#, Android, iOS). Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a bare backend framework in this sense — every existing recipe is a complete, self-contained end-user application with its own UI (password manager, photo library, notes, monitoring dashboard, etc.). Para is infrastructure for a developer to build a *different* app on top of, not an app a customer installs and immediately uses.
usefulness_rationale: The AF catalogue targets self-hosters who want a working application reachable at a domain, not a bare BaaS layer that only becomes useful once someone writes custom client code against it. A customer who deploys Para gets an empty JSON store with no screens to look at — there is no comparable "why would I install this standalone" case the way there is for every other recipe. It would fit a developer-platform or PaaS-adjacent catalogue, not this consumer/prosumer self-hosted-app catalogue.
summary: Para is a single-container Java/Spring app (image erudikaltd/para, latest stable 1.54.7) listening on one HTTP port (8080), embedding H2 + Lucene by default so it needs no external database or search cluster to boot — mechanically it would sit behind Traefik like any other recipe. Its only first-boot secret is `para.app_secret_key`, a signing key for its "root app" that Para itself never requires a customer to choose — it can be generated server-side with no customer input, the same pattern used for other apps' JWT/session-signing secrets — so there is no structural blocker under the current /compose mechanism. Upstream is unambiguously active (multi-release-per-month cadence, feature work as recent as April 2026). The recommendation is not_recommended purely on fit: Para is a headless backend framework with no web UI and no standalone end-user value — a customer installs it to write a custom app against its REST API, which is a different product category from every app currently in the catalogue and a poor match for a self-hosted-app storefront aimed at people who want a finished application, not a library to build one.

name: Parse Server
source_description: Open-source mobile app backend with REST, GraphQL, auth, and push notifications
version_health_notes: ~3 weeks since the latest release (9.10.0, 2026-07-13) as of 2026-08-05. Repo is one of the most established projects in the open-source-BaaS space (spun out of the original Parse.com shutdown in 2016), still receiving frequent releases (security fixes for GraphQL schema disclosure and file-upload validation shipped in this very release) and active PR/commit traffic on both `release` and `alpha` branches. No sign of slowing or abandonment.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue offers a Backend-as-a-Service for mobile/web app developers (REST + GraphQL data API, user auth, push notifications, cloud functions, file storage). Closest neighbors are gitea/opengist (developer tooling) but those are source hosting, not an app backend. A customer building a mobile or web app who wants to self-host their own BaaS instead of Firebase/Supabase would use this; nobody else in the catalogue serves that need.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely differentiated and the project is mature/stable, but Parse Server itself has no web UI at all — it's a pure REST/GraphQL API server, so on its own it's only useful to a customer who is also writing application code against it (a narrower, more technical audience than most of our self-contained-app recipes). The optional companion, Parse Dashboard, adds a web UI for managing classes/data/users and would be the natural pairing to make this feel like a complete "recipe" rather than a bare API endpoint.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: PARSE_SERVER_MASTER_KEY; PARSE_SERVER_APPLICATION_ID; MONGO database credentials; PARSE_DASHBOARD_USER_PASSWORD
blocking_issues:
Parse Server has no web UI of its own — it is a bare REST/GraphQL API with no login screen to gate at all. Shipping it alone (no dashboard) means there is nothing for Traefik `basic_auth` to usefully protect beyond the raw API surface, and no interactive way for a customer to confirm the instance is alive/working after provisioning, which is a weak recipe experience even though it isn't a hard installability blocker (masterKey already gates all data access at the API layer).

If Parse Dashboard is bundled to give the recipe a real web UI, its admin login (PARSE_DASHBOARD_USER_ID / PARSE_DASHBOARD_USER_PASSWORD) is settable via env vars at container start, so USER_ID could be fixed (e.g. "admin") and USER_PASSWORD projected via `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` — same pattern as Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN. This is not a blocker, just extra scope beyond a bare Parse Server recipe.
summary: Parse Server is a mature (10 years old), actively maintained, Apache-2.0 BaaS for mobile/web apps with no equivalent in our current catalogue — genuine differentiation. All secrets it needs (master key, app ID, DB credentials) can be server-generated with no customer input, so it is installable today as a bare API-only recipe. The catch is that on its own it has no web UI and nothing for a customer to click through after provisioning; the recipe would be far more useful (and demo-able) paired with Parse Dashboard, whose admin login maps cleanly onto the generated_from root-password mechanism. Recommend building with Parse Dashboard included rather than as a bare Parse Server instance.

name: Parseable
source_description: Open-source observability data lake for logs, metrics, and traces
upstream_docker_image: quay.io/parseablehq/parseable (also mirrored on Docker Hub as parseable/parseable)
version_health_notes: v2.9.5 shipped 2026-07-22, ~2 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Recent history shows a steady near-weekly cadence: v2.9.4 (2026-07-11), v2.9.3 (2026-06-27), v2.9.2 (2026-06-23), v2.9.1 (2026-06-16), v2.9.0 (2026-06-13), v2.8.0 (2026-05-28). No signs of slowing, maintenance-only status, or archival.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers a logs/metrics/traces data lake. Uptime Kuma (our only monitoring recipe) is a lightweight up/down status checker, a different niche entirely. Parseable would let a customer running other AF apps (n8n, Immich, Gitea, etc.) centralize ingestion and querying of logs/metrics/traces with a built-in web console, single Rust binary, columnar on-disk/S3 storage. Same broad niche already covered on the gap-analysis side by openobserve.yaml and grafana-loki.yaml (neither built yet), so this is one of several competing candidates for the same observability slot rather than a unique gap — see CLAUDE.md note that catalogue overlap between candidates is not itself a reason to reject one.
usefulness_rationale: Observability/log-aggregation is a real, recurring self-host need with no representative in the shipped catalogue, and Parseable's single-binary/single-container local-storage mode keeps the resource floor low. It's a developer/ops-facing tool rather than a broad-appeal consumer app, and most of its value depends on pointing other services' log/metric shippers at it after install — setup work outside what the recipe itself provisions.
blocking_issues:
Parseable has its own mandatory built-in login (HTTP Basic Auth against P_USERNAME / P_PASSWORD, default admin/admin) that gates the entire console and API — there is no way to use the app without authenticating to it directly, so a Traefik basic_auth gate cannot substitute for it (same shape as apps-gaps/openobserve.yaml).

P_PASSWORD is read by the container as a plaintext credential set directly via env var at startup — the app does not accept a pre-computed hash in any algorithm. Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md this is the genuine-plaintext case: generated_from only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel to populate this variable with a customer-meaningful value today.
summary: Parseable is an actively maintained (near-weekly releases, latest v2.9.5 from 2026-07-22), single-binary/single-container Rust observability data lake with a genuine web console and no equivalent already shipped in the 24-recipe catalogue. It is otherwise mechanically simple to deploy behind Traefik (one public HTTP port for local-storage mode, local-disk or S3 backing storage), but its own mandatory admin login only accepts a plaintext P_PASSWORD env var at startup, which the current /compose mechanism has no channel to supply (generated_from projects a hash, not plaintext, and a basic_auth gate can't substitute for a login the app itself enforces). Structurally identical blocker to apps-gaps/openobserve.yaml; revisit as build_now once a plaintext-password (or app-side hash support) projection channel exists.

name: Passbolt
source_description: Open-source team password manager with end-to-end OpenPGP encryption and sharing
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (CE) + commercial license for Pro/Enterprise-only features
version_health_notes: 5.14.0-1-ce pushed to Docker Hub ~20 hours before this analysis (2026-08-05), preceded by 5.13.0-1-ce about 22 days earlier — a steady monthly-ish CE release cadence. Repo is not archived and shows ongoing commit activity. Actively maintained by Passbolt SA.
differentiation: Passbolt targets team/organizational credential sharing with granular per-user, per-group, per-resource permissions and an admin-managed directory of users, whereas Vaultwarden (a Bitwarden-protocol reimplementation) is oriented around individual vaults with simpler org-sharing. Passbolt's auth model is fundamentally different too: it's OpenPGP keypair-based (each user generates their own keypair in the browser extension) rather than a master-password-derived encryption key, which the CE edition markets as end-to-end encrypted team credential sharing rather than personal vault sync.
usefulness_rationale: There is genuine differentiation from Vaultwarden for a team/business use case (shared folders, per-resource ACLs, admin user directory), so this isn't pure duplication. But it comes with a materially heavier onboarding flow (GPG keypair setup per user, browser extension dependency, admin-driven invite-by-email) that is a poor fit for the single-tenant self-host customer profile the rest of the catalogue targets, which caps the practical value below "high."
secrets_required_at_first_boot: DATASOURCES_DEFAULT_PASSWORD; SECURITY_SALT; PASSBOLT server GPG keypair passphrase; EMAIL_TRANSPORT_DEFAULT_USERNAME / EMAIL_TRANSPORT_DEFAULT_PASSWORD (SMTP relay credentials, needed to deliver the first-admin invite email); first-admin registration (email/name via `bin/cake passbolt register_user`, no password field)
blocking_issues:
Passbolt has no server-side admin password field at all — there is no login form our `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` mechanism can project a hash into. Authentication is OpenPGP-keypair based: each user (including the first admin) generates their own personal GPG keypair client-side in the browser extension during setup, choosing their own passphrase interactively. This is not a server-known secret of any kind, hashed or plaintext — there is nothing for af-api to derive from the customer's root password.

Creating the first admin user is a manual, out-of-band step (`docker exec passbolt bin/cake passbolt register_user -u <email> -f <first> -l <last> -r admin`) that produces a single-use registration URL. Completing setup requires that URL to reach the admin, normally via an outbound SMTP relay the customer must supply (EMAIL_TRANSPORT_DEFAULT_HOST/USERNAME/PASSWORD) — an externally sourced credential with no projection mechanism today, the same class of blocker recorded for apps-gaps/bitwarden.yaml's admin-login-by-email flow. Without SMTP (or a manual operator pulling the URL from container logs, which is not part of the automated install.sh model), first boot cannot reach a working admin account at all.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` does not solve the above — that pattern only substitutes for a missing *app-level* login, but here the blocker is that no admin account can be provisioned in the first place without SMTP or manual intervention, independent of whether the app sits behind an extra auth gate.
summary: Passbolt is an actively maintained (monthly CE release cadence, latest 5.14.0-1-ce pushed 2026-08-05), reverse-proxy-compatible web app that adds genuine team-sharing differentiation over recipes/vaultwarden/, so it isn't pure duplication. It is not installable under the current mechanism, however: its OpenPGP-keypair auth model has no server-side password field for `generated_from` to project into, and provisioning the first admin account requires either a customer-supplied SMTP relay (to deliver a single-use invite link) or manual CLI intervention — neither of which our automated install.sh / `/compose` flow supports today. Revisit as blocked_on_platform if/when the platform gains an SMTP-relay input channel or an alternative admin-bootstrap path; not a candidate to build now.

name: Password Pusher
source_description: Self-hosted secret sharing with one-time, expiring links for passwords and files
