Project has run since well before 2020 and continues shipping new features (e.g. "Auto-dispatch" email delivery added in v2.9.0) as well as a self-hosted "Pro" tier, both signs of an actively maintained, commercially backed OSS project rather than maintenance-only.
differentiation: Distinct from Vaultwarden (long-term password vault for the customer's own credentials) — Password Pusher is a one-shot, expiring-link mechanism for handing a secret (password, file, or URL) to a third party who does not have an account on the instance. No existing recipe in the catalogue covers ephemeral secret/file sharing.
usefulness_rationale: Useful, narrow-purpose tool (onboarding credentials, one-off file drops) that a subset of customers — IT/ops teams, agencies handing off client credentials — would value; not a broad-appeal app like a password manager or dashboard, so demand is likely lower-volume than top-tier catalogue entries.
summary: Password Pusher is a single-container (SQLite-backed), single-HTTP-port app with no mandatory login of its own — anonymous push creation/viewing is the default behavior — so it fits the recipe mechanism cleanly via a Traefik basic_auth gate on the whole app, exactly the pattern already used for n8n/Immich/Open WebUI. Upstream is actively released (multiple tags in the last month, security fixes still landing) and Apache-2.0 licensed. It fills a real gap (ephemeral secret/file sharing) with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue; the optional multi-user "admin dashboard" feature requires a shell-exec + email-reset flow to provision (no automated channel), but that's a non-required bonus feature, not a blocker for shipping the core app. Recommend build_now.

name: Pastefy
source_description: Pastefy is a self-hosted pastebin for secure code snippet sharing
version_health_notes: 7.2.6 shipped 2026-06-01, roughly 2 months before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases in the same run — 7.2.5/7.2.4/7.2.3 also on 2026-06-01, 7.2.2 on 2026-05-31, 7.2.1 on 2026-03-18, 7.2.0/7.1.7 on 2026-03-17, 7.1.6 on 2026-03-01, 7.1.5 on 2025-10-15 — show a steady multi-release cadence with feature work as recent as the latest batch (AI-assisted summaries/comments, i18n for 17 languages). Not archived, not EOL, not slowing.
differentiation: Pastefy is a MySQL/MariaDB-backed pastebin with rich file-type previews (Markdown, Mermaid, SVG, CSV, GeoJSON, diff, calendar), paste forking, folders, an API, and optional AI-generated summaries/comments (via a customer-supplied Anthropic API key). OpenGist — already in the catalogue but currently `enabled: false` — covers the same "self-hosted Gist/pastebin" niche with a Git-backed storage model and SSH clone support, which Pastefy does not offer. The two are close substitutes aimed at the same "share a code snippet" use case; Pastefy's edge is richer previews and forking, OpenGist's is Git-native storage and SSH access.
usefulness_rationale: Standalone pastebins are a real, recognizable self-hosted-app category and Pastefy has a clean single-page web UI, so it clears the "would a customer want this on its own" bar. But it directly overlaps an existing catalogue entry (OpenGist) for the same job, and — see installability below — Pastefy's account/admin system only works through third-party OAuth, which our platform cannot provision for a customer today. Without OAuth it degrades to a fully open, anonymous, unauthenticated paste box with no working admin panel, which is a materially weaker product than what upstream actually ships.
blocking_issues:
Pastefy has no local username/password login of its own — the only documented login mechanism is OAuth2 (InteraApps, Google, GitHub, Discord, Twitch) or a custom OIDC provider, each requiring an externally-registered client ID/secret. There is no input channel for that today.
The admin panel (/admin) is reached by manually editing the `type` column to `ADMIN` in the `pastefy_users` table via direct MySQL access — this presupposes a user account already exists, which itself requires OAuth. With no OAuth provider configured, no accounts (and therefore no admin) can ever be created; the app runs as a fully open, anonymous pastebin with nothing to gate access except a Traefik basic-auth wrapper we add ourselves.
Optional AI summary/comment features require a customer-supplied AI_ANTHROPIC_TOKEN (external API key) — no input channel for that either, so this feature would have to ship permanently disabled.
summary: Pastefy is mechanically simple to ship: single web container (interaapps/pastefy, pin 7.2.6) plus a MariaDB sidecar, one HTTP port behind Traefik, domain-only to boot, upstream is unambiguously active. But its entire account/admin system is gated behind third-party OAuth registration, which the current /compose mechanism cannot supply — so without OAuth the app has no logins, no admin panel, and no owner control at all, leaving Traefik `basic_auth` as the only expressible access gate. It would ship as a degraded, feature-stripped version of what upstream actually offers, and it overlaps an existing (if currently disabled) catalogue entry, OpenGist, covering the same "share a code snippet" use case. Recommend `build_with_caveats` only if the overlap with OpenGist and the OAuth-less degraded mode are explicitly accepted; otherwise this is a good re-candidate once OAuth-app registration gets an input channel.

name: PatchMon
source_description: Self-hosted Linux patch management and fleet monitoring platform

Before that, 1.4.0 (2026-02-13) and 1.4.2 (2026-02-20) landed compliance scanning, OIDC/SSO, and a web SSH terminal. As of today (2026-08-05) it has been just over 3 months since 2.0.2 with no newer tag, but the cadence across the preceding six months (multiple releases roughly every 2-6 weeks) reads as actively developed, not slowing.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes does OS-level Linux/FreeBSD/Windows package patch management. Uptime Kuma covers uptime/service monitoring, not patching, and WUD (What's Up Docker) tracks container *image* update availability, not OS packages on the host. PatchMon gives a customer a fleet-wide view of pending OS updates, patch policies (immediate / maintenance-window / delayed), and compliance scanning (OpenSCAP/Docker Bench) across any number of their own Linux servers via a lightweight outbound-only agent — a genuinely new capability for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: High value for a customer who runs multiple servers and wants central patch visibility/compliance; lower value for a customer whose only infrastructure is the single VPS running the recipe itself, since the interesting payoff (fleet-wide patching) only shows up once other hosts are enrolled as agents against it.
summary: PatchMon ships as a single web app (Go server with embedded React UI, port 3000) behind Postgres 17 and Redis 7, with an optional bundled guacd container for its web SSH terminal feature — a four-container stack comparable in shape to paperless-ngx/n8n, and it works fine behind Traefik on a single HTTP(S)+WSS port. Like n8n, the app itself has no pre-provisioned admin login: the first visitor to the web UI creates an arbitrary admin username/password with no customer-value channel today, so it needs the same Traefik basic_auth:true gate (password projected from the customer's root password via generated_from) as the actual auth boundary in front of the app's own setup wizard. Postgres/Redis passwords and the JWT signing secret are all patternless secrets the server can generate itself, with no customer-facing value. OIDC/SSO and AI-assistant API keys are optional, added post-deployment through the UI, not required at first boot. Nothing today blocks shipping this as a recipe; recommend building it, noting the differentiated fleet-patching use case is strongest for multi-server customers.

name: Paymenter
source_description: Open-source billing and subscription management platform for hosting companies
version_health_notes: v1.5.7 published 2026-07-25, ~11 days before this analysis (2026-08-05). Prior releases (v1.5.4 through v1.5.6) landed roughly every 2-4 weeks through June-July 2026, a steady active cadence. Repo is not archived, ghcr.io/paymenter/paymenter image is actively pushed alongside tagged releases, and recent releases include ongoing security fixes (e.g. GHSA-5gmm-hjfj-8ff7 in v1.5.7, CVE-2026-55219 in v1.5.5), indicating a maintained project responding to its own vulnerability reports.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes address billing, invoicing, or subscription/order management for a hosting or SaaS business — the closest adjacent tools (n8n for workflow automation, portainer for container ops) don't overlap functionally. Paymenter would be a net-new category: a client portal + invoicing + product/order management + payment-gateway (Stripe/PayPal) system aimed at customers who resell hosting or subscriptions themselves.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely new ground for the catalogue with a plausible customer (hosting resellers, small SaaS operators), but it's a narrower business-vertical tool than most of the current general-purpose self-host catalogue, and its usefulness is gated on a working payment-gateway integration (Stripe/PayPal), which itself needs an external API key our platform has no channel for today (see installability below) — so even a customer who wants it can't finish setup without manually entering that key themselves post-install.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: MYSQL/MariaDB root and app passwords; APP_KEY (Laravel encryption key); admin username, email, and password (via interactive `php artisan app:user:create`); payment gateway API credentials (Stripe/PayPal secret keys — needed to actually process billing, the app's core function)
secrets_expressible_today: MYSQL/MariaDB root and app passwords:server_generated_no_customer_input; APP_KEY (Laravel encryption key):server_generated_no_customer_input
blocking_issues:
There is no env-var or config-file path to pre-seed the first admin account. Per upstream's own Docker install docs, the sequence is: `docker compose exec paymenter php artisan app:init` (interactively prompts for the install URL), `... db:seed --class=CustomPropertySeeder`, then `... php artisan app:user:create`, which interactively prompts for username, email, and password with no documented non-interactive flags. Even if install.sh scripted TTY input, the value it would need to supply is the customer's **plaintext** root password so their normal login works — `generated_from` only ever produces a bcrypt/argon2 hash of that password, and this command hashes whatever string it receives internally, so feeding it a hash would double-hash and silently break login. This is a structural mismatch, not merely a missing algorithm, so it isn't just `blocked_on_platform` on the `generated_from` algorithm list — there is no hash-shaped input this command will accept correctly.

Traefik `basic_auth` in front of the app does not resolve the above: it would gate the whole site, but `app:init`/`db:seed`/`app:user:create` still need to run once against the container directly at first boot to produce a working install and an admin account at all, independent of any outer HTTP auth gate.

The core value proposition (processing payments) depends on a customer-supplied Stripe/PayPal API secret with no projection mechanism today — even a customer who gets past admin-account creation cannot make billing functional without manually pasting a gateway key into the admin UI after the fact.
summary: Paymenter is an actively maintained (releases roughly every 2-4 weeks, latest v1.5.7 on 2026-07-25), reverse-proxy-compatible, MIT-licensed billing/subscription platform that would fill a genuinely uncovered business-tools niche in the catalogue. It is not installable under the current mechanism, however: first-boot setup requires a multi-step interactive `php artisan` sequence (init → seed → user:create) with no env-var or non-interactive path to plant an admin account, and the password that command needs is plaintext (to match the customer's real login), which `generated_from` structurally cannot supply since it only ever produces a hash. On top of that, the app's actual purpose (processing payments) needs a customer's own Stripe/PayPal key with no input channel at all. Revisit as blocked_on_platform if the platform gains either a scripted/non-interactive admin-bootstrap path plus a plaintext credential channel, or a general external-API-key input mechanism — building today would ship an app customers can't finish setting up.

name: PdfDing
source_description: Self-hosted PDF manager with cross-device sync and browser-based annotation
version_health_notes: v1.12.0 shipped 2026-08-02, 3 days before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases show a steady ~2-4 week cadence: v1.11.0 (2026-07-24), v1.10.0 (2026-07-09), v1.9.0 (2026-06-22), v1.8.0 (2026-06-05), v1.7.2 (2026-04-12), v1.7.0 (2026-03-29, a security fix for CVE-2026-34376, "shared PDF authentication bypass"). Frequent feature releases plus a recent CVE fix indicate an actively maintained project, not archived, not slowing.
differentiation: PdfDing is a lightweight, PDF-specific manager/viewer focused on cross-device reading progress sync, in-browser annotation (highlights, drawings, signatures), collections/tagging, markdown notes per document, and link/QR sharing. Paperless-ngx — already in the catalogue — is a broader OCR-driven document archive that ingests scanned paper documents of any type into a searchable, tagged store; it is not built around interactive PDF reading/annotation. The two share "manage your documents" territory but solve different jobs: PdfDing is a personal PDF reader/annotator for files a user already has, not a paper-to-searchable-archive pipeline.
usefulness_rationale: Cross-device PDF reading with annotation and sharing is a recognizable, standalone self-hosted use case (manuals, contracts, ebooks, research papers) distinct from the OCR-archive niche paperless-ngx covers, so it clears the "would a customer want this on its own" bar. It is not a top-tier draw compared to categories like password managers or photo backup, but it is a clean, minimal, single-container app with an active upstream.
blocking_issues:
PdfDing's own accounts are created through a self-service email/password sign-up form (django-allauth) rather than an env var the recipe could set — there is no ACCOUNT_EMAIL/ACCOUNT_PASSWORD-style variable to project a hashed root password into, so the generated_from mechanism does not apply to PdfDing's own login. Left with default settings (DISABLE_USER_SIGNUP unset), the app would be an open, anyone-can-register PDF store on the public internet until a Traefik basic_auth gate is added in front of it.
Promoting a registered user to admin requires `python manage.py make_admin -e <email>` executed inside the running container's shell — no env var or API equivalent exists. This is not a hard blocker: PdfDing's admin role only grants user-management/deletion rights over other accounts, which a single-tenant install behind a basic_auth gate does not need, so the app is fully usable as a non-admin account.
summary: PdfDing ships as a single container (mrmn/pdfding, pin v1.12.0) with a bundled SQLite option, one HTTP port (8000), and no external service dependencies at first boot — a straightforward fit behind Traefik on <slug>.<base_domain>. Its own login is self-service sign-up with no env-settable admin credential, so it needs the Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password projection) rather than generated_from to avoid sitting open to public registration; that mechanism is fully expressible today. Upstream is active with a healthy release cadence and a recent CVE fix, and while it has some conceptual overlap with paperless-ngx, the two target different jobs (PDF reading/annotation vs. OCR archiving). Recommend build_now.

name: PeerTube
source_description: Federated peer-to-peer video platform for self-hosted YouTube-style hosting
upstream_docker_image: chocobozzz/peertube (production tag family, e.g. v8.2.4-bookworm; companion chocobozzz/peertube-webserver image ships the bundled nginx)
version_health_notes: v8.2.4 shipped 2026-08-04, one day before today (2026-08-05). Recent history shows a steady, security-driven cadence: v8.2.3 (2026-07-20), v8.2.2 (2026-07-02), v8.2.1 (2026-06-12), v8.2.0 (2026-05-27), v8.1.8 (2026-05-23, patched a SQL-injection vulnerability that had been exploited in the wild since at least 2026-05-18), v8.1.7 (2026-05-22). No archival or EOL signal; upstream is actively developed and quick to ship security patches.
differentiation: Immich (our only "media" recipe) is a personal photo/video backup and library tool for one household; PeerTube is a federated (ActivityPub), public-facing video-hosting platform — a self-hosted YouTube/Vimeo alternative with channels, subscriptions, comments, and optional P2P delivery across a federation of instances. No existing recipe covers public video publishing/streaming, so this is a genuinely new niche for the catalogue rather than a duplicate of Immich.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted video publishing is a well-known, recurring "escape YouTube/Vimeo" use case (creators, communities, educational orgs), and PeerTube is the dominant open-source project in that space with an active federation and healthy release cadence. It would meaningfully broaden the catalogue's consumer/creator appeal beyond the current dev-tools/monitoring/personal-storage slant.
blocking_issues:
PeerTube has its own mandatory built-in login for the `root` admin account (email + password, gating the whole admin UI and most publishing features), so a Traefik `basic_auth` gate cannot substitute for it — same shape as apps-gaps/parseable.yaml and apps-gaps/openobserve.yaml.

Upstream does document a `PT_INITIAL_ROOT_PASSWORD` env var (docs.joinpeertube.org/maintain/configuration, added in github.com/Chocobozzz/PeerTube#1814) that sets the root admin password on first boot instead of the default auto-generated one (which otherwise surfaces only by grepping startup logs). But per that PR's change to `server/initializers/installer.ts`, it is read only once, inside `createOAuthAdminIfNotExist()` during initial root-user creation — it has no effect on subsequent restarts — and it is assigned straight into `password` with no hashing, i.e. it only accepts a plaintext value (min 6 characters), never a pre-computed hash. `generated_from` on our platform only ever projects a hash of the customer's root/server password onto an app-read parameter; it has no plaintext channel. So even with this env var, there is still no way to feed PeerTube's root password from the customer's server-root-password hash without the platform holding or transmitting the plaintext, which per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's installability table is a structural blocker (a genuine plaintext-only requirement can't be satisfied by a hash-only mechanism), not a missing-algorithm gap.

The interactive CLI helper `npm run reset-password -- -u root` also exists post-boot but likewise prompts for a new plaintext password rather than accepting one as an argument, env var, or pre-computed hash, so it offers no additional channel beyond `PT_INITIAL_ROOT_PASSWORD`.

The official docker-compose stack bundles its own nginx (`chocobozzz/peertube-webserver`) and certbot containers for TLS/reverse-proxy duties; upstream docs confirm these can be commented out to front the `peertube` app container directly with an external reverse proxy (Traefik), so this is a mechanical, not structural, integration issue.
summary: PeerTube is an actively maintained (latest v8.2.4, shipped one day before this analysis, with a fast security-patch cadence) federated video-hosting platform that would fill a real, currently-empty niche in the catalogue — no existing recipe covers public video publishing, and it is not a duplicate of Immich's personal-photo-library use case. It is a multi-service Postgres+Redis stack similar in shape to n8n/paperless-ngx, and its bundled nginx/certbot containers can be dropped in favor of Traefik per upstream's own documented guidance, so reverse-proxy integration is not a blocker. The hard blocker is the root admin account: upstream does offer a `PT_INITIAL_ROOT_PASSWORD` env var to set it on first boot, but that var (and the interactive CLI reset helper) only ever accepts a plaintext password, never a pre-computed hash, and it applies only once during initial root-user creation. Our platform's `generated_from` mechanism only ever projects a hash of the customer's server-root-password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel to drive PeerTube's root password from it without the platform handling plaintext credentials — and its mandatory built-in login means a Traefik basic_auth gate cannot stand in for it either. Revisit as build_now if upstream adds a hash-accepting (rather than plaintext-only) root-password input, or if a broader plaintext-credential-injection mechanism is added to our platform.

name: Pelican Panel
source_description: Modern open-source game server management panel, successor to Pterodactyl
version_health_notes: v1.0.0-beta36 shipped 2026-08-05 — today. Prior releases: beta35 (2026-06-22), beta34 (2026-05-08), beta33 (2026-02-18), beta32 (2026-02-09), beta31 (2026-01-18), beta30 (2025-12-19), beta29 (2025-12-09), beta28 (2025-11-09), beta27 (2025-10-20). Roughly monthly releases with no gap over a year, still under active development (6,600+ commits on main). Not archived, not EOL. Still formally in beta/pre-1.0 (has been "v1.0.0-betaNN" for well over a year), which is a maturity caveat worth noting but not a health concern — the project is clearly active, not stalled pre-release.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers game server hosting/management. Pelican Panel is a community-driven fork/modernization of Pterodactyl (rewritten on current Laravel/Filament), providing a web UI to deploy and manage isolated Docker-based game servers (Minecraft, SteamCMD titles, Discord bots, voice servers, etc.), with Pterodactyl egg/node import for easy migration. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue, not a re-skin of anything already present.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for self-hosted game panels, and the Panel container alone (web UI, DB, cache/queue) is cleanly single-container and reverse-proxy-compatible. But the Panel by itself cannot run any game server — that requires a separate "Wings" daemon component that needs Docker socket access, its own raw ports (8080 API, 2022 SFTP, not HTTP-proxyable), and a manual pairing step (an admin-generated node token pasted into Wings' config, only possible after the Panel is fully set up) that cannot be scripted by install.sh because the token doesn't exist until a human completes setup in the browser first. Shipping the Panel alone would put a functionally empty game panel in the catalogue; shipping Wings alongside it in the same compose stack means a service that crash-loops until manually reconfigured post-deploy — a rough first-run experience relative to our other recipes.
blocking_issues:
Core product value (running a game server) requires the separate Wings daemon, which needs Docker-socket-level host access and a manual Panel-generated node token pasted into its config after first boot — this pairing step can't be pre-populated by install.sh since the token only exists after a human finishes the Panel's own web setup wizard. A recipe shipping Wings in the same compose stack would crash-loop until the customer manually intervenes.
Wings' SFTP port (2022) and API port (8080) are raw TCP, not HTTP — usable as public: false / non-Traefik ports (precedent: Portainer's edge-agent port), but this means the 'panel + one working node' experience needs more manual host-level follow-up than a typical single-container recipe.
summary: Pelican Panel is upstream-healthy (monthly releases, active development, though still formally pre-1.0/beta) and fills a category gap — no existing recipe covers game server hosting. The Panel container itself is mechanically installable today: no external secrets are needed (DB/cache/APP_KEY are all server-generated), and the first admin account is created by the customer directly through the Panel's own web installer wizard, the same self-service pattern already accepted for n8n's owner setup. The real problem is usefulness: without the Wings daemon paired to at least one node — a step requiring Docker socket access, raw non-HTTP ports, and a manual token handoff that can't happen before the Panel's own setup wizard is complete — the deployed panel can't actually run a single game server. Recommend `build_with_caveats`: worth building only if the recipe (or its documentation) clearly separates "Panel deploys clean" from "Wings pairing is a manual, non-scripted, second step," rather than promising a plug-and-play game server host.

name: PentAGI

The catalogue's existing AI-agent entries (openclaw, hermes-agent) are general-purpose messaging-first assistants; PentAGI is a purpose-built autonomous pentesting platform (13+ specialized agents driving Nmap, Metasploit, and similar tooling inside sandboxed containers, producing vulnerability reports with exploitation guides). Genuinely distinct audience (security professionals/red teams) and use case, not a reskin of anything already in the catalogue.

blocking_issues:
PentAGI will not function without at least one LLM provider credential configured before the container starts (one of OPEN_AI_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, AWS Bedrock creds, Ollama endpoint, etc. — confirmed in upstream README and docker-compose.yml). Unlike openclaw/hermes-agent, PentAGI's web UI "Settings -> Providers" screen only manages provider *profiles* (model selection, routing, pricing metadata) for an already-configured backend; it does not accept raw API keys post-boot — those remain env-var/config-file only. The pentagi service mounts the host's /var/run/docker.sock to spawn sandboxed task containers. Not a novel blocker — the same pattern is already shipped in portainer, wud, and runtipi — but worth flagging as an operational caveat given the app's purpose is running attack/exploit tooling.
summary: PentAGI is an active, differentiated addition (autonomous AI-driven pentesting, no overlap with existing recipes) but is blocked today by a hard requirement for an external LLM provider API key that must be present as an env var before first boot, with no post-provision UI path to add it later (unlike openclaw/hermes-agent, whose provider keys are optional at boot and settable via the authenticated dashboard afterward). The fixed default admin login is not a blocker on its own — it can be gated behind Traefik basic_auth like Adminer — but the missing API-key input channel is. Revisit once a customer-supplied-secret mechanism beyond root-password hashing exists, or if PentAGI's UI adds a way to set provider credentials after boot.

differentiation: No existing recipe in the 24-app catalogue covers ticketing/helpdesk (Zendesk/Jira-style customer request tracking with a markdown editor, file uploads, and client history). If upstream were healthy this would be a genuinely distinct category for the catalogue, not overlap with any current recipe.
usefulness_rationale: Ticketing/helpdesk is a real, recognizable self-hosted category with no current catalogue entry, so demand exists in principle. However the concrete usefulness of shipping *this* app is undermined by its archived status — a customer would be adopting a frozen product with no security-patch path.
blocking_issues:
No version-pinned Docker Hub tag exists — pepperlabs/peppermint only ships :latest and :nightly, both frozen since Nov 2024. RFC-002's 'never :latest, always a pinned current stable tag' requirement cannot be satisfied because no such tag was ever published.
The app's own admin account is a hardcoded default (admin@admin.com / 1234) baked into the seed data; the docker-compose.yml upstream ships only DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_HOST and SECRET as env vars — there is no ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_PASSWORD-style variable to project a hashed root password into, so generated_from does not apply. This alone would not block installability (per SCHEMA.md, a fixed unchangeable default credential is fine behind a Traefik basic_auth gate), but is noted because it means the app's own login provides zero protection on its own.
Upstream repository is archived (read-only) and the last release is ~21 months old with no image rebuild since — shipping a recipe on top of a frozen, unpatched codebase is a security-support risk independent of the mechanical installability question.
summary: Peppermint is architecturally simple to run (single app container plus Postgres, one HTTP port, a Traefik basic_auth gate would cover its hardcoded default admin login) and would fill a real gap — no ticketing or help-desk recipe exists in the current catalogue. But the upstream project is archived on GitHub as of a recent push in 2025-09 with the archive flag now set, the last numbered release is 0.5.5 from 2024-11-14 (nearly two years ago), and the Docker image was never published with a pinned version tag — only a stale :latest/:nightly from November 2024. Combined with an ambiguous, non-standard license grant, this is a dormant/archived project with no patch path. Recommend not_recommended; revisit only if the project is un-archived and resumes releases, or if a maintained fork emerges.

name: Percona PMM
source_description: Open-source database monitoring with query analytics and Grafana dashboards
version_health_notes: v3.9.0 shipped 2026-07-30, six days before this analysis (2026-08-05), adding an Alert Status page, MongoDB/PostgreSQL dashboard improvements, and CSV export for Real-Time Query Analytics. Prior releases landed roughly monthly through 2026: v3.8.1 (2026-06-16, security patches for gRPC/Grafana/nginx CVEs), v3.8.0 (2026-05-28, Grafana 12.4 upgrade, encrypted PMM dumps), v3.7.1 (2026-04-30, security release), v3.7.0 (2026-04-01, real-time MongoDB query analytics), v3.6.0 (2026-02-05, native PMM navigation, HA cluster tech preview). Repo is not archived, the PMM 2.x line is in maintenance mode while active development is on the 3.x line, and Percona publishes security-focused patch releases promptly. No ambiguity on identity — Percona's own "PMM", not a different project.
differentiation: PMM is purpose-built for monitoring database servers (MySQL, MongoDB, PostgreSQL) it doesn't itself run: a lightweight pmm-client/exporter is installed on each target database and reports metrics, slow-query logs, and Query Analytics (QAN) back to a central PMM Server, which ships with its own bundled Grafana-based dashboards out of the box. This is distinct from every other monitoring-adjacent candidate considered so far: Uptime Kuma (external endpoint pings), Netdata (generic host/ container telemetry), Checkmk (generic infra/service auto-discovery), and Grafana (a bare dashboarding shell with no built-in data source or database-specific collectors). None of the 24 shipped recipes offer database-specific query analytics or pre-built DB dashboards.
usefulness_rationale: Database performance monitoring and query analytics is a distinct, well-recognized need for anyone running production MySQL/Postgres/ MongoDB, and PMM is the leading purpose-built open-source tool in that niche with dashboards included out of the box (no separate Grafana wiring needed, unlike a bare Grafana install). Value depends on the customer separately running pmm-client against their own database servers (which may or may not be on this platform), similar to Grafana's data-source caveat, but the server component alone still provides real out-of-the-box dashboards rather than an empty shell.
blocking_issues:
PMM Server's admin account (username "admin", used for both the native PMM UI and its underlying Grafana) is provisioned on first boot from the plaintext GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variable — documented by Percona itself as applying only "on first startup" and being ignored thereafter. There is no pre-hashed- credential option (unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN), so `generated_from` (hash-only) cannot populate it.

Unlike Grafana (which can fully disable its own login via GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED / GF_AUTH_DISABLE_LOGIN_FORM, shifting the sole auth boundary to a Traefik basic_auth gate) or Alerta (AUTH_REQUIRED=False), no documented mechanism exists to disable PMM's own login screen. Percona's FAQ explicitly covers setting or resetting the admin password but says nothing about anonymous access or disabling auth. A Traefik basic_auth gate in front of PMM would still leave the customer facing PMM's own admin login with no channel to learn or set that plaintext credential.

Secondary, non-blocking note: PMM Server terminates TLS itself and is documented to publish container port 8443 (mapped to host 443) rather than plain HTTP, which is a minor mismatch with our Traefik-terminates-TLS model but not a structural blocker on its own — it would need double TLS termination or PMM configured to serve HTTP internally.
summary: Percona PMM is actively maintained (v3.9.0, six days before this analysis, roughly monthly release cadence with prompt security patches) and would fill a genuine, high-value gap in the catalogue: none of the 24 shipped recipes offer database-specific query analytics or pre-built DB dashboards. It is blocked from shipping as a recipe today purely on the installability mechanism, in the same way as Checkmk: its admin account is created from a plaintext GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD env var honored only on first boot, with no pre-hashed-credential path and — unlike Grafana or Alerta — no documented way to disable its own login so a Traefik basic_auth gate could stand in as the sole auth boundary. This needs a genuine plaintext root-password-projection channel added to the platform (or Percona documenting an anonymous- access mode) before it's buildable — recommend `blocked_on_platform` rather than `not_recommended`, since the app itself is a strong catalogue candidate once that channel exists.

With that gate in place this is mechanically buildable, but the 4-month lull in upstream activity right after the Perplexica→Vane rebrand, plus real proximity to two other AI-answering-engine gap candidates, makes it a build-with-caveats rather than a priority pick.

name: pgAdmin
source_description: Open-source PostgreSQL administration and development platform for the web
version_health_notes: 9.17 shipped 2026-07-31, five days before today (2026-08-05) — the same release also fixed seven CVEs (CVE-2026-17346 through CVE-2026-17351, CVE-2026-17566). Prior releases: 9.16 (2026-06-18), 9.15 (2026-05-11), 9.14 (2026-04-02) — a steady roughly-monthly cadence with no gaps, plus intermediate daily-tagged snapshot builds (e.g. 2026-07-30-1) on Docker Hub. This is a well-maintained, actively developed project with an official upstream Docker image kept in lockstep with releases.
differentiation: No existing recipe provides a PostgreSQL administration/query UI. n8n and paperless-ngx both run on Postgres internally, but neither exposes it for general-purpose database administration. pgAdmin would let a customer browse schemas, run queries, and manage permissions on their own Postgres instance(s) — a genuinely distinct, developer-tool-oriented use case not covered by anything currently in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for a hosted Postgres admin UI among customers running Postgres-backed apps (their own or ones deployed via other recipes), and pgAdmin is the de facto standard tool for this. Value is somewhat narrower than a general productivity app since it's aimed at technically inclined customers who already run Postgres, but within that audience it is high-value and low-effort to deploy (single container, no extra services required).
blocking_issues:
pgAdmin's container entrypoint requires PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD (or PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD_FILE, which just reads the plaintext from a file instead of an env var) to set up the initial admin account — the upstream docs give no mechanism to seed the account from a pre-computed hash. generated_from only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel to supply this value. Per SCHEMA.md this is the one genuine structural blocker case: 'a genuine requirement for the plaintext password (not any hash) is a structural blocker.'
PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL is also required and must be a syntactically valid email address (the login is validated as an email, not an arbitrary username) — a fixed placeholder like admin@<domain> would work mechanically, but the real blocker is the plaintext-password requirement above, which makes this a moot secondary issue.
summary: pgAdmin is a healthy, actively released project (monthly cadence, recent CVE fixes shipped promptly, official pinned Docker image) and would fill a real gap — no database-administration UI exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It is architecturally simple to deploy (single container, no dependent services, one HTTP port, reverse-proxy friendly). However, its container entrypoint requires PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD as plaintext to bootstrap the initial admin login, with no supported way to instead supply a pre-hashed value — exactly the structural gap the root-password-projection mechanism cannot cross today. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once either a plaintext customer-supplied credential input channel exists, or pgAdmin adds support for seeding the admin account from a hash (neither exists today).

summary: pgBackWeb has no env var or CLI flag to preset its own admin account — on first boot, whichever visitor reaches the app first is shown a "create first user" form and picks an arbitrary name/email/password themselves (internal/view/web/auth/create_first_user.go), identical in shape to n8n's owner-setup wizard. That makes it installable today the same way: gate the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth (projected from the customer's root password via generated_from), so only the customer can reach the create-first-user page and no one else can race them to claim the admin account. It's a single container plus a bundled Postgres backing service (same shape as recipes/n8n), single HTTP port 8085, no other raw ports — reverse-proxy-compatible. The main caveat is version health: releases have gone quiet for ~8.5 months and the project has an announced-but-unexecuted rebrand to "UFO Backup" that could change the image/repo name; worth a quick re-check before scheduling a real af-create-recipe pass.

name: PgHero
source_description: Open-source PostgreSQL performance dashboard for query and index monitoring
version_health_notes: v4.0.0 tagged 2026-08-05 — the same day as this analysis — dropping support for Postgres < 14 and several legacy Ruby/Rails/dependency versions. Prior releases: v3.8.0 (2026-04-15, ~4 months earlier), v3.7.0 (2025-05-26, ~11 months before that), v3.6.2 (2025-03-21), v3.6.1 (2024-10-14), v3.6.0 (2024-07-10). Cadence is irregular (gaps from 2 to 11 months) but has never gone dormant — at least one release every year since the project started, with the changelog showing continuous maintenance-style fixes (dropped legacy support, CSP/CSS fixes, bug fixes) between major version bumps. Repo is not archived, has 8.9k GitHub stars, MIT license, and the Docker image on Docker Hub is published in lockstep with tags (linux/amd64 + linux/arm64). This is a healthy, actively maintained single-maintainer project (Andrew Kane / "ankane"), not a corporate-backed one with a fixed release train — cadence reflects that but shows no sign of abandonment.
differentiation: PgHero is a narrow, single-purpose read-only dashboard for one Postgres instance — slow queries, missing/unused/duplicate indexes, live queries, connection/space stats, and a query-explain view. It is lighter-weight and more focused than a general admin tool like pgAdmin (schema browsing, arbitrary SQL execution, user/permission management) or a fleet-wide monitoring platform like Percona PMM (multi-database-engine, Grafana-based, client/server architecture). None of the 24 shipped recipes offer Postgres-specific performance insight; n8n and paperless-ngx each run Postgres internally but expose no monitoring UI for it.
usefulness_rationale: Useful to a technically inclined customer who already runs Postgres and wants performance visibility, but its value is entirely contingent on which database it points at. Pointed at a customer's own external, self-managed Postgres server it is genuinely valuable; pointed at nothing (or at a fresh, empty database we'd have to bundle just to make the recipe self-contained) it has little to show. Unlike pgAdmin — where the customer adds server connections through the UI after logging in — PgHero's target database is fixed by a single `DATABASE_URL` environment variable set once at container start, so the "which database" question has to be answered at install time, not left to the customer to configure later.
blocking_issues:
PgHero has no login of its own by default — it ships with optional basic auth via plaintext `PGHERO_USERNAME`/`PGHERO_PASSWORD` env vars, which is not itself a blocker since the app works fine with those vars simply left unset and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate placed in front instead (same pattern as Adminer/WUD).

The real blocker is `DATABASE_URL`: PgHero's one required environment variable, read once at container start with no post-boot UI to change it, must contain the host, port, database name, and a username+password for the actual Postgres server to be monitored. That connection string is either (a) an arbitrary external customer-owned Postgres instance — a third-party credential with no input channel today, same category as an external API key — or (b) a database we'd have to stand up ourselves inside the recipe's own compose stack purely to give PgHero something to point at, which sidesteps the mechanism constraint but produces a recipe that monitors an empty, purpose- built database instead of anything the customer actually runs, defeating the point of a performance dashboard. Neither `generated_from` (hash-only, and only ever the customer's *root* password) nor Traefik `basic_auth` (gates HTTP access, not an app's internal DB connection config) can supply an arbitrary external connection string.
summary: PgHero is a small, actively maintained (MIT, v4.0.0 shipped the same day as this analysis, no dormancy despite an irregular release cadence), genuinely differentiated addition — nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue offers Postgres-specific query/index performance monitoring. Its own optional auth is a non-issue (a Traefik `basic_auth` gate covers it cleanly), but it is blocked on a more fundamental gap than pgAdmin or Percona PMM: its single required `DATABASE_URL` must name an actual external Postgres server with real credentials, and our platform has no channel today for a customer to supply an arbitrary third-party connection string — only a hash of their own root password or a static basic-auth gate. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once a genuine customer-supplied-value input channel exists; bundling a throwaway Postgres just to satisfy the env var would ship a recipe with no real content to display.

name: Pgweb
source_description: Cross-platform web-based PostgreSQL database browser with zero dependencies
version_health_notes: 0.17.0 published 2025-11-22 — about 8.5 months before today (2026-08-05) — and is still the newest tagged release/Docker Hub image; no follow-up release has shipped since. The tag history shows the same pattern repeatedly: roughly quarterly point releases through 2023-2024 (0.14.1 2023-06-17, 0.14.2 2023-10-30, 0.14.3 2024-01-29, 0.15.0 2024-03-15, 0.16.0 2024-06-05, 0.16.1 2024-09-07, 0.16.2 2024-11-02), then a 12.5-month gap before 0.17.0. Despite the sparse tagging, the repo itself is clearly not dormant: `pushed_at` is 2026-07-26 and commits landed as recently as 2026-07-03 (read-only mode hardening, PostgreSQL 18 support in the dev docker-compose). So this reads as an actively-developed project that batches infrequent, irregular releases rather than one going stale — "sporadic" cadence, not "slowing" or "dormant".
differentiation: A separate gap analysis already covers pgAdmin (apps-gaps/pgadmin.yaml) for the same "Postgres admin UI" niche; that file should be read alongside this one since both target the same slot. Pgweb is architecturally the lighter-weight alternative: a single ~50MB zero-dependency Go binary with no admin-account bootstrap flow at all, versus pgAdmin's full email/password account system and heavier Flask-based stack. Functionally it's narrower (browse/query/export, no server-wide user/permission management), but for a customer who just wants to point a browser at their own Postgres and run queries, pgweb is simpler to deploy and — critically, see installability below — is not blocked by the same plaintext-password requirement that blocks pgAdmin today.
usefulness_rationale: Same audience as pgAdmin (customers running Postgres-backed apps, their own or via other recipes, who want an ad hoc query/browse UI) — technically inclined, not a mass-market need, but real and recurring. Within that audience pgweb is arguably the better first recipe to ship of the two: it is mechanically installable today with zero blocking issues, whereas pgAdmin is blocked_on_platform. Shipping both would be redundant unless there's a specific reason to want pgAdmin's fuller admin/permissions surface.
summary: Pgweb is a single-container, zero-dependency Go binary (official image sosedoff/pgweb, pin e.g. 0.17.0) serving one HTTP port (default 8081) with no database of its own and no built-in admin-account bootstrap — it has no login at all unless one is explicitly configured, and it connects to whatever Postgres instance/URL the end user supplies through its own UI or PGWEB_DATABASE_URL at runtime, not at image-boot time. It does ship its own optional --auth-user/--auth-pass (or PGWEB_AUTH_USER/PGWEB_AUTH_PASS) HTTP basic-auth flags, but since those only ever accept plaintext, generated_from can't feed them directly either — same as any other no-login app. The clean path is to leave pgweb's own auth off and put a Traefik basic_auth:true gate in front of it instead (identical pattern to Adminer/n8n/WUD), which is fully expressible today via generated_from projection of the customer's root password into the gate credential. That leaves zero blocking issues: no external API key, no OAuth, no plaintext-password requirement. Combined with an active-if-irregular upstream (recent July 2026 commits, if a thin 8.5-month gap since the last tagged release) and a real, currently unmet "Postgres browser" niche in the catalogue, this is a build_now candidate — plausibly a better first pick than the related but currently blocked pgAdmin candidate (apps-gaps/pgadmin.yaml) for the same use case.

name: Phoenix
source_description: Open-source AI observability and tracing platform for LLM applications
upstream_license: Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2) — source-available, not OSI-approved OSS; free to self-host and use, restrictions apply to offering it as a hosted service to third parties
version_health_notes: Releasing near-daily: 19.15.0 (2026-08-03) -> 19.16.0 (2026-08-04) -> 19.17.0 (2026-08-04) -> 19.18.0 (2026-08-05, today). Over 9,000 GitHub stars, backed by Arize AI (funded observability vendor), Docker Hub image updated within hours of each tagged release plus a rolling `nightly`. Unambiguously active, not archived/maintenance-only/EOL.
differentiation: Functionally the same niche as apps-gaps/langfuse.yaml (already evaluated build_with_caveats): open-source LLM tracing/observability/ eval for developers building on top of LLM APIs, complementary to ollama/open-webui rather than competing with them. Phoenix is the lighter-weight deployment (2 containers: app + Postgres, vs Langfuse's 5-service ClickHouse/Redis/MinIO stack) and has a large OpenTelemetry- native instrumentation ecosystem (OpenInference), but it targets the same developer audience and same job-to-be-done as Langfuse. No functional overlap with any of the 24 built recipes (ollama, open-webui, n8n, etc. are inference/automation, not tracing).
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct demand (widely used self-hosted LLM-ops tool, 9k+ stars, active vendor backing) from the same developer/self-hoster audience as Langfuse. Medium rather than high for the same reason as Langfuse: developer-tooling for people building their own LLM-integrated products, not a broad consumer app. Given Langfuse already covers this niche and is already catalogued as a gap-analysis candidate, Phoenix is a "which one" prioritization question rather than adding new category coverage — see CLAUDE.md note that overlapping candidates are still evaluated independently rather than auto-rejected for the overlap.
blocking_issues:
Not a hard blocker but a real functional caveat: Phoenix's trace- ingestion path is not purely the HTTP UI port. The official image exposes :6006 (web UI + OTLP/HTTP collector) and :4317 (OTLP/gRPC collector) — customer applications sending traces need to reach whichever collector protocol their OTel SDK is configured for, not just a browser reaching the UI. Traefik can front a TCP entrypoint for :4317, but that is a second public routable endpoint beyond the single-HTTP-port-on-<slug>.<base_domain> pattern the rest of the catalogue uses, and if the whole app is gated behind Traefik basic_auth (see below) that gate would also need to cover the ingestion endpoint, which OTLP exporters don't handle as smoothly as a browser login.

Phoenix ships with authentication OFF by default (no login at all, full UI/API/trace data open to anyone reaching the port). Turning it on requires PHOENIX_ENABLE_AUTH=true and PHOENIX_SECRET (both fine — opaque, server-generatable), which scaffolds a FIXED default admin account (admin@localhost / admin) that the docs say must be changed on first login. There is a PHOENIX_DEFAULT_ADMIN_INITIAL_PASSWORD env var to preset that password on first boot, but it takes the plaintext password directly — not a hash — so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash of the customer's root password) has no matching input channel for it. Per SCHEMA.md's guidance for "a fixed/default admin credential the app itself gives no way to change" being fine behind a Traefik basic_auth gate: the practical fix here is to leave PHOENIX_ENABLE_AUTH off (or leave the default admin/admin as-is) and put the entire app behind Traefik basic_auth using generated_from on the customer's root password — same pattern as Adminer/WUD. That resolves the login-secret problem but compounds the port-4317 caveat above (the gate now sits in front of the ingestion endpoint too).
summary: Phoenix (Arize AI) is an active, well-adopted (9k+ stars, near-daily releases) open-source LLM observability/tracing platform, functionally overlapping apps-gaps/langfuse.yaml's niche rather than filling a new gap in the 24-recipe catalogue. Deployment is lighter than Langfuse (2 containers: arizephoenix/phoenix + postgres:16, vs Langfuse's 5-service stack), and its only first-boot secret is the Postgres password (server-generatable, no customer input needed). The install-mechanism wrinkle is auth: Phoenix has no login by default, and its opt-in auth scaffolds a fixed admin/admin account whose initial-password override env var wants a plaintext password (no hash-based input channel exists for it) — so the actual auth boundary has to be a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the whole app, per SCHEMA.md's guidance for fixed-credential apps. That gate, however, would sit in front of both the web UI (:6006) and the OTLP trace-ingestion ports (:6006 HTTP / :4317 gRPC) that customer apps need to reach programmatically, which is a functional caveat beyond the usual single-HTTP-port pattern. Mechanically installable today (build_with_caveats), but given Langfuse already covers this same job-to-be-done and is already flagged for the backlog, Phoenix is best treated as a "which observability tool" prioritization choice rather than an independent build.

Repo is not archived, last push was 2026-08-05 (today), and 35 open issues are still being triaged. Clearly active, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: Photofield is a read-only viewer/gallery over an existing photo tree (file system is the source of truth, no ingestion pipeline, no mobile backup client, no user accounts), whereas Immich is a full backup + library platform (mobile auto-upload, ML search/face-recognition pipeline, multi-user accounts, albums/sharing). Photofield's pitch is raw browsing speed/zoom over very large collections rather than being a Google-Photos replacement. It is lighter (single Go binary + SQLite cache, no Postgres/Redis/ML containers) but strictly less capable as a product for a typical self-hosting customer who wants to also *upload* photos from a phone.
usefulness_rationale: On the AF platform, a customer has no built-in way to get photos onto the server other than SFTP/file-manager style access to a mounted directory, since Photofield has no upload/ingestion UI of its own. That makes it a viewer for photos a customer already got onto the box some other way — a much smaller and more technical audience than Immich, which already covers "back up and browse my photos" for the mainstream case. Photofield adds a real niche (huge local collections, zero accounts, minimal resource footprint) but it's thin compared to what we already ship.
summary: Photofield is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8080) Go app with an embedded SQLite cache and no built-in authentication or user accounts at all ("no user accounts... not the focus right now" per upstream docs), so it is mechanically installable today behind a domain param plus a mandatory Traefik basic_auth:true gate (password projected from the customer's root password), the same pattern used for Adminer/WUD/n8n. The project itself is healthy and actively released. The gap is product fit, not platform mechanics: it only displays photos already present in a mounted directory and gives the customer no way to get photos there in the first place, so it largely duplicates and is strictly weaker than the already-catalogued Immich for the mainstream "back up and browse my photos" use case. Recommend build_with_caveats — technically buildable, but low priority given the overlap and thin ingestion story.

name: PhotoPrism
source_description: PhotoPrism is an AI-powered photo management application for the decentralized web
version_health_notes: PhotoPrism uses rolling, date-stamped build tags rather than semver releases (e.g. 260728-bbde8f452, 260601-a7d098548, 260523-..., 260305-...). Releases land roughly every 4-8 weeks, most recently 2026-07-28 — 8 days before today (2026-08-05). This is a continuously maintained, actively developed project, not a stalled one.
differentiation: Direct functional overlap with recipes/immich: both are self-hosted, AI-powered photo/video libraries with face recognition, geo/map view, and automatic tagging behind a single web UI. PhotoPrism's edge is a lighter footprint (can run on SQLite with no external DB/cache, vs. Immich's mandatory Postgres+pgvecto.rs+Redis stack) and a filesystem-first "index don't import" model that some users prefer over Immich's managed-library approach. It lacks Immich's official mobile app with background auto-backup, which is Immich's main consumer-facing draw. Per CLAUDE.md, catalogue overlap alone is not a reason to reject a candidate — but it does mean PhotoPrism would need to earn its slot on its own merits rather than "we don't have a photo app yet."
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct audience (users who prefer PhotoPrism's UX, its library-scanning model, or want a DB-free/lighter deployment than Immich) but it's competing directly with an app we already ship, and its most attractive features (world map, enhanced search, some AI labeling) are gated behind a paid membership rather than fully free in the self-hosted Community Edition.
blocking_issues:
PHOTOPRISM_ADMIN_PASSWORD must be a plaintext password known to the customer at first boot — it's what they type into PhotoPrism's own "admin" login every time, not a pre-computed hash. The official compose file ships it as a literal env var (default "insecure" in the upstream example) with no support for supplying a pre-hashed value; PhotoPrism hashes it internally only after receiving the plaintext. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever produces a hash string, so it cannot be projected into this field — structurally the same blocker documented for Ackee (apps-gaps/ackee.yaml): there is no channel today to hand the app a plaintext credential the customer actually knows, short of leaking their real root password verbatim.

Auto-generating PHOTOPRISM_ADMIN_PASSWORD server-side and never showing it to the customer doesn't work either, for the same reason it doesn't work for Ackee: this is a customer-facing login field (not an internal secret like a DB password), so a hidden random value would lock the customer out of the app's own admin UI.

Fronting the whole app with a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (using `generated_from` on the root password) does not resolve this either: PhotoPrism has its own login screen, so the SCHEMA.md "no login of its own → gate with basic_auth" allowance doesn't apply, and using a fixed/shared PHOTOPRISM_ADMIN_PASSWORD across every customer install just to have *something* in the field would mean every instance shares the same internal admin credential, which is the anti-pattern the mechanism is meant to avoid.
summary: PhotoPrism is an actively maintained, single-container-plus-optional-DB photo/video manager with a single reverse-proxy-friendly HTTP port (2342) and can run standalone on SQLite, making it mechanically simple to package. It fails installability today on the same credential-input gap as Ackee: its only login field, PHOTOPRISM_ADMIN_PASSWORD, requires a plaintext password the customer knows, and neither `generated_from` (hash-only) nor Traefik `basic_auth` (app already has its own login) covers that. It also directly overlaps recipes/immich, which is more actively developed on the consumer side (official mobile app with auto-backup) — PhotoPrism's differentiation is a lighter deployment footprint and a different UX philosophy, not a missing capability. Recommend revisiting only if a customer-known-plaintext credential channel is added to the platform; even then this competes for build priority against the photo-management slot Immich already fills.

Net: active development and even security patching, but no real versioned release cadence to point a pin at — the "2.4.0" tag today is not the same image bytes it was in 2024, which matters for reproducible pins.
differentiation: Nearly identical value proposition to Immich already in the catalogue — both are self-hosted photo galleries with RAW support, EXIF browsing, and face recognition/grouping, which is exactly Hostinger's description of this app. The real difference is architectural, not feature-level: Photoview is a read-only browser over an existing directory tree the operator already has on disk/NAS (no upload/backup pipeline, no mobile app), so it is lighter weight (single Go binary + one DB) than Immich's full backup-and-sync suite (ML service, Redis, Postgres, mobile clients). That's a real but narrow niche: a customer who already has an organized photo library and just wants a browsing/sharing UI over it, rather than a phone-backup target.

Photoview's only edge — being lighter weight for browsing an already-organized library — is a thin wedge against an existing recipe, and its stale-tag/floating-release situation (see version_health) makes it a weaker pick for a second "photo gallery" slot than the alternative of just pointing such a customer at Immich.
summary: Photoview is mechanically installable today: the official docker-compose example is just the `photoview/photoview` app container plus a MariaDB (or Postgres/SQLite) database behind one HTTP port (80, typically mapped to 8000), no extra raw ports. It needs no external API keys or OAuth registration — the only first-boot secret is the database password, which the platform can generate server-side and never has to reach the customer. The admin account itself is created interactively through Photoview's own first-visit setup wizard (username, password, and root photo path), the same self-serve pattern already accepted for immich and uptime-kuma, so no root-password projection or basic_auth gate is needed either. Despite being technically buildable, this is a not_recommended pick: it duplicates Immich's core pitch (RAW, EXIF, face recognition) almost exactly while being less actively released (no versioned tag in 2+ years, now tracking a floating master build instead) and narrower in scope (browse-only, no backup/mobile story). Note the app name is ambiguous — a same-named but unrelated Android library (Baseflow/PhotoView, an ImageView zoom widget, Apache-2.0) exists on GitHub and was ruled out as the wrong project for this analysis.

name: phpBB
source_description: Classic open-source PHP bulletin board software for self-hosted forums
version_health_notes: Latest stable is 3.3.17, released 2026-06-06 (~2 months before today, 2026-08-05) — a maintenance/security release of the 3.3.x line, which has been the sole actively supported branch since 3.2 went EOL in 2019. phpBB's own endoflife.date entry describes releases as irregular rather than on a fixed schedule; only the latest 3.3.x point release gets fixes. In parallel, phpBB 4.0.0-a2 (a ground-up rewrite on Symfony 7.4) shipped 2026-04-27 as an early alpha explicitly marked "should not be used on any live sites." No EOL announcement or archival for 3.3.x — the project is active but slow-moving, with the real forward momentum concentrated in an unreleased 4.0 rewrite.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers forum/community hosting — the nearest neighbours (Gitea for code, Anytype for notes, Opengist for pastes) serve different purposes. A customer wanting a public discussion forum would reach for this instead of a hosted SaaS. Two other forum candidates in this niche (Flarum, NodeBB) were evaluated separately and hit the identical structural blocker documented below — phpBB does not change that picture, it's the same gap with the same platform-side obstacle.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted forums are a genuine but narrow need next to the automation/dev-tooling/security apps dominating the current 24 recipes. phpBB is the most recognizable classic option in this space (20+ years of history, huge extension/theme ecosystem), but it is also the most dated: PHP-native with no first-party container story, and its forward development energy is going into an unreleased 4.0 rewrite rather than the 3.3.x line a recipe would have to pin to.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: admin.name (admin username); admin.password (admin password); admin.email (admin email); dbpasswd (MySQL/MariaDB password)
blocking_issues:
phpBB's own installer — the web installer and its CLI equivalent (`php install/phpbbcli.php install install-config.yml`) — takes the admin username/password/email as plaintext in an `installer.admin` config block and hands it to phpBB's own account-creation code, which hashes it internally (`phpbb_hash()`). There is no supported install path that accepts a pre-computed hash instead, so `generated_from` (which only ever carries a hash) cannot express this credential — the same genuine plaintext-password requirement documented for Flarum and NodeBB, not merely an unsupported hash algorithm.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` is mechanically available but wrong here: phpBB's entire surface is the public forum itself (topics, member posts, registration), not an admin-only tool like n8n or Adminer. Basic-auth-ing the whole domain would block real forum visitors and members, defeating the product's purpose, just as concluded for Flarum and NodeBB.

phpBB has no official production Docker image — the phpBB project's own `phpbb/docker` repo is explicitly scoped to CI and local development, not production, and the project's public guidance is to install phpBB directly rather than run it in Docker. Community images exist (e.g. `selim13/phpbb`, `blueimp/phpbb`) but the once-common `bitnami/phpbb` image is no longer maintained, and none of the remaining actively-updated community images were found tracking the current 3.3.17 stable with a version-pinned tag rather than an unversioned `latest`. This is an independent blocker on top of the plaintext-password issue.
summary: phpBB is the best-known classic self-hosted forum platform and would fill the same community/discussion-board gap already identified for Flarum and NodeBB, but it is blocked today for the same structural reason as both: its installer (web or CLI) requires the admin password as plaintext so phpBB can hash it internally, which `generated_from` cannot supply, and gating the whole public forum behind Traefik `basic_auth` would block real visitors rather than just protect an admin surface. It is further hampered by having no official production Docker image and no well-maintained community image publishing a current, version-pinned tag — the project explicitly recommends against Docker for production use. Revisit if the platform gains a genuinely customer-chosen credential channel, or if a maintained, version-pinned image with a pre-hashed-admin install path appears; until then this sits alongside Flarum and NodeBB as the same unresolved forum-niche blocker, not a reason to build a bespoke image ourselves.

Treated as `active` on the strength of the 2026 release pickup and live build activity, despite the ~3.5-month gap since the last actual release.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers IP address management. A separate gap analysis for NetBox (apps-gaps/netbox.yaml) targets the same IPAM niche with a heavier DCIM/network-documentation tool; that file is blocked_on_platform today. phpIPAM is the lighter-weight, IPAM-only alternative in the same slot: a single PHP/Apache app plus MariaDB versus NetBox's Django/PostgreSQL stack. phpIPAM does have a Racks module (rack creation, rack diagram view, device-to-rack placement, subracks, with active 2026 work per the v1.8.0 changelog), but it is lighter and less comprehensive than NetBox's full DCIM feature set — phpIPAM stays primarily an IPAM tool with rack modeling as a secondary feature, not a DCIM-first platform. Shipping both would be redundant; phpIPAM is arguably the better first pick for this niche since — see installability below — it is not structurally blocked the way NetBox is.
usefulness_rationale: Real, recurring need among technical customers/MSPs managing their own network address space (subnet tracking, VLANs, DNS/DHCP audit trail), but it's a specialist admin tool rather than a broad-appeal app — narrower audience than most of the catalogue, similar in kind to NetBox or Guacamole.
summary: phpIPAM (official image phpipam/phpipam-www, pin e.g. v1.8.1) ships no admin account and no env-var/CLI channel to seed one — first boot presents its own unauthenticated, multi-step web installer (choose "New phpipam installation", let it create the DB schema, then define the admin password directly into the app's own form). Unlike NetBox, where the container refuses to create any login without a plaintext SUPERUSER_PASSWORD env var and there is no self-service alternative, phpIPAM's installer *is* the vendor-documented, built-in way a customer provisions their own admin account — nothing needs to flow through af-api/`/compose` for it. The only real gap is that this installer page is open to anyone who reaches the domain before the customer completes it, so the whole app must sit behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate (credential projected from the customer's root password via `generated_from`) until setup is done — the same "no login of its own yet" pattern used for Adminer/n8n/WUD. The MariaDB password is a server-generated secret nothing customer-facing reads. Caveats keeping this at build_with_caveats rather than build_now: (1) the customer must manually click through phpIPAM's installer once after deploy — real UX friction most of our recipes avoid; (2) the web and cron containers both require NET_ADMIN/NET_RAW capabilities for ping/SNMP discovery, an elevated-privilege ask beyond our typical recipe footprint; (3) upstream recommends setting IPAM_DISABLE_INSTALLER after setup completes, which is a customer follow-up step, not something install.sh can safely do before the wizard has run. None of these are hard platform blockers, but together they're more integration work than a typical single-container recipe.

name: PicoClaw
source_description: Ultra-lightweight Go AI assistant with native MCP support and 30+ LLM providers
version_health_notes: v0.3.1 published 2026-07-03, 33 days before today (2026-08-05). Release history shows a roughly monthly cadence through 2026: v0.2.6 (Apr 8), v0.2.7 (Apr 22), v0.2.8 (Apr 30), v0.2.9 (May 29), v0.3.1 (Jul 3), with nightly builds published in between (e.g. v0.3.1-nightly.20260702). Docker Hub tags for sipeed/picoclaw confirm the same cadence, with matching "-launcher" variant tags for every version. Repo is not archived and shows ongoing commits — active development, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: Same "self-hosted AI agent with a messaging-bot gateway plus a web console" shape as the two existing recipes openclaw and hermes-agent: a long-running gateway that relays tasks through chat platforms (Telegram, Discord, Matrix, IRC, WeCom, and others — 19+ channels claimed), backed by a web launcher/dashboard, routed through 30+ LLM providers via user-supplied API keys, with MCP server support recently added (v0.2.8+). PicoClaw's actual pitch (ultra-lightweight, <10MB RAM, runs on a $10 Raspberry Pi, sub-1s startup, written from scratch in Go) is a genuine differentiator on constrained edge/embedded hardware, but that specific value proposition mostly evaporates on an IONOS cloud VM with GBs of RAM to spare — the resource floor a customer here cares about is "does it run at all," which openclaw and hermes-agent already clear. No feature (channel count, provider count, MCP support) is exclusive to PicoClaw relative to the other two.
usefulness_rationale: Active, MIT-licensed, monthly-shipping project, but its headline selling point (extreme resource efficiency on tiny/embedded hardware) is largely irrelevant in a cloud-VM hosting context, and the catalogue already has two recipes (openclaw, hermes-agent) covering the same "messaging-bot AI agent with web dashboard" niche with more mature dashboards. A third entry adds redundancy without a use case a typical IONOS customer would reach for over the existing two.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the upstream docker/docker-compose.yml and web/backend/launcherconfig/config.go (sipeed/picoclaw @ main): the launcher web console does have its own login, but the admin password is set through an interactive first-run setup wizard in the browser, not via any environment variable read at container start. The config struct stores a `DashboardPasswordHash` (bcrypt) once a password has been chosen, but there is no `PICOCLAW_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` / `..._HASH`-style env var to pre-seed it before first boot — the legacy `PICOCLAW_LAUNCHER_TOKEN` env var that once served this purpose was removed upstream (migrated once into the password-login flow, then dropped). This is the same shape as Agent Zero and Adminer in apps-gaps precedent: no channel exists today to project a generated_from ROOT_PASSWORD hash into the app's own login, whether because the comparison is plaintext or, as here, because there is no env-var input at all for the hash.

Workaround, same pattern as n8n/OpenClaw/WUD/Open WebUI/Immich/Agent Zero: leave the launcher's first-run wizard unconfigured behind the scenes and gate the single public port (18800) with Traefik `basic_auth: true`, projecting the root-password hash there instead. This also closes the unauthenticated-setup-wizard race window (anyone hitting the URL before the customer completes first-run setup could otherwise claim the admin account).

LLM provider credentials (Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini/DeepSeek/etc.) and messaging-channel tokens (Telegram bot token, Discord webhook, etc.) are configured post-provision through the web console's setup wizards, not required as an env var at first boot — same deferred pattern already shipped in openclaw and hermes-agent, not a blocker.

The gateway's webhook listener (port 18790) binds to 127.0.0.1 by default and is only exposed on 0.0.0.0 when `PICOCLAW_GATEWAY_HOST` is set for the launcher profile; it does not need to be publicly routed through Traefik — only the 18800 web console port does, so the app is still reverse-proxy-compatible on a single public HTTP port.
summary: PicoClaw is an active, MIT-licensed, monthly-shipping Go rewrite of the same "messaging-bot AI agent with a web console" idea already covered by openclaw and hermes-agent. It is mechanically installable today — gate the single public web-console port (18800) with Traefik basic_auth instead of driving the app's own first-run password wizard, which has no env-var input channel for a projected root-password hash — but its actual differentiator (running on $10 embedded hardware with <10MB RAM) has little bearing on a cloud-VM customer, and the catalogue already has two recipes in this exact niche with more mature web dashboards. Not recommended as a third entry without a concrete customer ask.

name: PicoShare
source_description: Minimalist self-hosted file sharing with expiring links and no size limits
version_health_notes: v1.5.4 released 2026-05-26, ~2.3 months before this analysis (2026-08-05). Releases have landed roughly every 1-3 months over the past year (1.5.0 2025-07-28, 1.5.1 2025-08-24, 1.5.2 2026-05-13, v1.5.3 2026-05-25, v1.5.4 2026-05-26), and commit activity continues past the last tag (a docs commit merged 2026-07-14). Single maintainer (mtlynch) describes it as a hobby project, but it is not archived and is clearly still triaged and shipped.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers ad-hoc file/link sharing. Syncthing does continuous multi-device folder sync, not one-off shareable download links with expiry; Immich/Paperless are media/doc archives, not general file drop tools. PicoShare fills a distinct "send someone a file with a link that expires" use case with no size or file-type restriction.
usefulness_rationale: Handy, low-friction utility for anyone who wants a private WeTransfer/Firefox-Send alternative on their own domain. Single maintainer and modest feature set (no teams, no encryption at rest) keep it a niche/personal tool rather than a broad-appeal app.
blocking_issues: PicoShare's admin login has no separate hashed-secret storage path. The server holds PS_SHARED_SECRET (or PS_SHARED_SECRET_FILE) and, on each login attempt, runs the SAME key-derivation function over both the stored value and the value the admin types in before comparing the derived keys (handlers/auth/shared_secret/shared_secret.go: StartSession()). That means whatever string is placed in PS_SHARED_SECRET must be the exact literal passphrase the customer types at login — functionally a plaintext requirement, not a hash PicoShare separately knows how to verify against (unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN, which does accept a pre-hashed value). Our platform's only channel, `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext — so there is no way to hand the customer a passphrase they know and also satisfy PS_SHARED_SECRET's literal-match requirement. A Traefik basic_auth gate in front does not resolve this either: it would add a second, independent login, but the customer would still need the real (unknowable, since server-generated) PS_SHARED_SECRET to get past PicoShare's own admin screen and actually use the app (upload files, create share/guest links) — there's no anonymous-admin path. This is a structural requirement for a plaintext customer-known secret, not merely an unsupported hash algorithm, so it doesn't fit the "flag as blocked_on_platform with the algo named" carve-out in SCHEMA.md.
summary: PicoShare is a small, actively maintained (releases every 1-3 months, latest v1.5.4 on 2026-05-26), reverse-proxy-friendly single-container app that would add a genuinely new "expiring file link" capability not covered by the existing 24 recipes. It is blocked today only because its admin login requires the literal passphrase the customer will type, and af-api's only secret-projection mechanism (`generated_from`) ever supplies a hash of the root password, never the plaintext. Revisit if the platform ever adds a plaintext-secret projection channel; until then this is not mechanically installable via the current recipe mechanism.

Shipping a recipe on top of an app the author has publicly abandoned is a poor long-term bet regardless of mechanical installability.
blocking_issues: Picsur's only login is a fixed "admin" username whose password comes from the `PICSUR_ADMIN_PASSWORD` env var. Checked against the backend source (`user-db.module.ts` / `user-db.service.ts`): this value is consumed as plaintext at container start and bcrypt-hashed internally by the app itself — there is no way to hand it an already-hashed credential, so `generated_from` (which only ever produces a hash of ROOT_PASSWORD) cannot be projected into it directly. Workaround: generate `PICSUR_ADMIN_PASSWORD` randomly server-side (customer never needs it) and put the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate carrying the actual customer-facing credential (bcrypt hash of ROOT_PASSWORD) — the same pattern used for Chibisafe and Alerta's equivalent plaintext-only admin passwords. This is a design-choice workaround, not a hard blocker.
summary: Picsur is mechanically installable today: it's a single app container (ghcr.io/caramelfur/picsur) plus Postgres behind one HTTP port (8080), no extra raw ports, no external API key or OAuth requirement. Its plaintext-only admin-password env var can't take a `generated_from` hash directly, but the standard workaround — random server-generated admin password internally, real customer credential enforced via a Traefik `basic_auth` gate — makes it installable now. The blocker is upstream health, not mechanism: the maintainer has explicitly and publicly declared the project "NOT MAINTAINED" (README, as of the 2025-10-12 commit), it never progressed past self-declared beta, and the last release was 21 months ago. Combined with `chibisafe` already covering the identical "upload image/file, get shareable link" niche while being actively released, Picsur is not_recommended: overlap alone wouldn't disqualify it, but abandonment by its own author on top of a healthier same-niche alternative already in the backlog does.

name: PieFed
source_description: Federated Reddit-style link aggregator with strong moderation tools
