Tags in the preceding month show a very tight cadence — v1.7.9 (2026-08-03), v1.7.8 (2026-07-24), v1.7.7 (2026-07-19), v1.7.6 (2026-07-17), v1.7.5 (2026-07-10), v1.7.4/v1.7.3 (2026-07-08), v1.7.2 (2026-07-06) — multiple releases per week. Repo shows 78 releases and 7000+ commits on main. Clearly an actively developed, non-EOL project with an engaged single-lead (rimu) + contributor community (Matrix room, in-app devs community).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers federated link-aggregation / forum-style social software. Gitea and Opengist are code-hosting tools, not discussion platforms. PieFed (a Lemmy/Kbin-style ActivityPub federated Reddit alternative) would be a genuinely new category for customers wanting to run their own fediverse community.
usefulness_rationale: Federated forum software has real demand (Lemmy/Kbin communities exist and grow), and PieFed differentiates on moderation tooling. But it is a multi-service stack (Postgres + Redis + Celery workers) requiring a real domain for ActivityPub federation, background cron jobs, and ongoing moderation attention — a heavier commitment than most of our current single-purpose utility recipes, which narrows the addressable customer base somewhat.
blocking_issues:
There is no official pre-built image on a registry. The shipped `compose.yaml` builds the app image from a Dockerfile in the checked-out git tag (`git checkout v1.7.x && docker compose up --build`); third-party images exist (e.g. elestio/piefed, dockur/piefed) but are unofficial repackagings, not the upstream recommended path. A recipe would need to pin a git ref and build on first boot rather than pull a tagged image — workable, but a different pattern than our other docker-compose recipes.

The admin account is created by `flask init-db` (run once via `docker exec` after first boot), which collects username, email, and password through interactive `input()` prompts in app/cli.py — not via any environment variable. Critically, `User.set_password()` (app/models.py) always calls `generate_password_hash(password)` on whatever plaintext it is given; there is no code path that accepts a pre-computed hash instead. Our platform's only secret-projection mechanism, `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, only ever supplies a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so it cannot be threaded through this flow. This is the same structural problem documented for PicoShare (`apps-gaps/picoshare.yaml`): a genuine requirement for a plaintext customer-known secret, not an unsupported hash algorithm, so it is not the "flag as blocked_on_platform with the algo named" carve-out in SCHEMA.md by itself — see the mitigation note below.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front would not resolve the second issue: PieFed has its own login separate from any gate, and the admin account still needs a password the customer knows, which our mechanism cannot supply as plaintext.
summary: PieFed is an actively developed (releases multiple times a week, latest v1.7.10 on 2026-08-05), reverse-proxy-friendly federated link-aggregator that would add a genuinely new social/community category to the catalogue. It is blocked today for two independent reasons: there is no official pre-built image to pin (the app is built from source at a git tag), and its one-time `flask init-db` admin setup requires the plaintext admin password via an interactive prompt, which our `generated_from` mechanism (hash-only) cannot supply. The image-building issue is a recipe-design problem we could likely work around; the plaintext-admin-password issue is the same structural blocker seen with PicoShare and requires a platform change (a plaintext-secret projection channel) before this can ship.

source_description: Self-hosted multi-user podcast manager with cross-device playback sync
version_health_notes: v0.9.0 released 2026-06-26, about 6 weeks (~1.4 months) before this analysis (2026-08-05) — "Video, CarPlay, Android Auto, and a Whole New Look", a 220+-commit release. Not archived, not in maintenance-only mode; clearly active.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers podcast subscription management. Immich and Paperless-ngx are media/document archives with a completely different content type; nothing else touches audio/RSS-feed consumption. PinePods adds a genuinely new "self-hosted Spotify-for-podcasts" category: multi-user subscriptions, per-episode progress synced across web/desktop/mobile (including CarPlay/Android Auto as of v0.9.0), a built-in gpodder-compatible sync server so third-party apps like AntennaPod can point at it, and OIDC/SSO plus MFA/TOTP support.

blocking_issues:
PinePods' official docker-compose example provisions the sole admin account via USERNAME/PASSWORD/FULLNAME/EMAIL environment variables, consumed by the startup.sh script (which exports them verbatim and hands off to a compiled pinepods-db-setup binary) with no documented support for accepting a pre-hashed value — unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN, which explicitly supports either a plaintext or an Argon2-hash comparison. PASSWORD appears to be treated as the literal passphrase the admin will type at every future login. Our platform's only projection channel, `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, supplies a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext — setting PASSWORD to that hash would create an account whose real credential is an opaque hash string the customer doesn't know, not their actual root password, so they could never log back in. This is the same structural "app needs the literal plaintext" problem documented in apps-gaps/picoshare.yaml.

If USERNAME/PASSWORD/FULLNAME/EMAIL are omitted entirely, PinePods instead boots with zero users and presents an open account-creation screen to the first visitor of the public URL — whoever reaches it first becomes the sole admin. This is the identical "first-visitor self-registration race" already documented as a platform blocker in apps-gaps/airtrail.yaml, apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml, and apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml: a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front would stop a random internet stranger from reaching the registration form, but it only supplies one root-password-derived credential for the gate itself — it cannot also hand the customer a second, distinct credential for the in-app signup form, so the race is only pushed one layer deeper (to "first person through the shared basic_auth gate").
summary: PinePods is an active, actively-developed (release 6 weeks ago, nightly builds ongoing), reverse-proxy-friendly (single port 8040, internal nginx fronts both the main API and the gpodder-sync API) podcast manager that would be a genuinely new, high-appeal category for the catalogue — nothing else in the current 24 recipes touches podcasts. It is blocked today for the same reason as PicoShare and AirTrail: its only two provisioning paths for the initial admin account are (a) an env var that appears to require the literal plaintext password, which `generated_from` cannot supply since it only ever carries a hash, or (b) an open first-visitor self-registration screen that a `basic_auth` gate cannot fully secure end to end. Revisit if the platform gains a plaintext-capable secret channel, or if upstream documents pre-hashed PASSWORD support.

summary: Piwigo is an active, well-maintained gallery/publishing app distinct from Immich's personal-backup niche, and it is mechanically deployable today: bundle a MariaDB/MySQL sidecar with a server-generated DB password (no customer input needed, same pattern as n8n/paperless-ngx), and put the whole app — including the first-run install wizard — behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate whose password is projected from the customer's root password via generated_from. That gate is necessary rather than optional here: without it, anyone who reaches the domain before the customer completes Piwigo's own install wizard could claim the admin account. The wizard itself still requires the customer to manually choose their in-app admin username/password on first visit after logging in through the gate; that hop is unavoidable since Piwigo gives no other input channel, but it's an acceptable one-time manual step rather than a structural blocker. Recommend build_with_caveats: installable now, narrower audience than Immich, and the install-wizard hand-off should be called out clearly in the recipe's post-install instructions.

name: Plandex
source_description: Open-source terminal AI coding agent for large multi-step coding tasks
version_health_notes: Cadence was roughly monthly through mid-2025 (v2.1.6 2025-05-27, v2.1.7 2025-06-04, v2.1.8 2025-06-08, v2.2.0 2025-07-01, v2.2.1 2025-07-16), then stopped entirely: no release since v2.2.1, over 13 months before this analysis (2026-08-05). The last commit to `main` of any kind was on 2025-10-03, a docs/README update announcing that "Plandex Cloud is winding down as of 10/3/2025 and no longer accepting new users" — i.e. the vendor's own hosted product was discontinued, and there has been no commit activity (~10 months) since that announcement. The GitHub repo is not marked archived and issues/PRs remain open, but the combination of a killed commercial offering and total code silence since is a strong dormancy signal rather than a quiet-but-healthy project. The docs subdomain (docs.plandex.ai) and marketing site (plandex.ai) both failed to resolve (DNS SERVFAIL) during this research session — noted as a soft signal only, since search engines still have both indexed; not treated as a confirmed outage.
differentiation: All three are terminal AI coding agents, but Plandex's actual differentiator is architectural, not cosmetic: it maintains a persistent, versioned "plan" per task (multi-file diff sandbox, full change history, ability to review/rewind before applying to the real repo) backed by a Postgres-persisted server, versus claude-code/ gemini-cli which apply edits directly with no separate review/rollback layer. It also indexes up to ~20M tokens of project context via tree-sitter maps and supports a real multi-user/team server mode (shared plans across an org) that neither existing CLI recipe offers. Per CLAUDE.md's overlap policy this is evaluated on its own merits, not penalized for covering similar ground.
usefulness_rationale: The differentiation above is real, but the specific self-hosted-server mode that delivers it (team plans, Postgres persistence) is exactly the part now unmaintained for over a year with the vendor's own cloud version of the same feature discontinued. Shipping a recipe whose unique selling point rides on the least-maintained part of a single-maintainer project that has gone quiet is high risk for low reward — a customer gets a CLI tool materially inferior in support and momentum to the two comparable tools already in the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
The self-hosted server ships two modes. "Local mode" (LOCAL_MODE=1, the Docker Compose example in app/docker-compose.yml) is explicitly documented as "designed for local use with a single user" and skips real account verification entirely — anyone who can reach the API port can sign up as an org member. That is not safe to expose on a public <slug>.<base_domain> without a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the whole API surface (expressible today, listed above).

"Production mode" (GOENV=production, the mode meant for real multi-user exposure) instead requires SMTP_HOST/SMTP_PORT/ SMTP_USER/SMTP_PASSWORD for email-based PIN verification — an external third-party service credential with no customer-supplied value channel in the current /compose mechanism. Production mode is therefore not installable_today; only the local-mode-plus-basic-auth path is.

Either way, actually using Plandex to code requires the customer to supply their own LLM provider API key (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, or a Claude Pro/Max login) at CLI-usage time. Per the claude-code/gemini-cli precedent this is not a first-boot blocker — it's entered interactively by the CLI user themselves, same as the existing recipes' ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / GEMINI_API_KEY parameters.

No web UI at all — it is a CLI (`plandex`/`pdx`) talking to an HTTP API server, so `reverse_proxy_compatible` in the browsable-app sense is false even though the API port itself could sit behind Traefik.
summary: Plandex is mechanically installable as a docker-compose recipe (Postgres + plandexai/plandex-server, run in LOCAL_MODE with the whole API gated behind Traefik basic_auth, LLM API key supplied by the customer interactively via the CLI) — production mode is blocked on an SMTP credential with no input channel, but the local-mode path clears the installable_today bar. The recommendation is not_recommended anyway: the project's one commercial cloud offering was wound down on 2025-10-03 and there has been no commit of any kind since, versus a steady near-monthly cadence before that. Its genuine architectural differentiation over claude-code/gemini-cli (persistent reviewable plans, team server mode) is precisely the unmaintained self-hosted-server part of the project, making it a weak bet to ship a recipe around right now.

name: Plane
source_description: Open-source project management tool for issue tracking and sprints
version_health_notes: v1.4.0 (stable) released 2026-07-31, about 5 days before this analysis (2026-08-05); v1.4.1-rc1/rc2 release candidates followed on 2026-08-04 and 2026-08-05 respectively, so upstream is actively cutting new builds right up to today. Prior stable releases: v1.3.1 (2025-05-14), v1.3.0 (2025-04-06), v1.2.3 (2025-03-05), v1.2.2 (2025-02-23) — roughly monthly cadence sustained over more than a year. Not archived, not in maintenance-only mode; clearly active, well-funded (backed by Plane the company, YC-funded) open-core project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers project management / issue tracking / sprint planning. Gitea is the closest existing recipe by audience (developer-tools) but is a git-hosting server whose issue tracker is a secondary feature bolted onto repository management — it has no sprints, cycles, roadmaps, or Kanban/Gantt views. Plane is a dedicated Jira/Linear-style tool: issues, cycles (sprints), modules, pages/docs, and a "God mode" instance-admin panel — a genuinely new category for the catalogue and one with mainstream, everyday-use appeal (every team doing software work needs some form of this).
usefulness_rationale: Project/issue tracking is a category most self-hosting customers actively look for by name (as a Jira/Linear/Asana alternative), and Plane is one of the most complete, actively developed, and widely deployed open-source options in that space (its own blog cites 100,000+ Docker and 44,000 Kubernetes self-hosted deploys). High everyday utility, unlike some of the narrower niche apps triaged elsewhere in this pipeline.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the official self-host release artifacts (docker-compose.yml + variables.env published on the v1.4.0 GitHub release, and developers.plane.so/self-hosting docs): there is no admin-username/admin-password environment variable anywhere in the stack. All internal secrets (SECRET_KEY, LIVE_SERVER_SECRET_KEY, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, RABBITMQ_PASSWORD, MinIO root credentials) are inter-service plumbing with sensible defaults, not the customer-facing account. Instead, the first visitor to reach the deployed URL is shown a "Let's secure your instance" screen where they type any email and password of their choosing to become the sole Instance Admin with access to /god-mode. This is the same first-visitor self-registration-race shape already documented in apps-gaps/pinepods.yaml, apps-gaps/airtrail.yaml, apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml, and apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml — there is no `type: password` login parameter on Plane's own account to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var or accepted as a pre-hashed value.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would stop a random internet stranger from reaching that signup screen, but per the same precedent it only supplies one root-password-derived credential (for the gate itself) — it cannot also hand the customer a second, distinct credential for the in-app instance-admin signup form, so the race is only pushed one layer deeper (first person through the shared gate becomes Instance Admin instead of first person on the open internet). Compounding this, Plane's default instance setting "Allow anyone to sign up without an invite" is ON out of the box, meaning even after an admin is set, further open self-registration into workspaces continues until someone manually visits /god-mode → Authentication and disables it — a step with no automated hook in our current install flow.
summary: Plane is an active, well-funded, actively-released (stable build 5 days before this analysis, release candidates cut daily) project-management tool that would fill a genuinely new, high-appeal category — nothing in the current 24 recipes covers issue tracking / sprints / Kanban. It is architecturally reverse-proxy-compatible: the official stack ships its own bundled proxy container (makeplane/plane-proxy) fronting five internal services (web, api, space, admin, live) on a single port 80/443, which Traefik can sit in front of exactly like it already does for other multi-service recipes (immich, anytype-server). It is blocked today for the same structural reason as PinePods, AirTrail, 2FAuth, and Activepieces: there is no env var to preset the sole Instance Admin account, only an open first-visitor self-registration screen that neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely hand to the customer exclusively. Revisit if upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow, or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond root-password projection.

Plausible is one of the best-known self-hosted GA alternatives (cookie-free, no personal-data collection, GDPR-friendly by design) and a genuinely common ask for anyone running a marketing site or SaaS product who wants analytics without Google.

summary: Plausible CE's official `plausible/community-edition` compose stack is three containers — `postgres:16-alpine` (user/account data), `clickhouse/clickhouse-server:24.12-alpine` (events data), and the app itself, `ghcr.io/plausible/community-edition:v3.2.1` — fronted by a single HTTP port (default 8000, reconfigurable via `HTTP_PORT`) that Plausible's own entrypoint can even TLS-terminate directly, so it sits behind Traefik exactly like Immich's or Paperless-ngx's multi-service stacks already do. The two required env vars, `BASE_URL` and `SECRET_KEY_BASE` (a random ≥64-byte secret used for session signing), are both server-side — `BASE_URL` derives from the assigned domain and `SECRET_KEY_BASE` is exactly the kind of patternless secret AF already generates with no customer input. Postgres's own password is likewise internal-only (default `postgres`, container-to-container, never customer-facing). The one real credential concern: Plausible has no admin env var at all — the first person to open the assigned domain gets a plain signup form and becomes the instance's first (and effectively admin) user. `DISABLE_REGISTRATION` defaults to `invite_only`, but the shipped registration plug (`PlausibleWeb.Plugs.MaybeDisableRegistration`, confirmed by reading `lib/plausible_web/plugs/maybe_disable_registration.ex` in the v3.2.1 source) explicitly bypasses that restriction on "first launch" (no users yet in the DB) — so registration is open by design for exactly the window that matters. That's the same open-first-registration race n8n and WUD already ship with in this catalogue; per SCHEMA.md the fix is a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate keyed off the customer's root-password hash, which closes the race without needing any Plausible-side change. With that gate, `installable_today` is true. Version health is strong (active app-repo commits days before this analysis, tightening tagged-release cadence, a promptly-patched CVE) and the product niche (privacy-first web analytics) has zero overlap with the existing 24 recipes. Recommend `build_now`.

name: Plex
source_description: Popular media server for streaming movies, TV shows, music, and photos
upstream_license: Proprietary (closed-source; free core server, paid Plex Pass tier; remote streaming of personal media now requires Plex Pass or Remote Watch Pass as of 2025-04-29 enforcement)
version_health_notes: plexinc/pms-docker gets new PMS point-release tags roughly every 1-4 weeks (1.43.1.10611 -> 1.43.2.10687 beta -> 1.43.3.10828 (~23 days before today) -> 1.43.3.10861 (~2 days before today, 2026-08-05)). Repo is not archived and Plex Inc. is an active commercial company; no dormancy or EOL signal on the server product itself. Note the separate, unrelated 2025-04-29 policy change requiring Plex Pass/Remote Watch Pass for *remote* streaming of personal media — a monetization/licensing shift, not a maintenance or EOL signal.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24 covers general-purpose personal video/TV library streaming. Immich is the closest existing recipe by "self-hosted personal media" flavor but is strictly a photo/video backup and AI-organized gallery, not a transcoding library server for movies and TV shows with broad smart-TV/mobile client support. Plex is the best-known brand in this category; apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml and apps-gaps/emby.yaml already analyze the same "Plex-style media server" gap and were both found high-usefulness but blocked_on_platform on unrelated grounds (interactive local admin setup wizard with no env-var seed hook). Plex is architecturally different from both: it has no local admin account at all — every server is bound to a plex.tv cloud account instead.
usefulness_rationale: Home media/TV streaming is one of the most commonly requested self-hosting use cases, and Plex specifically is the most widely-recognized brand in the category (more so than Jellyfin or Emby), which gives it strong pull for a customer browsing the catalogue. That demand is real, but see installability below — the blocker here is structurally different from, and arguably harder than, Jellyfin/Emby's "open setup wizard" problem.
blocking_issues:
Plex has no local admin account of any kind — unlike Jellyfin/Emby, there is no username/password the app itself manages. Every Plex Media Server must be bound ("claimed") to a real plex.tv cloud account before it does anything useful; the web UI's first-run flow is "Sign In" or "Create Account" against plex.tv, not a local admin signup form. This is the canonical "OAuth app registration / third-party account linking" case the SCHEMA.md fit-table already calls out as having no input channel today, and it is structurally worse than Jellyfin/Emby's problem: even if this platform gains a way to inject a preset admin credential via env var or a `generated_from`-style hash, that mechanism would have nowhere to attach on Plex, because Plex was never going to accept a platform-issued credential for its own account — it only accepts the customer's real, pre-existing (or newly created) plex.tv identity.

The one first-boot input Plex *does* accept, `PLEX_CLAIM`, does not change this: it is a claim token the customer must fetch themselves, interactively and while already signed into plex.tv, from https://plex.tv/claim, and it expires ~4 minutes after being issued. It is not a value af-api's JWE bootstrap token can derive or pre-generate — it is a live, single-use, externally-issued secret tied to a specific plex.tv account, i.e. exactly the "external API key/token the app can't function without" row the SCHEMA.md fit-table already marks as not installable. Skipping PLEX_CLAIM only defers the same sign-in requirement to the web UI on first visit; it does not remove it.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not help here either: it can keep a stranger from reaching the setup page first, but the customer themselves still cannot get a working server out of the wizard without linking a plex.tv account, which is outside anything `generated_from`/root-password projection or basic_auth can supply.

Secondary, non-blocking note: Plex's own docs recommend host or macvlan networking for full functionality (GDM local-network discovery, DLNA, and the more reliable path for Plex clients' "automatic remote access" port-mapping probe). The core web UI only needs TCP/32400 and works fine in bridge mode behind a single-domain Traefik reverse proxy for basic library browsing/streaming, so this is not a structural blocker the way the account-linking issue is — just a functionality caveat that would need documenting if the account-linking blocker were ever lifted.
summary: Plex Media Server itself is healthy and actively released (plexinc/pms-docker gets a new PMS point-release roughly every 1-4 weeks, most recently 2 days before today) and would fill a real, currently-empty "Plex/Jellyfin-style home media streaming" gap that customers plausibly search for by name — more so than the already-analyzed Jellyfin or Emby, given Plex's brand recognition. It is not installable today, and its blocker is a harder variant of Jellyfin/Emby's "no env-var admin seed" gap: Plex has no local admin account to seed at all — every server must be claimed to a real, customer-owned plex.tv cloud account via an interactive sign-in or a short-lived, externally-issued PLEX_CLAIM token, the same third-party account-linking / external-token case SCHEMA.md already rules out (and the same shape of blocker apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml hit for the same reason). Recommend `blocked_on_platform`, consistent with that precedent, but flag that this is a stronger case than Jellyfin/Emby's: those two are fixable in principle with a config-seeding hook and/or an extended `generated_from` algorithm list, whereas Plex would need an entirely different mechanism — a way for the customer to supply a live third-party credential/token at provisioning time, not a root-password-derived hash — before it could ever qualify. Revisit only if/when the platform gains that kind of customer-supplied external- credential channel.

name: Plone

Plone follows a published policy (5 years of security support per major version from its initial release date, minor versions roughly every 12-18 months), which is a healthier, more explicit maintenance signal than most candidates in this catalogue. Not dormant, not archived, not EOL.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes are a general-purpose content management system / website builder. Paperless-ngx and Gitea/Opengist are adjacent in "manage documents/content" spirit but serve document-archival and code-hosting workflows respectively, not building and publishing a public-facing website with pages, versioning, and role-based access control. Plone would open a genuinely new "build a website" category for the catalogue, and its enterprise/government heritage (accessibility, fine-grained permissions, audit trail) is a distinct value prop from lighter CMS competitors.

Per the schema's guidance this is not a hard blocker on its own: a fixed, unchangeable default credential behind a Traefik `basic_auth` gate is an accepted pattern (the gate becomes the real auth boundary), so this app is installable_today provided the whole stack sits behind mandatory basic_auth rather than exposing the admin/admin login directly to the internet.
summary: Plone is a mature, actively maintained enterprise CMS (6.2.1, released 2026-06-26, ~6 weeks before today with a healthy multi-year support policy) and would fill a genuine gap: none of the current 24 recipes cover general-purpose website/content management. It is mechanically installable today, but only via the Traefik basic_auth workaround — the official plone/plone-backend image has no supported way to set the Zope admin password at boot (it ships hardcoded admin/admin), so the customer's own password can't be projected into it via generated_from the way Vaultwarden or n8n do. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building, but plan for a mandatory basic_auth gate up front and expect a heavier multi-container stack (Volto frontend, Zope backend, and ZEO or Postgres/RelStorage for object storage) than our typical single-app+DB recipes.

name: Pocket ID
source_description: Passkey-only OIDC provider for passwordless SSO across self-hosted apps
version_health_notes: v2.12.0 shipped 2026-07-29, about a week before today (2026-08-05), and is described upstream as containing security fixes with an explicit "highly recommended to update" note. Releases through 2026 have landed roughly every 2-4 weeks (v2.6.1/v2.6.2 on 2026-04-21, v2.7.0 on 2026-05-11, v2.8.0 on 2026-05-31, v2.9.0 on 2026-06-16, v2.10.0/v2.11.0 in July, v2.12.0 on 2026-07-29). Repo is not archived; this is a genuinely active, fast-moving project.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes provide identity/SSO functionality. Pocket ID occupies the same conceptual niche already flagged for Authentik and Keycloak in prior gap analyses (neither shipped yet) but is a much lighter-weight alternative: a single Go binary + embedded SQLite by default, no worker/Postgres services, purpose-built for homelab/small-team OIDC SSO rather than full enterprise IAM. It specifically differentiates on being passkey-only (no password/TOTP login path at all), which is a distinct selling point for customers who want WebAuthn-based SSO without running a heavier IdP.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted SSO is a recurring ask for customers running several AF recipes side by side, and Pocket ID's low resource footprint (SQLite, single container) makes it a much easier operational fit than Authentik/Keycloak for that same demand. Passkey-only auth is also a genuine differentiator worth having in the catalogue on its own merits.
blocking_issues:
Pocket ID has no admin-bootstrap environment variable of any kind (confirmed against the full env-var list in backend/internal/common/env_config.go — no ADMIN_* or *_PASSWORD* field exists). The first admin account is provisioned entirely client-side: whoever first navigates to https://<app-url>/setup registers a WebAuthn passkey and becomes the sole admin. There is no plaintext password or hash involved at any point — a passkey is a public-key credential generated on the visitor's own device — so this is categorically outside what `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` can produce (it only ever emits a password hash, never a key pair). This is a harder blocker than Authentik/Keycloak's plaintext/ unsupported-hash problem: there is no hash-shaped value to project at all.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front of the whole app does not cleanly substitute either, for two independent reasons: (1) Pocket ID's own login/setup UI is the ongoing product surface end users must keep reaching for SSO into other apps, not just an admin panel being protected — the same reasoning that ruled out a gate for Authentik; and (2) even used narrowly to close the /setup race window, "gate + client-side self-registration behind it" is the same shape already flagged as unvalidated on 2FAuth's gap analysis, not an accepted combo today.
summary: Pocket ID is an active, lightweight, BSD-licensed passkey-only OIDC provider that would fill the same real catalogue gap already identified for Authentik and Keycloak — self-hosted SSO — with a notably smaller footprint (single container, embedded SQLite, no worker/DB services). Mechanically it's a clean single-port web app, fully reverse-proxy compatible. It fails installability today for a more fundamental reason than its heavier IdP cousins: there is no admin-bootstrap credential of any kind to project, because the first admin account is created via an open /setup race and a client-generated WebAuthn passkey rather than any password or hash. Revisit as `build_now` once the platform gains either a way to pre-seed/lock the first-admin setup flow to the deploying customer, or a genuinely validated "gate then self-register" pattern — until then this sits alongside Authentik/Keycloak as blocked on the same class of platform gap.

name: PocketBase
source_description: Open-source backend for your next SaaS and mobile app in a single file
version_health_notes: Confirmed via the GitHub releases page (not training-data recall): the project ships on two parallel branches — v0.39.x (current line, v0.39.7 2026-07-16 → v0.39.8 2026-07-19 → v0.39.9 2026-07-22 → v0.39.10 2026-07-30) and v0.22.x (backport line, receiving matching releases the same days for security/stability fixes). As of today 2026-08-05, the latest release (v0.39.10) is only 6 days old, and the repo shows releases multiple times a month on both branches — clearly active, not slowing. 60.5k GitHub stars, 2,443+ commits. Project explicitly notes it is pre-1.0 ("full backward compatibility is not guaranteed before reaching v1.0.0") but has been in this state for years without signs of abandonment.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes cover a general-purpose app backend (embedded SQLite database, realtime subscriptions, auth, file storage, and a REST-ish API behind an admin dashboard). n8n is workflow automation and Anytype Server is personal knowledge sync — neither serves the "backend for your own SaaS/mobile app" use case PocketBase targets. This would be a genuinely new category: a self-hosted Supabase/Firebase-style BaaS for customers building their own apps on top of the AF-hosted instance.
usefulness_rationale: Very high real-world adoption (60k+ stars) and fills a gap none of our existing recipes touch — a lightweight backend a customer's own app/mobile client talks to, not just an end-user-facing tool. Held back from being a slam dunk only by the installability gap below.
blocking_issues:
No official Docker image: pocketbase/pocketbase ships as a single prebuilt binary (confirmed on the GitHub Releases page and pocketbase.io/docs/going-to-production, whose own Docker example is a hand-rolled Dockerfile that downloads and unzips the release binary). A docker-compose recipe would have to depend on an unofficial third-party image (e.g. ghcr.io/muchobien/pocketbase, the most widely-used community build) rather than a vendor-published one — a supply-chain/maintenance risk beyond the usual "pin a tag" concern.

No channel to project generated_from onto the superuser login: the only two supported ways to set the initial superuser email/password — the CLI command `pocketbase superuser create EMAIL PASS` (or `upsert`), and the community image's PB_ADMIN_EMAIL / PB_ADMIN_PASSWORD env vars which just call that same command — both take a plaintext password and bcrypt-hash it internally on write. PocketBase's underlying auth record model can technically store an already-hashed bcrypt value directly (`record.SetRaw("password", "$2a$...")`, confirmed via PocketBase JSVM docs/discussions), which is the same trick Vaultwarden uses for ADMIN_TOKEN — but that path is only reachable by writing a custom Go/JSVM migration script executed at container startup, not through any documented CLI flag or env var. Today's recipe mechanism (env-var templating over a fixed docker-compose file) has no way to run that custom script, so `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` cannot actually reach this app's login yet, even though bcrypt is a supported algorithm in principle.

Traefik basic_auth is not a clean substitute here: PocketBase's core value is the REST/realtime API that a customer's own mobile or web app calls directly, not just the admin dashboard a human logs into. Gating the whole public port behind basic_auth (the pattern used for apps with no login of their own, e.g. Adminer) would also block that API traffic, breaking the actual product this recipe would be installed for. Scoping basic_auth to just the /_/ admin path would dodge that, but leaves the superuser login itself ungated by anything root-password-derived, and path-scoped Traefik auth isn't a mechanism this catalogue currently uses in any recipe.
summary: PocketBase would be a strong, differentiated addition — a genuinely new BaaS/backend category with no overlap among the current 24 recipes, MIT licensed with no commercial-hosting restriction, a single reverse-proxy- friendly HTTP port, and an active project (latest release 6 days old as of 2026-08-05, multiple releases a month across two branches). The blocker is mechanism, not merit: there is no official Docker image (would have to ship on an unofficial community build), and more importantly the superuser login only accepts a plaintext password through every documented interface (CLI command and the community image's env vars), with no supported way to inject an already-hashed value without writing and running a custom migration script the current install.sh/env-var mechanism has no channel for. Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit once either an official image ships or the platform gains a way to run a one-off setup script at first boot (which would also make the bcrypt SetRaw trick usable).

name: Polaris
source_description: Lightweight self-hosted music streaming server written in Rust with web UI
version_health_notes: 0.16.1 shipped 2026-05-08, about 3 months before today (2026-08-05); the most recent commit on master is also 2026-05-08 ("Updated changelog for 0.16.1"), with steady commits through April/May 2026 (0.16.0 on 2026-03-05, 0.15.0 on 2026-02-05, and further back 0.14.3, 0.14.2, 0.14.1, 0.14.0 at roughly 1-3 month intervals). Repo is not archived, 28 open issues, single maintainer (agersant) but consistently active — reads as a genuinely maintained small project, not dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 built recipes covers personal music streaming; Immich is the closest neighbor by "self-hosted personal media" flavor but is strictly photo/video. This is the same niche already surfaced by two prior gap analyses, [[airsonic-advanced]] (rejected: dormant 2+ years, no stable release ever cut) and [[ampache]] (recommended build_now: actively maintained, no blocker). Polaris is a third entrant in that niche — smaller/lighter than either (single Rust binary, no bundled DB server) but with a narrower installability story than Ampache due to its auth mechanism (see below).
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted music streaming has a real recurring audience and Polaris is lightweight and actively maintained, but Ampache already fills this niche with a clean build_now path; Polaris only adds value as an alternative if Ampache's footprint (bundled MariaDB) is a concern, and that upside is undercut by the auth-provisioning blocker below.
blocking_issues:
Polaris has no default user and no first-run web setup wizard: at least one user must be pre-declared in polaris.toml before the app is usable, via either a plaintext `initial_password` or a `hashed_password` field (confirmed against docs/CONFIGURATION.md). Only the hashed form is a viable customer-derived credential channel (plaintext values never reach /compose today), but Polaris hashes with PBKDF2-SHA256 ("$pbkdf2-sha256$i=10000,l=32$..."), which is not in the current `generated_from` supported-algorithm list (argon2, bcrypt). Per SCHEMA.md this is a genuine hash-format gap, not a plaintext-only requirement — not a hard structural no, but it does block `installable_today` until `generated_from` supports pbkdf2-sha256.

agersant/polaris publishes no official Docker image; the only packaged option is the third-party, community-maintained registry.gitlab.com/connectical/container/polaris (also mirrored on Quay.io), adding an extra maintenance dependency outside upstream's own release process.
summary: Polaris is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (5050) music streamer that would sit behind Traefik the same way Vaultwarden/Uptime Kuma do, and upstream is small but genuinely active (monthly-ish releases through 2026, last one 3 months ago). It's blocked from `installable_today` because Polaris requires at least one pre-declared user at first boot and only accepts that user's password as plaintext or a PBKDF2-SHA256 hash — neither of which our current `generated_from` mechanism (argon2/bcrypt only) can project into. It also depends on an unofficial third-party Docker image rather than one agersant publishes. Given Ampache already covers this niche with a clean build_now path, recommend blocked_on_platform rather than prioritizing pbkdf2-sha256 support just for Polaris.

version_health_notes: Confirmed via GitHub releases API: 15 releases between 2026-06-13 (2.2.49) and 2026-08-04 (3.2.0), i.e. one day before today (2026-08-05) — averaging roughly one release every 3-4 days over the last 8 weeks, including a 2.x -> 3.x major bump on 2026-07-13. Posterizarr is not a media server itself — it is a companion utility that connects to an *already-running* Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby instance and fetches/generates textless poster art, background art, season posters, and title cards from Fanart.tv, TMDB, TVDB, and the media server's own metadata. It has zero standalone value: it needs a working Plex/Jellyfin/Emby deployment to point at, none of which are installable in our catalogue today (apps-gaps/plex.yaml, apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml, and apps-gaps/emby.yaml are all blocked_on_platform for unrelated reasons — no admin-seed channel or, for Plex, no local account at all).

Shipping Posterizarr on its own, disconnected from any media server the customer could get from us, is a niche, low-demand offering on its own merits.
blocking_issues:
Posterizarr's config.json requires three mandatory third-party API credentials before it can do anything useful: a TMDB API token (themoviedb.org), a Fanart.tv API key, and a TVDB Project API key (thetvdb.com). All three are external accounts the customer must register for themselves and paste in manually — exactly the "external API key/token the app can't function without" case SCHEMA.md already marks as having no input channel today.

It also requires the URL and auth token/API key of an existing Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby server to scan and enrich. We have no installable recipe for any of those three media servers today (see apps-gaps/plex.yaml, apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml, apps-gaps/emby.yaml), so even a customer willing to hand-enter Posterizarr's own API keys would have nowhere to point it — this is a second, independent external-credential blocker on top of the first.

The web UI (port 8000) ships with no built-in login of its own ("Default credentials: none required" per upstream docs), so it would need a Traefik basic_auth gate to avoid sitting open — that piece alone is expressible via generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD projection, but it does not unblock the two API-key/media-server issues above.
summary: Posterizarr is a healthy, fast-moving project (15 releases in the last 8 weeks, latest 3.2.0 shipped one day before today) that fills no gap in our catalogue on its own: it is a pure companion utility for an already-running Plex/Jellyfin/Emby library, none of which we can currently provision as recipes. Beyond that dependency problem, it also requires three mandatory external API keys (TMDB, Fanart.tv, TVDB) that have no customer-input channel under the current /compose mechanism. Even with a Traefik basic_auth gate covering its own login-less web UI, two independent, unrelated blockers remain. Recommend not_recommended — revisit only if the platform gains a general external-API-key input channel *and* at least one of Plex/Jellyfin/Emby becomes installable, since Posterizarr provides no value without the latter regardless.

name: PostgreSQL
source_description: PostgreSQL is a powerful, open-source object-relational database system
latest_version: 18.4 (current stable line); 17.10, 16.14, 15.18, 14.23 also maintained; 19 Beta 2 in testing
version_health_notes: 18.4 (and the parallel 17.10/16.14/15.18/14.23 point releases) shipped 2026-05-14, about 2.9 months before today (2026-08-05) — well inside PostgreSQL's normal quarterly minor-release cadence. PostgreSQL 19 Beta 2 landed 2026-07-16, with GA expected around September/October 2026, showing active major-version development on top of the maintenance releases. This is the official PostgreSQL Global Development Group project and the `postgres` Docker Hub image is the official, actively-updated packaging (docker-library/postgres).
overlaps_with: gitea; guacamole; immich; n8n; paperless-ngx; runtipi
differentiation: None of the listed recipes expose Postgres as a standalone, customer-usable service — each runs its own Postgres (or, for Immich, a Postgres-based fork with pgvecto.rs) internally, on the bridge network only, purely as private storage for that one app. A standalone PostgreSQL recipe would target a different use case: a customer running their own external app (a custom script, a BI tool, a self-hosted SaaS) that needs a Postgres backend to connect to from outside the VM. That's a real, distinct need in principle, but it requires publishing the database port to the internet, which is exactly what the catalogue's own rules forbid (see `blocking_issues`).
usefulness_rationale: Would be useful to technical customers who want a managed Postgres backend for something they run themselves, but it's a developer/ power-user tool with no UI of its own, and its one useful exposure shape (a public 5432) is one our own recipe rules already reject on security grounds. Same structural class as MySQL and MariaDB (apps-gaps/mysql.yaml, apps-gaps/mariadb.yaml) — both raw-protocol RDBMS engines with no application-layer presence to gate behind Traefik — and harder to ship than Adminer (apps-gaps/adminer.yaml), which at least has an HTTP UI to gate.
blocking_issues:
The only useful shape for a standalone PostgreSQL recipe is a publicly reachable Postgres-protocol port so an external customer app can connect to it. Publishing host port 5432 is exactly what RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` rule forbids (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226) — 5432 is explicitly on the forbidden-host-port list. There is no alternate exposure path today: Traefik only routes HTTP, and Postgres speaks a raw binary wire protocol, so it cannot be fronted the way our web-UI recipes are (no `basic_auth`, no subdomain routing).

Even setting the port rule aside, the superuser password is only projectable via `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` (a plaintext env var, which `generated_from` does not produce) — the official image has no pre-hashed-password input at all (unlike MySQL/MariaDB's `*_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASH` variants). So this credential is not even a `blocked_on_platform`-shaped gap waiting on a new supported hash algorithm; Postgres structurally requires the plaintext password at container start, which `generated_from` can never supply. Moot anyway given the public-port blocker above.
summary: PostgreSQL is an actively maintained, healthy upstream project (18.4 released under 3 months before this analysis, 19 Beta already out), but a standalone PostgreSQL recipe has no viable shape in the current catalogue. Its only useful exposure — a public, customer-reachable 5432 — is explicitly forbidden by our own `no-public-db-port` rule, and it has no web UI to gate behind Traefik/basic_auth the way our other no-login apps do. None of the existing 24 recipes expose Postgres externally either (they all run it as private internal storage), so there's no literal duplication, but also no "internal-only" niche left for a standalone recipe to fill. This is the same structural mismatch documented for MySQL and MariaDB — a raw internet-facing DB port that our security rules and Traefik-only routing model don't support — and is if anything a harder blocker for the credential channel, since Postgres has no pre-hashed-password env var at all. Recommend not_recommended rather than blocked_on_platform, since no plausible mechanism change fixes this without relaxing a deliberate security rule.

version_health_notes: 3.8.1 shipped 2026-07-30, less than a week before today (2026-08-05); 3.8.0 landed just a week before that (2026-07-23), and 3.7.x point releases shipped roughly weekly through June-July 2026 (confirmed via GitHub releases API). Dev pre-releases are cut almost daily. This is an unusually active project even by our catalogue's standards. On 2026-07-13 Prefect announced it is acquiring Dagster Labs (a competing orchestrator), consolidating the two leading successors-to-Airflow under the Prefect name — a strong positive signal for the project's health and market position, not a distress signal (both products continue as independently maintained, the acquirer is Prefect itself). No indication of maintenance-only mode, archival, or EOL.
differentiation: Superficial category overlap with n8n only ("workflow orchestration"), but a different audience and a structurally different product. n8n (and the rejected activepieces candidate, apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml) are no-code/low-code tools: a non-developer builds and runs an entire automation visually in the browser, and the web UI IS the product. Prefect is a Python orchestration control-plane for data/ML engineers: workflows ("flows") are Python code the customer writes and deploys themselves via the `prefect` CLI/SDK from their own development environment; the self-hosted server's web UI is a monitoring/scheduling dashboard (run history, logs, work-pool and deployment management), not an authoring canvas. A customer cannot build a working pipeline through the UI alone the way they can in n8n. This makes it a genuinely different capability (bring-your-own- code pipeline orchestration for technical/data teams) rather than a duplicate of n8n's no-code automation niche, but it also means the self-hosted server alone is only half the product — running actual flows additionally requires the customer to run a Prefect *worker* (polling the server's work pool) and to have written and deployed Python flow code from outside the VM, none of which the recipe mechanism provisions.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct capability not covered by any of the 24 existing recipes, and Prefect is a legitimate, well-known, actively developed project (its own health signals are strong). But the value it delivers out-of-the-box is narrower than most catalogue entries: a customer gets an orchestration dashboard with nothing running yet, and needs outside developer effort (their own Python code, `prefect deploy`, and a running worker process) before it does anything useful. That's a fine value proposition for a technical customer who already knows Prefect and wants a managed control-plane, but it's a much thinner "works immediately after signup" experience than n8n or Activepieces, capping usefulness at medium rather than high for a general AF audience.
blocking_issues:
The self-hosted server (`prefect server start`, the official `prefecthq/prefect` image, single port 4200 for both UI and API) ships with NO authentication enabled by default — anyone who reaches the URL has full read/write access to all flow runs, deployments, and (via the UI's "blocks" feature) any stored credentials/secrets. Confirmed via upstream docs (docs.prefect.io/v3/advanced/security-settings): opt-in auth is a single shared Basic Auth string, `PREFECT_SERVER_API_AUTH_STRING`, in plaintext `user:pass` form compared directly by the server — not a hash, so `generated_from` (which only ever emits a hash) cannot target it. That said, this is not a structural blocker the way Postgres's plaintext-only `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` is (apps-gaps/postgresql.yaml): since the server has no auth at all by default, a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app (leaving `PREFECT_SERVER_API_AUTH_STRING` unset) is a complete, supported substitute — same pattern as n8n and Adminer use for apps with no login of their own.

Even with the UI gated, the recipe would deliver a dashboard with no workers and no deployed flows — not a blocker on the installability schema's terms (no external API key/OAuth/second customer credential is needed to boot the container), but worth flagging: this is the only catalogue candidate so far where "installable today" and "does something useful out of the box" are this far apart. Not a mechanism-channel gap, just a product-shape caveat for whoever prioritizes it.
summary: Prefect is healthy and actively developed (weekly releases, and a just-announced acquisition of rival Dagster that consolidates rather than threatens its position), ships an official single-container image with a single HTTP port and no mandatory database, and is mechanically installable today by gating its otherwise-unauthenticated web UI behind Traefik `basic_auth` — no external secrets or API keys required at first boot. It doesn't duplicate n8n despite the shared "workflow orchestration" label: Prefect targets developers who bring their own Python code, while n8n is a no-code tool where the UI builds the automation. The catch is that a freshly-booted Prefect recipe is just a monitoring dashboard with nothing running until the customer separately writes flow code and runs a worker from outside the VM — a thinner immediate payoff than most of the catalogue. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building for the distinct developer/data-team niche it fills, but set expectations that it's a control-plane, not a turnkey automation product.

name: PrestaShop
source_description: Open-source e-commerce platform for creating and managing online stores
version_health_notes: Confirmed via the GitHub releases page, not training-data recall. As of today 2026-08-05: latest stable is 9.1.4 (2026-06-04, released alongside a matching 8.2.7 maintenance release on the older 8.2.x line), and a 9.2.0-beta.1 followed on 2026-07-22 — about 2 weeks ago — with 9.2 reportedly in feature-freeze per PrestaShop's own build blog. The 9.1.x line has shipped 5 releases since March 2026 (9.1.0 → 9.1.1 → 9.1.2 → 9.1.3 → 9.1.4), with 8.2.x receiving matching security/maintenance releases the same days (8.2.5, 8.2.6, 8.2.7) — the same dual-branch support pattern seen in other actively maintained candidates. No dormancy signal.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-app catalogue covers e-commerce/online storefronts — closest neighbors (gitea, opengist, portainer, n8n) are dev-tooling/ops, not customer-facing storefronts. PrestaShop (PHP/Symfony, MySQL-backed, one of the most widely deployed self-hosted e-commerce platforms globally) would be a genuinely new category. Note: `apps-gaps/bagisto.yaml` already analyzed a competing self-hosted e-commerce candidate (Laravel-based) and found it blocked_on_platform for a different reason (no admin-credential override at all) — the two are not mutually exclusive per the "overlapping apps are fine" convention, so `overlaps_with` is left empty rather than pointing at bagisto.
usefulness_rationale: Fills a real category gap (self-hosted online store) with an upstream that has by far the largest install base and community of any self-hosted e-commerce project. Usefulness is high on fit grounds; see installability below for why it can't ship as-is today.
blocking_issues:
The official prestashop/prestashop image's automated-install path (PS_INSTALL_AUTO=1) only accepts the back-office admin password as a plaintext value via the ADMIN_MAIL/ADMIN_PASSWD env vars (confirmed against PrestaShop's own Docker devdocs page); the install script hashes it internally (PrestaShop has used bcrypt for employee/admin passwords since 1.7). There is no documented CLI flag, env var, or install option to inject an already-hashed value instead — no channel reachable by `generated_from`, which only ever carries a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext. This is the genuine-plaintext-requirement case called out in SCHEMA.md as a structural blocker (distinct from "app only supports an unsupported hash algorithm", which would just be `blocked_on_platform` pending algorithm support).

Traefik basic_auth is not a viable substitute either, for the same reason `apps-gaps/bagisto.yaml` found with the competing Bagisto candidate: PrestaShop serves the public storefront (/) and the back-office admin login (a configurable but still same-port, same-domain path, default /admin-dev) out of one container on one port. Gating the whole domain behind basic_auth to protect the back-office login would also lock out every storefront visitor, defeating the purpose of an e-commerce recipe. There is no path-scoped basic_auth mechanism in the current platform to gate only the admin path while leaving the storefront open.
summary: PrestaShop is upstream-healthy (active dual-branch releases, latest stable 9.1.4 from 2026-06-04, a 9.2 beta already out) and would fill a genuine category gap — no existing recipe covers self-hosted e-commerce. It fails installability today for the same class of reason as the competing Bagisto candidate: the only mechanism available for a customer-facing admin credential (Traefik basic_auth on the whole port) would also block the public storefront, since both share one container and port. Unlike Bagisto, PrestaShop does support setting the admin password via env var at install time (ADMIN_PASSWD) — but only as plaintext, hashed internally by the install script, with no way to feed in a pre-hashed value the way `generated_from` produces. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once either a path-scoped basic_auth capability exists (gate /admin-dev only) or PrestaShop's install path gains a way to accept a pre-hashed admin password.

name: PrivateBin
source_description: PrivateBin is a zero-knowledge encrypted pastebin for secure text sharing
upstream_license: Zlib/libpng (core code); bundled third-party libs under GPLv2, BSD-3-Clause, MIT, Apache-2.0, CC-BY-4.0
version_health_notes: v2.0.5 was tagged 2026-07-11, about 3.5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Per endoflife.date, the 2.x line has shipped 2.0.0 (2025-07-28), 2.0.2 (2025-10-28, security fix for CVE-2025-62796), 2.0.3, 2.0.4 (~2026-06), and 2.0.5 (2026-07-11) — a steady cadence of patch releases every 1-3 months, several explicitly security-motivated, with the 1.7.x line still receiving a backport as late as 2025-11-13 before its support window closed 2025-07-28. Official Docker Hub image privatebin/nginx-fpm-alpine mirrors releases closely: the "2.0.5" and "stable" tags were both pushed 26 days ago (matching the GitHub tag date), with "edge"/"nightly"/"latest" rebuilding roughly daily. This reads as a healthy, actively maintained project with a responsive security-patch cycle, not a stale or maintenance-only one.
differentiation: OpenGist (already in the catalogue) is the nearest neighbor — both are self-hosted, browser-based text/snippet sharing tools reachable behind Traefik on a single HTTP port. They serve different niches, though: OpenGist is a Git-backed, GitHub-Gist-style tool built around optional user accounts, persistent gist history, and syntax-highlighted code files. PrivateBin is deliberately account-less and zero-knowledge — all encryption/decryption happens client-side in the browser via a key in the URL fragment that the server never sees, pastes are typically one-time/burn-after-read or short-TTL, and there is no server-side admin surface at all. It fills the "quickly hand someone a secret snippet without either party creating an account or the host being able to read it" use case, which OpenGist's account/history model does not target.
usefulness_rationale: Zero-knowledge, ephemeral paste sharing is a distinct and legitimate self-hosting want (incident responders, support teams, and privacy- conscious users sharing secrets/logs without a third-party pastebin seeing the plaintext), and it is not exactly duplicated by OpenGist's Git/account-oriented model. It is a narrower utility than a general dev tool, though, and the customer gets no admin UI or user management to speak of — it is a single-purpose appliance, which caps demand relative to broader productivity or developer-tools recipes.
summary: PrivateBin is a single-container PHP app (official image privatebin/nginx-fpm-alpine:2.0.5) listening on one HTTP port (8080 inside the container), with a data volume for stored pastes and no database dependency — a clean fit behind Traefik on privatebin.<domain>, structurally close to the existing Uptime Kuma/ Vaultwarden single-container recipes. It has no admin panel, no login, and no environment-variable secret to project at boot: the entire security model is client-side, zero-knowledge encryption, so there is nothing for `generated_from` or Traefik `basic_auth` to gate — and gating it behind basic auth would in fact break the app's core use case of letting an unauthenticated recipient open a shared paste link. Upstream is actively maintained with a healthy, security-responsive release cadence (latest tag 2026-07-11, ~1 month old). It does not duplicate OpenGist's Git/account-based gist model, filling a real zero-knowledge/ephemeral-sharing niche instead. Recommend build_now: mechanically simple, no blocking secrets, healthy upstream, and adds genuine differentiation to the catalogue.

name: PrivateGPT
source_description: Self-hosted RAG engine for chatting with private documents using local LLMs
version_health_notes: v1.0.1 shipped 2026-06-18, about 1.5 months before today (2026-08-05), following v1.0.0 (2026-06-03) two weeks earlier — that pair looks active. But the version line before it tells a different story: the prior public release was v0.6.2 on 2024-08-08, meaning the project went ~22 months with zero public releases before v1.0.0 landed. Per the "PrivateGPT 1.0 is out" announcement (Zylon-ai/private-gpt discussion #2259, posted 2026-06-04), that gap is explained — Zylon built a commercial product on a private fork of PrivateGPT for two years and only merged it back into the open repo at v1.0.0, closing the private fork going forward. So the repo is not dormant/archived (57k+ stars, hundreds of commits, two releases in the last 2 months, no archival notice), but it also is not the same application Hostinger's description refers to: v0.6.2 and earlier were the lightweight "chat-with-your-documents" RAG tool; v1.0+ is a full API backend framework (Claude-compatible messages API, agentic tools, MCP connectors, code execution, text-to-sql) aimed at developers building AI products, not an end-user RAG chat app. Cadence is rated "sporadic" because the sample since the relaunch is only two releases across two months, following a two-year public silence.
differentiation: On paper PrivateGPT still exposes a single HTTP port with a bundled "workbench" UI at /ui for chatting, uploading documents, and inspecting API calls, and it still fronts local LLMs via any OpenAI-compatible server (the same Ollama pairing already used by open-webui). But the project itself has moved off the "chat with your documents" use case Hostinger describes and repositioned as a developer-facing backend framework: a Claude-compatible messages API, MCP connectors, code execution, database/text-to-sql tools, and skills, meant to be built on top of rather than used directly. Its actual RAG-chat surface area (ingest a doc, ask questions with citations) is a strict subset of what anythingllm already does with a more end-user-oriented UI, and the "any OpenAI-compatible backend + browser chat UI" pairing is exactly open-webui + ollama. There is no capability here a customer can't already get from the existing catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: The application Hostinger's description advertises (a turnkey self-hosted RAG chat tool) is effectively the abandoned pre-1.0 PrivateGPT; the application that actually ships today under that name and image is a developer backend/API framework whose intended integration surface (custom clients calling a Claude-compatible messages API, MCP tooling, code execution sandboxes) doesn't map well to a self-service AF customer clicking "install" and expecting a chat app. Combined with heavy functional overlap against open-webui, ollama, and anythingllm — all more end-user-appropriate for the exact use case being advertised — this doesn't add distinct value to the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
The app ships no customer-facing login of its own: server.auth in settings.yaml defaults to enabled: false, and unlike almost every other setting in that file (which are all ${VAR:default} env-var-interpolated), the auth secret is a single hardcoded base64 "Basic secret:key" string with no corresponding env var — it can only be changed by mounting a custom settings.yaml, not through any documented environment variable. That rules out generated_from-based root-password projection onto the app's own auth entirely (there is no env var to project into). A Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the single public port (:8080, same pattern as n8n/OpenClaw/WUD/Open WebUI/Immich) is required and fully expressible today via generated_from targeting the Traefik gate credential.
Full-feature usage (task queues, multi-tenant storage, observability) pulls in Postgres, Redis, RabbitMQ, S3-compatible storage, and Celery workers per settings.yaml, but every one of those has a working local default (sqlite skills DB, local Qdrant path, in-memory broker/cache), so a minimal single-container deployment pointed at a bundled Ollama service via OPENAI_API_BASE is possible and does not require any of that extra infrastructure or any customer-supplied secret for it.
summary: PrivateGPT is mechanically installable today — a single container behind Traefik basic_auth, pointed at a bundled Ollama via OPENAI_API_BASE, with no external API key or unreachable secret required. The problem is fit, not installability. The upstream project quietly pivoted at v1.0 (2026-06-03), after ~22 months of building a commercial product on a closed fork, from the lightweight "chat with your private documents" tool Hostinger's description still describes into a developer-oriented AI backend framework (Claude-compatible messages API, MCP, code execution, text-to-sql). What ships under this name today no longer matches the advertised use case, and the RAG-chat surface it does retain is already better covered by anythingllm (document workspaces, purpose-built end-user UI) and open-webui + ollama (the same local-LLM-backend pairing). Recommend not building this recipe: the value proposition Hostinger's catalogue entry implies isn't the product that would actually be installed.

Profilarr manages and syncs Radarr/Sonarr quality profiles and custom formats (optionally pulling curated rule sets from a community "Dictionarry" repo) across one or more *arr instances. Like Bazarr (see apps-gaps/bazarr.yaml), it has zero standalone value: it is a pure companion tool that must be pointed at existing Radarr and/or Sonarr installations, entered through its own UI after boot. Neither Radarr nor Sonarr exists as an AF recipe today, so a customer installing Profilarr alone gets a configuration tool with nothing to configure until they separately run Radarr/Sonarr themselves.

Shipping it in isolation would hand customers a dead-end app; it only makes sense bundled with a future "media automation stack" decision that also adds Radarr/Sonarr.
summary: Profilarr is a two-container app (ghcr.io/dictionarry-hub/profilarr web UI on port 6868, plus a companion "parser" sidecar with no public port) that is mechanically simple to deploy behind Traefik — single public HTTP port, no raw protocols, structurally close to uptime-kuma/ anytype-server in the catalogue. Auth defaults to built-in mode ("on"): the first visitor to the web UI creates their own admin username and password directly in-app, the same pattern already accepted for uptime-kuma, so no customer-supplied secret or basic_auth gate is required to boot safely. The actual blocker is usefulness, not mechanics: Profilarr does nothing without at least one Radarr or Sonarr instance to sync against (their URL/API key entered through Profilarr's own UI post-login, not needed to boot), and neither exists in our catalogue. installable_today is true, but recommend build_with_caveats pending a decision on whether Radarr/Sonarr — and the broader media-automation stack (Bazarr, Profilarr) — get added alongside it; shipping this alone is low value.

name: ProjectSend
source_description: Client-focused file sharing platform for securely sending files to clients
version_health_notes: Confirmed via the GitHub API, not training-data recall. As of today 2026-08-05: latest tagged release is r2029 (2026-03-29), part of a burst of three releases in March 2026 (r1994 -> r2002 -> r2029) after a longer r1720 (2024-08-03) -> r1945 (2025-10-10) gap. No new tag in the ~4 months since r2029, but the default `develop` branch is not stalled: `pushed_at` is 2026-08-04 and commits land multiple times a week (latest 2026-07-17), including active dependency bumps and bug fixes, with 352 forks / 1956 stars and 176 open issues still being triaged. Repo is not archived. Reading this as active development with irregular (not dormant) tagging, not a maintenance-only or EOL project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers client-facing file delivery. Syncthing is peer-to-peer file sync (no client-portal concept), Vaultwarden is a password manager, and immich/paperless-ngx are personal media/document archives rather than tools for sending files to external clients with per-client access lists and public download links. ProjectSend's niche (accountant/agency/freelancer sending deliverables to named clients) is genuinely new ground.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for a lightweight "send files to clients" tool as a Nextcloud alternative, and the upstream is healthy and widely deployed (1956 stars, official LinuxServer image with >1M pulls). Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because the deployment model available today (see installability) undermines the app's actual selling point — reaching external clients who have no account on the server.
blocking_issues:
ProjectSend has no env-var-driven admin account provisioning. The LinuxServer image only documents PUID/PGID/TZ/UMASK; the admin username and password are created interactively through the app's own browser-based install wizard on first visit (confirmed against ProjectSend's own install docs: DB connection can be pre-seeded by writing includes/sys.config.php before first boot, but "system and administrator user information" is still collected by the wizard itself, with no documented pre-seed or CLI path for that step). That install wizard sits open and unauthenticated on the public domain until someone completes it, so whoever reaches the URL first claims the admin account — a real race condition our recipe mechanism has no channel to close (there is no admin secret we could project via `generated_from`, since the app never accepts a pre-set/pre-hashed credential).

The only available mitigation, a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate on the whole domain (same pattern used for Adminer/n8n), would close that install-wizard race but comes at a cost specific to this app: ProjectSend's core feature is giving external clients (who have no account of their own, and in many cases use the app's public/guest download links — see the "public download" feature referenced in upstream's own commit history) direct access to files sent to them. A permanent whole-domain basic_auth gate would force every client to also learn and enter the tenant's shared root-password-derived credential before they can reach their files or a public download link, defeating the product's actual purpose. This is the same class of blocker `apps-gaps/prestashop.yaml` and `apps-gaps/bagisto.yaml` hit: gating an entire single-port app behind basic_auth to protect one admin/setup surface also locks out the public-facing audience the app exists to serve, and there is no path-scoped or setup-only-then-auto-removed basic_auth mechanism today to gate just the install wizard/admin login without touching client-facing paths.
summary: ProjectSend is upstream-healthy (active `develop` branch, latest tagged release r2029 from 2026-03-29, an official LinuxServer Docker image with broad adoption) and would fill a genuine gap in the catalogue — no existing recipe covers client-facing file delivery. It cannot ship as a recipe today: the app has no way to accept a pre-set or pre-hashed admin credential (admin creation only happens via an unauthenticated first-visit web wizard), and the one available gating mechanism, whole-domain Traefik basic_auth, would permanently block the external clients the app is built to serve, not just the setup window. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit if a path-scoped or setup-only basic_auth gate becomes available (protecting the install wizard and admin login without also gating client/public-download paths), or if ProjectSend adds an env-var/CLI path to provision the admin account non-interactively.

name: Prometheus
source_description: Open-source monitoring and alerting toolkit with time-series database
version_health_notes: v3.13.2 shipped 2026-07-30, six days before today (2026-08-05); v3.13.1 landed 2026-07-10 and v3.13.0 about a month before today (confirmed via the GitHub releases API and Docker Hub tag timestamps). Point releases have been landing roughly every 2-3 weeks through mid-2026, consistent with the project's long-running steady cadence. Prometheus is a CNCF graduated project with 18k+ commits, hundreds of open issues/PRs, and active CI (including fuzzing and vulnerability scanning) — no indication of maintenance-only mode, archival, or EOL.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers this ground. uptime-kuma (the closest "monitoring" entry in the catalogue) is black-box uptime/ping checking of external endpoints; Prometheus is a pull-based time-series metrics database that scrapes numeric metrics (CPU, memory, request rates, custom app instrumentation) from targets the customer configures, and exposes them for PromQL querying and alerting. WUD monitors Docker image freshness only, not general metrics. Distinct capability, not a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Prometheus is the de facto standard metrics toolkit and would be a legitimate, well-known addition, but the value out of the box is thin: the official image ships with an empty default scrape config (just itself), so a freshly-booted recipe has nothing meaningful to show until the customer edits prometheus.yml (via SSH/volume access, outside the recipe mechanism) to add scrape targets and, in most real setups, deploys exporters (node_exporter, cAdvisor, etc.) alongside the workloads being monitored — none of which this recipe provisions. It is also commonly paired with Grafana for dashboarding, which the bare recipe wouldn't include. Real capability, but "works immediately after signup" is a weaker story than most of the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
Prometheus ships with no authentication on its web UI/API (port 9090) by default. Confirmed via upstream docs (prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/https/): opt-in auth is `basic_auth_users` in a separate `--web.config.file` YAML file, with bcrypt-hashed passwords compared against that file on every request. This is not a structural blocker — since the server has no auth at all unless that file is supplied, a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app (never supplying `--web.config.file`) is a complete, supported substitute, the same pattern used for n8n and other apps with no login of their own.

Not a blocking issue but a caveat worth flagging alongside `usefulness_rationale`: default-booting Prometheus with no scrape targets configured is mechanically installable (no external secret needed) but functionally close to a no-op until the customer edits its config file from outside the provisioned stack — this recipe mechanism has no channel for a customer to supply scrape-target configuration at first boot either.
summary: Prometheus is healthy and actively developed (CNCF graduated, releases every few weeks, large active community), ships an official single-container image with a single HTTP port and no mandatory external database, and is mechanically installable today by gating its unauthenticated-by-default web UI behind Traefik `basic_auth` — no external API keys or OAuth needed at first boot. It doesn't duplicate anything in the current 24-recipe catalogue (uptime-kuma is uptime pinging, not metrics collection). The catch is that Prometheus alone monitors nothing useful until the customer configures scrape targets (and typically deploys exporters) from outside the recipe, so the freshly-booted experience is thinner than most of the catalogue. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building for a real, distinct capability, but set expectations that it's a metrics backend awaiting configuration, not a turnkey dashboard.
