name: PsiTransfer
source_description: Lightweight self-hosted file sharing with expiring links and no accounts
version_health_notes: v2.4.4 was tagged 2026-06-02, 64 days before today (2026-08-05). The matching Docker Hub tag psitrax/psitransfer:v2.4.4 was pushed the same day. Recent cadence is healthy: six releases in six months (v2.3.1 2025-12-26, v2.3.2 2025-12-30, v2.4.0 2026-01-31, v2.4.1 2026-02-14, v2.4.2 2026-04-13, v2.4.3 2026-04-14, v2.4.4 2026-06-02), including security-hardening notes on v2.4.3 and a path-traversal fix on v2.3.1. That said, the project's longer history is bursty rather than steady: v2.1.2 (2022-11-14) to v2.2.0 (2024-04-05) is a ~17-month gap, and v2.2.0 to v2.3.0 (2025-06-04) is another ~14-month gap. A single maintainer (psi-4ward) appears to revive the project in concentrated bursts after long dormant stretches rather than shipping on a predictable cadence. Current state reads as active, but the history argues for treating "active" as provisional — another multi-year gap after this burst would not be a surprise.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers this niche. Syncthing is continuous P2P folder sync between devices you control, not link-based one-off sharing with an outside recipient. PrivateBin and OpenGist share text/code snippets, not arbitrary large files. PsiTransfer is a WeTransfer/Dropbox-Transfer alternative: upload one or more files, get a bucket URL, hand that URL to someone outside your org who does not have (and should not need) any credential for your server, and the bucket expires after a configurable retention window or one-time download.
usefulness_rationale: Ad-hoc large-file handoff to an external party without a third-party SaaS is a genuine, distinct self-hosting want, and no current recipe covers it. It is a narrower single-purpose appliance than most of the catalogue, though (no accounts, no admin surface beyond an optional stats page), which caps demand relative to broader productivity tools.
blocking_issues:
PSITRANSFER_ADMIN_PASS and PSITRANSFER_UPLOAD_PASS are compared as plaintext against the literal `x-passwd` header the browser sends (`req.get('x-passwd') !== config.adminPass` in lib/endpoints.js — confirmed by reading the upstream source). There is no hashing support at all, so `generated_from` — which only ever carries a hash of the root password, never the plaintext — has no way to produce a value this app will accept. This is the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case SCHEMA.md calls a hard structural blocker, not the softer "unsupported hash algorithm" case.

Traefik `basic_auth` is not a substitute here the way it is for Adminer or n8n: it gates the whole public port, and PsiTransfer's entire value proposition is handing an unauthenticated download URL to a recipient who has no relationship with the customer's server. Gating the domain behind basic auth would block every recipient from opening their download link — the same conflict noted for PrivateBin in apps-gaps/privatebin.yaml, but arguably worse here because PsiTransfer's default retention windows (up to 8 weeks) mean links are expected to stay externally reachable for a while.

Both passwords are optional and ship disabled by default (`adminPass: false`, `uploadPass: false`), so leaving them unset (the only mechanically installable option today, since neither can be projected and basic_auth can't be scoped to just the upload path) is not a benign no-op: it deploys a fully open, unauthenticated public file-upload endpoint with no channel to lock it down. That's a real abuse surface (anonymous hosting of arbitrary or illegal content on the customer's server) beyond the usual "no secrets needed" case.
summary: PsiTransfer is a single-container Node app (official image psitrax/psitransfer, pin v2.4.4) on one HTTP port (3000) with a single data volume and no database — structurally as simple as Uptime Kuma or PrivateBin, and it would add genuine differentiation as the only external-link file-transfer tool in the catalogue. Upstream is currently active (six releases in the last six months) though historically prone to multi-year dormant stretches between bursts. It is blocked today, however, on a structural mismatch rather than a missing platform feature we can just wait out: its admin/upload passwords require the literal plaintext (no hashing), which `generated_from` cannot supply, and Traefik `basic_auth` can't substitute without breaking the app's core unauthenticated-recipient download flow. Left with neither password set — the only combination installable under current mechanics — it ships an open anonymous upload endpoint. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: worth revisiting only if a plaintext (not hash) customer-secret projection channel, or a path-scoped auth gate that can protect uploads while leaving download links public, becomes available.

name: Pterodactyl
source_description: Open-source game server management panel with Docker isolation
version_health_notes: Panel v1.15.0 and Wings v1.13.2 both shipped 2026-08-03 — 2 days before today (2026-08-05). Panel release history in 2026 alone: v1.12.0 (2026-01-06), v1.12.1 (2026-02-14), v1.12.2 (2026-03-26), v1.12.3 (2026-05-23), v1.12.4 (2026-05-30), v1.13.0 (2026-06-15), v1.14.0 (2026-06-22), v1.14.1 (2026-06-29), v1.15.0 (2026-08-03) — roughly monthly, sometimes more often. Repo is not archived, pushed_at is same-day as the latest release, 171 open issues actively triaged. Clearly active, not dormant or maintenance-only.
differentiation: No recipe in the current catalogue addresses game server hosting; portainer is the closest existing analogue (a Docker-management web UI) but manages arbitrary containers generically rather than provisioning per-customer game server instances with resource limits, file managers, and console access the way Pterodactyl does. If it were mechanically installable it would open a genuinely new category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for self-hosted game server panels, but Pterodactyl is a hosting platform in its own right (multi-tenant, multi-node) more than a single-tenant "app" — its value to one AF customer running one instance for their own game servers is narrower than to someone reselling game hosting, which is arguably out of scope for a single-VM recipe.
blocking_issues:
The admin-creation CLI (`p:user:make`) does accept non-interactive flags (--email, --username, --password, --admin=1), so the password itself could in principle be projected via generated_from and passed to install.sh — that part alone would not be a hard blocker.
The real structural blocker is Wings, the daemon that actually runs customer game servers: it is designed to run on a separate node with direct access to the host's Docker daemon (mounting /var/run/docker.sock or an equivalent), not as an isolated service inside our recipe's own docker-compose stack. That is a materially different trust boundary than any other recipe in the catalogue and is not something the current recipe mechanism (or Traefik-fronted single-tenant model) is built to express.
Each hosted game server needs its own directly-reachable raw TCP/UDP port (e.g. 25565 for Minecraft) assigned dynamically per game server instance — these are not HTTP, so Traefik cannot front them, and the recipe metadata model has no concept of a dynamic, customer-managed port range.
Wings node registration is an inherently two-actor, multi-step flow: an admin logs into the Panel's web UI, creates a Node, and the Panel mints a one-time configuration token that Wings then consumes. There is no customer-supplied secret path for this in the current /compose bootstrap flow, and unlike the admin-password case there is no non-interactive CLI equivalent documented for generating that token outside the web UI.
Architecturally this is a hosting platform (Panel + one-or-more Wings nodes) rather than a single self-contained app; even solving the secrets-projection gaps above would only make the Panel installable in isolation, with no game servers actually running until a Wings node is manually paired.
summary: Pterodactyl (Panel + Wings) is actively maintained with a roughly monthly release cadence (latest v1.15.0, 2026-08-03) and is not at risk of EOL. However it fails our installability bar for reasons that go beyond a missing secrets-projection mechanism: Wings, the component that actually runs hosted game servers, requires direct host Docker socket access and dynamically assigns raw per-server TCP/UDP ports that Traefik cannot front, and pairing Wings to the Panel is an inherently manual, multi-step admin-console flow with no scriptable secret we could project today. Even the one piece that could be projected (the initial admin password) leaves the recipe as a Panel with no working game-server backend. Recommend not_recommended: this is a structural mismatch with the single-tenant, reverse-proxy, docker-compose recipe model, not a gap that IF-1420/1312 alone would close.

name: PufferPanel
source_description: Open-source web panel for managing Minecraft, Factorio, Rust, and other game servers
upstream_docker_image: pufferpanel/pufferpanel (pin to a version tag, e.g. 3.0.9 — do not follow upstream examples that use :latest)
version_health_notes: v3.0.9 tagged and pushed to Docker Hub 2026-07-14, about 3 weeks before today (2026-08-05). GitHub API confirms the repo is not archived and was last pushed to on 2026-08-01. Release cadence over the last ~7 months is roughly monthly to bi-monthly (3.0.4 2026-03-02, 3.0.5 2026-03-03, 3.0.6 2026-03-17, 3.0.7 2026-04-21, 3.0.8 2026-05-27, 3.0.9 2026-07-14). 119 open issues, actively triaged. Note: an initial web search summary mis-dated these same releases as 2024 (likely a training-data year-guessing artifact from the source page's date formatting); the dates above were re-verified directly against the GitHub Releases API and Docker Hub tag-push timestamps, which are authoritative. Clearly active, not dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches game server hosting/management. PufferPanel would be a genuinely new category (gaming) — it lets a customer run and administer Minecraft, Factorio, Rust, and other game server processes from one web panel, distinct from anything else offered today.
usefulness_rationale: Well-known, actively maintained open-source alternative to Pterodactyl in the self-hosted game-panel space, and would open a net-new category for the catalogue. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because of the SFTP port (see below) and, more importantly, the installability blocker below — a customer cannot actually log into the panel without a step our current mechanism has no way to perform.
blocking_issues:
PufferPanel has no first-run web setup wizard and no environment-variable path to provision the initial admin account. The official image's entrypoint.sh only runs `pufferpanel db upgrade` then `pufferpanel run` — it does not read any ADMIN_*-style env vars. The only supported way to create the first (admin) user is the CLI command `pufferpanel user add --admin`, which must be run interactively or with --name/--email/--password flags *inside the already-running container* (i.e. via `docker exec` after `docker compose up`). Our install.sh mechanism performs a single `docker compose up` and does not perform a post-boot exec step, so there is no channel to create the admin account at all today.

Even if a post-boot exec step existed, the `--password` flag on `pufferpanel user add` expects the user's plaintext password (it is hashed in-process via bcrypt and stored), not a pre-computed hash. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, so it could not be handed to this flag even with an exec channel — this is a genuine plaintext-only requirement, not just a missing supported-algorithm entry.

Web UI (port 8080) is reverse-proxy compatible, but the panel also needs port 5657 for SFTP (file transfer to/from managed game servers) — a raw TCP protocol, not HTTP, so it cannot be fronted by Traefik's HTTP routing the way the rest of our catalogue is. This is a secondary concern next to the admin- account blocker above, but would still need a raw TCP exposure mechanism (NodePort/LoadBalancer per CLAUDE.md guidance) for the SFTP feature to work at all.
summary: PufferPanel is an actively maintained (latest 3.0.9, 2026-07-14), Apache-2.0 game-server panel that would open a genuinely new "gaming" category for the catalogue with no existing overlap. It is not installable under the current recipe mechanism, though: the official Docker image provides no way to provision the first admin account except an interactive/flagged CLI command run via `docker exec` after the container is already up, and even that command requires a plaintext password rather than the hash our `generated_from` projection supplies — so there is no boot-time channel for the required admin credential today, structurally distinct from the "no channel for an external API key" case. A secondary concern is the SFTP port (5657), a raw TCP protocol that doesn't fit our Traefik-fronted HTTP model. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit if/when the install mechanism gains a supported post-boot provisioning step, and treat the plaintext-vs-hash mismatch as a real blocker to resolve, not just an extensible-algorithm gap.

name: Pulsarr
source_description: Real-time Plex watchlist monitor that syncs to Sonarr and Radarr with routing
upstream_docker_image: lakker/pulsarr (pin to a version tag, e.g. 0.18.0 — do not follow upstream docs' :latest example)
version_health_notes: Very active, fast-moving project: v0.16.0 (2026-06-03), v0.17.0 (2026-07-03), v0.17.1 (2026-07-03), v0.17.2 (2026-07-04), v0.17.3 (2026-07-06), v0.17.4-beta.2 (2026-07-19), v0.17.4 (2026-07-23), v0.18.0 (2026-08-05, released the same day as this research). The lakker/pulsarr Docker Hub image tracks releases within a day (0.18.0/0.18/0.18-node/latest tags all pushed ~1 day before today). Repo is not archived, no EOL notice; clearly active, well-maintained development.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches Plex watchlist automation. Pulsarr monitors a customer's Plex watchlist in real time and automatically adds matching titles to Sonarr/Radarr with predicate-based routing (e.g. by genre, user, or quality profile) — a narrower, more automation-focused sibling of Jellyseerr/Overseerr (request-and-approve UI) rather than a duplicate of it. Like apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml, apps-gaps/overseerr.yaml, and apps-gaps/prowlarr.yaml, its entire reason for existing depends on upstream apps (Plex, and at least one of Sonarr/Radarr) that do not exist as AF recipes today — Pulsarr has no independent function of its own; it is pure glue between three external services.
usefulness_rationale: Well-regarded, actively developed tool in the self-hosted media community and a real quality-of-life upgrade over polling-based alternatives (e.g. watchlistarr) for Plex Pass users. Its value is entirely conditional on the customer already running Plex plus Sonarr and/or Radarr elsewhere — none of which exist in this catalogue — so on its own it would ship as an automation tool with nothing to automate, mirroring the same "dependent piece of a pipeline that doesn't exist yet" pattern seen in prowlarr/jellyseerr.
blocking_issues:
Pulsarr's setup wizard requires a Plex Token before it can do anything — the customer must fetch this themselves from an existing, real plex.tv account (per Plex's own support docs on authentication tokens) and paste it into Pulsarr's setup screen. This is the same "external API key/token the app can't function without" case the SCHEMA.md fit-table rules out, and the same third-party-account-derived-credential shape already documented in apps-gaps/plex.yaml (PLEX_CLAIM) and apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml — af-api's JWE bootstrap token has no channel to carry a value the customer must obtain from a separate service.

Beyond the Plex Token, full operation also requires adding at least one Sonarr and/or Radarr instance by URL plus that instance's own API key. Those are credentials for services that don't exist as AF recipes today, and even if they did, each would be a second/third independent external secret — root-password projection only covers one credential, and none of these are generatable server-side (they are issued by, and only meaningful to, the external Plex/Sonarr/Radarr services themselves).

Pulsarr does have its own local admin account (created interactively on first web UI visit, not tied to Plex sign-in) — unlike Plex or Jellyseerr/Seerr, this part alone would in principle be projectable via `generated_from` if the app exposed an env-var seed hook for it. That does not rescue installability here, though: the Plex Token and Sonarr/Radarr API key requirements are independent, mandatory blockers that a local-admin fix would not touch.
summary: Pulsarr is a small, actively developed (v0.18.0 shipped the same day as this research), single-container app (lakker/pulsarr, port 3003, SQLite by default, no separate database service needed) that is mechanically simple and reverse-proxy compatible — the deployment shape itself is not the problem. It cannot be installed via the current recipe mechanism because its setup flow hard-requires a Plex Token the customer must obtain from their own plex.tv account, plus at least one Sonarr/Radarr instance URL and API key, none of which have an input channel today (not a root-password hash, not something Traefik basic_auth can substitute for). It also depends functionally on Plex, Sonarr, and Radarr, none of which exist as AF recipes, so even setting installability aside it would land as automation glue with nothing to connect to. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`, consistent with apps-gaps/plex.yaml and apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml; revisit only if/when the platform gains a customer-supplied external-credential channel, and ideally alongside a Plex/Sonarr/Radarr recipe decision.

name: Pulse
source_description: Real-time monitoring dashboard for Proxmox, Docker, and Kubernetes
latest_version: v6.1.2 (stable); v6.2.0-rc.8 in active pre-release as of today, 2026-08-05)
version_health_notes: Extremely active: v6.1.0, v6.1.1, and v6.1.2 stable tags shipped within a 15-day span (2026-07-11 through 2026-07-26), and a v6.2.0 release candidate line has been cutting near-daily rc builds since (rc.1 on 2026-07-27 through rc.8 on 2026-08-05, today). No sign of slowdown, archival, or maintenance-only mode.
differentiation: Pulse is a unified observability dashboard for virtualization/container infrastructure itself (Proxmox nodes/VMs, Docker hosts, Kubernetes clusters, TrueNAS, vSphere) — CPU/memory/disk metrics, backup-failure detection, restart-loop and capacity alerts, pulled via API tokens/agents against the customer's own infra. This differs from Uptime Kuma, which checks external-facing service availability (HTTP/TCP/DNS pings) with no concept of hypervisor or container-host internals, and from Portainer, which is a Docker management/control-plane UI (start/stop/deploy containers) rather than a metrics-and-alerting layer. A customer running Proxmox or a small Docker/K8s fleet outside AF's own infra would want Pulse for visibility that neither existing recipe provides.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful to the homelab/small-IT-team audience AF's catalogue targets, and distinct from what's already offered. Capped at medium rather than high because its value is entirely dependent on the customer separately owning and connecting Proxmox/Docker/Kubernetes infrastructure elsewhere — unlike a self-contained app, an AF customer who installs Pulse purely to monitor the AF VM it runs on gets comparatively little (it has no built-in target to monitor until the customer supplies external API credentials through the UI).
summary: Pulse is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (7655, WebSocket-capable) web app with an MIT license, an actively maintained upstream (multiple stable releases in the last month, daily rc builds ongoing today), and a pinnable numbered Docker Hub tag (rcourtman/pulse:6.1.2). Its admin login is set via the `PULSE_AUTH_PASS` environment variable, which upstream explicitly documents as accepting either a plaintext password (auto-hashed at startup) or a pre-computed bcrypt hash — a direct match for `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` — with `PULSE_AUTH_USER` set to a fixed default username, avoiding the app's normal interactive bootstrap-token flow entirely. No external API key or OAuth registration is needed for the app itself to boot and be usable; connecting it to the customer's actual Proxmox/Docker/Kubernetes infrastructure is a post-login, in-app configuration step the customer performs with their own credentials, same as any other admin task. Recommend build_now: it's mechanically installable today, fills a real gap (hypervisor/container host observability) distinct from Uptime Kuma and Portainer, and rides an actively developed upstream.

name: Pydio Cells
source_description: Self-hosted file sharing and document collaboration with team workspaces
version_health_notes: Confirmed via the GitHub API, not training-data recall. As of today 2026-08-05: latest tagged release is v5.0.2 (2026-06-30), five weeks ago, following v5.0.1 (2026-06-10) and the v5.0.0 major release (2026-05-26, a ground-up rewrite adding a new "Pages" display, a revamped metadata system, and PostgreSQL support). Before v5.0.0 the project was still shipping v4.4.x patches (v4.4.17 on 2026-01-08, v4.4.16 on 2025-12-02), so the v4 → v5 transition did not leave a gap in maintenance. `pushed_at` on the main repo is 2026-08-05 (today), repo is not archived, 2240 stars, 61 open issues. Reading this as actively maintained with a healthy, roughly monthly release cadence.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers general-purpose team file sharing with workspaces/ACLs. Syncthing is peer-to-peer sync with no server-side workspace or sharing-link concept, immich is photo/video-specific, paperless-ngx is a document archive/OCR tool, and vaultwarden is a password manager. Pydio Cells' actual niche (a Nextcloud-style "team drive" with per-workspace access control, web editing/preview, and share links) is genuinely new ground for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted "our own Nextcloud/Drive" is one of the most commonly requested self-hosting use cases, upstream is actively developed with an official multi-arch Docker image, and the app would fill a real gap rather than duplicate an existing recipe.
blocking_issues:
Pydio Cells has no first-boot channel that accepts a pre-hashed admin credential. Unlike ProjectSend (apps-gaps/projectsend.yaml), Cells does support a fully non-interactive `cells configure --yaml` / `CELLS_INSTALL_YAML` path (confirmed against docs.pydio.com/.../yamljson-installation and the `InstallConfig` proto in cmd/configure.go) that an install.sh could feed before the app is ever reachable, so the "unauthenticated setup wizard race" class of blocker does not apply here. The remaining problem is the shape of the `FrontPassword` field itself: every description of it (interactive wizard, YAML installer) treats it as the *plaintext* admin password, which Cells then hashes internally at account- creation time. Nothing in the upstream docs, forum threads, or configure command reference documents a way to hand Cells an already-computed bcrypt/argon2 hash and have it stored verbatim as the credential (the way Vaultwarden's `ADMIN_TOKEN` accepts a pre-hashed Argon2 value). Projecting `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` into `FrontPassword` would therefore not give the customer's real root password as their Cells login — it would hash the hash, silently locking the customer out of the account our install flow just created. This is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, which the schema calls out as a structural blocker (`generated_from` only ever carries a hash).

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate does not help here the way it does for no-login apps (n8n, Adminer): Cells has its own login screen, so gating the whole domain only adds a second credential in front of an admin account we still cannot provision correctly.
summary: Pydio Cells is upstream-healthy (v5.0.2 released 2026-06-30, active monthly cadence, official Docker image, no maintenance-mode or EOL signals) and would be a high-value, non-overlapping addition — the catalogue has no general-purpose team file-sharing/workspace recipe today. It is mechanically closer to installable than most blocked candidates, since Cells does support a genuine non-interactive `cells configure --yaml` install path, avoiding the unauthenticated- setup-wizard race that blocks apps like ProjectSend. It still cannot ship today: the admin account field that path fills (`FrontPassword`) takes a plaintext password that Cells hashes itself, and there is no documented way to instead hand it a pre-computed hash the way `generated_from` projection requires. name: Qdrant
source_description: Vector similarity search engine for AI and machine learning applications
version_health_notes: Extremely active as of today (2026-08-05): v1.19.0 shipped today, preceded by v1.18.3 (2026-07-17), v1.18.2 (2026-06-04), v1.18.1 (2026-05-22), v1.18.0 (2026-05-11), v1.17.1 (2026-03-27), v1.17.0 (2026-02-20) — a steady ~monthly minor/patch cadence going back years. Repo is not archived (last push today), 33.8k GitHub stars, official Docker Hub image tracks releases same-day. No EOL signals of any kind; this is a well-funded, fast-moving project (Qdrant also sells a managed cloud offering, which funds continued OSS development).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a vector/embedding database. Qdrant is backend infrastructure for customers already running Ollama, Open WebUI, n8n, or Hermes Agent from this same catalogue — a place to store embeddings for RAG/semantic-search pipelines instead of standing up Postgres+pgvector or a hosted vector DB elsewhere. Same role as apps-gaps/chroma.yaml and apps-gaps/milvus.yaml (both also previously researched, neither shipped), but Qdrant differs from both in one material way: it ships a genuine browser-based dashboard (collections browser, point/vector inspector, query console at /dashboard on its REST port) rather than being purely SDK/API-driven like Chroma (no UI at all) or Milvus (only a read-only health page).
usefulness_rationale: Real, growing demand from the self-hosted-AI/RAG audience, and Qdrant is widely regarded as the most polished/performant open-source vector DB in that space — it pairs naturally with Ollama/Open WebUI/n8n already in the catalogue. Still a developer-facing infrastructure piece: most customers deploying it are wiring it into a pipeline via SDK rather than using it as a stand-alone consumer app, so the addressable audience is narrower than a general-purpose UI-first app, same caveat noted for Chroma.
blocking_issues:
Qdrant ships with authentication fully disabled by default — the server (and its /dashboard UI) boots open to anyone who can reach the port. Optional auth is a single static env var, QDRANT__SERVICE__API_KEY, checked with a literal string/JWT comparison, not a hash-verify login screen — there is no "admin login parameter" to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`. Confirmed via the dashboard's own UX: when an API key is configured, the web UI prompts the user to type the exact key into a text box and stores it client-side; feeding it an opaque hash string (what `generated_from` produces) would mean the customer has to type that unreadable hash as their credential, defeating the point — same failure mode already documented for Ackee's plaintext-comparison password field (apps-gaps/ackee.yaml).

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole service (same pattern used for Adminer/WUD/Chroma) sidesteps this cleanly: leave QDRANT__SERVICE__API_KEY unset (Qdrant has no login of its own to conflict with) and let Traefik own the auth boundary. This is mechanically expressible today and closes the "open to the internet" gap without touching Qdrant's own credential handling.

Qdrant also exposes an optional gRPC port (6334) alongside the REST port (6333) that serves both the HTTP API and the dashboard. Unlike Milvus (apps-gaps/milvus.yaml), gRPC is not required — the REST API is fully functional standalone — so the recipe should only publish 6333 through Traefik and keep 6334 non-public (`public: false`, internal-network only), avoiding the "gRPC clients can't do an interactive basic-auth handshake" problem entirely rather than needing to solve it.
summary: Qdrant is a single official image (qdrant/qdrant, pin v1.19.0), actively maintained (same-day release as this research), Apache-2.0 licensed, and fills a genuine gap — no vector database exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It differs favorably from the two prior vector-DB candidates: unlike Chroma it has a real web dashboard, and unlike Milvus its primary protocol is plain HTTP/REST on one port, so it stays reverse-proxy compatible without touching gRPC. It has no built-in login, so a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate on the REST/dashboard port (6333 only; keep gRPC's 6334 non-public) is the correct and available mechanism to avoid shipping it open to the internet — mechanically installable today via the same pattern already used for Chroma/Adminer. The caveat is audience fit, not mechanism: it's primarily consumed by SDKs and other apps (Ollama/Open WebUI/n8n pipelines), so it should ship positioned as an AI-stack building block rather than a stand-alone destination app.

The core repo's `pushed_at` is 2026-07-29 (last week), 14.2k stars, 161 open issues, not archived — code activity (commits, issue triage) is clearly ongoing even though tagged releases are infrequent. Calling this `slowing` rather than `active` because the ~12-13 month gap between the last two releases is longer than the ~6-9 month gaps earlier in the project's history, but `eol_status: active` since there is no maintenance-only announcement, no archive, and visible recent commit activity.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches hotel/property management or booking-engine use cases; the closest business-app neighbors (paperless-ngx, n8n) are document management and automation, not reservations/PMS. A working QloApps recipe would be genuinely new ground, not an overlap.
usefulness_rationale: Hotel PMS/booking-engine is a real, recognizable self-hosting niche (QloApps is built on the PrestaShop 1.6 core and is one of the few open-source options in this space, 14.2k GitHub stars), but it is a narrower audience than general productivity/collaboration tools already well represented in the catalogue, and the packaging problems below make it considerably more expensive to ship than a typical recipe.
blocking_issues:
QloApps has no official Docker image at all. devdocs.qloapps.com's installation page documents only two supported paths — a browser GUI wizard and a CLI script (`install/index_cli.php`) — and does not mention Docker. The only Docker packaging that exists is a third-party community image, `webkul/qloapps_docker` (published by the vendor's own GitHub org but not referenced from QloApps' own docs), whose tags top out at 1.6.1 — it has never been rebuilt for 1.7.0 (released 2025-07-04, 13 months ago) and still ships Ubuntu 18.04 + PHP 7.2 + MySQL 5.7, all of which are themselves past their own upstream EOL, and PHP 7.2 in particular is below the PHP 8.1+ that QloApps 1.7.0 itself now requires per its changelog. Building a recipe on this image means shipping a customer-facing app on a three-versions-stale, EOL-on-EOL base; building our own image from the QloApps source instead is a materially bigger lift than the typical "pin an official tag" recipe.

The one image that exists bundles the web app, MySQL, and an SSH server into a single container (env vars `USER_PASSWORD` for SSH, `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`, `MYSQL_DATABASE`), rather than the app+db multi-service split every other compose recipe in this catalogue uses. It could still be fronted by Traefik on the HTTP port alone (leaving 3306/2222 unpublished), so this by itself is a packaging wart rather than a hard blocker, hence `reverse_proxy_compatible: false` above reflects the image's own design, not a Traefik incompatibility.

Per the image's own README, first boot does NOT auto-complete the QloApps install: "go to your browser and hit your IP or domain name and start qloapps installation process" — i.e. the unauthenticated PrestaShop-style setup wizard is exposed on the public HTTP port until a human manually finishes it, then must manually delete the `install/` directory and rename the admin folder. This is the same unauthenticated-setup-wizard race class of blocker noted for ProjectSend (apps-gaps/projectsend.yaml) and ships open on the internet by default.

Even switching to the documented non-interactive `install/index_cli.php --email=... --password=...` path (which would close the wizard-race problem and could feed ADMIN_EMAIL) does not resolve the credential channel for ADMIN_PASSWORD: that flag takes the admin account's *plaintext* password, which QloApps/PrestaShop core then hashes internally at account- creation time. There is no documented way to hand it a pre-computed bcrypt/argon2 hash instead. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever carries a hash of the customer's root password, so projecting it into `--password` would store the hash-of-the-hash as the login, silently locking the customer out — the same structural mismatch documented for Pydio Cells (apps-gaps/pydio-cells.yaml). A Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not substitute here either, since QloApps has its own admin login the gate would sit in front of without fixing the provisioning problem.
summary: QloApps fills a real gap (hotel PMS/booking engine, nothing comparable in the current 24 recipes) and the upstream project itself is still active (commits within the last week, releases roughly annually, not archived or EOL). It is not recommended today for two independent reasons rather than one platform-mechanism gap: first, there is no official Docker image — the only one that exists is community-maintained, three releases stale, and built on an EOL Ubuntu/PHP/MySQL base incompatible with QloApps' own current PHP 8.1+ requirement, meaning a real recipe would need a from-scratch image build, not a pinned-tag compose file. Second, even a fixed image would hit the same structural credential blocker as Pydio Cells: QloApps' only non-interactive install path takes a plaintext admin password that it hashes itself, with no channel for the hash-only value `generated_from` produces, and its own admin login means a Traefik `basic_auth` gate doesn't route around that. Revisit only if Webkul ships and maintains a current, split app/db Docker image AND a future platform mechanism can carry more than a single hash to an app's own install flow.

Document ingestion and hybrid keyword/vector search work without one, but that's not what "production-ready RAG framework" is sold as. R2R-Application (the web dashboard) ships a default admin login (admin@example.com / change_me_immediately, overridable only via env vars at boot) with no documented password-reset flow for a forgotten default — this is a fixed/default admin credential the schema says is fine to gate behind Traefik basic_auth rather than a blocker on its own, but it stacks on top of the API-key blocker above rather than resolving it.

Shipping a recipe on top of an actively-exploitable, publicly-disclosed vulnerability with no maintainer response is a reason to hold regardless of whether Traefik basic_auth could otherwise mask it at the edge.

Full-mode deployment is a five-service stack (R2R core API, R2R-Application dashboard, Postgres+pgvector, Hatchet workflow engine with its own web dashboard, MinIO object storage with its own web console) — only the main dashboard needs to be public; Hatchet's and MinIO's consoles would stay internal-network-only behind Traefik, similar to the gRPC-port pattern already used for Qdrant (apps-gaps/qdrant.yaml). summary: R2R is architecturally interesting — the only candidate researched so far that packages a full RAG pipeline (ingestion, hybrid search, knowledge graphs, agentic retrieval) rather than a single building block — but two independent problems rule it out today. Mechanically, its core RAG functionality needs a customer-supplied OpenAI/Anthropic API key set as a boot-time environment variable, with no runtime settings page to supply one later, which is the "external API key, no input channel" hard no per the schema. Separately, upstream health has visibly declined: no release in 14 months, no commits in 9 months, and most tellingly, a critical unauthenticated-admin-bypass vulnerability (#2295) reported over five weeks ago with zero maintainer response — the founding team's public profile now centers a different, unrelated product. usefulness_rationale: Real, durable demand — RabbitMQ is one of the most widely deployed message brokers and a natural pairing with self-hosted app stacks (decoupling n8n workflows, backing custom microservices a customer is developing). Capped at medium rather than high because, like Qdrant/Chroma/Milvus in this same analysis batch, the primary consumers are other applications and SDKs, not a human clicking around a browser — the management UI is an operations dashboard, not the product itself. The audience is developers standing up their own infrastructure, narrower than a general-purpose destination app.
blocking_issues:
RabbitMQ's built-in `guest` account is restricted to loopback connections by default for ALL protocols it serves, not just the management HTTP UI — AMQP (5672), the management API, and every other listener refuse `guest` logins from any non-loopback client. Since customers necessarily connect from outside the container (their own app publishing/consuming messages, or a browser hitting the management UI through Traefik), the broker is completely non-functional out of the box unless a real, remotely-usable admin user/password is provisioned at first boot — this is not optional the way a login screen usually is.

The official image's supported mechanism for provisioning that user, `RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER`/`RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS`, only accepts a plaintext password — RabbitMQ hashes it internally, but the env var itself must be the plaintext value, never a pre-computed hash. (A legacy `RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS_HASH` variable existed pre-3.9 but is deprecated and documented as no longer used.) `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever produces a hash string, so feeding that into `RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS` would set the broker's real password to an opaque hash the customer never sees and can't type — same plaintext-vs-hash mismatch documented for Qdrant's API key and Ackee's login field. This is a genuine plaintext requirement, not just a missing hash algorithm, which apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md calls out as an actual structural blocker rather than a "not a hard no" algorithm gap.

Unlike every other app in this analysis batch that hit a plaintext-login wall (Apache Hop, Apache Amoro, AstrBot, Agent Zero), the standard workaround — leave the app's own login unset/ default and gate its single HTTP surface with Traefik `basic_auth: true` — does not fully apply here. RabbitMQ's core function is served over AMQP (5672), a raw binary protocol that Traefik's HTTP-layer `basic_auth` cannot gate at all. Even if the management UI on 15672 were fully covered by a `basic_auth` gate, the AMQP port would still need its own working, non-default, customer-known credential to be secure and functional — and that credential has no expressible input channel today.

Net effect: there is no way to give the customer a working, secure broker without a plaintext admin credential neither `generated_from` (hash-only) nor `traefik_basic_auth` (HTTP-only, doesn't reach the AMQP port) can supply today.
summary: RabbitMQ is an extremely active, MPL-2.0 open-source message broker with an official, regularly-updated Docker image (`rabbitmq:4.3.4-management- alpine`) and no EOL signal whatsoever — a solid upstream by every version-health measure. It would also fill a genuine gap: nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a message broker/queue. It fails installability today for a reason distinct from the usual plaintext- login pattern seen elsewhere in this batch: RabbitMQ's `guest` account is loopback-only across every protocol it serves, so a real remote admin credential is mandatory (not optional) for the broker to work at all, the official image only accepts that credential as plaintext (no hash input), and — unlike single-HTTP-surface apps — the core AMQP protocol on port 5672 has no HTTP-layer gate that `basic_auth` could substitute in front of. This is a platform mechanism gap (a customer-supplied or projected plaintext credential, not just a hash), so `blocked_on_platform` rather than `not_recommended` — worth revisiting if the bootstrap mechanism ever gains a plaintext-credential input channel.

name: Readur
source_description: Modern document management system with advanced OCR for searchable archives
version_health_notes: Not archived. Releases have shipped roughly every 2-4 weeks over the past several months (2.7.3 on 2025-12-26 through 2.9.2 on 2026-07-09), and the default branch had a commit as recently as 2026-08-06 — one day after today (2026-08-05), i.e. development is ongoing right now. This is a young, fast-moving project, not a mature/slowing one.
differentiation: Same core pitch as paperless-ngx (OCR + full-text search over scanned documents/PDFs behind a web UI), but a lighter stack: single Rust/Axum binary plus Postgres, no Redis/Celery worker tier. Adds WebDAV/S3 ingestion and OIDC/SSO login that paperless-ngx doesn't have out of the box. It is a genuine alternative within a category we already cover, not a new category.
usefulness_rationale: A real, if narrower, audience wants a lighter/faster document-OCR stack than paperless-ngx, but it's the same job-to-be-done we already ship, and Readur is a much younger, less battle-tested project (first releases only in the past ~8 months) than the paperless-ngx line it would sit next to.
blocking_issues:
ADMIN_PASSWORD has no expressible mechanism today. Readur's admin seeding (src/seed.rs) takes the env var as a literal plaintext password (min 8 chars) and stores `bcrypt::hash(password, 12)`; login (src/routes/auth.rs) does `bcrypt::verify(submitted_password, stored_hash)` against the same value. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` produces an opaque hash string (e.g. "bcrypt:$2b$..."), not a plaintext credential — feeding that string into ADMIN_PASSWORD would make Readur bcrypt-hash the hash itself and require the customer to type the raw hash blob as their login password to match it. There is no channel today to hand Readur a plaintext credential the customer actually knows.

Auto-generating ADMIN_PASSWORD server-side (like POSTGRES_PASSWORD or JWT_SECRET) doesn't work either: unlike those internal secrets, this one is customer-facing — it's the literal password the customer must type into Readur's own login screen every visit. A random value never shown to the customer would lock them out of the document archive entirely.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` doesn't rescue this either — Readur has its own login (unlike Adminer), so a basic-auth wrapper would only add a second, equally undeliverable credential in front of the first; it doesn't solve access to Readur's own UI.
summary: Readur is a single-HTTP-port (8000), Traefik-friendly Rust document/OCR app backed by Postgres, with no extra raw ports or GPU/privileged needs. It overlaps squarely with paperless-ngx (and by extension paperless-ai) already in the catalogue — same OCR/searchable-archive pitch, lighter stack, younger and less proven project. It fails installability today for the same structural reason as other apps whose own login does a plaintext bcrypt compare: ADMIN_PASSWORD needs a customer-known plaintext credential and there is no channel to supply or safely auto-generate one today. Revisit if a future mechanism can pass a customer-known plaintext credential through, or purely as a differentiated-alternative candidate once paperless-ngx-style admin-password delivery is solved platform-wide.

name: Readyset
source_description: Streaming SQL cache for Postgres and MySQL with automatic result invalidation
upstream_license: BSL-1.1 (converts to Apache-2.0 four years after each release)
version_health_notes: Latest tag stable-260730 (readyset package version 1.29.0) published 2026-07-31, less than a week before today (2026-08-05). GitHub release history shows a consistent ~monthly cadence going back well over a year (stable-260720 on 2026-07-21, stable-260630 on 2026-07-01, stable-260528 on 2026-05-28, stable-260423 on 2026-04-23, etc. — tag names encode the release date as stable-YYMMDD). No archival notice, no maintenance-only signal; this is one of the more actively released upstreams evaluated so far.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes are a database caching/read-scaling layer — this is a structurally different category (infra plumbing, not an end-user application). It doesn't compete with anything in the catalogue; it competes with a customer's Redis/Memcached instance or query-cache middleware, and only for customers who already run a Postgres/MySQL workload elsewhere that they want to speed up.
usefulness_rationale: Real product with an active upstream, but it isn't a self-contained "application" in the sense the rest of the catalogue is — it's a caching proxy that must be pointed at a database the customer already operates (via UPSTREAM_DB_URL, a full connection string with credentials to an external, already-running Postgres/MySQL with logical replication enabled). An AF recipe has no such external database to attach to; bundling a fresh MySQL/Postgres in the same recipe just to have something to cache produces an empty demo instance with no real workload behind it, defeating the point of the product. There is also no web UI at all — interaction is exclusively via SQL client (CREATE CACHE statements) and a Prometheus metrics endpoint, so it doesn't fit the "visit a domain, log in" pattern the rest of the catalogue and the Traefik front-end assume.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: UPSTREAM_DB_URL (full connection string incl. credentials for the customer's existing external Postgres/MySQL database)
blocking_issues:
UPSTREAM_DB_URL is an arbitrary, customer-specific connection string (host, port, database name, username, and password) pointing at a database the customer runs outside of this recipe. This is exactly the "external API key / arbitrary customer-chosen credential" case SCHEMA.md rules out — there is no channel today for af-api to accept or inject a customer-supplied value at `/compose` time, and it is not a hash that `generated_from` could project from the root password (it's a plaintext DSN for a system entirely outside this recipe's control).

No web UI to gate or log into. Readyset's only interfaces are the Postgres/MySQL wire protocol (SQL client) and a Prometheus /metrics HTTP endpoint — Traefik `basic_auth` (our other supported mechanism) protects HTTP routes, not a raw SQL wire-protocol TCP port, so it doesn't apply here either.

Even disregarding the secret-input problem, the app's value only exists in front of a real, already-populated production database. An AF single-instance recipe with no external DB to attach to would ship as cosmetically "installed" but functionally useless out of the box.
summary: Readyset is an actively maintained (near-monthly releases, latest 5 days before this analysis), BSL-1.1-licensed SQL caching proxy for Postgres and MySQL. It fills no gap versus the current catalogue since nothing else here does database-layer caching, but it is a poor fit for the AF recipe model on two independent counts: it requires a customer-supplied external database connection string with credentials as its core bootstrap input (no expressible mechanism under the current `generated_from`/`basic_auth` constraints), and it exposes no web UI at all — only a raw SQL wire-protocol port and a metrics endpoint, so it isn't reverse-proxy-compatible even if the secret problem were solved. Recommend not_recommended; this is a developer infrastructure component meant to sit in front of an existing production database, not a standalone self-hosted application suited to a single-tenant AF instance.

REDAXO's own angle within that group: unlike WordPress/ClassicPress/Bludit (blog-post-first, fixed content model) or Drupal/Joomla (heavier, more opinionated enterprise CMS), REDAXO is explicitly a thin content-management framework — it ships no default theme or forced markup and expects the site builder to write their own PHP/HTML templates via its module/template addon system (AddOns "YForm", "YRewrite", etc.), closer in spirit to a headless-ish build-your-own-frontend tool than a turnkey blog. It also happens to be the cleanest of the PHP-CMS candidates from an automation standpoint (see installability) — several of the other CMS gap files needed extra engineering (wp-cli, scripted installer POSTs) to avoid a browser-driven setup wizard; REDAXO's community image supports that natively.
blocking_issues: CONFIRMED (Task 4 sanity-check audit, 2026-08-24): the admin credential's install mechanism hashes plaintext internally (or, for alist/nextcloud, the post-boot CLI/occ command does) - generated_from can only emit an already-hashed value, so the customer's real root password will never match. Needs either a platform plaintext-passthrough mechanism or a per-recipe redesign (drop the auto-config, expose the app's own setup wizard behind basic_auth) before this is genuinely installable.
summary: REDAXO is a two-container recipe — friendsofredaxo/redaxo (PHP/Apache, port 80, pinned e.g. to the "5" tag; no per-patch-version tag is currently published, only floating 5/5-stable/5-edge, so pinning would need to be by image digest rather than an immutable version tag, a minor authoring caveat, not a platform blocker) plus a MariaDB sidecar, structurally close to Gitea/Paperless-ngx in this catalogue. Its install flow is the cleanest of the PHP-CMS gap candidates seen so far: the image documents that "REDAXO is auto-installed within the container if the web root is empty and all required environment variables are provided" — REDAXO_DB_HOST/NAME/LOGIN/PASSWORD plus REDAXO_ADMIN_USER/REDAXO_ADMIN_PASSWORD (min 8 chars) — fully non-interactive, no browser wizard and no wp-cli-style workaround needed. REDAXO's own setup code (rex_login::passwordHash) always hashes whatever plaintext is handed to it, so `generated_from`'s root-password hash projection cannot feed REDAXO_ADMIN_PASSWORD directly (it would be double-hashed and the customer's real root password would never match). That is not a blocker, though: the same pattern already accepted for Gitea's GITEA_ADMIN_PASSWORD and ClassicPress's admin account in this repo applies just as well here — auto-generate a random admin password entirely server-side and surface it to the customer post-provision, the same "server_generated_no_customer_input" mechanism, no plaintext round-trip through the customer's root password required. With an actively released upstream (patch roughly every 3-5 weeks, latest two days before today) and zero structural blockers, this is a build_now candidate — though the decision of which general-purpose CMS(s) to actually ship should weigh REDAXO against the other CMS candidates already analyzed in this directory rather than in isolation.

name: Redis
source_description: High-performance in-memory data store for caching, sessions, and real-time workloads.
upstream_license: Tri-licensed: AGPLv3, RSALv2, SSPLv1 (customer/deployer choice, per redis.io/legal/licenses)
version_health_notes: 8.10.0 released 2026-07-29, about 1 week before today (2026-08-05) — an aggressively active cadence. The same day-of-batch release (2026-07-23) also shipped point releases across every parallel- maintained line (8.8.1, 8.6.5, 8.4.5, 8.2.8, 7.4.10, 7.2.15, 6.2.23), showing a healthy multi-branch maintenance ladder, not just a single latest line. Redis went through public licensing turmoil (SSPL/RSAL dual-license switch in 2024, prompting the Linux Foundation's Valkey fork) but reversed course in May 2025 by adding AGPLv3 as an OSI-approved option starting with Redis 8 — upstream is healthy and actively developed, the license churn is resolved, not an EOL signal.
differentiation: Both `immich` and `paperless-ngx` already run Redis internally, on the bridge network only, purely as a private cache/queue backend for that one app — never customer-reachable. A standalone Redis recipe would target a different use case: a customer running their own external app (a custom script, a self-hosted SaaS, a queue worker) that needs a Redis instance to connect to from outside the VM. That's a real, distinct need in principle, but it requires publishing the Redis port to the internet, which is exactly what the catalogue's own rules forbid (see `blocking_issues`).
usefulness_rationale: Would be useful to technical customers who want a managed cache/queue backend for something they run themselves, but it's a developer/ power-user tool with no UI of its own, and its one useful exposure shape (a public 6379) is one our own recipe rules already reject on security grounds. Same structural class as MySQL/MariaDB/PostgreSQL (apps-gaps/mariadb.yaml, apps-gaps/postgresql.yaml) — a raw-protocol data store with no application-layer presence to gate behind Traefik — and harder to ship than Adminer (apps-gaps/adminer.yaml), which at least has an HTTP UI to gate. Unlike those recipes, Redis also has no bundled web UI equivalent (RedisInsight is a separate, unaffiliated-image tool, not part of the official `redis` image) that could serve as the reverse-proxy-friendly front door.
blocking_issues:
The only useful shape for a standalone Redis recipe is a publicly reachable Redis-protocol port so an external customer app/worker can connect to it. Publishing host port 6379 is exactly what RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` rule forbids (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226) — 6379 is explicitly on the forbidden-host-port list. There is no alternate exposure path today: Traefik only routes HTTP, and Redis speaks a raw RESP binary protocol, so it cannot be fronted the way our web-UI recipes are (no `basic_auth`, no subdomain routing).

Even setting the port rule aside, the official `redis` image has no pre-hashed-password input at all. Auth is set via the `requirepass` directive in `redis.conf`, or equivalently via `REDIS_ARGS="--requirepass <plaintext>"` on `redis/redis-stack`- style entrypoints — both take the password in plaintext at container start. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash (argon2/bcrypt), never plaintext, so it cannot project the customer's root password into Redis auth. This is not a supported-algorithm gap waiting on a new hash type (`blocked_on_platform`); Redis structurally requires the plaintext secret, which `generated_from` can never supply — the same structural mismatch documented for PostgreSQL (apps-gaps/postgresql.yaml). Moot anyway given the public-port blocker above.
summary: Redis is an actively maintained, healthy upstream project (8.10.0 shipped about a week before this analysis, with a full ladder of parallel-maintained branches all patched the same week; the 2024 licensing controversy was resolved in 2025 with an AGPLv3 option, not an EOL event). But a standalone Redis recipe has no viable shape in the current catalogue: its only useful exposure — a public, customer- reachable 6379 — is explicitly forbidden by our `no-public-db-port` rule, and it has no web UI to gate behind Traefik/basic_auth the way Adminer or other no-login apps do. `immich` and `paperless-ngx` already run Redis internally as private, non-exposed caches, so there's no literal duplication, but also no "internal-only" niche left for a standalone recipe to fill. This is the same structural mismatch already documented for MySQL, MariaDB, and PostgreSQL — a raw internet-facing data-store port our security rules and Traefik-only routing model don't support, compounded by an auth mechanism (`requirepass`) that only ever accepts a plaintext secret, which `generated_from` can never supply. Recommend not_recommended rather than blocked_on_platform, since no plausible mechanism change fixes this without relaxing a deliberate security rule.

name: Redpanda Console
source_description: Web UI for managing Kafka and Redpanda topics, schemas, and live message streams
upstream_license: BSL-1.1 (Business Source License; converts to Apache-2.0 per the Change Date in redpanda-data/redpanda's licenses/bsl.md)
version_health_notes: v3.9.0 published 2026-07-23, ~13 days before today (2026-08-05). Recent release history shows a steady near-monthly cadence: v3.8.0 (2026-06-29), v3.7.4 (2026-05-29), v3.7.3 (2026-05-20), v3.7.2 (2026-04-29). Note the repo is also still cutting parallel v2.8.x patch releases (v2.8.16 on 2026-06-22, v2.8.15/v2.8.14 on 2026-05-29) alongside the v3 line — likely an LTS/backport branch for customers not yet on v3, not a sign of stagnation. No archival notice; repo pushed to as recently as today. Clearly active.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes touch message streaming/Kafka at all — this would be a new category (dev/ops tooling for event streaming) rather than competing with an existing recipe. Closest is arguably Portainer/Adminer in spirit (an ops UI in front of infrastructure the customer already runs) but for Kafka/Redpanda instead of Docker or a SQL database.
usefulness_rationale: Real, actively developed tool with a clear niche use case, but that niche is narrower here than it looks: Console's whole value proposition is pointing at a Kafka/Redpanda cluster the customer already operates, typically in production, elsewhere. AF customers provisioning a single self-hosted app instance don't generally have an existing external Kafka cluster to manage. A recipe could bundle its own single-node Redpanda broker (as upstream's own demo docker-compose does) to make the app self-contained, but then it's a Kafka/Redpanda sandbox with a UI attached, not "manage the Kafka cluster I already have" — a materially smaller value prop than the Hostinger description implies.
blocking_issues:
Redpanda Console's built-in login (OIDC or basic-auth, configured via `authentication.jwtSigningKey` etc.) is an enterprise-license-gated feature per upstream docs — without a license key, unauthenticated users hit a "license expired" page and login is unavailable. The community-edition app is therefore open-by-default with full cluster-management access (topics, consumer groups, ACLs, schema registry) unless something else gates it. Traefik `basic_auth: true` on the app's single public port covers this cleanly (no license needed, no customer-facing credential of the app's own), so this is not a hard blocker — just something the recipe must remember to set.

Only self-contained (bundled own Redpanda broker) deployment is installable under current constraints. If a customer instead wants Console pointed at their real, already-running Kafka/Redpanda cluster — the actual common use case — that requires supplying `KAFKA_BROKERS` plus, for anything beyond a trivially open local cluster, SASL/TLS credentials (`KAFKA_SASL_USERNAME`, `KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD`, client certs) for a system entirely outside this recipe. That is exactly the "external, already-running service + arbitrary credential" case SCHEMA.md rules out — no channel exists for af-api to accept or inject such a value at `/compose` time. This doesn't block the bundled/self-contained variant, but it does mean the recipe can only ever manage a fresh sandbox cluster it created for itself, not a customer's real one.
summary: Redpanda Console is an actively maintained (near-monthly releases, latest 13 days before this analysis), BSL-1.1-licensed web UI for Kafka/Redpanda that fills a genuine gap in the current 24-recipe catalogue — nothing else touches event streaming. It clears the mechanical bar for installable_today only in a self-contained form (Console + a bundled single-node Redpanda broker, gated by Traefik basic_auth since the app's own login is enterprise-license-only), which keeps every input server-generated with no customer-supplied secrets. However, that self-contained form is also its main weakness: the product's real value is managing an existing external Kafka/Redpanda cluster, and that path requires arbitrary broker addresses and SASL/TLS credentials with no expressible input channel today. Recommend build_with_caveats — worth building as a bundled Redpanda-sandbox recipe, but be explicit in the recipe description that it manages its own bundled cluster, not an external one the customer may already run.

name: Reitti

name: Reiverr
source_description: TV-friendly Jellyfin, TMDB, Sonarr, and Radarr discovery and playback frontend
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/aleksilassila/reiverr (pin to a version tag such as v2.2.0 — do not follow upstream README's :latest example)
version_health_notes: v2.2.0 shipped 2025-02-22 (marked a pre-release on GitHub, not even a full stable release) and is, as of today 2026-08-05, about 18 months old with no newer tag. `git log` on `master` confirms the same date for the last real commit — the only push activity visible since then is a dependabot dependency-bump branch (2026-02-19), not a merge to master. The repo is not archived and the maintainer is still responsive: in issue #188 ("Status Project", opened 2026-01-13 asking if the project is still supported), the maintainer replied on 2026-02-13 saying they "recently started working on the project again" with "a pretty comprehensive and big plan," promising a timeline update "in the next couple of months." As of the most recent comments on that same issue (2026-06-12 and 2026-06-28, both community members asking for a progress update with no maintainer reply), six months have passed since that promise with nothing landed on master. This is a stalled/dormant project with a stated-but-unfulfilled revival intent, not an actively maintained one — treat the "still supported" framing with the same skepticism the maintainer's own community is now expressing.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a combined discovery+playback frontend for a media-server stack. Conceptually closest is the previously gap-analyzed (not yet built) Jellyseerr, which is request-management-only (no playback) — Reiverr additionally plays media back directly via a Jellyfin plugin and can stream via a Jackett/torrent-stream plugin, so it is not a pure duplicate even against that unshipped candidate. However Reiverr's entire value (TMDB discovery, Jellyfin playback, Sonarr/Radarr library status) is structurally dependent on external services the customer must already run and manually connect after first login — none of Jellyfin, TMDB accounts, Sonarr, Radarr, or Jackett exist as AF recipes today, so like Jellyseerr this is a dependent piece of a larger media-stack pipeline, not a self-contained destination a customer can install and use alone.
usefulness_rationale: Niche within an already-niche self-hosted-media-stack audience (its own README describes it as "still in early stages" even before the 18-month development stall), requires the customer to already run and hold admin credentials for at least one other self-hosted service (Jellyfin) not present in our catalogue to get any value from it, and that upstream dependency is itself stalled. Low priority relative to building the media-server pieces (Jellyfin) this app would actually sit on top of.
blocking_issues:
Reiverr's admin account is seeded via the optional `ADMIN_USERNAME` / `ADMIN_PASSWORD` environment variables — a config-seed hook that Jellyfin, for comparison, lacks entirely. However, inspection of the upstream source (backend/src/auth/auth.service.ts, backend/src/users/users.service.ts) confirms the app does not hash passwords at all: `user.password === password` is a plain string comparison, and `users.service.ts` even has a `// TODO: Hash password` comment marking it unimplemented. `ADMIN_PASSWORD` must therefore be supplied as the literal plaintext credential the customer will type to log in. Per SCHEMA.md, `generated_from` only ever carries a hash of the root password, never the plaintext — this is a genuine plaintext-only requirement, which SCHEMA.md calls out explicitly as a structural blocker (distinct from the softer "unsupported hash algorithm" case, which would not block on its own).

Leaving `ADMIN_USERNAME`/`ADMIN_PASSWORD` unset falls back to "whoever submits any username/password first becomes admin" — the same unauthenticated-race self-registration pattern the existing `jellyfin.yaml` gap analysis already treated as insufficient even when combined with a defensive Traefik `basic_auth` gate, since the customer still ends up hand-picking their own in-app credential rather than the platform projecting one it already controls. Kept consistent with that precedent here rather than treated as a workaround.
summary: Reiverr is a single-container, reverse-proxy-friendly Svelte/NestJS web app (ghcr.io/aleksilassila/reiverr, port 9494) structurally similar to Uptime Kuma/Vaultwarden-style single-container recipes, but it fails installability on the same plaintext-admin-credential problem as Jellyfin — worse, in fact, since its source confirms passwords are stored and compared in cleartext with no hashing at all, so there is no possible `generated_from` projection, hashed or not. Its practical value is also structurally capped: it is a discovery/playback frontend for an existing Jellyfin (plus optionally Sonarr/Radarr/Jackett) stack the customer must already run elsewhere, none of which exist as AF recipes today. On top of both problems, upstream development has been stalled for roughly 18 months (last real commit 2025-02-22) despite a maintainer promise in early 2026 to resume work, which six months of follow-up community comments show has not yet materialized. Recommend `not_recommended` — low standalone value, no catalogue pairing, a genuine plaintext-credential blocker, and a dormant upstream with an unfulfilled revival promise.

name: Relaticle
source_description: Open-source CRM with native AI agent support and REST API automation
version_health_notes: v3.3.19 shipped 2026-07-29, about a week before today (2026-08-05). Releases are landing multiple times a week (v3.3.10 through v3.3.19 all within a roughly six-week window, June 22 - July 29), a very healthy cadence for a project at 1.5k GitHub stars / 167 forks with 1,300+ commits, 5 open issues and 9 open PRs. Modern stack (Laravel 13, Filament 5, PHP 8.4) with a public roadmap. No signs of slowing, maintenance-only, or archival.
differentiation: No existing recipe in the 24-app catalogue covers CRM/sales-pipeline use cases. Relaticle's specific angle is native AI-agent integration (an MCP server exposing 30 tools plus a full REST API) on top of a conventional contacts/companies/deals CRM, which pairs naturally with the catalogue's existing AI-adjacent recipes (ollama, open-webui, hermes-agent, openclaw) as something an agent could actually operate against. Genuinely new ground, not a variant of anything already shipped.
usefulness_rationale: CRM is a common SMB/freelancer need with no self-hosted representation in the catalogue today, and the AI-agent/MCP angle is a differentiator IONOS could market distinctly from generic "yet another CRM" self-host guides. Single reverse-proxy-friendly web UI, standard Postgres+Redis backing services matching the existing n8n/paperless-ngx/immich pattern this catalogue already supports well.
blocking_issues:
Relaticle has no CLI-free, env-var-driven way to seed an initial admin account. The upstream self-hosting guide's documented path is `docker compose exec app php artisan make:filament-user`, an interactive CLI prompt with no non-interactive/env-var equivalent — not expressible via `generated_from` (there is no single admin password parameter on the app to project a hash into).

The actual first-run path is web self-registration at `/app/register`. With the default `REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true` and no SMTP configured (there is no channel for a customer-supplied mail-relay credential either), nobody can complete verification and sign in. Setting `REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=false` removes that block but upstream's own docs warn "anyone who can reach `/app/register` can create a working account" — i.e. whoever visits the domain first after deployment becomes the CRM owner, a race any internet scanner wins if the domain is reachable before the customer's first visit.

This race is closeable with the same tool used for no-login apps: gate the entire domain behind Traefik `basic_auth` (customer's root password hash) so no unauthenticated request reaches `/app/register` before the customer does. That is a workable fit for our mechanism, not a structural blocker — but it is a caveat on the recipe design (permanent basic_auth in front of an app that has its own login), not a zero-caveat `build_now`.
summary: Relaticle is an actively maintained (weekly releases), AGPL-3.0 Laravel/Filament CRM with a distinctive AI-agent/MCP angle that fills a genuine gap — no CRM exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It runs as a standard multi-container docker-compose stack (app + horizon worker + scheduler + Postgres 17 + Redis 7) matching patterns already proven in n8n/paperless-ngx/immich, behind a single reverse-proxy-friendly port. The one real wrinkle is initial-admin bootstrapping: there's no env-var or `generated_from` path to seed an admin account directly, only an interactive CLI command or open self-registration at `/app/register`. That registration endpoint is a first-come-first-served race if exposed unauthenticated, so the recipe needs a permanent Traefik `basic_auth` gate (root-password hash) in front of the whole app plus `REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=false` (no SMTP input channel exists) to be safely installable today — workable, but a caveat-laden design rather than a clean `build_now`.

Preceding releases (v1.16.0 2026-05-22, v1.16.1 2026-06-02, v1.16.2/1.16.3 2026-07-09) show a steady multi-week cadence through 2026, following a slower 2024-2025 period (v1.14.0 2024-10-27, v1.15.0 2025-12-24). Repo is not archived; project is actively maintained.
differentiation: Nothing in the current catalogue covers embeddable comment/discussion widgets for external blogs or static sites — this is a distinct use case from any of the 24 existing recipes (no CMS, forum, or comment-system recipe exists today). It would appeal to customers running a static site or blog elsewhere who want a privacy-respecting Disqus alternative.
usefulness_rationale: Real niche demand (Disqus-alternative-seekers), but it's an embed widget consumed by an external site rather than a destination app the customer visits directly — narrower audience than a general-purpose tool, and its value is gated behind the OAuth setup described below.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: AUTH_GITHUB_CID / AUTH_GITHUB_CSEC (or another OAuth provider's client ID/secret — Google, Facebook, Microsoft, Telegram, GitLab)
blocking_issues:
Remark42 has no built-in admin username/password. Site visitors log in via OAuth (GitHub/Google/Facebook/Microsoft/Telegram/GitLab client ID+secret) or SMTP-backed email magic links; becoming a comment moderator/admin additionally requires pasting that OAuth-derived user ID into ADMIN_SHARED_ID after a manual first login. None of these credentials are the customer's server root password, and none are a value af-api can derive or generate server-side — there is no input channel for an external OAuth app registration or a customer's own SMTP credentials today.

Anonymous commenting (AUTH_ANON=true) works without any credential, but nobody can be promoted to admin without first authenticating via one of the OAuth providers above, so the moderation surface is unreachable in a zero-external-credential deployment.

Gating the whole site behind Traefik basic_auth would not substitute for real admin auth here — the app does have its own login mechanism (OAuth), it's just one we have no channel to configure, so this isn't the "app with no login of its own" case basic_auth is meant to cover.
summary: Remark42 is an actively maintained (latest release 2026-07-10), single small Go binary/container comment-engine widget with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It is mechanically simple to run behind Traefik (one HTTP port, no extra protocols), but every path to a working admin/moderator role requires an external OAuth app registration (client ID + secret) or the customer's own SMTP credentials for email login — neither of which has an input channel under the current root-password-projection / basic-auth mechanism. Revisit once a general-purpose "arbitrary customer-supplied API key/secret" channel exists on af-api; until then this is blocked_on_platform, not a not_recommended app.

differentiation: None beyond what guacamole already covers, and materially worse fit for a hosted-recipe model. Remmina is a native GTK desktop application, not a server product — it has no first-party server or web mode. The only containerized path is linuxserver/remmina, a "webtop"-style image that boots a full KasmVNC Linux desktop in the browser and runs the Remmina GUI inside it, plus a passwordless sudo terminal alongside it.
