The image's pinned tag (1.4.40dfsg-2ubuntu1) trails the current upstream release (1.4.43) by three point releases, so the recipe would ship a stale build from day one.
summary: Remmina is a native desktop remote-desktop client, not a server app; the only Docker packaging (linuxserver/remmina) works by running a full browser-accessible Linux desktop (KasmVNC-based) with Remmina and a root-capable sudo terminal inside it. Mechanically it is installable today — a domain plus a Traefik basic_auth gate covers the one first-boot secret — but it directly overlaps with guacamole, which already covers the "reach RDP/VNC/SSH from a browser" use case as a purpose-built gateway rather than a full sudo desktop workaround, and its only container image lags upstream by three releases. Recommend not adding it to the catalogue.

name: Resilio Sync
source_description: Peer-to-peer file synchronization across devices using the BitTorrent protocol
version_health_notes: Resilio Sync itself is still developed (3.1.2.1076 shipped 2025-10-31, ~9 months before today, 2026-08-05), but the vendor's own Docker Hub image, `resilio/sync`, has not been rebuilt since ~mid-2024 and is frozen at `2.8.1` — a pre-3.0 build, ~2 years stale. The only image tracking current releases is the third-party `linuxserver/resilio-sync` (currently shipping the 3.0.3 binary as of this writing), which repackages Resilio's proprietary binary rather than being vendor-maintained. Resilio also discontinued its separate "Sync Business" product in favor of "Resilio Active Everywhere" in 2024, narrowing the vendor's own focus away from the self-hosted Sync line this recipe would target. Net: the product line is not abandoned, but the officially-published container is, and only a community rebuild tracks the app that's actually current.
differentiation: Functionally near-identical to the existing syncthing recipe: both are peer-to-peer, no-cloud-middleman file sync tools with a web UI and a dedicated sync port. Resilio adds LAN-sync speed via BitTorrent-derived swarming and one-click folder "read keys" for sharing, but Syncthing already covers the core "sync files across my own devices without a cloud" use case with a fully open-source, no-account, no-license stack.
usefulness_rationale: A customer who wants P2P sync already has syncthing in the catalogue with no licensing friction. Resilio's value-add (swarming speed, selective sync UX) is real but marginal for a self-hosted single-tenant VM, and is undercut by the licensing blocker below.
blocking_issues:
As of Sync 3.0 (Aug 2024), Resilio requires every install — including free, non-commercial use — to register an account on resilio.com and confirm non-commercial usage online before the app is functional ("Licensing in Resilio Sync 3.0"). This is exactly the "OAuth app registration / third-party account linking" case the schema calls a hard no: there is no channel today for a customer to complete that registration through `/compose`.

The only way to avoid the 3.0 licensing wall is pinning to the vendor's stale `resilio/sync:2.8.1` image (pre-3.0, no forced registration) — but that ships a build the vendor itself has moved past and stopped publishing updates for, which conflicts with shipping a recipe on current, supported software.

Resilio's own WebUI login (set via `sync.conf`'s `webui.password`) takes a plaintext password, not a hash — `generated_from` can only project a hash, so this field cannot be populated from the customer's root password. Leaving it unset (Traefik `basic_auth` as the real gate, same as WUD/Open WebUI) works for the local WebUI, but does not touch the account-registration blocker above, which is unrelated to the local login.
summary: Resilio Sync overlaps almost entirely with the already-catalogued syncthing (P2P, no-cloud file sync, web UI, dedicated sync port), and brings no differentiator strong enough to justify the overlap on its own. More decisively, Sync 3.0 (the only actively-developed line) requires mandatory online account registration and license activation even for free non-commercial use — a third-party account-linking flow with no input channel in the current `/compose` mechanism. The alternative, pinning the vendor's stale, un-updated 2.8.1 image to dodge that requirement, means shipping software the vendor has already moved past. Recommend not building until either the licensing model changes or an external-account input channel exists on the platform.

name: Restreamer
source_description: Easy-to-use live video streaming server supporting RTMP, HLS, SRT, and WebRTC
version_health_notes: No tagged release since v2.12.0 (2024-09-13) — almost 2 years (~23 months) before today (2026-08-05). Prior cadence (v2.11.0 2024-06-07, v2.10.0 2024-04-23, v2.9.0 2024-04-05, v2.8.0 2024-02-02) was roughly monthly through 2024, then stopped entirely. Not a clean abandonment, though: Docker Hub's untagged "dev" image was pushed ~9 days ago, and the GitHub issue tracker is still active, so upstream is doing unreleased work rather than being archived — but customers today only get the frozen 2.12.0 image, so treat it as maintenance-only in practice.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does live video ingest or restreaming (RTMP/SRT/HLS/WebRTC) — this would open a new category. Two other streaming-server candidates (Ant Media Server CE, MistServer) were separately gap-analyzed and hit the same structural blockers (raw non-HTTP ingest ports, no expressible first-boot credential mechanism), so this isn't a unique opportunity so much as a third data point in a niche the platform can't yet serve.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists (creators/small broadcasters wanting a self-hosted RTMP restreaming hub for OBS → YouTube/Twitch/Facebook), but the audience is narrower and more technical than the catalogue's typical productivity/monitoring/media-library apps, and the frozen ~2-year-old image adds risk on top of that.
blocking_issues:
Restreamer's own admin login (RS_USERNAME/RS_PASSWORD env vars, or the newer CORE_API_AUTH_USERNAME/CORE_API_AUTH_PASSWORD naming documented for the in-development next version) only accepts a plaintext username/password pair — there is no hash-based field for generated_from to project into. The workable path is to hardcode a fixed, non-customer-facing value for RS_USERNAME/RS_PASSWORD and put the actual customer-facing gate in front of the whole app via Traefik basic_auth (root-password hash), the same pattern used for n8n/Immich/Open WebUI. That mechanism (IF-1312) is still unmerged, so this is blocked on the same platform work as MistServer, not on anything specific to Restreamer.

Core function needs RTMP (1935/1936) and SRT (6000/udp) ingest ports exposed raw to the internet — Traefik can front the HTTP dashboard (8080) and HTTPS API (8181) but does nothing for these. Restreamer does support a per-stream publish token (set from inside the UI after login, not read from an env var at boot), which mitigates anonymous-publish risk once an admin configures it, but it isn't a first-boot secret our mechanism needs to supply — it's a caveat for whoever builds this, not a blocker on its own (same shape as MistServer's RTMP/RTSP/UDP ports).
summary: Restreamer would fill a genuine catalogue gap (no live-streaming/RTMP restreaming recipe exists today), but it's blocked on the same unmerged Traefik basic_auth mechanism (IF-1312) needed for MistServer and other no-hash-login apps, since its own admin login only takes a plaintext password with no field for a projected hash. Even once that lands, its RTMP/SRT ingest ports stay raw by design (mitigated only by an in-app-configured publish token, not a first-boot secret), and the upstream image has been frozen at v2.12.0 for ~23 months despite ongoing unreleased dev-branch activity — worth revisiting after IF-1312 merges, but not a near-term build.

name: Rocket.Chat
source_description: Open-source team messaging with real-time chat, video calls, and integrations
upstream_license: MIT (Expat) for the core; `ee/` and `apps/meteor/ee/` directories are under a separate proprietary Rocket.Chat enterprise license (repo LICENSE is dual, GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
version_health_notes: 8.6.1 is the newest non-prerelease tag, published 2026-07-10 — 27 days before today (2026-08-06). The 8.7.0 line is mid-release-candidate (8.7.0-rc.0 on 2026-07-21 through 8.7.0-rc.5 on 2026-08-04, all marked prerelease on GitHub and pushed as `8.7.0-rc.N` tags on Docker Hub), so a recipe would pin 8.6.1, not an RC. Rocket.Chat ships a new minor roughly monthly (8.5.x, 8.6.0 on 2026-07-03, 8.6.1 on 2026-07-10) and maintains an unusually wide set of parallel patch branches — on 2026-07-10/11 alone it cut 7.10.14, 8.0.8, 8.1.7, 8.2.7, 8.3.7, 8.4.5, 8.5.2 and 8.6.1 in one coordinated sweep. `develop` has commits from today. Clearly active and commercially backed, not maintenance-only, archived, or EOL. Separate commercial caveat, not a version-health problem: the free self-managed Community tier is user-capped (workspaces crossing 25 users / 100 monthly active contacts are auto-enrolled in a 30-day trial and must then upgrade, reduce users, or fall back to Community), and the Pro plan was retired to legacy on 2026-04-29.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers team chat/messaging, so this would open a new category rather than duplicate anything. Against the other messaging candidates already analysed under apps-gaps/, Rocket.Chat is the closest sibling to apps-gaps/mattermost.yaml (self-hosted Slack/Teams alternative, single HTTP app + one database), and unlike apps-gaps/matrix-synapse.yaml + apps-gaps/element.yaml it is a single self-contained product — server and web client in one image — so no second recipe is needed to make it usable.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted team chat is a mainstream, frequently requested workload (avoiding Slack/Teams SaaS pricing and keeping message data on the customer's own server), and Rocket.Chat is one of the two best-known options in that space. It serves its own full web UI on a single HTTP port (3000) with WebSocket upgrades, which Traefik fronts fine on `<slug>.<base_domain>`, so it fits the existing proxy model without raw ports. The Community user cap tempers this for larger teams but not for the small-team case the catalogue mostly targets.
blocking_issues:
Rocket.Chat's only supported way to preseed the first admin account is the documented `INITIAL_USER=yes` + `ADMIN_USERNAME` / `ADMIN_EMAIL` / `ADMIN_PASS` env-var set (plus `OVERWRITE_SETTING_Show_Setup_Wizard=completed` to skip the wizard). `ADMIN_PASS` takes the **plaintext** password — Rocket.Chat hashes it itself on first boot and there is no env var, setting, or API field that accepts a pre-computed hash. Per SCHEMA.md's decision table this is a structural blocker: `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever carries a hash, so it has nowhere to project. Same shape as the blocker in apps-gaps/matrix-synapse.yaml.

Skipping the env vars and letting the customer run the built-in setup wizard doesn't help either: that route creates the admin credential client-side in the browser, so again there is no `type: password` metadata parameter on Rocket.Chat's own login for the root-password projection to target — and until someone completes it the fresh workspace sits on the public domain with an open wizard/registration form (`Accounts_RegistrationForm` defaults to public), so whoever reaches the domain first owns the workspace.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate is a poor substitute here for exactly the reason given in apps-gaps/mattermost.yaml: Rocket.Chat is explicitly multi-user team software, so a permanent gate over the whole hostname would also lock out every teammate the customer invites (none of whom know the customer's server root password), and would break the mobile and desktop clients' REST/WebSocket connections to the same port. Removing the gate after bootstrap needs a manual out-of-band step the install flow doesn't support today. The single root-password projection is also already consumed by the gate, leaving no channel for a second, distinct in-app admin credential.

Secondary, not boot-blocking: teammate email invites, password resets and push notifications beyond the Community tier's 10k/month cap depend on customer-supplied external SMTP / cloud-workspace credentials, and `ROCKETCHAT_LICENSE` (needed for any paid tier) is likewise a customer-supplied value — none of which has an input channel in `/compose`. A Community-tier install boots fine without them.

Mechanical caveat for whoever builds this later, not a platform blocker: Rocket.Chat requires MongoDB configured as a **replica set** (`?replicaSet=rs0`), not a standalone mongod. Upstream's compose ships an entrypoint script that runs `rs.initiate()` on first start; the recipe would have to carry that init step, which is more involved than the plain `postgres:16-alpine` sidecar in recipes/n8n or recipes/paperless-ngx.
summary: Rocket.Chat is an actively developed (monthly minors, 8.6.1 on 2026-07-10, 8.7.0 currently in RC, commits today), commercially backed team-chat platform that would fill a genuine messaging gap in the current 24-recipe catalogue with no overlap against anything shipping. Architecturally it fits well — one image serving both server and web UI on a single HTTP port behind Traefik — with the one mechanical wrinkle that its MongoDB must be a replica set rather than a plain sidecar. It is not installable today because the only supported first-admin provisioning path (`INITIAL_USER` + `ADMIN_PASS`) demands the plaintext password, which the hash-only `generated_from` mechanism cannot supply, while the alternative — the built-in setup wizard on an openly registerable domain — creates the credential client-side and can't be safely gated behind Traefik basic auth for multi-user chat software. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`, revisit alongside apps-gaps/mattermost.yaml and apps-gaps/matrix-synapse.yaml once the platform can seed or surface a first-boot plaintext credential.

name: RomM
source_description: Beautiful self-hosted ROM manager for scanning, browsing, and playing retro games
version_health_notes: Stable 5.1.0 released 2026-07-29, 7 days before today (2026-08-05); 5.1.1-beta.1 followed on 2026-08-02 and the default branch was pushed 2026-08-06, so the project is in continuous active development. The release feed shows a dense alpha/beta/stable train (5.0.0 on 2026-07-15, then ten 5.1.0 pre-releases across 2026-07-22..07-27 before 5.1.0 stable) — a mature project shipping stable minors every few weeks with pre-releases in between. ~11.9k GitHub stars, not archived, no EOL notice, multi-maintainer org (`rommapp`) with a docs site (docs.romm.app) and companion clients.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers gaming or emulation — the nearest neighbours (immich for photos, syncthing for files) are library/sync tools for other media types. RomM is a single-HTTP-port web app that scans a customer-supplied ROM library, enriches it with metadata/artwork from online providers, and plays games in-browser via EmulatorJS/RuffleRS, plus save-state sync and companion-app APIs. It does overlap with the already-analysed candidate `retroassembly.yaml` (also browser-based retro gaming); RomM is the larger, better-staffed project (~11.9k vs ~1.1k stars) with richer metadata/library management, while RetroAssembly is the simpler single-container one. Per CLAUDE.md, overlap between candidates is not itself a reason to reject either.
usefulness_rationale: Strong hobbyist/enthusiast appeal and by far the best-known app in this niche, but it is entertainment rather than broad business utility, and the customer supplies (and is solely responsible for the legality of) their own ROM files — the app ships no copyrighted content. Active upstream and a category the catalogue does not touch argue for building it; niche audience argues against high priority.
summary: RomM is a two-service compose stack (rommapp/romm plus a mariadb:11 sidecar; Redis/Valkey is bundled inside the app image and needs no separate service) exposing one HTTP port, 8080, which fronts cleanly behind Traefik on romm.<base_domain>. Its three mandatory secrets — ROMM_AUTH_SECRET_KEY, the app DB password and the MariaDB root password — are all patternless values no customer ever reads, so they can be generated server-side; the admin account is created by the customer in the browser through RomM's first-boot setup wizard (the uptime-kuma pattern), so no root-password projection and no Traefik basic_auth gate are needed. Metadata providers (ScreenScraper, MobyGames, SteamGridDB, RetroAchievements, IGDB) each need an external API key that has no input channel today, but they are optional: the keyless Hasheous provider (HASHEOUS_API_ENABLED=true) can be enabled server-side, so scanning and artwork work out of the box and the missing key channel degrades a feature rather than blocking the install. Recommend building now, pinned to Docker Hub tag `5.1.0` (not `latest`, and not the `-slim` variant, which drops the bundled EmulatorJS/Ruffle assets and pulls emulator cores from a CDN at runtime instead).

version_health_notes: Very healthy. v12.9.2 shipped 2026-07-17, 19 days before this analysis (2026-08-05), and the repo was last pushed 2026-08-05 itself. Cadence is roughly monthly: v12.7.3 (2026-01-29), v12.7.4 (2026-03-06), v12.7.5 (2026-03-14), v12.8 (2026-04-03), v12.8.1 (2026-05-08), v12.9 (2026-06-05), v12.9.1 (2026-06-26), v12.9.2 (2026-07-17). 475+ releases and ~7.9k commits since 2018, 642 GitHub stars, ~20 open issues, single principal maintainer (François Jacquet) with a commercial plugin/support business behind it. Canonical development is on GitLab; the GitHub repo is a mirror (its license autodetect reports GPL-2.0, matching the LICENSE file — an older GitLab metadata field showing "AGPL v1.0" is a mis-detection, not a relicensing). The Docker image is built from a separate repo (gitlab.com/francoisjacquet/docker-rosariosis, GitHub mirror francoisjacquet/docker-rosariosis), last pushed 2026-07-20, i.e. it does track releases — its Dockerfile pins ROSARIOSIS_VERSION=v12.9.2.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes addresses the education sector; the closest structural cousins (paperless-ngx, gitea) are PHP/Python+DB web apps with an entirely different purpose. RosarioSIS is a student information system — enrolment, grades, gradebook, scheduling, attendance, billing — which is a different product category from an LMS like Moodle (course delivery) that was analysed separately and is currently blocked on image sourcing. RosarioSIS, unlike Moodle, has a self-contained official image.
usefulness_rationale: Serves a real, distinct segment (small/mid-size schools, private academies, tutoring centres — many in exactly the SMB/hosting bracket IONOS sells to) that no current recipe touches, and it is the leading free SIS with a live upstream. Audience is narrower and more vertical than our general-purpose infrastructure and productivity recipes, and the free core intentionally leaves some functionality to paid plugins, so medium rather than high.
summary: Mechanically straightforward two-service stack — rosariosis/rosariosis (PHP 8.1 + Apache, single HTTP port 80, one /var/www/html volume) plus postgres:15, exactly the shape of paperless-ngx/n8n minus the extra workers — with no external API key, OAuth registration or customer-chosen credential anywhere in the boot path, so nothing needs to pass through /compose. The Postgres password is a patternless server-generated value; the one customer-facing secret is a Traefik basic_auth gate, which is mandatory here rather than optional: first boot leaves an unauthenticated /InstallDatabase.php wizard exposed and then seeds a hardcoded admin/admin login, so the basic_auth boundary (IF-1312) is what actually protects the instance until the customer changes that password in-app. Upstream is clearly alive (v12.9.2 on 2026-07-17, monthly cadence, repo pushed the day before this analysis) and fills an education-sector gap the catalogue currently has. Caveats for the build: the official image publishes only a moving `master` tag (no per-version tags exist on Docker Hub), so the recipe must pin by digest — sha256:38044ee4c81b672eda37ff90cf3b8d4719685ac5dabf342b9eb256397941c03b was current at analysis time, built 2026-07-20 from ROSARIOSIS_VERSION v12.9.2 — which satisfies image-tag-pinned but makes WUD update detection and version bumps a manual, digest-tracking chore rather than the usual tag bump; the image is amd64-only; DB schema creation still requires a human to walk the /InstallDatabase.php wizard once behind the gate; and the app's Postgres major-version upgrades are documented as manual, so pin postgres:15 and treat upgrades as a recipe-maintenance item.

name: Rotki
source_description: Rotki is a privacy-first crypto portfolio tracker with DeFi support
version_health_notes: Healthy, actively developed project (~4.0k stars, not archived). Recent tags on Docker Hub and GitHub: v1.42.0 (2026-02-20), v1.42.1 (2026-03-26), v1.43.0 (2026-05-08), v1.43.1 (2026-05-18), v1.43.2 (2026-06-18) — roughly a release every 4-6 weeks. Today is 2026-08-06, so the newest stable tag is 49 days (~7 weeks) old, which is within the project's normal gap between releases and not a dormancy signal. The repo's last push was 2026-08-06 (today) and `nightly`/`edge` images are rebuilt daily, so development is ongoing between releases. No archival, maintenance-only, or EOL signal.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes touch personal finance; the closest thing in spirit is Vaultwarden (self-host-your-own-sensitive-data), not a functional overlap. Rotki is specifically a crypto/DeFi portfolio tracker and tax-accounting tool with a fully local, SQLCipher-encrypted database — it differs from a general investment tracker (Ghostfolio, an apps-gaps candidate, not a recipe) by covering on-chain/DeFi position discovery and jurisdiction-specific tax report generation.
usefulness_rationale: Strong appeal for the crypto-holding subset of self-hosters: it is the best-known open-source tool for local, non-custodial portfolio and tax accounting, and its whole value proposition ("your keys/positions never leave your server") maps directly onto why a customer rents a VPS. Marked medium rather than high because the audience is narrower than a general finance app, and because upstream's own docs treat Docker as a secondary deployment mode behind the desktop app.
summary: Rotki ships a single official all-in-one container (rotki/rotki, pin v1.43.2) that serves backend + frontend over one HTTP port (80) with /data, /logs and optional /config volumes and no required environment variables beyond cosmetics (TZ, LOGLEVEL), so structurally it is a single-container web app like Uptime Kuma or Vaultwarden and works fine behind Traefik on rotki.<base_domain>. It needs no first-boot secret of its own: the account (profile name + password, which is the SQLCipher key for the local DB) is created by the customer in the UI after install, and all external API keys (Etherscan, exchanges, rotki Premium) are optional and entered in-app later — so nothing needs a customer-supplied value through /compose. The catch is that the login screen is open to whoever reaches the URL first, and upstream states outright that "rotki was not designed to run over a public network," recommending exactly a Traefik reverse proxy with basic auth and TLS if it must be exposed; that gate credential is the one first-boot secret and is expressible today via traefik_basic_auth (IF-1312). Note the app's own password can never be root-password-projected, because SQLCipher needs the plaintext and generated_from only carries a hash — hence the gate is mandatory, not optional, and this is build_with_caveats rather than build_now.

name: Roundcube
source_description: Browser-based IMAP webmail client with a modern interface and plugin support
latest_version: 1.7.2 (current stable); 1.6.17 (1.6.x LTS branch, maintained in parallel)
version_health_notes: 1.7.0 landed 2026-05-10 as the first stable of the 1.7 line (after a long rc cycle), followed by 1.7.1 on 2026-05-24 and the security release 1.7.2 on 2026-07-05 — about one month before today (2026-08-06). The 1.6.x branch moved to LTS/security-only mode when 1.7.0 shipped and still gets coordinated releases (1.6.17, same day as 1.7.2, fixing CVE-2026-54432 and CVE-2026-54433 among others); 1.5.x is explicitly no longer maintained. Repo is not archived and was pushed to on 2026-08-05 (yesterday); the official Docker images (roundcube/roundcubemail) were rebuilt 2026-08-03, so both source and image publishing are live. Two supported branches, regular security response, no dormancy signal. Name is unambiguous — roundcube/roundcubemail is the only project using it; roundcube/roundcubemail-docker (also active, pushed 2026-07-07) is the same org's image-build repo, not a competing upstream.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches email. Roundcube is the best-known self-hosted webmail client — a single PHP app on one HTTP port (80) that speaks IMAP/SMTP to a mail server the customer already has, so it gives them a private browser inbox for their existing mailboxes without a third-party webmail provider. Structurally it is a uptime-kuma/vaultwarden-shaped recipe (one container, SQLite by default, one public HTTP port, no raw protocol ports of its own) and sits behind Traefik on roundcube.<base_domain> with no special handling; the only proxy-related knob is ROUNDCUBEMAIL_REQUEST_PATH, and that stays "/" for a subdomain deployment.
usefulness_rationale: Webmail is one of the most recognizable self-hosting asks and Roundcube is the default answer to it — huge install base, shipped by most hosting control panels, so customers arrive already knowing the name. It pairs naturally with IONOS mail products (the customer points it at their own IMAP/SMTP), which makes it more commercially relevant than most single-purpose utilities in the catalogue. Rated high rather than medium for that recognition plus the empty category, with the honest caveat that it is only useful to a customer who already has a mailbox somewhere — it is a client, not a mail server.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: ROUNDCUBEMAIL_DES_KEY (session/password encryption key); ROUNDCUBEMAIL_DB_PASSWORD (only if MariaDB/Postgres is used instead of the default SQLite; internal); basic_auth_password (Traefik gate in front of the login page)
secrets_expressible_today: ROUNDCUBEMAIL_DES_KEY (session/password encryption key):server_generated_no_customer_input; ROUNDCUBEMAIL_DB_PASSWORD (only if MariaDB/Postgres is used instead of the default SQLite; internal):server_generated_no_customer_input; basic_auth_password (Traefik gate in front of the login page):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
Not a blocker, but the central design decision for the recipe: the image's documented "required" env vars ROUNDCUBEMAIL_DEFAULT_HOST and ROUNDCUBEMAIL_SMTP_SERVER are exactly the kind of arbitrary customer-specific value /compose cannot carry (each customer's mail server hostname differs). They cannot simply be left unset either — the entrypoint defaults both to `localhost` and unconditionally writes `$config['imap_host'] = '<host>:<port>'`, so an unconfigured instance points at a non-existent local IMAP server and every login fails. The fix needs no new platform mechanism: the entrypoint appends `include()` lines for every `/var/roundcube/config/*.php` file *after* the generated docker config, so a small PHP override shipped with the recipe and bind-mounted there wins. Setting `$config['imap_host'] = '';` makes Roundcube render a "Server" textbox on the login page (documented behaviour in config/defaults.inc.php: "Leave blank to show a textbox at login"), and `$config['smtp_host'] = 'tls://%h:587';` routes outgoing mail to whatever host the user logged in against (`%h` = user's IMAP hostname). The customer then supplies their own mail host and credentials interactively at first login — no /compose input needed. This must be spelled out in the recipe; copying the upstream example compose verbatim would hardcode mail.example.org and ship dead.

Consequence of the blank-host approach, and why the Traefik `basic_auth` gate above is treated as required rather than optional: with `imap_host` blank, an unauthenticated visitor can make the instance open IMAP/SMTP connections to any hostname they type, i.e. use the customer's box as a credential-probing / outbound-connection springboard. Roundcube does have its own login (the customer's IMAP credentials — no admin account and no `generated_from` projection needed), but that login is not the boundary that stops this, so the public port should sit behind Traefik `basic_auth` projected from the customer's root password (IF-1312), same pattern already used for n8n/WUD/Immich.

OAuth2/OIDC login (ROUNDCUBEMAIL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, Gmail/M365 XOAUTH2) is genuinely unsupportable today — it needs a third-party app registration with no input channel — but it is entirely optional and off by default, so it does not gate first boot. The recipe should just not advertise it.
summary: Roundcube is a healthy, actively maintained (stable 1.7.2 on 2026-07-05, 1.6.x LTS in parallel, repo pushed yesterday), GPL-3.0-or-later PHP webmail client with an official pinned image (roundcube/roundcubemail:1.7.2-apache), one HTTP port, SQLite by default, and no raw protocol ports — a uptime-kuma-shaped single-container recipe that fronts cleanly on Traefik and fills an empty category (no email app among the current 24 recipes). It is installable today with no new platform mechanism, but not by copying the upstream compose: the customer's IMAP/SMTP hostname is an arbitrary per-customer value /compose cannot supply, so the recipe must bind-mount a config override into /var/roundcube/config setting `imap_host = ''` (login page then prompts for the server) and `smtp_host = 'tls://%h:587'`, letting the customer enter their own mail host and credentials at first login. Because a blank host lets anonymous visitors aim the instance at arbitrary mail servers, the public port should be gated with Traefik `basic_auth` from the root password; all other secrets (des_key, optional DB password) are server-generated and never customer-facing. Hence build_with_caveats — high value, but the recipe author must get the blank-host + gate design right.

name: RSS Bridge
source_description: Self-hosted bridge that creates RSS feeds for sites without them
version_health_notes: Upstream development is unambiguously alive — the repo was last pushed on 2026-08-06 (today) and the GitHub API returns a full page (100+) of commits since 2026-02-01, mostly bridge fixes tracking third-party site changes. What is sporadic is *tagging*: releases are date-named and irregular (2022-06-14, 2023-03-22, 2023-07-11, 2023-07-13, 2023-09-24, 2024-02-02, 2025-01-02, 2025-01-26, 2025-06-03, 2025-08-05), and the newest tag, 2025-08-05, is exactly 12 months (366 days) old as of today (2026-08-06). The project's own delivery model is effectively rolling: Docker Hub (rssbridge/rss-bridge) and GHCR publish per-commit `sha-*` tags plus `latest` on every push, and the date tags are occasional snapshots of that stream. Not archived, not maintenance-only, no EOL announcement; 9.1k stars, 267 open issues actively triaged.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches web feeds. The nearest adjacent recipe is n8n, which can technically poll a page and emit items, but that is a general workflow builder requiring the customer to hand-build scraping logic per site; RSS-Bridge ships ~400 maintained site-specific bridges (YouTube, Reddit, Mastodon, Telegram, Bluesky, Substack, plus generic CssSelector/XPath bridges) behind a point-and-click form. It is also a feed *producer*, not a reader — it complements rather than replaces any aggregator a customer already runs.
usefulness_rationale: A genuinely useful, well-known utility (9.1k stars) for a real recurring need: following sites that dropped or never had a feed. But it is a single-purpose helper for a fairly technical, RSS-literate audience rather than a headline app most VPS customers would buy hosting for, and its value depends on the customer already having a feed reader somewhere. Cheap to host (one small PHP/nginx container, no database) which keeps the cost/benefit reasonable even at medium demand.
summary: RSS-Bridge is structurally one of the easiest candidates seen so far: a single Debian/nginx/php-fpm container (rssbridge/rss-bridge, pinnable date tag 2025-08-05), one HTTP port (80 internally, upstream's own compose maps 3000:80), no database, one bind mount for /config, and no external API key or account linking needed for the default bridge set — so it fits the single-container-web-app shape of recipes/uptime-kuma and recipes/opengist and sits cleanly behind Traefik on rss-bridge.<base_domain>. It ships with authentication disabled and all bridges enabled by default, so it must not be left open on the internet (it would otherwise be a free fetch-any-URL scraper for strangers); the gate is Traefik `basic_auth: true` with the root-password hash, per IF-1312, since RSS-Bridge's own basic auth wants a plaintext password in config.ini.php (or RSSBRIDGE_authentication_password) and therefore cannot consume a `generated_from` hash. Caveats, none blocking: a basic-auth gate means feed URLs must carry credentials (https://user:pass@host/... — widely but not universally supported by readers), and pinning to the newest date tag ships a build that is already 12 months old even though upstream commits daily, so a recipe here should expect either regular version bumps or a decision to pin a `sha-*` tag instead.

name: RSSHub
source_description: Open-source RSS feed generator for websites missing native RSS support
version_health_notes: RSSHub does not cut semver releases at all — the GitHub releases list is empty and there are no version tags. Distribution is continuous: every master commit produces a commit-SHA image plus a dated tag (diygod/rsshub:YYYY-MM-DD, with chromium-bundled-YYYY-MM-DD variants), ~15,200 tags on Docker Hub. Tags 2026-08-03, 2026-08-04, 2026-08-05 and 2026-08-06 all exist, and the repo's last push was 2026-08-06 (same day as this analysis), so the project is very actively developed, not archived and not maintenance-only. latest_version above is the most recent complete dated tag (2026-08-05); the 2026-08-06 tag was still being pushed while this was written. Consequence for a recipe: there is no upstream "stable release" to pin — app_version has to be a date tag, which is a moving snapshot of master with no changelog or stability guarantee behind it.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches RSS at all, and RSSHub is not a reader — it is the opposite half of the stack: it scrapes sites, social accounts and APIs that publish no feed and emits RSS/Atom/JSON Feed for them. It therefore does not overlap the reader-side candidates already analysed (apps-gaps/freshrss.yaml, apps-gaps/fusion-rss.yaml, apps-gaps/miniflux.yaml, apps-gaps/commafeed.yaml) — it complements them, and per CLAUDE.md overlap would not be a rejection reason anyway. Note the "web UI" is thin: a landing page and HTML error pages, with the real interface being feed URLs like /github/issue/DIYgod/RSSHub fetched by the customer's reader. Everything is one HTTP port, so Traefik on rsshub.<base_domain> fronts it the same way it fronts uptime-kuma or opengist.
usefulness_rationale: A well-known project (45k+ stars) solving a real problem for anyone who tracks sites without feeds, and self-hosting it is the standard answer to the public rsshub.app instance being rate-limited or IP-blocked. But it is a power-user tool: value depends on the customer already running a reader, and a large share of the ~5000 routes target Chinese platforms or need per-site cookies/tokens, which our mechanism cannot supply today — so the usable-out-of-the-box surface is narrower than the route count suggests.
summary: RSSHub boots with zero configuration: the official diygod/rsshub image listens on a single HTTP port (1200) and needs no database and no API key to serve feeds — upstream's compose adds Redis (CACHE_TYPE=redis) and browserless only as optional accelerators, and the plain image with CACHE_TYPE=memory, or a Redis sidecar with a server-generated password, needs no customer input either way. It has no login of its own, so it must not sit open on the internet (an unauthenticated instance is a fetch-anything proxy that will attract abuse and get the customer's IP blocked by target sites); the correct gate is Traefik basic_auth: true with generated_from on the root password, which readers can consume as https://user:pass@rsshub.<domain>/<route>. RSSHub's own ACCESS_KEY is not a usable alternative — the customer has to know that value to build feed URLs, and there is no channel to hand a server-generated one back to them. Caveats behind the build_with_caveats verdict, none of them blocking: no semver releases at all, so app_version can only pin a dated master snapshot that goes stale within days; individual routes break routinely when target sites change, with no per-route SLA; and routes requiring site cookies or third-party API keys stay unavailable until an arbitrary-secret input channel exists.

version_health_notes: Two upstreams matter here and both are healthy. The IDE itself (Posit, rstudio/rstudio) shipped 2026.07.1 on 2026-07-21 — 16 days before today (2026-08-06) — on a steady named-release train: 2026.01.0 (2026-01-06), 2026.04.0 (2026-04-22), 2026.05.0 (2026-05-26), 2026.06.0 (2026-06-29), 2026.07.0 (2026-07-14), 2026.07.1 (2026-07-21), with point releases between. The container (rocker-org/rocker-versioned2) tagged 4.6.1 on 2026-07-22 and its repo had commits on 2026-08-03, i.e. within the last week; tags track R releases (4.5.3, 4.6.0, 4.6.1 all in the last two months). Note that Posit is also pushing its newer Positron IDE, but that has not put RStudio into maintenance mode — the 2026.04 release added new RStudio features (Posit Assistant) and Posit moved to a *more* frequent release cadence. No archival, maintenance-only, or EOL signal on either side.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a coding or analysis workbench. Gitea is a git host, Ollama + Open WebUI is local LLM chat inference, and the native claude-code/gemini-cli recipes are terminal assistants — none give the customer an interactive REPL, plotting pane, and data frame viewer. RStudio Server is the R-ecosystem counterpart to the JupyterLab and code-server candidates already analysed in apps-gaps (neither of which is a shipped recipe yet); it targets the statistics /R crowd specifically, with knitr/R Markdown/Quarto authoring and CRAN package management built in.
usefulness_rationale: RStudio is the dominant IDE in the R world and "my own R box in the browser, with my data staying on my server" is a real self-hosting want for researchers, statisticians, and analysts. Marked medium rather than high because the audience is narrower than the Python/JS-flavoured JupyterLab or code-server candidates, and because it is a fat recipe by catalogue standards: the image is multi-GB and a useful R session wants ~2 GB RAM plus disk headroom for compiled CRAN packages.
summary: RStudio Server runs as a single container (rocker/rstudio:4.6.1) on one HTTP port (8787), needs no database or sidecar, and only wants a volume for /home/rstudio — structurally the same shape as Uptime Kuma or Vaultwarden, and fine behind Traefik on rstudio-server.<base_domain> (Traefik v3 proxies its websocket sessions natively; the awkward sub-path rewriting in upstream's nginx examples does not apply when it gets its own subdomain). The one mechanism catch is authentication: RStudio Server OSS authenticates via PAM against a real Linux user, and the image's init script sets that user's password with `chpasswd`, so it needs the *plaintext* password — `generated_from` only ever carries a hash, so the app's own login cannot be root-password-projected the way code-server's HASHED_PASSWORD or JupyterLab's hashed_password can. Leaving PASSWORD unset is not a way out either: the image then prints a random password to the container log, which no customer-facing channel surfaces. The workable shape is therefore DISABLE_AUTH=true with a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (IF-1312) as the real auth boundary — installable today, but the gate is not optional, since an unauthenticated RStudio session is a shell with arbitrary code execution on the VM. build_with_caveats rather than build_now for that reason plus two operational ones: the container is community-maintained (Rocker) rather than vendor-official, and its footprint (multi-GB image, ~2 GB RAM floor) is well above the current catalogue average.

name: Rundeck
source_description: Open-source runbook automation for self-service ops and workflow orchestration
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (Rundeck Open Source / Community); PagerDuty also sells a closed-source "Runbook Automation Self-Hosted" edition on top of the same codebase — SSO, ACL editor UI and the `RUNDECK_SECURITY_DBLOGIN_*` admin-bootstrap variables are Enterprise-only
version_health_notes: 6.1.0 shipped 2026-08-03, three days before today (2026-08-06), with 6.0.1 (2026-07-15) and 6.0.0 (2026-06-29) immediately before it — a steady ~monthly GA cadence going back at least a year (5.20.1 2026-05-18, 5.20.0 2026-04-02, 5.19.0 2026-02-03, 5.18.0 2025-12-16, 5.17.0 2025-11-03, 5.16.0 2025-10-06, 5.15.0 2025-09-02), plus tagged rc builds between each. Repo is not archived, last push 2026-08-05 (yesterday), 6.3k stars, 692 open issues actively triaged, Docker Hub tags rebuilt continuously. PagerDuty acquired Rundeck in 2020 and now fronts it as "Rundeck by PagerDuty"; despite the commercial Self-Hosted edition alongside it, the OSS line is still receiving monthly GA releases and there is no EOL or maintenance-only announcement for the community edition. One tagging oddity to be aware of when pinning: Docker Hub carries a `7.0.1` tag published 2026-04-09, i.e. *before* 6.0.0, with no matching GitHub release — it belongs to PagerDuty's separate commercial version line, not the OSS one. Pin `6.1.0`, not `7.x`.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes does operational job execution against a fleet of servers. n8n (automation) is a drag-and-drop canvas for wiring SaaS APIs together; Rundeck is an ops runbook engine — define a job as shell/script steps, target a set of nodes over SSH (or the local node), schedule it with cron, and hand a scoped "run this button" to someone who has no shell access, with per-job ACLs and a full execution/audit log. That self-service-delegation plus node-inventory model is the part n8n has no equivalent for. It is also distinct from the Jenkins and Kestra candidates analyzed separately: Jenkins is a build/CI pipeline server, Kestra a DAG data-pipeline scheduler, Rundeck an ops-task runner. Single HTTP port (4440), works behind Traefik with `RUNDECK_GRAILS_URL` set to the public https URL and `RUNDECK_SERVER_FORWARDED=true`.
usefulness_rationale: Well-known, long-lived tool with a real audience (ops/SRE teams standardizing manual procedures), and it fills a genuine catalogue gap. Capped at medium rather than high because its core value — delegating jobs across many managed nodes — mostly materializes for a customer who already runs a server fleet; on a single AF-provisioned VM it degrades to "a nicer cron with an audit trail". The resource floor is the other drag: upstream's own minimum is 8 GB RAM / 4 GB JVM heap / 2 vCPU, far above every current recipe (n8n asks 2 GB), so it does not fit the entry-level VM sizes most of the catalogue targets.
summary: Rundeck is an actively maintained (monthly GA releases, latest 6.1.0 on 2026-08-03), Apache-2.0, single-web-port, Postgres-backed ops runbook engine that fills a real gap — no current recipe does scheduled/delegated job execution across servers with ACLs and an audit log. It is installable under today's mechanism: the community edition has no admin-password env var (`RUNDECK_SECURITY_DBLOGIN_ADMINPASSWORD` is Enterprise-only) and otherwise boots with the fixed default admin/admin, but its Jetty `realm.properties` file accepts a pre-computed bcrypt hash (`admin: BCRYPT:<hash>,user,admin`), so install.sh can render that file from `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` and give the customer a working login on first boot — the same shape as the Jenkins candidate, and no Traefik basic_auth gate is needed since Rundeck has its own login. Two caveats keep this at build_with_caveats rather than build_now: upstream's bcrypt support rejects `$2y$` salt revisions (only `$2a$` works), so the projected hash's prefix must be verified against what `generated_from` actually emits before shipping; and the 8 GB RAM / 4 GB heap JVM footprint is well above anything else in the catalogue, making this a larger-VM-only recipe. Everything else is routine — pin `rundeck/rundeck:6.1.0`, add Postgres with a server-generated password (the bundled H2 database is explicitly not production-safe), bind-mount `/home/rundeck/server/config/realm.properties` and the data/ssh dirs, and point `RUNDECK_GRAILS_URL` at the Traefik hostname.

name: RustDesk
source_description: RustDesk is an open-source remote desktop software for secure remote access
version_health_notes: The self-hostable component is rustdesk-server (hbbs/hbbr), a separate repo from the RustDesk client (github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk). Server releases are lumpy: 1.1.12 (2024-10-07), 1.1.13 (2025-01-20), 1.1.14 (2025-01-25), then a ~12-month gap to 1.1.15 (2026-01-13) and 1.1.16 (2026-07-20) — 16 days ago as of today (2026-08-05). Between-release commit activity is continuous (latest commits on master 2026-07-27), so the gaps reflect a small, stable Rust daemon rather than abandonment; 1.1.16 itself shipped a fix for an unauthenticated UDP punch-hole request and an i32 overflow that mis-reported peers offline 24.9-49.7 days as online. The client repo is clearly active (1.4.9 on 2026-07-06, 1.4.8 2026-06-23, 1.4.7 2026-06-02). Docker Hub carries a matching pinned tag rustdesk/rustdesk-server:1.1.16 (pushed 2026-07-20, amd64/arm64/armv7). Note the vendor also sells RustDesk Server Pro (closed source, paid) — the web console, user management and API server live only there; the OSS server analysed here is the rendezvous/relay pair only.
differentiation: RustDesk's OSS server is a self-hosted rendezvous (hbbs) + relay (hbbr) pair for RustDesk's own native clients — the self-hosted equivalent of TeamViewer/AnyDesk's infrastructure. That is architecturally the opposite of guacamole, the only remote-access recipe in the catalogue (currently `enabled: false`): guacamole is a clientless browser gateway that must be able to reach already-listening RDP/VNC/SSH ports on the target, so it only works for machines the customer can route to. RustDesk's targets dial *out* to the rendezvous server, so it reaches laptops and desktops behind NAT with no inbound firewall rules and no RDP/VNC exposed at all, and it prefers direct P2P hole-punched connections, falling back to the customer's own relay only when hole-punching fails. Complementary to guacamole rather than a replacement.
usefulness_rationale: "Self-hosted TeamViewer replacement" is one of the highest-demand self-hosting use cases, and RustDesk is the leading open-source answer to it with a mature multi-platform client set. The server is tiny (two small Rust daemons, ~256 MB RAM) so it is a cheap, high-perceived- value VM occupant. The catch is that the value is realised in the customer's *clients*, not on the VM: the recipe ships infrastructure with nothing to look at in a browser.
summary: RustDesk Server OSS (AGPL-3.0, rustdesk/rustdesk-server:1.1.16) is a two-container hbbs + hbbr stack that needs no customer-supplied value at all: hbbs generates its own ed25519 key pair into its data volume on first boot and enforces key validation by default, there is no login, no admin credential and no external API key, so `secrets_required_at_first_boot` is genuinely empty and the /compose parameter gap does not bite here. It is, however, a raw-port app, not a Traefik one — hbbs needs tcp 21115/21116 plus udp 21116 and hbbr needs tcp 21117 (optionally ws 21118/ 21119 for the web client), all of which must be declared `http: false` host-bound public ports in the wg-easy shape; there is no HTTP surface for Traefik to route or for `basic_auth` to gate, and the health check has to be a TCP probe rather than a curl. Two caveats for whoever builds it: the OSS server has no web console (that is a paid Pro feature), so after install the customer must SSH to their own VM and read `id_ed25519.pub` out of the data volume to configure their clients — there is no output channel in the recipe mechanism for handing that key over — and being a relay, sustained sessions consume the VM's bandwidth. No overlap problem with guacamole (different, NAT-traversing, agent-dials-out architecture; guacamole is disabled besides). Worth building, with the key-retrieval step documented prominently.

name: RustFS
source_description: S3-compatible distributed object storage system built with Rust
version_health_notes: Very active: open-sourced July 2025, ~30k GitHub stars, 130+ contributors, and a weekly-to-biweekly beta train (beta.10 on 2026-07-17, beta.11 on 2026-07-23, beta.12 on 2026-07-30 — the newest is 6 days old as of 2026-08-05). The catch is the opposite of dormancy: every tag ever cut is a pre-release, there is no stable 1.0 yet, and the release notes carry breaking-change entries between betas. Not an EOL/abandonment risk, but a pre-GA-stability risk for a component whose whole job is not losing customer data. Name is not ambiguous upstream-wise, though note the unrelated fork/mirror github.com/Altailab/rustfs-s3 and the historical "rustfs" FUSE toy projects — the object store analyzed here is github.com/rustfs/rustfs.
differentiation: The catalogue has no object storage at all — the closest neighbours are syncthing (peer-to-peer file sync, not an API) and immich/paperless-ngx (apps that store files but expose no storage API); anytype-server embeds a MinIO purely as an internal dependency, not as a customer-facing endpoint. RustFS would be the first S3 endpoint a customer can point their own backups, CI artifacts, Terraform state, or app SDKs at, and its Apache-2.0 licence is a genuine differentiator against MinIO's AGPL + closed-console turn.
usefulness_rationale: "Give me an S3 bucket on my own VPS" is one of the most common self-hosting asks and nothing in the 24-recipe catalogue answers it. It would also unlock backup targets for other recipes. Value is high; the obstacle is delivery of the credential pair (see installability), not demand.
blocking_issues:
RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY (with RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY) is a plaintext shared secret, not a login hash: the customer must type the exact same value into every S3 client, SDK, or backup tool that talks to port 9000. generated_from only ever projects a hash of the root password, and a server-generated-random value has no channel back to the customer, so neither supported mechanism can deliver a usable S3 credential. This is the plaintext-requirement case SCHEMA.md calls a structural blocker.
Traefik basic_auth cannot substitute for that credential on the S3 API port. S3 clients authenticate with SigV4 headers and do not send HTTP basic-auth credentials, so a basic_auth gate on port 9000 breaks every S3 client instead of protecting it. Gating only the console (9001) still leaves 9000 reachable with whatever access/secret pair is configured — i.e. the well-known rustfsadmin/rustfsadmin default, which would put an unauthenticated-in-practice object store on the public internet.
Two distinct public HTTP surfaces (9000 S3 API, 9001 console) versus the one-public-port-per-recipe pattern every current recipe follows, and virtual-hosted-style bucket addressing additionally wants wildcard DNS under the app domain (RUSTFS_SERVER_DOMAINS). Path-style-only operation on a single host is possible but needs a routing decision the current recipe shape does not express.
Pre-GA: no stable release exists (all tags are 1.0.0-beta.*), with breaking changes between betas. Shipping a data-durability component in permanent pre-release to customers deserves an explicit product sign-off even once the credential channel exists.
summary: RustFS is a healthy, fast-moving, Apache-2.0 S3-compatible object store with a real web console, an official pinnable image (rustfs/rustfs:1.0.0-beta.12, ports 9000/9001, data volume owned by UID 10001), and no overlap with anything in the 24-recipe catalogue — object storage is a genuine gap and the demand is obvious. It is nonetheless not installable under today's mechanism: the app's primary secret is a plaintext S3 access/secret pair that the customer must reuse in external clients, and neither generated_from (hash only) nor Traefik basic_auth (breaks SigV4) can deliver it, while leaving the documented rustfsadmin default in place would expose an open bucket store on port 9000. A reviewer could argue for build_with_caveats by projecting argon2:ROOT_PASSWORD into RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY, gating the console with basic_auth, and telling the customer to SSH in and read the value out of the env file — that works mechanically but makes out-of-band retrieval part of the product, so the honest verdict is blocked_on_platform pending a real customer-value input (or output) channel. Revisit once that exists and RustFS has cut a stable 1.0.

name: Rybbit
source_description: Open-source privacy-first web analytics alternative to Google Analytics
version_health_notes: v2.8.0 was tagged 2026-07-27, ~10 days before today (2026-08-06). Preceding tags from the releases feed: v2.2.3 (2025-12-12), v2.2.4 (2025-12-14), v2.3.0/v2.3.1 (2026-01-02), v2.4.0 (2026-02-11), v2.5.0 (2026-03-29), v2.6.0 (2026-05-14), v2.6.1 (2026-05-16), v2.7.0 (2026-07-07), v2.8.0 (2026-07-27) — a minor release roughly every 4-8 weeks with no gap longer than ~2 months over the last eight months. `master` has commits as recently as 2026-08-02 (4 days ago). Repo is not archived or marked maintenance-only; ~12.6k stars, ~2.5k commits, active issue triage. Pinned container tags `v2.8.0` were confirmed present on GHCR for both `rybbit-io/rybbit-backend` and `rybbit-io/rybbit-client` (the shipped compose file otherwise defaults to `:latest` via `${IMAGE_TAG:-latest}`, which a recipe would pin). A commercially-operated cloud offering (rybbit.com) funds the project; the self-hosted build carries no license key or feature gate that surfaced in the docs.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers website/product analytics; Uptime Kuma is the nearest shape (dashboard + small backing store) but measures availability, not visitor traffic. Rybbit is a newer, notably polished cookie-free GA alternative with session replay, funnels, retention and web-vitals reporting on top of plain pageview counting — a fuller product-analytics feature set than the lighter tools in this space, at the cost of a heavier stack (Postgres + ClickHouse + Redis + two app containers).
usefulness_rationale: Privacy-respecting, GDPR-friendly self-hosted analytics is a recurring ask from anyone running a site they don't want to feed to Google, and it pairs naturally with IONOS-hosted sites (the tracked site does not have to live on the same server — only the tracking snippet points here). Upstream is young but fast-moving and well maintained. Note the catalogue already has competing gap analyses for the same niche (`plausible-analytics`, `matomo`, `ackee`, `goatcounter`, `countly`); per CLAUDE.md overlap between candidates is not itself a reason to reject, but a human should pick which one or two actually get built.
blocking_issues:
No way to close the open-signup window. Rybbit has no admin env var and no CLI seeding path — the documented first-boot flow is "browse to https://<domain>/signup and create your admin account", after which the operator is told to set DISABLE_SIGNUP=true and restart. Until the customer does that, whoever reaches the domain first becomes the instance owner. The catalogue's standard fix for that race (a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate on the public port) does not work here: Rybbit is an analytics collector, so the very endpoints anonymous website visitors must reach unauthenticated — the tracking script and the event-ingest POSTs, both served under the backend's `/api/*` prefix — sit behind the same port and would be 401'd by a blanket gate, breaking the app's only function. Closing the race needs path-scoped basic auth (gate the UI and `/signup`, leave the ingest paths open), which the current per-port toggle cannot express. Note this contradicts `apps-gaps/plausible-analytics.yaml`, which reaches `build_now` by proposing exactly such a blanket gate over an equally ingest-dependent app; a human should reconcile the two — the same objection applies to any analytics recipe.

Not a single-HTTP-port app out of the box. Upstream splits the web surface across two containers — `rybbit-client` (Next.js UI, 3002) and `rybbit-backend` (API + tracking ingest, 3001) — and requires path-based routing (`/api/*` and `/.well-known/oauth*` to the backend, everything else to the client), which upstream's own bundled Caddy does. Our Traefik labels are injected per recipe against one public port on `<slug>.<base_domain>`, so the split cannot be expressed at the platform layer. This one is solvable inside the recipe rather than on the platform: ship upstream's Caddy as an in-recipe container listening plain HTTP on a single port (replace the `{$DOMAIN_NAME}` site block with `:80`, drop the TLS automation) and let Traefik front that. Listed here because it makes the recipe structurally unlike anything currently in `recipes/` — every existing entry proxies straight to the app container.
summary: Rybbit is a healthy, fast-moving (v2.8.0 on 2026-07-27, commits four days before this analysis) AGPL-3.0 privacy analytics platform with official pinned GHCR images and a documented external-reverse-proxy deployment mode, filling a category the current 24 recipes do not cover at all. Its machine secrets are all fine for us — BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, the Postgres password and the ClickHouse password are patternless values nothing customer-facing reads, exactly what AF already generates server-side. It fails `installable_today` on the admin account: Rybbit only creates one through an open `/signup` page with no env or CLI alternative, and the usual Traefik `basic_auth` gate cannot be used to cover that window because a blanket gate would also block the anonymous tracking-script and event-ingest requests the product exists to serve. A secondary, recipe-level (not platform-level) wrinkle is the two-HTTP- container path split, which needs an in-recipe Caddy to collapse onto one port. Recommend revisiting once path-scoped basic auth exists, or a mechanism that seeds a first admin from the root-password hash — the product case for building it is strong, and this same gate-vs-ingest conflict should be settled once for the whole analytics category.

name: Ryot
source_description: Self-hosted tracker for media, fitness, books, and daily habits
version_health_notes: Very active single-maintainer project (IgnisDa). Latest release v10.4.2 was tagged 2026-07-23, two weeks before today (2026-08-06), and v10.3.x shipped roughly fortnightly through May–July 2026. Docker Hub `ignisda/ryot` carries matching `v10`, `v10.4`, `v10.4.2` tags plus per-commit `develop` builds. Open-core: the community edition is GPL-3.0, while "Ryot Pro" (profile sharing, recommendations, supercharged collections) is a paid licence key — the free edition is fully usable without it. Not to be confused with the unrelated `saketchopra/ryot` fork or the "Ryot" name used by other small projects; the IgnisDa repo is the upstream Hostinger lists.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue tracks personal media consumption or fitness. Immich is the only adjacent media recipe and it stores photos rather than tracking what a user watches, reads, plays or lifts. Ryot is a single-container Rust app plus Postgres serving one HTTP port (8000), so it fronts cleanly on `ryot.<base_domain>` with the existing Traefik setup.
usefulness_rationale: A genuinely popular consumer self-hosting app (Goodreads/Trakt/Letterboxd replacement in one) with importers and Jellyfin/Plex/Kodi sync, which is a good fit for the hobbyist end of the VPS market. It is a personal-use app rather than a business tool, so it broadens catalogue appeal without serving the prosumer/infra segment most existing recipes target.
summary: Ryot is mechanically installable today: `ignisda/ryot:v10.4.2` plus `postgres:18-alpine`, one HTTP port (8000), and only two secrets the server can generate itself — `SERVER_ADMIN_ACCESS_TOKEN` (validated non-empty at boot, but never needed by the customer for normal use) and the Postgres password. Ryot has its own login, but registration is controlled solely by the env var `USERS_ALLOW_REGISTRATION` (default true) with no runtime admin toggle, and there is no seeded first admin — so the recipe must either leave signup permanently open on a public URL or put a Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front (IF-1312) and let the customer register behind it; the gate is the right call and is the one first-boot credential needing projection. The main caveat is feature degradation, not a blocker: movies/TV need a customer TMDB or TVDB token and video games need Twitch/IGDB or GiantBomb credentials, and those external API keys have no input channel today, so a shipped recipe would boot with books, anime/manga, audiobooks, podcasts, music, fitness and habits working and the movie/show/game trackers dark until the customer edits the env file by hand. Also note the basic-auth gate breaks the Jellyfin/Plex webhook integrations and the mobile clients, which is an acceptable trade for a first pass but should be documented.

name: SABnzbd
source_description: SABnzbd is an automated Usenet downloader for binary newsgroup content
upstream_docker_image: lscr.io/linuxserver/sabnzbd (pin a version tag, e.g. 5.0.4-ls265 — never :latest, and avoid the "unstable"/"nightly" tags that currently track 5.1.0RC2)
version_health_notes: As of today (2026-08-05) the current stable release is 5.0.4 (2026-06-11), i.e. about 8 weeks old, and sabnzbd.org still advertises it as the "mature and stable" download. The 5.0.x line landed in a tight burst this year — 5.0.0 and 5.0.1 (2026-05-01), 5.0.2 (2026-05-14), 5.0.3 (2026-05-15), 5.0.4 (2026-06-11) — and the 5.1.0 cycle is already in public testing (Beta1 2026-06-14 through RC2 2026-08-03, two days before today). The repo is not archived, has ~10.2k commits with ongoing activity on `develop`, and a small open issue count (~14), so it is genuinely maintained rather than maintenance-only. linuxserver.io mirrors it promptly: their 5.0.4-based tag is current and their `unstable` tag already carries 5.1.0RC2. No EOL or hand-over signals. Note the project name is not ambiguous, but the download domain is: sabnzbd.org is the live site; sabnzbd.net (the old changelog host) did not resolve during this research — use .org for links.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers Usenet or any other media-acquisition role — there is no *arr app, no indexer and no download client of any kind. SABnzbd would be the first, and it is the reference implementation of the category: a single Python container serving one HTTP port (8080) with its own web UI, no companion database or worker services. It sits behind Traefik on `sabnzbd.<base_domain>` with no raw protocol port needed at all — unlike qBittorrent/Syncthing, all Usenet traffic is outbound NNTP, so this is a cleaner reverse-proxy fit than the BitTorrent candidates. Separate candidates exist for NZBGet (`apps-gaps/nzbget.yaml`) and the *arr/indexer apps, which cover adjacent or overlapping ground; per repo convention that overlap is not itself a reason to reject this one.
usefulness_rationale: SABnzbd is the best-known and most widely deployed Usenet downloader, and it is the app the *arr ecosystem integrates with first, so it is a natural anchor if we ever build out media automation. Appeal is nonetheless bounded: the customer must already hold a paid Usenet provider account and an indexer to get any value, and we ship no companion Sonarr/Radarr/Prowlarr recipes to pair it with yet — a narrower audience than broad-appeal recipes like Vaultwarden or Uptime Kuma.
summary: SABnzbd is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8080) web app on the well-maintained lscr.io/linuxserver/sabnzbd image, with only PUID/PGID/TZ as environment inputs and /config plus download volumes — structurally the same shape as recipes/uptime-kuma and recipes/syncthing, and simpler than either since all Usenet traffic is outbound NNTP and no inbound raw port is required. Its own login is disabled by default (fresh installs serve the setup wizard to anyone who reaches them) and the image exposes no env var for credentials, so a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate projected from the root-password hash is mandatory, not optional, and is the only secret needed (IF-1312); the app's API key is self-generated and never customer-supplied. Two implementation caveats for whoever builds it: SABnzbd's hostname-verification check rejects requests whose Host header is not in `host_whitelist`, so install.sh must seed `host_whitelist = <APP_DOMAIN>` into sabnzbd.ini before first start (the `HOST_WHITELIST_ENTRIES` env var belongs to third-party images, not the linuxserver one), and the recipe must pin a stable tag such as 5.0.4-ls265 because the image's `unstable`/`nightly` tags currently carry 5.1.0RC2. Recommend build_with_caveats — mechanically ready and upstream is healthy, but the app only earns its keep for customers who already have a Usenet provider, and we carry no indexer or *arr recipes to pair it with.

name: Saltcorn
source_description: Open-source no-code application builder for database-driven apps

Upstream's example compose already carries Traefik router labels for exactly the <slug>.<base_domain> pattern our recipes use, so reverse proxying is proven rather than assumed. The only boot-time inputs are SALTCORN_SESSION_SECRET and the Postgres password — both patternless server-generated values no customer ever sees — plus one real gap: there is no env var that seeds an admin, so the first visitor to the root URL gets the setup wizard and becomes the instance admin. That first-come- first-served window must be closed with a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate (the n8n/WUD/Open WebUI pattern) until the customer completes the wizard; Saltcorn's CLI `create-user` path is plaintext-only and therefore not usable via `generated_from`, but it is not needed. Recipe caveats for the build pass, not blockers: the schema must be initialised (`reset-schema`, or the initdb script upstream ships) before `serve`, and the instance's Base URL is set post-install in the admin UI. Nothing here needs a platform capability we lack — recommend build_now.

name: Screego
source_description: Self-hosted WebRTC screen sharing server with built-in TURN relay
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/screego/server:1.12.4 (mirrored as screego/server:1.12.4 on Docker Hub)
version_health_notes: 1.12.4 shipped 2026-05-13, ~2.7 months (84 days) before today (2026-08-05); the matching multi-arch image tag `1.12.4` was pushed to Docker Hub the same day (amd64/arm64/armv6/ppc64le/riscv64), so the published image tracks the release. Recent tags are largely dependency bumps and build- target additions rather than features, which reads as a feature-complete single-purpose Go daemon in low-maintenance mode, not abandonment: the repo is not archived, has ~10.5k stars and only ~15 open issues, and upstream is still cutting releases within the last quarter. No EOL or maintenance-only announcement.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does real-time screen sharing. The nearest neighbour is guacamole (currently `enabled: false`), but that is a clientless gateway for *controlling* a remote machine over RDP/VNC/SSH — Screego is the opposite direction: an ad-hoc, browser-to-browser, view-only broadcast of one participant's screen to others via a shared room link, with no agent on either end beyond a WebRTC-capable browser. It is also much narrower than the Jitsi Meet candidate analysed separately (no audio/video conferencing, no rooms with cameras, no recording) — a deliberately single-purpose "share my screen at high resolution and low latency" tool aimed at developers doing pairing or demos.
usefulness_rationale: Real, well-scoped demand — teams who want a privacy-preserving, self-hosted alternative to screen sharing through Teams/Zoom/Slack, at much better resolution than those tools deliver. Capped at medium rather than high because the app has no persistence, no accounts to speak of and no standing value between sessions: it is infrastructure for a meeting that must be running when someone wants it, and most prospective users already have *some* screen sharing bundled with a conferencing tool they pay for. Value is highest as a companion to a conferencing app, not a replacement for one.
summary: Screego (GPL-3.0, `ghcr.io/screego/server:1.12.4`) is a single Go container that needs no customer-supplied value: `SCREEGO_SECRET` is a patternless cookie-signing key nothing customer-facing reads, so it is server-generatable, and the one real login is a `user:bcrypt_hash` line in the file named by `SCREEGO_USERS_FILE` — bcrypt is exactly what `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` projects, so install.sh can render that file from the projected hash and the customer logs in with their own root password (the Vaultwarden pattern, with the §7.1 `$`- doubling caveat since bcrypt hashes are `$`-heavy). Traefik `basic_auth` is deliberately *not* the right gate here — it would also block the invited guests the room link exists for — so the users-file route is the one to take, keeping the default `SCREEGO_AUTH_MODE=turn` so guests can join a room without an account while only the authenticated host can burn the VM's bandwidth on the TURN relay. Caveats for whoever builds it, none of them blocking: (1) it is not a pure Traefik app — the web UI on 5050 is fine behind Traefik with `SCREEGO_TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` (and Traefik's TLS satisfies Screego's hard requirement that it be served over HTTPS, since `getDisplayMedia` needs a secure context), but the built-in TURN relay additionally needs raw host-bound 3478/tcp and 3478/udp plus a UDP relay port range set via `SCREEGO_TURN_PORT_RANGE`; (2) `metadata.ports[]` takes one integer per entry with no range syntax, so upstream's default 50000-50200 must be shrunk to a handful of explicitly enumerated ports (each an `http: false` entry, watch `no-duplicate-public-port`) — upstream's own answer to this is `network_mode: host`, which does not fit the renderer's Traefik model and should not be used; (3) `SCREEGO_EXTERNAL_IP` is mandatory for TURN to advertise usable candidates, but Screego resolves DNS names there, so pointing it at the app's own `APP_DOMAIN` avoids needing the VM's literal public IP; (4) relayed sessions consume VM bandwidth whenever peer-to-peer hole-punching fails.

source_description: High performance home video integration platform and NVR with smart detections

The upstream compose file uses an untagged image plus a bundled Watchtower auto-updater; a recipe must pin and drop Watchtower. Variants: -noble-lite (no ML runtimes), -noble-full, -noble-intel, -noble-nvidia, -noble-amd.
