The *server/container* line has been quiet: stable 0.143.0 was published to npm and tagged on GitHub on 2025-10-28 — 281 days (~9.3 months) before today (2026-08-05) — the newest beta is 0.144.1 (2025-11-07), and the newest container tags in ghcr.io/koush/scrypted are v0.144.1-noble-*, with the :latest manifest (== v0.143.0-noble-full) built 2025-11-16, ~8.6 months ago. The *project* is anything but dormant: main has commits dated 2026-08-05 (the day before this analysis: "snapshot: work around vips load crash", "rebroadcast: fix socket leak"), ~8.5k commits, 5.8k stars, ~30 open issues, not archived, no EOL notice. The reason is architectural: functionality lives in plugins that install and update from npm into the volume at runtime, and those ship constantly — @scrypted/nvr published 0.12.105 on 2026-08-06. So the pinned image is stale-but-supported rather than abandoned; cadence is marked slowing (not active) because the artefact a recipe would actually pin has not moved in ~9 months, and dormant/EOL would be plainly wrong. Practical consequence for a recipe: pinning the image does NOT pin behaviour, because plugins self-update inside /server/volume.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does video: Scrypted would be the first camera/NVR app. The overlap with recipes/home-assistant is partial and real — both are local-first smart-home hubs that bridge devices to HomeKit/Google Home/Alexa — but Home Assistant is a general automation engine with weak video, whereas Scrypted is a video-first hub (ONVIF/RTSP onboarding, hardware-accelerated rebroadcast, HomeKit Secure Video) with an NVR and object detection bolted on. Per CLAUDE.md that overlap is not itself a reason to reject it.
usefulness_rationale: The value proposition does not survive the move to a public cloud VM. Scrypted must pull RTSP/ONVIF streams *from* the cameras, and a customer's cameras sit on their home LAN behind NAT — an IONOS VM cannot reach them without the customer first building port forwards or a VPN, which is exactly the kind of setup our one-click install cannot do for them. Even where reachable, continuous NVR recording of remote streams means permanent inbound WAN bandwidth plus a large data disk, and the advertised "smart detections" want a GPU/Coral/QuickSync device that our VM flavours do not offer. On top of that the NVR plugin carrying the headline features is a paid Scrypted subscription, so the free install a customer would get is the camera hub only. This is a LAN-appliance app (NAS, Pi, home server), not a hosted-VM app.
summary: Mechanically, Scrypted fits our mechanism: one container, one volume (/server/volume), no database, no companion services once upstream's bundled Watchtower is dropped, and a pinnable tag (v0.143.0-noble-full). It serves its own web UI on 10443 (self-signed HTTPS) and, per server/src/server-settings.ts, an equivalent plain-HTTP listener on 11080 — Traefik should front 11080 on scrypted.<base_domain>, and the UI's WebSockets are transparent to Traefik; note the server sets `trust proxy` to loopback only, so it will not believe X-Forwarded-Proto and issues its `login_user_token_insecure` cookie, which is functional but means TLS must be terminated at Traefik. Auth needs a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (IF-1312): there is no seeded credential — the first HTTP caller to POST /login simply creates the admin account (addUserInternal in scrypted-server-main.ts), so an ungated install is claimable by whoever finds it first, and the app's own password path is unusable for projection because it stores sha256(salt+password) in an internal database, not an env var (SCRYPTED_ADMIN_USERNAME only creates a user with a random password for token/ingress auth). That is the only secret needed, so installable_today is true. Recommend not_recommended anyway, on fit rather than mechanism: the cameras Scrypted exists to record live on the customer's NAT'd home LAN and are unreachable from an IONOS VM, "smart detections" want accelerator hardware we do not offer, recording remote streams burns continuous WAN bandwidth and disk, and the NVR plugin behind the headline feature set is a paid subscription — leaving customers a bare camera hub with no cameras. Also worth flagging for whoever revisits this: dropping upstream's `network_mode: host` for our bridge+Traefik shape costs multicast/mDNS camera discovery and the HomeKit/Google Home bridges, which is moot on a cloud VM but is a real functional difference from every install guide the customer will find.

name: ScyllaDB
source_description: High-throughput NoSQL database compatible with Cassandra and DynamoDB APIs
upstream_license: "ScyllaDB Software License Agreement" v1.1 (last updated 2026-04-12) — source-available, NOT open source. Since the December 2024 licensing shift, ScyllaDB OSS AGPL 6.2 was the final AGPLv3 release; everything from ScyllaDB Enterprise 2025.1 onward ships under this single source-available license with a free tier. The free tier is capped at 10TB total storage and 50 vCPUs across all deployments/clusters, is restricted to "Never Customers" (no paid ScyllaDB relationship in the preceding 12 months), and explicitly forbids offering the software as a SaaS or commercial DBaaS, or using it to compete with ScyllaDB's existing or future products. (Scylla Manager moved to AGPL separately; the Kubernetes operator is Apache-2.0 — neither covers the database itself.)
version_health_notes: Very active. 2026.2.3 was pushed to Docker Hub on 2026-08-05 — the same day as this analysis (today, 2026-08-05) — and the 2026.1 LTS line got 2026.1.10 one day earlier (2026-08-04). Patch releases land every 1-3 weeks on each maintained line (2026.1.6 2026-06-24, .7 2026-07-01, .8 2026-07-09, .9 2026-07-22, .10 2026-08-04; 2026.2.0 2026-06-29, .1 2026-07-13, .2 2026-07-26, .3 2026-08-05), the previous 2025.1 LTS and 2025.4 lines are still receiving patches, and 2026.3.0-rc1 was tagged 2026-08-05. Upstream runs a parallel LTS/STS ladder and the repo is not archived. The 2024-12 license change (AGPL → source-available) is a commercial-model change, not an abandonment signal — development is healthier than ever, the risk here is legal, not decay.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is a standalone database — where Postgres/Redis appear (immich, paperless-ngx, n8n) they are private bridge-network backing services the customer never connects to. A ScyllaDB recipe would be the first customer-facing wide-column store, aimed at a developer who wants a Cassandra-CQL- or DynamoDB-API- compatible database to point their own external application at. It is also the only Cassandra-family server the catalogue would have — the separate `cassandra-reaper` gap-analysis covers a repair UI for a cluster hosted elsewhere, not a server.
usefulness_rationale: ScyllaDB is a scale-out database designed for dedicated multi-core, high-memory nodes; the single-container, single-VM, no-tuning shape our recipes deliver is precisely the deployment it is worst suited to (it would need `--developer-mode 1`/`--smp 1`/`--memory` clamps just to boot on a small customer VM, which upstream explicitly labels non-production). It has no web UI of any kind — monitoring is a separate Prometheus/Grafana stack — so there is nothing for Traefik to front, and the audience is a narrow slice of developers rather than the end-user apps that make up most of the catalogue. Structurally the same class as apps-gaps/redis.yaml, apps-gaps/postgresql.yaml and apps-gaps/apache-kvrocks.yaml, with a heavier resource profile than any of them.
blocking_issues:
No exposure path. ScyllaDB's primary client interface is CQL on port 9042 (plus 19042 shard-aware, 9160 Thrift, 10000 REST admin, 7000/7001 inter-node) — a raw binary protocol, not HTTP. Host port 9042 is on RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` forbidden list as an ERROR (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226, "9042 (Cassandra)"), and Traefik only routes HTTP, so there is no subdomain route and no `basic_auth` gate that could apply. The one useful shape for a standalone ScyllaDB recipe — a client-reachable CQL port — is the shape our own rules forbid.

The Alternator (DynamoDB API) port 8000 is HTTP and is not on the forbidden list, but it does not rescue the recipe. With `alternator_enforce_authorization: true`, the AWS secret access key IS the CQL role's `salted_hash` from `system_auth.roles` — a server-side, randomly-salted value the customer cannot derive from their own root password. Handing it to them needs an *output* channel for a generated secret, which the recipe mechanism does not have any more than it has an input channel. Leaving authorization off instead (the default) means an unauthenticated public database; and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate is not a substitute, because AWS-SDK/boto3 clients sign SigV4 requests and do not send HTTP basic credentials, so gating 8000 would simply break every supported client.

Licensing. The ScyllaDB Software License Agreement v1.1 forbids offering the software as a SaaS or commercial DBaaS and forbids using it to compete with ScyllaDB's own products or services — a hosting provider provisioning per-customer ScyllaDB instances as a paid catalogue item reads as exactly that, and directly competes with ScyllaDB Cloud. The free tier is additionally capped at 10TB storage and 50 vCPUs *in aggregate across all deployments* and limited to "Never Customers", so the terms do not even scale to a catalogue, and IONOS's own commercial relationship with ScyllaDB (if any) could void eligibility outright. This needs a commercial agreement with ScyllaDB, not an af-recipes change (cf. the ArangoDB and AFFiNE gap-analyses for milder versions of the same issue).
summary: ScyllaDB is a vigorously maintained project (2026.2.3 shipped 2026-08-05, the day of this analysis, on a 1-3 week patch cadence across parallel LTS and STS lines) with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue, but it fails our mechanism on two independent counts. Its client interface is CQL on port 9042, a raw binary protocol whose host port RFC-002 forbids outright, and it has no web UI at all, so there is nothing for Traefik to route or gate; the HTTP Alternator/DynamoDB port is no escape hatch, because enforced authorization makes the AWS secret key a server-generated salted hash we have no way to hand the customer, and basic auth in front of it would break SigV4 clients. Notably the *credential* itself would have been expressible — ScyllaDB supports `CREATE ROLE WITH HASHED PASSWORD` in crypt(3) bcrypt format, which `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` produces — so unlike Redis/Kvrocks this is not a plaintext-password gap; the exposure model is what blocks it. On top of that, the post-2024 source-available license explicitly forbids SaaS/DBaaS offerings and competing use and caps the free tier at 10TB/50 vCPUs in aggregate, which a per-customer hosting catalogue cannot satisfy. Not recommended: no near-term platform change unblocks it, and the licensing question would need a commercial agreement even if one did.

differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers general-purpose self-hosted file sync and sharing with a server-side web UI. recipes/syncthing/ is the nearest neighbour but solves a different problem — peer-to-peer device-to-device replication with no server-side library browser, no share links, no per-user accounts; recipes/immich/ is photos/video only and recipes/paperless-ngx/ is a scanned-document archive. Seafile's specific angle within the "self-hosted Drive" category is its block-level storage engine (fast delta sync of large files, the reason it is usually benchmarked ahead of Nextcloud) plus genuine client-side encrypted libraries, which is the "end-to-end encryption" the Hostinger blurb refers to — the library password never leaves the client, so the server stores only ciphertext. Reviewer note: Seafile targets the same customer need as the Nextcloud (apps-gaps/nextcloud.yaml), ownCloud (apps-gaps/owncloud.yaml), OpenCloud (apps-gaps/opencloud.yaml) and Pydio Cells (apps-gaps/pydio-cells.yaml) gap-analyses; none of those are recipes yet, so there is no catalogue overlap to reject on, but they should be weighed as one group.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted file sync/share is one of the most-requested self-hosting use cases and the catalogue has no recipe for it at all. Seafile is a well-known, mature entrant with first-party desktop and mobile clients, an official multi-arch Docker image, and the differentiating encrypted-library feature the Hostinger listing leads with.
blocking_issues:
Seafile's only first-boot channel for the admin account, INIT_SEAFILE_ADMIN_EMAIL / INIT_SEAFILE_ADMIN_PASSWORD (documented default `me@example.com` / `asecret`), takes the *plaintext* password. The entrypoint hands it to Seahub's account-creation path, which stores Seafile's own internal hash of whatever string it receives — Seahub is Django-based and its stored credential is a `pbkdf2_sha256$...` value. Projecting `generated_from: "argon2:ROOT_PASSWORD"` (or bcrypt) into that variable would make the *hash string* the login password: Seafile would hash the hash, and the customer, who only ever knows their root password, could not log in to the account our install flow just created. Per SCHEMA.md this is the structural case — a genuine plaintext-password requirement, which `generated_from` can never satisfy because it only ever carries a hash. Same shape as apps-gaps/pydio-cells.yaml.

No documented way to hand Seafile a pre-computed credential instead. The nearest theoretical path — seeding the Seahub `EmailUser` row with an already-hashed password — needs the hash in Django's `pbkdf2_sha256` format, which is not in `generated_from`'s supported algorithm list (`argon2`, `bcrypt`) today. SCHEMA.md classes an unsupported-but-addable algorithm as `blocked_on_platform` rather than a hard no, so naming it here: `pbkdf2_sha256` (Django-format, including the iteration count and salt encoding) would be the required addition, and it would additionally need upstream (or the recipe) to guarantee that pre-seeding the user table before first login is supported and survives Seafile's own schema migrations — neither of which upstream documents.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate does not rescue this the way it does for no-login apps: Seafile has its own login screen and its desktop/mobile sync clients authenticate against it, so an extra HTTP-basic layer would both leave the un-provisionable admin account behind it and break the native clients' sync endpoints.
summary: Seafile is upstream-healthy and a high-value catalogue gap: 13.0.25 was released on 2026-07-13 (24 days before today, 2026-08-06) on a roughly monthly patch cadence following the 13.0 GA on 2026-01-05, the official seafileltd/seafile-mc image is rebuilt per release, and no recipe in the current 24 covers general-purpose file sync and sharing. It is structurally a Paperless-ngx/Immich-shaped stack — app container plus a private MySQL/MariaDB and Redis — and it is reverse-proxy-friendly: since 12.0 the bundled Caddy is an optional compose file that can be dropped, after which the seafile container serves its whole UI plus the /seafhttp file-transfer endpoint on a single internal HTTP port 80, exactly what Traefik on <slug>.<base_domain> wants (the optional websocket notification server on 8083 can simply be left disabled). The blocker is the admin credential: INIT_SEAFILE_ADMIN_PASSWORD is a plaintext-only input that Seafile re-hashes itself, so root-password projection would set the customer's login to a hash string they never see, and there is no documented pre-hashed-credential path — the DB-seeding alternative would need `pbkdf2_sha256` support that `generated_from` does not have. Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit if Seafile documents a pre-hashed admin-credential input, or if the platform gains either a `pbkdf2_sha256` projection algorithm or a real channel for a customer-supplied value.

Syncthing (recipes/syncthing/) is the only storage-adjacent recipe and solves an unrelated problem — P2P device-to-device file sync, no server-side API, no buckets, no programmatic access. SeaweedFS would add the "self-hosted S3 endpoint" primitive: a backing store other applications write to via the AWS SDK, plus a filer with WebDAV and an Iceberg REST catalog. Note this is infrastructure a developer consumes from code, not an end-user product like Nextcloud (apps-gaps/nextcloud.yaml) or ownCloud (apps-gaps/owncloud.yaml) — those target humans browsing files, SeaweedFS targets applications storing objects. The two do not substitute for each other.

But the audience is developers and operators rather than the general self-hosting customer, and the value of a *single-node* SeaweedFS is much lower than the distributed deployment the project is designed for: on one VM it is essentially a local-disk S3 gateway, with none of the replication or horizontal scaling the description advertises. Useful, not headline.

The `weed mini` all-in-one command (upstream's own documented single-node production mode) starts master, volume server, filer, S3 gateway, WebDAV, Iceberg catalog and Admin UI in one process from chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.41 (pin the numeric tag; never :latest or :dev, which are rebuilt weekly), so the recipe is closer in shape to recipes/uptime-kuma/ than to the six-service upstream docker/seaweedfs-compose.yml. Both first-boot secrets are expressible: the Admin UI (port 23646) takes `-admin.password` / WEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD as an arbitrary string with a fixed default username "admin", which fits generated_from:"<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD" the same way ownCloud's ADMIN_PASSWORD does (apps-gaps/owncloud.yaml); and the S3 gateway needs one identity seeded server-side in its -s3.config JSON, because with zero identities configured it runs in documented "Allow-All Mode" where every S3 operation succeeds unauthenticated — a wide-open bucket store on a public IP. That bootstrap key can be random and never shown to the customer, since the authenticated Admin UI's Object Store Users page lets them create their own access/secret pairs afterwards (existing secret keys are masked there, so the seeded one is genuinely server-only). The caveats are about exposure, not secrets. reverse_proxy_compatible is false: this is two distinct public HTTP services, not one. The Admin UI can sit on <slug>.<base_domain> behind Traefik (upstream even ships `-admin.urlPrefix` for that), but the S3 endpoint on 8333 cannot share that hostname — path-style S3 requests are `/<bucket>/<key>` at the root and collide with the admin routes, virtual-host-style needs wildcard DNS we do not issue, and a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of S3 would break every AWS SDK client because basic auth and SigV4 both claim the Authorization header. So S3 has to be published as a raw port (8333, like recipes/syncthing/'s 22000), which means plain HTTP with no TLS termination unless a second Traefik route is added — acceptable for a first cut, but it should be a conscious decision by the reviewer, and the master (9333) and filer (8888) UIs must stay unpublished since they have no authentication at all. Recommend build_with_caveats: healthy, very actively maintained upstream filling a real catalogue gap, but the routing story needs agreeing before anyone writes the recipe, and the weekly release cadence means the pinned tag will need regular maintenance.

Note the catalogue slug overlap: this file, along with apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml and apps-gaps/overseerr.yaml, all describe the same lineage — `seerr` is the current, canonical entry of the three, and the other two should be treated as historical names rather than separate build candidates.

Seerr is a single-container web app on one HTTP port (5055) with SQLite by default (Postgres optional) — structurally the same shape as recipes/uptime-kuma/ or recipes/vaultwarden/, so it would sit behind Traefik on seerr.<base_domain> with no raw ports or extra protocols. Its function is to sit in front of a customer's existing Jellyfin, Plex, or Emby server and let household users browse TMDB and submit media requests, which an admin approves and routes to Sonarr/Radarr. The nearest catalogue neighbour, Immich, is a photo library, not a request front end — no real functional overlap. It does duplicate the two dormant-name gap entries (jellyseerr, overseerr), and supersedes both.
usefulness_rationale: Well-known, heavily used tool in the self-hosted media community and the obvious companion to a media server, but the whole value proposition depends on a Jellyfin/Plex/Emby instance the customer already runs elsewhere — AF has no media-server recipe to pair it with, so on its own it is a request UI with nothing to serve requests. High value to the subset of customers already running a media stack, low value to everyone else.
blocking_issues:
Seerr has no local-only admin account. Its mandatory first-run setup wizard requires picking Jellyfin, Plex, or Emby and authenticating against that server before the instance is considered initialized — Plex via a plex.tv OAuth token exchange, Jellyfin/Emby via server URL plus that server's own admin username and password. The first administrator (user ID 1) is imported from the connected media server, not created inside Seerr.

That credential is third-party account linking, which per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md has no input channel today: it is neither a hash of the customer's server root password (so `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` has no parameter to attach to — there is no env var that pre-seeds an admin login or skips the wizard) nor something the platform can generate server-side, since it must match an account on an external system the customer already controls.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate would keep the URL from sitting open while unconfigured, but it does not unblock installation: the app stays permanently stuck at the setup wizard until a real, working media-server credential is supplied, so the delivered instance would be non-functional.

Secondary (not the primary blocker): to actually fulfil requests the customer must also supply Sonarr/Radarr URLs and API keys, another arbitrary customer-supplied value with no input channel. Seerr is usable read-only without them, but that is not the product.
summary: Seerr is a healthy, actively maintained project — the February 2026 merger of Overseerr and Jellyseerr into one MIT-licensed codebase, releasing about monthly with v3.4.1 shipped 2026-07-30 (7 days ago) and security fixes landing regularly. Mechanically it is an easy recipe: one official image (`seerr/seerr`), one HTTP port (5055), one data volume, SQLite by default, fully reverse-proxy-compatible behind Traefik. It is nonetheless not installable under today's mechanism: the mandatory setup wizard requires authenticating against an external Jellyfin, Plex, or Emby server, which is third-party account linking with no `/compose` input channel, and basic_auth cannot substitute for it. Recommend blocked_on_platform — revisit once a customer-supplied external-credential channel exists, ideally alongside a media-server recipe to pair it with; treat apps-gaps/jellyseerr.yaml and apps-gaps/overseerr.yaml as superseded by this entry.

Paperless-ngx is the nearest neighbour and is not close: it archives scanned documents, whereas SENAITE models the analytical-lab domain — clients, samples, analysis services and profiles, worksheets, result entry with verification workflow, specifications and out-of-range flagging, certificates of analysis, and instrument interfaces. It is also the heaviest-configuration app of any candidate reviewed here: a fresh instance is an empty shell that needs a lab's clients, contacts, analysis services, calculations, and specifications set up before it does anything useful, so the "provisioned in minutes" value story is weak even though the container itself starts cleanly.
blocking_issues:
Not a hard blocker, but the reason a basic_auth gate is mandatory rather than optional: the image's only admin-credential knob is the `PASSWORD` environment variable, which sets the Zope admin user's password as **plaintext** and defaults to the documented, published value `admin`. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever produces a hash, so it cannot feed `PASSWORD`, and there is no config path that accepts a pre-computed hash for the Zope inituser — this is the same structural situation as the plone candidate in this directory (SENAITE is built on Plone/Zope). Per SCHEMA.md this is explicitly not a blocker on its own: leave the credential at its default and make Traefik `basic_auth` (root-password projection, argon2 or bcrypt) the real, mandatory auth boundary in front of the whole app, with the customer changing the admin password from inside the UI afterwards. The gate must not be presented as optional — without it, `admin/admin` is directly reachable on the internet.

Reverse-proxy caveat that needs design work, not a platform change: SENAITE is a Zope application and the site lives at a sub-path (setting `SITE=senaite` at first boot auto-creates it at `/senaite`), and Zope generates absolute URLs from the request path rather than from `X-Forwarded-Host`. Serving it at `senaite.<base_domain>/` therefore needs a Traefik `ReplacePathRegex` middleware injecting the VirtualHostMonster prefix (`/VirtualHostBase/https/<domain>:443/senaite/VirtualHostRoot`) — upstream's own Apache/nginx guidance uses exactly this rewrite. It is expressible in compose labels because the domain is known at compose time, but no recipe in the catalogue does path rewriting today, so it needs end-to-end validation before shipping.
summary: SENAITE LIMS is a real, credible laboratory information management system (successor to Bika LIMS, GPL-2.0, Plone/Zope-based) and would open a category the current 24 recipes do not touch at all. Upstream is still being developed — senaite.core commits and Docker Hub 2.x rebuilds as recent as 2026-07-31 — but its release cadence has clearly slowed: 2.6.0 from 2025-04-04 is still the latest tag, ~16 months old, with nothing in 2026. Mechanically it is the easy kind of app: one official container (`senaite/senaite`), one HTTP port (8080), no external database (ZODB in a /data volume), and no secret the customer must supply. It is installable today, but only via the Plone-style workaround — the Zope admin password can only be set as plaintext and defaults to admin/admin, so a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate has to be the actual auth boundary — and it additionally needs a VirtualHostMonster path-rewrite middleware, which no existing recipe uses. Recommend build_with_caveats and treat it as lower priority than broader-audience candidates: the effort is real and the addressable customer set (analytical labs willing to configure a LIMS from an empty shell) is narrow.

The only pinnable release tag on GHCR (0.9.0) is over two years stale — the sole newer artefact is the mutable `main` tag, which RFC-002 pinning does not allow — so a recipe would ship a frozen llama.cpp build that can never receive a security fix. Functionally it is a weaker single-container version of the open-webui + ollama pairing the catalogue already ships, so there is no capability gap to justify adopting an abandoned codebase.

name: SerpBear
source_description: Self-hosted SEO rank tracker for Google, Bing, and other search engines
upstream_docker_image: towfiqi/serpbear (pin `3.1.0`; upstream's own compose example uses `:latest`, which RFC-002 forbids)
version_health_notes: Release history is bursty rather than steady, driven by a single maintainer (towfiqi): 0.x/1.x through early 2024, v2.0.0-v2.0.2 in March 2024, v2.0.4-v2.0.6 in November 2024, v2.0.7 on 2025-02-23, then a 13-month silence until v3.0.0 on 2026-03-01 and v3.1.0 on 2026-03-27. v3.1.0 is the newest release as of today (2026-08-06), i.e. 132 days (~4.3 months) old, and the matching Docker Hub tag `3.1.0` was pushed 2026-03-27 — the `latest` tag points at the same build and has not moved since. `main` is quieter still but not dead: the last commits landed 2026-05-13/14, 84 days (~2.8 months) ago, after a cluster of activity in March. Repo is not archived, carries no deprecation or EOL notice, ~6-7k stars, ~265k total image pulls. Treat as active-but-thin: the project is alive and the v3 line is recent, but a recipe should expect long stretches with no upstream fix and a bus factor of one. A second, softer risk is that SerpBear's value depends on third-party SERP scraping services staying usable — upstream's own README already marks three of its integrations (scrapingrobot.com, scrapingant.com, spaceserp.com) as "Doesn't work Anymore", so integration rot outpaces the release cadence.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches SEO or marketing analytics. The nearest neighbour, uptime-kuma, watches whether a site is reachable; SerpBear watches where that site ranks in search results for chosen keywords — adjacent audience, entirely different job. It is a single Next.js container on one HTTP port (3000) with SQLite in one data volume, structurally the same shape as recipes/uptime-kuma/ and recipes/vaultwarden/, and it takes its public URL from an env var (NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL) that is derivable from APP_DOMAIN, so it sits cleanly behind Traefik on serpbear.<base_domain> with no raw ports or extra protocols.
usefulness_rationale: Rank tracking is a real, recurring cost for anyone running a site commercially (hosted equivalents start around $30-100/month), and it fits IONOS's website-owner customer base better than most homelab apps in the gap list. The catch is that SerpBear itself does no scraping: the customer must bring a paid third-party SERP API account or their own proxy IPs before a single keyword position appears, so an out-of-the-box install is an empty dashboard rather than a working product. Also note the Hostinger description oversells it — SerpBear tracks Google (plus Google Ads/Search Console integrations), not Bing or "other search engines"; scraper choice does not change that.
blocking_issues:
SerpBear's own login cannot be wired to the customer's root password. pages/api/login.ts compares the submitted password to the PASSWORD env var as a literal string — no hashing, no pre-hashed input form — and `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever carries a hash, so projecting it would set the account password to a hash string the customer never sees. Per the schema's fixed-default-credential rule this is not a hard blocker: leave SerpBear's documented default pair (USER_NAME=admin, PASSWORD=0123456789) in place and make the Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate — projected from the root-password hash — the real customer-facing auth boundary. Recipe docs must then state plainly that the inner login is a known public default.

Not blocking installation, but blocking usefulness: keyword position checks need either a third-party SERP scraper API key (serper.dev, serpapi.com, SearchApi.io, valueserp.com, HasData, ...) or a list of the customer's own proxy IPs. Both are arbitrary customer-supplied values with no `/compose` input channel. They are, however, entered in the running app's own Settings screen rather than as env vars, so the customer can supply them post-install through the web UI without any platform change — the same shape as the optional OPENAI_API_KEY note in apps-gaps/karakeep.yaml, except here the app tracks nothing at all until it is done. Upstream's only free option (scrapingrobot.com) is marked dead in its own README, so in practice this means a paid account.

Also post-install-only and optional: Google Search Console integration (SEARCH_CONSOLE_CLIENT_EMAIL / SEARCH_CONSOLE_PRIVATE_KEY) and Google Ads keyword-volume data need service-account credentials, and email alerts need customer SMTP details. None are needed to boot; none have an input channel today.
summary: SerpBear is a mechanically easy recipe — one official MIT-licensed image (`towfiqi/serpbear`, pin `3.1.0`), one HTTP port (3000), one SQLite data volume, public URL derived from APP_DOMAIN — and it opens an SEO/marketing category the current 24 recipes do not cover at all. Its two boot secrets that nobody reads (SECRET for JWT signing, APIKEY for its own API) are server-generatable; its admin login is a plaintext PASSWORD comparison that `generated_from` cannot fill, so the Gotify pattern applies: keep the documented default admin credential and put a root-password-projected Traefik `basic_auth` gate in front as the actual auth boundary. That makes it installable today. Two caveats keep it out of build_now: the delivered instance tracks nothing until the customer pastes a paid third-party SERP scraper API key or proxy list into the in-app Settings screen (doable via the UI, no platform change needed, but it is manual work with a recurring external cost), and upstream is thin — single maintainer, 13-month release gap before the March 2026 v3 line, newest release 132 days old, last commit 84 days old, and three of its scraper integrations already marked broken in its own README. Worth building if a marketing/SEO slot is wanted, with explicit documentation of the default inner login and the required external scraper account.

name: ServerStatus
source_description: Multi-server real-time monitoring dashboard with lightweight client agents
version_health_notes: "ServerStatus CN Build 2.0.0" was tagged 2026-07-10, under a month before this analysis (2026-08-05), and rewrote the server side in Go ("Go重构服务端，更轻更快"). It was the third release in ten days (1.1.8 on 2026-07-01, 1.1.9 on 2026-07-09, 2.0.0 on 2026-07-10), following a much slower earlier line (1.1.7 2025-09-03, 1.1.6 2025-08-15, 1.1.5 2024-09-13). Commits on master continue past the release — most recently 2026-07-23 — and the `server` image on Docker Hub was rebuilt the same day, so the project is clearly alive, not archived, MIT, ~4.7k stars. Caveat on pinning: the Docker Hub tag list has no `2.0.0` tag at all. The Go server is published only as the rolling `cppla/serverstatus:server` (and `:latest`), both rebuilt 2026-07-23; the newest numeric tag is `1.1.7` (pushed 2026-02-27), which is the *previous*, pre-rewrite server. Name ambiguity: several unrelated upstreams share the name. `zdz/ServerStatus-Rust` (Rust rewrite, ~1.5k stars) was ruled out as the weaker pick — its last release is v1.8.1 from 2024-03-19, i.e. ~2 years 5 months stale, with commits trickling to 2026-04-01; `BotoX/ServerStatus` (last commit 2016-01-06) and the original `mojeda/ServerStatus` (last commit 2015-04-21) are both long dead. Hostinger's own page names no repo but references a third-party image (`jiasongji/serverstatus`); the description ("lightweight client agents", real-time multi-server dashboard) matches the cppla server/client pair, which is the canonical maintained line and the one analysed here.
differentiation: Uptime Kuma — our only monitoring recipe — probes endpoints from the outside and says up/down; ServerStatus reports from inside each host: CPU, load, memory, disk, per-interface traffic with monthly baselines, TCP ping/packet loss, plus service and SSL-certificate checks, all in one live table covering many machines. Nothing in the current 24 recipes shows host resource telemetry. Its distinguishing feature against the other host-metrics candidates already triaged in this sweep (Beszel, Netdata, Glances) is the fleet view: one dashboard aggregating agents from arbitrarily many servers, which is also exactly the part that sits awkwardly inside a single-VM recipe.
usefulness_rationale: The fleet dashboard is genuinely useful for a customer running several IONOS VMs, and the agent is tiny. Capped at medium for two reasons: the recipe can only deliver the local half (the customer must install and credential an agent by hand on every other server, and the agent port must be publicly exposed), and the project is Chinese-first — README and web UI are Mandarin with no documented i18n or language switch, which is a poor fit for a catalogue whose recipes carry seven-language `short_description` blocks. Beszel or Netdata are the stronger picks if only one host-metrics dashboard is wanted.
blocking_issues:
ADMIN_TOKEN and the config.json node password are both patternless values the recipe can generate server-side, so neither blocks — but the customer does need to *read them back* to manage nodes in the UI and to bring up agents on their other servers. That means SSHing into their own VM and reading /opt/serverstatus/.env (or config.json). Same shape as the Glances/Prometheus/Dozzle findings: a documentation and first-five-minutes cost, not a missing input channel.

The "multi-server" selling point is only half-deliverable by a recipe. Each additional monitored host needs the customer to run `cppla/serverstatus:client` there with SERVER/USER/PASSWORD matching an entry in the dashboard's config.json — outside AF's single-VM provisioning scope — and the server's agent listener (35601/tcp) must be published publicly as a raw port (`http: false`), like syncthing's 22000 or wg-easy's 51820. The HTTP UI itself is clean behind Traefik on `<slug>.<base_domain>`; `reverse_proxy_compatible` is false only because of that mandatory second raw port. A local client sidecar (the beszel-agent shape) can make the recipe useful out of the box for the AF host alone.

No version-pinned image exists for the current server. The Go 2.0.0 server ships only as the rolling `cppla/serverstatus:server` / `:latest`; the newest semver tag, `1.1.7`, is the older Python server. `image-tag-pinned` would technically pass on `:server` (it is not literally `:latest`) while giving none of the reproducibility that rule exists for, and `app_version: "2.0.0"` would not correspond to any pullable tag. A recipe should either pin by digest or accept a floating tag and say so explicitly.

config.json is not auto-created — the server refuses to run without one and upstream expects you to download the sample, which contains the well-known default node credential (`s01` / `USER_DEFAULT_PASSWORD`). install.sh would have to template a fresh one; shipping the sample verbatim is not acceptable.
summary: ServerStatus (cppla/ServerStatus, MIT, ~4.7k stars) is healthy and actively developed — a Go rewrite landed as 2.0.0 on 2026-07-10, under a month before this analysis, with commits and image rebuilds through 2026-07-23. It fills a real catalogue gap: nothing among the 24 recipes shows host resource telemetry, and its fleet table goes further than the single-host candidates triaged elsewhere in this sweep. It is installable today — a domain, a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (the dashboard has no login of its own and stays world-readable otherwise), and server-side generated values for ADMIN_TOKEN and the config.json node password, none of which need a customer input channel. The caveats are what hold it to build_with_caveats rather than build_now: a second public raw TCP port (35601) for agents plus manual per-server agent rollout, no version-pinned image tag for the 2.0.0 server (only rolling `:server`), a config.json that install.sh must template instead of copying upstream's default-credential sample, and a Chinese-only README and UI with no documented i18n — which for our seven-language catalogue makes Beszel or Netdata the better first host-metrics build.

name: SFTPGo
source_description: Full-featured SFTP, FTP, and WebDAV server with web-based administration
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0-only with additional terms (see NOTICE, invoked under AGPL sections 7.3(b) and 13.1). SFTPGo Enterprise is a separate proprietary product; only the AGPL Community/Open Source edition is relevant here.
version_health_notes: Verified against the GitHub releases page and Docker Hub tag metadata, not recall. v2.7.5 was released 2026-07-17 — 20 days before today (2026-08-06) — a bug/security-fix release (httpd share connection close; improper handling of malformed SSH channel requests). Preceding releases: v2.7.4 (2026-06-27), v2.7.3 (2026-05-30), v2.7.1 (2026-03-13), v2.7.0 (2025-10-23, a feature release: post-quantum mlkem768x25519-sha256 key exchange, go-jose JWT rewrite, French/German WebUI translations, share-page disclaimers; it also *removed* Git and rsync support on security grounds), plus continued 2.6.x maintenance (v2.6.6 on 2026-02-24, v2.6.5 on 2026-02-07). The official image is rebuilt in lockstep — v2.7.5/v2.7.5-alpine/latest pushed 2026-07-17, the rolling 2.7.x and edge tags as recently as 2026-08-04. Repo is not archived, ~10k stars, active issue traffic. One structural caveat a reviewer should know: since SFTPGo Enterprise launched, upstream states plainly that primary development effort goes to the Enterprise edition (faster cadence, major new features first) while the Open Source edition "remains maintained" with bug fixes and essential updates and only selective backports. That is a slower-feature-flow signal, not an EOL one — the OSS line still shipped genuinely new features in v2.7.0 and four fix releases in the last five months — so `active` is the honest reading, but the open-source edition should be expected to lag the commercial one feature-wise.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a file-transfer *server*. recipes/syncthing/ is the nearest neighbour but solves the opposite problem — peer-to-peer replication between devices the customer controls, with no standard-protocol endpoint a third party can connect to. SFTPGo's value is precisely that: it exposes per-user, quota'd, virtual-folder-scoped accounts over SFTP (and optionally FTPS/WebDAV) with a real web admin UI plus an end-user WebClient for browsing, upload links and public shares, backed by local disk or S3/GCS/Azure Blob. Typical customer need: "give my client/agency/CI job an SFTP drop-box on my own server" — the classic replacement for hand-rolling OpenSSH chroot users, which nothing in the catalogue covers. `reverse_proxy_compatible: false` in the strict sense of this field: the web admin/client is a single plain-HTTP port (8080) and sits behind Traefik on <slug>.<base_domain> without trouble, but the app's core function needs a raw published TCP port for SFTP (2022 by default), which Traefik does not front — the same shape as recipes/syncthing/'s 22000 or recipes/wg-easy/'s UDP port, both of which the recipe schema already handles via `http: false` port entries.
usefulness_rationale: A managed SFTP/WebDAV server with per-user accounts and a web admin UI is a common, concrete self-hosting need with no catalogue coverage at all, and SFTPGo is the strongest OSS option in that niche (single Go binary, SQLite by default, multi-arch official image, small footprint). It also composes well with the rest of the catalogue as the "give something else a place to drop files" building block.
summary: SFTPGo is a single-container Go app (drakkan/sftpgo pinned at v2.7.5) with a SQLite data provider by default, so no sidecar database: web admin/WebClient on HTTP 8080 for Traefik, plus a raw published TCP 2022 for SFTP itself (FTPD and WebDAVD are bound to port 0 — disabled — in the shipped sftpgo.json, so a first recipe would sensibly ship SFTP + web UI and leave FTPS, which additionally needs its own TLS material and a passive-port range, off). It clears the /compose constraint cleanly: the only customer-facing credential is the first admin login, created at startup from SFTPGO_DEFAULT_ADMIN_USERNAME (a fixed recipe value such as "admin") and SFTPGO_DEFAULT_ADMIN_PASSWORD with SFTPGO_DATA_PROVIDER__CREATE_DEFAULT_ADMIN=1 — and, verified in internal/dataprovider/admin.go, `Admin.hashPassword()` stores the value verbatim when it already carries an internal hash prefix, so a pre-computed hash from `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` (or argon2) is accepted directly and the customer logs in with their own root password. Host keys, tokens and the DB are all generated by SFTPGo itself, and there is no external API key or OAuth registration in the boot path (the OIDC block is opt-in and empty by default). Two things for the recipe author to verify rather than assume: (1) `internalHashPwdPrefixes` is exactly `$argon2id$` and `$2a$` — a bcrypt hash emitted with the `$2b$` or `$2y$` prefix would be treated as plaintext, re-hashed, and lock the customer out, so the projection must produce `$2a$`-prefixed bcrypt (Go's x/crypto default) or an alexedwards/argon2id-style `$argon2id$v=19$...` string; (2) upstream's AGPL NOTICE adds attribution terms that bite exactly our case — an app offered through our own frontend must carry clear attribution to the SFTPGo project and a link to the corresponding source — cheap to satisfy but worth doing deliberately. Recommend build_now.

summary: Shaarli is an actively released (v0.16.5, 2026-07-31), non-EOL, single-container flat-file bookmarking service with an official GHCR image that is fully in step with upstream releases, one HTTP port (container port 80) and no database — upstream's own docker-compose example already fronts it with Traefik, so reverse-proxy compatibility is proven rather than assumed. It fills a real catalogue gap: no existing recipe manages bookmarks. Like Baikal and Bludit it has no env-var path to seed an admin account — credentials are set on an unauthenticated first-run install page and stored as a salted SHA-1 digest of password+login+salt in data/config.json.php, which `generated_from` (argon2/bcrypt, hash-only) cannot produce — so the install page must be gated with a Traefik basic_auth credential projected from the customer's root password so no stranger can claim the instance first. It boots and renders useful keyless layers (USGS seismic, satellite TLEs, news, Telegram OSINT, partial ADS-B) with an empty env, so no API key blocks install; but OPENSKY_CLIENT_ID/SECRET (flagged critical upstream) and AIS_API_KEY (ships layer empty without it) have no customer input channel, so customers get a permanently degraded subset of the advertised "60+ feeds" — that is the main caveat and an argument for prioritising this behind apps that are fully functional out of the box. Two further caveats for a recipe author: the shipped compose defaults join a Tor-onion peer mesh and a public Meshtastic MQTT broker (MESH_INFONET_FLEET_JOIN=true, MESH_BOOTSTRAP_SEED_PEERS pointing at a .onion, MESH_MQTT_* with baked-in credentials) which should be explicitly disabled in an IONOS recipe, and ADMIN_KEY is empty by default (acceptable only because the basic_auth gate is the real auth boundary). Pre-1.0 with ~fortnightly releases means ongoing version-bump maintenance.

There is no env var for the admin account: the first account created through the web setup form becomes root, and the `setupPassword` config option that exists for exactly this "provider sets up on behalf of the customer" case is confirmed in source (packages/backend/src/server/api/endpoints/admin/accounts/create.ts) to be a plaintext string-equality check, so `generated_from` — which only ever carries a hash — cannot project into it. Left unset, that gate is absent and the standard Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate (projected from the customer's root-password hash) is what guarantees the customer reaches the signup form first, the same pattern already accepted for Immich, Open WebUI, n8n and WUD. Caveats, hence `build_with_caveats` rather than `build_now`: (1) a basic_auth gate left permanently in place blocks inbound ActivityPub delivery and public profile fetches, so the instance cannot actually federate until the gate comes off, and `/compose`+`/bootstrap` have no lifecycle hook to lift it after the customer claims root — the honest framing is "private instance out of the box, federation needs a manual post-setup step"; (2) upstream is a small-team fork in security-fix-only mode for the last 12 months while the Misskey upstream it soft-forks ships monthly, so `misskey` is the stronger build in this niche if only one fediverse recipe gets bandwidth; (3) the image lives only in the project's self-hosted GitLab registry (no Docker Hub or GHCR mirror), a single point of failure for pulls that the rest of the catalogue does not have.

blocking_issues: NOT a mechanism blocker, but a policy/legal one that a human must decide before any recipe work starts: Shelfmark's purpose is searching and downloading books from shadow-library and P2P sources (its `AA_*` / Direct Download settings target Anna's Archive-style mirrors, alongside torrent, Usenet and IRC clients). Upstream's own readme carries a disclaimer pushing copyright compliance onto the user. Shipping this as an official IONOS Application Factory recipe would put the brand behind a copyright-circumvention tool; that is a legal/product call, not an engineering one, and it should be answered before the app is queued for `af-create-recipe`.
summary: Shelfmark (ghcr.io/calibrain/shelfmark, pin v1.3.5 — the tag is published and resolvable on GHCR, as is the `shelfmark-lite` variant) is a single-container MIT-licensed Python/Flask app on one HTTP port (8084, configurable via FLASK_PORT) with a SQLite store inside its `/config` volume and a `/books` output volume — structurally the same shape as recipes/uptime-kuma and recipes/vaultwarden, no external database, no privileged capabilities in the standard image (the Tor and WireGuard variants need NET_ADMIN/NET_RAW and should simply not be used). Upstream documents root-path reverse-proxy deployment with websocket/Socket.IO passthrough and exposes an unauthenticated `/api/health` endpoint, so Traefik fronting and health-check wiring are both straightforward. Every external credential it can use — Hardcover, Google Books, Prowlarr, qBittorrent, SABnzbd, AA donator key, SMTP — is optional and settable in the app's own UI after install, so none of them touch the /compose constraint. What it does need at first boot is a gate: AUTH_METHOD defaults to `none` and there is no env var to seed a local admin, so without a Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password the instance would sit fully open on the internet — that mechanism exists (IF-1312), so this is installable_today. The reason this is build_with_caveats rather than build_now is not technical: it is primarily a shadow-library/torrent download front-end, and putting an IONOS-branded recipe behind that needs an explicit legal/product sign-off (if that sign-off is refused, the correct outcome is not_recommended). Secondary caveat: upstream self-declares the project stable but "not under active maintenance" with a closed feature scope, even though releases are still landing weekly.

name: ShinyProxy
source_description: Open-source server for hosting R Shiny, Dash, and Streamlit apps with auth
upstream_docker_image: openanalytics/shinyproxy:3.2.4 (vendor-published, self-described 'official ShinyProxy Docker image'; Dockerfile in openanalytics/shinyproxy-docker)
version_health_notes: v3.2.4 shipped 2026-04-30, ~3.2 months before today (2026-08-05), and is a security release rolling up dependency CVE fixes. Recent history: 3.2.3 (2026-01-15), 3.2.2 (2025-11-12), 3.2.1 (2025-10-28), 3.2.0 (2025-07-07) — four releases in the ~10 months to 3.2.4, so the current cadence is healthy. Worth noting for context: there was a ~13-month quiet stretch between 3.1.1 (2024-06-20) and 3.2.0 (2025-07-07), so the project is not on a metronome; it moves in bursts. Repo is not archived (last push 2026-05-15, 69 open issues actively triaged), and the Docker Hub image was rebuilt as recently as 2026-08-02. Commercially backed by Open Analytics (Belgium), who sell support/enterprise services around it — no EOL or maintenance-only signal. Upstream is steering Docker/Kubernetes users toward the "ShinyProxy Operator" for production, but the plain containerised deployment is still documented and the official image is still published per-release.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue hosts a customer's own data apps — ShinyProxy would be a new category. It is a Java/Spring Boot front door that serves a catalogue page of Shiny/Dash/Streamlit apps and spawns a fresh container per user session for each one, giving per-session isolation and lifecycle management the customer would otherwise hand-roll. Its container-orchestration angle brushes against `portainer` (Docker management UI) and `runtipi` (self-hosting app launcher), but neither serves R/Python analytical apps and neither is a substitute. Single HTTP port (8080) with WebSocket traffic, which Traefik proxies natively, so it fronts cleanly on `shinyproxy.<base_domain>` like the rest of the catalogue — no raw ports or extra protocols leave the host.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely valuable to R/Python data-science teams, and the best-known open-source answer to Posit Connect for self-hosters — but the addressable customer is narrow: ShinyProxy ships no content of its own, so it only pays off for someone who already has (or will build) containerised Shiny/Dash/Streamlit app images. Worse for our mechanism, there is no channel to supply those app specs at `/compose` time, so the recipe would land as a working ShinyProxy serving only upstream's demo apps, with the real work — build/pull your images, edit `/opt/shinyproxy/application.yml`, restart — done by the customer over SSH afterwards. Also resource-hungry relative to most recipes: a JVM (~238 MB image) plus one ~450 MB R container per active session.
summary: ShinyProxy is an actively maintained, Apache-2.0, commercially backed project (v3.2.4, 2026-04-30, four releases in the preceding ~10 months) with an official vendor-published Docker image and a single reverse-proxy-friendly HTTP port (8080, WebSockets — fine behind Traefik). It is installable today, but only in one shape: our recipe would set `proxy.authentication: none` in the application.yml we author and gate the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth` middleware fed from the root-password projection. ShinyProxy's own `simple` auth is not usable as the customer-facing login — it stores passwords as plaintext in application.yml with no hash-accepting form, so `generated_from` (which only ever emits a hash) cannot feed it, and its LDAP/OIDC/SAML modes all need external registration with no input channel today. That design choice costs ShinyProxy one of its headline features: with `authentication: none` there are no per-user accounts, groups, or admin panel, so the install is effectively single-tenant behind one shared basic-auth credential. Two further caveats for whoever builds it: the container needs `/var/run/docker.sock` mounted plus `group_add` with the host's docker GID resolved at install time (root-equivalent access, though `portainer`, `runtipi`, and `wud` already do this), with `proxy.docker.internal-networking: true` and a shared `container-network` so spawned app containers are reachable; and the demo app image `openanalytics/shinyproxy-demo` publishes only a `latest` tag (last pushed 2025-07-08), so satisfying the pinned-tag rule means pinning it by digest. Recommend `build_with_caveats`, and low priority against apps that deliver value out of the box — this one needs the customer to bring their own apps before it does anything.

name: ShipShipShip
source_description: Self-hosted changelog and roadmap with community voting and newsletters
version_health_notes: v1.3.5 (2026-02-18) is the latest tagged release and matches the last commit to the repo (both `main` and `dev` branches) — no commit or release in the ~5.5 months since, as of today (2026-08-05), despite a very active cadence beforehand (multiple releases per month from v1.1.3 in 2025-09 through v1.3.5 in 2026-02). The maintainer (GauthierNelkinsky) directly confirmed the slowdown in https://github.com/GauthierNelkinsky/ShipShipShip/issues/31 (2026-07-24): "I just don't have the time to actively work on this right now, so it's more in maintenance mode than active development. It's not abandoned though... Might pick it back up myself." Repo is not archived and the maintainer says PRs are still reviewed, but there is currently zero active development — treating this as maintenance-only rather than active.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers a public changelog/roadmap with community voting and newsletter announcements — this is a genuinely uncovered category. (A prior gap analysis for Fider covers similar "feedback board" ground but was found blocked_on_platform for an unrelated reason — no password login at all, requiring SMTP/OAuth. ShipShipShip is architecturally different: it does have its own password login, but that login can't be projected today either, for a different reason — see below.)
usefulness_rationale: A self-hosted "what's new / what's coming" page with voting is a real, recurring ask for SaaS builders who want to keep product-update communication in-house, and the category is otherwise empty in our catalogue. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high given the maintenance-only status and the single-maintainer, still-young (first tag 2025) project.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: ADMIN_USERNAME / ADMIN_PASSWORD (the app's own content-authoring login — used to create/publish changelog and roadmap entries, not merely a perimeter gate); JWT_SECRET
blocking_issues:
ADMIN_PASSWORD is checked as a plaintext string equality (`backend/middleware/auth.go`: `username == adminUsername && password == adminPassword`, read straight from the env var) — the app has no bcrypt/argon2 hash-comparison path at all. `generated_from` only ever projects a *hash* of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no way to make ADMIN_PASSWORD equal the customer's actual root password through the supported mechanism.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` does not substitute here the way it does for n8n/WUD: ADMIN_USERNAME/ADMIN_PASSWORD is the same credential the customer needs to log into ShipShipShip's own admin UI to author changelog/roadmap content — it is not a redundant security perimeter around an otherwise-open app. If we randomize ADMIN_PASSWORD server-side (as we would for a true no-customer-input secret), the customer can never log in to use the app's actual admin functionality. This matches the schema's "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case, which is called out as a structural blocker distinct from a merely unsupported hash algorithm.
summary: ShipShipShip is a simple, single-container Go/SvelteKit app (SQLite, one HTTP port, no other services) that would otherwise be an easy, reverse-proxy-friendly fit and fills a category — public changelog/ roadmap with voting and newsletters — that our 24-recipe catalogue currently lacks. It is blocked today because its admin login (ADMIN_USERNAME/ADMIN_PASSWORD), which is the actual content-authoring credential rather than a perimeter gate, is checked as plaintext with no hash-comparison path, and `generated_from` can only ever supply a hash of the customer's root password. Traefik `basic_auth` doesn't substitute since the customer still needs working admin credentials to publish content. Separately, the maintainer confirmed on 2026-07-24 that the project is now maintenance-only, not actively developed. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit if a plaintext-password projection channel is ever added, and re-check upstream activity before building even then.

blocking_issues: Shopware's first-boot installer (the official Deployment Helper, invoked via `system:install`/`user:create`) creates the admin account from `INSTALL_ADMIN_USERNAME` / `INSTALL_ADMIN_PASSWORD` env vars, and it hashes whatever plaintext value it receives internally — it has no "accept a pre-hashed password for comparison" mode the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password, never the plaintext itself, so there is no way to make the customer's actual root password become their working Shopware admin login: feeding the hash string into `INSTALL_ADMIN_PASSWORD` would just set that opaque hash as the literal admin password, which the customer does not know and cannot type in. Gating the storefront/admin behind Traefik `basic_auth` (also root-password-derived) does not solve this either — it only adds a second, separate wall in front of an admin panel the customer still can't sign into with a password they know, unless the admin password is left at a fixed, server-generated value the customer is simply never told (workable per the SCHEMA.md "fixed/default credential behind a Traefik gate" allowance, but then the customer has no route to Shopware's own admin panel at all — a shop they cannot administer isn't a usable recipe outcome, just a basic_auth-gated storefront front page).
summary: Shopware is a mature, actively developed (release today, 2026-08-05), MIT-licensed, single-HTTP-port eCommerce platform (app + worker + scheduler containers behind one Traefik-friendly port, plus MySQL/MariaDB and optional Elasticsearch) that would fill a genuine gap — the catalogue has no storefront/shop recipe today. It fails the current installability test on one specific point: its admin account is created from a plaintext password env var that Shopware hashes itself, and `generated_from` only ever supplies a hash, so the customer's root password cannot become a working Shopware login the way it does for Vaultwarden. A random server-generated DB password is no problem, but the admin credential has no expressible channel today. Worth building once either `generated_from` gains a plaintext-passthrough mode or Shopware exposes a way to accept a pre-hashed admin password directly — `blocked_on_platform`, not `not_recommended`.

differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers social-media scheduling, so this would be a new category for the catalogue. However, it is not a novel gap: apps-gaps/postiz.yaml already analyzed the same product category (self-hosted Buffer/Hootsuite alternative) and recommended build_with_caveats. Postiz is the more mature, broader candidate — it already supports X, LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, Reddit, Threads, Mastodon, Bluesky, TikTok, and YouTube, plus AI content generation and team collaboration, versus Shoutrrr's newer and narrower feature set (X, Bluesky, LinkedIn, with Meta/Threads/Discord added only in its most recent releases). A customer choosing between the two today would most likely prefer Postiz's platform coverage and longer track record.
usefulness_rationale: Real, common self-hosting ask (self-hosted social scheduler), and the single-container SQLite-by-default deployment is operationally lighter than Postiz's multi-service Temporal stack. Capped at medium rather than high because Postiz already covers the same job more completely, and because — as detailed below — two of Shoutrrr's three headline networks (X, LinkedIn) can't actually be used without a customer- supplied OAuth app registration that has no input channel today, which undercuts the exact use case in Hostinger's own description.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the upstream README and docker-compose.production.yaml: Shoutrrr has no admin-credential environment variable at all. The container boots with zero users; the first visitor to the app's URL is presented with an open registration form ("register the first account, and you're in") and becomes the sole owner. Per the precedent already accepted for n8n and Postiz (self-service signup on a URL only the customer knows is not treated as a blocker), this on its own does not block installability — there is no `type: password` parameter to target with `generated_from`, but none is needed since the customer sets their own credential directly in the browser after deployment, not through /compose.

The structural blocker is different: X and LinkedIn publishing — two of the three networks named in Hostinger's own description — require operator/customer-obtained OAuth app credentials (X_CLIENT_ID/X_CLIENT_SECRET, LINKEDIN_CLIENT_ID/LINKEDIN_CLIENT_SECRET) set as environment variables before those integrations work at all. These are external, customer-registered developer-portal credentials (X in particular now requires business verification), not a hash of the root password and not something af-api can generate — this is exactly the "external API key/token the app can't function without" case with no supported channel per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md. Only Bluesky (via a per-user app password entered live in the UI, no pre-boot secret) and Discord (webhook URL, also entered live) would work out of the box; X and LinkedIn would sit visibly present in the UI but permanently non-functional for every customer unless we ship a manual per-instance setup step outside the recipe mechanism.
summary: Shoutrrr is a very young (five and a half weeks old) but fast-shipping self-hosted social-media scheduler that would open a new category for the catalogue — except apps-gaps/postiz.yaml already covers the same category with a broader, more established candidate. Its self-service admin signup is not a blocker on its own (same accepted pattern as n8n/Postiz), but two of its three headline networks — X and LinkedIn — require a customer- supplied OAuth app registration with no input channel in the current recipe mechanism, leaving only Bluesky and Discord functional out of the box. That gap matters more for Shoutrrr than for Postiz, since Postiz's pitch spans many more platforms and losing two is proportionally smaller. Revisit only if the platform gains a channel for customer-supplied external credentials, and even then, prioritize Postiz first given its maturity and broader coverage.

Repo is not archived (`archived: false` via GitHub API) and has 63 open issues, so it isn't formally EOL, but the pattern reads as an occasionally-revived single-maintainer project rather than one under active development — "sporadic" fits better than "active" or even "slowing".
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers website analytics/traffic tracking. Shynet is a cookie-free, no-JS-required alternative to Google Analytics in the same space as Plausible, Matomo, Ackee, and GoatCounter (all currently `apps-gaps` candidates, none yet built) — a real, recognizable category, just one we'd be picking a specific implementation within rather than introducing.
usefulness_rationale: Privacy-first analytics has a genuine recurring audience, but Shynet specifically is the weakest-maintained option among the analytics candidates already surfaced (Plausible and Ackee both show more recent/active upstream work); a customer comparing options would likely be steered toward one of those instead once they're built.
blocking_issues:
Shynet has no environment variable for setting an admin username/password at first boot. The only way to create the first account is `./manage.py registeradmin <email>` (shynet/core/management/commands/registeradmin.py), a one-off management command that must be run via `docker exec` (or `docker run`) against the running container, after which it generates a random 10-character password (`get_random_string(10)`) and prints it to stdout/console — it is never customer-supplied, never hash-verified, and there is no channel in the current `/compose` flow to run an interactive post-boot exec step or surface console output back to the customer. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` doesn't apply — this isn't a hash-verified field, it's a command whose entire output is a random secret with no input side at all.

Gating the app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead (root password) doesn't fully solve it either: with no admin account ever created, a customer who gets past the gate lands on Shynet's own login screen with nothing to log in with. Public self-signup (`ACCOUNT_SIGNUPS_ENABLED=true`) would let a customer create *a* account, but by default only superusers can create tracked "services" (sites to monitor) per the `ONLY_SUPERUSERS_CREATE` setting, and self-signup does not grant superuser — so even that path leaves the customer with an account that can log in but can't do the one thing the app is for, short of a second manual exec/DB step to promote the user.
summary: Shynet is a reverse-proxy-friendly, single-HTTP-port (8080) Django + Postgres app with no direct overlap in the current catalogue — cookie-free web analytics is a real category we don't cover yet. It fails installability today for a harder reason than a missing `generated_from` mapping: there is no environment-variable or hash-verified credential field at all for the admin account. The only bootstrap path is an interactive `manage.py registeradmin` exec that prints a random password to console output, which the current `/compose`-only mechanism has no way to run or surface, and public self-signup doesn't grant the superuser role needed to add tracked sites. Combined with a sporadic release history (a ~2.6-year gap between v0.13.1 and v0.14.0) and stronger-maintained alternatives already in `apps-gaps` (Plausible, Ackee), this is a `not_recommended` rather than a `blocked_on_platform` — even if a future admin-bootstrap mechanism existed, Shynet specifically isn't the analytics app worth spending it on.

name: SigNoz
source_description: OpenTelemetry-native APM with unified traces, metrics, and logs
upstream_license: Open-core: MIT for the core repo, with the ee/ and cmd/enterprise/ directories under a separate proprietary license (ee/LICENSE)
version_health_notes: v0.136.1 published 2026-08-05T19:38Z (today) per the GitHub Releases API, with v0.136.0 also shipping earlier the same day and v0.135.1/ v0.135.0 on 2026-07-31/07-29 — sub-weekly release cadence throughout July-August 2026. 31.6k GitHub stars, 1539 open issues. Clearly active, not slowing or dormant.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue does APM/tracing/log aggregation; Uptime Kuma (our only "monitoring" recipe) is blackbox up/down ping checking, a different use case entirely. SigNoz would fill a genuine gap the same way HyperDX and OpenObserve would (both already analyzed, apps-gaps/hyperdx.yaml and apps-gaps/openobserve.yaml) — it is one of several credible OTel-native "unified observability" candidates competing for the same niche, not a duplicate of anything already shipped.
usefulness_rationale: Real, well-adopted open-source APM tool (31.6k stars) that a customer running several other self-hosted services (our own n8n, Gitea, Immich, etc.) could point OpenTelemetry-instrumented workloads at. But like HyperDX/Jaeger/OpenObserve it only has value for a customer who has other instrumented services to feed it — no standalone utility — and it carries a heavier resource/operational footprint (ClickHouse + ClickHouse Keeper + Postgres + OTel Collector + backend) than a typical single-container recipe.
blocking_issues:
Not a single-HTTP-port app: SigNoz's entire purpose is receiving telemetry pushed by OpenTelemetry-instrumented services, which requires the OTel Collector's raw ingestion ports (4317 gRPC, 4318 HTTP) to be reachable directly by whatever external service is pushing traces/metrics/logs — not just a browser routed through Traefik on 80/443. This is the identical structural mismatch already flagged for Apache SkyWalking, HyperDX, and Jaeger (apps-gaps/hyperdx.yaml, apps-gaps/jaeger.yaml): every current recipe is a single browser-facing HTTP port fronted by Traefik, and exposing raw ingestion ports per customer VM is a product decision that hasn't been made.

Heavier multi-container stack than most of the catalogue: the official deployment is five containers — the SigNoz backend/UI, OpenTelemetry Collector, ClickHouse, ClickHouse Keeper, and PostgreSQL (metadata store) — comparable in weight to Immich/ anytype-server rather than the single-container recipes that make up most of the catalogue, and needs a real ClickHouse data volume.

Upstream has deprecated static docker-compose manifests entirely in favor of "Foundry" (foundryctl), a CLI that generates the Docker Compose files at install time from a casting.yaml config rather than shipping a fixed compose file to fork from. A recipe would need to either pin to the last pre-Foundry compose manifest (a dead end, since upstream no longer maintains it) or wrap the foundryctl install flow itself, which doesn't fit the current metadata.yaml/ docker-compose.yaml recipe shape.

No first-boot secret is required by the platform itself: on first visit to the UI (port 8080) the app presents its own signup screen where the visitor creates their own admin account directly (no env-var-injected admin credential, no API key gate) — the same self-serve pattern already accepted for n8n and Immich in this catalogue, so authentication alone is not what blocks this recipe.
summary: SigNoz is an actively developed (multiple releases per week, latest v0.136.1 shipped today, 2026-08-05), open-core APM platform with no equivalent already in the catalogue. Its own first-run account creation is unproblematic (self-serve signup, same pattern as n8n/Immich/HyperDX), so it is not blocked by the usual root-password/basic_auth secrets mechanism. What blocks it is structural, identical to HyperDX and Jaeger: its core purpose requires exposing raw OTel ingestion ports (4317/4318) directly to whatever external, separately-hosted services are pushing telemetry, a fundamentally different exposure shape than our Traefik-only, single-HTTP-port recipes — compounded here by a five-container ClickHouse/Postgres-backed stack and upstream's move away from a maintainable static docker-compose manifest toward the Foundry/foundryctl installer. Recommend blocked_on_platform pending a product decision on exposing non-HTTP ingestion ports per recipe; revisit alongside HyperDX and Jaeger if/when that decision is made.

blocking_issues:
Confirmed against upstream self-hosting and environment-variable docs: there is no admin-username/admin-password environment variable to preset the owner account. Sim ships an open, persistent email/password self-registration screen (`better-auth`-based) with knobs to restrict it after the fact — `DISABLE_REGISTRATION`, `DISABLE_EMAIL_SIGNUP`, `ALLOWED_LOGIN_DOMAINS`, `ALLOWED_LOGIN_EMAILS`, `BLOCKED_SIGNUP_DOMAINS` — but every one of those needs a customer-specific value (the customer's own email or domain) that has no channel into `/compose` today, or is a static boolean that would have to be `true` from boot (locking the intended customer out too) or `false` forever (leaving registration open to any visitor indefinitely). This is the same structural shape as the 2FAuth and Activepieces gap analyses (see `apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml`, `apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml`): no `type: password` parameter on the app's own login exists to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because the credential is created client-side via self-registration rather than injected via env var. Unlike n8n/AnythingLLM/Uptime Kuma's first-run setup wizard (which creates exactly one owner account and then permanently closes further signups), Sim's registration screen is designed to stay open long-term for additional team members, so it is not a one-time race that resolves itself — it is a standing open door.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would close the "stranger reaches the URL first" race, but per the 2FAuth/Activepieces precedent, today's basic_auth mechanism has no channel to also hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential for the in-app registration form beyond the single root-password projection already used for the gate itself — so it does not fully resolve the underlying provisioning gap, and it does not stop additional signups by anyone who already has the gate password either.

Separately from the auth gap: the official `docker-compose.prod.yml` needs six services (app, realtime/websocket, Postgres+pgvector, Redis, cron, migrations) and the docs state a 2 CPU / 12 GB RAM / 20 GB SSD floor — a heavier footprint than most of the catalogue, and the realtime websocket service needs its own path-based route (`/socket.io/`) under the same domain, which is workable behind Traefik but is not the simple single-service-single-port shape most recipes use. Not a blocker on its own, just an added operational cost on top of the auth gap above.
summary: Sim Studio is an active, well-funded, fast-shipping AI agent workflow builder (Apache-2.0, 29.4k stars, several releases a day), but it fails the installability test on the same structural grounds as the 2FAuth and Activepieces gap analyses: there is no env-var hook to preset the sole admin account, and the app's registration screen is designed to stay open indefinitely rather than closing after a one-time setup wizard, so neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely hand the customer exclusive control of their own instance. The three core secrets (BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, ENCRYPTION_KEY, INTERNAL_API_SECRET) plus the Postgres password are trivially server-generatable and not blocking on their own. It also duplicates ground n8n already covers as a visual workflow builder, so even once the auth gap is resolved this lands as medium rather than high value. Revisit if upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond root-password projection, and weigh it against n8n's existing recipe before prioritizing.
