The two most recent gaps are 16 days (v2.11.2 -> v2.11.3) and 39 days (v2.11.3 -> v2.12.0), so the current rhythm is roughly monthly, not weekly. Cadence is still recorded as `active` rather than `slowing` because the deceleration reads as normalisation after a post-launch burst rather than as a stall: in absolute terms the project shipped a feature release 6 days ago and has never gone more than ~6 weeks without one. A recipe author should nonetheless expect monthly-ish tag bumps, not weekly. The other flip side is immaturity: a ~4-month-old codebase has not yet had time to prove long-term stability, and breaking or security-relevant changes could land at any pinned-tag bump.
differentiation: Nothing currently in the 24-recipe catalogue covers anonymous, link-based file/note sharing with true client-side (browser) end-to-end encryption — the server and its operator never see plaintext content or the decryption key (carried only in the URL fragment, never sent to the server). OpenGist is the closest neighbor but is Git-backed code/text snippets with server-side plaintext storage and no encryption; Syncthing is P2P folder sync between a customer's own owned devices, not one-off link sharing with third parties; Vaultwarden is a password manager, not a share-a-link tool. The `anonupload` gap-analysis (not built, not_recommended — eol) covers similar ground conceptually but that specific project has been abandoned since 2023, so SkySend is a live, actively-maintained alternative to that unfilled niche.
usefulness_rationale: Zero-knowledge encrypted file/note drop (with burn-after-read notes and view limits) is a genuinely useful, currently-unfilled niche for a self-hosting customer who wants to share a sensitive file or secret with someone outside their org without trusting a third-party service. Usefulness is medium rather than high because it is a narrow, single-purpose utility (not a platform customers build on) and the underlying project's newness (~4 months, pre-1.0-in-spirit release velocity) adds real stability/security risk for something whose whole value proposition is trustworthy handling of sensitive data.
blocking_issues: The only auth mechanism expressible today cannot express the configuration this app actually needs. Traefik `basic_auth: true` is a boolean gate on the recipe's public HTTP port, not a path-scoped rule (see apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md), and SkySend serves both the upload UI and the recipient-facing share/download URLs (`BASE_URL/<share path>`) on that one port (3000). Gating the port therefore prompts every share recipient for the customer's basic-auth credential — which is derived from their own server root password and so cannot responsibly be handed to an outside party — before they can fetch a file or read a note. That defeats the app's stated purpose (sharing a secret with someone outside the org). Leaving the gate off keeps share links usable but exposes an unauthenticated upload endpoint to the internet, i.e. anyone who finds the URL can write arbitrary files to the customer's disk. Upstream's own answer to exactly this is OIDC with `OIDC_PROTECT_FILES` / `OIDC_PROTECT_NOTES`, which gates upload/note creation only while "downloads always public" — the split our whole-app boolean cannot express. Enabling it needs registering the instance with an external identity provider (client ID/secret/issuer URL), for which /compose has no input channel today.
summary: SkySend ships as a single official container (skyfay/skysend, pin to v2.12.0) on one HTTP port (3000), backed by SQLite and local bind-mounted `/data` + `/uploads` volumes with no external database — a clean fit for our single-container-behind-Traefik pattern. The app has no built-in account system or admin login by design (that's the whole "zero accounts, zero knowledge" pitch); its only auth option is OIDC/SSO, which requires registering the instance with an external identity provider and has no input channel in our current /compose flow. That leaves an unavoidable trade-off, because IF-1312's Traefik `basic_auth` is a whole-port boolean and SkySend serves uploads and recipient download links on the same port: gate it and outside recipients are locked out of the share links the app exists to produce; leave it open and anyone who finds the URL can upload to the customer's disk. A recipe author should ship it gated — an open write endpoint on a public VM is not a defensible default — and document that this reduces the instance to single-operator use until path-scoped basic_auth or an OIDC input channel exists, which is the platform work that would unlock the app's headline external-sharing use case. The project itself is new (~4 months) and its release cadence has slowed from near-daily during the April/May launch burst to roughly monthly since late May 2026, with the most recent release 6 days ago — still actively maintained, just no longer sprinting. Recommend building with the caveat above, plus a note to the recipe author to track upstream releases for security-relevant fixes given the sensitive-data use case, and to treat a gap beyond ~2 months as the signal to re-check project health.

differentiation: No recipe today covers browser/RPA-style automation specifically — Skyvern drives a real headless/headful browser via LLM + computer vision to fill forms, navigate sites, and complete workflows it has never seen before, without brittle site-specific selectors. openclaw and hermes-agent are the closest existing entries (also "self-hosted AI agent" positioning) but both are messaging-app-first (Telegram gateway/bot with a secondary dashboard) and don't operate a browser as their core mechanism. Skyvern is web-UI-first (workflow builder, livestreaming of the browser session, artifact/file management) and its use case — automating web-based tasks a business already does by hand (data entry, form submission, scraping behind logins) — is genuinely distinct from "chat with an agent over Telegram." Real differentiator, but conceptually adjacent enough to both existing agent recipes that it should be weighed against them, not treated as filling an empty niche.
usefulness_rationale: Popular, well-funded, actively-developed browser-automation-via-LLM tool with a distinct RPA-flavored use case versus the catalogue's existing chat-first AI agents. Capped at medium rather than high because it is presently blocked on installability (see below) and because two adjacent "AI agent" recipes already exist, so the incremental catalogue value depends on whether a customer specifically wants browser-driving automation rather than a chat-driven agent.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against upstream self-hosting docs and the shipped docker-compose.yml: at least one LLM provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq, or a self-hosted Ollama endpoint) must be enabled and its API key set in the `skyvern` container's `.env` *before* first startup — ENABLE_<PROVIDER>=true, <PROVIDER>_API_KEY=..., and LLM_KEY=... are read at container start, not configured later through the UI. This is a mandatory external API key with no projection channel under the current `/compose` mechanism (root-password hashing cannot produce a third party's LLM API key), matching the "external API key the app can't function without" no-channel case in apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md. Ollama does not remove the blocker: it just shifts the requirement to standing up and reaching a separate LLM endpoint, which the customer still has to configure post-boot and which the compose stack does not include.

The `skyvern-ui` frontend has no built-in username/password login surfaced in the docs or compose env — it would need a Traefik `basic_auth` gate (root-password hash) to avoid sitting open on the internet, the same pattern used for n8n/OpenClaw/WUD/Open WebUI/Immich. That gate alone is expressible today; it just doesn't resolve the LLM-key blocker above.

The app's own internal API_KEY (used for API-server auth) is generated automatically on first container startup — that piece is server_generated_no_customer_input and not a blocker on its own, only called out for completeness.
summary: Skyvern is an active, fast-shipping (multiple releases in the last month, latest v1.0.48 today, 2026-08-05), well-funded browser-automation tool that fills a real gap — no current recipe drives a real browser via LLM + computer vision the way Skyvern does, distinguishing it from the catalogue's existing chat-first agents (openclaw, hermes-agent). It is reverse-proxy-compatible (skyvern-ui on a single HTTP port) and would otherwise be a reasonable build. It is blocked today purely on the external-API-key problem: at least one LLM provider's API key must be baked into the `skyvern` container's `.env` before the stack can do anything useful, and there is no channel today for a customer to supply that at `/compose` time. Revisit once the platform has a real arbitrary-secret input channel (beyond root-password hash projection); until then this is blocked_on_platform, not build_now.

name: slskd
source_description: Web-based Soulseek client for peer-to-peer music and file sharing
version_health_notes: No new stable numbered release since 0.26.0 on 2024-07-19 — over 24 months before today (2026-08-05). However the project is not dormant: master/canary builds are pushed within days of today (canary Docker tag updated ~2 days ago per Docker Hub), the repo has ~5k commits, ~3.7k stars, ~156 open issues, and is not archived. This is a project that develops continuously but has stopped cutting tagged stable releases — worth re-checking before a recipe pins to 0.26.0, since that tag is now over two years old relative to what canary actually ships.
differentiation: Nothing else in the current 24-recipe catalogue talks to the Soulseek P2P network. Syncthing (recipes/syncthing) is superficially similar (web UI, P2P transport, extra raw sync port) but solves a different problem — private device-to-device file sync, not joining a public file-sharing network. slskd is the only candidate that adds "P2P network client" as a category. reverse_proxy_compatible is false for the same reason Syncthing needs its raw 22000 and apps-gaps/resilio-sync.yaml is marked false: the web UI (HTTP 5030, HTTPS 5031) can sit on <slug>.<base_domain> behind Traefik, but slskd additionally needs its Soulseek peer listen port (default 50300, SLSKD_SLSK_LISTEN_PORT) published as a raw TCP port reachable from the internet. Upstream docs/config.md: "configuring the listen port and port forwarding ensures full connectivity with other clients." That port carries the Soulseek wire protocol, not HTTP, so it is outside Traefik's HTTP-only reach and must be published directly on the VM. Without it the app still boots and serves its UI but degrades to outbound-only peer connectivity.
usefulness_rationale: Soulseek is a public P2P network primarily used for sharing copyrighted music. Even though the app itself is legitimate open-source software, hosting it as a one-click catalogue recipe puts IONOS in the position of provisioning infrastructure whose main real-world use is unauthorized media sharing/distribution — a reputational and abuse-vector risk that outweighs the niche audience (self-hosted P2P music enthusiasts) it would serve. This is a business/legal judgment call, not a technical one; flagging for human review rather than asserting it outright.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: slskd web UI login (basic-auth gate credential)
secrets_expressible_today: slskd web UI login (basic-auth gate credential):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
slskd's own web UI login (SLSKD_USERNAME/SLSKD_PASSWORD) only accepts a plaintext password at startup — there is no bcrypt/argon2-hash input path for it, so generated_from cannot project the customer's root password into it directly. Workaround: leave SLSKD_USERNAME/PASSWORD as a server-generated random value nothing customer-facing reads, and put the real auth boundary at Traefik basic_auth (root-password hash) in front of the whole app, same pattern as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI. This makes the app mechanically installable once IF-1312 (basic_auth) ships — not a hard blocker, just blocked_on_platform.

The app's actual purpose (searching/downloading on the Soulseek network) additionally needs the customer's own Soulseek network account username/password (SLSKD_SLSK_USERNAME/PASSWORD). These are NOT required to boot the container or reach the web UI — the app starts and serves its UI without them, just disconnected from the network — and slskd supports entering them post-login via its own Settings page (SLSKD_REMOTE_CONFIGURATION=true) triggering a reconnect, with no restart needed from us. This is customer self-service through the app's already-authenticated UI, the same shape as a user adding their own third-party API keys inside n8n after deploy, so it is not a blocker for our /compose mechanism.
summary: slskd is a well-built, actively-developed (canary-level) Soulseek P2P client with a real web UI and no category overlap in the current catalogue, but two things hold it back. Mechanically, its own web login only takes a plaintext password (no hash input), so it needs the not-yet-merged Traefik basic_auth gate (IF-1312) rather than generated_from to be installable — a real but temporary platform gap. Soulseek network credentials themselves are not a boot-time blocker since the customer can self-service those through the app's own UI after login. Routing is also not a pure Traefik story: the web UI fronts fine, but the Soulseek peer listen port (default 50300) is a raw TCP port that has to be published directly on the VM alongside the HTTP route, same shape as recipes/syncthing/'s 22000 — worth agreeing before anyone writes the recipe. Separately from mechanics, the app's primary real-world use case — joining a public network mostly used to trade copyrighted media — is a reputational/legal fit question for IONOS's catalogue that a human should weigh before this goes further, independent of whether IF-1312 ships.

name: Smocker
source_description: Open-source HTTP mock server and proxy with a live admin UI for API testing
latest_version: v1.1.2-preview (latest tagged release; latest non-preview/stable tag is 1.0.0)
version_health_notes: 1.0.0 shipped 2025-03-22 and was quiet for over a year. Development then resumed with v1.1.0-preview/v1.1.1-preview/v1.1.2-preview on 2026-07-18/2026-07-19 (a Go 1.26 + React 19 modernization, embedded-UI self-contained binary, and official multi-arch GHCR image) — roughly 2.5 weeks before this analysis (2026-08-05). The `latest` and `1.0.0` Docker tags on GHCR are still the March-2025 build; the actively-developed 1.1.x line is only published under `-preview` tags, so a recipe would have to choose between pinning a 16-month-old stable tag or an unstable preview tag.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers HTTP API mocking/stubbing or request-proxying for integration testing; the closest developer-tools entries (Gitea, Opengist, claude-code, gemini-cli) are unrelated (git hosting, gist hosting, CLI agents). Smocker would be a genuinely new capability, not an overlap.
usefulness_rationale: Useful for teams that want a persistent, shared mock/stub server for API integration testing rather than a per-CI-run throwaway container, but it's a developer/QA infrastructure tool rather than an end-user-facing app, which is a narrower fit for the catalogue's typical customer than apps like Uptime Kuma or Vaultwarden.
blocking_issues:
Smocker needs two independently-public HTTP ports: 8080 (the mock endpoint that test clients hit) and 8081 (the config/admin UI and API used to register and manage mocks). Per rfc/001-recipe-schema.md §4.3, a recipe may declare at most one HTTP port that gets a Traefik router/domain; a second HTTP port has no supported way to receive its own domain+TLS today. This is a structural blocker independent of the auth question below.

The 8081 config/admin port ships with no built-in authentication at all (it can create, delete, and inspect mocks, and Smocker's proxy mode can be pointed at arbitrary upstream hosts) — it must sit behind a mandatory gate. `traefik_basic_auth` is the correct mechanism, but it cannot be applied until the two-HTTP-port limitation above is resolved, since basic_auth is applied per Traefik router and only one port gets a router.
summary: Smocker is a small, MIT-licensed, single-container HTTP mock/proxy server with a genuinely new capability for the catalogue (no overlap with the 24 existing recipes) and shows renewed upstream activity as of July 2026 after over a year of dormancy. It is blocked from shipping today by a platform limitation rather than a usefulness problem: it needs two separate public HTTP ports (mock endpoint + unauthenticated admin UI), and the current recipe mechanism only routes one HTTP port per recipe through Traefik, so the admin UI has no way to get both a domain and the basic_auth gate it requires. Revisit once multi-HTTP-port routing (or an equivalent path-based split) is supported, or once a single-port operating mode is confirmed viable upstream.

Recommend build_with_caveats: technically installable with the basic_auth workaround, but low priority given its narrow appeal and the empty-by-default first-run experience.

blocking_issues:
Snac2 gives no way — in any form, hash or plaintext — to set an account's password to a chosen value at creation time. Verified against upstream source: `adduser()` (utils.c:290-388) takes only a uid and unconditionally calls `new_password()` (utils.c:278-286), which generates a random password internally, stores its hash, and prints the plaintext to stdout exactly once ("User password is %s", utils.c:377). `resetpwd()` (utils.c:391+) behaves identically. The only code path that accepts an operator-chosen password is the authenticated web UI's `passwd1`/`passwd2` fields on the user admin page (html.c:6062-6066) — reachable only after already logging in with the generated password. So the credential the customer needs is server-generated and customer-facing, which fits none of our three mechanisms.

`generated_from_root_password` has no target. The mechanism projects a hash onto a `type: password` metadata parameter that the app reads at boot from env or config (the Gitea recipe's `GITEA_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is the shape that works). Snac2 reads no such parameter: the credential lives only as the `passwd` field inside `<basedir>/user/<uid>/user.json`, written solely by adduser/resetpwd/ web-UI, and nothing in the server ever consults the environment for it. Two separate platform gaps would have to close: (a) a write path for the projected hash into user.json (recipe-side post-processing, or upstream accepting a pre-hashed credential), and (b) snac2's bespoke hash format added to `generated_from`'s algorithm list — it is `<nonce>:sha1hex("<nonce>:<uid>:<plaintext>")` (snac.c:144-161), not argon2 or bcrypt. Per SCHEMA.md that second item is the extensible-algo case rather than a hard no, since af-api holds the plaintext root password and could compute this form itself.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate does not substitute: snac2 has its own real password-based web login (it's not a no-login app), so gating the domain with basic auth would add an extra password in front of an account whose own credential the customer still has no way to learn or choose — same reasoning as apps-gaps/mitra.yaml.

`server_generated_no_customer_input` does not fit either, because the customer genuinely needs this credential — it is their login to their own Fediverse account, not an internal DB/JWT secret nothing customer-facing reads. The one partial mitigation is that the generated password is printed to container stdout, so a customer with root on the box could recover it from `docker logs`; that is an out-of-band manual retrieval, not one of the supported mechanisms, and a poor first-run experience to ship.

Note for completeness: the other one-time setup step, `snac init`, is NOT a blocker. It prompts for address, port, host name, URL prefix and an optional admin email (utils.c:171-221) — all non-secret and all derivable from APP_DOMAIN — and upstream's own `examples/docker-entrypoint.sh` already drives it unattended by piping answers on stdin. `snac adduser <basedir> <uid>` is likewise non-interactive when the uid is passed as an argument (main.c: `user = GET_ARGV(); return adduser(user);`; the "Username:" prompt at utils.c:301-304 fires only when uid is omitted), and the same upstream entrypoint runs it unattended. install.sh could therefore provision the account fine — it just cannot control what password that account ends up with.
summary: Snac2 is an actively maintained (near-monthly tags, latest 41 days old), extremely lightweight ActivityPub server with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue and a real differentiation angle (flat-file storage, minimal dependencies, far lighter than Mastodon). It's reverse-proxy friendly (single HTTP port, no raw protocols) and would open a new social/fediverse category alongside the already-analyzed Mitra and Iceshrimp.NET candidates. Provisioning itself automates fine — both `snac init` and `snac adduser <basedir> <uid>` run unattended, as upstream's own docker-entrypoint.sh demonstrates — but the resulting account's password is always generated by the server and printed once to stdout, and no code path accepts a caller-supplied password or hash. That credential is customer-facing, so it fits none of our three mechanisms: nothing for `generated_from` to target, a basic-auth gate doesn't replace snac2's own login, and it isn't a never-seen-by-the-customer server secret. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit if upstream accepts a preset credential at account creation, or if the platform gains both a write path into `user.json` and snac2's salted-SHA-1 hash format in `generated_from`.

name: Snapdrop
source_description: Local file sharing in your browser inspired by Apple AirDrop
version_health_notes: Project has never used GitHub Releases/tags — there is no versioned release history at all, only rolling commits to master. Last commit ("chore: update README.md") was 2025-02-10, roughly 18 months before today (2026-08-05); before that the last substantive commits were 2024-08-31. Repo itself is not marked archived and still has 19.7k stars, but the project has effectively been acquired by LimeWire (announced on the repo), whose focus is a hosted/commercial product — the open-source repo is left "as-is" for self-hosters rather than under active maintenance. The most telling third-party signal: LinuxServer.io, who packaged the only well-known Docker image for this app, has formally deprecated `linuxserver/snapdrop` ("This image is deprecated. We will not offer support for this image and it will not be updated.") and directs users to the community fork PairDrop instead. That is an external maintainer voting with their feet on this exact upstream going stale — a stronger dormant signal than the commit gap alone.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does ephemeral, no-account peer-to-peer file transfer between devices in a browser tab (WebRTC data channels, WebSocket signaling only, nothing persisted server-side beyond routing). Syncthing is the closest neighbor but solves a different problem — continuous background folder sync with durable state — not "drag a file, have it land instantly on another open tab."
usefulness_rationale: The AirDrop-style pitch depends on ambient discovery of nearby devices on the same local network; deployed as a single customer's hosted instance behind a domain, that discovery model is moot (it becomes "anyone with the link who has the tab open at the same time," not "devices on my WiFi"), so most of the product's actual value proposition doesn't survive the reverse-proxy/hosted deployment model. Combined with a stale, releaseless upstream and a deprecated reference Docker image, this reads as a novelty rather than a durable catalogue addition.
blocking_issues:
No official Docker image from upstream; the only widely-used third-party image (linuxserver/snapdrop) is formally deprecated by its own maintainer with no further updates, and no ports/tags will move going forward.
App itself has no login of any kind, so it would sit fully open on the internet without a Traefik basic_auth gate — expressible, but underscores how thin the app's own security model is for public exposure.
summary: Snapdrop is a small, well-known "AirDrop in the browser" toy — a single static/Node.js service (no official Docker image; the community reference image is linuxserver/snapdrop) doing WebRTC file transfer between browser tabs via WebSocket signaling. Upstream has no versioned releases ever and has gone quiet since 2025-02-10 following its acquisition by LimeWire, and LinuxServer.io — the maintainer of the only commonly-used Docker packaging — has explicitly deprecated that image and points users at the PairDrop fork instead. Mechanically it could be gated behind Traefik basic_auth like other login-less apps, but the app's core value (same-LAN device discovery) doesn't really translate to a single hosted customer instance behind a domain, and building on a deprecated, unmaintained image is a poor foundation regardless. Recommend not_recommended; if there's real customer demand for this style of tool, PairDrop (the actively maintained fork LinuxServer itself now recommends) would be the app to evaluate instead.

name: SnappyMail
source_description: Lightweight self-hosted webmail client for accessing IMAP email in any browser
version_health_notes: No tagged release since v2.38.2 on 2024-10-09 — roughly 22 months before today (2026-08-05), and the djmaze/snappymail Docker Hub tags stop at that same version ("almost 2 years ago" per Docker Hub, matching the release date). However master is not dormant: commits continue into 2026 (most recently seen around 2026-03-11, plus multiple commits through mid-2025), the repo is not archived, and issues/PRs are still being triaged. This is the same shape as apps-gaps/slskd.yaml — active development that has simply stopped cutting tagged stable releases — worth re-verifying the exact latest commit/tag before pinning a recipe.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches email/webmail — this would be the first recipe in that category. SnappyMail is a lightweight, single-container webmail *client* only: it needs no database for its simplest deployment (SQLite-backed), no mail is delivered or stored by the app itself, and it works behind a single HTTP port (8888) with no extra raw ports, confirmed by upstream's own examples/docker/docker-compose.traefik.yml. It gives a customer who already has IMAP/SMTP mailboxes elsewhere (their own mail server, a business email provider, etc.) a self-hosted webmail UI instead of relying on that provider's own webmail or a desktop/mobile mail app.
usefulness_rationale: Real value for customers who specifically want to keep webmail access off a third-party provider's UI, but the audience is narrower than a typical AF recipe because the app is a pure client — it does nothing useful until the customer already has a working mailbox elsewhere and then configures it in, which is an extra manual step most self-hosters of a "one-click app" won't expect. It doesn't compete with or replace a full mail server stack (e.g. Mailu, docker-mailserver), which nobody in the current catalogue offers either.
blocking_issues:
The admin panel's own login (username "admin", password auto-generated at first container start and written to /var/lib/snappymail/_data_/_default_/admin_password.txt inside the container) has no environment variable or hash-accepting input at boot — the only documented way to retrieve it is `docker exec ... cat admin_password.txt`, which is not a channel /compose exposes. Workaround: leave that internal password as an opaque server-generated value nothing customer-facing ever reads, and put the real auth boundary at Traefik basic_auth (root-password hash) in front of the app (or at least the /?admin path), same pattern as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI. This makes SnappyMail mechanically installable once IF-1312 (basic_auth) ships — not a hard blocker, just blocked_on_platform.

Separately from the auth mechanics: even once the admin panel is reachable, the app is not useful to an end user until someone visits /?admin at least once post-deploy to add a Domain (mapping the customer's email domain to their real IMAP/SMTP host) or enable manual server entry on the login form. That is a one-time app-configuration step, not a customer-supplied secret, so it does not block /compose mechanically — but it means this can't be a zero-touch "log in and go" recipe the way e.g. Vaultwarden is; onboarding docs would need to tell the customer to configure their mail provider before the webmail login screen does anything useful.
summary: SnappyMail would be the first email/webmail-category recipe in the catalogue and is mechanically simple — single container, no database required, one HTTP port, reverse-proxy friendly. It's currently blocked the same way apps-gaps/slskd.yaml is: its own admin-panel login only exposes a container-internal auto-generated password with no hash-accepting or env-var input path, so it needs Traefik basic_auth (IF-1312) rather than generated_from to gate it safely. Upstream is healthy but release cadence has gone sporadic (no tagged version since 2024-10-09, ~22 months ago, even though master keeps taking commits) — worth re-checking closer to build time. Usefulness is real but medium: it only serves customers who already have a mailbox elsewhere and are willing to do a one-time admin-panel setup step, a narrower fit than a typical single-purpose self-hosted app.

name: Snipe-IT
source_description: Free open-source IT asset management for tracking hardware, licenses, and depreciation
version_health_notes: v8.6.3 shipped 2026-06-15, about 1.5 months before today (2026-08-05). The project (upstream org renamed from `snipe` to `grokability` on GitHub, though the Docker Hub namespace is still `snipe/snipe-it`) has a tight, regular release cadence: v8.6.0 through v8.6.3 all shipped within about 6 weeks (late May-mid June 2026), following v8.5.0 in May 2026 and v8.4.x in Feb-Apr 2026. This is a mature, actively maintained project with frequent point releases (v8.6.3 was largely a security and SCIM/LDAP fix release) — no signs of slowing, sporadic tagging, or abandonment.
differentiation: Snipe-IT is an IT asset/license/depreciation tracker (hardware inventory, software license seat counts, warranty and depreciation schedules, checkin/checkout workflows, QR/barcode asset tags). Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers this ground — Portainer and Guacamole are infrastructure/remote-access tools, not asset-register tools, and Paperless-ngx is document management, not equipment tracking. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue, appealing to SMB customers who need to track owned hardware, software licenses, and warranties without a spreadsheet.
usefulness_rationale: IT asset management is a well-understood, broadly-needed SMB workflow (which laptop is assigned to whom, when does this license/warranty expire) and Snipe-IT is the best-known open-source tool in that space, with a polished web UI and an active, well-funded upstream. Clear differentiation from the rest of the catalogue and a real audience.
blocking_issues:
Snipe-IT has no unattended, env-var-driven install path. First boot either redirects the browser to an interactive setup wizard (collects site name plus a full admin identity: first/last name, email, username, and password) or requires an operator to exec into the container and run the interactive `php artisan app:install` command. Neither has a documented non-interactive/env-var mode.

The only scriptable admin-creation path is the rescue command `php artisan snipeit:create-admin --first_name=... --last_name=... --email=... --username=... --password=<plaintext>`. It requires the admin password in **plaintext** (Snipe-IT hashes it itself via Laravel's bcrypt on account creation) plus first/last name and email — none of which our root-password-hash projection (`generated_from`) can supply, since that mechanism only ever carries a pre-computed hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, and has no channel for arbitrary identity fields (name/email/username) at all.

A Traefik `basic_auth` gate does not substitute here: Snipe-IT does have its own login, so leaving the app itself unconfigured behind a gate would just mean the customer lands on the interactive setup wizard once past the gate, with the same unattended-install problem.
summary: Snipe-IT is a strong, high-value candidate — active upstream (tight release cadence, v8.6.3 as of 2026-06-15), a genuinely new category for the catalogue (IT asset/license/depreciation tracking, no overlap with any of the current 24 recipes), a clean single-port web UI, and a standard MySQL-backed multi-container shape (structurally similar to Paperless-ngx). It is blocked on the platform today for one specific reason: Snipe-IT's admin account can only be created through an interactive setup wizard or an interactive/rescue artisan command that both require a full identity (name, email, username) and, critically, the admin password in **plaintext** rather than a hash — a hard mismatch with the root-password-hash-only projection mechanism (`generated_from`), and not something a Traefik basic_auth gate can work around since the app has its own login. DB password and app key are trivially server-generated with no customer input needed. Recommend revisiting once there is either a customer-supplied-value input channel or a documented way to seed Snipe-IT's admin account from a value AF can actually produce (e.g. if Snipe-IT ever accepts a pre-hashed password on install).

Its three required values are DEFAULT_APP_ID / DEFAULT_APP_KEY / DEFAULT_APP_SECRET (which fall back to the hardcoded `app-id` / `app-key` / `app-secret` if unset, so they must be overridden); all three can be randomly server-generated at install with no customer input, then read back out by the customer to configure their client app. The reason not to build it is upstream, not mechanism: no release in ~28 months, no human commit on the default branch since March 2024, no code change since February 2024, and published images frozen since 2025-03-03. For an AGPL-3.0 network service that would sit on a customer's public domain terminating untrusted WebSocket connections, shipping a recipe on a codebase with no security-patch path is the wrong bet — hence not_recommended, to be revisited only if upstream resumes releases or a credible maintained fork emerges.

name: Solidtime
source_description: Time tracking for freelancers and agencies with billing rates and PDF reports
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers time tracking or freelancer/agency billing. Solidtime is a self-hosted, open-source alternative to Toggl/Clockify/Harvest — projects, tasks, billable rates, clients, multi-organization support, PDF invoicing/reports — which is a genuinely new, business-facing category distinct from the ops/dev-tooling lean of most existing recipes.

blocking_issues:
Solidtime's official Docker deployment ships with public registration disabled by default (APP_ENABLE_REGISTRATION); the documented path to a usable admin account is running `docker compose exec scheduler php artisan admin:user:create "Name" "email@example.com" --verify-email` after the containers are up, which prints a server-generated temporary password to the CLI output, then adding that account's email to the SUPER_ADMINS env var and restarting. There is no HTTP-reachable first-run setup wizard and no single admin-login field that `generated_from` could project the root-password hash into — the credential is minted by a one-off `artisan` CLI invocation, not read from an env var at container start. `/compose` has no channel to run a post-boot exec command, so this can't be wired up today.

Even if registration were left open, Solidtime requires a working SMTP relay for signup verification and password-reset email; no SMTP credential input channel exists either, though this is secondary to the admin-bootstrap blocker above.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth as a workaround does not solve this — the app still has no way for the customer to reach a working admin session behind that gate, since account creation itself requires the CLI step.
summary: Solidtime is an actively maintained (weekly releases, latest one day after today) open-source Laravel app — solidtime/solidtime image, Postgres + Redis backing services, single web port — that would fill a genuine catalogue gap (no time-tracking/billing app exists today) with a reverse-proxy-friendly single HTTP port. It is blocked from shipping as a recipe today purely on the installability mechanism: the only documented way to get a working admin login is a post-boot `artisan admin:user:create` CLI exec that mints its own temporary password and requires manually editing SUPER_ADMINS and restarting, which has no equivalent in `/compose`'s env-var-only bootstrap and no fit for either `generated_from` root-password projection or a Traefik basic_auth gate. SonarQube's own login has no customer-facing input channel: the image ships a fixed default admin/admin account and forces a password change via the web UI on first login, but there is no environment variable or API parameter to preset that password before first boot (unlike Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN or Gitea's GITEA_ADMIN_PASSWORD). Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's guidance for a fixed default credential the app itself gives no way to change at deploy time, the correct mitigation is a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app rather than treating this as a hard blocker — that moves the actual customer-facing auth boundary to the gate, with the still-default admin/admin behind it only reachable by someone who already holds the gate credential.

The bundled Elasticsearch component enforces standard ES bootstrap checks that require a *host*-level (not container-namespaced) kernel parameter, `vm.max_map_count >= 262144`, or the container fails to start. This is not expressible via Docker Compose `sysctls:` (that only sets namespaced sysctls; `vm.max_map_count` is host-wide) and no existing recipe in this catalogue currently sets a host sysctl from install.sh. It is very likely solvable — install.sh already runs with root/host privileges on the target VM in every existing recipe (e.g. `chown` in `recipes/n8n/install.sh`), so `sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144` (plus persisting it in `/etc/sysctl.d/`) should work — but it is an unprecedented pattern in this catalogue and needs a recipe author to actually verify it against the real IONOS VM image before shipping, not a soft assumption.
summary: SonarQube Community Build is a single official image (`sonarqube`, pin to `26.8.0.126808-community`) exposing one HTTP port (9000), reverse-proxy friendly, and under a genuinely OSS license (LGPL-3.0, core; bundled analyzers are SSALv1 source-available but still free to use). It fills a real, currently-empty gap in the catalogue (static code analysis/security scanning) with no overlap against existing recipes. Installability has two open items rather than a single hard "no": the app's own login (default admin/admin, no way to preset a password before first boot) is solvable today via a Traefik `basic_auth` gate per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's guidance on fixed default credentials; but the bundled Elasticsearch's host-level `vm.max_map_count` requirement is a genuinely new pattern for this catalogue (no existing recipe sets a host sysctl) that a recipe author needs to prove out against the actual IONOS VM image before this can ship, which is why `installable_today` is `false` and the recommendation is `build_with_caveats` rather than `build_now`.

name: Songloft
source_description: Self-hosted personal music server with Subsonic API and JS plugin sandbox
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (server binary and Docker image); GPL-3.0 applies to parts of the bundled Flutter client only
version_health_notes: v2.11.1 shipped 2026-08-03, 2 days before today (2026-08-05). The project's CHANGELOG shows the earliest entries around 2026-02-12 (project start, then under the name MiMusic before the v2.0 rebrand to Songloft), reaching v2.11.1 by 2026-08-03 — roughly 40 tagged releases in under 6 months, most spaced 1-4 days apart (e.g. v2.9.1 through v2.9.6 all landed within a single week, 2026-06-29 to 2026-07-04). This is a very young project (~6 months old) with a near-daily release rhythm, still well within its initial rapid-iteration phase rather than having settled into a stable maintenance cadence. That combination (young + fast-moving) means a pinned tag will likely be behind within weeks and breaking changes are more likely than in a mature project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue serves personal media libraries — the closest neighbors are Immich (photo/video library) and Syncthing (file sync), neither of which streams audio or speaks the Subsonic protocol. Songloft would be the catalogue's first self-hosted music server: it scans a customer's own audio/video files, serves them through a built-in web player and a Subsonic-compatible API (added via an official `songloft-plugin-subsonic` JS plugin, so existing Subsonic clients like Substreamer or DSub can connect), and additionally supports a QuickJS-sandboxed JS plugin system for extending metadata sources and device control.
usefulness_rationale: A self-hosted music/media server is a recognizable, popular self-hosting use case (Navidrome, Jellyfin, Plex-style demand) and would fill a real gap in the catalogue. Usefulness is medium rather than high because Songloft itself is a young, low-adoption project (~1.4k GitHub stars, single primary maintainer per commit history) relative to established alternatives in the same space (e.g. Navidrome), and its explicit "personal, non-commercial, music you legally own" framing narrows it to a single-user/household niche rather than a broader team tool.
blocking_issues: Songloft's admin login is configured via the `ADMIN_USERNAME` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD` environment variables, and the app compares login attempts directly against the plaintext value of `ADMIN_PASSWORD` — there is no documented option to supply a pre-hashed (argon2/bcrypt) admin password instead (confirmed by reading the upstream README's configuration and quick-start sections, which only show plaintext password examples and explicitly warn that the command-line `-password` flag "will appear in plaintext in shell history and the process list"). `generated_from` only ever produces a hash of the customer's root password, and Songloft has no field that accepts a hash for this purpose — so this is a genuine plaintext-only requirement, which SCHEMA.md calls out as an actual structural blocker rather than a soft `generated_from`-algorithm gap. Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead does not resolve this, because Songloft would still be left with its own default `admin / admin` login exposed behind that gate, and — unlike the fixed-default-credential case SCHEMA.md excuses (IF-1312) — the customer has no way to change that default to something derived from their own root password without knowing it in plaintext, so it stays a knowable, static credential to anyone who ever gets past the Traefik gate (e.g. a future customer of a reused instance, or a support engineer).
summary: Songloft is a clean single-container fit mechanically — one official image (songloft/songloft, pin to 2.11.1), one HTTP port (58091), SQLite storage, bind-mounted music/data volumes, and no other services — and it would be the catalogue's first dedicated music-server recipe, filling a real and currently-unfilled niche (Subsonic-API-compatible streaming plus a built-in web player). It is blocked today purely on the auth-projection gap: its admin login only accepts a plaintext password via `ADMIN_USERNAME`/`ADMIN_PASSWORD`, with no hash-accepting field for `generated_from` to target, and stacking Traefik `basic_auth` on top still leaves the app's own default admin/admin credential live behind the gate rather than actually being set from the customer's root password. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once either a plaintext-password projection channel exists, or check whether a future Songloft release adds a hashed-password env var. Separately worth tracking: the project is only ~6 months old with a very fast release cadence (roughly 40 tags since February 2026), so even once installable it would need closer-than-usual upstream-tracking for stability and security fixes.

name: SoulSync
source_description: Music platform syncing Spotify and Tidal playlists to your self-hosted library
version_health_notes: Extremely active — 3.1.9 shipped 2026-07-26 (10 days before today, 2026-08-05), and the preceding ~10 releases (3.0.3 through 3.1.8) all landed between 2026-07-15 and 2026-07-26, i.e. roughly one release every 1-2 days over the prior three weeks. Not archived, no EOL signals. This is a young, fast-moving hobby project rather than a mature stable release train — worth noting for pin-maintenance burden if ever built, but not a version-health concern in itself.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does streaming-service playlist sync into a self-hosted music library; the closest conceptual neighbor is Immich (photo/video library), a different media type. A customer already running a self-hosted music server (e.g. a Subsonic/Navidrome-style stack, none of which is in the catalogue either — see apps-gaps/airsonic-advanced.yaml) would find SoulSync a natural add-on to auto-populate that library from Spotify/Tidal playlists. The pitch is real, but see installability below: the app's actual download mechanism is not what the Hostinger description implies.
usefulness_rationale: The Hostinger description ("syncing Spotify and Tidal playlists to your self-hosted library") undersells what SoulSync actually is: an automation front-end over Soulseek (via a required slskd instance) and several other Hi-Res sources (Deezer, Qobuz, Amazon Music), with Spotify/Tidal used only for discovery/metadata/playlist definitions, not as licensed download sources. The primary download path is a public P2P network whose main real-world use is unauthorized copyrighted-media sharing — the same reputational/legal concern already raised in apps-gaps/slskd.yaml, which SoulSync makes worse by packaging that P2P client behind a friendlier "playlist sync" pitch aimed at a broader, less P2P-savvy audience.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: slskd API key (SOULSYNC_SLSKD_API_KEY) — connects SoulSync to a co-deployed slskd instance; Spotify API Client ID/Secret — required for playlist discovery/sync, the app's headline feature; SoulSync web UI login (no built-in strong auth — only per-profile PINs; needs a basic-auth gate)
secrets_expressible_today: SoulSync web UI login (no built-in strong auth — only per-profile PINs; needs a basic-auth gate):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
SoulSync's primary download source is Soulseek via a separately deployed slskd instance (see apps-gaps/slskd.yaml, also `blocked_on_platform`/flagged for legal review) — an external dependency this recipe would have to co-provision, with slskd's own API key then fed into SoulSync. Neither today's `/compose` mechanism nor a single-recipe scope has a channel to stand up and wire two cooperating apps' cross-service credentials automatically, and the underlying P2P-network exposure concern from apps-gaps/slskd.yaml applies here unchanged.

Spotify playlist sync — the feature the Hostinger description actually advertises — requires a customer-supplied Spotify API Client ID and Secret registered on developer.spotify.com. This is an external API key with no projection mechanism today (not a password hash, not a Traefik gate); `/compose` has no field for it. Tidal works via a device-flow OAuth login performed inside the app after deploy (self-service through the UI, not a boot-time blocker by itself), but without Spotify credentials the core "sync Spotify playlists" pitch does not function at all.

SoulSync's own web UI has no traditional single admin login — upstream describes "per-profile login passwords / quick-switch PINs" rather than a proper admin account, so there is nothing to hash a root-password into via `generated_from`. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate could cover the perimeter (same pattern as n8n/WUD), but that alone does not resolve the Spotify API key or slskd dependency blockers above.
summary: SoulSync is an actively-developed (releases every 1-2 days recently), MIT-licensed music automation platform with a real single-container web UI (port 8008) that would be reverse-proxy-compatible in isolation. But its architecture does not match Hostinger's "syncs Spotify/Tidal playlists" framing: Spotify/Tidal are discovery/metadata sources, while the actual downloading happens through a required, separately-deployed slskd (Soulseek P2P client) instance — already flagged in apps-gaps/slskd.yaml as blocked_on_platform and as a reputational/legal concern given Soulseek's primary real-world use for unauthorized media sharing. On top of that dependency problem, the app's headline feature needs a customer-supplied Spotify API Client ID/Secret with no projection channel in `/compose` today. Recommend not_recommended: this is blocked on multiple fronts (a P2P legal/reputational question, a missing external-API-key input channel, and a multi-service cross-credential wiring problem), not a simple `blocked_on_platform` wait-for-one-feature case.

name: Spacedrive
source_description: Open-source file manager for organizing assets across devices and cloud storage
upstream_license: FSL-1.1-ALv2 (Functional Source License; source-available today, converts to Apache-2.0 two years after each release)
version_health_notes: v2.0.0-alpha.3 shipped 2026-04-17, just under 4 months before today (2026-08-05). This is a ground-up Rust rewrite line: v2.0.0-alpha.1 (2025-12-26) came after the prior stable 0.4.x line was explicitly paused — the 0.4.3 release notes (2025-03-25) stated "we must temporarily pause our development roadmap ... due to current funding constraints and related challenges". differentiation: On paper Spacedrive's pitch (content-addressed dedup via BLAKE3, cross-device virtual filesystem, AI-safety-screened indexing of email/notes/cloud sources, P2P sync via Iroh/QUIC) goes well beyond Syncthing's plain folder-sync. In practice none of that is reachable through a browser: the self-hostable piece (`apps/server`, "sd-server") is an RPC-only headless backend with, per its own README, "no bundled web UI" and a "Future web UI (not yet implemented)" placeholder. A customer's actual interface to any of Spacedrive's features is the native Tauri desktop app or the React Native mobile app running on their own device and pairing with the server over RPC/P2P — neither of which our recipe mechanism installs or configures. So there is no deliverable differentiation over Syncthing for a browser-only customer today; Syncthing already covers the "sync files across my own devices, no cloud" niche with a real web UI on port 8384.
usefulness_rationale: A customer who provisions this recipe would get a domain that serves a bare `/health` check and a `/rpc` JSON-RPC endpoint — nothing resembling the file manager described in the Hostinger listing. Getting any actual value out of it requires installing and pairing a separate native client the recipe mechanism has no part in delivering, which is a fundamentally different customer journey than every other recipe in the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
sd-server has no reachable web UI to log into; its own SD_AUTH does HTTP Basic auth via a plaintext user:pass env var, so a Traefik basic_auth gate could stand in for it, but there is nothing behind the gate for a browser user to use.
sd-server ships no web UI at all. Its own README states it 'Provides only RPC endpoints (no bundled web UI)' with a 'Future web UI (not yet implemented)' note — fronting port 8080 with Traefik exposes only a health-check endpoint and raw JSON-RPC, not an application a customer can use in a browser. This is a product/architecture mismatch, not something the auth-projection or basic_auth mechanisms can fix.
ghcr.io/spacedriveapp/spacedrive/server does have published semver tags (0.4.0, 0.4.1, 0.4.2) plus a 'latest' tag pointing at 0.4.2 — but those are ~2 years stale and belong to the old, paused pre-rewrite 0.4.x line, not the actively developed v2 alpha. The v2 line (the one with any recent release activity, see version_health) has no maintained pinned tag: its only recent tags are per-commit SHAs (e.g. 61c0503) plus a 'staging' tag, and its own docker-compose.yml builds the image from source (`build: context: ../.. dockerfile: apps/server/Dockerfile`) rather than referencing a published tag. Pinning to the stale 0.4.2 tag would ship a different, superseded codebase than what upstream is currently developing/documenting.
The only actively developed line (v2 rewrite) is pre-1.0 alpha; upstream's own v2.0.0-alpha.2 release notes warn 'Many features are NOT working so test with caution', which is not a basis for a production recipe.
Core selling point (P2P device sync over UDP 7373) has no meaning in a single, customer-facing hosted-server deployment with no client to pair — the feature that would justify choosing this app over Syncthing is unusable in our delivery model.
summary: Spacedrive's headless server component (sd-server) has no web UI whatsoever — by upstream's own admission it is RPC-only, meant to be paired with the native Tauri/React Native client running on the customer's own device, not accessed through a domain in a browser. Even setting aside that there is no officially published pinned Docker tag (only per-commit SHAs and a "staging" tag) and that the only active line is a pre-1.0 alpha still recovering from a funding-driven development pause in 2025, the fundamental blocker is architectural: fronting this app with Traefik would give a customer a domain that returns a health-check string and JSON-RPC errors, not the file manager described in the Hostinger listing. Recommendation is not_recommended — this isn't a case of waiting on a platform mechanism (IF-1420/1312) to unblock it, since even solved auth wouldn't produce a usable app.

name: Speaches

That maps cleanly onto the existing Traefik basic_auth pattern (n8n/WUD/Adminer): gate the whole app behind basic_auth projected from the customer's root password, same as those recipes, making it mechanically installable today. The caveat is version health, not installability: the project is actively committed to but has not cut a final stable release in over 7 months, sitting on a release-candidate tag — recommend building, but pinning to the RC tag with awareness that upstream may still be stabilizing toward 0.9.0 final.

name: Speakr
source_description: Self-hosted AI transcription and intelligent note-taking platform
upstream_license: AGPLv3 (dual-licensed; a separate commercial license is offered for organizations that don't want AGPLv3's network-source-sharing obligation — running the unmodified upstream image as-is, without redistributing modifications, stays inside the AGPLv3 terms, same posture already accepted for Vaultwarden)
version_health_notes: Latest tag v0.10.2-alpha shipped 2026-07-15, ~21 days before today (2026-08-05). The run-up to it was near-daily: v0.9.5-alpha (Jul 6), v0.9.6-alpha (Jul 8), v0.9.7-alpha (Jul 13), v0.10.0-alpha (Jul 14), v0.10.1-alpha (Jul 14), v0.10.2-alpha (Jul 15) — six releases in nine days. Clearly active, well-maintained development. Caveat: every release to date, including the current one, is tagged "-alpha" — the project has not cut a 1.0/stable line yet, so breaking changes between point releases are plausible and should be expected when bumping the pinned tag later.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers audio transcription or AI-assisted note-taking from voice recordings. paperless-ai (closest AI-adjacent recipe) works on already-digitized documents, not audio; open-webui/ ollama provide general chat, not recording capture, diarization, or transcript summarization. Speakr fills a genuinely new niche: capture or upload audio, transcribe with optional speaker diarization, auto-generate titles/summaries, and semantically search across a recording library — a plausible standalone sell for meeting notes, interviews, or voice journaling that keeps audio off third-party SaaS.
usefulness_rationale: The privacy-first pitch (audio never leaves the customer's own infra) is a real differentiator, but the most useful configuration (cloud transcription/summarization APIs for good accuracy) is not exposable under the current recipe mechanism (see below), so the catalogue version would ship as a materially degraded, fully-local-only experience unless/until IF-1420/1312-style secret-projection is extended to a general external-API-key channel.
blocking_issues:
Speakr's own admin bootstrap is unusually well-shaped for this platform: ADMIN_USERNAME/ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_PASSWORD env vars create the sole admin account on first startup (no open self-registration race, no OIDC-only login) — a direct generated_from:"<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD" target on ADMIN_PASSWORD, the same shape as the shipping Vaultwarden ADMIN_TOKEN example. This part is NOT a blocker.
The app's core function (transcription + AI summary/chat) needs either a cloud provider credential (TRANSCRIPTION_API_KEY for OpenAI/WhisperX-cloud/Mistral/AssemblyAI, TEXT_MODEL_API_KEY for OpenRouter/OpenAI) or a fully local connector (ASR_BASE_URL pointing at a self-hosted WhisperX/faster-whisper container, TEXT_MODEL pointing at a local Ollama/LM Studio endpoint) — confirmed via upstream docs that ASR_BASE_URL requires no API key at all once set. Because a no-external-key local path exists, this does not meet the SCHEMA.md "can't function without [an external key]" bar for a hard block — but it does mean a recipe can only ship the local-only configuration; there is no channel today for a customer to supply their own cloud provider key for better transcription/summarization accuracy, which is the configuration upstream's own docs treat as the higher-quality default.
A local-only build requires bundling at least one extra sidecar container (a WhisperX/faster-whisper ASR service, likely CPU-only on standard recipe VM sizing since GPU passthrough isn't part of the current recipe pattern) plus a local LLM endpoint (Ollama-style) for summarization/chat — a heavier multi-service footprint than most current recipes, and CPU-only ASR transcription speed/quality will be noticeably worse than the cloud-API path Speakr is designed around.

Release health is also weak: the upstream is maintained by a single person, ships no formal GitHub Releases (only Docker Hub tags via "Bump version" PRs), and has irregular commit activity with multi-month gaps between bursts. build_with_caveats: installable and fills a genuine gap, but the minimal feature depth and thin release/maintenance signal warrant flagging before committing build time.

name: StarRocks
source_description: High-performance open-source OLAP database for sub-second analytics
upstream_docker_image: starrocks/allin1-ubuntu (single-container FE+BE quickstart image; production topologies use separate starrocks/fe-ubuntu and starrocks/be-ubuntu images), pinned tag 4.1.4
version_health_notes: 4.1.4 published 2026-08-05 — the same day as this analysis. Three branches are getting regular patches in parallel: 4.1.x (4.1.1 May-29, ..., 4.1.4 Aug-05), 4.0.x (4.0.9 Apr-16, 4.0.10 May-09, 4.0.11 Jun-05, 4.0.12 Jun-25, 4.0.13 Jul-16), and 3.5.x LTS (3.5.17 May-13, 3.5.18 Jun-05, 3.5.19 Jun-26, 3.5.20 Jul-23) — roughly a release every 2-4 weeks across the three lines. StarRocks became a Linux Foundation project in 2023 and shows no slowdown or archival signal; this is one of the most actively released upstreams seen in this batch.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is an analytics/OLAP database — this would be a genuinely new category. Structurally near-identical to two other database gap-analyses already on file: apps-gaps/clickhouse.yaml (same OLAP niche, different engine) and apps-gaps/apache-doris.yaml (StarRocks originated as a fork of Apache Doris/Baidu Palo and still shares its FE/BE architecture, MySQL wire protocol on port 9030, and root-account model). If either of those ships, StarRocks would be a third, largely redundant entry in the same niche rather than a distinct one.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand exists for a self-hosted OLAP/analytics backend, but StarRocks specifically targets larger-scale distributed deployments: the FE has a minimal web console at :8030 for cluster/query monitoring, not a query authoring surface, and the actual product value (SQL analytics for BI tools, ad-hoc queries, data-lake federation) is delivered over the raw MySQL wire protocol on :9030, not through a browser. That's the same "database is the product, not an app on top of one" shape as ClickHouse and Doris, aimed at data engineers rather than end users — a narrow, developer-only audience for an AF customer base, and one already covered twice over by existing gap analyses.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: root account password (shared by the FE web console at :8030 and MySQL-protocol access at :9030)
blocking_issues:
StarRocks provisions the root account with an empty password by default and offers no init-time hook to set one on the vanilla Docker image (starrocks/allin1-ubuntu, fe-ubuntu, be-ubuntu) — the only documented path is connecting via MySQL client with the empty password after boot and running `SET PASSWORD = PASSWORD('<plain>')` or `SET PASSWORD = '<sha1-hash>'` by hand. That second form does accept a pre-hashed credential directly (MySQL native-password / doubled-SHA1 format, per upstream's SET_PASSWORD reference), so this is the same shape as Apache Doris's fe.conf `root_password`: an unsupported hash algorithm gap, not a plaintext-only hard blocker. `generated_from` today only supports argon2/bcrypt, not SHA1/ mysql_native_password, so no expressible value exists yet — but extending `generated_from` to cover that algorithm would close this. The Kubernetes operator's Helm chart (`starrocks.initPassword.password`) is a separate, plaintext-only mechanism, but it isn't the only one upstream provides and isn't the path a Docker Compose recipe would use anyway, so it doesn't change the verdict.

StarRocks' primary interface is the raw MySQL wire protocol on port 9030, not HTTP — the FE web console on :8030 is a monitoring/status surface, not the way customers get analytics value out of the app. A recipe would either need to expose :9030 as a raw (non-HTTP) public port, which sits outside the Traefik-fronted browser flow every current recipe assumes, or restrict the app to internal-only use, which defeats the point of a standalone analytics database recipe.
summary: StarRocks is an aggressively active, Linux Foundation-governed OLAP database (a release landed the same day as this analysis, three branches in parallel maintenance) and would technically be a new category for the catalogue. It is a closable platform gap rather than a hard blocker: the root account ships with an empty password, and the documented post-boot recovery path (`SET PASSWORD = '<sha1-hash>'`) accepts a pre-hashed credential in MySQL native-password / doubled-SHA1 format — the same shape as Apache Doris's fe.conf `root_password`. `generated_from` just doesn't support that hash algorithm today (only argon2/bcrypt), so extending its supported-algorithm list would unblock this. Separately, its core value lives on the raw MySQL-wire-protocol port 9030 rather than behind a browsable, Traefik-frontable web UI, which remains a real concern independent of the credential fix. Combined with the fact that this exact niche (self-hosted OLAP analytics database) is already covered twice over by prior gap analyses (apps-gaps/clickhouse.yaml, apps-gaps/apache-doris.yaml), StarRocks would be worth revisiting once `generated_from` gains SHA1 support, but isn't a priority to unblock on its own. Recommend blocked_on_platform.

name: Statistics for Strava
source_description: Self-hosted Strava analytics dashboard with charts, heatmaps, and gear tracking
version_health_notes: "Statistics for Strava" no longer exists under that name. On 2026-07-19 the project rebranded to "Dreeve" (v5.0.0) and, per the release notes, explicitly dropped Strava as a dependency ("No more Strava or any 3rd party dependencies" — see the v5.0.0 announcement). The old GitHub slug `robiningelbrecht/statistics-for-strava` now contains only a migration stub (1 release, 4 stars, last push 2026-07-19) pointing at the new repo `dreeveapp/dreeve` (2,006 stars, last push 2026-08-06). All ongoing development is at the new repo/image (`robiningelbrecht/dreeve` on Docker Hub, `ghcr.io/dreeveapp/dreeve` on GHCR). Release cadence is very active: 30 releases in the 5 months prior to today (2026-08-05), averaging roughly one every 4-5 days, with the latest release (v5.1.5) landing on today's date itself. This is not ambiguity between two competing projects with the same name (per SCHEMA.md guidance) — it is one continuously-maintained project that renamed itself; the Hostinger catalogue entry is simply pointing at a name the upstream has retired.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers personal fitness/activity tracking or analytics (categories in use today are ai, automation, developer-tools, infrastructure, media, monitoring, productivity, security). This would be a new category: a personal dashboard for workout/activity data (charts, heatmaps, gear-wear tracking) built from imported FIT/TCX/GPX files or a Strava account sync.
usefulness_rationale: Appeals to individual hobbyist customers (cyclists/runners) wanting a private alternative to Strava's own dashboards, but it is a single-user, personal-use tool rather than a team/business app, which caps its addressable audience compared to most of the catalogue. Its value is further reduced under our platform's constraints (see installability) since the marquee "sync with Strava" feature isn't deliverable — see summary.
blocking_issues: The app's namesake feature — importing/syncing activities from a customer's Strava account — requires IMPORT_MODE=stravaApi plus customer-specific STRAVA_CLIENT_ID/STRAVA_CLIENT_SECRET/ STRAVA_REFRESH_TOKEN (a Strava OAuth app registration the customer creates themselves). There is no channel today for a customer-supplied external API key/OAuth credential, so this mode cannot be offered. The only deliverable configuration is the default IMPORT_MODE=files, where the customer manually drops FIT/TCX/GPX files into a watched folder — mechanically fine, but it means the recipe could not actually do what Hostinger's own description promises ("Strava analytics dashboard"); it would ship as a generic personal workout-file dashboard instead.
summary: The catalogue entry's name and description refer to a product that no longer exists under that name: upstream rebranded "Statistics for Strava" to "Dreeve" on 2026-07-19 (v5.0.0) and is actively maintained there (releases every few days, latest v5.1.5 on 2026-08-05). Mechanically the app is installable today: it's a single-image two-container (app + daemon) docker-compose stack sharing an on-disk SQLite database, one HTTP port (8080), and its admin login is a bcrypt password hash (ADMIN_PASSWORD_HASH) that maps cleanly onto generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"; APP_SECRET is a random signing key we can generate server-side. However, the feature the Hostinger description actually advertises — syncing analytics from a customer's Strava account — needs a customer-supplied Strava OAuth client ID/secret, which our platform has no input channel for; only the manual file-import mode is deliverable. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building only if positioned honestly as a self-hosted workout-file dashboard (FIT/TCX/GPX upload) rather than a "Strava" integration, and using the current upstream name/image (Dreeve / robiningelbrecht/dreeve), not the retired "Statistics for Strava" branding.

name: Steel Browser
source_description: Open-source browser API for AI agents with full Chrome DevTools Protocol access
version_health_notes: Confirmed against the GitHub API (steel-dev/steel-browser). Releases were roughly monthly through late 2025/early 2026 (v0.4.0 Sep 18, v0.4.1 Sep 24, v0.4.2 Sep 29, v0.4.3 Oct 14, v0.4.4 Oct 19, v0.4.5 Nov 4, v0.5.0 Nov 10, v0.5.1 Nov 19, v0.5.2 2026-03-15, v0.5.3-beta 2026-04-24), but no tag has been cut since v0.5.3-beta — over 3.5 months as of today (2026-08-05). That gap is on tagging only, not on the project itself: `pushed_at` is 2026-08-05 and the most recent commit is dated 2026-07-20, so main is still actively developed. Repo is not archived, has 7.4k stars and 54 open issues. Called `release_cadence: slowing` (tag cadence dropped from monthly to none in 3.5+ months) while `eol_status: active` (commit activity is current and heavy). All releases to date are tagged `-beta`; the project self-describes as "public beta and evolving every day," so treat the API/schema as not yet stable.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does headless-browser automation. n8n can drive browser-automation nodes but is a general workflow engine, not a dedicated Chrome/CDP sandbox; openclaw and hermes-agent are messaging-app-first AI agent runtimes with no browser control at all. Steel Browser fills a distinct niche: a self-hosted Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium-compatible remote Chrome instance (session management, proxy rotation, stealth/anti-detection, screenshot /PDF/markdown page conversion) that a customer's own AI agent code or n8n workflow can point at instead of a paid cloud browser API (Steel Cloud, Browserless, Browserbase).
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely novel capability for the catalogue and popular upstream (7.4k stars), but it is infrastructure a customer's own code calls into via API/SDK rather than an app they use directly day-to-day — the built-in "UI" is a debugging/session-inspection dashboard, not a product surface on its own. Value is real but narrower (developers building agents/ scrapers) than a typical high-usefulness recipe.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against upstream README, docs.steel.dev self-hosting docs, and the shipped docker-compose.yml: the self-hosted app has no login of its own at all. The REST API (session creation, page navigation, JS execution, screenshots, proxy configuration) and the debug UI at `/ui` are both served unauthenticated. This is a materially higher- risk "no auth" case than a typical dashboard: an open Steel instance lets anyone drive a full Chrome browser as an open relay/scraper from the server's IP, which is an abuse and SSRF surface, not just an information-disclosure one. A mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate on the public port is not optional here the way it might be judgment-call elsewhere — same pattern as Adminer/WUD, fully expressible today via `generated_from` → root-password hash → basic_auth gate.

Confirmed against the GHCR registry API: `ghcr.io/steel-dev/ steel-browser`, `steel-browser-api`, and `steel-browser-ui` each publish only a single `latest` tag — no version-pinned tags exist upstream at all. RFC-002's image-tag-pinned rule requires a pinned, current stable tag, never `:latest`. The only way to pin today would be a content digest (`@sha256:...`), which silently tracks whatever commit was HEAD at pin time rather than a named, upstream-published version — a materially worse pin than every other recipe in the catalogue has. Not a hard blocker (a digest pin is technically possible) but a real caveat against `build_now`.

Two ports are involved: 3000 (combined REST API + `/ui` dashboard, including the CDP-over-websocket endpoint that Puppeteer/Playwright clients actually connect to) and 9223 (a secondary "console debugger" CDP redirect for `chrome://inspect`-style tooling). Confirmed via docs.steel.dev that browser-automation clients use the port-3000 websocket, so only port 3000 needs to be public and Traefik-fronted; 9223 can stay internal-only. Single public port keeps this reverse- proxy compatible, but a recipe author should not assume both ports need exposing just because the upstream docker-compose.yml maps both.
summary: Steel Browser is mechanically installable today: it needs no external API key or OAuth registration to boot, and its total lack of built-in auth is fully covered by gating the single public port (3000) behind Traefik `basic_auth`, the same pattern already used for Adminer/WUD/Agent Zero. The catalogue gap is real — nothing else offers a self-hosted remote Chrome/CDP sandbox — but two caveats keep this at `build_with_caveats` rather than a clean `build_now`: upstream publishes no version-pinned Docker tags at all (only `latest` on all three images), forcing a digest pin instead of a normal version pin, and the project has gone 3.5+ months without cutting a release despite continuous active commits, so recipe maintenance would need to track main via digest bumps rather than tagged releases. Usefulness is capped at medium since this is developer infrastructure consumed via API/SDK rather than an app used directly.

source_description: Powerful locally hosted web-based PDF manipulation tool
upstream_license: MIT (core); open-core — several directories (app/proprietary, app/saas, engine, frontend/editor/src/{proprietary,desktop,saas,cloud}) ship under separate, more restrictive licenses gated behind a premium/enterprise license key
version_health_notes: v2.14.2 shipped 2026-07-08, ~28 days before today (2026-08-05); a v2.14.3 pre-release tag exists dated 2026-08-06 but is marked prerelease, so 2.14.2 is the latest stable. Release history shows a steady weekly-to-biweekly cadence through 2026: v2.14.0 (06-30), v2.13.2 (06-24), v2.13.1 (06-19), v2.13.0 (06-18), v2.12.0 (06-09), v2.11.0 (05-19), v2.10.1 (05-07), v2.10.0 (04-24), v2.9.x (04-02 to 04-04), v2.8.0 (03-24). Repo is not archived, last push 2026-08-06, ~89k GitHub stars. Clearly active, well-resourced project (backed by a company, "Stirling PDF Inc."), not slowing or EOL.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes offers general-purpose PDF manipulation (merge/split/convert/OCR/compress/sign/redact/edit — 50+ tools). Paperless-ngx and paperless-ai are archival/indexing systems for scanned documents, not editing toolkits, so there's no functional overlap with either. Stirling PDF is a much heavier, more feature-complete alternative to the other two PDF-tool gap-analysis candidates already written up in this batch (pdfding — a personal PDF reader/annotator with sync, and bentopdf — a lightweight client-side WASM toolkit): Stirling PDF runs actual server-side processing (LibreOffice-backed conversion, real OCR via Tesseract, digital signing, automation pipelines, a REST API) rather than a purely in-browser tool or a document library. If more than one of these three ships, they'd compete for the same "PDF utility" slot in the catalogue — a build-bandwidth call, not a reason to reject any one of them on its own merits.
usefulness_rationale: Broad, non-technical appeal (everyone occasionally needs to merge/split/convert/OCR/sign a PDF) combined with genuine self-hosting value: unlike bentopdf's client-side WASM tools, Stirling PDF does real server-side work (OCR, format conversion, digital signing, automation via its API/pipelines) that isn't available for free in a browser tab, making the "keep your files off third-party SaaS like smallpdf/ilovepdf" pitch stronger. A large, actively developed, company-backed project with a big community reduces upstream-abandonment risk relative to the other two candidates.
blocking_issues: Stirling PDF's own login system (SECURITY_ENABLELOGIN=true) requires SECURITY_INITIALLOGIN_USERNAME/SECURITY_INITIALLOGIN_PASSWORD to be supplied as a PLAINTEXT password at first boot — it is used to seed the initial admin account, not accepted as a pre-hashed value in any supported algorithm. generated_from only ever projects a hash, so it cannot supply this field; this is a genuine plaintext-password requirement, which SCHEMA.md calls a structural blocker for that specific parameter (distinct from an unsupported-hash-algo case, which would just need IF-1420 extended).
summary: Stirling PDF ships as a single container (stirlingtools/stirling-pdf, pin 2.14.2), single HTTP port (8080), no required external database (defaults to embedded H2; Postgres is optional) — a clean fit behind Traefik on <slug>.<base_domain>. Its upstream's own reference docker-compose.yml ships with SECURITY_ENABLELOGIN=false (no built-in auth at all) precisely for reverse-proxy-fronted deployments like ours, which sidesteps the plaintext-only initial-admin-password blocker entirely: leave the app's own login disabled and gate the whole subdomain with Traefik basic_auth (password projected from the customer's root password via generated_from), the same Adminer/bentopdf/WUD pattern already used elsewhere in the catalogue. That makes it fully installable today. Upstream is very active (weekly releases, ~89k stars, company-backed, not archived) and offers real differentiated value — server-side OCR, format conversion, and signing — well beyond the other two PDF-tool candidates already analyzed (pdfding, bentopdf). Recommend build_now, with a note that shipping more than one PDF-tool recipe is a prioritization call, not a quality issue.

Strapi lets a developer define content types and consume them over a generated REST or GraphQL API from an external frontend (static site, mobile app, JAMstack build) — distinct from anything already shipped (Gitea is source control, OpenGist is snippets, n8n is workflow automation, Paperless-ngx is document archiving).
