Strapi fills a real, currently-uncovered catalogue gap (headless CMS / custom API backend) and is the strongest of three competing candidates surfaced in this pass (Directus is legally encumbered by a "Competing Use" license clause; Cockpit CMS's release cadence has recently slowed) thanks to its active weekly release cadence, permissive MIT license, and market recognition. Recommend build_now, with a note for whoever picks the catalogue slot that Directus and Cockpit CMS were evaluated for the same niche and Strapi is the recommended pick among the three.

name: Stump
source_description: Self-hosted comic, manga, and ebook server with OPDS and e-reader sync
upstream_license: MIT (the bundled Expo mobile app is GPL-3.0; server/web is MIT)
version_health_notes: v0.1.6 shipped 2026-08-02, three days before today (2026-08-05). Recent cadence is roughly monthly through 2026 (v0.1.0 on 2026-03-29, v0.1.1 04-04, v0.1.2 04-18, v0.1.3 05-17, v0.1.4 05-29, v0.1.5 06-20, v0.1.6 08-02). There was a ~6-month gap between v0.0.12 (2025-10-05) and v0.1.0 (2026-03-29) that coincided with a major internal rewrite (Prisma to SeaORM), not a maintenance lapse. Repo is not archived; latest commit push was 2026-08-06 (yesterday relative to today). Upstream itself labels the project "beta" and pre-1.0 — active development, but the maintainer is explicit there is "no guarantee of any timeline for features or bug fixes" since this is a free-time project for a single primary maintainer (bus-factor risk worth flagging even though current activity is healthy).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes serves comics/manga/ebooks. Immich covers photos/video, Paperless-ngx covers scanned documents, Syncthing and Gitea are general file/code sync — none overlap with a dedicated reading server with OPDS feeds and Kobo/KoReader e-reader sync, which is a distinct, recognizable self-hosted-app category customers search for by name (comparable to Kavita/Komga/Calibre-Web in the space).
usefulness_rationale: Clear, well-scoped single-purpose app (single container, config/data volumes, no external DB) with a real niche audience among self-hosters who read digital comics/manga/ebooks. Capped at medium rather than high because it is still pre-1.0 beta software by the maintainer's own description, and the audience is narrower than general-purpose media tools already in the catalogue.
blocking_issues:
Stump has no admin-credential environment variable at all (confirmed against the official docker-compose install docs at stumpapp.dev/docs/getting-started/installation/docker — only PUID, PGID, and STUMP_CONFIG_DIR are configurable). The container boots with zero users; the first visitor to the public URL is presented with an open registration form and becomes the sole admin-account owner. There is no `type: password` login parameter to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` — the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var at container start, so root-password projection has nothing to attach to.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app does not close this race on its own: the gate uses the platform's single root-password-projection slot, but the app's own first-visitor-wins registration form is still reachable by anything that can present that gate credential — including our own automated first-boot health-check, which would race the customer to complete self-registration and could claim the admin account before the customer ever visits. There is no channel today to hand the customer a second, distinct credential to pre-seed Stump's own signup separately from the gate. This is the same structural blocker recorded for `apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml`, another open-self-registration app.

Name ambiguity check: "Stump" also refers to `stumpwm` (an unrelated X11 tiling window manager) and a couple of unrelated CLI/markdown tools of the same name. The Hostinger description ("comic, manga, and ebook server with OPDS and e-reader sync") unambiguously matches `stumpapp/stump`, the project analyzed here — no other candidate considered.
summary: Stump is an active, actively-released (beta, pre-1.0) single-container comic/manga/ebook server with OPDS and Kobo/KoReader sync that would fill a genuine content-type gap in the catalogue — nothing else covers this niche. It fails the installability test purely on the platform mechanism: like 2FAuth, its one admin account is provisioned via an open, unauthenticated self-registration form with no env-var hook, so neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely hand the customer their own exclusive first-run credential without racing our own health-check or any other early visitor. Revisit once the platform supports either a preset-admin-via-env-var injection (would require an upstream feature request to stumpapp/stump) or a second customer-facing credential channel beyond the single root-password projection.

name: SuggestArr
source_description: Automated media recommendation engine for Jellyfin, Plex, and Emby with Seer
version_health_notes: Released today (2026-08-05). Recent release cadence is very active: v2.9.0 (2026-06-12), v2.9.1 (2026-06-19), v2.10.0 (2026-07-14), v2.10.1 (2026-07-20), v2.11.0 (2026-08-03), v2.12.0 (2026-08-05) — six releases in under two months, several days apart. No archival or EOL signals; this is a healthy, actively-developed project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches media-server automation. SuggestArr watches a customer's Jellyfin/Plex/Emby history and auto-requests similar titles via Jellyseerr/Overseerr, optionally using an LLM for smarter suggestions. It is a satellite/companion app, not a standalone media server: it has no value unless the customer already runs a media server AND a request manager (Jellyseerr/ Overseerr) elsewhere — none of which are in our catalogue today. That dependency chain narrows the addressable audience considerably.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful quality-of-life automation for the specific audience that already self-hosts a full Jellyfin/Plex/Emby + Jellyseerr/Overseerr stack (elsewhere), but it's a niche add-on rather than something that stands alone. It's unlikely to attract a customer who doesn't already have that stack running, and the requirement on external API keys (see installability) further limits what we could actually ship.
blocking_issues:
The app has no built-in admin login of its own — all configuration (media server, Jellyseerr/Overseerr, TMDb) happens through an unauthenticated web setup wizard on first boot. Without a gate this would sit open on the internet; a Traefik basic_auth gate is expressible and would supply that boundary (same pattern as recipes/wud).

The app cannot function without a customer-supplied TMDb API key (mandatory for all similarity search) and a Jellyseerr/Overseerr API key + URL (mandatory to send requests) — both external, customer- obtained credentials with no env-var equivalent documented (the Docker image only exposes LOG_LEVEL and SUGGESTARR_PORT as env vars; everything else is entered through the web UI wizard and stored in a config file). There is no channel today for a customer-supplied external API key of this kind.

It also needs the customer's Jellyfin/Plex/Emby server URL and credentials/API key to read watch history — another external, per-customer credential outside the root-password-hash mechanism, and pointing at a media server that itself isn't part of our catalogue.
summary: SuggestArr (github.com/giuseppe99barchetta/SuggestArr, MIT, image ciuse99/suggestarr, latest v2.12.0 released 2026-08-05) is a healthy, actively-developed single-container Flask app with no direct catalogue overlap. Mechanically it is a simple docker-compose service on one HTTP port (5000) — reverse-proxy friendly — but it is fundamentally a companion/satellite app: it does nothing without a customer-supplied TMDb API key, a Jellyseerr/Overseerr API key + URL, and Jellyfin/Plex/Emby server credentials, none of which our platform has an input channel for today, and none of which are apps we host ourselves. Its own web UI also has no built-in login, so even a bare deployment would need a Traefik basic_auth gate just to avoid sitting open. Recommend not_recommended: blocked on multiple external-API-key inputs we cannot express, and of narrow value even if that were solved, since it only helps customers who already run a full media-server + request-manager stack elsewhere.

name: Sun-Panel
source_description: Server and NAS navigation panel with customizable homepage and app launcher
upstream_license: MIT (as stated in the repo/docs, but see notes below on how much of the shipped image this actually covers)
version_health_notes: v1.8.1 is the latest stable Docker Hub tag (pushed 2025-12-31), about 7 months before today (2026-08-05). On the surface this looks like a normally-paced project (v1.6.0 2024-11-10, v1.6.1 2024-12-23, v1.7.0 2025-03-26, v1.8.0 2025-10-28, v1.8.1 2025-12-31), but the GitHub tags for v1.6.0 through v1.8.1 all point at the exact same commit (25f46209, authored 2024-04-26 "Update README.md") — the public source repository has not received a real commit since April 2024, even though four "releases" have been tagged against it since. Docker Hub tells a different story: past the 1.8.1 stable line there is an active `2.0.0-dev-*` series with builds as recent as 2026-06-08 (about 2 months before today), i.e. the maintainer is still actively building and shipping newer compiled images, just not against the public open-source tree. The project's own README states "the author added some [PRO] function, so the project temporarily entered a closed source state," with the "latest open-source version" pinned at v1.3.0 — meaning even the v1.4.0-1.8.1 Docker images already ship closed-source code layered on the last public commit, and the upcoming 2.0 line continues that pattern. Repo is not archived and still has 159 open issues, so this is not abandonment, but it is functionally a closed-source product distributed as a Docker image with an increasingly stale open-source facade — worth flagging as a real concession versus a clean stable OSS release cadence.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a bookmark/homepage-style navigation dashboard (the space occupied by Homepage, Homarr, Heimdall, Dashy). Portainer manages Docker containers directly rather than presenting a customizable launcher grid, and none of the monitoring or productivity recipes overlap conceptually. Sun-Panel would be a genuinely new, easily-explained category for customers running several other self-hosted services who want one landing page linking to all of them.
usefulness_rationale: Real, recognizable self-hosted-app category with broad appeal to anyone running multiple services (which describes most AF customers). Capped at medium rather than high because of the version-health concerns above — the public source is effectively frozen while paid "PRO" development continues elsewhere, so the long-term openness and support trajectory of the free image is uncertain, and the optional Docker-socket-mounting feature (for container status/launch cards) would need to be left out of an AF deployment for security reasons, losing one of its differentiating features.
blocking_issues: Sun-Panel ships with a fixed, hardcoded default admin account (admin@sun.cc / 12345678, per the official quick-deploy docs) and no documented environment variable to set or override it at container start — the only way to change it post-boot is the in-app "reset password" flow or a `-password-reset` CLI flag run inside the container. Per the schema's guidance this is not a hard blocker: a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate projected from the customer's root password in front of the whole app makes the fixed internal default a non-issue, since the actual customer-facing auth boundary becomes the gate rather than Sun-Panel's own login.
summary: Sun-Panel is a single-container Docker/NAS navigation dashboard (port 3002, config/uploads/database volumes, no external DB) that would fill a real gap in the catalogue — nothing else offers a customizable homepage/app-launcher. It is mechanically installable today by gating the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth` credential in front of its own fixed default admin login, the same pattern already used for Adminer/HertzBeat. The open concern is upstream health: the public GitHub source has been frozen at an April 2024 commit for well over a year while four version tags were still cut against it, and the maintainer has explicitly moved active (2.0-line) development into a closed-source "PRO" track distributed only as compiled Docker images. Recommend build_with_caveats — worth shipping given the clear customer-facing use case, but flag the closed-source drift as a reason to re-check upstream health before or shortly after building.

It clears the installability bar today and the project is actively maintained (releases every 1-2 weeks). The caveat worth flagging before building: since all task data lives client-side in the browser, not on the server, this recipe delivers less "self-hosted value" than most of the catalogue unless a future iteration also wires up the optional WebDAV/SuperSync sync backend from upstream's docker-compose.yaml — recommend build_with_caveats rather than an unqualified build_now.

name: SuperTokens
source_description: SuperTokens is an open-source authentication solution with session management
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (core); a separate ee/ directory in the repo carries its own more restrictive license for enterprise-only features, not needed for self-hosted core usage
version_health_notes: v12.0.10 published 2026-08-06, essentially the day of this analysis (2026-08-05). supertokens-core maintains several parallel supported version lines (12.0.x, 11.4.x, 11.3.x, 11.2.x, 11.1.x, 11.0.x, 10.1.x) and backports patches across all of them — v12.0.10, v11.4.7 and v11.3.7 were all released within hours of each other on 2026-08-06, with v12.0.9 four days before that. Going back further, releases are frequent and continuous through 2026 with no gaps longer than a few weeks. Repo is not archived, 15.2k GitHub stars, last push 2026-08-06. Clearly a well-resourced, actively maintained project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is an auth/identity backend, so on paper this looks like a gap similar to the ones already flagged for Authentik and Casdoor. In practice it is a fundamentally different kind of app: SuperTokens core is a headless authentication microservice with no standalone UI of its own. Its only HTTP surface is a REST API (health-checked via GET /hello) meant to be called by a backend SDK (Node/Python/Go/Java) that a developer writes and deploys separately; the "user management dashboard" upstream advertises is not served by the core container itself — it's mounted by the customer's own backend app once that app integrates the supertokens SDK (e.g. reachable at <their-app-domain>/auth/dashboard, not at the core's own port). Deployed on its own, as any recipe here would deploy it, the container serves no page a customer could open in a browser and use — unlike Authentik or Casdoor, which ship a complete, usable web IdP UI out of the box.
usefulness_rationale: SuperTokens is a building block for developers who are already writing a custom backend application and choose it as their auth layer at development time — it is not a turnkey product an AF customer could stand up and start using the way they can with every other recipe in the catalogue. A recipe that boots the core container in isolation hands the customer a bare API with nothing to click on; all the value requires them to write, deploy, and wire up separate backend code with the SDK, which is entirely outside what a self-hosting recipe delivers. This is a stronger version of the caveat already flagged for Casdoor ("value only materializes once wired into other apps") — Casdoor at least has a working admin web UI reachable immediately after boot; SuperTokens core has none at all.
blocking_issues:
The recipe mechanism could technically boot the container (Postgres password and the optional API_KEYS core-auth secret are both patternless values nothing customer-facing needs to read, so they're server-generatable), but there is no customer-facing login screen to gate at all — 'has no login of its own, gate the whole thing with Traefik basic_auth' does not apply either, because the thing being gated is a JSON REST API consumed by a backend SDK, not a browser UI a human would visit. Fronting it with Traefik on <slug>.<base_domain> and basic_auth would just break normal API calls from the customer's own backend (which don't send interactive basic-auth credentials), so the standard no-login gate pattern used for Adminer/WUD/Stirling PDF doesn't transfer here.
Even if deployed successfully, the recipe would deliver nothing a customer can use standalone: functioning auth requires them to write and deploy their own backend application with the supertokens SDK pointed at this core instance, which is out of scope for anything a recipe can provision. This is a product-fit gap, not a secrets/mechanism gap.
summary: SuperTokens core (supertokens/supertokens-postgresql, pin 12.0.10) is a single-container, Postgres-backed service on one port (3567) with no customer-supplied secrets it can't get server-generated — mechanically it would be easy to boot. The upstream project is also very actively maintained (near-daily backported releases across multiple version lines, not archived). It fails on product fit, not mechanism: the core by itself has no web UI — its dashboard is served by a customer's own backend application after they integrate the SuperTokens SDK, something entirely outside a recipe's scope. Standing up just the core container would give an AF customer an unauthenticated-by-default REST API with nothing to open in a browser, not a usable self-hosted app. Recommend not_recommended: this is a developer library/dependency, not a self-contained application, and doesn't fit the "one container, one web UI behind Traefik" shape the rest of the catalogue follows.

name: SurrealDB
source_description: Multi-model database for documents, graphs, time-series, and vector data
upstream_license: Business Source License 1.1 (converts to Apache-2.0 on the per-release Change Date, 4 years out). The Additional Use Grant forbids using the Licensed Work "as a Database Service" — defined as any product, service, platform, or commercial offering that uses SurrealDB to provide database functionality to third parties who create, manage, or control schemas or tables. Worth a legal read before shipping a self-hosted-database recipe from a hosting catalogue, though the customer (not IONOS) would be the one creating/managing schemas on their own VM, which is the more common self-hosted-database reading of the grant.
version_health_notes: 3.2.4 shipped 2026-08-03, two days before today (2026-08-05). Prior patches/minors: 3.1.5 (2026-06-19), 3.0.5 (2026-03-27), 2.6.5 (2026-03-24), 2.5.0 (2026-01-22), 2.4.0 (2025-11-24), 2.3.10 (2025-09-19) — a steady roughly-monthly-to-bimonthly cadence across both patch and minor lines, with several lines (2.x, 3.0.x, 3.1.x, 3.2.x) receiving patches in parallel. Clearly active development, not slowing or dormant.
differentiation: None of the 24 current recipes is a standalone, customer-facing database — n8n, paperless-ngx, immich, etc. all run Postgres/SQLite purely as private internal storage. SurrealDB would be a first for that category (shared structurally with the other database candidates already analyzed: apps-gaps/apache-couchdb.yaml, apps-gaps/mongodb-4.yaml, apps-gaps/neo4j.yaml, apps-gaps/edgedb.yaml). Within that group it is the most differentiated on paper — a single engine covering document, graph, time-series, and vector workloads with one query language (SurrealQL) and one HTTP/WS API, rather than a single-model store — aimed at developers building an app that needs several of those data shapes without running separate databases. Like CouchDB it speaks HTTP/JSON natively (port 8000) rather than a raw binary wire protocol, so it doesn't have MySQL/MongoDB's structural raw-port problem.
usefulness_rationale: Real differentiated value for developers who want one datastore for mixed document/graph/vector/time-series workloads, and an actively developed, healthy upstream. Same ceiling as the other database candidates, though: it's infrastructure a customer's own app talks to, not an end-user product with day-to-day human use, and unlike CouchDB it ships no bundled admin UI at all (Surrealist, the only UI, is a separate desktop/web client, not part of the self-hosted server image) — reachable only via CLI/SDK/raw HTTP once deployed.
blocking_issues: Verified against the surrealdb/surrealdb source (server/src/cli/start.rs, server/src/dbs/mod.rs, core/src/kvs/ds.rs::initialise_credentials): the official image's startup root credential (`--user`/`--pass`, or the `SURREAL_USER`/`SURREAL_PASS` env vars) is typed as a plain `String` and passed straight into `DefineUserStatement::new_with_password`, i.e. SurrealDB itself hashes it internally with Argon2id at first boot. There is no startup-time passhash/env-var equivalent of SurrealQL's `DEFINE USER ... PASSHASH` clause — that clause only exists for a user manually running SurrealQL after the server is already up, not for seeding the initial root user from the container entrypoint. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash, never a plaintext value, so per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's own test table this is a genuine plaintext requirement — a structural blocker, not a missing-algorithm gap IF-1420 could close (even though Argon2id is exactly the algorithm `generated_from` already supports for other apps; the mismatch here is the entrypoint's input type, not the hash format).
summary: SurrealDB is an actively maintained, well-differentiated multi-model database (documents, graphs, time-series, vector) with a real gap-filling case: no current recipe offers a customer-facing database, and among the database candidates analyzed so far it's the healthiest upstream and least redundant feature set. It also avoids the raw-binary-port problem that blocks MySQL/MongoDB/Neo4j, since it speaks HTTP/WS on a single port (8000). It still fails the credential channel, though, in the same way MongoDB and Neo4j do: the initial root user can only be seeded as a plaintext password via `--user`/`--pass` (`SURREAL_USER`/`SURREAL_PASS`), confirmed directly against the CLI arg types and the `initialise_credentials` code path in the SurrealDB source — SurrealQL's `PASSHASH` clause isn't reachable from container startup. `generated_from` only ever supplies a hash, so there is no way to project the customer's root password into it today. Recommend `not_recommended`, in the same structural class as `apps-gaps/mongodb-4.yaml` and `apps-gaps/neo4j.yaml`, rather than `blocked_on_platform` — this isn't an unsupported-algorithm gap, the entrypoint doesn't accept a hash at all.

Upstream is very actively maintained (weekly releases, 3.3k stars, not archived). It fails on product fit, not mechanism: the self-hosted OSS server has no web dashboard of its own (that's a cloud-only SaaS feature) — its only surface is a Bearer-token JSON API meant to be consumed by a customer's own backend application via the Svix SDK. Standing up the container alone would give an AF customer an authenticated API with nothing to open in a browser, not a usable self-hosted app. Recommend not_recommended: this is a developer infrastructure dependency, not a self-contained application, and doesn't fit the "one container, one web UI behind Traefik" shape the rest of the catalogue follows — the same verdict already reached for SuperTokens.

summary: Swing Music (ghcr.io/swingmx/swingmusic, pin v3.0.0) is an actively maintained, single-container, single-HTTP-port (1970) music streaming server with a genuine browser web UI and no database dependency — mechanically simple to front with Traefik. The workable path — the same one used for apps-gaps/kitchenowl.yaml, which has an identical "first visitor claims the owner slot" problem — is to enable signup (ENABLE_SIGNUP=1) but gate the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` credential projected from the customer's root password, so only the customer can reach the signup form and claim the first (superuser) account; Postgres password and Django's SECRET_KEY are generated server-side with no customer input needed. That makes this installable today. Upstream is actively maintained with a dense release cadence and no EOL signals. The main open question is catalogue prioritization, not mechanics: this is the fourth candidate in the recipe/household-management niche to clear gap analysis (after Mealie, Grocy, and KitchenOwl), so a human reviewer should decide how many of these four are actually worth building rather than treating overlap as a rejection reason.

blocking_issues:
Licensing, not mechanism: the Sustainable Use License's Limitations clause restricts use to "your own internal business purposes or... non-commercial or personal use," and permits redistribution to others only "free of charge for non-commercial purposes." Offering TaskTrove as a paid, one-click hosted recipe on IONOS Application Factory is a commercial third-party hosting use that this clause does not appear to permit — the same shape of blocker previously flagged for Planka (apps-gaps/planka.yaml) and NocoDB (apps-gaps/nocodb.yaml). Needs explicit legal sign-off, or contact with the maintainer for a commercial arrangement, before this can ship regardless of the technical mechanism question below.

No project-level admin-bootstrap env var exists. By default TaskTrove ships with no login at all (any visitor has full access). Setting AUTH_SECRET (an encryption key, not a password) switches on auth, but the first person to visit the running instance is prompted to create the account interactively through the web UI — there is no env var carrying a plaintext or hashed initial credential, so `generated_from` has no field to project the customer's root password into. This is the same first-come-first-served exposure window seen with NocoDB: the fix is gating the whole app behind a Traefik `basic_auth: true` wall (auto-generated credential) until the customer visits and claims the account through TaskTrove's own signup screen, at which point that becomes the durable login.

No external database dependency — TaskTrove stores tasks as JSON files under a mounted volume (`/app/data`), so there is no additional server-generated secret beyond AUTH_SECRET itself, which needs no customer input.

Project appears dormant since 2026-01-09 (see version_health) — worth weighing alongside the licensing question, since it affects how much confidence to place in a timely licensing response from the maintainer if pursued.
summary: TaskTrove is mechanically installable today: a single official ghcr.io/dohsimpson/tasktrove image with one HTTP port (3000) that works cleanly behind Traefik, no database dependency, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate standing in for the missing admin-bootstrap env var (same NocoDB-style workaround) to close the first-come-first-served signup window. It would also fill a genuinely new category — no current recipe covers personal task/to-do management. The recommendation is `not_recommended` for two independent reasons: the Sustainable Use License's restriction to internal/non-commercial use does not clearly permit IONOS reselling it as a paid hosted recipe (same shape of blocker as Planka and NocoDB, needing legal sign-off before revisiting), and the upstream repo has had zero commits or releases for nearly 7 months as of 2026-08-05 after a very active prior cadence, an abrupt stop worth re-checking before committing build effort even if the licensing question clears.

name: Technitium DNS Server
source_description: Open-source DNS server with ad blocking, encrypted DNS, and web management
version_health_notes: v15.4.0 shipped 2026-07-11, less than a month before today (2026-08-05). Recent history shows a fast, steady cadence: v15.0.0 (2026-04-25, major release adding OIDC Single Sign-On) → v15.0.1 (2026-04-26) → v15.1.0 (2026-05-03) → v15.2.0 (2026-05-09) → v15.3.0 (2026-07-05) → v15.4.0 (2026-07-11). No archival notice, no EOL announcement, official Docker image kept in lockstep with releases. Clearly an actively maintained project.
differentiation: Technitium's core pitch — network-wide DNS-based ad/tracker blocking with a web console — is the same job already covered twice in the catalogue by adguard-home and pihole, both shipped as WireGuard-VPN-only recipes for the same structural reason (DNS runs on raw port 53, not HTTP, so it can't sit behind Traefik). Technitium adds real extra capability beyond either (authoritative + recursive DNS, DNS-over-TLS/HTTPS/QUIC, built-in DHCP, clustering, OIDC SSO), but none of that changes the primary customer-facing use case Hostinger's own description highlights ("ad blocking, encrypted DNS, and web management"), which a customer already gets from either existing recipe.
usefulness_rationale: A third DNS-ad-blocker recipe targeting the same narrow "customer runs their own network-wide resolver over WireGuard" niche adds maintenance surface without opening a new customer segment — the two recipes already in the catalogue saturate this use case.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against upstream's DockerEnvironmentVariables.md: DNS_SERVER_ADMIN_PASSWORD (or DNS_SERVER_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE) takes the admin web-console password as a plain-text string read once on first boot — there is no argon2/bcrypt hash format the server accepts instead. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever produces a hash, never the plaintext password, so it cannot be projected onto this field at all (not even a "not-yet-supported algorithm" case — this is the genuine plaintext-requirement blocker called out in apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md).

Auto-generating DNS_SERVER_ADMIN_PASSWORD server-side (the pattern pihole's WEBPASSWORD uses) doesn't solve it either: like Ackee's ACKEE_PASSWORD (see apps-gaps/ackee.yaml), this is the literal credential the customer must type into Technitium's own login screen to manage DNS zones, blocklists, and settings — the entire point of the app's "web management" pitch — so a random value never surfaced to the customer would lock them out of the product's main feature. Gating the console behind Traefik `basic_auth` doesn't help either, since the customer still needs to get past Technitium's internal login once through the gate.

Independent of the credential issue, DNS service itself runs on raw port 53/tcp+udp, not HTTP — same as adguard-home and pihole, this cannot sit behind Traefik and would need the same WireGuard-VPN-only exposure pattern those two recipes already use.
summary: Technitium DNS Server (technitium/dns-server, web console on 5380, DNS on 53/tcp+udp) is an actively maintained project with a fast release cadence and genuinely more DNS-protocol capability than either adguard-home or pihole. But its core customer-facing value — network-wide DNS ad blocking with encrypted DNS and web management — duplicates two recipes already in the catalogue, and it is not installable today regardless: DNS_SERVER_ADMIN_PASSWORD only accepts a plaintext password (no hash format `generated_from` could target), and that password is the customer's actual login for the web console's core functionality, so it can't be auto-generated and withheld either. Recommend not_recommended: low incremental value over existing DNS recipes, on top of a real installability blocker.

name: Teedy
source_description: Open-source document management system with OCR and full-text search
version_health_notes: No tagged version release since v1.11 (2023-03-12) — over 3 years ago as of 2026-08-05. Upstream commit history is not dead (last commit 2026-02-09, ~6 months ago; another 2024-09-07), so the project isn't archived or abandoned, but it has stopped cutting numbered releases: the `latest` Docker tag (last built 2024-09-07) sits ahead of `v1.11` with a handful of bug fixes and is the only image carrying those, which is a poor fit for AF's "pin a stable tag, never :latest" rule. 114 open issues, repo not archived. Best read as low-intensity maintenance mode rather than active development.
differentiation: Teedy is a general-purpose document repository (tags, folders, ACLs, workflows, webhooks, versioning, LDAP) rather than paperless-ngx's scan-consumption-focused pipeline. Feature overlap (OCR, full-text search, "digitize and search your documents") is substantial though, and paperless-ngx is the far more actively maintained and widely adopted project in the same space.
usefulness_rationale: The core value proposition (OCR + searchable document archive) is already covered by paperless-ngx, which is materially more active upstream. Teedy's differentiators (workflows, ACL, LDAP) are more relevant to team/enterprise document handling than a typical single-tenant AF customer's needs, and the stalled release cadence adds long-term maintenance risk without a clear compensating benefit.
summary: Teedy is mechanically installable today: it accepts its initial admin password as a bcrypt hash via DOCS_ADMIN_PASSWORD_INIT, which maps cleanly onto generated_from root-password projection, and it's a single-port, reverse-proxy-friendly web app. The blocker is fit, not mechanism: it substantially overlaps paperless-ngx (already in the catalogue and far more actively maintained), and upstream has not cut a numbered release since March 2023, forcing any pin onto a stale tag or an unversioned `latest` build. Recommend build_with_caveats only if there's a specific customer ask for Teedy's workflow/ACL/LDAP features beyond what paperless-ngx offers; otherwise not worth the added maintenance surface.

name: Temporal
source_description: Durable workflow execution platform with web-based monitoring and search
version_health_notes: Latest server release v1.31.2 shipped 2026-07-08, less than a month before this analysis (2026-08-05). Release history shows multiple tagged releases per month across the 1.29/1.30/1.31 lines (patch and minor releases both), consistent with an actively maintained project. The temporalio/auto-setup all-in-one image (historically the easiest single-container option) is deprecated by upstream for production use in favor of the split server/admin-tools/ui compose stack referenced below.
differentiation: Not a duplicate of n8n or any existing recipe. n8n is a no-code workflow-automation tool consumed entirely through its own web UI; Temporal is a durable-execution *backend platform* — customers write their own workflow/worker code in an SDK (Go/Java/Python/TypeScript/etc) that connects to the server's gRPC frontend to actually do anything. The bundled Web UI is read-only observability (monitoring + workflow search), not a place where end-user work happens.
usefulness_rationale: Valuable for engineering teams already building on Temporal, but it is a developer-infrastructure component rather than an end-user application, which is a mismatch for this catalogue's audience (compare to n8n, Immich, Vaultwarden — all fully usable through nothing but a browser). Its core function is unreachable without also standing up external SDK-based worker code, which is out of scope for what an AF customer clicks "install" to get.
blocking_issues:
The gRPC frontend (port 7233) is not an HTTP endpoint and cannot be gated by Traefik basic_auth; it needs its own network-level exposure (raw TCP passthrough, not a simple `<slug>.<base_domain>` HTTP route) to be reachable by external worker code, which is the entire point of running Temporal.

Temporal Server ships with no built-in authentication for that frontend: the default is the `noopAuthorizer`, which permits every request unauthenticated. The supported hardening path is mTLS client certificates or a custom Authorizer/ClaimMapper plugin — neither is a hash of the customer's root password, and there is no channel today for a customer to supply or generate a client certificate. Exposing 7233 publicly without one of these means an open, unauthenticated workflow-execution control plane.

The bundled Web UI has no native username/password login either (SSO/OAuth env vars are the only built-in option, which itself has no input channel today). A Traefik basic_auth gate can protect the UI, but that does nothing for the gRPC frontend risk above.

Full stack requires Postgres + (for the search feature Hostinger's description calls out) Elasticsearch in addition to the server, admin-tools, and UI containers — heavier than any current recipe, but this is a secondary concern next to the auth/exposure blockers.
summary: Temporal is an actively maintained, MIT-licensed durable-execution platform (v1.31.2, released 2026-07-08) with no overlap with anything currently in the catalogue. It does not fit the AF recipe model, though: its actual functionality is reached over an unauthenticated-by-default gRPC frontend meant for external SDK worker code, not through the bundled read-only Web UI, and neither our root-password-hash mechanism nor Traefik basic_auth can secure that surface. Even setting aside the security gap, it is a developer-infrastructure component rather than an end-user application, which is a poor match for this catalogue's audience regardless of platform mechanism changes — recommend not_recommended rather than blocked_on_platform.

name: TensorZero
source_description: Open-source LLMOps gateway with built-in observability and prompt optimization
version_health_notes: The GitHub repository was archived by the owner on 2026-06-12 and is now read-only — no commits, issues, or PRs are possible anymore. 2026.6.0 (2026-06-04) is the final release, itself a security fix for a high-risk vulnerability in the TensorZero Gateway (GHSA-824w-x939-6cmc). Per public reporting, the company (raised $7.3M, returned unspent capital to investors) shut down because the commercial layer built on top of the OSS gateway never reached sustainable product-market fit; the founders explicitly stopped maintaining the open-source project when they wound down. As of today (2026-08-05), that is under 2 months since the archive date — this is a fresh EOL, not a stale one, but it is unambiguous: no security patches, no LLM-provider API updates, no bug fixes will ever ship again for this project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is an LLM-gateway/LLMOps product. open-webui + ollama is a local-model chat front-end, not a multi-provider API gateway with observability, evaluation, and experimentation features. TensorZero would have filled a real gap for customers building their own AI applications against hosted model APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, etc.) who want a self-hosted logging/routing layer in front of them, rather than customers who just want to chat with a model in a browser.
usefulness_rationale: The underlying idea (self-hosted LLM gateway + observability) is useful and would have been a good differentiator, but shipping a recipe on top of an archived, unmaintained project handles security risk to the customer for no offsetting benefit — any future LLM-provider API change or CVE in the gateway will never be patched upstream. usefulness is scored on the app as it exists today (frozen), not on the idea.
blocking_issues:
TensorZero's entire purpose is routing inference calls to external LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Azure, Google Gemini, Mistral, Groq, etc.) declared in the gateway's tensorzero.toml config. At least one provider API key is required for the gateway to do anything useful, and there is no channel today for a customer to supply an arbitrary external API key at first boot — this alone blocks installable_today independent of the EOL finding.
Repo archived 2026-06-12 (read-only, final release 2026.6.0 on 2026-06-04) — shipping a recipe now means committing customers to an unmaintained gateway that will never receive security patches or provider-API compatibility updates.
The TensorZero UI (tensorzero/ui image) itself requires gateway auth to be configured (2026.5.0 made this mandatory) and is a thin observability/eval front-end over ClickHouse + the gateway, not a self-contained admin app with its own generatable login — no single-parameter generated_from projection covers the real secret the app needs (the provider key), only a basic_auth gate on the UI, which does not unblock the gateway's own API-key requirement.
summary: TensorZero is a two-container stack (tensorzero/gateway on :3000 backed by ClickHouse, plus an optional tensorzero/ui on :4000) that is structurally reverse-proxy-friendly — single HTTP surface per container, similar in shape to recipes/n8n's Postgres-backed pattern with ClickHouse standing in for Postgres. It would have filled a genuine gap (no LLM-gateway/LLMOps product exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue; open-webui/ollama serve a different job). However, two independent problems rule it out: the gateway cannot function without a customer-supplied external LLM-provider API key, which our current `/compose` mechanism has no channel to deliver, and — more decisively — the upstream repository was archived read-only on 2026-06-12 after the vendor shut down, meaning any recipe built on it today ships an unmaintained, permanently frozen gateway with no future security patches. Recommend not_recommended; revisit only if a maintained fork emerges.

name: TeslaMate
source_description: Self-hosted Tesla data logger with trip history and Grafana dashboards
version_health_notes: v4.0.1 tagged 2026-06-14, about 8 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Release history is dense through 2026: v3.0.0 (2026-02-28), v3.1.0 (2026-06-07), v4.0.0 (2026-06-13), v4.0.1 (2026-06-14) — a burst of three releases in a week resolving a Tesla refresh-token regression, following a steadier v2.x cadence back through 2025 (v2.0.0 2025-04-26, v2.1.0 2025-07-21, v2.1.1 2025-08-16, v2.2.0 2025-11-06). Repo is not archived, actively maintained by teslamate-org, clearly active rather than maintenance-only.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches personal vehicle telemetry. uptime-kuma and wud are the closest "monitoring" recipes but watch services/containers, not a physical device's location, battery, charging, and drive history. TeslaMate would be a new vertical: an always-on data logger for a customer's own Tesla, with a live dashboard and a pre-built set of Grafana reports (efficiency, charging cost, trips, vampire drain, etc.).
usefulness_rationale: Well-regarded within its niche (8.7k+ GitHub stars) but the addressable audience is narrow: it's only useful to someone who owns a Tesla, which is a small slice of a general VPS-hosting customer base compared to the broad-appeal apps already in the catalogue (n8n, paperless-ngx, immich).
summary: TeslaMate is a four-container Compose stack (teslamate + postgres + teslamate/grafana + eclipse-mosquitto) with two separate single-HTTP-port web UIs — the Phoenix live dashboard on :4000 and Grafana on :3000 — each reverse-proxy-friendly on its own subdomain. Postgres password and the Tesla-API-token ENCRYPTION_KEY are patternless secrets the server can generate with no customer input. Neither web UI has a login the customer needs to configure at boot: the teslamate app itself has no built-in auth at all (it shows live GPS location and drive history, so it needs a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate, same pattern as Adminer), and Grafana ships a fixed default admin/admin login that should likewise sit behind a basic_auth gate rather than rely on Grafana's own unchangeable-by-us credential. Linking the actual vehicle happens after deployment, when the customer signs into their own Tesla account directly inside the running app — that's a manual in-browser step the customer performs themselves (like configuring API keys inside hermes-agent or n8n post-provision), not a value af-api needs to inject, so it isn't a blocker. Mechanically this is build_with_caveats rather than build_now: it needs two basic_auth gates instead of the usual one, and given the very narrow (Tesla-owner only) target audience, it's a defensible but low-priority addition compared to broader-appeal gaps in the catalogue.

name: Text Generation Web UI
source_description: Web interface for running local LLMs with GGUF, GPTQ, and AWQ support
version_health_notes: Very active: v4.9 shipped 2026-05-20, less than 3 months before this analysis (2026-08-05), preceded by v4.8 (2026-05-07) and the v4.7.x series (2026-05-03) and v4.6.x series (2026-04-23) — multiple releases per month. Not dormant or EOL. However, the project itself has changed substantially: it was renamed from "text-generation-webui" to "textgen" (repo moved to oobabooga/textgen) and, per its own README as of v4.7.3 (2026-05-03), repositioned itself as "a desktop app for local LLMs" bundling an Electron shell as the primary distribution (portable downloads for Linux/Windows/macOS). Headless/Docker/server operation still exists but is now a secondary path, not the project's lead use case — a material shift in direction since the Hostinger listing (slug/description referencing the old "text-generation-web-ui" name and GGUF/GPTQ/AWQ framing) was presumably written.
differentiation: Functionally overlaps heavily with open-webui (also a browser-based chat UI for local LLMs, already bundled with Ollama in that recipe) and with ollama itself. TextGen's distinguishing features versus open-webui are backend flexibility (llama.cpp, ExLlamaV3, Transformers, TensorRT-LLM, chosen per-model instead of delegating to a separate Ollama runtime) and built-in LoRA training / image-generation tabs. Notably, current TextGen has dropped GPTQ and AWQ support entirely (neither format appears anywhere in its README or docs) — the exact formats Hostinger's description cites as differentiators no longer apply to the current upstream project.
usefulness_rationale: The "chat with a local LLM in your browser" use case this app targets is already served by open-webui, and open-webui already bundles Ollama for model management — covering the same customer need with a lower resource/operational footprint and a project that has stayed focused on the self-hosted server use case rather than pivoting to desktop-first distribution. TextGen's extra backends/training/image-gen tabs are power-user features unlikely to justify a second, largely-redundant catalogue entry for AF's audience.
blocking_issues:
No official prebuilt Docker Hub image exists to pin a tag against. Upstream only ships Dockerfiles (docker/cpu, docker/nvidia, docker/amd, docker/intel) that build the image at deploy time via `git clone https://github.com/oobabooga/textgen.git` against whatever is on the default branch — there is no tag/version ARG to pin. Every other recipe in the catalogue pulls a pinned, versioned image; adopting TextGen as-is would mean either building and hosting our own pinned image (extra maintenance burden with no upstream equivalent) or accepting an effectively unpinned, floating build.

The app's own login mechanism (`--gradio-auth username:password`) requires the plaintext password at process start (Gradio checks it directly), so it cannot consume a `generated_from` hash. This is not a hard blocker on its own — the app has no default-on auth, so the standard Traefik `basic_auth` gate pattern (as used for n8n, WUD, Open WebUI) is used instead and native `--gradio-auth` is simply left disabled.
summary: TextGen (formerly "text-generation-webui") is under active, fast-paced development and is mechanically installable today via a Traefik basic_auth gate — but it is not recommended for this catalogue. It duplicates ground already covered by open-webui (bundled with ollama), the very quantization formats (GPTQ/AWQ) Hostinger's description cites have been dropped from the current codebase, the upstream project has pivoted to a desktop-first Electron distribution model rather than staying focused on self-hosted server use, and there is no official pinned Docker image to build the recipe against — a real deviation from how every other recipe in this catalogue sources its image.

name: The Lounge
source_description: The Lounge is a web-based IRC client for always-on chat connectivity
version_health_notes: v4.5.2 shipped 2026-07-12, less than a month before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases: v4.5.1 (2026-06-24), v4.5.0 (2026-05-20, a "maintenance focused release" dropping Node.js 18/20 support and switching to built-in SQLite), v4.4.3 (~3 months before 4.5.0). A v4.6.0-pre.1 pre-release is already out (2026-07-22), confirming ongoing development. Repo is not archived, issues/PRs are actively triaged — this is a steady, actively maintained project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers IRC/persistent chat client hosting. The closest neighbors by shape are single-container web apps like Uptime Kuma or Vaultwarden, but none overlap in purpose. The Lounge fills a genuinely new category: an always-on web IRC client (bouncer- style) for customers who want a persistent presence on IRC networks without running their own client 24/7.
usefulness_rationale: IRC has a smaller but durable audience (open-source project channels, niche communities, some ops/on-call use), and a self-hosted always-on client is exactly the kind of "why would I run this on my own VPS" utility that fits our self-hosting audience. It's capped at medium rather than high because IRC usage skews toward a narrower, more technical demographic than e.g. password managers or automation tools.
summary: The Lounge is an active, single-container (Node.js, SQLite by default as of v4.5.0), reverse-proxy-friendly web IRC client with no overlap in the current catalogue — persistent/always-on IRC chat is a genuinely new category for us. Unlike most admin-credential apps we've evaluated, The Lounge stores each user's login as a directly-editable JSON file under `${THELOUNGE_HOME}/users/<name>.json` containing a bcrypt password hash (confirmed via upstream docs — the `thelounge add`/`thelounge reset` CLI commands are just interactive wrappers around writing that same file). install.sh can write that user file directly with a bcrypt hash derived from the customer's root password via `generated_from: "bcrypt: ROOT_PASSWORD"`, without needing the interactive CLI at all — the same pattern Vaultwarden already uses for its `ADMIN_TOKEN`. No blocking issues found; recommend building a recipe now.

name: ThingsBoard
source_description: Open-source IoT platform for device management and real-time dashboards
version_health_notes: v4.3.1.3 published 2026-06-30, about 5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Upstream runs two parallel maintenance lines (4.3.x and 4.2.x) with synchronized patch releases roughly every 4-8 weeks throughout 2026: v4.3/v4.2.1.1 (2026-01-20/2025-12-24), v4.3.0.1/v4.2.1.2 (2026-02-03), v4.3.1/v4.2.2 (2026-03-10), v4.3.1.1/v4.2.2.1 (2026-03-31), v4.3.1.2/v4.2.2.2 (2026-05-28), v4.3.1.3/v4.2.2.3 (2026-06-30). Repo is not archived and clearly actively maintained, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: home-assistant is the closest existing recipe by keyword ("IoT"/smart home) but serves a completely different use case: it's a consumer local-automation hub with hundreds of built-in integrations that talk directly to specific smart-home devices/hubs on the customer's own network. ThingsBoard has no built-in device integrations at all — it's a generic device-management and telemetry-dashboard backend that a customer's own hardware/firmware (sensors, gateways, industrial equipment) must be programmed to connect to over MQTT/HTTP/CoAP/LwM2M. Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers this "build your own IoT backend" developer-platform niche, so it would be a genuinely new vertical, not a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Well-known, widely deployed IoT platform (20k+ GitHub stars) with a real dashboard/rule-engine web UI a customer can use without writing backend code, unlike a pure SDK-only platform. But its core value — ingesting live telemetry from real devices — only materializes once the customer has hardware that can speak MQTT/CoAP/HTTP to it, which is a narrower, more technical audience than broad-appeal recipes like n8n or Vaultwarden.
blocking_issues: Real device connectivity — the actual point of an IoT platform — needs the MQTT (1883/8883) and CoAP/LwM2M (5683-5688/udp) transports reachable directly, not just the HTTP web UI on :8080. These are raw TCP/UDP ports rather than HTTP routes behind Traefik; the platform's `ports` metadata does support declaring raw tcp/udp ports (as wg-easy's VPN port already does), so this is an exposure-mechanism limitation to flag, not a hard secrets-input blocker: no customer value needs to be injected into those ports at boot, since device auth (per-device MQTT access tokens) is generated inside the running app after the admin logs in, the same "configure it in-browser after deploy" pattern already accepted for TeslaMate's Tesla-account link and n8n's post-install API credentials.
summary: A clean single-instance install (thingsboard/tb-node + Postgres, no LOAD_DEMO flag) creates exactly one login: sysadmin@thingsboard.org with a fixed default password the app gives no env var to set at container startup — same pattern as TeslaMate/Adminer, addressed by gating the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth credential rather than relying on the app's own unchangeable-at-boot default. Postgres's password is a patternless secret the server can generate with no customer input. Mechanically installable today, but two caveats keep it at build_with_caveats rather than build_now: the platform's real usefulness depends on exposing raw MQTT/CoAP/LwM2M ports beyond the reverse-proxied web UI (mechanically supported via the existing tcp/udp `ports` field, but a heavier network footprint than our typical single-HTTP-port recipe), and the addressable audience — customers with their own IoT hardware to connect — is narrower and more technical than the catalogue's broad-appeal apps.

name: ThinkDashboard
source_description: Minimalist self-hosted bookmark dashboard with keyboard shortcuts
version_health_notes: The project is very young: first tagged release (v0.2) and README history both start around 2025-10. From there it shipped ~15 tagged releases in about six weeks (0.2 through 0.7.6, 2025-11-24), an unusually fast cadence. Then activity stopped abruptly — the last GitHub commit (per the API) is 2025-12-06, and there has been no commit or release since, i.e. roughly 8 months of total silence as of today (2026-08-05). The repo is not archived and no EOL has been announced, so `eol_status: active` is the literal/technical answer, but the pattern (rapid-fire releases followed by a hard stop with zero activity for 8 months) reads as a strong dormancy signal for a 327-star, single-maintainer hobby project rather than a project in planned maintenance mode — treat this as a real risk factor, not a clean "active" project, when weighing whether to build on it.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes are a bookmark manager or start-page / dashboard app — this would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue (closest in spirit is Uptime Kuma's status-page style UI, but that monitors services rather than organizing links). ThinkDashboard's pitch is a fast, keyboard-driven personal home page for bookmarks, which is a plausible small-business/power-user want, but it's a niche, low-stakes utility rather than something customers are likely to seek out a hosted catalogue entry for.
usefulness_rationale: The app is simple, single-container, and genuinely fills a gap in the catalogue, but it stores everything in flat JSON files with no multi-user support, no built-in auth, and no data-portability story beyond raw file access — it's a personal, single-user bookmarklet page, not a product most AF customers would pay a hosting seat for. Combined with the dormancy signal above, value is marginal even setting aside installability.
summary: ThinkDashboard is a small, single-container Go app (one HTTP port 8080, one bind-mounted data directory of JSON files, a pinned image tag available on GHCR) that has zero built-in authentication — including on its `/config` settings page — so it must ship behind a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate, exactly like WUD or Adminer. Mechanically that is installable today with no blocking issues. The catalogue case is weaker: it's a genuinely new category (no existing bookmark-dashboard recipe) but a low-stakes, single-user personal utility, and the upstream project went from an unusually fast release cadence (15 releases in six weeks) to total silence for roughly 8 months with no announcement, which is a meaningful risk for a young, single-maintainer project. Recommend build_with_caveats: technically buildable now, but low priority given thin customer value and an unclear maintenance trajectory upstream.

name: Thruk
source_description: Multi-backend web interface for Naemon, Nagios, Icinga, and Shinken monitoring
version_health_notes: 3.28 published 2026-04-09, about 4 months before today (2026-08-05). Changes history shows a steady quarterly cadence through 2025-2026: 3.22 (2025-04-12), 3.22.2 (2025-05-28), 3.24 (2025-10-02), 3.26 (2026-02-06), 3.28 (2026-04-09). Repo is not archived, has 14k+ commits, and open issues/PRs are actively triaged — clearly active, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: uptime-kuma is our existing monitoring recipe, but it's a self-contained synthetic monitor: it performs its own HTTP/TCP/ping checks against URLs the customer enters in its UI. Thruk is not a monitoring engine at all — it's a Livestatus web frontend that visualizes and lets you acknowledge/schedule-downtime against an existing Naemon/Nagios/Icinga/ Shinken core. It has zero built-in checks of its own; all value comes from a backend monitoring core with host/service definitions that the customer (or the recipe) must configure separately. So it's adjacent to uptime-kuma by category, not a duplicate of its actual functionality, but it also can't stand alone the way uptime-kuma does.
usefulness_rationale: Thruk by itself is a UI shell with nothing to display until a Naemon/Nagios/Icinga backend exists with real host/service checks configured — a non-trivial sysadmin task (writing monitoring-object config files) that most self-hosting customers won't do. uptime-kuma already covers the "watch is my site up" use case with zero configuration burden, which is what most customers actually want from a monitoring recipe.
blocking_issues:
Thruk's own upstream (sni/Thruk) publishes no Docker image at all — it's a Perl/mod_perl application shipped via OS packages or bundled inside ConSol's OMD (Open Monitoring Distribution). The only actively-maintained container path found is consol/omd-labs-debian (or -rocky), which bundles Thruk together with a full Naemon core, rrdcached, npcd and Apache into one heavyweight image — this would ship as an "OMD monitoring stack" recipe, not a "Thruk" recipe, and is a materially different (and much larger) deliverable than what the candidate name implies.

Even with that bundled image, the omdadmin login gets a random password generated at container startup and printed to container logs — not something af-api's ROOT_PASSWORD-hash projection or any other current mechanism can retrieve and hand back to the customer. A Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the whole app (same pattern as Adminer/ThingsBoard) sidesteps needing that specific credential, but the underlying app is still unusable out of the box: an empty Naemon core has no hosts/services to monitor until the customer authors monitoring-object config by hand, which the recipe mechanism has no channel to pre-populate either.
summary: Thruk is not a standalone deployable app in the way our catalogue expects — it's a Livestatus frontend with no monitoring engine or Docker image of its own, only reachable in practice through ConSol's much heavier OMD bundle. Even setting the missing-official-image problem aside with a Traefik basic_auth gate, the resulting recipe would boot to an empty monitoring UI with nothing configured, since defining hosts/services requires hand-authored config the recipe mechanism can't inject. Combined with uptime-kuma already covering the "self-hosted monitoring" niche with a zero-config synthetic-check experience, this is a low-value, not cleanly installable candidate: not_recommended.

name: Thumbor
source_description: Smart open-source image server with face-aware cropping and on-the-fly resize
version_health_notes: Latest tag 7.8.0 was cut 2026-05-30 (~2.2 months before this analysis, 2026-08-05), closing several privately-reported security issues (file loader path bypass, URL signature validation, DoS in filters). The prior release (7.7.7) was 2025-05-15, so the 7.7.7->7.8.0 gap was ~12.5 months — but repo commit activity is continuous and recent (commits as late as 2026-08-02, three days before this analysis), 23 open issues still being triaged, not archived. Long gaps between tags with steady commit activity in between; treating as active rather than slowing/dormant given the ongoing daily development.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a headless image-processing/resize proxy. Immich is the closest thing by subject matter (photos) but is a full self-hosted photo library with its own web UI, auth, and mobile apps — a completely different product. Thumbor has no comparable counterpart in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Thumbor is an unauthenticated, API-only microservice: you call it with HMAC-signed URLs (e.g. /<sig>/300x200/smart/path/to/image.jpg) from your own website/app code, and it returns a transformed image. It has no dashboard, no login screen, and nothing to look at if a customer just visits the domain — the entire value only shows up once the customer writes integration code in their own separate application to generate signed URLs and point it at this service. Every other recipe in the catalogue gives the customer a working app UI on first boot; Thumbor gives them a bare backend that requires developer work elsewhere to do anything visible. That makes it a poor fit for AF's self-hosted-app customer model even though it is a solid, well-regarded piece of infrastructure for people who do build image-heavy sites.
summary: Thumbor is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8888) image server with MIT license and an actively-developed (if slow-tagging) upstream. It has no login of its own; its only "secret" is SECURITY_KEY, an HMAC signing key that can be generated server-side and never needs to reach the customer, so mechanically nothing blocks shipping it as a recipe today. The reason not to build it isn't the installability mechanism — it's that Thumbor has no web UI at all. Legitimate use requires the customer to already run a separate website/app and write code to produce HMAC-signed image URLs; gating the whole thing behind Traefik basic_auth (the usual fallback for no-login apps) would actually break its intended use, since browsers loading tags for anonymous site visitors don't supply basic-auth credentials. Recommend not building this recipe: it's a developer-integration component, not a stand-alone self-hosted app a customer installs and uses directly, which is a structural mismatch with the rest of the catalogue.

name: Tianji
source_description: All-in-one hub for website analytics, uptime, and server status monitoring
version_health_notes: Latest tag (1.32.21) was published the same day as this analysis (2026-08-05). GitHub releases show several tags per week in the run-up (1.32.17 on 2026-07-26, 1.32.19/1.32.20 on 2026-08-02, 1.32.21 on 2026-08-05) — rapid, ongoing development, not a stale or wind-down pattern.
differentiation: Uptime Kuma only does uptime/status-page monitoring. Tianji bundles that with self-hosted website analytics (page views/visitors, UTM tracking, a privacy-friendly alternative to Umami/Plausible, neither of which is in the catalogue) and server-status reporting in one deployable app. A customer wanting analytics + uptime today would need two separate recipes; Tianji covers both with one install.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted web analytics is a common ask with no existing catalogue entry, and folding uptime/server-status monitoring into the same app reduces the number of services a customer has to run. Active upstream development lowers abandonment risk.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: JWT_SECRET; POSTGRES_PASSWORD; Traefik basic-auth gate credential
blocking_issues: Tianji has its own login, but the account is created via a public self-registration page, not a fixed admin parameter — there is no env var that sets an initial admin username/password. Upstream's own docker-compose.yml ships with ALLOW_REGISTER: false, which means nobody (including the customer) can create an account on a stock deploy. To make the recipe usable at all, ALLOW_REGISTER must be set to true — but unlike n8n's one-shot "first visitor becomes owner" setup wizard, Tianji's registration page stays open indefinitely, so ALLOW_REGISTER: true left in place permanently would let ANY visitor to the domain self-register an account for the life of the deployment, not just before the customer's first visit. Our current mechanism has no channel to flip that env var back to false after the customer's first login (no customer-facing settings write-back, no post-deploy config channel). The only mitigation expressible today is fronting the whole app with a Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password projection) so only the customer can reach the registration page at all — this is a workaround for a persistent open-registration risk, not a clean fit for the generated_from/basic_auth decision table, which assumes the app has no login of its own or a single fixed admin credential to project into.
summary: Tianji is an actively developed, Apache-2.0, single-web-UI app (Postgres backend, reverse-proxy-friendly) that would add self-hosted analytics to the catalogue and partially overlaps Uptime Kuma on the monitoring side. It clears the mechanical bar for installable_today, but only via a double-gate workaround: a Traefik basic_auth wrapper (projected from the customer's root password) to keep the domain private, combined with ALLOW_REGISTER left permanently on so the customer can self-register their own Tianji admin account behind that gate. That's a heavier, less-precedented setup than our other single-login recipes and should be called out explicitly if this moves to af-create-recipe, rather than assumed to work the way n8n's one-time owner wizard does.

name: TiddlyWiki
source_description: Self-hosted non-linear personal wiki and knowledge management notebook
version_health_notes: 5.4.1 published 2026-07-10, about 4 weeks before today (2026-08-05); it was a quick regression/bugfix follow-up to 5.4.0. The repo has 8.6k stars, 930 open issues and 217 open PRs under active triage, an active Google Group / Discord / Reddit community, and a steady multi-release cadence through 2025-2026 (5.3.x line through most of 2025, 5.4.0/5.4.1 in mid-2026) — clearly active, not maintenance-only. Copyright of the project is held in trust by the UnaMesa Society non-profit, which adds long-term stewardship continuity beyond any single maintainer.
differentiation: The closest existing peer is recipes/anytype-server, described as "a privacy-focused note-taking and knowledge management app" in the same `productivity` category. It does not constitute overlap: anytype-server is a headless any-sync backend (any-sync-node, any-sync-filenode, any-sync-coordinator) with raw TCP sync ports (`http: false`) and no web UI of its own — it is consumed exclusively through the separate AnyType desktop/mobile client apps and is not reverse-proxy/Traefik- fronted the way our HTTP recipes are. TiddlyWiki, by contrast, is a fully browser-based wiki: point a browser at the domain and you get the entire non-linear, tiddler-based editing UI with no separate client install or sync protocol to expose. Beyond anytype-server, nothing else in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers personal wiki/note-taking either — Paperless-ngx and Paperless-AI are document management/OCR for existing files, Opengist is code-snippet sharing, and Gitea is source control — none of these serve TiddlyWiki's non-linear, tiddler-based personal knowledge base use case. It's a genuinely distinct niche (a "second brain" notebook) that would add real breadth to the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Personal wikis are a well-known, popular self-hosting use case (see also Wiki.js, Outline, TriliumNext) and TiddlyWiki's zero-database, single-file-or-Node-server model is lightweight and appealing for a small VPS deployment. Usefulness is medium rather than high because TiddlyWiki's own most common deployment mode is a single static HTML file edited locally in-browser with no server at all — the Node.js server mode we'd package is the less typical "always-on shared/synced wiki" path, a smaller slice of TiddlyWiki's actual user base.
blocking_issues:
The TiddlyWiki/TiddlyWiki5 upstream repo publishes no official Docker image or Dockerfile of its own — it ships as an npm package (`tiddlywiki`) plus a single-file HTML wiki, with Node.js server mode documented as an advanced/secondary usage path. Every recipe currently in this catalogue consumes a pre-built, officially published image (confirmed by scanning all 24 `docker-compose.yaml` files: none build a custom image), so this would be a first-of-its- kind departure from that pattern.

The two most visible third-party images are both weak substitutes: elasticdog/tiddlywiki rebuilds on a monthly cadence (most recent tag ~4 months before today) but the bundled TiddlyWiki version is pinned at 5.1.23 — three minor versions and roughly 2+ years behind the current 5.4.1 — so the "freshness" of its build dates is cosmetic, not a freshness of the actual app. m0wer/tiddlywiki bundles a newer 5.2.7 but the upstream repo commit history shows it was explicitly marked "UNMAINTAINED" in 2021 with no commits since April 2023. Neither is a safe long-term base image; shipping this recipe would mean either accepting a stale/unmaintained third-party image or authoring and maintaining a small custom Dockerfile around the official `tiddlywiki` npm package — extra ongoing maintenance burden this catalogue doesn't currently carry for any other recipe.

TiddlyWiki's Node.js server has no built-in login by default (anonymous read/write) unless the operator explicitly configures `username`/`password` or `readers`/`writers` ACL parameters at server startup — those are plain CLI arguments, not something `generated_from` (which only ever supplies a password *hash*) can populate. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate sidesteps this cleanly (same pattern as Adminer/ThingsBoard) since the app itself needs no login of its own to function.
summary: TiddlyWiki is an active, well-established project with no existing overlap in our 24-recipe catalogue, and its lack of built-in authentication is fully solvable today with a Traefik basic_auth gate — the auth mechanism is not the blocker. The real caveat is the Docker image: upstream publishes none, and the two community alternatives are either years out of date on the actual TiddlyWiki version or explicitly abandoned, meaning a recipe here would either ship a stale image or require authoring and maintaining a custom Dockerfile, a pattern this catalogue does not currently use anywhere else. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth doing, but plan for either accepting the version lag or owning a small custom image.

name: TimescaleDB
source_description: Time-series database built on PostgreSQL for fast ingest and analytics at scale
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (core extension); the official Docker image (timescale/timescaledb) additionally bundles Timescale-Licensed features — the Apache-2.0-only build is the "-oss" tagged image
version_health_notes: timescale/timescaledb-docker tags are pushed roughly monthly, with the latest-pg18/2.26.1-pg18 build landing within the last week (as of 2026-08-05). The upstream company (now branded "Tiger Data") is actively developing and shipping new PostgreSQL major-version support (pg18 added 2026). No archival, EOL notice, or slowdown signal — this is a commercially backed, actively released project.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a standalone, customer-provisioned database product — existing recipes (n8n, paperless-ngx, gitea, immich, etc.) all run Postgres/MySQL as an internal, unexposed implementation detail of the app, not as the product itself. TimescaleDB would be the first "bring your own client and connect over the wire" database recipe, aimed at developers who want managed time-series storage (IoT telemetry, metrics, sensor data) without provisioning Postgres + the extension by hand.
usefulness_rationale: Real technical value for a narrow developer/analytics audience, but it is a raw SQL server with no web surface at all — the customer's only interaction is a Postgres connection string over TCP 5432, and publishing that port is exactly what our own recipe rules forbid (see `blocking_issues`). Same structural class as PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB (apps-gaps/postgresql.yaml, apps-gaps/mysql.yaml, apps-gaps/mariadb.yaml) — raw-protocol RDBMS engines with no application-layer presence to gate behind Traefik.
blocking_issues:
The only useful shape for a standalone TimescaleDB recipe is a publicly reachable Postgres-protocol port so an external customer app can connect to it (timescale/timescaledb extends the official postgres image and speaks the identical wire protocol on 5432). Publishing host port 5432 is exactly what RFC-002's `no-public-db-port` rule forbids (rfc/002-recipe-rules.md:220-226) — 5432 is explicitly on the forbidden-host-port list. There is no alternate exposure path today: Traefik only routes HTTP, and Postgres speaks a raw binary wire protocol, so it cannot be fronted the way our web-UI recipes are (no `basic_auth`, no subdomain routing).

Even setting the port rule aside, the superuser password is only projectable via `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` (a plaintext env var, which `generated_from` does not produce) — same as upstream Postgres, the image has no pre-hashed-password input at all (unlike MySQL/ MariaDB's `*_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASH` variants). This is not a `blocked_on_platform`-shaped gap waiting on a new supported hash algorithm; Postgres/TimescaleDB structurally requires the plaintext password at container start, which `generated_from` can never supply. Moot anyway given the public-port blocker above.
summary: TimescaleDB is an actively released, commercially backed project (Tiger Data, monthly image cadence, PostgreSQL 18 support shipped days before this analysis) with no EOL or dormancy concerns. It doesn't overlap any existing recipe since every current Postgres usage in the catalogue is internal to another app, not customer-facing. But a standalone TimescaleDB recipe has no viable shape in the current catalogue: its only useful exposure — a public, customer-reachable 5432 — is explicitly forbidden by our own `no-public-db-port` rule, and it has no web UI to gate behind Traefik/basic_auth the way our other no-login apps do. This is the identical structural mismatch documented for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB (timescale/timescaledb is literally the postgres image with an extension bundled on top) — a raw internet-facing DB port that our security rules and Traefik-only routing model don't support, and a plaintext-only password variable with no hashed-credential channel. Recommend not_recommended rather than blocked_on_platform, since no plausible mechanism change fixes this without relaxing a deliberate security rule.
