name: Tinode
source_description: Open-source instant messaging server with mobile and web clients and group chats
upstream_docker_image: tinode/tinode-mysql (also published as tinode-postgres, tinode-mongodb, tinode-rethinkdb variants per database backend)
version_health_notes: v0.25.3 shipped 2026-07-04, about a month before this analysis (2026-08-05). Recent history shows a steady monthly-ish cadence: v0.24.6 (2025-10-10), v0.24.7 (2025-11-07), v0.25.0 (2025-12-21), v0.25.1 (2025-12-26), v0.25.2 (2026-03-03), v0.25.3 (2026-07-04). The main branch had commits as recently as 2026-08-01. Matching Docker Hub tags exist up to 0.25.3, pushed about a month ago. Clearly active, not maintenance-only, archived, or EOL — though upstream itself describes the project as "beta-quality: feature-complete and stable but probably with a few bugs or missing features," which is a product- maturity caveat distinct from release-cadence health.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers chat/messaging, so this would open a new category rather than duplicate anything. Against the other messaging candidates already analysed under apps-gaps/ (apps-gaps/matrix-synapse.yaml, apps-gaps/rocketchat.yaml, apps-gaps/mattermost.yaml), Tinode is architecturally closer to Rocket.Chat/Mattermost — a single self-contained server image with its own bundled web client — than to Matrix Synapse, which needs a separate client like Element. Structurally closest to recipes/n8n and recipes/paperless-ngx (single app container + one dedicated database container behind a single Traefik hostname).
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted chat/messaging is a recurring self-hosting request and would be the first entry in a "communication" category. Tinode is less well-known and less feature-complete than Rocket.Chat or Matrix (upstream self-describes as beta-quality), and its web client is more basic, so it is a reasonable but not standout option — usefulness is capped at medium relative to the stronger Rocket.Chat/Synapse candidates already in apps-gaps/, pending which of these the catalogue actually prioritizes for the "communication" slot.
blocking_issues:
Tinode has no admin/root login of its own that can be provisioned via config or environment variable at boot. Unlike Rocket.Chat's `ADMIN_PASS` or Synapse's `register_new_matrix_user` script, there is no first-run mechanism to seed a privileged account at all — `root` access is granted post-deployment by directly editing the database (pre-v0.18) or via the `tinode-db` init tool / manual `tn-cli` commands run against an already-running server, none of which take a customer-supplied value through `/compose`. There is therefore no `type: password` parameter for `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` to project into, and per SCHEMA.md's decision table a missing provisioning channel entirely (not just a plaintext-vs-hash mismatch) is a structural blocker.

Tinode's default auth config (`docker/tinode/config.template` / `server/tinode.conf`) has no toggle to disable open self-registration — any visitor who reaches the deployed domain can create a new account via the bundled web client or any Tinode mobile client. Combined with the lack of an admin credential, this means whoever reaches the domain first has no more or less access than the customer — there is no privileged account to protect and no way to close the door after boot.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate is not a workable substitute for the same reason given in apps-gaps/rocketchat.yaml and apps-gaps/mattermost.yaml: Tinode is inherently multi-user chat software served over one HTTP port carrying both the web client and the JSON/WebSocket (or gRPC) API every client — including the customer's own contacts — connects through. A permanent basic-auth gate over that port would block every other participant from ever reaching the chat, not just protect an admin panel, and there is no documented way to lift the gate for regular users while keeping any admin surface protected.
summary: Tinode is an actively developed (monthly-ish releases, v0.25.3 on 2026-07-04) GPL-3.0 instant-messaging server with its own bundled web client, fitting cleanly behind a single Traefik hostname as one app container plus one database container (MySQL/Postgres/MongoDB). It would open a currently-empty "communication" category with no overlap against the existing 24 recipes, but usefulness is only medium given upstream's own beta-quality framing and the stronger Rocket.Chat/Synapse candidates already in apps-gaps/. It is not installable today: Tinode has no first-boot admin-provisioning channel at all (root access is granted post-deployment via DB edits or CLI tools, not a config/env value), self-registration cannot be disabled, and a Traefik basic-auth gate can't substitute without blocking every legitimate chat participant on the same port. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`, revisit alongside apps-gaps/rocketchat.yaml and apps-gaps/matrix-synapse.yaml if the platform ever gains a way to seed a first-boot admin credential for chat-style apps.

name: Tiny File Manager
source_description: Single-file PHP web file manager for browsing and managing server files
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release 2.6 published 2024-11-05, about 21 months before today (2026-08-05) — no tagged release since. Release history is irregular: multiple releases in 2018-2019 and again 2019-2020, then a ~21-month gap to 2.4.7 (2022-02-12), a ~9-month gap to 2.5.0 (2022-11-19), a ~3-month gap to 2.5.3 (2023-02-22), and a ~21-month gap to 2.6. The repo itself is not dormant — GitHub API shows a push as recently as 2026-07-20 (about 2.5 weeks before today) and 5,959 stars — so classifying `eol_status: active` rather than `maintenance-only`, but `release_cadence: sporadic` because tagged cuts are far apart and unpredictable despite ongoing commit activity.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a general-purpose web file browser/manager for the server's own filesystem. Syncthing synchronizes files between devices rather than browsing a single server's disk through a UI; Portainer manages Docker containers, not arbitrary files; Paperless-ngx/Paperless-AI manage ingested documents with OCR, not raw file trees. Tiny File Manager fills a distinct, common self-hosting niche: browse/upload/edit/rename/delete files in a mounted directory (e.g. shared storage, backups, static-site assets) through a plain browser UI, no SSH/SFTP client needed.
usefulness_rationale: A lightweight web file manager is a genuinely useful utility recipe — it's one of the most commonly requested self-hosted tools precisely because it needs no client software. Usefulness is medium rather than high because it only manages whatever directory is mounted into the container (not the customer's full server filesystem, which would be a serious security exposure to run behind a web login), narrowing it to a "manage this one data volume" tool rather than the full sysadmin file-manager pitch its name implies, and because more actively maintained/more capable alternatives exist in the same space (e.g. FileBrowser, Filestash).
blocking_issues:
The app has no environment-variable-based credential input. Its shipped default admin/admin@123 and user/12345 logins are hardcoded in the PHP source and can only be overridden by mounting a `config.php` file containing a PHP `$auth_users` array whose values are `password_hash()` outputs (bcrypt by default — a supported `generated_from` algorithm). This is expressible today by having install.sh render that config.php from a template before `compose up` (the same file-templating pattern recipes/guacamole/install.sh already uses for its DB init script), not a hard blocker — but it's a file-mount workaround rather than a plain env var, more moving parts than most `generated_from` recipes to date.

The official `tinyfilemanager/tinyfilemanager` Docker Hub repo has no tag matching the latest 2.6 source release: the only pinned, versioned tags published are `2.5.3` (2023-02-22) and `2.4.7` (2022-02-12), both older than 2.6, which shipped a documented path traversal fix among its changes. The only tag that tracks current source is `master`, rebuilt on every upstream commit (most recently 2026-07-20) — a moving target, not a stable pin, and against this catalogue's never-`:latest`-equivalent pinning discipline. Building this recipe today means either pinning to the outdated 2.5.3 image (missing the 2.6 path-traversal fix) or tracking the unversioned `master` tag.
summary: Tiny File Manager is a genuinely distinct utility (no existing recipe browses/manages a mounted directory through a web UI) and its auth can be projected via generated_from, though only by templating a mounted config.php rather than a plain env var. The real caveat is image freshness: the official Docker Hub image is stuck two releases behind the latest 2.6 source tag, which includes a real security fix (path traversal), leaving a choice between an outdated pinned tag or an unversioned `master` tag. Combined with a sporadic, unpredictable release cadence, recommend build_with_caveats — worth doing, but flag the image-pin tradeoff explicitly before building.

name: Tiny Tiny RSS
source_description: Self-hosted, multi-user RSS aggregator with mobile client API support
upstream_docker_image: ghcr.io/tt-rss/tt-rss (paired with ghcr.io/tt-rss/tt-rss-web-nginx as the front-end container; Postgres for the database)
latest_version: rolling release, no semantic versions — most recent image build tag 20260803-212347
version_health_notes: Important context beyond a simple cadence check: the *original* tt-rss project (maintained by Andrew Dolgov, "fox", at git.tt-rss.org since 2005) was discontinued by its own maintainer on 2025-10-03, with all original infrastructure (git host, forum, cgit) scheduled for shutdown on 2025-11-01. A long-time contributor forked the project the same day (2025-10-03) as github.com/tt-rss/tt-rss, and ownership of the tt-rss.org domain was transferred to the fork's maintainer, so tt-rss.org now serves the fork's docs — this is why upstream docs read as continuous rather than describing a handoff. The fork has been building official multi-arch images (ghcr.io/tt-rss/tt-rss and ghcr.io/tt-rss/tt-rss-web-nginx) continuously since, with new tags roughly daily (e.g. 20260803-212347, 20260803-215733, 20260804-021224 observed within the days immediately before/after this analysis date of 2026-08-05). Given the project uses a rolling main-branch release model (no tagged versions even before the handoff), "release cadence" is best read as "is main still being built and shipped," which it clearly is. That said, the maintainer transition happened only ~10 months ago and is worth flagging: the original author explicitly said tt-rss had become unfun to maintain and infrastructure was in decline, so the fork's long-term continuity is less proven than a project with a multi-year post-handoff track record.
differentiation: No RSS/feed-reader recipe exists in the current 24-recipe catalogue, but this is not a novel gap: apps-gaps/freshrss.yaml (recommended build_now) and apps-gaps/miniflux.yaml (blocked_on_platform, same plaintext-admin-password issue analyzed below) already cover this niche. Tiny Tiny RSS's distinguishing feature over both is a documented Fever-API-compatible mobile client protocol used by several third-party RSS apps, plus native multi-user support — but FreshRSS already offers a Fever/Google-Reader-compatible API too, so the differentiation from FreshRSS specifically is thin. Architecturally it is a three-container stack (PHP-FPM app + nginx web front-end + Postgres), closest to recipes/n8n and recipes/paperless-ngx (app + dedicated Postgres behind one Traefik hostname), plus one extra nginx container for static/proxy duties.
usefulness_rationale: The feed-reader niche this would fill is already better served in apps-gaps/ by FreshRSS, which is installable today with no blocker and needs only a single lightweight container (SQLite default, no separate DB). Tiny Tiny RSS adds a heavier three-container footprint, the same installability blocker as Miniflux, and a maintainer-transition history less than a year old — there is no scenario where a reviewer would pick it over FreshRSS for this slot.
blocking_issues:
The admin account password is set via the `ADMIN_USER_PASS` environment variable, which the official docker entrypoint re-applies on every container startup by calling tt-rss's own user-management routine — this routine takes the plaintext password and hashes it internally (tt-rss stores credentials as a salted hash, e.g. `SHA1:<hash>`, in the `pwd_hash` column of `ttrss_users`). There is no documented way to supply a pre-computed hash directly into that column instead of a plaintext value. `generated_from` can only ever project a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext itself, so per SCHEMA.md's decision table this is the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case — a structural blocker, not a supported-algorithm gap IF-1420 could close.

Gating the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` (the n8n/WUD pattern) does not resolve this on its own, for the same reason noted in apps-gaps/miniflux.yaml: tt-rss presents its own separate login screen behind any such gate, and without a way to set the admin password to something the customer knows, the customer would be locked out of the app itself even after passing the basic-auth gate. Since tt-rss does not support open self-registration by default (only an admin can create additional users), there is no way for the customer to create their own account either.

tt-rss ships an `auth_remote` plugin that can trust an externally authenticated identity, but it reads PHP's `REMOTE_USER` server variable — natively populated by e.g. Apache's own Basic Auth module — not an arbitrary forwarded header from a separate reverse proxy. Community reports describe unresolved friction getting nginx `auth_request`/header-forwarding setups to populate it correctly, so unlike Miniflux's documented `AUTH_PROXY_HEADER` + `TRUSTED_REVERSE_PROXY_NETWORKS` path (itself still unvetted for our platform), tt-rss's remote-auth story is less mature and not a reliable bridge from a Traefik `basic_auth` login today.
summary: Tiny Tiny RSS is a three-container stack (PHP-FPM app, nginx front-end, Postgres) whose original maintainer discontinued the project on 2025-11-01, immediately succeeded by an active community fork (github.com/tt-rss/tt-rss, tt-rss.org domain transferred) that has shipped near-daily rolling image builds since — so it is not EOL, but its post-handoff track record is under a year old. It would fill a currently empty RSS-reader category, but that category is already better addressed by apps-gaps/freshrss.yaml (build_now, single lightweight container, no blocker) and shares the exact same structural blocker already documented for apps-gaps/miniflux.yaml: the admin account can only be seeded with a plaintext password via `ADMIN_USER_PASS`, which `generated_from` cannot supply, and a Traefik `basic_auth` gate would still leave the customer locked out of tt-rss's own login. Given FreshRSS already covers this niche installably, recommend `not_recommended` rather than `blocked_on_platform` — even if the plaintext-password blocker were lifted, this app would not add anything FreshRSS doesn't already offer more cheaply.

name: TinyAuth
source_description: Lightweight Traefik forward-auth middleware for protecting self-hosted apps
version_health_notes: Latest stable v5.1.3 shipped 2026-07-30, less than a week before today (2026-08-05), fixing a security advisory (GHSA-r27r-rr9v-vv37). Release history shows a rapid cadence — multiple point releases and release candidates per month (v5.1.1 on 2026-07-17, v5.1.2 with five betas 2026-07-18/20, v5.1.3 2026-07-30, nightly builds continuing through 2026-08-06). Repo is not archived, 8k+ stars, last push 2026-08-06 — this is a young but very actively developed project, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes is a forward-auth/SSO gateway. TinyAuth is architecturally a much lighter alternative to Authentik or Authelia (single small Go binary, one container, no database dependency in its simple username/password mode) that adds a login page plus OAuth/LDAP/TOTP options in front of whatever it's paired with via Traefik's `forwardAuth` middleware. However, TinyAuth's whole value proposition is centralizing login for *multiple* self-hosted apps sitting behind one Traefik instance — a customer wires TinyAuth's forwardAuth middleware onto several other containers' routers. AF's recipe model provisions each recipe as its own independently networked stack with its own Traefik router; there is no mechanism today for one recipe's middleware to be attached to a different recipe's router. So inside AF, a standalone TinyAuth recipe could only gate itself (or a demo service shipped alongside it) — a capability the platform already provides for any app via a Traefik `basic_auth: true` toggle, with no extra container, RAM, or moving parts.
usefulness_rationale: Mechanically sound and popular upstream, but under AF's current per-recipe, independently-networked deployment model its core use case (one shared login gate wired across several other apps) isn't reachable. Shipping it as a single-app recipe would only reproduce, at the cost of a whole extra container, what the existing Traefik `basic_auth` gate already does for any recipe today. Revisit if AF ever supports cross-recipe/shared-network middleware wiring — that's the scenario where TinyAuth's actual differentiation (one login for many apps, OAuth/LDAP/2FA options) becomes real value to a customer.
summary: TinyAuth is a small, actively maintained (v5.1.3, 2026-07-30) Traefik forward-auth gateway. Mechanically it is installable today: verified against the pinned v5.1.3 `.env.example` and getting-started docs, its only required-at-first-boot credential is `TINYAUTH_AUTH_USERS`, a comma-separated `username:bcrypt-hash[:totp]` list generated via `tinyauth user create --interactive`, which for a single pair maps cleanly onto `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, with no blocking secrets — v5.1.3 has no general session/cookie-signing secret variable (unlike older v2/v3 releases). `TINYAUTH_AUTH_TRUSTEDPROXIES` (recommended for reverse-proxy setups, e.g. `172.17.0.0/16` for Docker) is a non-secret config value to set in the compose file, not a customer secret. The reason not to build it isn't installability but fit: its entire reason for existing — one shared login wired via Traefik middleware across several independently-hosted apps — has no equivalent in AF's one-recipe-one-stack provisioning model, where the same self-protection it could offer is already covered by the existing Traefik `basic_auth` toggle at zero extra cost. Recommend `not_recommended` for now; worth revisiting only if AF gains cross-recipe shared-middleware support.

name: Traccar
source_description: Open-source GPS tracking platform supporting 200+ protocols and devices
version_health_notes: v6.14.5 shipped 2026-06-18, 48 days before today (2026-08-05). Release history shows a consistent multi-year cadence of roughly one minor/patch release every 2-8 weeks: v6.11.0/6.11.1 on 2025-12-07, v6.12.0-6.12.2 spanning 2026-02-22 to 2026-02-27, v6.13.0-6.13.3 spanning 2026-05-02 to 2026-05-06, and v6.14.0-6.14.5 spanning 2026-05-30 to 2026-06-18. The current ~48-day gap since 6.14.5 sits inside the normal range seen between prior minor-version clusters (the 6.12→6.13 gap was ~9 weeks), so this reads as a normal lull rather than a slowdown. Project is clearly still actively developed, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: Traccar is a GPS tracking/fleet-management server: it ingests live location reports from 200+ GPS tracker protocols and 2000+ device models, and presents a web UI for real-time map tracking, geofencing, trip history, and reporting. Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue touches IoT device connectivity or fleet/asset tracking; the closest neighbor by shape is Home Assistant (self-hosted device dashboard) but it serves a completely different device class and use case. Genuinely new ground for the catalogue. Note on "reverse_proxy_compatible: false": this applies to the app as a whole, not the web UI in isolation — the Web UI itself (port 8082, HTTP/WebSocket) fronts fine behind Traefik like any other recipe. But Traccar's actual value proposition is device connectivity: physical GPS trackers dial in over ~200 distinct plain TCP/UDP protocol listeners (commonly ports 5000-5150+, one port per protocol family, configured per-protocol in traccar.xml) that are not HTTP and cannot be fronted by Traefik. A deployment that only exposes the web UI is a tracking platform with no way for any tracker to report a location — it would ship a shell of the product. Making this useful means publishing a meaningful subset of those raw ports directly (the wg-easy recipe's `public: true, http: false` port pattern shows the mechanism exists), but Traccar needs dozens of them rather than the one or two seen in existing raw-port recipes, and the customer's actual device fleet determines which protocols/ports matter — a fixed built-in subset may not match what a given customer owns.
usefulness_rationale: Clear, recognizable use case (self-hosted fleet/asset tracking as an alternative to commercial GPS-tracking SaaS) for a real audience (delivery/logistics operators, vehicle fleets, personal device trackers). Capped at medium rather than high because the raw-port surface area needed for the core feature (device ingestion) is large and customer-fleet-dependent, which is an awkward fit for a fixed-port-list recipe model, and the target audience is narrower than general productivity/infra tools already in the catalogue.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: Traefik gate credential (Traccar has no admin credential of its own to project — see notes)
secrets_expressible_today: Traefik gate credential (Traccar has no admin credential of its own to project — see notes):traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
Traccar has no built-in default admin account and no config/env mechanism to pre-seed one: settings in traccar.xml for username/password are ignored, and there is no INITIAL_PASSWORD/INITIAL_PASSWORD_HASH-style env var. Instead, the very first user to register through the web UI (or POST to /api/users) automatically becomes admin — a self-registration race, not a login generated_from can project into. The only safe path is putting the real auth boundary at a Traefik basic_auth gate (keyed off the customer's root-password hash) so nobody but the customer can reach the registration endpoint at all; the customer then self-registers their own admin account from inside the gate. This is expressible today but is a different shape from our other recipes and should be called out in review.
Full device-tracking functionality needs dozens of raw TCP/UDP ports (one per GPS protocol family, commonly in the 5000-5150+ range) published directly, not proxied through Traefik. Mechanically expressible per-port (same pattern as wg-easy's UDP port), but the number of ports needed is large and depends on which tracker protocols the customer's own devices use — no fixed subset is guaranteed to cover a given customer's fleet without either publishing a large port block or asking the customer which protocols they need (an input we have no channel for today).
summary: Traccar is a mature (Apache-2.0), actively maintained GPS-tracking/fleet server with no existing overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue — genuinely new ground. It clears the installability bar in the narrow mechanical sense: it has no fixed admin credential to project, so the workable pattern is a Traefik basic_auth gate (keyed off the customer's root-password hash) as the real auth boundary, behind which the customer self-registers their own first-and-only admin account — no plaintext or hash-incompatible field to fight, unlike apps with a stuck INITIAL_PASSWORD env var. The bigger caveat is architectural rather than auth-related: Traccar's actual product value is ingesting live GPS reports over ~200 raw TCP/UDP device protocols, which Traefik cannot front, so a recipe that only exposes the web UI would ship a tracking platform no tracker can report into. Shipping this well means publishing a meaningful, customer-fleet-dependent block of raw ports — mechanically possible (wg-easy already proves the pattern) but a bigger and blunter raw-port footprint than anything currently in the catalogue. Recommend build_with_caveats: both the auth gate and the raw-port strategy need explicit sign-off before this becomes a recipe.

Installability needs a workaround, not a straight port: Traduora seeds a default admin (TR_SEED_DATA=true, TR_ADMIN_EMAIL/TR_ADMIN_PASSWORD), but per its own source (api/src/seeds/user.seed.ts → UserService.create) the password must arrive as plaintext — the app itself runs `bcrypt.hash(password, 10)` on whatever string is supplied, so it cannot accept a pre-computed hash and there is no `generated_from` channel to seed a customer-specific admin login. It also defaults to open self-signup (TR_SIGNUPS_ENABLED=true) with per-project roles rather than one instance-wide admin, so anyone reaching the URL could create their own account. The fix: set TR_SIGNUPS_ENABLED=false, treat the seeded default admin as an internal detail no customer needs, and gate the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth with `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` — the same "fixed/default credential behind a gate" pattern SCHEMA.md treats as acceptable (see Adminer), making Traefik the real customer- facing auth boundary instead of Traduora's own login. Recommend build_with_caveats: worth building, but the recipe must document and enforce TR_SIGNUPS_ENABLED=false plus the basic_auth gate rather than exposing Traduora's own login UI as the primary credential.

differentiation: TrailBase is a single-binary backend-as-a-service (BaaS): embedded SQLite (experimental Postgres support since v0.28), auto-generated type-safe REST + realtime APIs over existing tables, and a built-in auth system (password + OAuth, JWT-based) with client SDKs for eight languages. It occupies the same product category as Supabase/PocketBase — nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does auto-generated REST APIs over a database plus bundled auth/realtime for app developers; the closest neighbors (n8n, paperless-ngx) are end-user apps with their own fixed UI, not a generic backend a customer would build a separate frontend against. Genuinely new ground for developer-facing customers.
usefulness_rationale: Real, recognizable use case (a low-ops Supabase/Firebase alternative for small apps and prototypes) and a single container with no external dependencies, which is operationally simple to host. Capped at medium rather than high because the target audience (developers building an app against a generic backend) is narrower than the general productivity/infra tools already in the catalogue, and — see `blocking_issues` — the built-in admin dashboard, which is required to configure any of the record APIs/auth that make the product useful in the first place, has no reachable login for a customer under our current install mechanism.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: TrailBase admin login (admin@localhost / auto-generated random password); Traefik gate credential
blocking_issues:
TrailBase creates exactly one admin account on first boot with a hardcoded email (admin@localhost) and a random 20-character password generated in-process and only ever written to the container's stdout log (crates/core/src/app_state.rs: `random_alphanumeric(20)`, then `info!("Created new admin user: ... password: '{password}'")`). There is no env var, config field, or CLI flag to pre-seed this password at startup.
The only way to change it after the fact is `trail user change-password admin@localhost <new-password>` (or `trail user add` / `trail admin promote`), and every one of those CLI subcommands takes the password as a plaintext argument — there is no field anywhere that accepts a pre-computed hash. Our install mechanism only ever has a hash of the customer's root password (`generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`), never the plaintext, so install.sh cannot call any of these commands meaningfully. This is the 'genuine requirement for the plaintext password' case the schema calls a structural blocker, not a missing-algorithm gap IF-1420 would fix.
Unlike Traccar (also admin-credential-less at boot), TrailBase does not fall back to open self-registration for the first user — an admin already exists, just with an unknowable password — so gating the whole app behind Traefik basic_auth does not restore a usable admin path the way it did for Traccar. Nothing (not even a legitimate customer) can reach TrailBase's admin dashboard, which is required to define any record API, table, or auth setting before the backend does anything useful. A recipe built today would ship an inert, empty backend behind a login wall with no way in.
summary: TrailBase is an actively developed (near-weekly releases), genuinely novel addition to the catalogue's shape — a single-binary Supabase/ PocketBase-style backend-as-a-service with no existing overlap. It fails installability for a reason distinct from most other blocked candidates: it isn't missing an input channel for an external API key or OAuth registration, it's that TrailBase's own admin account is created with a random password that is never exposed through any config/env/CLI surface accepting a hash — only plaintext, which our root-password projection mechanism never carries. Because the admin dashboard gates all productive use (defining APIs, tables, auth), a Traefik basic_auth wall cannot substitute the way it does for apps with open self-registration. This is an upstream design gap (no ADMIN_PASSWORD/ADMIN_PASSWORD_HASH env var), not something IF-1420/1312 would unblock, so not_recommended rather than blocked_on_platform.

Transmission accepts rpc-password either as plaintext (which it re-hashes and rewrites into settings.json on daemon startup) or, if the value already starts with "{", as a pre-hashed credential in its own proprietary salted-SHA1 format ("{" + 40-hex-char SHA1 + 8-char salt). Capped at medium rather than high because: (1) the official single-container "testing" mode is explicitly documented by upstream as not a production deployment path — a real Trino install is a coordinator + worker cluster, which is a heavier operational commitment than most of our single-container recipes; (2) it ships with zero useful catalogs configured out of the box (only the built-in `tpch`/`memory` sample catalogs) — a customer gets a working SQL engine with nothing to query until they hand-edit catalog config files inside the container, which is a real but non-trivial post-install step outside our parameter/env-var model; (3) the target audience (data engineers federating multiple data sources) is narrower than the general-purpose productivity/infra tools already in the catalogue.
summary: Trino is active and well-maintained (steady ~monthly releases, no EOL signals) and fills a real gap — no query-federation/analytics engine exists in the current catalogue. Mechanically it is installable today: the official trinodb/trino image runs standalone in a single container on port 8080 with sane defaults and, critically, ships with no authentication configured by default (Web UI accepts any username with no password when the server has no authenticator configured), so a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate is the correct and sufficient fit — there is no app-native login to project a root-password hash into. Recommended `build_with_caveats` rather than `build_now`: upstream itself documents single-container mode as a testing/demo configuration rather than a production deployment (real Trino runs coordinator+worker clusters), and the shipped image has no real data source configured out of the box, so a customer installing this recipe gets a working but functionally empty SQL engine until they add their own catalog configuration by hand — a legitimate but not turnkey experience worth flagging to a human reviewer before committing build effort.

name: Trip
source_description: Self-hosted minimalist map tracker and trip planner for points of interest
version_health_notes: v1.47.0 released 2026-08-01, 4 days before today (2026-08-05). Release history is dense: v1.46.0 (2026-07-25), v1.45.2 (2026-05-30), v1.45.1 (2026-05-20), v1.45.0 (2026-05-19), v1.44.0 (2026-05-04), v1.43.2 (2026-03-21) — roughly every 1-4 weeks with occasional faster patch bursts. Repo created 2025-07-17, `pushed_at` is 2026-08-01, not archived, 1.8k stars / 103 forks, 6 open issues — clearly active and still under 1.5 development. The shipping `docker-compose.yml` pins the image to the floating major-version tag `ghcr.io/itskovacs/trip:1` rather than a specific release like `1.47.0`; a recipe would need to pin to an exact tag per RFC-002, not the upstream default.
differentiation: Nothing shipped in the current 24 recipes covers trip/travel planning or POI mapping. Two structurally similar apps have already been gap-analyzed but not built: apps-gaps/trek.yaml (Trek — collaborative group-trip planner with budgets/packing lists) and apps-gaps/airtrail.yaml (AirTrail — personal flight-log tracker) and apps-gaps/adventurelog.yaml (AdventureLog — travel diary/trip planner). Trip's own pitch is narrower than all three: a minimalist personal POI-map tracker plus lightweight multi-day trip itineraries, with no flight-import, budgeting, or collaboration-first framing. It is a smaller, simpler tool aimed at "pin places on a map and rough out an itinerary" rather than full group-trip logistics — a real but modest differentiator versus Trek/AdventureLog, not a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Clean single-container app (SQLite, bundled frontend+backend, one HTTP port, no unusual runtime needs), actively developed with a healthy release cadence and real GitHub traction (1.8k stars). Capped at medium rather than high because it competes directly with two other already-catalogued-as-candidates travel/POI tools (Trek, AdventureLog) for the same narrow audience segment, and none of the three has shipped yet, so the category's actual customer demand is unproven.
blocking_issues:
Confirmed against the upstream configuration docs (itskovacs.github.io/trip/docs/getting-started/configuration) and the admin-settings docs (.../docs/map-tracker/settings-admin): Trip has no admin-username/admin-password environment variable. The app boots with zero users; registration is open by default (`REGISTER_ENABLE` defaults to enabled) and docs state plainly "First user registered will be set admin." Whoever submits the signup form first — customer or a random internet visitor scanning the freshly exposed port — becomes the sole admin. This is the same structural gap already documented in apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml, apps-gaps/activepieces.yaml, and apps-gaps/airtrail.yaml: there is no `type: password` parameter on Trip's own login to target with `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"`, because the credential is created client-side via self-registration, not injected via env var.

`BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME` only promotes an *already-registered* username to admin on next startup — it does not create an account or set a password, so it cannot be used to pre-provision a customer credential either; a user still has to exist first via the same open signup form.

Setting `REGISTER_ENABLE="false"` before first boot would close signup entirely, including for the customer, since Trip then requires an admin-issued "Magic Link" to create the first account — there is no admin yet to issue one, a chicken-and-egg dead end without manual intervention.

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app would close the "random stranger races to register first" exposure window, but per the 2FAuth/Activepieces/AirTrail precedent it still can't hand the customer a *second*, distinct credential for Trip's own signup form beyond the single root-password projection already spent on the gate — so it doesn't fully resolve the underlying provisioning gap, it only narrows the race to whoever visits the URL immediately after the gate is entered.
summary: Trip is an active, well-maintained, single-container POI-map and trip-planning app (SQLite, one web port, Traefik-compatible) that would add a genuinely uncovered category to the catalogue, though it overlaps in audience with two other still-unshipped travel-planning candidates (Trek, AdventureLog). It fails the installability test for the same structural reason as those two and as 2FAuth/Activepieces/AirTrail: there is no env-var-driven admin account, only an open first-visitor self-registration screen, and neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone can safely hand that credential to the customer exclusively. Revisit once upstream adds an env-var-driven initial-admin flow, or the platform gains a second customer-facing credential channel beyond root-password projection.

name: Trudesk
source_description: Open-source help desk and ticketing system built on Node.js and MongoDB
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release (v1.2.11) and the matching Docker Hub image (`polonel/trudesk:1.2.11`, and `:latest`/`:1`/`:1.2`) were all published on 2024-07-24 — just over 2 years before today, 2026-08-05. The last commit on any branch (develop: "chore(deps): update node-sass") landed 2025-01-24, about 18.4 months ago, and nothing since. A `v1.3.0-beta1` prerelease (React-frontend rewrite, APIv2) shipped 2023-06-19 and never reached a stable release — the `next`/`ui-next` branches for that rewrite have had no visible follow-through since. The repo itself is not archived (`archived: false`, `pushed_at` shows sporadic pushes as recently as 2026-05-11, likely CI/dependency housekeeping rather than feature work) and still has 1,492 stars and 12 open issues, so this is not a dead/archived repo — but it is functionally stalled: no release, no meaningful commit activity, in ~2 years. The README states this is "the source for Trudesk Community Edition" and points users to "Trudesk Cloud" (trudesk.io) as "the more comprehensive, cloud-hosted version" — strongly suggesting the vendor's attention and any real development effort has moved to the paid SaaS product, leaving the self-hosted OSS edition in maintenance-only mode.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers help desk / customer-support ticketing. It is a genuinely distinct category — closest neighbors by stack shape are n8n and paperless-ngx (multi-container Node/Postgres- or-Mongo-backed web apps), but none of them address ticket queues, SLAs, or support-agent workflows.
usefulness_rationale: Help desk/ticketing is a plausible small-business use case with broad appeal, and the app is architecturally simple to run behind a reverse proxy (single HTTP port, no raw protocols). Capped at medium rather than high because the upstream project is functionally dormant (see version_health) — a customer adopting this in 2026 would be running software the vendor has stopped meaningfully improving for ~2 years, with the vendor's real effort steered toward its paid cloud product instead.
blocking_issues:
Trudesk has no admin-credential env var at all (confirmed against `src/controllers/install.js`): first boot serves an interactive, multi-step HTML install wizard where the customer types their own `account[username]` / `account[password]` / `account[cpassword]` / `account[email]` directly into a web form, and the app hashes and stores whatever they typed. This is actually a better fit for our model than most apps — no plaintext secret needs to flow through `/compose` at all, since the customer's own login is created in-band, in the app's own UI, with the plaintext never touching our platform. The Docker image's bundled MongoDB env var config (`polonel/trudesk` docker-compose ships `MONGODB_URI` pointed at a `mongo` service) skips the wizard's DB-connection step, so the only wizard step a customer sees is admin-account creation.

The gap is exposure, not a missing input channel: between container start and the customer completing that wizard, the unauthenticated install-wizard endpoint is reachable by anyone who requests the domain first and could claim the "Admin" account themselves. A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate (keyed off a hash of the customer's root password, per IF-1312) closes that race window during setup; it can be safely lifted or left in place afterward since Trudesk's own login screen takes over once the wizard completes.
summary: Trudesk is mechanically installable today — its admin account is created by the customer directly through its own first-run web wizard, so unlike most apps we evaluate it needs no secret projected through `/compose` at all, only a temporary Traefik `basic_auth` gate to prevent someone else from reaching the unauthenticated wizard first. It would also be a new category for the catalogue (help desk/ticketing, currently uncovered). The blocker to actually shipping it is upstream health, not the platform: the last release and Docker image are both from 2024-07-24 (~2 years ago), the last commit anywhere is from 2025-01-24 (~18 months ago), and the README itself redirects users to a paid "Trudesk Cloud" product — this reads as a vendor who has moved on from the self-hosted edition. Recommend revisiting only if upstream shows renewed release activity; shipping it now means putting a stalled help-desk app in front of customers who need active support-tooling maintenance.

name: TubeArchivist
source_description: Self-hosted YouTube archiver with channel sync, full-text search, and web playback
version_health_notes: About 4.3 months since the latest tagged release (v0.5.10, 2026-03-28) as of today (2026-08-05). Release history (v0.5.1 2025-05-11, v0.5.2 2025-05-14, v0.5.3 2025-06-08, v0.5.4 2025-06-11, v0.5.5 2025-07-31, v0.5.6 2025-08-18, v0.5.7 2025-08-21, v0.5.8 2025-11-08, v0.5.9 2026-02-07, v0.5.10 2026-03-28) shows cadence slowing from roughly monthly through mid-2025 to roughly quarterly since. However, this is not a maintenance slowdown of the project itself: the repo also ships a continuously-updated `unstable` Docker tag (pushed within the last 10 days) and commit history shows steady activity through at least 2026-07-27 (multiple commits/day from several contributors, not just the lead maintainer). TubeArchivist's practice is to batch fixes onto `unstable` and cut a versioned `v0.5.x` tag only periodically, so the ~4-month gap in named releases overstates staleness — treat as active development with a slow, deliberate formal-release cadence rather than dormant or maintenance-only.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 built recipes archives YouTube content; Immich is the closest by category (photo/video library) but manages media the customer already has rather than fetching it from YouTube. TubeArchivist is functionally close to apps-gaps/pinchflat.yaml — both are standing "subscribe to a channel, keep downloading" archivers rather than one-off URL-paste tools like apps-gaps/metube.yaml or apps-gaps/alltube.yaml. The differentiator is that TubeArchivist is a self-contained watch experience: it bundles its own Elasticsearch- backed full-text search and web video player, so the customer never needs a separate Plex/Jellyfin instance to consume the archive. Pinchflat instead produces a Plex/Jellyfin/Kodi-ready file layout for an external media server to serve. Which one a customer wants depends on whether they already run (or want to run) a separate media server.
usefulness_rationale: Distinct, popular niche (11k+ GitHub stars) with real demand for "archive channels I care about before they're taken down/demonetized/ deleted," and its built-in search+playback avoids a second app dependency that Pinchflat requires. Held to medium rather than high because it overlaps meaningfully with Pinchflat's use case (see apps-gaps/pinchflat.yaml) and because YouTube-scraping tools built on yt-dlp carry the same third-party-ToS and extractor-breakage exposure already flagged across the other video-download gap candidates in this directory.
blocking_issues:
TA_PASSWORD (the app's own initial-admin-user credential, required at first boot) is documented as accepting a plaintext password only — "no hashes" — with an optional `_FILE` (Docker secret) suffix for *where* it's read from, not what format it's in. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password, so it structurally cannot supply this field regardless of which hash algorithm is added to the supported list. This matches the SCHEMA.md "genuine requirement for the plaintext password" case, which is called out as a hard blocker, not a `blocked_on_platform` algorithm gap.

Gating with Traefik `basic_auth` in front (our other supported mechanism) does not resolve this on its own: TubeArchivist has its own required login (unlike Adminer/n8n/WUD, which have no native auth), so a customer who only knows their root-password-derived basic-auth credential would be locked out of the app's actual login screen if TA_USERNAME/TA_PASSWORD were instead set to a server-generated value the customer never sees.

TubeArchivist does support delegating auth to a reverse proxy (TA_ENABLE_AUTH_PROXY, using Django's RemoteUserBackend, reading a configurable header — default `Remote-User` — for the authenticated identity) which could in principle let a Traefik basic_auth gate double as the app's real login. This is a plausible future path but is not the same mechanism as either of our two supported patterns today: it needs the reverse-proxy layer to inject a specific trusted identity header rather than just gate access, and auto-provisions/trusts whatever username appears in that header with no documented tie-in to `generated_from` or the existing `basic_auth: true` toggle. Flagging as a platform gap worth revisiting, not as something achievable with the current two mechanisms.
summary: TubeArchivist is a well-regarded, actively-developed YouTube archiver (channel sync, yt-dlp downloads, Elasticsearch-backed full-text search, built-in web player) that would meaningfully extend the catalogue's media category alongside — not simply duplicating — apps-gaps/pinchflat.yaml. It is reverse-proxy-compatible (single HTTP port, no raw protocols) and the project shows no EOL/dormancy risk despite a slowing formal-release cadence. It is blocked today, though, on the same first-boot mandatory admin login as Immich/Vaultwarden-style recipes need to solve, except TubeArchivist's TA_PASSWORD field only accepts a plaintext value with no hash-based alternative, so `generated_from` cannot reach it, and its own built-in login means a plain Traefik `basic_auth` gate would either leave a server-generated credential the customer never learns, or expose the app's real login unprotected. TubeArchivist's auth-proxy header mode is a plausible bridge between the two but isn't equivalent to either supported mechanism as they exist today. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once auth-proxy-header projection (or a documented way to feed a plaintext credential derived from the root password) is supported, not `not_recommended` — the app itself is healthy and differentiated.

name: Twingate Connector
source_description: Zero trust network access connector for secure remote resource access
upstream_license: proprietary (connector binary/image; Twingate's own OSS projects — Terraform provider, Helm charts, k8s operator — are separate and not this component)
version_health_notes: Docker Hub shows 1.90.0/1.90/1/latest all pointing at the same digest, published "23 days ago" relative to today (2026-08-05), i.e. roughly 2026-07-13. Prior tags 1.89.0 (~2 months earlier, ~2026-06-05) and 1.88.0 (~4 months earlier, ~2026-04-05) show a steady monthly-ish cadence. No deprecation/EOL signals; this is a commercially maintained SaaS product's client-side agent, actively shipped.
differentiation: Twingate Connector is the outbound-only agent half of Twingate's commercial Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) SaaS: it runs inside a private network/VM and dials out to Twingate's cloud control plane to expose that network's resources to remote users, but it has no standalone server role, no exposed inbound port, and no local admin/login of its own — all policy, user, and device management happens in Twingate's hosted Admin Console (a third-party SaaS UI, not anything we would host). This is architecturally the closest match to the already-analyzed netbird-client (a headless agent that joins an externally-managed mesh/control-plane), not to wg-easy, which is a full self-hosted WireGuard server *with* its own web UI that customers administer directly on our infrastructure. Twingate's pitch — ZTNA with per-resource access policies rather than flat VPN mesh access — is a real product differentiator versus both existing recipes, but the Connector alone (with no self-hosted control plane, since Twingate has none to self-host) is a thin, tokens-only shim into a vendor SaaS rather than a product a customer "runs" on the domain we provision.
usefulness_rationale: Same shape as netbird-client: legitimate only for a customer who already has a Twingate account/network and wants a permanent cloud peer/gateway to expose a remote network's resources through it. There is no self-hosted control plane to stand up (unlike Headscale for Tailscale) — this is purely a client for a third-party paid SaaS — so it's a narrow accessory to an external product rather than a general-purpose self-hosted app in its own right.
summary: Re-evaluated as recipe_type: native, following the same precedent netbird-client's own gap-analysis established: Twingate's own docs (twingate.com/docs/connectors-on-linux) describe a native systemd install path — a single install command plus a config file at /etc/twingate/connector.conf — as an alternative to the Docker image, so there's no forced docker-compose framing here either. TWINGATE_NETWORK, TWINGATE_ACCESS_TOKEN, and TWINGATE_REFRESH_TOKEN have no `generated_from` mechanism (they're minted per-connector in the customer's own Twingate Admin Console, a third-party SaaS account the customer must already have), but per Twingate's Knowledge Base ("Repeating 'Token is expired' Error in Connector Logs") the connector self-refreshes the access token using the refresh token automatically once running — the pair is "time-expiring" only in the JWT-lifetime sense, not something the customer must re-supply on a schedule. That makes this functionally a one-time setup credential, the same shape as NetBird's NB_SETUP_KEY: declare all three as required:false documentation-only parameters, install the connector unconfigured, and let the customer populate connector.conf (or re-run the installer) with their own values over SSH post-provisioning, then start the systemd service. Mechanically installable today under the established native-CLI pattern, consistent with the differentiation section's claim that this is architecturally the closest match to netbird-client — same conclusion, build_with_caveats, for the same reason: a real but narrow accessory to an external paid SaaS control plane rather than a general-purpose self-hosted app, still low usefulness on its own merits even though it clears the installability bar.

name: Tyk Gateway
source_description: Open-source API gateway for auth, rate limiting, and traffic management
upstream_license: MPL-2.0 (core gateway; the `ee` subtree is commercially licensed and not part of the OSS build)
version_health_notes: Released about one month before this analysis (2026-08-05). Multiple parallel branches maintained (5.14.x latest, 5.13.x, and a 5.8.x LTS line), with alpha/rc builds for an upcoming 5.15 already on Docker Hub — indicates a healthy, actively-developed project, not maintenance-only.
differentiation: Nothing else in the catalogue is an API gateway/traffic-management layer; the closest neighbors (adguard-home, pihole, wg-easy) are network/DNS tools, not HTTP API proxying. Tyk would be a genuinely new category if it fit our install model.
usefulness_rationale: Tyk Gateway is developer infrastructure for teams building and fronting their own APIs, not an end-user self-hosted app in the mold of the rest of the catalogue (note-taking, media, VPN, monitoring). Out of the box it proxies nothing — it only becomes useful once a customer defines upstream API endpoints through its admin REST API, which is a materially different (and more advanced) usage pattern than "log into a web UI at <slug>.<base_domain>".
blocking_issues:
The gateway has no web UI or login form of its own — the open-source image ships only the proxy engine plus a REST admin API. The OSS Dashboard/Management UI is a separate commercial product (Tyk Self-Managed / Tyk Cloud), not part of this image.

The admin API is protected by a static shared-secret string set in tyk.conf and checked with a plain equality comparison on the X-Tyk-Authorization header — it is not a hashed password-verify flow, so `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` does not apply (that mechanism assumes the app itself hashes/verifies a login value; Tyk just string-compares a config literal against the header). There is also no built-in login page to gate with Traefik `basic_auth`, since the "product" a customer interacts with (arbitrary proxied upstream APIs, configured via the admin API) isn't a single browsable surface a basic_auth prompt in front of one port would meaningfully protect.

Even with a working credential channel, the deployment requires external Redis and post-boot API-definition configuration via the admin REST API before the gateway proxies anything — a materially different first-boot flow than our single-container-plus-domain recipes.
summary: Tyk Gateway is an actively maintained, healthy open-source project (latest v5.14.0, released ~1 month before this analysis), but it is developer infrastructure — an API proxy with no web UI, configured entirely through a REST admin API gated by a static shared secret rather than a hashed login. Neither `generated_from` root-password projection nor a Traefik `basic_auth` gate meaningfully fits its auth model or its "configure arbitrary upstream APIs" usage pattern, so it doesn't map onto the current recipe mechanism. It also doesn't fit the catalogue's end-user-app mold the way our 24 existing recipes do. Not recommended for a build pass today.

name: Typebot
source_description: No-code chatbot builder for conversational forms and interactive flows
upstream_license: Functional Source License 1.1 (FSL-1.1-ALv2) — converts to Apache License 2.0 two years after each release; source-available, not OSI-approved while under FSL
version_health_notes: v3.17.2 shipped 2026-06-17, ~7 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Prior releases (v3.17.0/3.17.1 in May, v3.16.x in April, v3.15.x in January 2026) show a steady cadence of roughly one release every 1-4 weeks through the past year, so a 7-week gap is within normal variance, not a slowdown. Repo is not archived and continues active commit activity.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers no-code chatbot / conversational-form building. n8n (automation) is a general workflow engine, not a chat-widget/form builder; open-webui and ollama are LLM chat frontends, not lead-gen or support-widget builders. Typebot would be a distinct category: embeddable conversational forms and chat flows for a customer's own site.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct use case (lead-gen forms, support/FAQ bots, surveys) with no catalogue overlap, but it's a narrower business tool than our infra/productivity staples and the self-hosting setup (Postgres + Redis + two web services + mandatory SMTP/OAuth) is heavier than most of what a typical customer would want to operate themselves.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: builder admin login credential (SMTP magic-link OR OAuth provider: Google/GitHub/GitLab/Facebook/Azure AD/custom OIDC — no username+password option exists); ENCRYPTION_SECRET; POSTGRES_PASSWORD
blocking_issues:
Typebot's builder has no username/password login of its own — NextAuth requires at least one configured provider: SMTP (email magic link) or an OAuth/OIDC app (Google, GitHub, GitLab, Facebook, Azure AD, or custom OIDC). Both require a customer- or operator-supplied external credential (SMTP host/user/password, or an OAuth client id/secret from a third-party console) that /compose has no channel to accept today.

A Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the builder does not solve this: it only blocks anonymous network access, but the customer still can't complete the app's own first-login flow (which needs a working email/OAuth provider) to create the admin account at all.

This is a genuine "no plaintext/no arbitrary secret" gap rather than a generated_from-algorithm gap (root-password projection only ever supplies a password hash into a password-type field; Typebot has no such field), so IF-1420 alone would not unblock it — it needs a new channel for arbitrary operator-supplied config (SMTP creds or OAuth registration), not a supported hashing algorithm.
summary: Typebot is an actively maintained (latest v3.17.2, 2026-06-17), source-available (FSL, not yet OSI-approved) no-code chatbot/conversational-form builder with no overlap in the current 24-recipe catalogue. It's structurally a reverse-proxy- friendly multi-container web app (Postgres + Redis + builder + viewer), but its builder login mandatorily requires SMTP or an OAuth/OIDC provider — neither of which has a customer-input channel in the current /compose mechanism, and a Traefik basic_auth gate can't substitute since the app's own first-login flow still needs a working provider. Blocked on platform support for a real external-credential input channel, not on recipe authoring.

name: Typesense
source_description: Fast in-memory search engine with instant results and typo-tolerance
upstream_license: GPL-3.0 (server binary/image); client SDKs are separately licensed (Apache-2.0/MIT depending on language)
version_health_notes: Latest *stable* tag is v30.2 (2025-04-19), ~15.5 months before today (2026-08-05) — preceded by v30.1 (2025-01-29) and v30.0 (2025-01-27), v29.1 (2025-04-19), v29.0 (2024-06-30). Stable-release cadence has clearly slowed: two stable releases in 2025, none at all so far in 2026. However the project is not dormant — v31.0 has been in active release-candidate iteration (rc12 pushed ~19 days before today, rc13 pushed ~6 days before today per Docker Hub tag timestamps), so development is ongoing, just held in a long pre-release phase rather than shipped as stable. Repo has 26k+ GitHub stars and a commercial company (Typesense Inc., also sells Typesense Cloud) behind it, which argues against abandonment. Net: active development, but a customer installing "latest stable" today would be running a build with no stable release in over a year — worth flagging as a slowing cadence, not treated as EOL.
differentiation: No existing recipe in the 24-app catalogue provides a standalone search/indexing engine — every current recipe is an end-user application (photo management, password manager, VPN, forms, monitoring, etc.) that at most embeds a database as a private internal dependency. Typesense would be the first "search-infrastructure-as-a- product" recipe, occupying the same slot already scoped out in apps-gaps/meilisearch.yaml and apps-gaps/elasticsearch.yaml — a developer bolts it onto their own site/app/docs for instant, typo- tolerant search rather than using it as a destination app itself.
usefulness_rationale: Typesense has no built-in web UI at all (unlike Meilisearch, which at least ships a search-preview console) — administration and querying are purely via REST API and client SDKs. Its actual consumer is a developer's own application code, so the value only materializes once the customer wires their own app to it; there's nothing for a customer to look at or click on immediately after install. Same audience mismatch already flagged for Meilisearch/Elasticsearch/EdgeDB, but weaker here since there isn't even a token web console to justify a Traefik-fronted "app" experience.
blocking_issues:
TYPESENSE_API_KEY (set via the mandatory `--api-key` flag/env var) is not an internal-only secret — it IS the product's sole authentication credential. Every API call other than a bare health check requires it as a header value, and the customer's own application must be configured with this exact plaintext string to do anything useful with the service. There is no channel today for surfacing a server-generated secret back to the customer for actual external use — the identical gap already documented in apps-gaps/meilisearch.yaml for MEILI_MASTER_KEY and in apps-gaps/edgedb.yaml for Gel's root credential.

generated_from only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) onto a parameter; Typesense's `--api-key` takes the plaintext value directly and compares it verbatim against the header the client sends — there is no hash-verify login screen to target, so even setting aside the "customer needs to read it" problem, a hash-shaped value would not work here regardless of which algorithm generated_from supports. A genuine plaintext requirement, treated as a structural blocker per the schema.

`--api-key` has no optional/disabled mode — the server refuses to start without one (confirmed against Typesense's own server- configuration docs), so there is no "run it open, gate with Traefik basic_auth instead" fallback the way Qdrant or Adminer allow; the credential is baked into the app's own required boot arguments, not an optional auth layer that can be swapped out.
summary: Typesense is a mechanically simple, single-container, single-official- image (typesense/typesense) search engine, GPL-3.0 licensed, backed by a funded company, with no catalogue overlap — it would be the first standalone search-infrastructure recipe. Stable-release cadence has slowed markedly (last stable tag 15+ months ago) even though pre-release (v31 RC) activity continues, so it's active but not fast-moving. Installability is blocked on the same structural gap already identified for Meilisearch: its mandatory --api-key is a plaintext credential the customer's own application must actually receive and use, not an internal secret we can generate and hide, and not something generated_from's hash-projection mechanism can carry. Unlike Qdrant it offers no basic_auth-behind-Traefik escape hatch either, since the API key is a required boot argument with no disable path. It also has no web UI of any kind, making it the weakest audience fit of the search-engine candidates reviewed so far (Typesense/Meilisearch/Elasticsearch/Qdrant). Not recommended to build until a channel exists for handing a server-generated plaintext credential back to the customer.

name: Ubooquity
source_description: Self-hosted home server for ebooks and comics with web reader and OPDS feed
upstream_license: Freeware, free for non-commercial use — proprietary, source not published (no SPDX id; not open source)
version_health_notes: 3.1.0 shipped 2025-08-18, just under 12 months before today (2026-08-05, ~11.6 months) — no release in nearly a year. The project's own archive shows a very uneven cadence even in its active periods: 2 releases in 2025, 2 in 2024, 1 in 2023, 1 in 2021, 1 in 2018, then bursts of 3-7 in 2013-2017. A 3-year gap (2018 to 2021) has happened before, so a 12-month silence isn't yet conclusive EOL, but it is a solo-developer freeware project with no public roadmap or repo to check commit activity against, and support threads (userecho forum) show long-standing unresolved bugs (e.g. admin password reset issues open for years). Treating as maintenance-only rather than active.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers ebook/comic library serving. Immich is photo/ video management, Syncthing is generic file sync, Paperless-ngx is scanned-document archiving — none render EPUB/CBZ/CBR/PDF as a browsable library with a web reader or expose an OPDS feed for e-reader apps. Ubooquity would be a genuinely new use case in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Real, well-understood self-hosting use case (home ebook/comic library, similar niche to Calibre-Web/Kavita) with no catalogue overlap, but it's a narrow hobbyist tool, built on a proprietary/closed-source freeware core rather than an actively-developed OSS project, which is a weaker long-term bet than most of the current 24 recipes.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: basic-auth gate credential (root-password-derived) for both public ports
secrets_expressible_today: basic-auth gate credential (root-password-derived) for both public ports:traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues:
Ubooquity's own admin password (and any per-library user accounts) can only be set through a first-visit web wizard at the admin port (/ubooquity/admin) — the linuxserver/ubooquity image has no environment variable, config-file seed, or API for presetting it before boot (confirmed via linuxserver/docker-ubooquity issues #17 and #19, "unable to set admin password"). Left open on the internet, this is a race: whoever loads the admin URL first claims the account. generated_from can't reach this field (there's no password-type parameter to project into), but gating both the admin port (2203) and the library/reader port (2202) behind Traefik basic_auth with the customer's root-password-derived credential closes the race — the customer authenticates to reach either port before anyone else can, then sets Ubooquity's own admin password themselves through the wizard. This is the same "no login of its own reachable pre-setup" pattern basic_auth already covers for adminer/n8n/WUD/Open WebUI, and per SCHEMA.md's practical-test table that mechanism is installable now, not contingent on anything unshipped — not a blocker.

Two separate HTTP services need exposing (library/reader + OPDS feed on 2202, admin panel on 2203) rather than the single public port most current recipes assume, each needing its own independent basic_auth gate. Both are plain HTTP and reverse-proxy friendly individually (e.g. reader.slug.<base_domain> and admin.slug.<base_domain>, or admin kept un-published and reached via an internal route), but whether af-core's Traefik label renderer supports two independently-gated public ports for a single recipe is unconfirmed — every existing basic_auth recipe (adminer, n8n, WUD, Open WebUI) gates exactly one port. This multi-port-with-per-port-basic_auth shape, not the basic_auth mechanism itself, is the real open question.
summary: Ubooquity is a niche but functionally distinct fit (ebook/comic library + web reader + OPDS feed, no overlap in the current catalogue), packaged via the well-maintained linuxserver/ubooquity community image even though the upstream Ubooquity server itself is closed-source freeware in maintenance-only mode (no release in the ~11.6 months to 2026-08-05). Mechanically the single-port case is already solved: the admin password can only be set through a first-visit web wizard with no preset channel, but a Traefik basic_auth gate (already usable today, same as adminer/n8n/WUD/Open WebUI) closes that setup race. What actually blocks this is that Ubooquity needs the gate applied independently to two separate public ports (library/reader 2202, admin 2203), and it's unconfirmed whether af-core's Traefik label renderer supports more than one independently-gated public port per recipe today. Revisit once that multi-port capability is confirmed or built.

Version health is strong and the product niche (privacy-first web analytics) has zero overlap with the existing 24 recipes, though two other analytics candidates (Plausible, Matomo) are already sitting in this same apps-gaps set covering similar ground. Recommend `build_now`.

name: Universal Media Server
source_description: Open-source DLNA media server streaming video and music to any compatible device
version_health_notes: universalmediaserver/ums:15.8.0 was pushed to Docker Hub 2026-07-13, about 3.5 weeks before today (2026-08-05). Tag history shows a consistent roughly-monthly cadence through 2025-2026 (15.0.0 2025-08-23, 15.1.0 2025-09-27, 15.2.0 2025-10-29, 15.3.0 2025-12-11, 15.4.0 2026-01-10, 15.5.0 2026-02-28, 15.6.0 2026-04-26, 15.7.0 2026-06-01, 15.8.0 2026-07-13). Repo is not archived; this is a fork of the long-running PS3 Media Server project and is clearly actively maintained.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24 covers general-purpose personal video/TV library streaming. apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml and apps-gaps/plex.yaml already analyzed the closest neighboring gap ("Plex-style" transcoding media server with a modern web/app-first UI) and both landed blocked_on_platform. Universal Media Server is a different flavor of the same broad category: its core identity and historical strength is DLNA/UPnP protocol compliance for streaming to physical devices (smart TVs, games consoles, DLNA-capable receivers) rather than a polished web/mobile-app streaming experience — the HTML5 web player is a secondary feature. That said, the DLNA discovery mechanism (SSDP on UDP 1900, mDNS on UDP 5353, per the official Dockerfile's EXPOSE list) is inherently LAN-broadcast-based and does not traverse a hosted VM sitting behind Traefik on the public internet — a customer's home smart TV or console cannot discover a cloud-hosted UMS instance the way it would one running on their home network. Deployed on this platform, UMS would only be reachable through its web player (port 9001, plain HTTP, single-port and reverse-proxy-friendly), which undercuts the specific "stream to any DLNA device" pitch in Hostinger's own description.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted home media streaming is a high-demand category, but Universal Media Server's specific value proposition (broad DLNA/UPnP device compatibility) is largely neutralized by cloud hosting, since DLNA discovery cannot cross from a datacenter VM onto a customer's home LAN. What's left — a browser-based web player behind Traefik — covers similar ground to the already-analyzed, more actively marketed Jellyfin/Plex gap without UMS's brand recognition. Real niche appeal for retro/DLNA-device compatibility (older smart TVs, PS3/Xbox-style UPnP clients on the same LAN as the server), but a weaker overall pitch for a hosted-in-the-cloud customer than the category's blocked front-runners.
blocking_issues:
UMS has no environment variable, CLI flag, or config-seeding mechanism to create the initial admin account non-interactively. The official universalmediaserver/ums Dockerfile (src/main/external-resources/docker/Dockerfile) starts the app with a bare `java -jar ums.jar` and no admin-related env vars — first boot always serves an interactive setup wizard. Whoever opens the web UI first is prompted to either create the first admin account (POST /v1/api/auth/create in net.pms.network.webguiserver.servlets. AuthApiServlet, confirmed by reading the servlet source) or disable authentication entirely (POST /v1/api/auth/disable) — the latter being available to any anonymous visitor as long as no admin exists yet, which is worse than Jellyfin's equivalent race.

Unlike Jellyfin, UMS's own password hashing (net.pms.iam. AccountService.hashPassword, confirmed in source) uses bcrypt at cost 12, which IS in the currently supported generated_from algorithm list. That removes one blocker Jellyfin has, but it doesn't help here: generated_from can only project a hash into an app's own admin-parameter at provisioning time if the app exposes some pre-boot channel (env var, config file field, seeded DB row) to receive it, and UMS has none — the admin row is only ever created by the interactive wizard hitting the API above. The compatible hash algorithm is necessary but not sufficient without a seed channel to put it in.

A Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password-derived) closes the "anonymous visitor disables auth or claims admin first" race the same way it does for Jellyfin, but the customer would still have to manually walk through UMS's own setup wizard and choose credentials by hand after authenticating past the gate — basic_auth secures the perimeter, it doesn't provision the app's own account.
summary: Universal Media Server is an actively maintained (roughly monthly Docker Hub releases, most recently 15.8.0 about 3.5 weeks before today) GPL-2.0 DLNA/UPnP media server with an official single-container image (universalmediaserver/ums), structurally similar to the Uptime-Kuma/Vaultwarden class of single-container recipes. It hits the same installability wall as apps-gaps/jellyfin.yaml: first boot is an interactive setup wizard with no env-var or config-seed hook for the admin account, and — worse than Jellyfin — an anonymous first visitor can outright disable authentication rather than just claim the admin account. UMS's own password hashing (bcrypt) is already in the supported generated_from list, but that's moot without any pre-boot channel to write the hash into. Beyond the mechanism blocker, the app's core pitch (DLNA streaming to any compatible device) depends on LAN-broadcast discovery (SSDP/mDNS) that cannot reach a customer's home devices from a cloud-hosted VM, leaving only the secondary HTML5 web player as functional once deployed — a weaker differentiator than the already-analyzed, similarly-blocked Jellyfin/Plex gap. Recommend blocked_on_platform; revisit only alongside Jellyfin/Plex if/when a config-seeding or admin-provisioning hook is validated for this platform, and note the DLNA-discovery caveat even then.

usefulness_rationale: Genuinely useful for anyone self-hosting a video library, but its value is conditional: it optimizes files already sitting in a mounted library path, and the catalogue has no Plex/Jellyfin/Emby-style media server recipe for it to pair with. A customer would need to bring their own media storage/mount and workflow, which is a smaller addressable slice of AF's customer base than a self-contained app.
summary: Unmanic is a single-container, single-HTTP-port (8888) app with no built-in login, so it fits the current recipe mechanism cleanly via a Traefik basic_auth gate — no external API keys, OAuth, or unsupported credential types are involved. It is mechanically installable today. The open question is priority, not feasibility: release cadence has slowed to roughly one tagged version every several months (though upstream commits are current as of this week), and its usefulness depends on the customer already having a video library mounted into the VM, which the catalogue currently has no companion media-server recipe to provide.

name: Unstructured
source_description: Unstructured is a document processing API for RAG and AI model fine-tuning
version_health_notes: 0.1.10 pushed to quay.io 2026-07-23, about two weeks before today (2026-08-05). Docker-tag history shows a tight cadence through 2026: 0.1.5 (2026-04-22), 0.1.6 (unreleased-tag gap), 0.1.7 (2026-05-27), 0.1.8 (2026-07-10), 0.1.9 (2026-07-21), 0.1.10 (2026-07-23) — several releases are CVE remediations (starlette, lxml, python-multipart, opencv/ffmpeg bundled libs) landing within days of disclosure.
