Sibling repo `Unstructured-IO/unstructured` (the underlying OSS library) shows commits as recent as 2026-07-23 and `pushed_at: 2026-08-04`. Neither repo is archived. Clearly active, no EOL or maintenance-only signal.
differentiation: Unstructured is a stateless REST API (port 8000) that ingests ~26 file formats (PDF, Office docs, images, HTML, email, etc.), auto-detects type, and returns structured elements — optionally chunked by title — ready for embedding into a vector store or feeding an LLM fine-tuning job. Nothing in the current 24 recipes does this: Paperless-ngx and Paperless-AI do document *archiving* with their own internal OCR, not a standalone parsing/chunking API another app calls; Ollama and Open WebUI are the inference/chat layer, not the ingestion layer feeding them. The niche is closest in shape to two other unbuilt apps-gaps candidates — Apache Tika (generic extract-only REST microservice, `apps-gaps/apache-tika.yaml`, verdict: not_recommended for lack of end-user value) and Gotenberg (headless PDF-generation API, `apps-gaps/gotenberg.yaml`, verdict: build_now) — both "developer calls it, no dashboard" tools. Unstructured sits between them: more special-purpose than Tika (RAG-chunking output, not bare extraction) and squarely useful to the same audience the catalogue's existing AI/LLM recipes (Ollama, Open WebUI) already target, but like both siblings it has zero interactive UI beyond an auto-generated Swagger page at `/general/docs`.
usefulness_rationale: Real, well-known capability gap — Unstructured is one of the most commonly referenced document-ingestion components in self-hosted RAG/AI stacks, and pairs naturally with the AI-tooling recipes already in the catalogue. But it is developer infrastructure, not a product a customer opens and uses directly: value only accrues to a customer already building or running their own RAG pipeline against it, a narrower audience than a standalone app with a UI.
summary: Unstructured ships as a single, stateless container (no database, no volumes) on one HTTP port (8000), with a pinnable image tag on quay.io/unstructured-io/unstructured-api and an actively, frequently patched upstream (multiple CVE-remediation releases in the last four months, latest 0.1.10 on 2026-07-23). It has no built-in login — an optional `UNSTRUCTURED_API_KEY` env var can require a bearer-style header, but that key would need to be read back out by the customer's own calling code, which our current mechanism has no channel for — so the right fit, same as Gotenberg and Tika, is a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate keyed off the customer's root-password hash, closing the "open document- parsing endpoint on the internet" exposure without needing any app-side change. With that gate, it is mechanically installable today. It duplicates nothing in the current 24 recipes and gives the catalogue's existing AI/LLM tooling (Ollama, Open WebUI) a natural ingestion counterpart, though its audience — developers wiring up their own RAG pipeline — is narrower than a standalone consumer app. Recommend `build_now`, comparable to Gotenberg rather than Tika.

name: Uptrace
source_description: Open-source APM for distributed traces, metrics, and logs via OpenTelemetry
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (full server, including the pre-built uptrace/uptrace image — unlike some AGPL projects there is no separate permissive license for the binary distribution)
version_health_notes: v2.0.3 (latest stable, non-prerelease) shipped 2026-05-13 — 84 days before today (2026-08-05). A parallel v2.1.0-beta track is moving faster: beta.5 (2026-04-14), beta.6 (2026-05-25), beta.7 (2026-06-05, 61 days ago), so the project has cut a release roughly every 3-6 weeks across both tracks over the last 6 months. No archival notice, no EOL announcement, active commit history. Cadence is active, though the stable (non-beta) line moves noticeably slower than the beta line — worth pinning to a stable tag rather than tracking beta.
differentiation: No current recipe touches distributed tracing/APM. Uptime Kuma is the closest existing neighbor by category (monitoring) but is a simple external uptime/ping checker with no relationship to application-level telemetry; Uptrace ingests OpenTelemetry traces, metrics, and logs emitted from inside a customer's own instrumented applications and gives them a real dashboard (traces, spans, error grouping, alerting) for debugging their own code. That is a genuinely new capability for the catalogue, not a variant of anything we ship today.
usefulness_rationale: High value, but only to a customer who has already instrumented their own application with an OpenTelemetry SDK and needs somewhere to send the data — a materially narrower audience than end-user apps like Vaultwarden or Immich, similar in kind to Unleash's audience limitation. It also carries real operational weight for a self-hosted box: the backing stack is four containers (Uptrace app, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Redis), with ClickHouse in particular being noticeably heavier on RAM/disk than anything else the current 24-recipe catalogue runs. That raises the bar for who this is a good fit for, hence medium rather than high.
blocking_issues:
Uptrace's own login (auth.users[].password in uptrace.yml) only accepts a plaintext password, either literal or via env-var substitution — there is no hashed-password field. generated_from can only ever project a hash, so the customer's root password cannot drive this app's own admin login directly. Worked around the same way as Unleash: the internal admin password is server-generated (never customer-facing) and the real access gate is Traefik basic_auth on the public port.
Ingesting telemetry needs a raw OTLP endpoint (gRPC on 4317 and/or HTTP on 4318) exposed publicly in addition to the web-UI port, since the customer's own external applications must reach it to send traces — this is not a single reverse-proxied HTTP port like most of the catalogue, closer to wg-easy's raw-port precedent than to a Traefik-only app. Also unclear how Traefik basic_auth (an HTTP-layer gate) would apply to the separate OTLP ports, which have no auth of their own beyond a per-project token baked into the SDK config — that token is server-generated and not customer-secret, but the port itself would sit open unless explicitly firewalled or paired with mutual TLS.
summary: Uptrace fills a real gap (no current recipe covers OpenTelemetry-based APM/tracing) and is actively maintained (latest stable release 84 days ago, faster-moving beta track alongside it, no EOL signal). Its own admin login only takes a plaintext password with no hash field, so — following the Unleash precedent — it can ship with a server-generated internal admin password and a Traefik basic_auth gate (projected from the customer's root password) as the real access boundary, which keeps it installable_today. The open caveats are operational rather than mechanism-blocking: a four-container backing stack (Postgres + ClickHouse + Redis + the app itself) with ClickHouse being noticeably resource-heavier than anything else in the catalogue, plus a raw OTLP ingestion port (4317/4318) that needs to be reachable by the customer's own external apps and doesn't fit the single-HTTP-port-behind-Traefik pattern most recipes use. Recommended as build_with_caveats: worth building, but plan for the extra resource floor and the non-standard port exposure before treating it as a drop-in template.

name: useSend
source_description: Open-source transactional and marketing email sending platform
version_health_notes: v1.9.6 published 2026-07-23, ~13 days before this analysis (2026-08-05). Prior releases: v1.9.5 (2026-07-12), v1.9.4 (2026-05-18), v1.9.3 (2026-05-17), v1.9.2 (2026-03-22) — roughly monthly with an occasional faster back-to-back patch pair. Repo pushed_at is 2026-07-24 and the GitHub Actions/issue tracker shows continued commit activity (e.g. PRs merged into v1.9.5/v1.9.6 in July 2026). Not archived, no EOL or maintenance-mode announcement found. Single primary maintainer (KMKoushik) but activity is steady and recent.
differentiation: None of the current 24 shipped recipes cover transactional/marketing email sending. useSend is closest in spirit to a self-hosted Resend/Postmark/SendGrid alternative: REST API + SMTP endpoint for transactional email, plus a marketing-campaign/contact-list builder on top, all riding on the customer's own AWS SES account for actual delivery. `apps-gaps/listmonk.yaml` and `apps-gaps/keila.yaml` cover the newsletter/campaign-only niche without a transactional-API angle; `apps-gaps/emailengine.yaml` covers a different niche (proxying existing IMAP/SMTP mailboxes to a REST API, not composing/sending new mail). useSend sits between these — a developer-facing "email infrastructure" product — considered here on its own merits, not a duplicate of any of the three.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct developer-facing use case (self-hosted transactional + marketing email API) with no functional overlap in the current catalogue, and an active, growing project (4.6k+ GitHub stars). Value is capped for our customer base by two mandatory external dependencies the app cannot function without at all: an AWS account (for SES/SNS) and a GitHub OAuth app registration (the only supported login method) — see blocking_issues.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: GITHUB_ID (GitHub OAuth app credential — the only supported login method); GITHUB_SECRET (GitHub OAuth app credential — the only supported login method); AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID (customer's own AWS account, used for SES send + SNS delivery-status callbacks); AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (customer's own AWS account, used for SES send + SNS delivery-status callbacks); NEXTAUTH_SECRET
blocking_issues:
useSend has no email/password login — authentication is GitHub OAuth only (the docs state plainly: "useSend uses GitHub authentication for login... If you want email/password login, please help us out with the code"). Login requires a GitHub OAuth App registered by the customer (GITHUB_ID/GITHUB_SECRET) with a callback URL pointing at the instance's own domain, which by definition can't be known until after the instance is provisioned — a chicken-and-egg OAuth app registration flow with no input channel in `/compose` today, and not something `generated_from` or `basic_auth` can substitute for since it isn't a password at all.

The app is non-functional for its core purpose without AWS SES (to send mail) and SNS (to receive delivery/bounce callbacks) credentials — AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY for an AWS account the customer must separately own and configure (attach AmazonSESFullAccess/AmazonSNSFullAccess policies, verify a sending domain, request SES production access). This is an arbitrary external third-party credential with no input channel today, same class of blocker as an API key.
summary: useSend is an actively maintained (monthly release cadence, most recent tag 13 days old), AGPL-3.0 self-hosted transactional/marketing email platform with an official Docker image and a Postgres+Redis+app stack structurally similar to recipes/n8n, exposing one HTTP port that would sit fine behind Traefik. It fills a real gap — nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue does transactional email sending — but cannot ship today: login is GitHub-OAuth-only with no email/password fallback (a chicken-and-egg OAuth app registration problem, not just an unsupported hash algorithm), and the app cannot send any mail at all without a customer-supplied AWS SES/SNS account. Both are external-credential input problems with no channel in `/compose` today. Recommend blocked_on_platform — revisit if a generic customer-supplied external-credential/OAuth-app input channel is added to the platform.

name: Vane
source_description: Privacy-focused AI answering engine with cited sources and local LLM support
version_health_notes: Vane is a March 2026 rebrand of the long-running Perplexica project (same repo, `ItzCrazyKns/Perplexica` -> `ItzCrazyKns/Vane`, Docker image `itzcrazykns1337/perplexica` -> `itzcrazykns1337/vane`) — not a separate fork, so its ~36k GitHub stars and history carry over. Latest tagged release is v1.12.2 (2026-04-10); the last commit to `master` is also 2026-04-11. As of today (2026-08-05) that is just under 4 months with zero commits and zero merged PRs, on a repo that previously shipped v1.12.1 -> v1.12.2 about 3.3 months apart — so the gap is longer than the project's own recent cadence, not just "normal quiet period." Meanwhile open issues have kept accumulating through July/August 2026 with no maintainer replies or merges in that window, including a still-open, unpatched security report (see installability). Repo is not archived and the maintainer was active as recently as April 2026, so this reads as "slowing / possibly under-resourced" rather than abandoned or EOL — worth re-checking before a build, not a hard pass.
differentiation: Vane is a Perplexity-style answering engine: it takes a natural-language query, runs it through a bundled, private SearXNG metasearch instance (or Tavily/Exa), and has an LLM (local via Ollama, or a customer-supplied OpenAI/Anthropic/Groq key) synthesize a cited answer with source links, plus image/video search, file-upload Q&A, and a "Discover" feed of trending articles. That's distinct from the existing `ollama` (bare model-serving API, no UI) and `open-webui` (general-purpose chat UI over local/remote models) recipes, neither of which does web search or source citation — Vane fills a "private Perplexity alternative" niche the catalogue doesn't currently cover.
usefulness_rationale: A self-hosted, cited-source search assistant is a recognizable, popular category (Perplexica has ~36k stars) and ships as a single container with a real end-user web UI out of the box, unlike infra-only tools. It lands at medium rather than high because it needs an LLM to be useful at all (either the customer brings their own API key entered post-install via the setup screen, or they pair it with a separately-run Ollama instance with enough RAM to host a model — neither is a zero-effort experience for a typical AF customer), and the maintenance-slowdown and open security issue (below) add real risk to recommending it today.
blocking_issues:
Vane ships with no authentication of any kind — no login screen, no users table, no session/API-key checks on any of its 16+ endpoints (documented in an open, unpatched report, ItzCrazyKns/Vane#1123, opened 2026-04-26 and still open as of 2026-08-05 with no maintainer response). Anyone who can reach the container can read chat history, trigger searches, and use whatever LLM credentials are configured. A recipe can compensate with a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate (same pattern as n8n/WUD/Open WebUI), but that's a workaround for a design gap the app has had open and unaddressed for ~4 months, not a fix.
To be useful past the setup screen the app needs an LLM: either the customer pastes a third-party provider API key into Vane's own settings UI post-install (no `/compose` input channel needed — that value never has to reach af-api, so this is not a structural blocker), or the customer separately runs Ollama with a pulled model. Either way, a fresh install is a non-functional shell until the customer does one more manual step — worth flagging as an onboarding caveat even though it doesn't block `installable_today`.
summary: Vane (the March-2026 rebrand of Perplexica) is a single-container, MIT-licensed, reverse-proxy-compatible AI answering engine with a real web UI and no overlap with the catalogue's existing `ollama`/`open-webui` recipes. It is mechanically installable today only by treating the whole app as needing a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate, because it ships with zero built-in authentication — a gap tracked in an open, unpatched security report that has sat unaddressed for about 4 months alongside a broader slowdown in commits and issue triage since the last release (v1.12.2, 2026-04-10). Combined with the extra post-install step of supplying an LLM (own API key or a paired Ollama), that's enough to recommend `build_with_caveats` rather than `build_now`: worth a recipe, but re-verify the auth situation and upstream activity haven't gotten worse before committing build time.

name: Vault
source_description: Secrets management platform for storing and rotating sensitive credentials
upstream_license: Business Source License 1.1 (BSL) — not OSI-approved open source; HashiCorp switched Vault from MPL-2.0 to BSL in August 2023
version_health_notes: Released the day before this analysis (2026-08-04); the 2.0.x line has shipped roughly every 4-8 weeks since 2.0.0 (2026-04-14). Actively maintained by HashiCorp, an IBM company. Not archived, not EOL. Note the name "Vault" is ambiguous: HashiCorp Vault (chosen here, matches the "storing and rotating sensitive credentials" description exactly) vs. OpenBao (a Linux Foundation fork of the last MPL-licensed Vault release, created specifically because of the 2023 BSL relicensing, fully open-source) vs. Vaultwarden (already in our catalogue as recipe `vaultwarden`, an end-user Bitwarden-compatible password manager, not an infra secrets-management platform). OpenBao was considered and ruled out only because the Hostinger catalogue entry names "Vault" specifically; it would be worth a separate gap-analysis pass on its own merits given the licensing caveat below.
differentiation: Functionally distinct from `vaultwarden`: Vaultwarden is an end-user password manager (personal logins synced across devices), while Vault is an infrastructure secrets-management platform — API tokens, dynamic database credentials, PKI issuance, encryption-as-a-service, secret leasing/rotation for applications and pipelines rather than for a person's browser. No other recipe in the current catalogue covers this ground, so it would be a genuine new category for developer/DevOps customers running their own apps or CI on the same infrastructure.
usefulness_rationale: High name recognition and real demand from developer/DevOps customers, but it's a specialist tool: most Application Factory customers running a handful of self-hosted apps don't need a dedicated secrets broker, and the BSL license (see below) adds a commercial-use caveat that a purely open-source alternative (OpenBao) would not carry.
blocking_issues:
Vault has no concept of a pre-supplied admin credential. Production mode requires running `vault operator init`, which the app itself generates: a root token and a set of Shamir unseal key shares. These are produced fresh at init time by Vault, not supplied by us or the customer, and there is no field to project a `generated_from` hash into — Vault's own auth methods (root token, userpass) require either a token minted by Vault itself or a plaintext password that Vault hashes internally, and there is no way to seed either from a pre-computed hash of the customer's root password. This is the table's explicit "app will only accept the plaintext password" case — a genuine structural blocker, not a missing-algorithm gap.

Even if the root token could be delivered to the customer some other way, Vault's default Shamir seal requires manually supplying a quorum of unseal keys after every restart (crash, host reboot, image update) before the API/UI becomes usable again. There is no auto-unseal available without an external KMS/HSM integration, which this recipe mechanism has no channel to configure. A Vault instance that silently stays sealed after an unattended restart is a broken recipe, not a degraded one.

Running in Vault's built-in "dev mode" sidesteps both problems (fixed root token, auto-unseal) but is explicitly in-memory, non-persistent, and unencrypted-at-rest per HashiCorp's own docs — shipping that as a "secrets management" recipe would misrepresent what it protects.

Licensing: Vault Community Edition ships under HashiCorp's BSL 1.1, which prohibits using the software to build a "competing product or service." Offering hosted Vault as an Application Factory recipe may qualify as competing with HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP Vault) — needs legal review independent of the technical blockers above.
summary: HashiCorp Vault is an actively maintained, well-known secrets-management platform with no functional overlap in our current 24-recipe catalogue, but it does not fit the current recipe mechanism: it has no admin login that accepts a projected password hash (root token and unseal keys are generated by the app itself at init time, and its userpass method needs a plaintext password we cannot supply), and its default seal requires manual unsealing after every restart with no auto-unseal path available today. Combined with a BSL license that raises its own commercial-hosting question, this is a hard no rather than a caveat — revisit only if a future platform change adds a way to capture and hand back app-generated secrets to the customer, plus a supported auto-unseal mechanism.

name: Verdaccio
source_description: Lightweight private npm proxy registry for JavaScript packages
version_health_notes: 6.9.2 shipped 2026-08-02 — 3 days before today (2026-08-05). Full patch history over the preceding ~3 months shows a release roughly every 1-3 weeks on the stable 6.x line (6.6.0 on 2026-05-10, 6.7.1 on 2026-05-16, 6.7.2 on 2026-05-25, 6.7.3/6.7.4 on 2026-06-21, 6.8.0 on 2026-07-13, 6.9.0 on 2026-07-26, 6.9.1 and 6.9.2 both on 2026-08-02). A parallel 7.0.0-next prerelease track and a 9.0.0-next track are also being published in step with the stable releases, and 6.9.0 added Node 22 + native ESM support, so this is active, forward-moving development, not maintenance-only patching. No archival notice, no EOL announcement.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a package-registry proxy. Gitea is the closest neighbor by category (developer-tools, self-hosted git) and does bundle a generic package registry (including an npm endpoint) as one of its many features, but that's a secondary capability riding on a full forge (issues, PRs, CI hooks) — a customer who only wants a private/cached npm registry without standing up a whole Git forge has no lightweight option today. Verdaccio is purpose-built for exactly that: proxy the public npm registry, cache what's pulled, and host private packages, in a single small container.
usefulness_rationale: Real, well-understood use case (private npm packages, CI-friendly registry caching) but a narrower audience than end-user apps like Vaultwarden or Immich — it's aimed specifically at teams/developers running their own JS build pipelines, and a customer already using Gitea's built-in package registry or a hosted registry (npm's own private packages, GitHub Packages) may not need a dedicated instance. Lightweight footprint (single container, no external DB) keeps the operational cost low relative to that narrower audience.
blocking_issues:
Verdaccio's built-in htpasswd auth plugin supports bcrypt-hashed entries (algorithm: bcrypt in config.yaml), so an admin user can be pre-seeded into the htpasswd file at first boot using a bcrypt hash of the customer's root password (generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD") rather than a plaintext value — same shape as the Vaultwarden ADMIN_TOKEN precedent, just projected into a htpasswd-format file line instead of an env var read directly by the app. Confirming that install.sh can render 'admin:<hash>' into the mounted htpasswd file (rather than passing the hash as a raw env var) is a small implementation detail for the actual af-create-recipe pass, not a mechanism gap.
Verdaccio's htpasswd plugin allows open self-registration by default (max_users defaults to +inf) — anyone who can reach the registry could otherwise create their own account and publish packages. This must be disabled in the shipped config.yaml (max_users: -1) so the pre-seeded admin account is the only way in; this is a static recipe-config decision, not a customer-supplied value, so it doesn't block installability.
summary: Verdaccio is actively developed (releases roughly every 1-3 weeks on the stable 6.x line, most recently 3 days before today) and fills a gap the current catalogue doesn't cover: a dedicated, lightweight private npm registry, distinct from Gitea's incidental package-registry feature. It's a single container behind one HTTP port (4873), no external database, genuinely reverse-proxy-compatible. Its htpasswd auth plugin supports bcrypt, so the customer's root password can drive the admin login the same way Vaultwarden's does, provided self-registration is disabled in the shipped config so that account stays the only entry point. No structural blockers found — recommend build_now.

name: VERT

latest_version: no tagged releases — GitHub Releases page is empty; only rolling commit-sha container tags exist (e.g. sha-e1c83ba)
latest_release_date: 2026-07-01 (date of the sha-e1c83ba commit/image, ~1 month before today, 2026-08-05)
version_health_notes: The project has never cut a formal GitHub Release or semver tag — it ships continuously via a commit-sha-tagged container image (also a floating `latest`/`main` tag). Commit history shows activity roughly every few weeks (July 1, June 24, June 2, April 1, Feb 24 2026 in the visible log), which is active but noticeably less regular than a scheduled-release project. No archival notice, no EOL announcement. Because there is no semver tag, "current stable" here means "most recent commit-sha image" rather than a vetted release — worth flagging to a human reviewer as a weaker version-pinning story than typical.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a file-format converter. VERT converts images, audio, and documents to other formats entirely client-side in the browser via WebAssembly — the server just serves a static/SSR frontend, so the customer's files never leave their own device for those formats. Rated medium rather than high because the tool has no accounts, no persisted state, and no admin surface of its own, so the value-add over just using the free public vert.sh instance is narrower than for apps that store customer data (Vaultwarden, Immich, Paperless) — the main reason to self-host it is data locality/compliance, not extra features.
blocking_issues:
No formal versioned release exists upstream (see version_health) — only commit-sha container tags. A recipe would have to pin to a commit-sha tag rather than a semver tag, which is a weaker upgrade/rollback story than every other recipe in the catalogue and worth a human decision before treating this as build_now.
PUB_HOSTNAME, PUB_VERTD_URL, and other PUB_* config values documented by upstream are baked in at image build time (per docs/DOCKER.md), not read at container runtime — the recipe's build/publish pipeline, not /compose, would need to produce a per-domain image if per-customer PUB_HOSTNAME correctness matters. This doesn't block installability (the app functions fine at any domain even with a mismatched PUB_HOSTNAME) but is a real customization gap versus the pattern of an env-driven APP_DOMAIN parameter.
summary: VERT needs no customer-supplied secret at all — no login, no admin surface, just a domain — so it clears the installability bar cleanly once a container tag is picked. The catch is upstream itself: there is no tagged release, only rolling commit-sha images, and per-domain config (PUB_HOSTNAME) is baked in at image build time rather than read from an env var at runtime. It fills a real, currently-empty niche (client-side file conversion, zero overlap with the existing 24 recipes) and is cheap to run as a single static-frontend container, but the lack of any versioned release and the build-time-only config make it a build_with_caveats rather than a straightforward build_now — worth a human decision on whether commit-sha pinning is acceptable before scheduling a real af-create-recipe pass. Repo is not archived and has no formal EOL/deprecation notice, but 11 months with no commits, no releases, and no maintainer response to a growing backlog of open issues/PRs is a real dormancy signal, not just a quiet period between releases.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers web/product analytics. Vince pitches itself explicitly as a Plausible-compatible, zero-dependency alternative (single static binary, no Postgres/ ClickHouse/Elixir runtime, drop-in replacement for Plausible's tracking script) — a genuinely lighter-weight footprint than either Umami or Plausible. Two other privacy-analytics candidates, `umami-analytics` and `plausible-analytics`, are already analyzed in this apps-gaps set and cover the same product niche; `matomo` is a fourth. All four would compete for the same customer intent if more than one is built.
usefulness_rationale: The product niche (privacy-first, cookie-free web analytics) is evergreen demand and the single-binary/zero-dependency design is a genuine differentiator versus Umami/Plausible/Matomo's multi-container stacks. Rated medium rather than high because of the version-health findings above (11 months dark, unaddressed community PRs and bug reports) and the small-project risk that implies (2,014 GitHub stars, effectively a single-maintainer project that has gone quiet) — a recipe built on top of it today could be shipping on an abandoned dependency.
blocking_issues:
Vince's admin account is provisioned by passing `VINCE_ADMIN_NAME` and `VINCE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` env vars to the `serve` command at boot (confirmed in `internal/cmd/run.go`), which calls `ops.CreateAdmin(name, password)`. That function (confirmed in `internal/ops/system_operations.go`) calls `bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword([]byte(password), ...)` itself — i.e. it expects the **plaintext** password as input and does its own hashing internally. `generated_from: "<algo>:ROOT_PASSWORD"` only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no way to hand Vince a value that both (a) satisfies its bcrypt-of-plaintext expectation and (b) lets the customer log in with the root password they actually know. This is exactly the "genuine requirement for the plaintext password, not any hash" row in SCHEMA.md's decision table — a structural blocker, not an unsupported-algorithm gap.

Vince is not a "no login of its own" app the way Adminer/WUD are — it has a real admin session (dashboard, site management, API-key creation under `/settings`) gated by `RequireAccount`. A Traefik `basic_auth` perimeter gate does not substitute for that: even with a basic_auth wall in front, `VINCE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` still has to be set to *something* at container boot, and whatever value we choose (random, server-generated) can't be the customer's actual root password, so the customer would have no way to authenticate into Vince's own admin UI to add sites or view non-public dashboards — not a zero-touch boot the way our other recipes deliver.
summary: Vince is a genuinely differentiated single-binary alternative to Umami/Plausible/Matomo (no external database, built-in autocert TLS, drop-in Plausible-script compatibility) and would occupy a currently-empty analytics category in the catalogue. But it fails installability today for a structural reason: its admin account is created from a plaintext `VINCE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` that the app itself bcrypts internally, and `generated_from` can only ever supply a hash of the customer's root password — never the plaintext — so there is no way to give the customer working login credentials to Vince's own admin UI, and a Traefik basic_auth gate only adds a perimeter without solving that access problem. On top of the platform blocker, upstream health is a separate concern: 11 months with zero commits or releases despite a growing backlog of unaddressed community issues and PRs is a real dormancy signal for what looks like a single-maintainer project. Recommend `not_recommended` — revisit only if upstream ships a hash-acceptable/headless admin-provisioning path (unlikely given current inactivity) and shows renewed maintenance activity.

name: Vitess
source_description: Database clustering system for horizontal scaling of MySQL databases
version_health_notes: CNCF-graduated project with a regular quarterly major-release cadence (v22 GA, then v23.0.0 GA 2025-11-04) plus frequent patch releases for open CVEs — v23.0.3 (2026-02-26, ~5 months before today, 2026-08-05) was itself a security patch. No sign of maintenance-only mode or slowdown.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers MySQL sharding/clustering infrastructure — the catalogue's database-adjacent recipes (n8n, paperless-ngx, immich, etc.) all consume a single Postgres/MySQL instance rather than operate one. Vitess itself isn't a customer-facing application; it's infrastructure that other applications would connect to as their database layer.
usefulness_rationale: Vitess exists to shard/scale MySQL across many nodes for large organizations (its origin is YouTube's MySQL fleet, later PlanetScale). A single-tenant self-hosted deployment for one customer has no natural use case matching the rest of the catalogue's "one useful app per customer" model — a customer needing a database for another app is far better served by a plain MySQL/Postgres container than by a sharded cluster with its own topology-consensus service.
blocking_issues:
Vitess's actual product surface is the MySQL wire protocol exposed by vtgate (port 15306 by default), not an HTTP application — a customer's real use of the deployment (connecting a MySQL client/app to the cluster) cannot go through Traefik's HTTP router the way every other recipe does; it would need raw TCP passthrough, which is a different exposure model than the rest of the catalogue.
Minimum viable topology requires a separate consensus/topology store (etcd, Consul, or ZooKeeper) plus vtctld, vtgate, and one or more vttablet+mysqld pairs — a multi-service cluster-of-clusters shape with no single-container or simple multi-container equivalent in any existing recipe.
VTAdmin (the only web UI) ships with no built-in authentication by design (upstream explicitly leaves auth to the operator), so it would need a Traefik basic_auth gate — expressible today — but that only covers the admin UI, not the underlying database access customers would actually want.
summary: Vitess is an actively maintained, CNCF-graduated MySQL clustering system, not an end-user application — it has no natural fit as a single-customer self-hosted recipe. Its primary interface is the raw MySQL protocol via vtgate rather than HTTP, its minimum deployment topology is a multi-node cluster with its own consensus store, and its only web UI (VTAdmin) has no built-in login of its own. Even with a Traefik basic_auth gate on VTAdmin, the core value of the product (a horizontally-scaled MySQL cluster) isn't reachable through our current reverse-proxy-only exposure model, and the operational complexity is a poor match for the rest of the catalogue.

There is no official VueTorrent Docker image; upstream ships only a dev-oriented docker-compose.yml for local testing. Deployment in practice happens one of three ways, none of which are "install VueTorrent on its own": (1) drop the built static assets into qBittorrent's own container as an alternate WebUI folder (the LinuxServer.io `qbittorrent` image supports this via a docker-mod env var, no separate container); (2) run qBittorrent normally and let its WebUI serve the VueTorrent theme directly, since LinuxServer's qbittorrent image has shipped VueTorrent bundled as the default WebUI for some time; or (3) run a third-party "standalone" image (e.g. `nukecat/vuetorrent-standalone`, unofficial, not maintained by the VueTorrent project) that is purely a reverse-proxying frontend requiring `QB_HOST`/`QB_PORT` pointing at a pre-existing qBittorrent backend it does not manage or provision. In every case a qBittorrent recipe (`apps-gaps/qbittorrent.yaml`, not yet in the 24-recipe catalogue, recommended build_now) is the actual dependency doing all the work; VueTorrent adds no capability a qBittorrent recipe couldn't ship on its own by simply enabling the bundled VueTorrent WebUI that modern linuxserver/qbittorrent images already default to.
usefulness_rationale: As a UI skin with a mandatory, unconfigurable qBittorrent dependency and no official container of its own, VueTorrent isn't a coherent unit of "install this app" the way every other catalogue entry is. The functionality customers actually want (a nice torrent-client web UI) is better delivered by building the qBittorrent recipe itself and simply enabling its already-bundled VueTorrent theme, rather than modeling VueTorrent as a second, separate recipe.
blocking_issues:
No official Docker image; the only 'standalone' path is an unofficial third-party image (nukecat/vuetorrent-standalone) not endorsed by upstream.
Every deployment path requires a separate, already-running qBittorrent instance reachable at a customer- or operator-supplied host/port (QB_HOST/QB_PORT) — this is external infrastructure the /compose mechanism has no channel to provision or point at, since it isn't a password/hash and isn't server-generatable.
Bundling qBittorrent alongside VueTorrent in one recipe just reproduces the qbittorrent recipe (apps-gaps/qbittorrent.yaml) with an extra unnecessary container, since linuxserver/qbittorrent already offers the same VueTorrent skin as a built-in theme option.
summary: VueTorrent is a WebUI theme for qBittorrent, not an independent application: it has no official Docker image and every known deployment method (drop-in WebUI folder, LinuxServer.io docker-mod, or the unofficial nukecat/vuetorrent-standalone reverse-proxy image) requires a pre-existing, separately-provisioned qBittorrent backend. Modeling it as its own recipe would either require bundling qBittorrent anyway (duplicating the not-yet-built `qbittorrent` gap candidate) or pointing at external infrastructure the platform has no input channel for. Recommend `not_recommended` as a standalone recipe; if a nicer torrent UI is wanted, the fix is enabling VueTorrent as the bundled WebUI theme when/if the qBittorrent recipe itself is built, not a separate recipe.

That is a first-come, first-served open registration form, not an injectable credential. (Note: some third-party guides claim Wakapi ships a hardcoded default `admin`/`admin` account on first boot; this could not be confirmed against the current official README, wiki, or config.default.yml and appears to be outdated or conflated with an unofficial fork/image — treated here as unverified, not as the fixed-default-credential case the schema would otherwise treat as installable via a `basic_auth` gate alone.)

A Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app (using the root-password projection) would close off the registration race from the public internet, but per the precedent set in `apps-gaps/2fauth.yaml` (the structurally identical case), that only moves the same open self-registration race one layer in — anyone who reaches the app through the gate is still racing to register the one account, and today's mechanism has no channel to hand the customer a second, distinct credential for the app's own login beyond the single root-password projection already spent on the gate itself.
summary: Wakapi is an active, well-maintained, lightweight single-container app (SQLite by default) that would add a genuinely new category to the catalogue — self-hosted developer time tracking — with no overlap among the current 24 recipes. It fails the installability test on the same platform-mechanism grounds as 2FAuth: the app provisions its one admin account via an open, unauthenticated self-registration form with no env-var hook, so neither `generated_from:ROOT_PASSWORD` nor a `basic_auth` gate alone gives the customer an exclusive, platform-provisioned credential. Revisit once the platform supports injecting a preset admin login via env var (would require an upstream feature request) or a second customer-facing credential channel beyond the single root-password projection.

usefulness_rationale: Fills a genuine category gap and, unlike Excalidraw, delivers real server-side real-time collaboration with the stock image rather than needing an extra websocket-relay build to earn the word "collaborative." Simple single-container footprint (~120MB image, one Node process, no database) makes it cheap to run per customer.
blocking_issues: WBO has no built-in username/password login of its own: any board URL is openly readable/editable by anyone who has (or guesses) the link unless the operator wires up its optional AUTH_SECRET_KEY JWT capability system (canOpen/canEdit/canClear claims). That JWT flow needs externally-issued signed tokens per board/user, not a single admin credential — there's no channel to project a customer value into it today. Not a hard blocker for the recipe overall since a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the whole app covers the same "don't sit open on the internet" need (the WUD/Excalidraw pattern), but it does mean the recipe ships without WBO's own per-board access control, just the outer gate.
summary: WBO is a single-container, single-port (HTTP) Node app with an official, actively-maintained, frequently-tagged Docker image (lovasoa/wbo, AGPL-3.0) — it is Traefik-friendly and mechanically installable today behind a mandatory basic_auth gate, since the app itself has no login of its own out of the box. It would be the catalogue's first real collaborative-whiteboard recipe, and does so with genuine server-side real-time collaboration built into the stock image (unlike the client-only Excalidraw candidate), making it a strong build_now candidate.

The only other required secret, WF_SECRET_KEY, is a patternless 32-byte random value the customer never needs to see. With zero blocking issues, an active upstream, and a differentiated (lighter, real-login) angle versus the Ghostfolio candidate, this is a strong build_now pick for the still-uncovered finance category.

name: Weaviate
source_description: Open-source vector database for AI applications and semantic search
upstream_docker_image: cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate (mirrored on Docker Hub as semitechnologies/weaviate)
latest_version: 1.37.0 GA (1.39.0-rc.0 in pre-release as of research date)
version_health_notes: Roughly monthly-to-bimonthly minor releases through 2026: 1.36.0 (2026-03-03), 1.37.0 (2026-04-16), with 1.39.0 already at rc.0 as of today (2026-08-05) — under 4 months since the last GA tag, well inside "active". Repo is not archived, has heavy commit/PR activity, and ships a built-in MCP server as of 1.37, signalling ongoing investment rather than maintenance-only mode.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is a vector database. Ollama and Open WebUI run/serve LLMs, and paperless-ai/hermes-agent/agent-adjacent tools may embed a vector store internally, but nothing today exposes a standalone vector DB a customer could point multiple AI apps at for semantic search/RAG. Weaviate would fill that specific gap.
usefulness_rationale: Vector databases are foundational infrastructure for RAG and semantic search, a real and growing AI use case, but Weaviate has no UI of its own — it's a backend a developer wires other apps (or code) up to. That caps its appeal to the more technical slice of the customer base compared with a ready-to-use end-user product.
blocking_issues:
Weaviate is REST (8080) + gRPC (50051) dual-port by design; official clients default to using both for full functionality (gRPC carries the fast batch/insert path), and gRPC is a raw protocol, not an HTTP route Traefik can front the same way as the REST API on a single `<slug>.<base_domain>` host. A recipe could expose gRPC only via a second raw TCP entrypoint (if the platform's Traefik config supports that) or accept REST-only operation with reduced write throughput — either way this is a real compatibility gap versus our single-HTTP- port recipes, not a hard blocker on its own.

Weaviate's own auth (`AUTHENTICATION_APIKEY_ALLOWED_KEYS`) requires the literal plaintext key value at every client call — it is not a password-verified-via-hash login form, so the `generated_from` hash- projection mechanism cannot supply it: a hash of the root password is not a value the customer's own client code could ever be expected to know or type in. The only expressible mechanism is running Weaviate with `AUTHENTICATION_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_ENABLED=true` (no internal auth) and gating the whole REST port behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead, same pattern as Adminer/n8n/WUD — installable, but it means every one of the customer's own applications that talks to this Weaviate instance has to embed the basic-auth credential on every REST call, which is a materially worse developer experience than Weaviate's native API-key model.
summary: Weaviate is an actively maintained (monthly releases, BSD-3-Clause, official pinned Docker image), API-only vector database with no bundled web UI — it fills a genuine gap versus the current 24 recipes, none of which is a standalone vector store. It is not cleanly installable under today's mechanism, though: it needs both an HTTP (8080) and a raw gRPC (50051) port for full functionality, which doesn't fit our single-HTTP- port-behind-Traefik pattern, and its own API-key auth wants a literal plaintext secret rather than a hash-verified login, so `generated_from` can't project a customer credential into it the way it does for Vaultwarden-style admin logins. The only expressible path is disabling Weaviate's own auth and gating the REST port with Traefik `basic_auth` (à la Adminer), which is installable but forces every client application to carry that gate credential on each call, and still leaves gRPC unaddressed. Recommend `blocked_on_platform`: revisit once the platform supports either a raw TCP entrypoint alongside HTTP, or a literal customer-chosen secret channel beyond root-password-hash projection.

name: WebCord
source_description: Privacy-focused Discord client with enhanced security and custom features
version_health_notes: v4.14.0 released 2026-07-12, about 24 days before today (2026-08-05). The LinuxServer.io Docker packaging (linuxserver/docker-webcord, built on their kasmvnc base image) tracks upstream releases and is likewise actively maintained.
differentiation: WebCord is not a server application — it is a desktop Electron app (an alternative Discord/SpaceBar client) that the LinuxServer.io image runs inside a virtual Linux desktop and exposes over a browser via KasmVNC (a noVNC-style remote-desktop protocol), on ports 3000 (HTTP) and 3001 (HTTPS). Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is a personal chat-client remote desktop; the closest structural cousin is Guacamole, which is a generic remote-desktop *gateway* rather than a single packaged app. WebCord's "web UI" is a rendered virtual desktop, not an HTTP application with real multi-user server value — it is functionally a single end-user's personal Discord session, streamed from a container instead of run locally.
usefulness_rationale: The appeal of self-hosting a chat client for personal Discord use inside a hosted VM is thin next to genuine infrastructure/productivity tools already in the catalogue: nearly every user already has a native or web Discord client, and running a full container + virtual desktop just to reach it adds cost and latency without a corresponding capability (no multi-user server role, no data ownership benefit — the account and messages still live on Discord's own servers).
summary: WebCord is an actively maintained, MIT-licensed Discord client with an official LinuxServer.io Docker image (lscr.io/linuxserver/webcord) exposing a single browser-reachable port via KasmVNC — mechanically it is installable today: the container has no built-in login by default, so a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate covers the one secret it needs, the same pattern used for n8n and WUD. However, this is not a server application in any sense that fits the catalogue: it packages a personal desktop chat client as a remote virtual desktop, with no multi-user or self-hosted-data value proposition, and it does not compete with or extend anything the current 24 recipes cover. Recommend `not_recommended` on fit/usefulness grounds despite being technically installable.

name: Weblate
source_description: Web-based translation management with version control integration
version_health_notes: Weblate uses calendar versioning with monthly releases plus point fixes: 2026.6 (2026-06-01), 2026.6.1 (2026-06-01), 2026.7 (2026-07-01), 2026.7.1 (2026-07-10), 2026.8 (2026-08-03). As of today (2026-08-05) the latest release is 2 days old — squarely within the project's steady monthly cadence. No sign of maintenance-only mode, archival, or EOL; this is one of the most consistently maintained candidates considered so far.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers localization/translation workflow management. Gitea (recipes/gitea) is the closest thing in spirit — both integrate with git — but Gitea hosts repositories generically while Weblate is a purpose-built continuous-localization tool that pulls/pushes translation strings against an existing git remote (GitHub/GitLab/self-hosted Gitea/etc.), with translation-specific UI (fuzzy matching, glossaries, machine-translation suggestions, QA checks) that a generic git host doesn't provide.
usefulness_rationale: Continuous localization is a common need for teams shipping multi-language software and is entirely uncovered by the current 24-recipe catalogue. Weblate is the de facto standard open-source tool in this space (used by KDE, phpMyAdmin, Fedora, etc.), actively maintained on a steady monthly cadence, and pairs naturally with the existing Gitea recipe for a fully self-hosted dev toolchain.
blocking_issues: Weblate's official docker-compose stack (weblate/weblate + postgres + valkey/redis + nginx front container) creates its admin account via WEBLATE_ADMIN_PASSWORD, which only accepts a plaintext password set directly as an env var (Weblate's own docs warn against storing it long-term for exactly this reason) — there is no pre-hashed- credential input, so generated_from (which only ever carries a hash) cannot project the customer's root password into it. Workaround, matching the pattern already used for n8n/WUD/OpenClaw/ Langflow: generate WEBLATE_ADMIN_PASSWORD server-side as a random value nobody needs to read, and put the real auth boundary at a Traefik basic_auth gate in front of the app. Caveat: unlike those single-purpose apps, Weblate is a genuinely multi-user tool (translators, project maintainers, and admins normally get distinct accounts, some via self-registration); a blanket basic_auth gate collapses that down to one shared credential, so this fits a single-team/private-instance use case rather than Weblate's intended open-collaboration model. Recipe should also set REGISTRATION_OPEN=False to prevent anonymous self-registration behind the shared gate.
summary: Weblate is an actively maintained (monthly release cadence, latest version 2 days old), GPL-3.0, official-image project that fills a genuinely open slot in the catalogue: continuous localization/ translation management with git integration, complementary to but distinct from the existing Gitea recipe. It ships as a multi-container stack (app + Postgres + Valkey/Redis + nginx), all reverse-proxy compatible on a single HTTP port. The blocker is that Weblate's admin account is provisioned via a plaintext WEBLATE_ADMIN_PASSWORD env var with no hashed-credential path, so generated_from can't project the customer's root password into it directly; the workaround is to server-generate that password and gate the app with Traefik basic_auth instead, the same pattern used for n8n/WUD/OpenClaw/Langflow. That makes it installable today, but with the caveat that basic_auth collapses Weblate's normal multi-user/self-registration model into a single shared credential — a reasonable fit for a private single-team instance, worth noting to whoever builds the recipe.

name: WebThings Gateway
source_description: Open-source Web of Things hub for unifying and controlling smart home devices
version_health_notes: Not archived and not dormant: the master branch has commits as recent as 2026-04-20, and a 2.1.0-beta.2 pre-release shipped 2026-04-01 (about 4 months before today, 2026-08-05). But tagged stable releases are infrequent — 1.1.0 (2023-01), 2.0.0-beta.1 (2025-08), 2.0.0 (2025-12-18, ~7.5 months ago) — roughly one stable release a year, from a small volunteer team (this was Mozilla's IoT project, spun out to the community as WebThingsIO after Mozilla discontinued IoT work in 2019). Classified active/slowing rather than maintenance-only or dormant.
differentiation: Directly overlaps with the existing home-assistant recipe: both are self-hosted smart-home hub web UIs for unifying and automating connected devices. WebThings' distinguishing angle is strict adherence to the W3C Web of Things standard and a lighter, simpler UI, but it has a far smaller integration/add-on ecosystem than Home Assistant's 1,000+ integrations, and a much smaller maintainer base. It adds no capability a customer can't already get from the recipe already in the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: WebThings Gateway's core value is bridging physical smart-home radios (Zigbee, Z-Wave, Bluetooth via USB dongles) to a web UI; upstream docs recommend running it with --network=host specifically so add-ons can reach that local hardware. A hosted cloud VM has no such dongles and no USB-passthrough path in this platform, so the app's main reason to exist is unusable here — the same physical-hardware gap that already limits home-assistant's usefulness on this platform, except home-assistant at least brings a much larger integration catalogue (cloud-API-based integrations that don't need local radio hardware) to partially compensate. WebThings brings that same hardware gap with a smaller ecosystem and no differentiator to offset it.
summary: WebThings Gateway is a single-container Node.js app (webthingsio/gateway, pin 2.0.0) serving its web UI on 8080/HTTP and 4443/HTTPS, storing state under a single volume (/home/node/.webthings) — structurally similar to home-assistant. Its first-time setup wizard has the customer create their own local admin account (name/email/password) directly through the app UI on first visit, with an optional (skippable) tunnel-subdomain step before it — the same "no customer secret needed through /compose, first visitor sets their own credential" pattern already accepted for home-assistant and actual-budget, so nothing here is mechanically blocked. The real problem is fit: it duplicates the smart-home-hub slot home-assistant already fills, brings a much smaller integration ecosystem, and its headline capability (Zigbee/Z-Wave/Bluetooth device bridging via local USB radios) is unusable on a hosted cloud VM with no hardware passthrough — the same constraint that already caps home-assistant's value here, but without home-assistant's compensating breadth of cloud-API integrations. Recommend not building this recipe: it is installable but adds no value over what's already in the catalogue.

Webtop is the opposite shape: a self-contained containerized Linux desktop (XFCE/ KDE/MATE/i3 on Alpine/Ubuntu/Fedora/Arch) that the customer runs and uses directly through the browser — no external target needed. Those env vars take a plaintext credential, which our recipe mechanism has no channel for (generated_from only ever projects a hash) — so the correct approach is to leave the app's built-in auth off and gate the public port with Traefik basic_auth instead, same pattern as Adminer/WUD/Web-Check. The main reservation is fit/value rather than mechanics: it overlaps conceptually with Guacamole's "browser-based remote desktop" niche (though serving a different use case — self-contained desktop vs. gateway to existing infra) and carries a heavier resource footprint than most of the catalogue. name: Wekan
source_description: Open-source Kanban board for visual project management and task tracking
version_health_notes: Confirmed via the GitHub releases API (not training-data recall): 100 tagged releases between v9.69 (2026-06-23) and v10.71 (2026-08-06) — an average of 2-3 tagged releases per day over the last ~6.5 weeks, i.e. effectively continuous delivery, not a normal versioned-release cadence. Repo is not archived, `pushed_at` is 2026-08-06 (same day as the latest tag), 21k+ stars, 356 open issues actively triaged. As of today (2026-08-05/06) this is unambiguously an actively maintained project — if anything, the release cadence is unusually fast for a self-hosted recipe to track (see blocking_issues).
differentiation: None of the current 24 built recipes cover kanban-style project/task management (Anytype Server is personal notes/knowledge sync, not a task board). Wekan would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue. Note for the reviewer: three other gap-analysis candidates already cover this same kanban/Trello-alternative niche — kan.yaml (build_now), planka.yaml (not_recommended, licensing), kanboard.yaml (build_now) — none of which are built recipes yet either, so this is not duplicate coverage today, but a prioritization call once one of these ships. Wekan is the oldest and most established of the four (21k+ stars vs. Kan's 5.3k, MIT license vs. Planka's restrictive Fair Use License) and is Meteor/MongoDB-based rather than a lighter PHP (Kanboard) or Next.js (Kan) stack.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand for a self-hosted Trello alternative, and Wekan is the most mature/widely-adopted option among the kanban candidates already in this gap-analysis set. Held to medium rather than high because Kanboard and Kan already cover the same customer need with a simpler installation footprint (single container / no bundled DB migration complexity), and Wekan's own default docker-compose.yml has shifted to a non-trivial FerretDB-binary-download-at-runtime setup (see blocking_issues) that adds operational fragility a hosted recipe would rather avoid.
blocking_issues:
No admin-login parameter to project a root-password hash into: Wekan has no ADMIN_USERNAME/ADMIN_PASSWORD-style env var. Per docs/Login/Adding-users.md, "First registered user will be admin, and next ones normal users" via the open /sign-up form — there is no way to disable self-registration before that first admin account exists (Admin Panel > Settings > Registration > Disable self-registration only becomes available after login). This is the same shape as the Kan finding: mitigated by gating the whole app behind a mandatory Traefik basic_auth wall (projected from the customer's root password via generated_from) so a stranger racing to /sign-up first can't claim the admin account — not a hard blocker, just a required mitigation.

Not a secrets-channel blocker but a real operational risk worth flagging: the project's current upstream docker-compose.yml (the one linked from the README) defaults to FerretDB v1 with an embedded SQLite backend, where the ferretdb container downloads a FerretDB binary from GitHub releases at first container start (`curl ... github.com/wekan/FerretDB/releases/...`). A recipe would need to pin FERRETDB_RELEASE explicitly or switch to the classic docker-compose-mongodb-v7.yml (plain `mongo:7`, no runtime binary fetch) to avoid a first-boot dependency on GitHub release availability/network egress from the customer's container.
summary: Wekan is mechanically installable: an official multi-registry image (ghcr.io/wekan/wekan, pin to a version tag like v10.71 rather than :latest per upstream's own recommendation), a single public HTTP port (8080, proxied to 80 in the sample compose) that works fine behind Traefik, and a MongoDB-compatible backend with no customer-facing database credential. It has no admin-login env var to seed via generated_from — the first person to hit /sign-up becomes admin — so, same as the Kan finding, it needs a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (projected from the customer's root password) to keep a stranger from claiming the admin account before the real customer logs in; with that gate in place there is no missing secrets channel. Two things temper the recommendation from a clean build_now: (1) the project's release cadence is unusually fast right now (2-3 tagged releases/day over the last ~6.5 weeks) which is a maintenance-burden signal for whoever tracks version bumps, not a version-health concern — the project is clearly active, just noisy to pin against; and (2) upstream's current default docker-compose.yml fetches a FerretDB binary from GitHub releases at first container start, which a recipe should avoid by using the classic MongoDB-7-based compose file instead. Net: build_with_caveats — genuinely differentiated (new kanban category, none of the 24 built recipes overlap) but lower priority than Kan or Kanboard, which cover the same customer need with a simpler install path, and worth a deliberate choice among the three kanban candidates rather than building all of them.

name: WeKnora

Repo created 2025-07-22 (Tencent-owned, "WeChat OpenAI" org publishes the images), last push 2026-08-07, not archived, 19.5k stars, 583 open issues. (Its latest tag lands essentially on the analysis date itself, underscoring how fast it ships.)
differentiation: Same "RAG over your own documents" core already covered by the anythingllm gap candidate, but WeKnora goes further with a ReAct agent that can orchestrate retrieval + MCP tools + web search, and a distinct "Wiki Mode" that distills a document set into a self-maintaining, interlinked markdown wiki with a knowledge graph (optional Neo4j) — neither open-webui/ollama (plain chat UI) nor paperless-ai (tagging assistant bolted onto document archiving) attempt that. WeKnora's value case rests on a smaller slice of that niche (teams wanting a living wiki/knowledge-graph output, not just Q&A), and it comes at a much heavier operational cost than either alternative (see below), so the net uplift per unit of complexity is moderate rather than clearly high.
summary: WeKnora ships its own signup/login system (JWT + optional API keys, RBAC roles, orphaned-space auto-promotion of the first real user to Owner), so — like uptime-kuma, immich, and the anythingllm candidate — the admin account is created through the app's own first-visit UI, not projected from the server root password. Everything the container stack needs to boot (Postgres/Redis credentials, JWT_SECRET, the SYSTEM_AES_KEY used to encrypt stored API keys) is a patternless value the platform can generate server-side; no LLM provider key is required at first boot since Ollama support is optional (OLLAMA_OPTIONAL=true) and other providers are added later through the UI, exactly the pattern already used for ANTHROPIC_API_KEY on claude-code. It is mechanically installable today with no blocking secret. The real caveat is operational weight: the default compose stack alone is frontend (nginx) + app (Go backend) + docreader (Python gRPC document/OCR parser) + Postgres (paradedb/pgvector) + Redis — five containers before any of the optional `full` profile add-ons (Neo4j, MinIO, SearXNG, Langfuse, a Docker-based agent-skills sandbox), noticeably heavier than open-webui+ollama or the anythingllm candidate for a comparable "chat with your docs" outcome. usefulness_rationale: Background removal is a common, recognizable task (e-commerce product photos, headshots, marketing assets) with an established paid-SaaS market, so the value proposition ("no per-image fees, your own server") is easy to explain to a customer. It's narrower in scope than most of the current catalogue (a single-purpose tool, not a platform), which caps it at medium rather than high usefulness.
summary: withoutbg's `withoutbg-openweights-v3-app-cpu` image is a single container serving a web UI plus API on one HTTP port (8080, CPU-only variant needs no GPU/NVIDIA toolkit), which sits cleanly behind Traefik on <slug>.<base_domain> — no database, no extra ports, no customer- supplied API key or OAuth needed since the model runs fully locally and the ~455MB weights are baked into the image at build time. The app has no login of its own, so it would need a mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (same pattern as Adminer/WUD) to avoid leaving an open, CPU-hungry image-processing endpoint reachable by anyone on the internet; that gate's password is expressible today via generated_from on the customer's root password. Mechanically installable now, but recommend build_with_caveats rather than build_now: the upstream Docker repo is only ~6 weeks old with no tagged releases yet (only rolling `latest`/commit-SHA tags), so there's real risk of breaking changes before pinning to a stable reference point, and it's worth a short wait-and-watch before committing to a recipe against a still-settling image.

Wizarr sits on top of an existing Plex, Jellyfin, Emby, Audiobookshelf, Romm, Komga, or Kavita instance and generates shareable invite links that auto-provision new users on that server, with expiring invites, per-invite library/permission presets, Discord invite integration, and optional linkage to Jellyseerr/Overseerr-style request systems.
