summary: Wizarr is a single-container, actively-maintained web app (MIT, ghcr.io/wizarrrr/wizarr, pinned tag v2026.7.1) listening on one HTTP port (5690, plain HTTP, no websocket/protocol quirks) that works fine behind Traefik. Unlike Jellyseerr, whose setup wizard imports its admin identity from the external media server, Wizarr's admin account is fully local and self-service: "the first user to register will be the admin user," created directly through Wizarr's own web UI with no environment-variable seeding needed — the same first-visitor-claims-root pattern already accepted unmitigated for n8n, Open WebUI, and Audiobookshelf in this catalogue. Connecting a Plex token or Jellyfin/Emby API key happens afterward as an in-app settings step the customer performs themselves once logged in, not a value `/compose` needs to inject at boot — so there is no first-boot secret this recipe mechanism can't express, and installable_today is true. The caveat is usefulness, not installability: Wizarr only does something useful paired with a Plex/Jellyfin/Emby server the customer already runs elsewhere, and no such recipe exists in the catalogue yet — recommend `build_with_caveats`, flagging that its value is capped until a media server recipe exists for it to onboard users into.

name: Woodpecker CI
source_description: Open-source CI/CD automation platform with native GitHub integration
version_health_notes: Consistent ~monthly stable releases through 2026 (3.14.0 on 2026-05-01, 3.14.1 on 2026-05-12, 3.15.0 on 2026-05-28, 3.16.0 on 2026-06-27, 3.17.0 on 2026-07-31 — 5 days before today, 2026-08-05). One larger gap between 3.13.0 (2026-01-14) and 3.14.0 (2026-05-01), otherwise steady cadence. Repo is not archived, 8,163+ commits, 7.6k stars, actively used as the main CI/CD engine at Codeberg. Clearly an active project.
differentiation: Gitea is a Git hosting/collaboration platform (repos, issues, PRs) with only a lightweight built-in Actions runner as an afterthought. Woodpecker is a dedicated CI/CD pipeline engine that attaches to an *external* Git forge (GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket, Forgejo) rather than hosting code itself — it targets customers who already host their code elsewhere (most commonly GitHub, per Hostinger's description) and just want a self-hosted build/deploy runner. Genuinely different job to be done than Gitea, not a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Real demand for self-hosted CI/CD as an alternative to GitHub Actions/GitLab CI (data residency, cost, custom runners), but the product is fundamentally a satellite to a third-party forge account — it is useless until the customer registers an OAuth application on that forge and pastes back a client ID/secret, which narrows the audience to technically confident users willing to do that setup step.
blocking_issues:
Woodpecker's server has no login of its own — every user, including the admin, authenticates by OAuth through a connected forge (GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket, or Forgejo). At least one forge must be configured at first boot via WOODPECKER_<FORGE>_CLIENT / WOODPECKER_<FORGE>_SECRET, which are the client ID and client secret of an OAuth application the customer must manually register on that forge's site (e.g. GitHub Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps) and paste back in. This is exactly the 'OAuth app registration / third-party account linking' case the schema calls out as having no input channel today — it isn't a password we could hash or generate, and a Traefik basic_auth gate wouldn't provide it either, since the app needs the actual forge credentials to function at all, not just a login gate.
The agent additionally needs privileged access to the host Docker socket (or an equivalent) to execute pipeline steps — not a blocker under the current secrets model, but worth flagging as an operational caveat for whoever builds this later.
summary: Woodpecker CI is an active, well-maintained (~monthly releases, not archived) two-container app (server + agent, both official images, SQLite-by-default so no separate database service is required) with a single reverse-proxy-friendly web UI. It doesn't duplicate Gitea — Gitea hosts code, Woodpecker builds code hosted elsewhere — so there's real differentiation if it shipped. However, it structurally cannot be installed under the current /compose mechanism: there is no admin password to hash and project via generated_from, and no bare app to gate with Traefik basic_auth, because Woodpecker requires a real GitHub (or other forge) OAuth application client ID/secret to boot into a usable state at all. That's a third-party credential with no customer-supplied input channel today. Recommend blocked_on_platform — revisit only if/when the platform grows a generic "customer-supplied arbitrary secret" input mechanism beyond root-password projection and basic-auth gating.

name: WordPress
source_description: WordPress is the world's most popular website builder and CMS
version_health_notes: WordPress 7.0 "Armstrong" shipped 2026-05-20 (slipped from an original 2026-04-09 target), with 7.0.2 as the current patch on the official Docker image as of 2026-08-05 — under 3 months since the last release. 7.1 Beta 1 was already out for testing by 2026-07-15, so the project remains on an active cadence. Since 2025 the project moved from 3 major releases/year to a single major release per year, but that's a deliberate cadence change, not a slowdown signal — patch/security releases and plugin/theme ecosystem activity remain continuous. No ambiguity on identity: "WordPress" here is the wordpress.org/self-hosted CMS (core project, official Docker image), not WordPress.com (hosted SaaS, no self-hosted image) or WooCommerce (a WordPress plugin, separate upstream).
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is a general-purpose website/blog CMS — the closest analogs (Gitea, n8n, Ghost-shaped tools) are developer or automation tools, not content-authoring platforms. WordPress covers a completely different customer intent (build a public website/blog with a WYSIWYG editor, themes, and a huge plugin ecosystem) and is, by a wide margin, the most widely-recognized self-hosted app name a hosting customer could ask for by name.
usefulness_rationale: WordPress alone powers a large share of the public web; brand recognition and existing customer familiarity make this one of the highest-demand candidates in the gap list, independent of how technically simple the stack is.
summary: Structurally this is a two-container stack (official `wordpress` php-apache image + a MySQL/MariaDB backend), single public HTTP port 80, directly reverse-proxy-compatible behind Traefik — the same DB-backed shape as recipes/n8n and recipes/paperless-ngx. The official image takes no admin-account env vars at all (WORDPRESS_DB_HOST/USER/PASSWORD/NAME and the AUTH/SECURE/LOGGED_IN/NONCE key+salt pairs are the only settings, and every one of those is either a server-generated opaque secret the customer never sees, e.g. the DB password, or fixed non-secret config). The WordPress admin account itself is created interactively by whoever first opens the site and completes wp-admin/install.php — the exact first-visitor-claims-admin pattern already accepted for Gitea, Uptime Kuma, and Kutt in this catalogue, so it needs no `generated_from` projection or Traefik basic_auth gate to be installable today. Recommend build_now: mechanically simple, zero platform blockers, and very high customer-recognition value.

name: Workout Cool
source_description: Self-hosted fitness platform with workout plans and exercise tracking
version_health_notes: No tagged release since v1.3.2 (2025-12-07), ~8 months before today (2026-08-05), despite the repo's early history (June-Dec 2025) shipping releases roughly weekly. Commit activity continues after that (default branch pushed as recently as 2026-07-31) but has become bursty rather than steady — a ~3.5 month gap between 2026-04-11 and 2026-07-30 with no commits at all, then a small cluster of ad-placement and calculator features. Repo is not archived and issues/PRs are still open, so this reads as a single-maintainer side project cooling off rather than abandonment — worth re-checking cadence before a build_now call rather than treating "active" as a solid green light.
differentiation: No existing recipe in the 24-app catalogue covers fitness/workout tracking; this would be a net-new category. It offers workout plan creation, an exercise database with video demos, and progress tracking, positioned as a privacy-focused alternative to commercial fitness apps.
usefulness_rationale: Fitness tracking is a plausible self-hosting niche (see also the long-established wger project), but Workout Cool is a young, single-maintainer app with a consumer-SaaS-shaped auth/billing model bolted on rather than a purpose-built self-hosted tool, which raises long-term maintenance risk for a recipe built on top of it.
blocking_issues:
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET are validated as required, non-optional server env vars in src/env.ts (z.string().min(1)), even though the .env.example comments and README present Google OAuth as optional. Without a real Google Cloud OAuth app registration the Next.js app fails env validation and will not boot at all. There is no channel today for a customer to supply an external OAuth client ID/secret via /compose.

The app has no single fixed admin account to project a root-password hash into — auth is open self-service signup/login (Better Auth email+password, admin() plugin grants the first/any registered user no special install-time credential). The generated_from mechanism needs one specific admin-login parameter to target, which doesn't exist here; a Traefik basic_auth gate would be the fallback, but the OAuth blocker above is sufficient on its own to block installability, so this is a secondary note rather than an independent blocker.
summary: Workout Cool would add a genuinely new category (fitness/workout tracking) to the catalogue with no overlap against the current 24 recipes, and is reverse-proxy-friendly (single Next.js web UI, Postgres backend). It is not installable today, though: the app hard-requires a Google OAuth client ID/secret to boot at all (env.ts marks both as required, not optional), and af-api's /compose has no channel for a customer-supplied external OAuth credential. There is also no single admin-login field to project a root-password hash into (open self-signup instead), though that alone is a secondary concern next to the OAuth blocker. Upstream does publish an official pinned image (ghcr.io/snouzy/workout-cool:1.3.2). Revisit if upstream makes Google OAuth truly optional; until then this is blocked on the platform, not just deprioritized.

name: WPS Office
source_description: WPS Office is a comprehensive office suite with document editing capabilities
upstream_license: Proprietary (Kingsoft/WPS Office, freeware desktop app) — container packaging itself is GPL-3.0 (linuxserver.io), but the packaged application is closed-source freemium software, not open source
version_health_notes: linuxserver.io ships a new container build roughly every 7-11 days (ls175 through ls180 span ~1 month as of 2026-08-05, most recent 4 days before analysis date). All recent tags carry the same underlying WPS Office application version (11.1.0.11723-2) — these are base-image / packaging maintenance releases, not application version bumps, so "active" reflects container upkeep more than upstream WPS Office release velocity. No visibility into Kingsoft's own WPS Office release cadence since it is closed-source; linuxserver.io is the only tracked upstream for this packaging.
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes provide document editing. However this is not a native web-based office suite (unlike OnlyOffice or Collabora Online) — it is a full Linux desktop environment streamed to the browser via KasmVNC, with the WPS Office desktop app running inside. Functionally it's closer to "remote desktop for one app" than to a lightweight embeddable document editor.
usefulness_rationale: A customer reading "office suite with document editing" expects a Google-Docs-like web editor, not a full remote-desktop session running a heavyweight (2.38GB image) proprietary Chinese office app with GPU/ shm requirements. Real self-hosted alternatives that actually match the expectation (OnlyOffice Docs, Collabora Online) are proper web-native editors and would serve this use case far better; this recipe would likely disappoint customers who click it expecting lightweight document editing in-browser.
blocking_issues:
The app has no strong login of its own — its optional built-in CUSTOM_USER/PASSWORD env vars provide only HTTP basic auth that linuxserver.io's own docs describe as "suitable only for securing the container on a trusted local network," not for internet-facing use. A Traefik basic_auth gate (root-password projected) can substitute for this, sidestepping the weak built-in mechanism.

Upstream explicitly warns the web interface ships a terminal with passwordless sudo access: "any user with access to the GUI can gain root control within the container, install arbitrary software, and probe your local network." Even gated behind Traefik basic_auth, every legitimate customer login is handed a root shell inside the container by design — a materially different risk profile than any other recipe in the catalogue.

This is an unofficial third-party packaging (linuxserver.io), not a product WPS/Kingsoft ships or supports for server/multi-tenant hosting; running their freeware desktop license as a hosted service product sits in licensing gray area.

Heavy resource footprint for what it delivers: 2.38GB image, requires `--shm-size=1gb` for Electron, and recommends GPU passthrough for usable rendering performance — well above the floor of comparable productivity recipes.
summary: WPS Office has no official server/web offering; the only packaging is linuxserver.io's unofficial KasmVNC wrapper that streams the full desktop app to a browser rather than providing a native web editor. It is mechanically installable today (Traefik basic_auth can gate the exposed port), but upstream's own security warnings — a passwordless root terminal reachable by any authenticated user, and basic-auth-only protection deemed unsuitable for internet exposure — plus its heavy resource needs and licensing ambiguity make it a poor catalogue fit. Customers wanting "document editing" would be far better served by a true web-native suite like OnlyOffice Docs or Collabora Online, neither of which we currently carry either.

name: WriteFreely
source_description: Minimalist Markdown publishing platform with ActivityPub federation and a distraction-free editor
version_health_notes: Source repo pushed to as recently as 2026-08-03 (2 days before this analysis), so the project itself is alive. Release cadence is uneven: v0.14.0 (2023-09-22) -> v0.15.0 (2024-02-03) -> v0.15.1 (2024-10-05) -> v0.16.0 (2025-08-29) -> v0.17.0 (2026-07-17) -> v0.17.1 (2026-07-20), i.e. roughly one release every 6-12 months historically, with two releases three days apart in the most recent burst (v0.17.1 fixed issues from v0.17.0). Not dormant, but not a fast-moving project either. IMPORTANT PACKAGING NOTE: the official Docker Hub image (docker.io/writeas/writefreely) is stale — last pushed ~5 years ago, frozen at 0.12.0, and the project's own docker-compose.yml in the repo still references "writeas/writefreely:latest" (that reference is itself stale/misleading). The actually-maintained image is published by the repo's own CI (.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml) to ghcr.io/writefreely/writefreely, tagged per release (e.g. v0.17.1) as recently as 4 days before this analysis. Any future recipe work must use the ghcr.io image, not the Docker Hub one the official docker-compose.yml still points to.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers blogging/publishing or ActivityPub federation; the closest category-adjacent recipes (opengist for code snippets, gitea for git hosting) serve a different content type entirely. WriteFreely would be the catalogue's first "public content platform" recipe, distinct from the largely private/internal-tool nature of the current 24.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely differentiated (Markdown blog + ActivityPub/fediverse publishing is a real customer want, and single-container SQLite mode keeps ops simple), but a niche audience compared to security/dev-tool recipes already in the catalogue, and the admin-auth mechanics below are awkward under current platform constraints.
blocking_issues:
WriteFreely has no env-var or config.ini field for bootstrapping an admin account, and no browser-based first-run setup wizard (unlike the "first visitor claims admin" pattern accepted for Gitea, Uptime Kuma, and WordPress in this catalogue). The only supported path is running "writefreely --create-admin <user>:<password>" as a one-off exec against the running container, and that command takes the admin password as PLAINTEXT (it hashes it internally). generated_from only ever projects a hash of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no way to get the customer's own credential into this flow, and install.sh itself never sees the plaintext root password either. Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md, a genuine plaintext requirement (not "a hash in an unsupported algorithm") is a structural blocker, not a soft one.

Traefik basic_auth is a whole-service gate in this repo's current recipes (no example of scoping it to a single path). Gating the entire app to work around the above would block public, unauth'd access to the blog itself and to its ActivityPub endpoints (webfinger/inbox), which is the actual point of the app — federation requires other fediverse servers to reach it without a login prompt. Only gating /admin (or /login) would preserve the product's purpose, and that path-scoped capability doesn't exist in the platform today.
summary: WriteFreely is an actively-developed, differentiated candidate (the catalogue's only fediverse-native publishing app) but is blocked on two platform gaps rather than app quality: no channel exists today for a customer-supplied plaintext admin password (generated_from only carries hashes), and whole-service Traefik basic_auth would defeat the app's public-blog/ActivityPub purpose where a path-scoped /admin-only gate is needed instead. Revisit once either a plaintext-capable credential channel or path-scoped basic_auth ships; also note for any future recipe work that the correct image is ghcr.io/writefreely/writefreely, not the long-abandoned docker.io/writeas/writefreely the upstream repo's own docker-compose.yml still references.

name: XBackBone
source_description: Self-hosted lightweight file and screenshot sharing server with ShareX support
version_health_notes: 3.8.2 (2024-06-27) is the last tagged release and, per its own release notes, was explicitly announced as "the final planned maintenance release of the legacy 3.x line" — roughly 2 years and 1 month before today (2026-08-05) with no further tags since. The upstream repo is not archived and remains genuinely active at the commit level: recent commits run through 2026-08-01 (a filename-sanitization security fix dated 2026-07-23, plus 2FA/activity-log/in-app-upgrade feature work in early July 2026), but all of that activity is on a ground-up rewrite ("the next-generation XBackBone, rebuilt from the ground up on Laravel 13 and Livewire 4") that has shipped zero tags, zero releases, and no published Docker image of its own — it is pre-release and not consumable today. There is no official upstream Docker image for either line; the only widely-used image is the third-party lscr.io/linuxserver/xbackbone build, itself frozen at the legacy 3.8.2 codebase since June 2024 (its own release stream just repackages base- image bumps around that same unchanged app version). So the only thing an operator can actually deploy today is a >2-year-stale, upstream-declared-final build of the legacy PHP codebase, while the actively developed successor has no release artifact yet.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue targets the "self-hosted ShareX/screenshot-tool backend" niche specifically: quick uploads from a desktop capture tool to short, shareable links with rich social embeds and per-user accounts. OpenGist is the closest neighbor but is scoped to Git-backed text/code snippets, not arbitrary image/video/file uploads; Immich is a full photo-library/backup product, not a lightweight link-sharing drop box; Syncthing is P2P folder sync between a user's own devices, not public link sharing. XBackBone would be a genuinely distinct category if the underlying codebase were healthier.
usefulness_rationale: "Self-hosted ShareX backend" is a real, recognized self-hosting use case with a dedicated audience, and the multi-user/admin-quota model is more capable than a bare anonymous-upload tool. But the only thing actually deployable today is a legacy codebase upstream itself calls end-of-line, over two years stale, with no security-patch path — the same category of concern (public-facing upload/serving surface on frozen code) that made a similar candidate (AnonUpload) a not_recommended in this catalogue.
blocking_issues:
No official upstream Docker image exists for either the legacy or rewrite codebase; any recipe would have to depend on a third-party image (lscr.io/linuxserver/xbackbone) that upstream does not publish or vouch for.

The image's documented first-boot path is a browser install wizard that POSTs a plaintext admin password to be hashed in-process — a recipe would have to route around the wizard entirely (pre-seed config.php, run the migration script, then INSERT the admin row directly with a precomputed bcrypt hash) to use generated_from:"bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD" instead of the wizard's own plaintext field. Mechanically possible (same shape as Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN row-seeding) but undocumented by upstream and would need to be re-validated against every future legacy point release.

The deployable codebase (3.8.2) is upstream-declared end-of-line for its legacy line with no further patches planned; the actively developed successor has no release or image to pin to yet.
summary: XBackBone is mechanically installable: a single-container PHP app, reverse-proxy-compatible on one HTTP port, whose admin login can be seeded with a generated_from:"bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD" hash by writing config.php and the admin DB row directly instead of using the browser install wizard. It would also fill a niche (self-hosted ShareX/ screenshot-sharing backend) genuinely absent from the current 24-recipe catalogue. However, the only artifact anyone can actually deploy today — the third-party lscr.io/linuxserver/xbackbone image — is frozen on 3.8.2, a release upstream itself titled "the final planned maintenance release of the legacy 3.x line" back in 2024-06-27, over two years before today (2026-08-05), with no official Docker image at all. The project's real current activity (commits through 2026-08-01, including a July 2026 security fix) is all on an unreleased ground-up rewrite with no tag or image yet. Shipping a customer-facing upload/serving surface on a >2-year-stale, upstream-declared end-of-line codebase is the same risk profile that made AnonUpload not_recommended in this catalogue. Recommend not_recommended; revisit once the Laravel/Livewire rewrite ships a tagged release and an official (or at least actively maintained) image.

name: XWiki
source_description: Enterprise wiki platform for knowledge management and team documentation
version_health_notes: 18.6.0 released 2026-07-27 — 9 days before today (2026-08-05). XWiki runs a strict monthly minor-release train through the year (18.0.0 Jan 2026, 18.1.0 Feb, 18.2.0 Mar, ... 18.6.0 Jul, 18.7.0 due Aug 2026), plus a parallel LTS branch (17.10.x) that gets its own patch releases. Repo is not archived, forum/chat/JIRA are active, roadmap page lists concrete plans through the rest of 2026. Clearly active, well-funded (XWiki SAS backs the open-source project commercially).
differentiation: None of the current 24 recipes is a wiki/knowledge-base tool, so on paper this fills the same gap already identified for An Otter Wiki, DokuWiki, Wiki.js, Apache JSPWiki, and TiddlyWiki — all separately under gap-analysis in this same batch. XWiki is the heaviest of that group: Java/Tomcat application server plus a mandatory external database (PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB — no supported embedded-DB path for production), versus e.g. An Otter Wiki's single Python process with git-backed storage and no DB at all. In exchange it offers materially more: structured "XClass" data objects and small in-wiki applications, fine-grained per-page/per-space permissions and groups, a WYSIWYG editor, built-in versioning/diff/comments, and multi-wiki farms — the feature set a mid-size organization ("enterprise wiki" per Hostinger's own description) would actually evaluate against Confluence, not against a lightweight personal wiki.
usefulness_rationale: Real, currently-unfilled category gap and a well-maintained, credible upstream — but this batch is already proposing several wiki candidates, and XWiki is by far the most resource-heavy of them (JVM + Tomcat + a separate database container, where the lighter candidates need one small container and no DB). If the catalogue only has budget for one wiki recipe, a lighter single-container option is the safer first pick; XWiki is the right choice only if the goal is specifically an enterprise-grade wiki with granular permissions and structured data, not "a wiki" in general.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: PostgreSQL database password; Web UI setup-wizard access gate credential
secrets_expressible_today: PostgreSQL database password:server_generated_no_customer_input; Web UI setup-wizard access gate credential:traefik_basic_auth
blocking_issues: XWiki has no environment variable to pre-provision the admin account. Instead, the first HTTP visit to a fresh install launches an interactive "Distribution Wizard" in the browser where whoever gets there first configures the database connection and creates the initial admin user — there is no `generated_from`-style hook into this flow. Left open, this is the same "first visitor wins the admin account" exposure already flagged for An Otter Wiki. It is coverable today by a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` gate (root-password projected) placed in front of the app for the setup window, but that is a workaround for a gap in the app's own first-run flow, not a clean fit — the customer would need to complete the wizard behind the gate before anything is safe to expose, and, unlike a normal app login, there's no way to have the app itself enforce that ordering.
summary: XWiki (xwiki:18.6.0-postgres-tomcat) is a Java/Tomcat wiki platform that requires an external PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB database and serves its UI on a single HTTP port (8080), so it is Traefik-compatible from a networking standpoint. It is actively maintained on a strict monthly release cadence with no EOL signal. The catalogue gap it fills — no wiki/knowledge-base recipe exists today — is real, but this same batch already proposes several lighter, DB-free wiki alternatives, and XWiki's own first-run flow (an interactive setup wizard with no env-var admin pre-provisioning) needs the same Traefik basic_auth workaround already used for An Otter Wiki, just to prevent an anonymous visitor from claiming the admin account before the customer does. Mechanically installable today with that gate, but recommended as build_with_caveats: a reasonable second wiki option for a customer who specifically wants enterprise-grade permissions and structured content over a heavier Java/DB footprint, not the default pick if the catalogue only needs one wiki recipe.

name: Yao
source_description: Open-source app runtime for building web apps and AI agents with JSON
upstream_license: "Modified Apache License 2.0" — standard Apache-2.0 plus additional conditions from the vendor (Infinite Wisdom Software): branding/logo and a "certificate verification system" must not be removed or altered, and organizations with 50+ employees or >$1,000,000 annual revenue must obtain a separate commercial license. Source-available, not a clean OSI-style permissive license.
version_health_notes: Very active: 10 release candidates (v1.0.0-rc1 through rc10) shipped between 2026-07-02 and 2026-08-03, roughly every 2-4 days, with rc10 just 2 days before today (2026-08-05). Repo is unarchived, 7.6k+ GitHub stars, ongoing feature work (agent/CLI/proxy-auth features landing in each rc). No EOL/maintenance-mode signal — but the project has not yet cut a GA v1.0.0; it is still pre-release by its own versioning.
differentiation: Closest existing recipes are the AI-agent pair Hermes Agent and OpenClaw, but those ship as finished, usable products (an agent that answers via Telegram/dashboard out of the box). Yao is a lower-level application *engine*/SDK — you write your own JSON/TS "app" (data models, API flows, UI pages) and Yao executes it; the bare image has no product of its own to offer a customer. No functional duplication with the current 24-recipe catalogue, but also no self-contained value without custom development work.
usefulness_rationale: Genuinely different from anything in the catalogue, but it is a developer framework, not an end-user application — a customer who "installs Yao" from a one-click catalogue gets an empty engine with nothing to click into until they author and deploy their own app code, which the AF one-click model has no path for. Every existing recipe is click-and-use; Yao would be click-and-then-go-write-code.
blocking_issues:
The official image (yaoapp/yao) ships no default application — it requires a project directory bind-mounted to /data/app containing the customer's own hand-authored app definition (JSON/TS models, APIs, UI pages) before it serves anything. /compose has no channel to accept or provision arbitrary customer source code, so a generic recipe would boot to an engine with no usable web UI at all, not to a configurable admin login the way a normal app would.

Licensing: the modified Apache-2.0 license requires a paid commercial license from Infinite Wisdom Software for organizations with 50+ employees or >$1M annual revenue — a threshold IONOS/AF itself clears, independent of any individual customer. Redistributing this as a one-click hosted recipe likely requires a commercial agreement with the vendor before any recipe work starts; this is a legal/business blocker, not a technical one.

The documented demo admin panel (accessible only once a project defines the built-in admin/"xiang" module) ships a fixed default login (xiang@iqka.com / demo@5099) with no environment-variable or compose-level override — moot given the app-definition blocker above, but would itself need a Traefik basic_auth gate if ever revisited.
summary: Yao is an actively developed (rc release every few days), Apache-2.0-plus (source-available, commercial-license-required-at-scale) application engine for building custom web apps and AI agents from JSON/TS definitions — not a ready-to-use product. The official Docker image requires a customer-authored project mounted into the container before it serves anything, which the current /compose mechanism has no way to provision, and IONOS's own scale likely triggers the vendor's commercial licensing requirement regardless of any per-customer parameter question. Recommend not_recommended: this is a developer framework outside the "click and use" shape of the catalogue, compounded by a licensing obstacle independent of the platform mechanism gaps tracked elsewhere.

name: Yarn
source_description: Self-hosted decentralized micro-blogging pod built on the open twtxt feed format
version_health_notes: v0.16.0 shipped 2026-07-12 (Docker Hub confirms the `0.16.0` tag pushed 26 days before this analysis, 2026-08-05), with a further commit to master on 2026-07-26 (text-encoding fix) — under a month old. 36 total tagged releases on the upstream Gitea instance (git.mills.io), a steady cadence for a single-maintainer-led project (James Mills / prologic). No archive notice, no EOL announcement; clearly active. Note: primary development happens on a self-hosted Gitea (git.mills.io/yarnsocial/yarn) with only a partial/lagging mirror on GitHub — some GitHub org/repo paths for "yarnsocial" 404'd during this research, so treat git.mills.io as canonical, not github.com.
differentiation: None of the current 24 shipped recipes touch social/micro-blogging. Yarn is a niche pick even within that empty category: it implements twtxt, a deliberately minimal decentralized feed format (a plain-text file per user, pulled by other pods/clients over HTTP) rather than the ActivityPub federation model of Mastodon/Pleroma/Misskey that most self-hosters mean by "decentralized social." It would be a genuinely new capability, not a duplicate, but the underlying protocol has a much smaller install base and ecosystem (clients, other pods to federate with) than ActivityPub alternatives.
usefulness_rationale: Fills an empty category on paper, but twtxt is a minority protocol even among self-hosted social software, so real-world demand from a small-business/solo-developer hosting audience is likely thin. A customer wanting a self-hosted "Twitter alternative" is far more likely to search for and recognize Mastodon than Yarn/twtxt.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: API_SIGNING_KEY; COOKIE_SECRET; MAGICLINK_SECRET; Traefik basic-auth gate credential
blocking_issues: Yarn's core purpose is a "pod" that other twtxt clients/pods pull user feeds from over plain HTTP (no auth) — putting a permanent Traefik basic_auth gate on the whole domain (the only way today to stop a stranger from grabbing the admin account during the open-registration window) would also block that pull-based federation once setup is done, defeating the app's actual purpose. The gate would need to be lifted after the customer claims the admin account and registrations are closed again — a config-and-restart step our current mechanism has no channel to trigger post-boot (install.sh runs once at provisioning, before the customer has had a chance to register).
summary: Yarn (yarn.social/yarnd) is an actively maintained (v0.16.0, 2026-07-12; 36 releases, commits within the last two weeks), AGPLv3-licensed, single-container Go app with an official Docker image and a single HTTP port (8000), reverse-proxy friendly. It fills an otherwise-empty social/micro-blogging category, but implements the niche twtxt protocol rather than the more recognizable ActivityPub model, which caps realistic customer demand. Mechanically it does not clear the current /compose constraint cleanly: there is no admin-password env var, so the admin account must be claimed through a temporarily-open self-registration page, and gating that page with Traefik basic_auth — the only tool we have — would need to be lifted afterward to let the pod serve its actual pull-based federation purpose, a post-boot step our install-once mechanism can't perform today. Not recommended: low expected usefulness and a genuine (not just cosmetic) installability blocker.

name: Yopass
source_description: Encrypted one-time secret sharing via self-destructing links
upstream_license: Apache-2.0 (core); newer features — OIDC auth, custom theming, audit logging, read receipts, webhooks — are gated behind a paid commercial license layered on top of the same repo/image
version_health_notes: Very active release cadence: 14.0.0 through 14.8.0 shipped between 2026-05-28 and 2026-07-28, roughly one tagged release every 1-2 weeks, with 14.8.0 only about 8 days before today (2026-08-05). No sign of slowdown, archival, or EOL — commit history and PRs are ongoing.
differentiation: Yopass solves a different problem than anything already in the catalogue: ephemeral, self-destructing one-time secret sharing (e.g. "send me the API key" over Slack/email safely) rather than persistent credential storage (Vaultwarden). No existing recipe covers transient secret transmission.
usefulness_rationale: A genuinely useful, low-friction utility for anyone regularly sharing passwords/tokens with teammates or clients, and it is extremely lightweight (two tiny containers, ~35MB image). Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because it is a narrow single-purpose tool compared to broader platforms elsewhere in the catalogue, and its core value proposition (anonymous one-time links) is intentionally account-free, so there isn't much for a customer to configure or grow into over time.
summary: Yopass is a two-container stack (jhaals/yopass web/API server + Memcached as the ephemeral secret store, per upstream's own deploy/docker-compose/insecure example) exposing a single HTTP port, cleanly reverse-proxy-compatible behind Traefik on yopass.<base_domain> — structurally similar to Uptime Kuma's single-public-port pattern, just with a small backing cache service like n8n's Postgres sidecar. It needs no customer-supplied secret at first boot at all: the free/open-source tier has no built-in accounts or admin login by design (secrets are encrypted client-side and shared via a one-time link containing the decryption key in the URL fragment — the app itself never sees plaintext and there is nothing for a customer to log into). This clears the current /compose constraint with zero blocking issues. The project is actively maintained with a fast release cadence, has no overlap with the existing catalogue, and is small and cheap to run, making it a solid build-now candidate — note only that the more advanced features (OIDC auth, audit logging, webhooks, read receipts) are commercially licensed add-ons not included in the free image, so the recipe would ship core secret-sharing functionality only.

name: Your Spotify

version_health_notes: Latest tagged release (1.20.0) is from 2026-05-24 — about 2.5 months old as of today (2026-08-05). Recent release history shows a steady ~1-2 month cadence: 1.19.0 (2026-03-30), 1.18.0 (2026-02-24), 1.17.0 (2025-12-26), 1.16.0 (2025-12-20). This is an actively maintained project with a good pinned-tag choice available (`1.20.0`).
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes does personal listening-history analytics. Closest neighbors are dashboard-style apps like Uptime Kuma or Home Assistant, but none touch music/streaming data. This would be a genuinely new category for the catalogue (personal media analytics) with broad casual appeal for anyone with a Spotify account.
usefulness_rationale: Popular, well-known self-hosted project with real demand (frequently recommended in self-hosting communities), but its value is entirely gated on the customer completing a Spotify Developer OAuth app registration before the recipe does anything useful — a meaningfully higher setup barrier than a one-click "give it a domain" app, which caps usefulness below apps that work immediately after install.
blocking_issues:
The app is functionally inert without `SPOTIFY_PUBLIC` (Spotify OAuth client ID) and `SPOTIFY_SECRET` (Spotify OAuth client secret) — both obtained by the customer registering their own app in the Spotify Developer dashboard and pointing its OAuth redirect URI at their deployed instance's domain. This is exactly the "OAuth app registration / third-party account linking" case the schema calls `no` — there is no channel today for af-api to project an externally-issued, customer-specific value like this into `/compose`.

Ships as two separate HTTP services (server on :8080, client on :3000) with no built-in reverse-proxy path-routing between them in the example compose file — the client is configured to call the server via its own `API_ENDPOINT`, so putting both behind one `<slug>.<base_domain>` Traefik router needs either a rewrite of the client's env-driven API base URL scheme or a second subdomain/path rule per service. Solvable at recipe-authoring time, but it is not "single port, drop-in" like most of the current catalogue — noted here since it compounds the OAuth blocker rather than standing alone.

No admin login of its own beyond the Spotify OAuth flow, so a Traefik `basic_auth` gate is not a substitute credential path here — it would just add an extra login in front of an app that still can't function without the customer's own Spotify app credentials.
summary: Your Spotify would fill a genuinely new niche (personal listening-history analytics) not covered by any of the current 24 recipes, and the upstream project is under active development with a healthy, recent release cadence (1.20.0, 2026-05-24). The sole blocker is that it hard-requires a customer-supplied Spotify OAuth client ID/secret, obtained by the customer registering their own app in the Spotify Developer dashboard, and there is no channel today for af-api to project an externally-issued, customer-specific credential like this into `/compose`. Revisit once the platform has an external API-credential input channel.

name: YOURLS
source_description: Self-hosted PHP URL shortener with click tracking, plugins, and REST API
version_health_notes: Latest tagged release is 1.10.4 (2024-05-23) — about 26 months / 2.2 years before today (2026-08-05) with no newer tag cut, and the official `yourls` Docker Hub image is still pinned at 1.10.4 for the same stretch. However the master branch itself is not dormant: commit history shows steady weekly-to-biweekly activity right up to 2026-08-05 (security hardening, cookie/session fixes, HTTP status code fixes, automated GeoIP/dependency bumps), so this reads as a project that has simply stopped cutting tagged releases rather than one that's unmaintained. Practical effect for a recipe: pinning to the only available stable tag (1.10.4) means shipping code that is over two years stale relative to master, with no newer official image to pin to instead.
differentiation: No existing recipe covers link/URL shortening. YOURLS gives a customer a self-hosted, branded short-link service with click analytics and a plugin ecosystem plus REST API — a genuinely new category versus the current 24 recipes (closest neighbors like Vaultwarden or Uptime Kuma solve unrelated problems).
usefulness_rationale: Useful for anyone wanting branded/self-hosted short links with click tracking instead of a third-party shortener, but it's a narrow, single-purpose utility rather than a platform customers grow into, and its primary web surface is a fairly small admin UI (bulk-shorten, stats) rather than a rich application.
blocking_issues:
YOURLS_PASS (the admin login password) has no input channel today. The official docker image's entrypoint writes whatever string it's given as a literal password value into config.php; if written as plain text, YOURLS auto-hashes it as its own custom `phpass:`-tagged format on first request, but that means the *plaintext* value written at first boot IS the login credential, not a hash of it — the customer would need to already know that plaintext, which generated_from cannot supply (it only ever emits a hash of ROOT_PASSWORD).

Notably this is not a hard structural dead-end once IF-1420 merges: YOURLS' own auth check (yourls_check_password_hash) DOES support a bcrypt-style hash checked via PHP password_verify() — but only if the stored value is manually pre-formatted as `phpass:<hash-with-$- replaced-by-!>` before it's written to config.php. A recipe's install.sh could plausibly perform that string transform on the `generated_from: "bcrypt:ROOT_PASSWORD"` value itself before writing config.php directly (bypassing the docker image's plaintext-env-var flow). This still requires IF-1420 to land first, so it is not installable_today, but it is a build_with_caveats path afterward rather than a permanent blocker.
summary: YOURLS is a single PHP container plus a MySQL sidecar — structurally close to n8n/Paperless-ngx's app-plus-database pattern — exposing one HTTP port and cleanly reverse-proxy-compatible behind Traefik. It fills a category gap (URL shortening) with no overlap in the current catalogue. The blocker is its admin login: the docker image's env-var flow wants a plaintext password rather than any hash, so it cannot be wired up via generated_from today; a workaround exists (pre-format the bcrypt hash as YOURLS' internal `phpass:` token and write config.php directly in install.sh) but depends on IF-1420 merging first. Separately, upstream has not cut a tagged release in over two years despite an actively committing master branch, so any recipe would ship on a stale pinned image with no fresher official tag available. Recommend blocked_on_platform: revisit once generated_from ships, and re-check for a newer tagged release at that time.

name: yt-dlp Web UI

version_health_notes: ~37 days since the latest release (v4.0.0, 2026-06-29) as of today (2026-08-05), and there is a follow-up bugfix commit on 2026-07-14 ("fixed non completing downloads after v4"), so the project is not dormant. But the release/commit history is bursty rather than steady: v3.2.6 (2025-03-15) to v4.0.0 (2026-06-29) is a ~15.5-month gap between tagged releases, and commit history in between shows long silences (2026-01-21 to 2025-09-01 is a ~5-month gap with a single throwaway commit). Repo is not archived (2,536 stars, 102 open issues, pushed_at 2026-07-14). GitHub username changed from marcopeocchi to marcopiovanello at some point (same repo/history, not a fork) — noting this so a reviewer doesn't mistake it for two different projects.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 built recipes covers "download a video/audio file from a URL" as a function. No overlap with existing built recipes, but the same niche is already covered by apps-gaps/metube.yaml (medium usefulness, build_now) and apps-gaps/alltube.yaml (not_recommended, dead project). yt-dlp Web UI adds a job queue, live progress via WebSocket, and livestream-capture support that MeTube's simpler UI lacks, but solves the same core problem MeTube already solves more cleanly.
usefulness_rationale: Single-container, single-HTTP-port (3033) app, actively maintained (not archived, recent bugfix commits) with more features than MeTube (download queue, livestream capture). Capped at medium rather than high for two reasons shared with MeTube: (1) the same third-party-ToS consideration around bulk-downloading video platforms' content applies here too, and (2) MeTube already fills this niche with a cleaner version-pinning story (date-stamped tags vs. this project's tag-less image, see blocking_issues) — shipping both would be pure overlap with no differentiated customer benefit big enough to justify carrying two yt-dlp front ends.
blocking_issues:
No pinned version tag on either registry the project publishes to. Docker Hub (marcobaobao/yt-dlp-webui) has exactly one non-signature tag, "latest" (151 total tags, all the rest are cosign .sig attestations) — there is no "v4.0.0" or equivalent to pin to. GHCR (ghcr.io/marcopiovanello/yt-dlp-web-ui) does publish versioned tags, but only up through v2.0.8 — it stopped tracking releases after that and never got v3.x/v4.x tags; "v4"/"v4.0.0" return 404 there. Building a recipe today means either violating RFC-002's `image-tag-pinned` rule by using `:latest`, or pinning to a `latest`-tag digest (sha256) with no semantic version attached to it — workable, but loses the "which release am I on" traceability MeTube's date-stamped tags give for free, and requires the recipe owner to manually re-check and re-pin the digest to pick up yt-dlp extractor fixes (this class of app breaks routinely as video sites change their frontends).

The app's own optional login (`--auth`/`--user`/`--pass` flags, backed by `JWT_SECRET`) takes a plaintext customer-chosen username and password with no hash-based option — `generated_from` cannot project into it. Not a hard blocker on its own: auth is optional and disabled by default, so the recommended path is to leave the app's own auth off and gate the whole app behind Traefik `basic_auth` instead, same as MeTube/WUD/n8n.
summary: yt-dlp Web UI is a single-container, single-port app with no auth enabled by default, so it slots behind a Traefik basic_auth gate with no structural secrets blocker — mechanically buildable today. It is actively maintained (not archived, a July 2026 bugfix commit following the June 2026 v4.0.0 release) but has a genuinely bursty release cadence (15.5 months between the last two tagged releases) and, more importantly, no reproducible versioned tag on either registry it publishes to (Docker Hub ships "latest" only; GHCR's versioned tags stop at v2.0.8). It duplicates the niche already covered by apps-gaps/metube.yaml, which has a cleaner tagging story and is already rated build_now for the same use case. Recommend build_with_caveats: not a platform blocker, but pin-to-digest tracking overhead and direct overlap with a better-tagged alternative make this a lower priority than MeTube for the same slot in the catalogue.

name: Zabbix
source_description: Enterprise open-source monitoring for networks, servers, and applications
version_health_notes: Zabbix ships two live tracks: 7.0 LTS (released June 2024, patch 7.0.29 on 2026-07-28, full support through 2027 and limited support through mid-2029) and 7.4 standard (patch 7.4.13 on 2026-07-29, support ends 2026-09-30 since standard releases only get ~1 year of life before the next one supersedes them). This is an actively maintained, corporately-backed (Zabbix SIA) project with no EOL/dormancy signal — for a recipe, the LTS 7.0.x line is the sane pin given its multi-year support window versus 7.4's ~1-year runway.
differentiation: Uptime Kuma is a lightweight external "is it up" status checker for a handful of HTTP/TCP/ping targets. Zabbix is a full enterprise monitoring platform: SNMP/agent-based polling of networked devices, servers, VMs and applications, historical metric storage and trending, templated item/trigger libraries per device type, distributed proxies, and alerting/escalation workflows. A customer who has outgrown Uptime Kuma's simple up/down checks (e.g. wants to monitor CPU/disk/network across a fleet of servers or network gear) would reach for Zabbix instead, so this is a genuinely different tier of the same broad "monitoring" category rather than a duplicate.
usefulness_rationale: Zabbix is one of the most widely deployed open-source monitoring platforms (used by large enterprises and MSPs) and IONOS customers running any nontrivial server/network footprint would have real use for it. It's a heavier, more IT-admin-oriented tool than most of the current catalogue, but that's exactly the gap: nothing here today does agent/SNMP-based infrastructure monitoring at this depth.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD; MYSQL_PASSWORD; Traefik basic-auth gate credential
blocking_issues: The official zabbix-web-nginx-mysql / zabbix-server-mysql images have no environment variable to set the frontend "Admin" account password at first boot (confirmed via zabbix/zabbix-docker issue #820 — this is a known, unresolved request). Every fresh deployment boots with the well-known default Admin/zabbix credential. Per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's guidance for a fixed default credential the app itself gives no way to change at deploy time, this is not a hard blocker on its own: the mitigation is a Traefik `basic_auth: true` gate in front of the whole app (same pattern as apps-gaps/sonarqube.yaml's admin/admin case), which moves the actual customer-facing auth boundary to the gate. The still-default Admin/zabbix login behind it is only reachable by someone who already holds the gate credential, so it is no longer customer-facing risk.
summary: Zabbix is a three-service stack (zabbix-server, zabbix-web frontend on nginx, MySQL/MariaDB — structurally close to n8n's app+Postgres pattern but with one more tier) exposing a single HTTP port for the web UI that is cleanly reverse-proxy-compatible behind Traefik; the server↔agent port (10051) stays internal-only for a basic single-node deployment. It fills a real gap versus Uptime Kuma's lightweight status checks with full agent/SNMP-based infrastructure monitoring, and upstream is actively maintained with a multi-year-support LTS line (7.0.29, 2026-07-28) to pin against. The frontend's fixed default Admin/zabbix login (no env var to change it at first boot) is solvable today via a Traefik `basic_auth` gate per apps-gaps/SCHEMA.md's guidance on fixed default credentials — the same pattern used for SonarQube's admin/admin — so it is not a hard blocker. No other blocking issue was found (MySQL credentials are server-generated with no customer input needed, and the multi-container wiring is a standard app+DB compose shape already used elsewhere in the catalogue). Recommend build_now.

name: Zen
source_description: Minimalist self-hosted note-taking app with markdown and full-text search
version_health_notes: The repo has exactly two git tags ever: 1.0.0 (2025-09-02) and 1.5.0 (2025-10-06), about a month apart, and nothing tagged since — just over 10 months as of today (2026-08-05). Untagged commit activity on `master` continued past the last tag (features like import frontmatter support, internal-note side panel) but the most recent commit of any kind is 2026-04-29, so the project has now also gone fully quiet on commits for just over 3 months. Not archived, AGPL-3.0 license intact, only 2 open issues, ~1.1k GitHub stars. The README states explicitly "This is a personal project built for my own use... I may not actively review pull requests or respond to issues due to time constraints" — a single-maintainer hobby project. This reads as a real but low-bandwidth, currently-dormant-for-months project rather than an abandoned one; worth re-checking before a build, not a hard EOL call.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue covers personal note-taking. Zen is a single Go binary storing Markdown notes in a local SQLite database (full-text search via BM25, tag-based organisation instead of folders, templates, pin/archive/soft-delete, import/export). It occupies the same "self-hosted Obsidian-alternative" niche already surfaced by prior gap-analyses of flatnotes, SilverBullet, and Many Notes — several strong candidates now compete for the same empty catalogue slot, which is fine to leave as-is per current prioritization guidance and doesn't count against any one of them on its own merits. Zen's differentiator within that niche is being the most minimal: a single ~small Go binary, no bundled search service or OAuth surface, with heavier features (semantic search, similar-image lookup, automated backups) split out into separate companion projects (zen-intelligence, zen-backup) rather than shipped in the main container.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted markdown note-taking is a well-understood, recurring self-hosting want, and Zen's low-resource single-binary/single-container footprint fits the AF profile well. Usefulness is capped at medium rather than high because Zen is thinner on features than SilverBullet or Many Notes (no multi-vault, no plugin/scripting system, no OAuth), is maintained by a single person who has explicitly flagged limited review bandwidth, and has had zero commits of any kind for the past 3+ months on top of an already sparse two-release tagging history.
blocking_issues: Zen has its own local login (email + password, hashed and stored in SQLite) but no admin-password env var or setup wizard — the very first account is created through an open, unauthenticated `POST /api/users` self-registration endpoint that is only disabled once exactly one user exists (`HasUsers()` check). There is no `generated_from` channel to project the customer's root-password hash into that registration call, since it's a plain unauthenticated API call rather than an app-managed credential field. Left unfronted, whichever visitor reaches the domain first (not necessarily the customer) could claim the sole account. A Traefik `basic_auth` gate keyed off the root-password hash closes that exposure at the perimeter, but the customer still has to complete in-app registration themselves on first authenticated visit — the recipe can only secure the door, not pre-provision the account behind it. This is the same pattern already documented for Many Notes.
summary: Zen is a single-container Go app (image `ghcr.io/sheshbabu/zen/zen:1.5.0`, default port 8080, two volumes `/data` and `/images`, no external database) that is reverse-proxy compatible and would fill a note-taking gap not covered by any of the current 24 recipes — though that same gap is already being separately evaluated via flatnotes, SilverBullet, and Many Notes candidates. It clears the installability bar only via a mandatory Traefik `basic_auth` perimeter gate, because its own account creation is an open, unauthenticated self-registration call with no root-password projection channel; the customer must still complete in-app registration themselves after first login, same caveat as Many Notes. Version health is the bigger concern here: only two tags exist in the project's history (1.0.0, 1.5.0, both in Sep-Oct 2025) and there has been no commit of any kind — tagged or not — since 2026-04-29, over 3 months ago. The repo isn't archived and the maintainer is still responsive to its low issue volume, but the README's own framing as a personal, limited-bandwidth project plus the recent activity gap argue for caution. Recommend build_with_caveats: mechanically installable today, but worth a freshness re-check before committing build time, and the basic_auth caveat must be called out explicitly in the recipe.

upstream_docker_image: glidea/zenfeed (backend); glidea/zenfeed-web (web UI); diygod/rsshub (bundled feed-scrape dependency)
version_health_notes: Tagged releases: v0.1.1 (2025-04-23) through v0.7.0 (2025-11-07), roughly monthly during 2025 then nothing tagged since. However, commit activity on `main` has continued well past the last tag — most recently 2026-07-10, with a small run of merged PRs (provider additions, README fixes) on 2026-07-03. differentiation: Nothing in the current 24-recipe catalogue is an RSS/feed reader or news-aggregation tool. Open WebUI and Hermes Agent are general AI chat/agent front ends, not feed aggregators; n8n could be wired up to poll feeds via automation but is not a reading/browsing product. Zenfeed's pitch — LLM-driven summarization, scoring/filtering, and semantic search over subscribed feeds, plus scheduled "daily briefing" digests and webhook/email alerts on tracked topics — is a genuinely distinct niche (personal AI news/monitoring hub) that none of the existing recipes cover.
usefulness_rationale: Real, distinct use case (self-hosted AI-curated RSS reading) with an actively-updated (if untagged) upstream, but it is a single-user personal tool rather than a business/team product, and its core value proposition (LLM summarization/semantic search) is non-functional out of the box without a customer-supplied LLM API key — see installability below.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: LLM provider API_KEY (SiliconFlow by default; OpenAI/Gemini/others configurable); Traefik basic-auth gate credential
blocking_issues:
The official docker-compose.yml requires an API_KEY env var for its LLM provider (defaults to SiliconFlow's Qwen3-8B/embedding models; the fallback literal "your-api-key" is non-functional). Without it, the app's only real feature — AI summarization, scoring/filtering, and semantic search — does not work at all; the app degrades to a bare RSS reader. This is a third-party API key with no customer-supplied-value channel in /compose today (the same class of blocker already tracked on the disabled `paperless-ai` recipe in this catalogue).

Upstream README states explicitly: "zenfeed does not yet have an authentication mechanism" for its web UI, and warns that exposing it publicly risks leaking the API_KEY. A mandatory Traefik basic_auth gate (expressible today via generated_from root password) mitigates the public-exposure risk but does not solve the missing-API-key blocker above.

No versioned upstream tag since v0.7.0 (2025-11-07); the official compose stack pins both first-party images (`glidea/zenfeed`, `glidea/zenfeed-web`) to `:latest`, which RFC-002's image-tag-pinned rule would reject — there is no stable numbered tag on Docker Hub to pin to instead as of today.
summary: Zenfeed is a three-container stack (zenfeed backend, zenfeed-web frontend, bundled diygod/rsshub feed-scraper) exposing a single primary web port (1400) that would sit cleanly behind Traefik, with the backend's other ports (query/gRPC API, MCP endpoint, Prometheus metrics) staying container-internal — structurally similar to other multi-container recipes like n8n. It fills a real gap: no existing recipe is an AI-curated RSS/news reader. It is blocked from shipping today for two independent reasons: it mandates a third-party LLM API_KEY with no supported input channel in /compose (the same structural blocker already tracked on the disabled paperless-ai recipe), and it ships no web-UI authentication of its own, upstream says so directly. On top of that, upstream has not cut a version tag since 2025-11-07 even though `main` is still being committed to, leaving no pinnable stable tag for the two first-party images. Revisit once IF-1420/1312-style secret projection is extended to arbitrary external API keys and upstream resumes tagging releases.

blocking_issues:

Not a persistent production service by design: the official Docker image is documented upstream as not intended for hosting the built site, and the built-in preview server is explicitly dev-only (not for production exposure) — there is no admin UI or long-running app process for the recipe model to gate or install into.
summary: Zensical is an actively maintained, fast-moving static site generator (latest 0.0.53, 2026-08-04) built by the Material for MkDocs team as a Rust-core successor to MkDocs — no EOL or dormancy concern, though it's still pre-1.0. It doesn't overlap with anything in the current 24-recipe catalogue, but structurally it's a CLI build tool, not a self-hosted application: no admin UI, no login, and no value without customer-supplied Markdown source content, for which the recipe mechanism has no delivery channel today. Upstream itself disclaims both the official Docker image and the built-in preview/search server as unsuitable for production hosting, directing users to a separate web server for anything live. Recommend not pursuing this as a recipe — the same structural mismatch already identified for Hugo, independent of the root-password/basic-auth secret mechanism.

This reads as maintenance-only for a narrowed scope, not active development, and not archived/hard-EOL only in the technical sense of the repo still existing.
differentiation: No recipe in the current 24-recipe catalogue offers a standalone full-text search/log-indexing engine — ZincSearch would be a new category. It ships as a single Go binary/container (Elasticsearch- compatible bulk ingest API plus a bundled Vue web UI for querying and user management), which is a lighter footprint than standing up Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for the same job.
usefulness_rationale: Search/log-indexing infrastructure is typically consumed by other applications via API rather than used directly by an end customer through a web UI, which is a weaker fit for AF's self-hosted-app catalogue than for our existing user-facing recipes. That usefulness gap is compounded by the maintainers' own 2023 statement steering the "log indexing" use case (the one Hostinger's description advertises) away from ZincSearch and toward OpenObserve, and by the 2.5-year gap since the last tagged release.
blocking_issues:
ZincSearch's only login mechanism is its own admin account, set via the ZINC_FIRST_ADMIN_USER / ZINC_FIRST_ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variables read once on first boot. ZINC_FIRST_ADMIN_PASSWORD must be supplied as plaintext — there is no documented option to seed it from a pre-computed hash. `generated_from` only ever projects a hash (argon2/bcrypt) of the customer's root password, never the plaintext, so there is no channel to give the customer a working login built from a value they already know. Randomly generating the admin password server-side instead would satisfy the boot requirement but leave the customer with no way to discover it and log into the one UI the app has, since AF has no generated-secret display/handoff channel today — that would make the app installable but functionally unusable as a standalone product.

A Traefik `basic_auth` perimeter gate does not resolve the above: it would add a second credential in front of an app that still needs its own separately-known admin login behind it, and the app's own login is the one the customer would actually need to operate the product (create indexes, run queries in the UI).
summary: ZincSearch (public.ecr.aws/zinclabs/zincsearch:v0.4.10, single port 4080 for both UI and API, reverse-proxy compatible, no external database) is not installable under the current recipe mechanism: its only login is a first-boot plaintext admin password with no `generated_from`-hash channel and no way to hand a server-generated password back to the customer. Even setting installability aside, this is not a strong candidate to wait on a platform fix for: no tagged release since 2024-01-14 (2.5+ years), only sparse minor commits since, and — most tellingly — the upstream maintainers explicitly said in 2023 that ZincSearch is kept alive only for app search and pointed users wanting log indexing (exactly what Hostinger's description offers) to their other project, OpenObserve. Recommend not_recommended.

name: Zipline
source_description: ShareX-compatible file and image upload server with a modern dashboard
version_health_notes: v4.6.5 released 2026-07-28, 8 days before today (2026-08-05). Tagged releases run roughly monthly through 2026: v4.6.4 (2026-07-06), v4.6.3 (2026-06-26), v4.6.2 (2026-06-03), v4.6.1 (2026-05-20), v4.6.0 (2026-05-11), v4.5.3 (2026-04-07), v4.5.2 (2026-03-29). GHCR also publishes near-daily `trunk-<sha>` build tags (latest 2026-08-06), confirming ongoing active development. Repo is not archived, releases include regular security-advisory fixes (e.g. v4.6.4, v4.6.2, v4.6.1) that are being triaged promptly. Clearly active.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes covers ShareX-style screenshot/file upload hosting. Immich is a photo/video library with albums and ML search, aimed at personal media backup rather than generating quick shareable links; Syncthing continuously syncs files between the customer's own devices rather than serving public/shared upload links; Opengist shares text/code snippets specifically, not arbitrary files or images. Zipline's niche — a personal "screenshot/file drop" server that ShareX, Flameshot, and similar tools upload directly to, returning a shareable URL — is distinct from all of these.
usefulness_rationale: Popular among a specific but sizeable audience (people replacing imgur/Discord-CDN-style screenshot hosting with a self-hosted ShareX-compatible endpoint), with a modern dashboard and URL shortener features. Narrower appeal than a general-purpose consumer app like a password manager or budgeting tool, but a clean, well-defined, frequently-requested self-hosting use case.
summary: Zipline is a two-service stack (its own Node app plus a PostgreSQL database, matching the n8n/paperless-ngx template) serving its dashboard and upload API on a single HTTP port (3000) — fully Traefik-compatible. It needs a `CORE_SECRET` cookie-signing key and a `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` database password at boot, but both are patternless server-side secrets nothing customer-facing ever needs to read, so af-api can generate them internally with no input channel required (mechanism: server_generated_no_customer_input for both). Confirmed against current (v4) docs (zipline.diced.sh/docs/config/core) and the official docker-compose (github.com/diced/zipline docker-compose.yml): on first browser visit the customer is redirected to a one-time setup page to create their own super-admin username and password directly through the app's UI (the same self-locking first-visit pattern already accepted for the shipped Uptime Kuma and gap-analyzed Actual Budget recipes) — unlike an open-ended self-registration app (e.g. An Otter Wiki), this setup path closes itself off permanently once the first admin account is created, so it does not need a Traefik basic_auth gate to avoid an indefinite registration-race window. That clears the /compose constraint today with zero blocking issues and no customer-supplied secret needed at all — just the domain param. Release cadence is active (latest release 8 days old, near-daily trunk builds) with no maintenance-only or EOL signal. Recommend building the recipe: it fills a real, currently-unfilled niche in the catalogue with a well-maintained upstream project.
