source_description: Open-source identity and access management with SSO, OIDC, passkeys, and multi-tenancy
upstream_license: AGPL-3.0 (core, Console, and Login moved from Apache-2.0 to AGPL-3.0 with the v3 release, 2025-03-31; proto/API/SDK packages remain Apache-2.0)
version_health_notes: Latest v4.16.2 shipped 2026-07-29, 7 days before today (2026-08-05). Recent tag history shows a steady multi-times-per-month cadence on both the current v4 line (v4.15.1 2026-06-08, v4.15.2 2026-06-17, v4.15.3 2026-06-22, v4.16.0 2026-07-10, v4.16.1 2026-07-17, v4.16.2 2026-07-29) and a still-maintained v3 LTS line (v3.4.11 2026-06-10 through v3.4.13 2026-07-17). No dormancy or EOL signal; this is a well-resourced, VC-backed project (Zitadel GmbH) with an active commercial cloud offering funding upstream development.
differentiation: No existing recipe in the 24-app catalogue provides SSO/OIDC/SAML identity-provider functionality — Vaultwarden and Guacamole are the closest security-adjacent recipes but solve different problems (password vaulting, remote-desktop gateway). ZITADEL would let a customer stand up their own IdP to centralize login for other self-hosted apps (OIDC/SAML relying parties), passkey/WebAuthn login, and multi-tenant org management — a genuinely new category for the catalogue, not a variant of anything already offered.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted SSO/IAM is a common "grow into" need once a customer runs several other self-hosted apps, and ZITADEL is one of the more actively developed, modern options (OIDC, SAML, passkeys) compared to older incumbents like Keycloak. Its web console + login UI are the only customer-facing surfaces needed to operate it, matching our Traefik-fronted model well.
summary: ZITADEL is an actively maintained, well-funded open-source IAM/SSO platform (latest v4.16.2, 2026-07-29, multiple releases per month) that fills a genuine gap — no existing recipe offers identity/SSO. It has a web console and login UI, runs behind a reverse proxy on standard HTTP ports, and its only first-boot secrets (a 32-byte masterkey, two Postgres passwords) can all be server-generated with no customer input needed, matching the "server_generated_no_customer_input" mechanism. The one wrinkle: ZITADEL's bootstrap admin account (zitadel-admin@zitadel.localhost) only accepts its initial password as plaintext via ZITADEL_FIRSTINSTANCE_ORG_HUMAN_PASSWORD in steps.yaml — there is no pre-hashed/bcrypt-hash input path, so `generated_from` cannot project the customer's root-password hash into it the way Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN does. The practical fix is to ship it with the documented fixed default password (Password1!/PasswordChangeRequired=true, forcing an in-app change on first login) and gate the whole public surface behind Traefik basic_auth using the root-password hash, the same "fixed admin credential behind a mandatory gate" pattern already accepted for other recipes. That keeps it installable today, though the stack itself (ZITADEL API + separate Login v2 container + Postgres, all needing to share one public domain via path-based Traefik routing) is more complex to wire up than our single-container recipes, hence build_with_caveats rather than a clean build_now.

name: ZNC
source_description: Always-on IRC bouncer that maintains persistent network connections with replay
version_health_notes: Mature, single-purpose C++ project. Tag history: 1.9.0 (2024-02-22), 1.9.1 (2024-07-03), 1.10.0 (2025-06-09), 1.10.1 (2025-07-01), 1.10.2-rc1 (2026-04-23), 1.10.2 (2026-05-07, ~3 months before this analysis on 2026-08-05) — roughly one release every 6-12 months, i.e. slowing relative to a typical actively-developed web app, but not a red flag on its own: this has been ZNC's release cadence for years and is typical for a feature-complete bouncer. GitHub repo (znc/znc) is not archived and shows a commit pushed 2026-08-01, four days before today (2026-08-05) — clear evidence of ongoing maintenance, 390 open issues being triaged, 2100+ stars. No EOL or sunset announcement found. Verdict: active, low-velocity, not dormant.
differentiation: Nothing in the current 24 recipes touches IRC or bouncer/relay functionality — this would be a genuinely new category. Closest conceptual neighbor by shape (raw protocol port + companion web UI) is wg-easy, not any messaging/chat app, since we don't have one. Worth noting for prioritization: `apps-gaps/convos.yaml` already analyzed a browser-based IRC bouncer (Convos) that serves the same underlying need — persistent IRC presence — through a single HTTP port with no raw protocol exposure and no separate desktop IRC client required. Convos is architecturally simpler to build (reverse_proxy_compatible: true) but is blocked on having no pinned stable tag today. Neither is built yet, so this isn't a catalogue-overlap issue, just context for whoever weighs the two IRC-bouncer candidates against each other.
usefulness_rationale: IRC bouncers serve a real but shrinking niche: users who want persistent presence on IRC networks (Libera.Chat, OFTC, etc.) with backlog replay while their client is offline. The audience is almost entirely retained from IRC's earlier era (open-source maintainers, sysadmins, old-school communities) rather than a broad self-hosting audience; most newer chat platforms displaced IRC for mainstream use. Real demand exists but it's narrow and technical.
blocking_issues:
ZNC's own user-password hashing (src/User.cpp, CUser::CheckPass) calls argon2id_verify() against a self-contained PHC-format string ($argon2id$v=19$m=...,t=...,p=...$salt$hash) stored verbatim in the config's Hash field (Method = Argon2id) — argon2id_verify decodes its own params/salt from that string, so it does not need to match ZNC's own default hash parameters. This is structurally the same shape as Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN: generated_from: "argon2:ROOT_PASSWORD" produces exactly this kind of string, so the customer's root password can become the login for both ZNC's IRC-protocol auth and its webadmin panel. Username is not customer-chosen and can be hardcoded (e.g. "customer") in install.sh, same as other recipes.

Caveat, not a blocker: the official znc/znc Docker image ships no env-var-driven bootstrap at all — first run normally requires an interactive `znc --makeconf` (TTY) wizard. Our install.sh would need to generate a minimal znc.conf from a template (embedding the generated_from hash directly into the Hash field) and mount it, bypassing the wizard entirely, rather than the usual pattern of passing a generated_from value through a docker-compose environment var. This is more templating work than our typical recipe, but the mechanism itself (a metadata parameter fed by generated_from) is not blocked by it.

Core function needs a raw TCP port (default 6667 plain / 6697 TLS) exposed directly to the internet for actual IRC client connections — Traefik's HTTP-only routing can't carry this. reverse_proxy_compatible is false for this reason alone. ZNC's optional webadmin module confusingly multiplexes HTTP and IRC-bouncer protocol on the *same* listener port (protocol-sniffed per connection), which is workable (publish that port directly for raw clients, and separately point an internal Traefik HTTP router at the same container port over the docker network for a friendly domain+TLS webadmin URL) but is an unusual, more fragile topology than our single-HTTP-port recipes.

Once inside webadmin (behind the generated_from-projected login), the customer still has to type their actual IRC network credentials (e.g. their Libera.Chat NickServ password) directly into ZNC's own per-network settings screen. That's normal in-app configuration after boot, not a /compose-time secret, so it does not block installability — flagged here only so a reviewer doesn't mistake it for one.
summary: ZNC is a mature, still-maintained (if slow-cadence) IRC bouncer with no overlap in the current catalogue. Its own admin/user login is mechanically installable today: ZNC's Argon2id password check (argon2id_verify against a self-contained PHC hash string) lines up exactly with our generated_from:argon2 root-password projection, the same shape as Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN. The real friction is architectural, not credential-shaped: the official Docker image has no env-var bootstrap (needs a hand-templated config file instead of makeconf), and the app's core value requires a raw, non-Traefik-routable TCP port for actual IRC client connections, with an optional webadmin HTTP UI multiplexed onto that same port. Recommend build_with_caveats — it's buildable, but a genuinely different recipe shape (raw-port-first, config-file templating) for what is a narrow, technical, low-broad-appeal audience.

name: Zulip
source_description: Open-source team chat with organized topic threading and 100+ integrations
version_health_notes: Latest stable 12.1 published 2026-06-26, ~41 days before today (2026-08-05). Release history shows a steady cadence: 12.0 (2026-04-27), 12.0-beta1/beta2 (2026-03-12, 2026-04-26), 11.6 (2026-03-31), 11.5 (2026-02-05), 11.4 (2025-10-23) — roughly a major/minor every 1-2 months plus interleaved patch releases on the prior LTS-ish line. No dormancy or EOL signal; Zulip is a well-established, actively commercially backed (Zulip, Inc.) open-source project with continuous development.
differentiation: No existing recipe in the 24-app catalogue covers team chat / threaded messaging. Zulip's differentiator versus generic chat tools is topic-based threading (each message belongs to a topic within a channel, unlike flat channel timelines), aimed at teams that want organized, searchable, asynchronous-friendly conversation history — a genuinely new category for the catalogue.
usefulness_rationale: Self-hosted team chat is a common need once a customer has more than a couple of self-hosted apps and people collaborating on them, and Zulip is one of the more actively developed open-source options in this space with a modern web UI and broad integration ecosystem (100+ integrations per Hostinger's description). It runs as a single HTTP(S)-fronted web app, matching our Traefik model well on the surface — see installability below for the first-boot login caveat.
secrets_required_at_first_boot: ZULIP_POSTGRES_PASSWORD; ZULIP_MEMCACHED_PASSWORD; ZULIP_RABBITMQ_PASSWORD; ZULIP_REDIS_PASSWORD; ZULIP_SECRET_KEY; ZULIP_EMAIL_PASSWORD; initial_organization_admin_credential
blocking_issues:
ZULIP_EMAIL_PASSWORD (outgoing SMTP relay credential) has no supported input channel. Zulip's docs state outgoing email is required so it "can confirm new users'" accounts — both the self-serve organization-creation flow (visiting /new/, gated by the OPEN_REALM_CREATION setting) and the standard EmailAuthBackend signup path depend on being able to send a confirmation email. The needed credential is a third-party SMTP account (e.g. a transactional email provider) that the customer would have to supply — an external credential with no projection mechanism today, per SCHEMA.md's "external API key/token the app can't function without" case.

Independent of the email problem, the two ways to create the first admin/organization both fail the plaintext-vs-hash test: (1) the web /new/ self-serve flow lets the customer type their own password directly into the browser (no projection needed at all, matching the n8n/Immich "customer sets their own credential live" pattern) but is blocked on the SMTP issue above; (2) the non-interactive fallback, `manage.py create_user ... --password=<value>`, requires the password as plaintext on the command line — Zulip hashes it internally with Django's own hasher, and there is no pre-hashed-password input flag. `generated_from` only ever produces a hash, never plaintext, so this path is a structural blocker, not merely an unsupported-algorithm gap.
summary: Zulip is an actively maintained (12.1, 2026-06-26), Apache-2.0 team-chat app with a genuinely new catalogue category (topic-threaded chat) and no overlap with the existing 24 recipes. Its official docker-zulip compose stack (app + Postgres + Redis + RabbitMQ + Memcached, all behind a single HTTP(S) port) is otherwise a good structural fit for our Traefik-fronted model, and all its infra secrets are server-generatable. The blocker is the first-admin/organization bootstrap: Zulip mandates outgoing SMTP to send confirmation emails for either its self-serve /new/ signup or standard account creation, and that SMTP credential is an external, customer-supplied secret with no input channel today; the CLI fallback (`create_user --password`) sidesteps email but needs a plaintext password that `generated_from` cannot provide (hash-only). If the platform were to provision a shared outgoing-mail relay (so no per-customer SMTP credential is needed), the self-serve /new/ flow would let the customer set their own admin password directly in the browser with no projection required at all — hence blocked_on_platform rather than not_recommended.
